stories.title: FBI depicts Tumbler Ridge shooter's guns, including 'SKS' once confiscated by RCMP
stories.summary: An FBI complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter for months provides extensive new details about the guns that May have been used in the attack, and how the teenage killer May have obtained them.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An FBI complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter for months provides extensive new details about the guns that may have been used in the attack, and how the teenage killer may have obtained them.

Oct. 7, 2026

JJF[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/fbi-depicts-tumbler-ridge-shooter-s-guns-including-sks-once-confiscated-by-rcmp/article_0d507c5b-1f71-5b3c-ae8d-542c09cd342a.html)

By The Canadian Press

The complaint sworn by an FBI agent in Seattle says James Bryant, who is charged with conspiracy to murder in a foreign country, told officers that Jesse Van Rootselaar stole firearms and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and hid them in her room “in preparation for a mass shooting.”

It also says in claims not tested in court that 18-year-old Van Rootselaar told Bryant in online chats that she had convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf, and that one of the weapons she intended to use had been returned after previously being confiscated by the RCMP.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Van Rootselaar killed eight victims on Feb. 10, including her mother and brother at their home, and five students and an educational assistant at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

The RCMP criminal investigation into the shooting is ongoing, despite Van Rootselaar having killed herself at the school.

Assistant RCMP Commissioner Elija Rain, who is acting commanding officer in B.C., says “investigators have made substantial progress in the criminal investigation.”

Rain says in a statement that the RCMP’s release of information about the case has recently been limited “because of the need to ensure our investigative theories and actions were not compromised.”

The FBI complaint released on Tuesday says Van Rootselaar told Bryant on the Discord platform that she possessed a 3D-printed foregrip, firearm magazines and a “switch” device for an SKS rifle, which the FBI says likely referred to a “machine-gun conversion device.”

Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, Wash., allegedly told the FBI that Van Rootselaar “ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

A photo in the complaint depicts a person the FBI says is Van Rootselaar, posing on their knees in a black miniskirt and fishnet stockings, while holding an olive-green rifle with a telescopic sight on the morning of the attack.

On the end of the barrel is what appears to be a suppressor, decorated in the blue, white and pink bands of the transgender Pride flag.

Van Rootselaar was trans, and the FBI said Tuesday that Bryant identifies as female.

The FBI says that in December 2025, Van Rootselaar discussed a gun she said she was planning to use in the attack.

“The police knocked my SKS sights off zero a lil bit when they roughly confiscated it, so the gun has been hitting high and to the left,” she allegedly told Bryant.

Adjusting the sights would be “a lot of work and I may end up doing my plan with a gun with sights that are super off,” Van Rootselaar allegedly said, before adding “I’m sure I can still do fine.”

Another photo shows a Canuck-branded shotgun that Van Rootselaar said would also be used in the attack.

It is decorated with a sticker, also in blue, white and pink.

Bryant allegedly tells Van Rootselaar: “Love the stickers … stickers would be so funny to be seen in photos of the incident.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. NDP Leader Eby says not everybody shares his concerns about Trump
stories.summary: Victoria - The Ndp's election campaign in British Columbia has moved on from the threat of Donald Trump's tariffs to focus on affordability issues.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When NDP Leader David Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22, he said British Columbia needed a “firebreak” against Trump’s economic attacks and Trump-style politics, which he said were threatening to infect the province.

But Eby says he accepts that not everyone shares his anxieties about the U.S. president, even as Trump’s actions make B.C.‘s challenges much worse.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 9Image 10

He says the key matter for voters on Oct. 24 will be deciding which party can support families during these tough times.

Interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson said at the start of the campaign that Trump is an “absolute bully,” and that standing up to him requires action, not press releases.

Eby says he is trying to express his own sense of anxiety about Trump’s threats as best as he can, and while not everybody shares his concerns, there is no question Trump’s actions continue to have an impact on British Columbians.

“Whether you believe and accept that Trump is making it much worse, it doesn’t matter because you’re still understanding that the cost of living is significant, that we need a strong public health-care system if you and your family get sick,” he said on Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: To get a suitable home, buyers figure out what they'll accept as a trade-off: Re/Max
stories.summary: Toronto - Canadians are willing to make compromises to afford a home that better meets their needs, a new survey from Re/Max finds.
stories.author: Daniel Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The survey, released Wednesday, said 65 per cent of respondents would compromise in at least one way to afford a larger or more suitable place to live. Such compromises might include living further away from city centres or choosing an older home that May need renovations.

“Rather than giving up on home ownership, Canadians are making different choices about how to get there. For some, that means looking outside their current community or reconsidering the type of home they buy,” Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said in a news release.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

“For others, it means making different financial choices. Buyers are identifying what matters most and where they have room to be flexible.”

The survey found that 63 per cent indicated they would relocate for a home that better fits their needs, including 47 per cent who said they would move up to an hour from the community they currently live in.

Re/Max said the report comes amid a slowdown for the housing market. Data from its own brokers and agents shows home sales saw annual declines in 81 per cent of markets that were analyzed over the first half of the year. During the period, average home prices increased across 56 per cent of markets.

Slower sales and more choice in certain markets could provide more time to compare properties, Re/Max said, allowing buyers to keep focused on their top priorities.

“The market has not become easy for buyers, but in many regions, it is allowing for a more deliberate purchasing process,” said Kottick in the release.

“That matters for people who are already rethinking location, property type or condition to make the numbers work. More time and choice can help buyers compare their options and understand where their budget goes further without feeling like they have to compromise.”

Conditions favourable to buyers are also more common than anticipated heading into the year, Re/Max said, with 32 per cent of markets analyzed currently in buyers’ favour, compared with 15.2 per cent a year earlier.

Canadians were also willing to make trade-offs beyond the property itself in order to afford a home, Re/Max found. Forty-one per cent of respondents said they would reduce discretionary spending, like travel and dining out, while 24 per cent said they would extend their amortization period.

Seventeen per cent would take on a second job or another source of income to afford a home. Another 17 per cent said they would delay retirement or other longer-term savings.

The online survey was conducted by Leger between July 17 and July 19, and responses were taken from 1,532 Canadian adults.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Oct. 7 anniversary marks three years of threats on Jews living in Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa - Security guards searching bags before bar mitzvahs.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Students who hide their Star of David necklaces for fear of being attacked.

Synagogue services that start with staff pointing out where the emergency exits are.

In the three years since Hamas unleashed a deadly terrorist attack on Israel, and Israel responded with a relentless war it says is aimed at eliminating Hamas in Gaza, life for Jews in Canada has changed dramatically.

“The society we’re living in is not quite the society we thought,” said Lisa Grushcow, senior rabbi of Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom in Montreal. “There’s this feeling of a world that’s really been turned upside down.”

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 16Image 17Image 18

Canadian Jews are facing a spike in antisemitic attacks — firebombings at synagogues like Grushcow’s, shootings at Jewish schools and physical assaults which police have classified as hate crimes.

Spy agency Csis mentioned in its annual report for 2025 a number of disrupted plots targeting Canadian Jewish institutions, including the arrest in August 2025 of a Montreal youth who intended to target Jews.

It said religiously motivated violent extremism has “increased significantly since the beginning of the Israel-Hamas conflict,” which has “fuelled violent extremist organization narratives and has the potential to inspire a new generation of extremists.”

Since 2023, Jewish communities have been the most frequently targeted group in police-reported hate crimes, despite representing less than one per cent of Canada’s population.

Toronto police said in September it had made 573 arrests and laid 1,398 charges in connection with demonstrations, protests and hate-motivated offences, targeting Jewish communities, since Oct. 7, 2023.

The Ottawa Police Service Board report issued last week said “Jewish residents have reported fear about wearing a kippah, Star of David or other visible expressions of Jewish identity in public.”

“Community organizations have adopted heightened security measures for religious, cultural and commemorative gatherings — including advance registration, identification requirements, restrictions on attendance and, in some circumstances, limiting public disclosure of event details.”

Grushcow’s synagogue has existed since 1883, and represents one of the most progressive branches of Judaism. In June someone attacked the temple with a firebomb. In February 2025, a swastika was spray painted on the building’s exterior.

“There’s been a lot that’s become normalized over the past three years that I think is just deeply disturbing — for us as a community, but also for us as a society,” Grushcow said.

She encourages non-Jewish Canadians to ask a Jewish friend if they can attend a synagogue. What they would find is communities grappling with ensuring security while not making those attending services feel too afraid to attend.

Last month, after a gunman shot at a Belleville, Ont., synagogue and a police officer, Conservative deputy leader Melissa Lantsman said the incident added to existing fear and shock.

“The next day, our synagogue, as it often does, starts with a security briefing of what to do when things go south, ON where the doors are,” she said.

Grushcow said there are immediate safety concerns for Jewish communities, along with longer term questions around how to restore civic dialogue.

“I was at the Pride March last summer. Somebody looks at me, and sees me with a rainbow Star of David on my shirt and calls me a baby killer. What is that? How has that become our new normal,” she said.

“How is it that any connection or care for Israel — which is the reality for the vast majority of Canadian Jews, for all kinds of historical, religious, spiritual reasons — how does that become something … that becomes perceived as a reason to keep people out of academic and professional and personal relationships?”

At the centre of some of the concern, is a wave of anti-Israel protests that erupted following Oct. 7.

Some groups behind some of those protests say they are targeting organizations that actively support the Israeli military — such as business owners who fundraise for foreigners who serve in the Israeli Defense Force, or a synagogue that appeared to be promoting the sale of land in the occupied West Bank.

Independent Jewish Voices has argued antisemitism is being weaponized to suppress pro-Palestinian advocacy.

But many Canadian Jews feel targeted for being Jewish, irrespective of whether or not they support the Israeli government.

Grushcow said Canadians needs to find a way to balance open dialogue with respect and safety.

She said Canadian society in general has “become very quick to write people off” over their perceived loyalties, losing the skills of maintaining “dialogue across difference.”

Grushcow is among many Jewish leaders who question whether Iran has played a role in inflaming tensions in Canada, and she says it’s hard to imagine who benefits from Jews being threatened and Canadian society losing its civility.

In June, Ruby Sahota, the secretary of state for combating crime, told the House of Commons that people who fired shots recently at synagogues were hired and paid by a “foreign entity.”

Ottawa has boosted funding for security at synagogues and expanded hate-speech laws, but Grushcow said Canadians need to do more.

“We have to stop saying this isn’t who we are — and recognize that it’s who we’ve become, and then how do we change that,” she said. “That work can’t come entirely from the Jewish community.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.summary: Officials in northwestern Ireland say they're working to recover a large Canadian buoy that floated across the Atlantic Ocean and washed up on a coastal island.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Officials in northwestern Ireland say they’re working to recover a large Canadian buoy that floated across the Atlantic Ocean and washed up on a coastal island.

Oct. 7, 2026

LW[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/canadian-buoy-drifts-across-atlantic-washes-up-on-shore-of-irish-island/article_3cfadcf1-8db1-58b1-b471-737273b7d661.html)

By Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press

A news release from Mayo County Council says the mariner marker, weighing in at roughly 3.5 tonnes, came ashore on Achill Island, known for its rugged mountains and bright sandy beaches.

It says council was told by the Canadian Coast Guard that its buoys, while “very friendly,” have quite the habit of drifting far from home.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

The council is looking to recover the buoy so as to prevent it from floating away and becoming a hazard to vessels or coastal infrastructure.

The release says the unusual visitor to the island can carry a navigation light and make a distinctive wave-powered whistling sound to alert nearby vessels.

The council adds the discovery is a lighthearted reminder of Mayo County’s connection to Canada through generations of emigration, before demanding a blithe bit of a ransom.

“Should the Canadians wish to see their buoy again, they may have to make a special trip to Mayo to collect it,” the release said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Three finalists named for inaugural Writers' Trust non-fiction editing prize
stories.summary: Toronto - Award-winning poet katherena vermette is among the three finalists for the Writers' Trust's inaugural prize for non-fiction editing.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nancy Flight Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction Editing awards $25,000 to an editor whose work has made an outstanding contribution to a full-length book of literary non-fiction. The organization says the award is the largest of its kind in Canada, with runners-up receiving $2,500 each.

vermette is nominated for editing “Carry Your Heart: Indigenous Helping Wisdom and the Science of Psychological Flexibility” by Cree psychotherapist Louis Busch, who blends Indigenous teaching wisdoms and Western psychology in the self-help title.

Article continues below

Guests arrive for the 90s exhibition opening party at Tate Britain

Image 14Image 15Image 16Image 17

The Winnipeg-born vermette previously won the Governor General’s Literary Award for English-language poetry in 2013 for her collection “North End Love Songs.” She also won the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize for her 2021 novel “The Strangers.”

Also among the finalists is Victoria’s George Galt for Sarah Ellis’ memoir “My Year in Fairyland: Grief, Maid and a Lifetime of Books,” which details the 12 months before her wife’s medically assisted death.

Rounding out the contenders is Vancouver’s Rachel Rose for “Humanitarienne: A Doctor’s Stories from the Conflict Zone” by physician and public health specialist Kirsten Johnson. The memoir explores her career in war-torn and disaster-affected regions.

The Writers’ Trust says the prize will be handed out annually until 2033 as part of a multi-year commitment of $483,000.

A three-person jury selected the finalists. The winner will be announced on Nov. 10 in Toronto.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Stephen Galloway tells court he was shocked by rape allegations
stories.summary: The former UBC professor believed his two-year relationship with his student had ended amicably, he told the court
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Bestselling author Steven Galloway acknowledged his two-year affair with a University of B.C. creative writing student was “inappropriate, ill-advised and stupid” during testimony on the second day of a trial where this woman and three others are defending themselves against accusations that they later defamed him.

Mr. Galloway told B.C. Supreme Court on Tuesday that he believed the relationship had ended amicably. And so, he said, he was surprised to learn shortly afterward that his former partner had filed a sexual harassment complaint with the school’s administration – an allegation which would eventually publicly explode and torpedo his personal and professional life.

“Without being crass, there was enthusiastic and ongoing consent at all times,” he said when his lawyer Daniel Burnett asked him about their sex life.

The high-profile trial is more than a decade in the making. Ubc’s announcement of a formal investigation of “serious allegations” involving Mr. Galloway in 2015 led to an online firestorm over the CanLit luminary’s rights to due process versus the rights of his alleged victim. UBC fired Mr. Galloway in 2016, but a retired judge hired by the university to investigate the complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established he committed sexual assault or assault.

He was never charged by police. In 2018, he sued nearly two dozen people for defamation, saying they had falsely claimed online that he had sexually and physically assaulted the woman. She is known publicly as A.B. because her identity is protected by a publication ban until 45 days after Justice Neena Sharma makes her final judgment.

Only A.B. and three other defendants remain: Mandi Gray, Dana Kagis and Glynnis Kirchmeier.

During Tuesday’s afternoon court session in Vancouver, Mr. Galloway’s lawyer directed the 51-year-old to explain how the student first began joining him for post-lecture drinks with a fellow professor in one of their offices before the pair began a sexual relationship around April 2011.

Mr. Galloway testified that he and A.B. initially had fun together, even if he now realizes their relationship was not appropriate given the power dynamic between a professor and a master’s student.

“I’d never had moments where I thought this person’s not enjoying this relationship,” he said.

After their affair ended in April, 2013, Mr. Galloway testified, they kept texting regularly and remained cordial. But his lawyer told the court that in July of that year A.B. filed a formal sexual harassment complaint with the university, alleging that Mr. Galloway repeatedly gave her several drinks of scotch in his office and propositioned her for sex.

Upon learning of this complaint, nearly three years later during the university’s investigation, Mr. Galloway testified that he had two reactions: shock that she was complaining even as she was texting him regularly asking him to go to concerts and other social events, and a feeling that her allegations were ridiculous since their relationship had ended cordially.

He also testified how in 2013, he dealt with a similar sexual harassment complaint from A.B. against a visiting scholar. She alleged the academic, who was a candidate for a professorship, had groped and choked her in an elevator while touring the campus, Mr. Galloway testified. After hearing her account and her refusal to file a formal complaint, Mr. Galloway stated that he and two of his colleagues decided to do what they could to stop him from being hired.

“Shamefully, the three of us lowered our interview scores to the point where the candidate dropped out,” he said.

Mr. Galloway said he was about to go on stage in Dayton, Ohio, for a speaking engagement when Ubc’s Dean of Arts first notified him he was being suspended in November, 2015, pending an internal review of an allegation of sexual assault.

He began his testimony detailing how he rose from an arts undergrad at his hometown college in Kamloops to become one of only a handful of Canadian authors with a New York agent, with lucrative speaking engagements across North America.

stories.title: Elections Alberta notifies thousands of referendum voters about invalid mail-in ballot packs
stories.summary: Agency has been working to assuage concerns about election integrity in the home stretch of the referendum campaign
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Thousands of Albertans May not have their ballots counted for the province’s coming referendum after Elections Alberta said more than 3,000 voters failed to properly identify themselves in the mail-in voting process.

The provincial elections agency said it has reached out to those electors, most of whom incorrectly filled out the voter declaration form that must be submitted alongside their ballots, asking them to resubmit documentation over e-mail.

“If they provide the required information, by email, we can process their special ballot,” Maia Hanrahan, spokesperson for Elections Alberta, said in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail.

“If they do not, we cannot process their special ballot, and it will be rejected.”

The agency has been working to assuage concerns about election integrity in the home stretch of the referendum campaign.

Elections Alberta has verified nearly 221,000 completed mail-in ballots, Ms. Hanrahan said, representing roughly one-third of the 652,000 electors who have been sent voting packages ahead of the province’s Oct. 19 referendum.

The errors add to a list of problems that have plagued the mail-in voting process, just one component of a referendum that Elections Alberta says is one of the biggest electoral events in Canadian history.

The referendum centres around 10 questions – all designed by Premier Danielle Smith’s government – asking voters to weigh in on provincial separation, immigration and constitutional issues.

The sweeping vote has forced Elections Alberta to order 45 million ballots for the 10 separate questions, more than twice the number of ballots cast nationwide in the 2025 federal election.

It has also hired more than 41,000 election workers and received roughly 65,000 applications, Ms. Hanrahan said on Tuesday. The agency is hoping to hire an unprecedented 60,000-plus election workers – more than four times the number who helped in Alberta’s 2023 provincial general election.

Nearly one-fifth of Alberta voters, meanwhile, have seized the opportunity to vote by mail, the first time Albertans have had unrestricted access to the process for a provincewide election.

The agency is asking voters to mail their ballots by Oct. 9 to ensure their votes are counted.

In order to vote by mail, Alberta requires electors to request a special ballot package and return the ballots along with a copy of their valid identification, and a declaration form containing their personal information and signature.

Ms. Hanrahan wrote that some voters filled out their declaration incorrectly by putting their birthdate in the signature line, not signing the declaration, or failing to fill out the entire form. She added that other voters either neglected to send a copy of their ID or there were other issues with the document.

Elections Alberta is asking those voters to rectify those issues by e-mailing the agency a new declaration form or copy of their ID.

“Without these two pieces of information, we are unable to verify and count their submitted special ballot, and it would be rejected,” she wrote.

The agency has been proactively responding on social media to voters who were notified that they need to send in more documentation.

Elections Alberta has been forced to address a crop of issues in the lead up to the referendum. Some of the first declaration forms sent to electors, for example, incorrectly included a section asking voters to testify that they’re unable to vote in person. Alberta voters were previously prohibited from voting by mail unless they could prove they were unable to.

Elections Alberta also found 313 mail-in packages sent to electors that were missing ballots.

Some observers have pointed to repeated warnings from Elections Alberta – an arm’s-length government agency – that it is underfunded and understaffed.

In its annual report, published in November, 2025, chief electoral officer Gordon McClure referenced “systemic deficiencies” at the agency, including high staff turnover, insufficient resources and a “lack of backup in critical positions and areas.”

That report was published roughly three months before Ms. Smith unveiled her plans for the October referendum. In May, Mr. McClure told a legislative committee that he’s “drinking from a firehose.”

Federalist campaigns have embraced mail-in voting, while separatist camps have been split over the system. Last month, lawyer and pro-independence organizer Keith Wilson said it’s critical his supporters vote at the mailbox. Prominent separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre, meanwhile, said he has “no faith in the system at all.”

stories.title: Rally calls on council candidates to pledge support for expanded licensing of landlords’ buildings
stories.summary: Members of tenants’ advocacy group London Acorn held a rally outside City Hall on Tuesday, calling on council candidates to pledge that they will support expanding municipal licensing of rental properties operated by landlords.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Members of tenants’ advocacy group London Acorn held a rally outside City Hall on Tuesday, calling on council candidates to pledge that they will support expanding municipal licensing of rental properties operated by landlords.

Currently, only residential buildings with up to four units, and converted dwellings with five or more units, require a Residential Rental Unit License.

“That leaves out the majority of landlords, all of the large landlords, and all of the corporate landlords,” said Jordan Smith, chair of London Acorn’s East of Adelaide Chapter. “So, that’s obviously really ineffective as a policy.”

The municipal licenses are intended to provide regulations for rental units, protect the safety of renters, and ensure property standards are maintained.

However, Acorn wants landlords to pay annual per-unit fees to fund a broader licensing program that would include proactive inspections and public reporting of the results.

Smith says with less than three weeks to go until the municipal election, candidates are being asked to pledge their support for the changes, “We’ve been presenting to the city for the last six years, literally that resolve this issue, you know, so we’re looking for a little bit of common sense here. We’re looking for a champion coming into it with our new council.

Mayoral candidate Tariq Khan was among a small number of candidates who attended the rally, “The rental protection office is not working, or there is a lack of accountability. There is a lack of supervision, and I just want to fix it.”

Following a meeting of the Strategic Priorities and Policy Committee (Sppc) on Tuesday afternoon, CTV News asked incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan and mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson about potentially expanding rental unit licensing.

“I wouldn’t make any changes without a robust consultation on the extent of the licensing regime,” Morgan said. “What I will say is, there are costs and enforcement implications of licensing widely. Often those costs get passed on to tenants. So I think we’d want to be cautious about that.”

He added, “I do think we need to continue to work with community partners on modernizing our rules. We brought in a renoviction by-law. We’ve made other changes to protect renters, and I’m always open to discussion about things that we could do.”

Stevenson acknowledged the concerns expressed by Acorn, “We’re hearing a lot of concern about apartment buildings where people have gone a long period of time without elevators, without heat, access to hot water, or water itself. So, I think that’s the underlying issue. I wouldn’t want to go broad and create a lot of red tape and costs in areas where it’s not needed. We want to focus all the efforts on the problems.”

She added that consultation would be important, “Getting people involved and listening to what the issues are, where are they, and at what level of government are we able to make a difference.”

A list of all 12 candidates for mayor can be found on the City of London website along with the registered candidates in all 14 wards.

Election day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Hanover shooting leaves man injured, suspect arrested
stories.summary: At least three schools and the town’s hospital were placed in a “hold and secure” Tuesday after gunshots were heard in Hanover.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
One person has been taken into custody following a shooting investigation in Grey County.

According to police, one person was injured in the shooting shortly before noon at a residence in the 300 block of 14th Avenue in Hanover, Ont.

Police said a 37-year-old man was taken to Hanover and District Hospital by Grey County paramedics with gunshot wounds that were not considered life-threatening.

Investigators said a 50-year-old suspect was arrested a short time after the incident, however they have not released details on any charges. Officers also recovered a firearm near the scene.

Hanover police are asking for the public’s help identifying and locating a black van that was seen leaving the area immediately after the shooting.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Hanover Police Service investigators or Crime Stoppers.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Parti Québécois Leader says independence vote won’t be early priority for incoming minority government
stories.summary: Mark Carney played down the separatist threat from the PQ’s win and emphasized the benefits of co-operation
stories.author: Maura Forrest, Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon vowed to work with opposition parties and played down the potential for conflict with Ottawa on his first day as premier-designate of Quebec after securing a minority government.

The PQ’s pledge to hold an independence referendum has been complicated by the low level of popular support the party earned from voters in Monday’s provincial election, a result that revealed a divided province deeply ambivalent about the separatist project.

Election night saw the governing Coalition Avenir Québec wiped off the political map, losing all of its seats. Outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette resigned as leader of the party on Tuesday.

In a Quebec City press conference earlier in the day, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon suggested sovereignty won’t be a top priority in the first part of his mandate, and repeated a promise not to hold a referendum while U.S. President Donald Trump is in the White House.

“We’ve got time. We’ve got plenty of urgent problems to solve, so I think the upcoming months will more be about … things that are urgent,” he said.

The PQ’s 59 seats put it five shy of its hoped-for majority, and its 28 per cent share of the popular vote is the lowest of any government in Quebec history. A five-way race splintered the 70 per cent of Quebeckers who say they don’t want a referendum.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon did not waver on his commitment to sovereignty, though he acknowledged his minority government would need the support of opposition lawmakers to launch a referendum.

“Once we make a commitment during a campaign, we work to carry it out,” he said, brushing off questions about the strength of his mandate to pursue Quebec’s independence.

On Parliament Hill, Prime Minister Mark Carney sought to play down the separatist threat from the PQ’s win and emphasized the benefits of co-operation.

“It’s a crucial time for Quebec. It’s a crucial time for our country. This is not a time to wait for something a few years down the road. It’s a time to act. It’s a time for boldness,” Mr. Carney told reporters on his way into a cabinet meeting.

The Prime Minister is navigating a delicate moment for national unity, with a referendum in Alberta less than two weeks away, and persistent threats to Canada’s sovereignty and economy by the Trump administration.

Asked if the Parti Québécois had a mandate to separate with just 28 per cent of the vote, the Prime Minister did not answer the question but noted that he won last year’s federal election with a 43 per cent mandate from voters.

Mr. Carney spoke Tuesday with the premier-designate, and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon described their conversation as “perfectly respectful and constructive.” He said he will meet soon with the Prime Minister.

The PQ Leader said he is ready to collaborate with the federal government and the other provinces “provided that it serves Quebec’s interests,” but cautioned that collaboration “doesn’t mean asking for nothing and then agreeing to anything.”

“The federal government’s position, in principle, must follow the will expressed by the people of Quebec – not the other way around,” he said.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon repeated his desire to abolish the office of lieutenant-governor in Quebec, a move to buck the British monarchy that critics see as an attempt to foment conflict with Ottawa. He said he has sought a legal opinion on the matter.

The premier-designate said one of his first moves in office will be to assemble a negotiating team to protect key sectors of Quebec’s economy during the trade dispute with the United States.

Upon announcing her resignation Tuesday, Ms. Fréchette said her party needs someone to lead the CAQ into the next election and beyond, although it is unclear whether the once-dominant party can be revived after being shut out of the National Assembly.

The Caq’s “third way” nationalism, which seeks to defend Quebec’s identity and powers without the disruption of independence, is still the best option after eight years in government, Ms. Fréchette said.

“We allowed our nation to affirm itself,” she said.

Meanwhile, other opposition party leaders spoke about their plans for wielding the balance of power in a possibly short-lived minority parliament.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard was upbeat after his party more than doubled its caucus by winning 40 seats, and called on former CAQ supporters to “come home” to the federalist party.

“We’re the only ones who can realistically block the PQ’s referendum project,” he said.

The left-wing separatist party Québec Solidaire did not rule out supporting the PQ in launching a referendum, which would require a majority vote in the National Assembly. The nine seats won by QS in the downtowns of Montreal and Quebec City would be enough to help the PQ trigger an independence vote, but the two separatist parties differ widely on immigration and identity issues, as well as the economy.

Ruba Ghazal, the co-leader of QS, remained vague about her intentions but suggested that cost-of-living issues were more urgent for many Quebeckers, and that holding a referendum would be more promising when a larger share of the population wants one. Currently, just 30 per cent of Quebeckers say they support independence, a historically low level.

“Anything is possible,” Ms. Ghazal said of supporting a PQ referendum initiative in the National Assembly. “We’ll do everything to rally a majority of the population to this beautiful project.”

“Quebec isn’t 70 per cent federalist. 70 per cent of people are anxious, or don’t know. There are those who have an attachment to Canada – it’s very diversified.”

The new PQ government will also have to contend with the wild card of the Quebec Conservative Party, which enters the National Assembly for the first time with a flourish after winning 19 seats.

Leader Éric Duhaime, the election’s breakout star, campaigned on aggressively shrinking the size of the Quebec state and sharply cutting immigration levels, which the province partly controls.

A self-described nationalist, Mr. Duhaime also opposes a referendum and has said his party will vote against one, but with a surprisingly large and mostly inexperienced caucus, controlling his troops will be a tall order.

“Our first challenge is to show Quebeckers we’re capable of taking on the functions we’ve been given … to play our role of watchdog well,” he said in a press conference Tuesday. “We’ll have a steep learning curve.”

With a file from Marieke Walsh

stories.title: Universities in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver brace for Oct. 7 protests
stories.summary: Jewish groups have decried the demonstrations as insensitive and deliberately provocative
stories.author: Colin Freeze, Kelly Grant
stories.content:
University officials in Canada’s largest cities say they are working with police and security services to prepare for protests Wednesday, the third anniversary of Hamas ’s deadly Oct. 7 attacks on Israel .

Protests are being planned at or near the University of Toronto, Montreal’s McGill University, and the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, as campuses continue to be flashpoints for demonstrations over conflicts in the Middle East.

About 1,200 Israelis and foreigners were killed and 250 people taken hostage when Hamas, which has been designated a terrorist entity by the Canadian government, invaded Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s subsequent invasion of Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in the territory.

In Canada and the United States, pro-Palestinian protesters have set up encampments on university campuses, demanding that the institutions divest from weapon manufacturers connected to the Israeli military and sever ties with Israeli universities that operate in the occupied territories.

Meanwhile, Jewish groups and students have demanded protection from alleged antisemitism on campus and demonstrations they say include threats and intimidation.

Pro-Palestinian groups in Canada organizing the campus protests have said they are intended to honour those killed in Gaza by Israel, while some Jewish groups have decried the demonstrations as insensitive and deliberately provocative.

McGill says it is in contact with the Service de Police de la Ville de Montréal ahead of a planned rally by pro-Palestinian groups outside the gates of that campus. “The university’s security services will enhance their staffing and are working closely with the Spvm,” said Katherine Cuplinskas, a spokeswoman for the school.

In an e-mail, Ms. Cuplinskas said the university has “dedicated intervention teams available to address unauthorized occupations, property damage, safety concerns, or significant operational disruptions.”

In Toronto, pro-Palestinian groups have been planning what they call an “honouring our martyrs” event at the University of Toronto’s downtown campus. The university has told student groups among the protesting factions that this event should not take place on campus.

An unsigned U of T statement says safety concerns are paramount and include “physical safety risks to participants and to members of the broader university community.” The statement says those concerns have been heightened by “the online promotion of counter-protests to take place at the same time.”

Some protest activity is still expected to take place on or around the downtown campus. The Toronto Police Service said it will be on hand Wednesday to monitor events. “We are aware and will be present,” said Nadine Ramadan, the force’s spokeswoman.

Protest activity is also being planned in Vancouver, according to UBC officials.

While the B.C. RCMP would not say whether they will be monitoring that event, university spokeswoman Thandi Fletcher said some security measures will be in place. “UBC is aware that two pro-Palestinian groups are organizing gatherings on the Vancouver campus on Oct. 7,” she said in an e-mail.

In October, 2024, McGill officials restricted access to the campus and asked professors to move classes online, citing an elevated potential for disruption on the first anniversary of the Hamas attacks.

And pro-Palestinian groups held an “honouring our martyrs” event last Oct. 7 on U of T’s Mississauga campus.

In an unsigned statement, the Boycott, Divest and Sanction caucus of the U of T graduate students union said the use of the term “martyrs” for the Oct. 7 protest refers to Palestinians killed in Gaza during the Israeli invasion.

However, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs counters that the term is a provocation meant to glorify Hamas.

“People are out there celebrating what happened,” said Danielle Keenan, a spokeswoman for Cija. “It would be more credible if these events were not taking place on Oct. 7 … This is the day that 1,200 people lost their lives.”

The concerns over this year’s Canadian campus protests coincide with mounting fears in Jewish communities worldwide. With the U.S. and Israel still at war with Iran, the Israeli government is warning Jews around the world that they May be at heightened risk of attacks this Oct. 7.

stories.title: Santé Québec releases report touting nearly $2-billion in savings
stories.summary: The report was released after the election victory of Parti Québécois, which has promised to dismantle the provincial health authority
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Hours after the election of the Parti Québécois, which pledged to dismantle Santé Québec, the provincial health authority released a Deloitte Canada report stating it had achieved nearly $2-billion in cost savings since it started operations in December, 2024.

PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose party will form a minority government, promised during the campaign to abolish Santé Québec, calling it “a bureaucratic monster.”

The Deloitte report was officially released Tuesday morning although it had been leaked to La Presse previously. Santé Québec wanted to wait until the end of the election campaign so it wouldn’t interfere in the political debate, Catherine Brousseau, the health authority’s spokeswoman, said.

The report was commissioned by Santé Québec’s board of directors in July. It said the organization had saved $1.9-billion since its creation, mostly by reducing the use of travel nurses and other agency temporary staff, which saved $1.7-billion in almost two years.

Many of those savings can be traced back to the outgoing Coalition Avenir Québec government, which made it a priority to eliminate agency personnel and reduce health care staffing – but the Deloitte report includes updated numbers.

The total time worked by temporary agency staff in Quebec’s health care system has shrunk by 86 per cent in nearly two years and overtime costs are also down, according to the report. Furthermore, the increase in health care personnel slowed from an annual average of 4.7 per cent in the 2019-2023 period to 0.8 per cent for 2025-2026.

The Deloitte analysis added that there were also unquantified savings from having Santé Québec act as a sole purchaser on behalf of the 30 regional health authorities and university hospital networks that it oversees.

“The initiatives undertaken have generated tangible benefits. In light of trends observed during major mergers and integrations, additional investments could support the continued realization of synergies and benefits,” the report said.

During the election campaign, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon floated different scenarios to replace Santé Québec, with either a smaller agency, a task force or a branch of the provincial Health Department.

Meeting reporters following the election, he said a “governmental efficiency secretariat” would be created to reduce bureaucracy and “superfluous programs.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has said that abolishing Santé Québec would save up to $100-million a year and complained that its staffing was bloated, calling it “a second mammoth” since it took over some of the functions previously handled by the province’s Health Department.

The Deloitte report, however, noted that 94 per cent of the 1,192 headquarter’s employees had been transferred from the Health Department and only 66 were new hires.

Santé Québec has been the public body providing health care services and managing the system daily since it was formed, while the Health Department sets strategic goals.

Contacted for comments on Tuesday, Christian Dubé, the former CAQ health minister who initiated Santé Québec, referred The Globe and Mail to the findings in the Deloitte report and to an open letter he made public in September.

“Quebeckers want a better healthcare system, not another reform,” Mr. Dubé wrote in the open letter, arguing that the changes he initiated in 2024 couldn’t show its full impact within a four-year electoral cycle.

Santé Québec was created by legislative act and abolishing it would require another law.

The PQ is five seats short of a legislative majority. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged that his government will need the collaboration of opposition parties to pass its bills.

He noted that he shared similar views on tightening public spendings with Eric Duhaime’s Conservatives, who won 19 seats. “Our desire to better manage public finances after years of wastage should find a friendly ear among the Conservatives,” the premier-designate said.

stories.title: Thousands of Alberta referendum mail-in ballots invalid due to errors: officials
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says some ballot packages have been returned with declaration forms missing, errors or issues with I.D. — but there's still time to submit the correct info.
stories.author: Global News
stories.content:
With less than two weeks to go until the Alberta referendum , the province’s election administrator says more than 3,000 mail-in ballots have been returned with errors that make them invalid.

Elections Alberta says some ballot packages were returned with either declaration forms missing, errors or issues with identification.

But they say there’s still time to submit the correct information via email.

Albertans are to vote on a series of questions on Oct. 19, including whether to stay in Canada or begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

Elections Alberta says they’ve verified about a third of more than 652,000 ballot packages that went out to eligible voters.

Hiring of extra staff continues, with more than two-thirds of the 60,000 workers needed having been hired.

stories.title: 'Curious' Air Canada IT worker tried to think like a crook to trace how airport gold heist was pulled off
stories.summary: “I tried to put myself in the mindset of how I would have done something like this,” Joshua Priebe testified at Parmpal Sidhu's trial.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Air Canada technology specialist Joshua Priebe was on a trip to Jamaica with dozens of airline colleagues when he heard about the spectacular gold heist at Air Canada’s Toronto cargo warehouse.

“When we were down there we all got a message,” Priebe told court Tuesday at the trial for one of the men accused of pulling off the largest gold heist in Canadian history. “We were talking about it at the pool, in the pool, and speculating on what could have happened.”

Once Priebe got back from the trip, which was a prize in the airline’s employee awards program, and returned to work at the scene of the crime, he heard more about the high-profile heist in which thieves mysteriously made off with a shipment of gold and cash worth more than $22 million.

“I’m a curious fellow by nature and I like to understand things. My mind automatically jumped into how I would have done it,” he said from the witness stand. It seemed like an inside job.

Priebe is now a program manager at Air Canada. At the time of the gold heist — April 17, 2023 — he was manager of application development and maintenance at Air Canada, an IT job at the airline’s large cargo facility at Pearson airport, where he helped keep the airline’s cargo management system running.

As an IT worker, he was asked by corporate security to preserve the corporate computer logs and to help Peel Regional Police investigate the heist, he said.

Analyzing more than 400,000 lines of code that documented employee computer usage from a week before the heist to a week afterwards, he looked for patterns matching the way he figured the heist could have been pulled off.

“I tried to put myself in the mindset of how I would have done something like this. I hope I’m not criminally minded, but I find it interesting. So that’s why I delved into the data,” Priebe testified.

“If I wanted to plan this out, how would I have done it? And looking at the data, I looked at the transactions that I would have done leading up to something like this,” he said.

“I started to piece together the story of what happened.”

Priebe described for Judge Gordon Cudjoe of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton the suspicious data trail at the second day of the trial for Parmpal Sidhu, a 56-year-old former Air Canada cargo warehouse employee who is one of the men accused of conspiring to steal the valuable crate.

Sidhu has pleaded not guilty.

Priebe said whoever was involved in the heist appeared to have deep knowledge of Air Canada’s shipping and cargo procedures and had credentials with access to its computer systems.

He looked for online activity in the logs for someone using Air Canada’s systems to search incoming air traffic for arriving shipments. He said that’s where a heist plot would likely start, trying to identify a specific high-value shipment as a target.

An employee with credentials could do that search remotely, from anywhere, not just in the office. Priebe figured the person would probably do it from home, where they had more free time and greater privacy, and so Priebe filtered out in-office inquiries and found a profile fitting that pattern — repeated searches over a couple of days made off-site, apparently of flights from Zurich, a financial centre in Switzerland known for shipping high-value precious metals, currency and luxury watches. Such shipments can be a daily occurrence at Pearson, he said.

The login credentials used for those searches, court heard, were for Simran Preet Panesar, who was an Air Canada manager who Sidhu reported to, and who is considered a fugitive wanted by police on charges of being part of the gold heist.

Priebe also found the credentials of a different Air Canada employee were then used to log into the system to change the designation of a specific crate on a flight from Zurich by deleting its code that it was a high-value shipment. This was done while the plane was in the air.

That change meant the crate would not be sent to a secure storage area at the airport, which is locked and guarded, but instead sent to general storage, where any employee could access it.

The timing of the change was a red flag, Priebe said.

“It was suspicious for me because it bypasses the automatic lockdown” on a shipment’s data that kicks in once it touches down and unloading begins. “It looks like it’s trying to bypass the security elements that we had in place.”

Another login, using yet another employee’s computer credentials, made a different but important change to the shipping data for the crate. This change made it so the crate would not be unpacked by warehouse staff and divided for the two different customers picking up the contents — TD Bank collecting the gold and a Vancouver foreign exchange picking up the foreign banknotes — but rather kept intact.

That made sure the entire load of gold and cash stayed together.

That was suspicious to Priebe because he saw the change was made on a mobile phone using the cargo warehouse’s guest Wi-Fi, rather than one of the desktop computers used by staff.

“That is not normal,” he said.

“This is unionized work that they’re doing and a unionized person would have no reason to go on a mobile device on the guest Wi-Fi to perform their duties. They’re provided with a computer at their desk.”

Priebe also described how the corporate digital logs also traced the login credentials used to print off an air waybill — a shipping contract that shows ownership of cargo — that was used by a driver to collect the diverted crate. The access was in the credentials for Sidhu, court heard.

Court heard from the second and third employees whose credentials were used to set up the heist.

On Monday Elizabeth Zaritskaya, now the manager of Hub Operations at Air Canada, testified that she was not at work at the time of the heist and was mystified with her credentials being used. She said she had nothing to do with the heist.

On Tuesday, Rachel Pearce, a former Air Canada manager whose last name at the time of the heist was Bailey, testified was she also was away at the time. When she came back to work, she heard from colleagues that people were talking about her ID being used.

“It was quite shocking,” she said. She said she thinks someone got her credentials or logged into her account by using an access password saved in her browser, before Air Canada changed their systems.

Court has heard that digital hygiene and computer security was woeful at the warehouse at the time and has since been overhauled.

Witnesses described credentials, profiles and logins being shared among employees out of convenience, shared workspaces, shared computers and staff forgetting to log out.

stories.title: Cornell rape allegations prompt Canadian student to share her university experience
stories.summary: The headlines out of Cornell University, where a former student alleges she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a fraternity party in 2024, have prompted some Canadian survivors to go public.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Brantford, ONT. – The headlines out of Cornell University, where a former student alleges she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a fraternity party in 2024, have prompted some Canadian survivors to go public.

One of those students is Melissa Stark, who took to her Instagram page to share her story.

“The recent news about the Cornell 7 has really brought back some unresolved rage for me. During my time at Saint Mary’s University in Halifax, I was sexually assaulted,” she wrote.

Stark said she was in her third year of university when the alleged assault took place.

“This was someone who I met through our friend circles. He became a friend and he came to my off-campus apartment, and the story goes from there.”

Speaking with CTV News from Brantford, Ont., Stark said she didn’t consent and that, “this individual forced himself upon me.”

Stark said she spent weeks in denial about what happened before she reported the alleged incident to a sexual violence co-ordinator at the university. She said her report was initially well received, though as it escalated, she said the administration refused to remove her alleged attacker from campus.

“I wanted him expelled, not only for myself, but in an effort to protect other students. The school instead said they could offer the person who assaulted me counselling, have him take some online courses and they asked if I wanted a written apology, which I declined because I didn’t think that would help me in any way,” she said.

Stark added that the alleged attacker continued his studies and flourished while her grades declined and her mental health suffered.

“He was given honours at graduation and able to walk the stage with everyone else.”

Saint Mary University’s Sexual Violence and Harassment Policy outlines that the disciplinary tools at its disposal include suspension and expulsion.

“The policy is very much a box for them to check off,” said Stark.

The school’s security department did issue a notice of no contact to each of the students, saying if the two find themselves in “a common academic activity, they shall leave as much physical space between them as possible and shall not communicate in any way.”

For Stark, she said the order was of little help. She still saw the man on campus and would avoid certain areas. She also dropped out of some classes because his friends were in the same program.

“I remember thinking at one point, ‘I’m going to drop out,’” she said.

Schools must support survivors, advocate says

Stark’s story isn’t an isolated incident. Candice Shaw, executive director of the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada , told CTV News that 11 per cent of female students and four per cent of male students experience sexual assault in a post-secondary setting.

Shaw believes that Canadian universities need to do more than simply come up with sexual violence policies.

“Canadian universities and colleges need to ensure there are clear pathways for survivors to find community-based support systems, like those offered through sexual violence support organizations,” she said.

Shaw said her national organization and others are well equipped to support survivors in a way that many educational institutions cannot.

CTV News sent Saint Mary’s University multiple emails before publication. They have not responded.

Stark did manage to graduate and is now focused on her future, which includes taking a master’s in criminology at another university in Ontario.

She said she’s sharing her story in hopes of reaching survivors.

“I want them to know that they’re not alone. There are people ready to listen and to help.”

If you or someone you know is struggling with sexual assault or trauma, the following resources are available to support people in crisis:

Call 911 if you are in immediate danger or fear for your safety.

The Canadian Association of Sexual Assault Centres ’ website has a comprehensive list of sexual assault centres in Canada that offer information, advocacy and counselling.

The Ending Violence Association of Canada ‘s website has links to helplines, support services and locations across Canada that offer sexual assault kits.

stories.title: FBI reveals what was in the killer's mind in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting
stories.summary: Seattle - A complaint by the FBI against James Bryant in U.S. District Court provides extensive new allegations about the mass killings in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., where eight victims died on Feb. 10, 2026.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
SEATTLE - A complaint by the FBI against James Bryant in U.S. district court provides extensive new allegations about the mass killings in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., where eight victims died on Feb. 10, 2026.

FBI special agent Joseph Rico swears in the complaint that Bryant, who lives in Bellingham, Wash., met shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar online about three years ago.

But they fell out of contact while the killer was institutionalized after setting her room on fire. After that, they spoke daily in the six months before the murders, Rico says.

U.S Investigators say a 30-year-old in Washington state gave advice and money to the Tumbler Ridge mass killer and even offered to livestream the attack on Facebook. (Oct. 6, 2026)

The complaint says they communicated via the Discord platform, where Van Rootselaar used two accounts.

Here’s what the FBI is alleging in its case against Bryant, who is charged with conspiracy to murder in a foreign country. The claims have not been tested in court.

HOW DID BRYANT ALLEGEDLY HELP THE KILLER

Bryant is said to have encouraged and advised Van Rootselaar for months, then helped set up a livestream to broadcast the murders.

Rico says Bryant admitted helping Van Rootselaar test the livestream equipment. Bryant also allegedly explained that Van Rootselaar purchased a tactical chest rig designed to carry additional bullet magazines, and during a test of the livestream, Van Rootselaar mounted a cellphone to the chest rig.

The complaint says Bryant gave Van Rootselaar tactical advice as to how to carry out the murders. In August 2025, while discussing possible target locations, Bryant allegedly said: “Hallways also mean a lot of ways people can escape. Corners to turn. Wide open spaces means numbers.”

He is also said to have advised Van Rootselaar that she “should have a handgun … this is smart.”

Bryant is said to have told Van Rootselaar in the days leading up to the attack that she did not need to go through with it, but continued to help test the livestream and did not alert police.

On the day of the killings, Bryant is said to have helped Van Rootselaar, who did not know how to drive, start the car in which she drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School, where six victims died.

THE CCTV FOOTAGE

Rico says CCTV footage shows Van Rootselaar enter Tumbler Ridge Secondary school through a side entrance, where she begins shooting at students and staff.

After Van Rootselaar has “killed and/or incapacitated several victims” she is allegedly seen lighting an explosive device, then throwing it near the school’s computer room and library. “The device ignited and left obvious blast marks,” Roco says.

A photo in the complaint shows what Rico says is the same device, consisting of a plastic bottle filled with liquid and taped with items including a lighter.

It says Van Rootselaar then tries to enter other parts of the school but is deterred by locked doors. “Van Rootselaar fired numerous shots into several of the doors,” it says.

Rico says police are then seen entering the building and Van Rootselaar retreats into an empty room, where she shoots herself dead.

THE LIVESTREAM

Rico says Bryant helped post a livestream on the day of the attack that lasted about 20 seconds on the Twitch platform.

“The livestream showed Van Rootselaar sitting in a vehicle with a rifle and another long gun in her lap,” he says.

During the livestream Van Rootselaar allegedly says to Bryant: “I’m going now. Fr (for real). Live. I shot them.”

Bryant allegedly responds: “Watching now.”

The complaint includes photos of guns, including one allegedly taken on the morning of the attack that the FBI says shows Van Rootselaar, posing on her knees in a black miniskirt and fishnet stockings.

The person in the photo, whose head is not shown, is holding an olive-green rifle with a telescopic site. On the end of the barrel is what appears to be a suppressor, decorated in blue, white and pink bands of the transgender pride flag. Van Rootselaar was trans, and the FBI said Tuesday that Bryant identifies as female.

Another photo shows a Canuck shotgun that Van Rootselaar says will be used in the attack. It is decorated with a sticker in the same blue, white and pink colours.

Bryant allegedly tells Van Rootselaar: “love the stickers … stickers would be so funny to be seen in photos of the incident.”

The FBI says that about six months before the shooting, Van Rootselaar told Bryant she had stolen guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe “and was hiding them in her room in preparation for a mass shooting.”

“Van Rootselaar also said she convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf,” the complaint says.

The FBI says Van Rootselaar told Bryant about the types of guns and accessories she possessed, “including a 3D printed foregrip, firearm magazines, and a ‘switch’ for the SKS (likely referring to a machine-gun conversion device).”

It says that according to Bryant, Van Rootselaar “ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

THE LOCATION

Before settling on Tumbler Ridge Secondary School as the site of the attack, Van Rootselaar allegedly discussed other locations with Bryant.

He allegedly says somewhere “like Walmart or Costco would have a lot of people” but would be “too wide and open.”

“Plus, I don’t wanna die in a shitty Walmart, I’d rather a mall because at least that’s a nice place to buy things lol,” Van Rootselaar adds in the August 2025 chat.

She says she wants to avoid a school, but “there’s just so many reasons why it’s ideal.”

She also sends Bryant a map of Northern Lights College in Dawson Creek.

“Out of the places I’ve looked at this seems to give me the best chance at getting a lot of time to shoot before the cops show up,” she says.

The complaint says Bryant told the FBI that after Van Rootselaar was institutionalized for setting her room on fire, she became “increasingly angry and suicidal.”

“Van Rootselaar often spoke about planning to use guns to murder her family members and others because she felt she had been mistreated,” it says.

It adds that Bryant believed “Van Rootselaar was fixated on mass shootings and watched livestreamed recordings of past shootings to learn from them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: New details in extensive FBI account of Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting
stories.summary: A complaint by the FBI against James Bryant in U.S. district court provides extensive new allegations about the mass killings in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., where eight victims died on Feb. 10, 2026.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
SEATTLE — A complaint by the FBI against James Bryant in U.S. district court provides extensive new allegations about the mass killings in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., where eight victims died on Feb. 10, 2026.

FBI special agent Joseph Rico swears in the complaint that Bryant, who lives in Bellingham, Wash., met shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar online about three years ago.

But they fell out of contact while the killer was institutionalized after setting her room on fire. After that, they spoke daily in the six months before the murders, Rico says.

The complaint says they communicated via the Discord platform, where Van Rootselaar used two accounts.

Here’s what the FBI is alleging in its case against Bryant, who is charged with conspiracy to murder in a foreign country. The claims have not been tested in court.

HOW DID BRYANT ALLEGEDLY HELP THE KILLER

Bryant is said to have encouraged and advised Van Rootselaar for months, then helped set up a livestream to broadcast the murders.

Rico says Bryant admitted helping Van Rootselaar test the livestream equipment. Bryant also allegedly explained that Van Rootselaar purchased a tactical chest rig designed to carry additional bullet magazines, and during a test of the livestream, Van Rootselaar mounted a cellphone to the chest rig.

The complaint says Bryant gave Van Rootselaar tactical advice as to how to carry out the murders. In August 2025, while discussing possible target locations, Bryant allegedly said: “Hallways also mean a lot of ways people can escape. Corners to turn. Wide open spaces means numbers.”

He is also said to have advised Van Rootselaar that she “should have a handgun … this is smart.”

Bryant is said to have told Van Rootselaar in the days leading up to the attack that she did not need to go through with it, but continued to help test the livestream and did not alert police.

On the day of the killings, Bryant is said to have helped Van Rootselaar, who did not know how to drive, start the car in which she drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School, where six victims died.

THE CCTV FOOTAGE

Rico says CCTV footage shows Van Rootselaar enter Tumbler Ridge Secondary school through a side entrance, where she begins shooting at students and staff.

After Van Rootselaar has “killed and/or incapacitated several victims” she is allegedly seen lighting an explosive device, then throwing it near the school’s computer room and library. “The device ignited and left obvious blast marks,” Roco says.

A photo in the complaint shows what Rico says is the same device, consisting of a plastic bottle filled with liquid and taped with items including a lighter.

It says Van Rootselaar then tries to enter other parts of the school but is deterred by locked doors. “Van Rootselaar fired numerous shots into several of the doors,” it says.

Rico says police are then seen entering the building and Van Rootselaar retreats into an empty room, where she shoots herself dead.

THE LIVESTREAM

Rico says Bryant helped post a livestream on the day of the attack that lasted about 20 seconds on the Twitch platform.

“The livestream showed Van Rootselaar sitting in a vehicle with a rifle and another long gun in her lap,” he says.

During the livestream Van Rootselaar allegedly says to Bryant: “I’m going now. Fr (for real). Live. I shot them.”

Bryant allegedly responds: “Watching now.”

The complaint includes photos of guns, including one allegedly taken on the morning of the attack that the FBI says shows Van Rootselaar, posing on her knees in a black miniskirt and fishnet stockings.

The person in the photo, whose head is not shown, is holding an olive-green rifle with a telescopic site. On the end of the barrel is what appears to be a suppressor, decorated in blue, white and pink bands of the transgender pride flag. Van Rootselaar was trans, and the FBI said Tuesday that Bryant identifies as female.

Another photo shows a Canuck shotgun that Van Rootselaar says will be used in the attack. It is decorated with a sticker in the same blue, white and pink colours.

Bryant allegedly tells Van Rootselaar: “love the stickers … stickers would be so funny to be seen in photos of the incident.”

The FBI says that about six months before the shooting, Van Rootselaar told Bryant she had stolen guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe “and was hiding them in her room in preparation for a mass shooting.”

“Van Rootselaar also said she convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf,” the complaint says.

The FBI says Van Rootselaar told Bryant about the types of guns and accessories she possessed, “including a 3D printed foregrip, firearm magazines, and a ‘switch’ for the SKS (likely referring to a machine-gun conversion device).”

It says that according to Bryant, Van Rootselaar “ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

THE LOCATION

Before settling on Tumbler Ridge Secondary School as the site of the attack, Van Rootselaar allegedly discussed other locations with Bryant.

He allegedly says somewhere “like Walmart or Costco would have a lot of people” but would be “too wide and open.”

“Plus, I don’t wanna die in a shitty Walmart, I’d rather a mall because at least that’s a nice place to buy things lol,” Van Rootselaar adds in the August 2025 chat.

She says she wants to avoid a school, but “there’s just so many reasons why it’s ideal.”

She also sends Bryant a map of Northern Lights College in Dawson Creek.

“Out of the places I’ve looked at this seems to give me the best chance at getting a lot of time to shoot before the cops show up,” she says.

The complaint says Bryant told the FBI that after Van Rootselaar was institutionalized for setting her room on fire, she became “increasingly angry and suicidal.”

“Van Rootselaar often spoke about planning to use guns to murder her family members and others because she felt she had been mistreated,” it says.

It adds that Bryant believed “Van Rootselaar was fixated on mass shootings and watched livestreamed recordings of past shootings to learn from them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Power outage affecting White Oaks area in London, Ont.
stories.summary: Over 1,300 London Hydro customers are without power Tuesday evening.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Over 1,300 Londoners in the city’s south end are without power Tuesday evening.

London Hydro took to social media, saying, “There are a number of elements impacting restoration including a pole down, pole fire, and grass fire.”

A large part of the White Oaks and Westminster areas are without power, including parts of White Oaks mall.

The estimated time of restoration is 10:30 p.m.

stories.title: Alberta's gopher museum closed until further notice as owners find new facility
stories.summary: A quirky Alberta roadside attraction that has delighted travellers for decades with its stuffed rodents in tiny costumes is closed until further notice.
stories.author: Daniela Germano The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The World Famous Gopher Hole Museum, located in Torrington, a hamlet about 120 kilometres north of Calgary, made the announcement online earlier this week.

Laural Kurta, museum director, said she was forced to close the doors because the two historical buildings that house the exhibits need to be replaced.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 16Image 17

“We have done every patch repair, staple, spackle, everything we could possibly do, and it is just at its end,” Kurta said in an interview Tuesday.

She added that the collection needs to be heat and humidity controlled because of the taxidermy, and the buildings can no longer sustain it.

“Nobody thought this place would last more than five years,” she said. “The museum has now been open for 30, and it’s busier than ever.”

The museum closed its doors last Tuesday. It was in a former century-old schoolhouse joined by a small hallway to a grain elevator office.

It opened in 1996 and features stuffed Richardson’s ground squirrels, commonly called gophers in Western Canada, in dioramas dressed in costumes.

There’s a rodent in an Edmonton Oilers jersey playing hockey, a rodent blacksmith hammering on an anvil, a Mountie gopher, a bank robber gopher, a three-gopher musical and medal-winning rodents on the Olympic dais.

Kurta’s parents helped set up the museum and her mother ran it for 24 years until she fell ill. A group of retired seniors volunteered their time to run the museum until the COVID-19 pandemic when Kurta then took over.

The museum was launched with a provincial startup grant but has been self-sufficient since, relying on admission fees by donation.

The community has started an online fundraiser to build a new museum and hopefully keep it in Torrington.

It has a long way to go. As of Tuesday afternoon, about $13,500 has been raised. About $300,000 is needed.

Until then the gophers will hit the road.

Kurta has been lending out the dioramas to some small museums and they even provided some displays for the Calgary Comic Expo earlier this year.

“We’re not completely gone,” she said.

“We’re just going to focus more on how we’re going represent in the community until we’re able to rebuild.”

Kurta said she never wanted to run the gopher museum, but felt compelled to keep it open for her family and for everyone else who loves it.

“Yes, it’s silly and the gophers are wearing funny clothes, and that’s part of why people come, but it also does tell the history of the community,” she said.

“It’s not just Torrington — it’s also the stories of small town Alberta.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

The Canadian Press
