stories.title: Quebec’s anglophones approach PQ win with optimism, skepticism
stories.summary: Quebec's new premier-designate has made several promises for anglophones, but the community is watching to see if they'll be kept with an independence referendum also possible.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Quebec’s new minority government made several promises to its English-speaking community, but anglophones say they’re approaching the new government with both optimism and skepticism.

The Parti Québécois (PQ) was elected to a minority government in Monday’s provincial election, just five seats shy of a majority, meaning it will have to work with opposition parties to pass legislation.

During the campaign, premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon stressed the importance of the anglophone community, defending their right to election documents in both official languages and suggesting changes to the province’s language law, Bill 96.

But Sylvia Martin-Laforge, director general of Talq, which advocates for the province’s English-language communities, said they will be watching to see what actions Plamondon takes.

This includes whether will reverse a challenge by the government on whether English-speaking Quebecers can receive voter information in English and French.

“He had questioned the vallue of challenging bilingual voter information during the campaign, noting that was a fundamental right,” she said. “So that would be an important first message to the English-speaking community if he recognizes that voter information should be in both languages.”

Yet, she also said his stance on applying the Charter of the French Language to CEGEPs is “not good news.”

Martin-Laforge told Global News that education is important for the “vitality” of anglophones, and would like to hear more information on how the new government wants to handle education and if any restrictions could be in place for attending English-language schools.

Daniel Béland, the director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada, said Tuesday that the PQ won’t want to be “at war” with anglophones especially as many did not vote for them.

Statistics on how many anglophones voted for each party are not yet available, but several electoral districts with strong English-speaking communities primarily voted Liberal.

On the Island of Montreal, the Quebec Liberals (PLQ) took 19 of 27 seats with just two PQ MNAs elected.

“In a minority context, with two parties that are explicitly willing to defend the anglophone minority, and I will even add Quebec Solidaire to the Conservatives and the Liberals in a sense, I think that he (Plamondon) will have to be careful the way we move forward in terms of policies that will affect anglophones directly,” Béland said.

He added the PQ doesn’t want to appear “mean” to English-speaking communities just because the party supports independence, an issue many anglophones are against.

Early in the campaign, Plamondon promised to hold a referendum on Quebec independence – something he had promised even before the election began. But he said he wouldn’t hold one until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029.

With a minority government, getting that referendum to a voting day would likely require additional support from at least one other party.

The Quebec Liberals and Conservatives (PCQ) have been staunch on their opposition to a referendum, but at least one party could lend support.

“There’s another party that’s been elected to the legislature that also supports a referendum and separation and that’s Quebec Solidaire,” said Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus of political science at the University of Toronto. “So between the two of them, they have a majority. So, forgetting Donald Trump, they could act on it sooner, or if they want they can act on it later.”

He added being a minority government, there is the risk it could fall to a confidence vote before 2029 setting the stage for an election before a referendum is ever held.

A referendum question in Quebec can’t head to the public for a vote without moving through the National Assembly. The PQ won 59 seats in Monday’s vote, while the PLQ and PCQ received 40 and 19 respectively totaling 59 together. Quebec Solidaire won nine seats, meaning they could join with the PQ to support the referendum.

“The timing is problematic and also there is the Trump problem or issue,” Beland said. “So the PQ will have to break its promise and organize a referendum that’s already really unpopular among Quebecers before the deadline they had set for themselves.”

stories.title: Small community’s development application tests local control and province’s commitment to Ontario farmland
stories.summary: A planning application before the Lucan-Biddulph council is drawing close scrutiny from farming advocates and potentially testing the provincial government's commitment to protecting Ontario's agricultural land.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
A planning application before the Lucan-Biddulph council is drawing close scrutiny from farming advocates and potentially testing the provincial government’s commitment to protecting Ontario’s agricultural land.

The proposal seeks to convert over 100 acres of prime farmland into residential development, a move that highlights the ongoing tension between municipal growth needs and the preservation of a critical food resource.

The application, submitted by Siv-ik Planning & Design Inc., requests an Official Plan Amendment to expand the Village of Lucan’s settlement area boundary by 45.47 hectares (approximately 112.36 acres).

These lands, located east of Saintsbury Line and south of Fallon Drive, are currently designated Agricultural and zoned General Agricultural (A1). The proposal aims to redesignate these fertile fields to ‘Residential’ to accommodate future housing growth. The application was deemed complete by the township on Sept. 1, 2026, with a statutory public meeting to be announced at a future date.

This application arrives at a critical juncture, being the first to request an urban growth boundary change since the province removed the ‘Municipal Comprehensive Review’ requirement. This review previously mandated detailed analysis of growth projections, economic impacts, and farmland loss.

“Now that review process has been taken away, it has now opened it up so that developers can apply on their own privately to have their lands considered,” explained Lucan-Biddulph Mayor Cathy Burghardt-Jesson.

She added that this change has diminished municipal control, noting, “I’ve been on council for 16 years, and I have found that the ability to do that is consistently stripped away.”

Burghardt-Jesson acknowledged the delicate balancing act her community faces.

“There have always been limitations and parameters set up for municipalities to grow in a responsible way that isn’t too fast, that doesn’t put a strain on infrastructure,” she stated. “Well, that’s always been the biggest challenge for small urban and rural communities across Ontario. We don’t have the infill opportunities that our neighbors like London have. And so, when we grow, the lands that we take away are agricultural.”

She emphasized the need for responsible growth to meet residents’ needs: “We just want to make sure that we’re growing appropriately, responsibly and can answer the needs of our residents.”

The Ontario Farmland Trust, an agency dedicated to farmland preservation, is closely monitoring the situation.

Executive Director Martin Straathof is raising “red flags” about the long-term implications. “This is a resource that once it’s paved over, we can’t get it back,” Straathof warned.

He highlighted the alarming rate of farmland loss in Ontario, citing that 2.8 million acres have been lost in just over three decades, an 18 per cent reduction.

“We’re now losing 319 acres a day,” he stated.

Straathof articulated the complex challenge, “We’re in that difficult place where we need to be protecting our farmland as a finite and critical resource for our communities and food security and our economic resilience. Yet at the same time, we’re also in a housing crisis and housing affordability issues.”

He stressed the growing global importance of Ontario’s food production capacity, adding, “Places like Canada and in particularly Ontario is going to be that much more depended upon globally for food production.”

He also pointed out the necessity of a buffer for less successful harvest years, stating, “We still need to make sure that we have not just, you know, farming up to the point that we can say, okay, this will feed everybody. We want that buffer for those years that it might not be as successful.”

Burghardt-Jesson, who is not seeking re-election in the upcoming November municipal election, noted that the next council will inherit the responsibility of navigating these growth decisions.

The township has provided notice for the application, inviting public input. Residents who wish to participate in future discussions or appeal decisions are advised to submit comments and attend upcoming public meetings, details of which will be announced by the Township of Lucan Biddulph.

As Lucan-Biddulph grapples with its future development, the decision on this application will reverberate beyond its borders, serving as a key indicator of how Ontario intends to balance the pressing need for housing with the irreplaceable value of its agricultural heritage.

stories.title: Delta plane clips Air Canada aircraft at LAX
stories.summary: Incident occurred around 10:30 a.m. local time as the Delta plane was taxiing for departure, and the Air Canada plane was being towed toward the gate
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration says it is investigating after a Delta Air Lines plane “clipped” an Air Canada aircraft at Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday.

The aviation agency says the incident occurred around 10:30 a.m. local time as the Delta plane was taxiing for departure, and the Air Canada plane was being towed toward the gate.

An Air Canada spokesperson says there are no reported injuries.

Sean Davidson says in a statement that Air Canada Flight 785 had arrived from Toronto before “an aircraft operated by another airline made contact with its tail.”

He says the plane will be taken out of service for inspection and repairs.

The U.S. agency says the Delta plane’s left wingtip clipped the Air Canada aircraft’s horizontal stabilizer, a wing-like structure at the tail of a plane.

stories.title: RCMP orders review of software supplied by company with alleged Russian ties
stories.summary: Oxygen Forensics allegedly presented itself as an American company to land government contracts and evade sanctions against Russia
stories.author: Sara Mojtehedzadeh
stories.content:
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police will not renew their contract with a software company accused of concealing its Russian ownership, and have ordered a probe of any security risks posed by the firm’s digital forensics tools, a spokesperson for the federal law enforcement agency says.

Earlier this year, the RCMP signed a licensing agreement with Oxygen Forensics, which is now at the centre of a criminal complaint in the United States alleging its owners falsely presented the firm as American to land government contracts.

In fact, the company was controlled by Russian nationals who were concerned about the effect on their business of increasingly strict economic sanctions against Russia, according to the criminal complaint filed by the U.S. Justice Department in late September.

Oxygen Forensics is tied to a Russian software developer that counts Russian security services amongst its clients, the criminal complaint alleges. The company’s software allows investigators to collect and extract data from digital devices.

In January, the RCMP spent around $34,000 on a licence for Oxygen Forensics’ software, publicly available procurement data show. In a statement to The Globe and Mail, a spokesperson for the agency, Ian Lordon, said there is “no plan” to renew the agreement, which expires in December.

The RCMP have also asked the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cccs) to launch a “supply chain integrity assessment” of Oxygen Forensics’ software, a process that looks at potential risks involved with technology products used by government agencies.

Oxygen Forensics’ digital forensics tools were deployed only in “limited circumstances when no other technical options were available,” Mr. Lordon told The Globe.

Any computers using the software have been isolated from the broader RCMP network, he added.

U.S. authorities have not alleged that Oxygen Forensics’ software contained malicious code or that it was used to gain unauthorized access to clients’ computer systems or data.

Communications Security Establishment Canada, which houses Cccs, did not respond to questions from The Globe about the supply chain assessment being conducted for Oxygen Forensics.

Several European law enforcement agencies, including London’s Metropolitan Police, have suspended their use of Oxygen Forensics’ software in the wake of the allegations.

Mr. Lordon said the RCMP’s licence with the firm was procured by Shared Services Canada, a federal department that manages information technology procurement and conducts due diligence on vendors to the government.

U.S. authorities arrested Oxygen Forensics’ chief executive officer, Lee Reiber of Boise, Idaho, in September and charged him with conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

A Russian national, Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, was also arrested last month at London Heathrow Airport while in transit to Istanbul. The United States is expected to seek Mr. Davydov’s extradition, according to the Justice Department.

Oxygen Forensics was incorporated in Virginia in 2013, publicly available corporate records show. An annual report from the following year lists Mr. Davydov as a vice-president and provides a Moscow address. Another Moscow-based individual was listed as the company’s CEO.

In the summer of 2022, the Moscow-based individuals were removed from the company’s corporate filings and Mr. Reiber was appointed CEO, the records show.

These changes were part of a conspiracy to conceal Oxygen Forensics’ true ownership in light of expanded U.S. sanctions against Russia in response to its invasion of Ukraine, according to an affidavit filed with the criminal complaint.

Oxygen Forensics’ leadership falsely claimed that no one in Russia was involved with developing its software, when its code was actually written, reviewed and managed by a team in Russia, an affidavit from a U.S. special agent specializing in cyber investigations says.

The RCMP previously secured two contracts worth a total of around $90,000 with Oxygen Forensics, according to procurement data provided to The Globe by the law enforcement agency. Those contracts have been closed and completed, agency spokesperson Mr. Lordon said.

Mr. Lordon did not say when the law enforcement agency learned of the allegations made by the U.S. Justice Department against Oxygen Forensics.

“The RCMP is constantly sharing and receiving information related to commercial products with partner agencies,” he said.

Oxygen Forensics did not respond to The Globe’s requests for comment.

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives maintain five-point lead over NDP as voting day nears: survey
stories.summary: Back on Sept. 24, 47 per cent of B.C. Conservative supporters were “very certain” of their choice. 65 per cent say that now.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Half (48 per cent) of leaning and decided B.C. voters are saying they would vote for the Conservatives, says ARI, adding that 43 per cent indicate support for the NDP.

Overall, says ARI, almost half of British Columbians (46 per cent) say they are “very certain” about their voting intentions. That’s an increase from the one-third (35 per cent) during the first week of the campaign. This growth in certainty “is reflected much more among B.C. Conservative supporters than those who would support the B.C. NDP,” says ARI.

Back on Sept. 24, half (47 per cent) of B.C. Conservative supporters said they were “very certain” of their choice. Two-thirds (65 per cent) say that now. For the B.C. NDP, 44 per cent are firm in their voting intent, which is an increase of just three points since the beginning of the campaign.

When the writ was dropped at the end of September, B.C. NDP leader David Eby pointed to President Donald Trump and the U.S. tariffs as the key reason his party should be given a majority mandate. However, according to the ARI, this was not among the top six issues for voters, even at the start of the campaign. Since then it has fallen further down the list. Only 10 per cent of voters say the U.S. tariffs/Donald Trump/alcohol ban is the “most important” issue to them when deciding how to cast their vote.

That’s behind concerns such as cost of living (57 per cent), health care (42 per cent), the economy/jobs (26 per cent), housing affordability (24 per cent), the deficit (24 per cent) and public safety (24 per cent). It’s even behind secondary issues such as the opioid crisis (15 per cent), climate change (14 per cent) and poverty (13 per cent).

B.C. voters haven’t had much time to get to know Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson, but a growing number now have an opinion about him, says ARI. “There are as many who view him positively (38 per cent) as negatively (37 per cent),” says ARI. “That is better than Eby performs on the same question. Three-in-five (58 per cent) say they view the B.C. NDP leader unfavourably; one-third (36 per cent) favourably.”

Geoff Russ: Repealing Dripa is only the first step to fixing Eby's reconciliation overreach

Colby Cosh: David Eby's election call is perfectly legitimate

Doerkson has a slight edge (36 per cent) over Eby (33 per cent) on the question of who British Columbians believe would be the best premier. Though, almost as many say neither is the best choice to lead the province (31 per cent), notes ARI.

There is a gender divide in party support, especially among voters older than 54. Three-in-five men in that age bracket say they are planning to vote Conservative, while a majority (54 per cent) of women plan to support the NDP. The Conservatives are preferred among both men and women aged 35-to 54, while the NDP have more support among voters under 35.

The NDP needs to convince the 2024 voters who elected them to return at even higher rates, states ARI. However, the survey shows that one-quarter of people who voted for the party two years ago say they are undecided or voting for the Greens (6 per cent) or Conservatives (8 per cent).

Meanwhile, the Conservatives are retaining 86 per cent of supporters from the 2024 election.

British Columbians go to the polls on Oct. 24.

The Angus Reid Institute conducted this online survey from Oct. 1-3, 2026, among a randomized sample of 1,013 Canadian adults who are residents of British Columbia. For comparison purposes only, a probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of +/- 3 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. Discrepancies in or between totals are due to rounding. The survey was self-commissioned and paid for by ARI.

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives plan to repeal no-fault insurance, leaked letter shows
stories.summary: The NDP government introduced the no-fault insurance system in 2021, that generally prevents car accident victims from suing.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The British Columbia Conservatives plan to repeal the province’s no-fault auto insurance system, in a major policy proposal revealed by a leaked letter from the party’s interim leader to lawyers and insurance executives.

Lorne Doerkson says in the letter that if elected on Oct. 24, the Conservatives would bring in legislation to restore accident victims’ rights to sue, under a new “hybrid system” designed to keep rates affordable while protecting people hurt by reckless drivers.

Doerkson has told reporters that the policy is needed to allow people with serious injuries to be properly compensated to manage their post-accident lives.

The NDP government introduced the no-fault insurance system in 2021, that generally prevents car accident victims from suing, in response to what NDP Leader David Eby called a “financial dumpster fire” at Icbc with losses in the billions.

Eby now says the letter leaked by the union representing Icbc workers amounts to a “secret deal” between Conservatives and trial lawyers.

But Doerkson says no-fault insurance has been “very challenging” for the residents for multiple reasons.

“Obviously we have to provide affordable insurance coverage for all of our residents, but for those that have experienced catastrophic injury and potentially life-altering injury, this program has not supported them well,” he said at an unrelated news conference in Vancouver.

“And in so many cases, we need to improve that and we absolutely have to contemplate this insurance model.”

Doerkson said he had made “no promises” about the plan.

But in the Sept. 29 letter to the vice-president of the Insurance Bureau of Canada, and the presidents of the Law Society of B.C., the Trial Lawyers Association of B.C., and the Canadian Bar Association, he says new legislation would be passed within a year of the Conservatives being elected.

“Accident victims will get back their right to recover for their serious injuries, and government will get out of the legal profession’s business.” he says.

He says B.C. can look to Ontario, Alberta, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, P.E.I., and Newfoundland and Labrador, which “all have hybrid insurance models.

“We can learn from them and do better,” he adds.

The NDP says trial lawyers have been lobbying to end the no-fault system “that lowered car insurance rates for drivers and has kept them frozen for seven years.”

It describes the Trial Lawyers Association as “the organization representing personal injury lawyers who previously worked on Icbc cases.”

stories.title: Ontario asks OPP to look into Osap payments at private career colleges
stories.summary: Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said the ministry launched targeted inspections of career colleges last year in response to growing concerns about Osap usage.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario has asked provincial police to look into student financial assistance payments at private career colleges after auditors identified “serious concerns” about possible criminal activity and “egregious” use of public money, the government said Tuesday.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said the ministry launched targeted inspections of career colleges last year in response to growing concerns about Ontario Student Assistance Program usage and asked Kpmg in August to begin an audit.

“While that work is ongoing, preliminary findings have identified serious concerns about the integrity of the Osap system in the private post-secondary sector,” he wrote in a statement.

“These include common ownership, the involvement of immigration services firms and co-location between private career colleges and immigration recruitment or immigration services firms, inadequate student validation and verification of course enrolment and outcomes, and unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations.”

As a result, the government notified the auditor general last week and referred the matter on Friday to the Ontario Provincial Police, Quinn wrote.

The Canadian Press reported on Friday that government officials who inspected three career colleges alleged in reports filed in court that they found evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program. Those schools deny most of the allegations made against them, and they have not been proven in court.

Quinn and the government have been under increasing pressure to explain what critics describe as a lack of oversight and inaction on unusually rapid Osap growth at a small number of career colleges.

“It’s a colossal mess,” interim Liberal leader John Fraser said. “The minister should have taken responsibility today and resigned.”

Quinn earlier this year drastically reduced the amount of Osap grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive, while restricting career college students to Osap loans.

He cited “unsustainable” costs, but a freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press showed that 95 per cent of the year-over-year growth in 2024-25 was due to career colleges.

A subsequent freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press showed that most of that growth was concentrated among a small number of schools. Just seven career colleges accounted for about $385 million in Osap grants in 2024-25, the same amount that went to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges.

He denied that it was a mistake to make online-only programs eligible in the first place.

“There is a lot of value in having options for online learning,” he said at a press conference on Tuesday. “Unfortunately, this comes down to criminal nature, criminal allegations, and the bad actors, unfortunately, taking advantage of taxpayer dollars and students, for that matter.”

“Unfortunately, there will be some colleges that are not going to be able to survive through this,” Quinn said. “But understanding that we’re talking about egregious use of taxpayer dollars here, criminal allegations, and we need to take that very seriously.”

“Doug Ford and his government originally blamed students for their decision to cut Osap support, but today they’ve finally admitted to the truth: the Ford government grossly mismanaged the system and is punishing every student in Ontario for their incompetence,” she wrote in a statement.

“We hope the government will introduce a policy that promptly addresses improper conduct and targets those who have acted wrongly,” the association wrote in a statement.

“I’m privileged enough to have a decent amount of savings, but that’s only to keep me afloat until the end of first semester. So after that, I wouldn’t really know what I’m going to do. But a lot of people are right now not focused on their exams just because they’re thinking like, ‘Is there any point?’ Because if Osap doesn’t come in the next month, they might as well drop out.”

stories.title: ‘Tipping recession’: Atlantic Canadian hospitality workers feeling the pinch
stories.summary: A new report finds that economic pressures mean people are not only dining out less, they're being less generous when it comes to tipping.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
A new report finds that economic pressures mean people are not only dining out less; they’re also being less generous when it comes to tipping.

And hospitality workers in Atlantic Canada say they’ve noticed it firsthand.

“I find tipping and business has been down. I think people just can’t afford it right now,” said Sam Molloy, the manager at Whiskey’s Lounge in Dartmouth, N.S.

A couple of streets over, the owner of Chanoey’s Pasta says the drop has been striking.

“We noticed a difference since last year that tipping culture has been really decreasing. We saw like a 50 to 60 per cent decrease on tipping,” said Catherine Paulino.

The report found 60 per cent of Atlantic Canada’s hospitality workers said their tips have decreased over the past two years.

Nationally, the figure was 67 per cent. Workers in Ontario were hardest hit, with 72 per cent of tipped workers reporting a decline.

Meanwhile, 43 per cent of respondents said they rely on tips to cover essential expenses such as rent and groceries. This reliance was highest in Atlantic Canada and British Columbia, at 51 per cent.

“The tips definitely help with trying to keep up with the cost and those expenses as well,” said Molloy.

The survey was conducted online by pollster Angus Reid on behalf of Actual, a Toronto-based company that offers automated tip management and payroll systems for businesses. The online survey sampled 506 Canadian adults who currently work in the hospitality industry.

Actual’s CEO, Afshin Mousavian, says the industry is in a “tipping recession,” and that’s leading to reduced income for workers.

“It’s important to understand that while consumers are frustrated that their bills have (an added) tip, those individuals, those employees, those businesses live in the same economy that everybody else does. So they’re also feeling the pinch,” said Mousavian.

The report also highlighted the importance of being transparent about how tips are divided.

Ninety per cent of respondents said they are aware of how tips are divided at their own workplace, with transparency being the strongest in Atlantic Canada at 96 per cent.

Last month, the province tabled amendments to the Labour Standards Code that included protections for workers’ tips and gratuities. The changes, which come into effect April 1, 2027, will “ensure tips and gratuities go to the people who earn them.”

Some restaurants, however, are bucking the trend and eliminating tipping altogether.

The Bonfire in Halifax has a no-tip policy , and its co-owner says the approach is resonating with the community and has drawn a loyal customer base since opening last year.

“In place of tips, everyone gets paid $20 an hour and then half of the profits from the business gets split amongst the employees at the end of every pay period,” said Vincent Morley.

“We feel like the responsibility of paying our employees properly should be on us as business owners and not relying on the generosity of people as they come in the door.”

Restaurant industry organizations say they’re keeping an eye on this trend but don’t expect tipping to go away anytime soon.

“It’s a big part of our culture,” said Natasha Chestnut with the Restaurants Association of Nova Scotia.

“And we know that (the) majority of diners, they’re still more than happy to tip for dining out experiences.”

Still, those who work in restaurants say they understand why customers are tipping less, but are hoping for some relief nonetheless.

“Everything is expensive right now, so it takes a toll on everybody,” said Molloy.

stories.title: Westwood Hills residents welcome work on new emergency exit, but want more routes
stories.summary: Work will begin on the emergency exit from the community of Westwood Hills in early October, and the municipality is also gathering the public's input on more connector roads.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
Residents in the Tantallon and Hammonds Plains area of Halifax have been voicing concerns about access roads and emergency egress from the growing subdivisions ever since the devastating wildfires of 2023.

At the time, residents shared stories of being stuck in traffic trying to flee on Hammonds Plains Road, as the sky grew black with smoke.

The fire forced the evacuation of more than 16,000 people and ultimately destroyed over 150 structures.

Halifax Regional Municipality said this week that work will begin on the emergency exit from the community of Westwood Hills this month, and the municipality is also gathering public input on more connector roads.

It’s welcome news for Richard O’Fegan, the president of the Westwood Hills Residents Association.

“It’s good to see that some momentum has taken place. It’s good see some actions have taken place to support our commu-nity,” he said.

A staff report was commissioned by municipal councillors in the months after the 2023 wildfire, which recommended moving ahead with a new emergency-only connection between the Westwood Hills subdivision and nearby Highway 103.

But O’Fegan says he has reservations about the placement of the road, and the fact that it will remain locked by a gate when there isn’t an emergency.

“It’s difficult for the community to be 100 per cent behind the placement of this and understand the positive impacts it’ll have if we do face a situation similar to what we did in 2023,” he said.

As part of the egress project, connector roads between the subdivision and Upper Hammonds Plains as well as Highland Park North are also being considered. The proposed plan states the purpose of these roads “would be to improve access and egress in case of emergencies, as well as to increase transportation network connectivity between these three communities.”

O’Fegan says he feels the placement of the connector roads could cause problems later on.

“All roads pointing to Hammonds Plains doesn’t really seem like the most effective strategy when you’re talking about 880 homes and more, (you’re) talking about a long-term care facility, you’re talking about neighbouring subdivisions,” said O’Fegan.

Debbie Miller, a member of the neighbourhood group Pockwock Corridor Safe, says residents want to know if there will be more roads heading in the other direction that lead to Highway 101.

“This isn’t enough. This is maybe step one, depending on what their goals are. If their goal is to have more development without better planning, then that’s not going to work,” she said.

Residents will have the opportunity to share their thoughts during in-person engagement sessions or take part in an online survey.

The meetings will be held:

Wednesday, Oct. 7 from 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. at Upper Hammonds Plains Community Centre, 711 Pockwock Road, Upper Hammonds Plains

Thursday, Oct. 15 from 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. at Tantallon Public Library, 3646 Hammonds Plains Road, Upper Tantallon

stories.title: Alberta separatists see an ally in Quebec premier-designate St-Pierre Plamondon
stories.summary: Separatist leaders feel the Party Quebecois victory could change the political dynamic of Canada, especially since its leader has shown willingness to support Alberta independence.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Leading figures in the push for Alberta separation are celebrating the election of Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Jeffrey Rath said Tuesday that St-Pierre Plamondon’s election victory could change the political dynamic of Canada, especially since the premier-designate has already shown his willingness to support Alberta’s separatist movement.

“For the first time in Canadian history, we have a government in Quebec that supports Alberta independence,” Rath said in an interview.

St-Pierre Plamondon and the separatist Parti Québécois are set to form a minority government after Monday’s election in Quebec, which saw the governing Coalition Avenir Quebec wiped from the assembly.

2:13 Quebec election 2026: What a projected win for the sovereigntist PQ means for the province

The premier-designate has pledged to hold what would be Quebec’s third separation referendum, but he’s said it won’t happen until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office.

During a visit to Calgary last year, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would recognize an independent Alberta should the province vote to separate.

Rath said he had met with the Party Quebecois leader in Calgary. He said the pair, who are both lawyers, talked for three hours over dinner and have maintained contact since.

“I’ve gotten to know him relatively well over the last year. I think people are going to be very surprised at how well he governs,” Rath said.

Corey Morgan, an online commentator and separatist advertiser in the upcoming Alberta referendum, also said the premier-designate was an ally and that his victory bodes well for Alberta’s movement.

“I believe it’s in the interest of independence movements on both sides of the country to … maintain pressure and instability on the federal system,” Morgan said.

1:52 Alberta separatists remain in close contact with U.S. officials ahead of referendum

On Oct. 19 Albertans will vote on whether they want to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on quitting Canada.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the vote earlier this year citing two competing petitions on either side of the separation debate that both received hundreds of thousands of signatures. Smith has said she supports Alberta staying in Canada and that she will vote accordingly.

Smith congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon on Monday in a social media post, saying she’s looking forward to working with his government.

“Our provinces and our country are stronger when we work together, stand united and build a stronger future for all Canadians,” Smith wrote.

Smith didn’t address the issue of separation in her congratulatory note, nor did Prime Minister Mark Carney in his own social media post.

Morgan said he thought the two leaders were ignoring the elephant in the room.

“People are kind of dodging that fact that, whether you like it or not, even if that wasn’t the prime driver in this provincial election, Quebec just elected an overtly separatist party to be their government,” he said.

“That’s significant, and that’s going to make a difference in policy in the next two to four years.”

5:58 Quebec Election: Separatist party to form a minority government after crushing defeat for the CAQ

Rath, a fierce critic of Smith for putting off a binding separation vote, also said he took inspiration from St-Pierre Plamondon’s path to victory.

The Party Quebecois saw much of its electoral support come from outside of Quebec’s two major cities and it managed to form government despite an overall vote share of about 28 per cent.

Rath said he thought something similar could happen in Alberta should Smith’s United Conservative Party fracture over the separation issue.

Smith has been adamant that her party, government and caucus are committed federalists, but in recent weeks the premier has seen calls for a leadership review come from two of her UCP constituency associations.

Rath said despite the premier’s assurances that the UCP isn’t a separatist party, he thinks rank-and-file members who want Alberta to go its own way represent a “supermajority” within the party.

“I think this is going to be really interesting for Alberta politics,” Rath said.

stories.title: Air Canada flight from Toronto struck by Delta plane at LAX, no injuries reported
stories.summary: An Air Canada flight that was travelling from Toronto was struck by another aircraft at Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday.
stories.author: Denio Lourenco
stories.content:
An Air Canada flight from Toronto was struck by another aircraft on the tarmac at Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday.

An Air Canada spokesperson told CityNews that flight AC785 was being towed to the gate after landing safely, when the left wing of an Airbus A350-900 operated by Delta Airlines made contact with its tail at approximately 10:30 a.m. local time.

There were no reported injuries to any passengers or crew.

The Air Canada spokesperson said the aircraft will be taken out of service for inspection and repairs.

A spokesperson for Delta Airlines confirmed the incident Tuesday afternoon.

“Nothing is more important than the safety of our customers and people, and we apologize to our customers for the experience and delay in their travels,” the spokesperson said.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said it is investigating.

stories.title: With a $1.5-million budget for a new home, what did this expecting Toronto couple buy?
stories.summary: They were open to a fixer-upper and said a finished basement that could serve as a guest suite would also be ideal
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
Maddie Timlin, a quality improvement manager, began dating Anthony Smith, a senior project manager, in 2023. At the time, they were both living in condos that they owned: Ms. Timlin in a one-bedroom unit in Toronto’s CityPlace neighbourhood and Mr. Smith in a one-bed-plus-den west of her in Fort York. A year later, in August, 2024, Mr. Smith, 39, moved in with Ms. Timlin, 35, and rented out his unit for $2,700 a month.

Two months after moving in together, the couple was engaged. But they prioritized having a child before getting married. “We wanted to put the family planning first,” Ms. Timlin explains. “We’re a little bit older.” They knew their current living situation wouldn’t work once they added a kid to the mix, so once the couple found out they were pregnant in March, 2026, they started thinking about buying a house together.

They connected with realtor Catherine Young from Right at Home Realty to guide their search. Ms. Young says that the majority of her clients are, like Ms. Timlin and Mr. Smith, couples upgrading into bigger properties to start a family. “I’m a mom myself, so I’ve gone through that transition of going from condo life to a house,” Ms. Young explains. “I understand what the pain points can be.” She encourages expecting families to look beyond the aesthetics and think practically. “You don’t think of things like, ‘I’ll have to take the stroller up the stairs,’ or ‘Where am I going to leave all the little shoes and boots when they get dirty,’” says Ms. Young.

Both Ms. Timlin and Mr. Smith planned to keep their condos and rent them out. That left them with a budget of around $1.5-million. The couple was open to a fixer-upper, since Mr. Smith enjoys doing renovations and handiwork (he fully renovated Ms. Timlin’s condo before he moved in), and they wanted to stay central in Toronto. “Walkability and access to transit were big factors for us,” Mr. Smith explains.

The couple was looking for at least three bedrooms and two bathrooms. A finished basement that could serve as a guest suite would also be ideal since Ms. Timlin’s mom, who lives in Ottawa, planned to stay with them after the birth to help with the baby. A garage was also a bonus for Mr. Smith’s hobby work. “I have a lot of tools and things,” he says.

Here were their top three options:

Three-bedroom subdivided townhouse near Trinity Bellwoods Park

The couple loved the location of this townhouse. It was a few minutes from Trinity Bellwoods Park and the restaurants and bars on Ossington Avenue. The property came with a 1½-car garage with decent space for storage. And the home itself had been recently renovated, but as two separate suites with a total of three bedrooms plus a den and two bathrooms. It would require significant renovations to turn back into a cohesive home. The above-grade bedrooms were small, which meant making the basement bedroom their primary, which they didn’t love. The property was listed at $1,519,900, which they figured was overpriced.

Four-plus-one bedroom semi in Brockton Village

Mr. Smith loved the spaciousness of this semi-detached home near Lansdowne Avenue and College Street. It appeared to have been owned by the same family for decades and had a spacious two-car garage for Mr. Smith’s tools and workshop. The bedrooms were a good size, and the basement was renovated with a separate entrance, kitchen and direct outdoor access – ideal for a guest suite. The home was in good condition and was move-in-ready, but its kitchen and flooring were old and outdated (however, the couple saw this as potential to improve the home over time). The home was well-connected by transit and close to Dufferin Grove Park, but it was slightly further from the city centre. The home was listed for $1,199,000, which Mr. Smith thought was too low. He called it a “honeytrap” to entice multiple bids.

Three-plus-one bedroom semi in Seaton Village

Located on a tree-lined street in Toronto’s Seaton Village, the couple happened to cycle past this home on the day it was listed for sale. The three-plus-one bedroom, two-bathroom semi-detached home had a large front porch, a fireplace, and well-sized bedrooms. The basement was equipped with a bedroom and a full bathroom for visiting guests. The home was move-in ready, but there were some quirks, like creaky hardwood flooring and a bedroom door that didn’t close properly. And it only had a one-car garage, which offered limited space for a workshop, compared to the other homes they considered. The home was priced at $1,399,000, which they thought was slightly overpriced.

Their home: Three-plus-one bedroom semi in Seaton Village

While the couple figured the subdivided townhome near Trinity Bellwoods had room in its listing price for negotiation, they worried that renovating it would be costly and wouldn’t add to the property value. It ended up selling for $1,458,000. Mr. Smith and Ms. Timlin did put an offer in on the “honeytrap” home in Brockton Village, bidding $100,000 over the listing price of $1,199,000, but the property eventually went to someone who bid more than $350,000 over asking. That left the three-plus-one semi in Seaton Village, which they loved for its character – the home was built in 1908 – and its backyard, which Mr. Smith likened to a secret garden. They figured the creaky floors and bedroom door would be easy fixes for Mr. Smith to tackle.

They decided to offer $1,360,000 on the home, eventually settling on a final price of $1,385,000. “I was surprised,” Ms. Timlin says of their offer being accepted. “We had only been actively seeing properties for two and a half weeks, so it was very early. But we felt really excited.” The couple moved into their new home at the end of June and have made a few improvements since then: installing some new light fixtures, fixing that bedroom door that didn’t close properly, and painting some walls, doors and trim. They also plan on fixing the creaky floors soon with some new, solid hardwood, as well as upgrading their HVAC system.

“I’m really ecoconscious,” says Mr. Smith. “We want to put in a heat pump and a high-efficiency furnace and water heater.” They’re also getting ready for the arrival of their new baby, who is due on Nov. 8. “The baby room is pretty much ready,” Ms. Timlin says. While they weren’t familiar with Seaton Village before their house hunt, they’re happy to discover that it’s a family-friendly, community-minded neighbourhood.

Their purchase also came in time for Mr. Smith’s father, who had been in the hospital recently, to enjoy a meal at their new home before he sadly passed away 10 days later. “He thought it was a good house,” Mr. Smith explains. “It was quite sentimental that he could come and just have a hamburger on the back patio. He was really proud of us to have made this choice for our family.”

stories.title: Canada at a ‘crucial time,’ Carney says after speaking with incoming Quebec premier
stories.summary: Carney and Quebec’s incoming opposition party leaders pledge to work with the sovereigntist Parti Québécois as it prepares to form a minority government
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec’s incoming opposition party leaders pledged Tuesday to work with the sovereigntist Parti Québécois as it prepares to form a government with a minority mandate.

On his way into a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney told reporters he spoke with Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon after Monday’s provincial election.

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to call an independence referendum in his first term, but not until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in 2029.

Carney called it a “crucial time” for the country, and said it’s important to focus on the now – not issues that are years into the future.

“This is a crucial time for our country, it’s a crucial time for Quebec,” he said. “This is not a time to wait for something a few years down the road. It’s a time to act. It’s a time for boldness.”

Carney said being bold was what his own government has been doing, including on promoting affordable housing, big projects such as the Churchill Falls energy agreement with Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, and support for workers affected by American tariffs.

Carney said he and the PQ leader discussed some of those issues, including infrastructure funding and support for Quebec workers hurt by the U.S. trade war .

St-Pierre Plamondon told supporters in Montreal he will work with Quebec’s English speakers and with Carney when it serves Quebeckers.

Parti Québécois candidates were elected in 59 ridings in Monday’s election, falling five seats short of the 64 needed for a majority government.

While the party had strong support across much of Quebec, it had its weakest level of support in the province’s two largest cities where the Liberals and Conservatives largely dominated. While the PQ failed to win a single riding in the Quebec City region, it won only two seats on the Island of Montreal.

Quebec’s opposition party leaders also said they were open to working with the new government, but made it clear that their support has limits.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, whose party finished with 40 seats, said the election results show that Quebeckers want the parties to work together. He said he was open to collaborating on issues such as health care and support for families and businesses, but that none of his members would support a referendum.

“It’s not worth crossing the room to come see us, because for us, it’s no,” he said.

Milliard said St-Pierre Plamondon would likely seek support for his referendum among the members of left-wing sovereigntist party Québec solitaire, which won nine seats.

The Quebec Liberal leader also invited the Coalition Avenir Québec’s defeated candidates and volunteers on Tuesday to rally to his side.

“If you want to continue to move Quebec forward within Canada, come over to us,” he said.

Québec solitaire co-spokespersons Ruba Ghazal and Sol Zanetti indicated Tuesday that they would work to grow support for independence, but said it was important that the public be on board.

“If there is a single condition for independence, it is that the population wants it,” Ghazal said.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, who will soon be leading a 19-member caucus, following a historic breakthrough, said his party would fulfill its promise to act as a “watchdog” for taxpayers. St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to call an independence referendum in his first term, but not until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in 2029.
Carney called it a “crucial time” for the country, and said it’s important to focus on the now – not issues that are years into the future.
“This is a crucial time for our country, it’s a crucial time for Quebec,” he said. “This is not a time to wait for something a few years down the road. It’s a time to act. It’s a time for boldness.”

Carney said being bold was what his own government has been doing, including on promoting affordable housing, big projects such as the Churchill Falls energy agreement with Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, and support for workers affected by American tariffs.
Carney said he and the PQ leader discussed some of those issues, including infrastructure funding and support for Quebec workers hurt by the U.S. trade war .

stories.title: Expert insight: How ‘technoference’ can disrupt parent‑child connections
stories.summary: What is parental technoference? New research finds parents distracted by devices are more likely to miss young children’s signals.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
Have you ever been telling someone a story when their phone lights up, and their eyes flicker toward their device?

Maybe they check the notification or they send a quick reply. Although the interruption only lasts a few seconds, the conversation, and your connection, has been disrupted.

There’s a name for these small, everyday technology-related interruptions that disrupt in-person interactions: “technoference.”

What happens when the person seeking the attention is a small child, and the person looking at their screen is their parent? In our new research, we wanted to see what actually happens when technology interrupts parent-child interactions.

Screens on phones, tablets and smart watches are now part of everyday life, and technoference is common. One study from the United States found that 89 per cent of parents report that digital devices interrupt interactions with their children at least once a day.

Another recent study from the U.S. found that parents spent an average of five hours a day on their phones while they were with their babies.

Babies and young children often share their feelings and ideas using looks, sounds, gestures and words as they learn about themselves and the world around them. It’s best for their learning and development when adults respond quickly to these signals.

When a parent is distracted by a device, it can interrupt these important moments of connection.

That doesn’t mean that parents need to put away their phones whenever their children are nearby; that would be unrealistic for most. Parents use technology to work, connect with family and friends, make appointments, schedule play dates, find information and manage family logistics.

Screens can both connect and disconnect families, depending on when and how they are used.

Much of what we know about parental technoference came from studies where parents are asked to report how often it happened. Self-reports are valuable, but it can be difficult to remember every time we glance at our phones.

We wanted to see in real time how parents might be unintentionally distracted by technology during play time.

We invited parents and their 13- to 18-month-old children to the university to participate in a research study. As part of their visit, we recorded parents and children while they were playing with books and toys. We then told parents about the recording and asked if they were willing to give permission for us to use these observations. Parents also reported information about their child’s language development, including the words their children understand and say.

We found that in the moments when parents checked their phones or smart watches, they were almost six times more likely to miss their children’s signals.

Greater observed technoference was also associated with children producing and knowing fewer words.

These findings could suggest that the parents’ observed technoference reflects cumulative missed opportunities to notice and respond to their child and shape language learning.

Over time, repeated interruptions could mean a child is having fewer opportunities to learn new words.

This May hinder children’s future development, as children’s vocabulary in the early years is also a building block for later communication and school readiness.

Much of the research on screens and children have tended to focus on children’s screen time. However, our findings suggest that we should also be thinking about the technology used by the adults around them – an idea reflected in the most recent screen time guidelines from child development experts.

An occasional digital interruption is unlikely to define a child’s development. Children benefit from warm, caring interactions that happen repeatedly over time. What May matter more is when technology repeatedly competes for a parent’s attention during opportunities for connection.

The goal then isn’t for parents to be screen-free, but rather to protect some time that can be free from digital disruptions. Putting devices away during meal, story and play time, a walk to the park or taking the train to grandpa’s house can create predictable opportunities for parent and children to focus on each other, and to connect.

The challenge isn’t to eliminate technology, but to be thoughtful about when we let it interrupt us.Image 1: The Conversation

Gizem Keskin, Postdoctoral Researcher, Determinants of Child Development Lab (Dcdl) at the Department of Psychology, University of Calgary; Penny Pexman, Professor of Psychology, Western University, and Sheri Madigan, Professor, Canada Research Chair in Determinants of Child Development, Owerko Centre at the Alberta Children’s Hospital Research Institute, University of Calgary.

stories.title: In ‘Tenzing,’ the Everest-scaling Sherpa Tenzing Norgay finally gets the spotlight
stories.summary: Toronto (AP) — The first image ever taken of a human being standing atop Mount Everest was of Tenzing Norgay.
stories.author: Jake Coyle The Associated Press
stories.content:
Toronto (AP) — The first image ever taken of a human being standing atop Mount Everest was of Tenzing Norgay.

When he and Edmund Hillary reached the summit of the world’s highest mountain on May 29, 1953 , one of the first things Hillary did was take out his camera and aim it at his fellow climber, the Sherpa Norgay, as he waved an ice ax tied with flags for Britain, India, Nepal and the United Nations.

Since that moment, camera lenses have seldom been pointed at Norgay, or the many Sherpa who have followed in his history-making footsteps. But the new Apple Studios film “Tenzing,” directed by Jennifer Peedom, puts Norgay back in the center of the frame, telling the life story of the Nepalese-Indian Sherpa mountaineer.

“Tenzing’s story is the ultimate underdog heroic story but had been pushed to the margins,” Peedom says. “Everest occupied such a large part of our imaginations. It’s become this icon of human achievement, yet the story of one of the first men to climb to the summit was largely unknown.”

“Tenzing,” which opens Friday in theaters before streaming Oct. 16 on Apple TV+, chronicles Norgay’s path leading up to Everest and the daring ascent that he and Hillary (played by Tom Hiddleston) made in 1953. Both were outsiders — Norgay was born in Tibet before moving to the Khumbu region of Nepal — in a British expedition led by Col. John Hunt (Willem Dafoe).

The film is a rousing mountain adventure and biopic but one made with uncommon authenticity. Tenzing’s son Norbu Tenzing is an executive producer. Cultural consultants Dr. Lhakpa Norbu Sherpa and Dr. Nima Namgyal Sherpa were leaned on. Most of the Sherpas portrayed in the film are played by real mountaineering Tibetan people.

And Norgay, a role shared across time frames, is principally played by Genden Phuntsok, a Chinese actor of Tibetan descent. Phuntsok had appeared in two acclaimed films by the Tibetan filmmaker Pema Tseden. But “Tenzing” is his first Hollywood film. To prepare for the role, he lived for 10 days with Phurba Tashi Sherpa, the subject of Peedom’s 2015 documentary “Sherpa.”

“From the top of the hill outside his village, you can see the top of Everest,” Phuntsok says. “All the people in the village were really kind to me. For them, Tenzing Norgay is their hero.”

Hiddleston’s Hillary takes a supporting role

Hiddleston plays Hillary, the New Zealand climber, with the kind of dashing charisma that many Hollywood productions would have put front and center. Instead, “Tenzing,” about an international expedition, itself became an operation of multiculturalism. At the center is the friendship between Norgay and Hillary, a relationship forged on the southeast ridge of Everest and that continued after their ascent.

For Phuntsok and Hiddleston, making “Tenzing” was likewise a partnership.

“Genden and I saw Everest with our own eyes for the first time at the same time,” Hiddleston says. “Jennifer’s insistence and inspiration was for us to trek as far as we could toward base camp when we started.”

For Peedom, the terrain was familiar. The Australian filmmaker has spent much of her career as a documentarian shedding light on the Sherpa, including “Sherpa,” about the avalanche in the Khumbu Icefall that killed 16 Nepali mountain workers. “Being a young camera operator, I’d notice the extent to which the Sherpa were written out of the story or would end up on the cutting room floor,” Peedom says.

“I hope the film stands as a testament to the beauty of Nepal and the beauty of the culture there, and reminds us of our delicate balance with nature,” he adds.

That balance was tragically felt in August when a deadly flood tore through a Himalayan river valley in Nepal. The destruction, in which at least 1,400 people were killed, was set off by a 2,000-foot-wide (609.6-meter-wide) chunk of ice that broke off a mountain glacier due to the effects of climate change.

Last month, Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah addressed the U.N. General Assembly , noting that Nepal, where electricity is overwhelmingly generated from hydropower, has contributed less than one-tenth of 1% of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. He called it “not just a local tragedy, but a warning to the world.”

As Peedom has screened “Tenzing” at fall festivals, she has reminded viewers of the tragedy in Nepal, and the possibility of more like it to come.

“Those mountains are starting to crumble,” Peedom says. “There are 15,000 glaciers alone in Nepal, 1,500 of them have glacier lakes in front of them. When those things collapse, there’s going to be more and more of these catastrophes.”

Meanwhile, record numbers of climbers ascend Everest. After China closed the ascent route from Tibet, numbers swelled on the Nepal side. Kami Rita Sherpa , a renowned guide who has summited the mountain more than 30 times, urged authorities to limit the endless stream of climbers on Everest. In May, a record 274 climbers reached the summit in a single day.

Since that moment, camera lenses have seldom been pointed at Norgay, or the many Sherpa who have followed in his history-making footsteps. But the new Apple Studios film “Tenzing,” directed by Jennifer Peedom, puts Norgay back in the center of the frame, telling the life story of the Nepalese-Indian Sherpa mountaineer.

“Tenzing’s story is the ultimate underdog heroic story but had been pushed to the margins,” Peedom says. “Everest occupied such a large part of our imaginations. It’s become this icon of human achievement, yet the story of one of the first men to climb to the summit was largely unknown.”

“Tenzing,” which opens Friday in theaters before streaming Oct. 16 on Apple TV+, chronicles Norgay’s path leading up to Everest and the daring ascent that he and Hillary (played by Tom Hiddleston) made in 1953. Both were outsiders — Norgay was born in Tibet before moving to the Khumbu region of Nepal — in a British expedition led by Col. John Hunt (Willem Dafoe).

The film is a rousing mountain adventure and biopic but one made with uncommon authenticity. Tenzing’s son Norbu Tenzing is an executive producer. Cultural consultants Dr. Lhakpa Norbu Sherpa and Dr. Nima Namgyal Sherpa were leaned on. Most of the Sherpas portrayed in the film are played by real mountaineering Tibetan people.

And Norgay, a role shared across time frames, is principally played by Genden Phuntsok, a Chinese actor of Tibetan descent. stories.title: Christine Fréchette resigns as Coalition Avenir Québec leader after election loss
stories.summary: Resignation comes after the CAQ was wiped off the map in Monday’s election, losing every one of its 79 seats
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Outgoing Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette says she is leaving politics with her head held high despite a crushing defeat in Monday’s provincial election.

She told reporters she had resigned as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec Tuesday afternoon, less than a day after her party failed to win any seats.

“I accept Quebeckers’ decision and take responsibility for the results,” she said at a news conference in Quebec City. “Serving Quebec has been the greatest honour of my life.”

The CAQ, founded in 2011, was in power for eight years in Quebec and held 79 seats in the provincial legislature before Fréchette triggered the election campaign in August. But the Parti Québécois capitalized on voters’ desire for change, winning enough seats in the election to form a minority government.

Fréchette said she would remain as premier until the premier-designate, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, is sworn in.

Fréchette spent about six months as premier, after replacing François Legault as leader of the CAQ in April. Legault had stepped down in January after the party tanked in the polls.

But Fréchette attempted to breathe new life into the party, and seemed to gain some momentum by claiming her governing party was best placed to weather the effects of American tariffs. A few days before the campaign was launched, polls suggested her party neck-and-neck with the PQ.

Throughout the campaign, she also said that Quebeckers needed the Caq’s approach as a so-called “autonomist” party, suggesting it was allowing the province to make more gains by shunning the old labels of federalists and sovereigntists. She championed the party as being “nationalist, economic and pragmatic.”

But the approach opened her up to criticism from her rivals who noted how she had repeatedly declined to say how she would vote if there was another referendum on sovereignty. Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, whose party made historic gains, repeatedly accused her of being a closet separatist. Fréchette had previously worked as a staffer for the PQ.

“I remain deeply convinced that the third way is the right way for Quebec,” Fréchette said. “When it comes to defending and promoting Quebec’s interests, we must do so in our own name, by ourselves, for ourselves.”

The CAQ had also been mired in scandals throughout its second mandate, from major investments into failing projects to massive cost overruns for the digitization of government services. Fréchette acknowledged that her party struggled to shake off that baggage.

Legault defended Fréchette’s efforts on social media, saying she has been “a competent minister and premier.”

“She showed a great deal of courage during this election campaign. She is not responsible for the ‘wear and tear of power’ that affects all governments,” he wrote.

Fréchette was first elected under the Caq’s banner in 2022. She served as immigration minister before taking over the energy and economy portfolio.

She is the first woman to serve as premier since PQ leader Pauline Marois, who won a minority government in 2012. Fréchette said she hopes her short time in office will open the door to more women in political leadership roles.

“Quebec was led by women for a total of 25 months in 159 years,” Fréchette said. “It’s too little.”

Experts are divided on whether the CAQ can survive after being wiped off the political map following a vote that handed the sovereigntist Parti Québécois a minority government.

Thierry Giasson, a political-science professor at Université Laval, says many Quebeckers still believe in the Caq’s core autonomist position.

“It could survive because there are people who believe in this idea of a third way, who have championed it, and who will likely want to ensure that it survive,” he said.

His colleague André Bodet agrees, saying the PQ was also expected to disappear after the last election.

“The Coalition Avenir Québec is not a fringe party in Quebec politics; on the contrary, it has governed for two terms,” he said. “Today’s electorate is primarily looking for charismatic leaders.”

But Martin Papillon, a political-science professor at Université de Montréal, points out that Legault did not have the same deep historical roots. Without a single seat, the party is fragile, he adds.

“It will become very difficult for that party to survive, especially since it is a coalition of people who have or had political ties elsewhere and who May return to their former parties, just as voters have decided to do,” he said.

The CAQ has 30 days to name an interim leader. A spokesperson for the party said meetings will be held in the next few days to determine next steps.

stories.title: GM confirms end of light-duty Silverado in Oshawa, boost heavy-duty truck output
stories.summary: Employment levels expected to stay the same, company spokesperson says
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
General Motors Co. GM-N is set to end production of the light-duty Chevrolet Silverado 1500 pickup at its plant in Oshawa, Ont., in November, and replace the volume by boosting output of the heavy-duty Silverado as the automaker retools the plant to make the GMC Sierra HD by 2028.

The Detroit-based automaker announced the $144-million investment to make the GMC Sierra HD in Oshawa after recent collective bargaining talks in August with Unifor, which represents 1,800 workers at the factory east of Toronto.

GM spokesperson Jennifer Wright confirmed Silverado 1500 production will stop in November but declined to say when GMC Sierra HD output will begin. Employment levels will stay the same with the loss of the Silverado 1500, Ms. Wright said.

Jeff Gray, president of Unifor Local 222, which represents workers at the plant, said the new GMC truck will be produced in Oshawa by late 2028.

Mr. Gray said he has not heard of any coming job losses. “The company has indicated to us there will be no change of volume in the plant, but that’s always subject to change, right?” he said by phone.

The factory currently makes the light-duty Silverado and its larger cousin, the Silverado HD. The GMC Sierra HD is much the same as the Silverado HD, with different trim and options.

“We felt that just building the Chevrolet Silverado HD wouldn’t give us enough volume to maintain two shifts. So that’s why when we went into negotiations in August, we fought for the GMC truck in our plant,” Mr. Gray said, “so that having those two trucks, the GMC HD and the Chevy Silverado HD will give us that volume to maintain two shifts.”

Total production at the plant in 2026 is expected to be 114,000 trucks, nearly evenly split between the light- and heavy-duty Silverado models, said Sam Fiorani, vice-president of global vehicle forecasting at Pennsylvania-based AutoForecast Solutions.

He expects Sierra output to be about 40,000 in the first year of production.

Ms. Wright said the automaker does not disclose production volumes.

GM last year announced plans to increase employment and production of the Silverado 1500 at its factory in Fort Wayne, Ind., eliminating one shift – about 500 jobs – in Oshawa. GM plants in Pontiac, Mich., and Silao, Mexico, also make the Silverado, which was 2025’s second-best-selling vehicle in the U.S., according to Automotive News and Cox Automotive, behind only the Ford F-150 pickup.

“The union’s position has always been that they’re moving the 50,000 units of light duty a year to Fort Wayne for political purposes to appease Donald Trump,” Mr. Gray said.

GM has also announced a $215-million investment at its propulsion plant in St. Catharines, Ont., that will make the factory the sole source for new transmissions.

Similarly, Ford Motor Co. F-N concluded its recent labour talks with the announcement it will spend US$500-million at its Essex, Ont., engine factory and US$400-million at its Oakville, Ont., Super Duty pick-up assembly plant. Production at long-idled plant is expected to begin this month, Mr. Fiorani said. Ford did not respond to e-mailed questions.

The United States has imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on the non-U.S. content of Canadian-made cars in what Mr. Trump has said is an attempt to restore domestic manufacturing while weakening Canada’s economy. The tariff is scheduled to rise to 50 per cent by Jan. 1 and include auto parts. Canada has responded with similar tariffs, with exceptions based on a car company’s Canadian production.

About 90 per cent of the cars produced at Ontario’s plants are shipped to the U.S.

The trade war has hit Ontario’s auto sector hard, with GM idling its electric van plant in Ingersoll and Stellantis NV in talks to sell its Brampton factory, which has not made a car since 2023.

Mr. Fiorani noted Ford’s Oakville investment announcement was made before Mr. Trump ratcheted up his tariff threat to 50 per cent, but said the trucks have a high U.S. content that makes eating the U.S. tariffs on the popular trucks a bit easier for Ford.

“Ford needs Super Duties,” he said. “It’s a very profitable vehicle and their [U.S.] plants that build them rely on overtime, so adding another plant to alleviate some of that pressure is important here,” he said. And GM is counting on continued strong sales of GMC trucks in Canada, thus avoiding U.S. tariffs, he said.

Like GM, Ford is investing in Canadian plants for several years down the road, he said.

“These investments take years to implement and a decade or more to pay off. So it’s very rare that an investment in a plant will disappear shortly after it’s announced or any investment is made. Automotive manufacturers need to look long term, and it goes beyond one administration on the U.S. side or Canadian side,” Mr. Fiorani said. “And that’s good news for Canadians.”

Still, Greig Mordue, an engineering professor at McMaster University whose specialties include automaking, said investment announcements made by automakers during collective bargaining talks often get abandoned. Such spending is a management prerogative, not a labour decision, he said, pointing to commitments made and reversed in recent years by the Detroit Three.

These include Stellantis’s commitment to build cars in Brampton, GM’s van plant in Ingersoll and Ford in Oakville, where the automaker abandoned plans to retool to make electric vehicles.

stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Winning a minority government with just 28 per cent of the vote puts the Parti Québécois in uncharted territory.

“It’s exceptional; we’ve never seen that in Quebec, certainly, that a party can win enough seats to form government with such low numbers,” said Daniel Béland, a professor of political science at McGill University.

“It’s a relatively strong minority government, in a sense. But we know that minority governments have a lower life expectancy.”

Monday’s outcome means the separatist PQ likely won’t be pushing for a referendum on leaving Canada any time soon, say political watchers.

The party won 59 of the National Assembly’s 127 seats and will need support from some members of the three opposition parties to reach 64 votes and get legislation passed.

The PQ held just seven seats when the writ dropped.

Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, or Pspp as he is known, has said he will wait to hold a referendum on Quebec independence until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in January 2029.

“Considering the average life expectancy of a minority government in Quebec, or even in Canada in general, it’s not sure (the PQ will still be in office when Trump makes his exit),” Béland said. “And that’s an issue that will be front of mind” for the governing party.

“The minority government renders a referendum on independence much less likely,” said André Lecours, a political scientist at the University of Ottawa.

Sébastien Dallaire, chief insights officer with Leger Marketing, agreed that we’re unlikely to “see a push for a referendum, especially not in the near future.”

Would it be possible “to create the winning conditions in the current context?” Dallaire said. “Right now, it looks unlikely.”

It wouldn’t be “impossible,” for the PQ to “pull the trigger on a referendum with the support of the Québec Solidaire,” Béland said.

“But Québec Solidaire and the PQ, although they both support the independence of Quebec, they don’t see the process leading to independence in the same way.”

Dallaire pointed out that about half of those who voted for Québec Solidaire “are not in favour of sovereignty.”

It would “likely be very hard for Québec Solidaire to convince their voters and their base that now is the time to go into a referendum period,” Dallaire said.

“It would be very tricky for Québec Solidaire to form a formal alliance with the PQ to push for a referendum.”

Québec Solidaire won nine seats Monday, compared to 11 in the last election.

“Québec Solidaire is a left-wing party, they’re pro-immigration, they are critical” of Quebec’s Bill 21, Béland said, while the PQ wants to “double down” on the provincial law enforcing state secularism that prohibits some public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols at work.

“These are very different political animals, these two parties, so in some areas they could collaborate. But in other areas the most logical dance partner for the PQ minority government would be the Conservatives.”

Conservatives jumped from zero seats in 2022 to 19 on Monday.

“Conservatives could push the PQ even further to the right in terms of tax cuts and spending cuts,” Béland said.

“Because it’s a minority government Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will have to, as we say in French, put some water in his wine to compromise in order to get things done, in order to pass a budget.”

The Conservatives could prove “quite influential,” Béland said. “Because it’s unlikely that the official opposition, the Liberals, will collaborate that much with the PQ.”

The Liberals jumped from 19 seats to 40 in Monday’s election.

“They were able to regain a lot of their old strongholds” in the Outaouais, Montreal’s South Shore and Lavalle, said Lecours, pointing out they also took a Quebec City riding.

“They’re starting to make some headway in Francophone Quebec,” he said.

Under the leadership of Christine Fréchette, the Coalition Avenir Québec — which formed a majority government in 2022 with 90 seats under former Premier François Legault — was reduced to zero seats.

The CAQ had “a horrible night” on Monday, Dallaire said.

The “complete wipeout” is unheard of “for a party that had a super majority,” he said. “Is there a tomorrow for the CAQ? That’s a question that a lot of people are asking today.”

Conservatives May well replace the CAQ as an alternative to the Liberals and the PQ, who have dominated since the 1970s, Dallaire said.

“Could the Conservatives now really establish themselves as the third option? That’s the hope after the win (Monday) night. We’ll see how things evolve in coming months.”

He expects a “rocky political environment” as the National Assembly is flooded with “rookies.”

“Close to 80 per cent of MNAs are new in this assembly,” Dallaire said. “So, it’s going to be a lot of learning and it’s going to be learning on the fly in a minority government situation where you need to collaborate and you need to compromise.”
