stories.title: Exports to the U.S. spiked in August before Trump’s 50% tariffs: StatCan
stories.summary: Canadian exports to the U.S. surged 8.1 per cent in August, just before a new round of 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods hit at the end of the month, according to StatCan.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canadian exports to the U.S. surged 8.1 per cent in August, just before a new round of 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods hit at the end of the month, according to Statistics Canada.

Some economists say this was largely because of tariff “front-running,” when businesses try to get as much product out the door as possible before tariffs take effect.

The agency released the balance of trade report for August on Tuesday, and Canada’s trade surplus with the U.S. — which happens when an economy exports more than it imports — nearly doubled from $6.1 billion in July to $11.2 billion in August, as imports from the U.S. fell 2.5 per cent.

This also marked the largest positive monthly change in Canada’s trade balance with the U.S. ever documented, Statistics Canada says.

U.S. President Donald Trump threatened Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of goods, and focusing on what his administration considered trade irritants, including automotive, alcohol and dairy industries.

Those tariffs took effect on Aug. 22.

Although Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar counter-tariff measures in September, the data released by Statistics Canada Tuesday does not take into account trade data beyond August.

“The strength in exports in August was tied largely to the front-running of U.S. tariffs that came into effect late in the month,” said senior economist Katherine Judge at Cibc in a statement, adding: “That means that the spike in exports is temporary and will ease in September.”

Statistics Canada also suggested some businesses May have had a sense of urgency in August, saying, “The announcement of tariffs May influence trade patterns and prompt importers to increase shipments before the tariffs take effect in order to avoid additional costs.”

Canada’s total exports to all countries increased 2.5 per cent in August compared to July, while imports fell two per cent. Meanwhile, Canada had a trade surplus with the world for the sixth straight month, and topped $4.2 billion in August, up from $787 million in July.

Energy products as a sector made up more than a quarter of the increase in all exports in August, driven by diesel fuel sales to countries including the U.S., as well as Peru, the U.K. and the Netherlands. The increase in export values for the category, Statistics Canada says, was not only because of demand but also that prices for petroleum based energy products are up more than 50 per cent year-over-year.

Consumer goods exports also increased by 6.6 per cent, with a more than 43 per cent increase in exports of miscellaneous goods and supplies. More specifically, this was driven mainly by shipments of gold and silver coins to the U.S., Statistics Canada says, and adds that many other goods within the category were targeted by new U.S. tariffs.

Statistics Canada also says miscellaneous consumer goods May include personal care items, including hair dryers and electric shavers, toiletries and cosmetics, as well as personal effect items, including jewelry and watches.

11:30 Ottawa and Washington relationship ‘the worst in modern history’: Ex-US Ambassador to Canada

Canada also sent about 10 per cent more industrial machinery, equipment and parts to international customers, which was the highest monthly amount since January 2025. That was mainly because of higher exports to the U.S., with customers buying more general-purpose machinery and equipment, as well as heating, cooling and air purification equipment.

New U.S. tariffs introduced in August also targeted imports of Canadian electronic and electrical equipment and parts, and that category saw exports rise 11 per cent in August. Statistics Canada says although some of those U.S. tariffs were removed in September, exports to the U.S. in August “significantly contributed to the increase in the month.”

“Some U.S. buyers clearly rushed to import ahead of new tariffs imposed on Aug. 22nd on another [approximately] five per cent of U.S. imports from Canada — and that boost will reverse in September,” said Nathan Janzen, assistant chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada in a statement.

“We continue to expect the new tariffs imposed by the U.S. administration will have a significant impact on directly targeted sectors.”

Canadian exports to countries other than the U.S. fell 8.5 per cent in August, and after reaching a record high in July. Statistics Canada says that’s mainly because August saw a sharp drop in comparable sales and shipments of unwrought gold to the U.K., energy products to the Netherlands, and aircraft and crude oil to France.

Overall, 30.2 per cent of all Canadian exports were sent to countries other than the U.S. in August, down from 33.9 per cent in July.

stories.title: Canadian Stellantis workers to hold strike vote as auto talks stall, union says
stories.summary: Unifor walked away from bargaining after automaker confirmed plans to sell Brampton plant to defence contractor
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Unifor says it will hold a strike authorization vote for its Stellantis NV Stla-N workers as contract talks are stalled over the automaker’s plans to sell its idled car plant in Brampton, Ont.

The union, which represents 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada, walked away from collective bargaining on Sept. 11 after the automaker confirmed it has a preliminary agreement to sell the Brampton plant to Roshel , a defence contractor that makes armoured vehicles.

The plant northwest of Toronto closed for retooling in 2023, and Stellantis moved planned production of the Jeep Compass to Belvidere, Ill., last year after the United States imposed tariffs on Canadian-made cars.

The strike vote will take place on Oct. 17 and 18, and the results will be made public on Oct. 19, Unifor said on Tuesday. A majority vote for a strike would give the union executive the option to use as leverage work stoppages at Stellantis’s minivan plant in Windsor and parts plant in Toronto.

“Strike action remains a last resort, but the ability to strike is an important part of collective bargaining and can help create the conditions for an agreement,” Unifor said in a statement.

The union said the issues unresolved at the table include job security for all Stellantis workers and the future of all the automaker’s Canadian operations.

Stellantis said on Sept. 11 it has a memorandum of understanding to sell the plant to Brampton-based Roshel.

“Stellantis believes that Roshel represents a strong path to restoring sustainable operations at Brampton assembly, preserving the site’s strategic role in Canada’s advanced manufacturing sector and helping to avoid a prolonged period of inactivity,” Stellantis said at the time.

The automaker cited “changing market and trade conditions” as the impetus for the sale. Since 2025, the U.S. has imposed tariffs of 25 per cent on Canadian-made cars.

The Stellantis plant, which employed more than 3,000 people when it closed for retooling in 2023, still has about 2,200 people on layoff.

The federal government has said any sale would put Stellantis in violation of a funding agreement that saw the company receive millions of taxpayer dollars to retool the plant.

stories.title: U.S. police arrest suspect from Washington state in connection with Tumbler Ridge shooting
stories.summary: A 30-year-old allegedly conspired with the shooter to murder people in the B.C. town and broadcast the killings online
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The teenager who perpetrated the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., spent at least six months planning for maximum carnage aided by a conspirator in Washington State who allegedly provided advice, money and technical assistance, U.S. and Canadian law enforcement officials said Tuesday.

Representatives from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation and the B.C. RCMP announced the developments at a joint news conference in Seattle, revealing for the first time that authorities had been investigating a second suspect in connection with the February attack.

James Cody Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, was arrested by U.S. authorities Tuesday and is alleged to have conspired with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, to execute the killings and broadcast them over the internet for the public to view, the officials said.

The arrest is the latest chapter in one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history, which left eight victims dead, including six children, and devastated the small mining community in northeastern B.C. Its aftermath has been far-reaching, triggering lawsuits, scrutiny of Canada’s firearms oversight and a cross-border reckoning over the lax regulations that govern technology giants when credible threats arise.

At least 37 lawsuits have been filed against OpenAI in California in connection with the shooting, after it was revealed that the shooter had queried the tech giant’s ChatGPT chatbot about gun violence scenarios in June, 2025.

B.C. RCMP, who have been working with the FBI, are continuing their criminal investigation in the province and have signalled a possibility of pursuing further charges in Canada.

Mike Herrington, special agent in charge of the Fbi’s Seattle office, said the accused “enabled” the shooter and agreed to livestream the attack to “maximize notoriety.”

“I read a lot of court documents, including some that discuss incredibly heinous acts of violence,” he said. “But this complaint was particularly difficult to read, in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned.”

Special Agent Herrington said it was his understanding that the alleged conspirator, like the shooter, “identifies as female.”

Ms. Bryant’s next court appearance is Oct. 13 in U.S. District Court in Seattle, where a judge will determine whether she can be released pending trial.

The teen shooter killed her mother and half-brother at their family home on Feb. 10 before proceeding to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School, where she killed five students and an educational assistant. She then turned a gun on herself.

The news conference, paired with a federal criminal complaint filed in U.S. District Court, provide a disturbing window into the pair’s friendship and the months they allegedly spent planning the attack. The allegations have not been tested in court.

Officials said Ms. Van Rootselaar and Ms. Bryant are believed to have met about three years ago on Omegle, a once-popular website that randomly paired users for one-on-one text or video conversations. The website, which shut down in November, 2023, was free to use and did not require an account or registration.

The two continued to stay in touch on other platforms, including Discord, which allows users to chat via text, voice and video.

About six months before the attack, “Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she had stolen guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and was hiding them in her room in preparation for a mass shooting,” according to the court document. “Van Rootselaar also said she convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf.”

According to the accused, Ms. Van Rootselaar was “fixated on mass shootings and watched livestreamed recordings of past shootings to learn from them,” the document said. She asked Ms. Bryant to livestream her planned attack and Ms. Bryant agreed.

Police announce that a 30-year-old from Washington state has been charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in connection with the February mass shooting that left eight victims dead in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.

The two discussed possible locations, with the shooter wanting one that would “lead to the largest number of victims.” The accused said it would be a “bad idea to attack a school because there would be too many young victims” and suggested instead a grocery store or church.

The accused is also alleged to have provided money to the shooter to purchase items for use during the attack, including the shoes she intended to wear, a lighter to ignite an explosive device and stickers to decorate the firearms. They tested the livestream at least twice, once in August, 2025, and again in January, 2026.

“They spoke daily during the six months prior to the Tumbler Ridge school shooting,” said the court document, which sets out the facts supporting the charge.

The day of the attack, the shooter told Ms. Bryant over Discord that she would commit the murders that day. She sent photographs showing that she was wearing the shoes that the accused had purchased and had a cellphone holster attached to a chest rig for the livestream.

Canadian officers later found that, shortly before opening fire, Ms. Van Rootselaar logged into her Twitch account and began a livestream, the document said. The video, which lasted for about 20 seconds, depicted the shooter sitting in a vehicle with a rifle and a separate long gun in her lap.

The accused told Ms. Van Rootselaar that the livestream was “coming through” but that it went “down” shortly after.

Michelle Kramer, a Discord spokesperson, said Tuesday that the company undertook an investigation to identify any related activity immediately following news of the mass shooting. Within hours, an account believed to be associated with the shooter was identified along with private messages.

Ms. Kramer said communications about the shooting were confined to direct one-on-one messages; none were identified through a public Discord server or through group direct messages. There were no user reports related to the event, she added.

“Once we were confident in the shooter’s identity and the associated account, our team conducted a thorough human review of all related direct messaging content,” Ms. Kramer said.

“Following our investigation, we proactively disclosed relevant information to law enforcement agencies and removed the suspect’s account for violating our policies.”

Discord declined to provide details on how many messages were shared in total between the two and if any other accounts were flagged to the authorities.

Twitch spokesperson Megan Kay said the platform does not comment on active legal matters but is co-operating with law enforcement. The company has “invested heavily in machine learning tools that detect content that could contain graphic violence,” she said in an e-mailed statement.

When asked if investigators believe Ms. Van Rootselaar was chatting with other people about her plans, U.S. officers said they are still assessing the totality of those communications via social media.

Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain, acting commanding officer for the B.C. RCMP, said Tuesday that as part of the force’s probe into the attack, investigators in the province have completed and reviewed more than 90 interview statements from students, educators and first responders. Digital and physical evidence has been collected and processed.

“Our focus remains on supporting the ongoing criminal proceedings in Washington State and continuing our close cooperation with the FBI,” he said. “Our RCMP criminal investigation remains ongoing, and the possibility of further charges being pursued in Canada remains under active consideration.”

B.C. Attorney-General Niki Sharma told media that the “chilling and disturbing” details revealed on Tuesday have left her with a lot of questions. She said artificial intelligence and chat sites should be properly regulated but would not say whether the B.C. government will sue other online platforms, such as Discord, named in the indictment.

stories.title: Ontario refers private career college Osap concerns to OPP
stories.summary: Referal comes after a provincial audit raised ‘serious concerns’ about three career colleges
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario has referred the issue of Student Financial Assistance payments at private career colleges to the provincial police after preliminary audit findings identified “serious concerns,” the government said Tuesday.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said in a statement that the ministry launched targeted inspections of career colleges last year in response to growing concerns about Ontario Student Assistance Program usage and in August had Kpmg begin an audit.

“While that work is ongoing, preliminary findings have identified serious concerns about the integrity of the Osap system in the private postsecondary sector,” he wrote.

“These include common ownership, the involvement of immigration services firms and co-location between private career colleges and immigration recruitment or immigration services firms, inadequate student validation and verification of course enrolment and outcomes, and unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations.”

As a result, the government notified the Auditor-General last week and has also referred this matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, Quinn wrote.

The Canadian Press has reported that the total of provincial grants sent to students at just seven career colleges in 2024-25 was about $385-million, the same amount that went to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges.

Court records show that Career Colleges Ontario, an association representing the sector and the body that processes their students’ Osap applications, has been warning the province about possible “suspicious” Osap activity for years, dating back to January, 2023.

At the same time, the government has paused all Osap payments for career college students while the audit is ongoing.

It has thrown the entire sector into uncertainty.

The ministry often approves which schools can accept Osap funding over the summer, but news of the pause Tuesday came as the academic year is already well under way.

Career Colleges Ontario said the approval delays are causing significant disruption for schools, which have to make operational decisions without clear information or timelines, and for students who don’t know if they can afford to start – or remain in – classes.

“We hope the government will introduce a policy that promptly addresses improper conduct and targets those who have acted wrongly,” the association wrote in a statement.

“Career Colleges Ontario was instrumental in bringing these concerns forward to the government in the first place, and it is not fair that students across the sector who have done nothing wrong are now being impacted as a result.”

The sector-wide delays are affecting not just schools that Career Colleges Ontario raised concerns about, but also schools such as Mothercraft, which has been offering early childhood education programs for decades and has a “stellar” compliance record, said executive director Michele Lupa.

“We’re still waiting to hear if we continue to be an eligible institution for Osap,” Lupa said in an interview.

“So, needless to say, that’s a little concerning. We’re six weeks into the academic year, and we have students who are relying on Osap to be able to carry out their studies. So they’re getting anxious, needless to say, and we are too.”

Mothercraft graduates about 125 new ECEs every year, and those graduates are especially critical at a time when the child-care sector is trying to expand under the national affordable child-care program, Lupa said.

Also in high demand at the moment are dental hygienists, and first-semester student Daliah Gardoque’s program at the Toronto College of Dental Hygiene and Auxiliaries is in Osap limbo, too.

“It’s extremely stressful,” said Gardoque, who started an online petition asking the ministry to “urgently address the ongoing uncertainty.”

“I’m privileged enough to have a decent amount of savings, but that’s only to keep me afloat until the end of first semester. So after that, I wouldn’t really know what I’m going to do. But a lot of people are right now not focused on their exams just because they’re thinking like, ‘Is there any point?’ Because if Osap doesn’t come in the next month, they might as well drop out.”

stories.title: How early morning classes affect Fanshawe College students
stories.summary: Many Fanshawe College students start their day with early morning classes, but having a lack of sleep with ear...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
Many Fanshawe College students start their day with early morning classes, but having a lack of sleep with early classes May affect students’ focus and attendance.

“I prefer not to attend the morning class if it is not important. I try to skip it and save my energy for the other classes,” said Fanshawe student Kulvir Multani.

“Not on everyday basis, but if I am, I’m sleeping late at night or I have some late activities to do,” she said.

Multani said she doesn’t sleep well because she has to think about waking up early.

“Whenever I have a morning class, I always think at night oh I have to get up early at so-and-so time and I cannot sleep well. That’s why I feel lazy in the morning, and that’s why I think I get late to the classes,” she said.

Multani said that catching the bus makes it difficult to make it to class on time.

“Definitely getting up and preparing for the classes, reaching to the busses or on time. And in the winters, it will get like worse and worse,” she said.

She said that 12 p.m. would be the perfect time for her.

“I prefer to start classes from 12, I guess. So that will be perfect for me,” she said.

A 2017 McGill University study found that students with earlier start times got less sleep and were more likely to feel tired in the morning. The findings raise questions about how early classes May affect Fanshawe student’s sleep, concentration and ability to stay focused throughout the school day.

The study said that 9:30 a.m. start times would be more beneficial to students because it gives them an opportunity to get more sleep in order to focus better.

“Real life people have to go to work sometimes earlier than 9 a.m., so one thing I try to do is encourage them to make sure they’re getting to bed earlier, and getting up in good time, and eating breakfast,” said Nancy French, pre-media and dual credit professor.

French’s earliest class is 9 a.m. and she finds that the time of day does affect students’ concentration.

“I do notice that more students come in for the 9 o’clock class tired and more disengaged than they do for say an 11 o’clock class,” she said.

stories.title: Feds create new Crown corporation 'to move with urgency' on defence procurement
stories.summary: The Carney government announced Tuesday that it will create a new crown corporation for defence procurement.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Carney government announced Tuesday that it will create a new Crown corporation for defence procurement, the latest new wing of the federal bureaucracy at a time of public service cuts.

Ottawa said it will create new legislation to turn its Defence Investment Agency (DIA), created as a stand-alone organization within a federal department only a year ago, into a Crown corporation so that it will have a permanent structure and a clearer mandate and reporting path. That will make the organization, which is to operate at arm’s length to the Department of National Defence, better able to make quick decisions and reduce “fragmentation.”

“We need to move with urgency,” Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters.

Five months earlier, the government created the DIA and gave it considerable procurement authority, saying the move would mean improved consolidation and efficiency and would better allow Ottawa to tie its military purchases to Canadian industry.

Government officials said Tuesday that the new Crown corporation will mean that it will be easier to recruit experts and structure contracts so that they’re more like private sector purchases and offer taxpayers better value. The new structure will also mean the organization will be more independent to manage investments and procurement, although the government will still advise and provide oversight.

Officials emphasized the importance of buying Canadian and helping the domestic defence industry gaining greater access to capital. “We have a limited tool kit,” said one official.

Under the model for the new Crown corporation, DND and the Canadian Armed Forces will continue to define Canada’s military needs and priorities, while the Crown corporation will be responsible for procurement, production and investment.

Beyond the creation of the new Canadian Corporation for Defence Investment, the move will also mean the creation of a new cabinet post, the associate minister of national defence for procurement. The organization would also have its own board of directors, chief executive, employees and annual plan.

It’s not the Carney government’s first attempt to make the government more nimble by setting up new structures that don’t have to follow all of the usual public service processes. The government also established a new Major Projects Office last year to make decisions on infrastructure and other key project investments quicker.

But at the same time, the government is reducing the size of the federal bureaucracy, in part to deal with its massive deficit and to pay for new spending on priority matters, such as defence.

The new Crown corporation is also the Carney government’s latest effort to overhaul Canada’s defence, in the wake of both economic and sovereignty threats from U.S. President Donald Trump.

The government has dramatically boosted spending, including on soldiers’ wages, and invested in new technology.

In February, Carney also launched Canada’s first Defence Industrial Strategy (DIS) , a long-term plan to strengthen national security and economic growth by supporting Canada’s defence industry. The government says it’s already made strides on that front, through new partnerships and purchases, such as deals to buy new modular assault rifles from Colt Canada and the selection of Saab as the preferred supplier for early warning and control systems for remote regions. Traditionally, procurement at DND has been slow.

The Canadian Army also announced this week that it has adopted a new structure to strengthen defence and readiness. The new structure includes four primary formations: the 1st Canadian Division in Edmonton, the 2nd Canadian Division in Montréal, a Canadian Army Support Division in Kingston, Ont. and a Canadian Army Doctrine and Training Centre, also in Kingston.

The government also announced Tuesday that McGuinty will visit Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Edmonton on Wednesday with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to “highlight” defence investments.

stories.title: Separation is unpopular in Quebec. Why did the province elect sovereigntists?
stories.summary: Quebecers chose a new government on Monday, handing the Parti Québécois (PQ) minority power in the province’s legislature, raising questions about why a sovereigntist party was elected when polling shows little interest in separating from Canada.
stories.author: Jordan Fleguel
stories.content:
Quebecers chose a new government on Monday, handing the Parti Québécois (PQ) minority power in the province’s legislature, raising questions about why a sovereigntist party was elected when polling shows little interest in separating from Canada.

“I think for now, Quebecers wanted a divided government,” David Heurtel, political analyst and former Quebec cabinet minister, told CTV News Channel on Tuesday.

“They wanted to give the PQ a minority government, and I think right now, what Quebecers want most is to deal with the priorities, the same priorities you see across Canada.”

Quebec’s premier-designate, PQ Leader Paul-St Pierre Plamondon has said that his party will work towards holding a third Quebec sovereignty referendum, but that he will wait until U.S. President Donald Trump has left office .

Minority saves province from ‘fraught territory’

That timeline keeps a referendum off the table for the next two years, by which point Plamondon May no longer be in charge, Heurtel said, noting that minority governments typically only last between 18 and 24 months.

“It’s, for most Quebecers, a big sigh of relief that (the PQ) didn’t get a majority, because then we would have been in some very fraught territory,” Tom Mulcair, CTV News’ political commentator and former federal NDP leader told CTV News Channel Tuesday.

“The fact that they were held to a minority came as a surprise to the PQ but not to those of us who kept our eyes on one number, which was 70 per cent. That’s the percentage of Quebecers that didn’t want another referendum,” he said.

Heurtel made the same observation, noting that even as the PQ surged in the polls during the campaign, “support for sovereignty has not wavered.”

5 takeways from Quebec election as Parti Québécois forms minority government

“Seventy per cent of Quebecers, including 63 per cent of Francophones, do not want a referendum and do not want independence,” said Heurtel.

Mulcair argued that while the PQ’s overarching separatist message was attractive to some voters in Quebec, Plamondon’s campaign mainly revolved around a promise to govern differently than the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which formed majority governments in 2018 and 2022.

Even Plamondon said in the final stretch of the campaign that the election was going to be about who Quebecers trusted most to lead them through the turbulent economic and political times ahead.

“It’s not totally accurate to say that this election is only about whether we would hold a referendum in three years from now,” Plamondon told Cjad, The Canadian Press reported .

“It’s about changing or not changing a government that has catastrophic results in many areas of our society and choosing who could do a good job and who could be reliable in terms of what they do and what they say.”

Collapse of the CAQ

Despite the PQ’s victory, the party received just 28 per cent of the total number of votes cast on Monday, and it has very little representation in the province’s largest urban centres of Montreal and Quebec City.

The collapse of the (CAQ), which failed to win any seats in the legislature, helped other parties gain ground as well. The provincial Liberals maintained opposition status after receiving 24 per cent of the popular vote, while the provincial Conservatives got roughly 21 per cent.

While both parties have said they would not support a referendum, Quebec’s other sovereigntist party, Québec solidaire, won enough seats in the legislature to form a majority with the PQ.

“They’ve got nine seats, so they could support the PQ if it decides to go ahead with the referendum bill, but there’s a lot of differences; they don’t get along very well on the political level,” said Heurtel.

Another important aspect of the political landscape in Quebec to keep in mind, Heurtel argued, is the current popularity of the prime minister.

“So, it’s not like you have that dichotomy with a Justin Trudeau, a Stephen Harper, or even a Jean Chrétien. The dynamic is completely different, and Quebecers don’t have an appetite… for a referendum.”

“It’s, for most Quebecers, a big sigh of relief that (the PQ) didn’t get a majority, because then we would have been in some very fraught territory,” Tom Mulcair, CTV News’ political commentator and former federal NDP leader told CTV News Channel Tuesday.

“The fact that they were held to a minority came as a surprise to the PQ but not to those of us who kept our eyes on one number, which was 70 per cent. That’s the percentage of Quebecers that didn’t want another referendum,” he said.
Heurtel made the same observation, noting that even as the PQ surged in the polls during the campaign, “support for sovereignty has not wavered.”
5 takeways from Quebec election as Parti Québécois forms minority government
“Seventy per cent of Quebecers, including 63 per cent of Francophones, do not want a referendum and do not want independence,” said Heurtel.

Mulcair argued that while the PQ’s overarching separatist message was attractive to some voters in Quebec, Plamondon’s campaign mainly revolved around a promise to govern differently than the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which formed majority governments in 2018 and 2022.
Even Plamondon said in the final stretch of the campaign that the election was going to be about who Quebecers trusted most to lead them through the turbulent economic and political times ahead.
“It’s not totally accurate to say that this election is only about whether we would hold a referendum in three years from now,” Plamondon told Cjad, The Canadian Press reported .

“It’s about changing or not changing a government that has catastrophic results in many areas of our society and choosing who could do a good job and who could be reliable in terms of what they do and what they say.”
Collapse of the CAQ

Despite the PQ’s victory, the party received just 28 per cent of the total number of votes cast on Monday, and it has very little representation in the province’s largest urban centres of Montreal and Quebec City.

The collapse of the (CAQ), which failed to win any seats in the legislature, helped other parties gain ground as well. The provincial Liberals maintained opposition status after receiving 24 per cent of the popular vote, while the provincial Conservatives got roughly 21 per cent.
While both parties have said they would not support a referendum, Quebec’s other sovereigntist party, Québec solidaire, won enough seats in the legislature to form a majority with the PQ.

“They’ve got nine seats, so they could support the PQ if it decides to go ahead with the referendum bill, but there’s a lot of differences; they don’t get along very well on the political level,” said Heurtel.
Another important aspect of the political landscape in Quebec to keep in mind, Heurtel argued, is the current popularity of the prime minister.

“So, it’s not like you have that dichotomy with a Justin Trudeau, a Stephen Harper, or even a Jean Chrétien. The dynamic is completely different, and Quebecers don’t have an appetite… for a referendum.”

stories.title: Can the Coalition Avenir Québec survive with no elected officials?
stories.summary: Montreal - The Coalition Avenir Québec did not win a single seat at the provincial legislature in Monday's election after eight years in power.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Outgoing Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette says she is leaving politics with her head held high despite a crushing defeat in Monday’s provincial election.

She told reporters she had resigned as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec on Tuesday afternoon, less than a day after her party failed to win any seats.

“I accept Quebecers’ decision and take responsibility for the results,” she said at a news conference in Quebec City. “Serving Quebec has been the greatest honour of my life.”

The CAQ, founded in 2011, was in power for eight years in Quebec and held 79 seats in the provincial legislature before Fréchette triggered the election campaign in August. But the Parti Québécois capitalized on voters’ desire for change, winning enough seats in the election to form a minority government.

Fréchette said she would remain as premier until the premier-designate, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, is sworn in.

Fréchette spent about six months as premier, after replacing François Legault as leader of the CAQ in April. Legault had stepped down in January after the party tanked in the polls.

But Fréchette attempted to breathe new life into the party, and seemed to gain some momentum by claiming her governing party was best placed to weather the effects of American tariffs. A few days before the campaign was launched, polls suggested her party neck-and-neck with the PQ.

Throughout the campaign, she also said that Quebecers needed the Caq’s approach as a so-called “autonomist” party, suggesting it was allowing the province to make more gains by shunning the old labels of federalists and sovereigntists. She championed the party as being “nationalist, economic and pragmatic.”

But the approach opened her up to criticism from her rivals who noted how she had repeatedly declined to say how she would vote if there was another referendum on sovereignty. Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, whose party made historic gains, repeatedly accused her of being a closet separatist. Fréchette had previously worked as a staffer for the PQ.

“I remain deeply convinced that the third way is the right way for Quebec,” Fréchette said. “When it comes to defending and promoting Quebec’s interests, we must do so in our own name, by ourselves, for ourselves.”

The CAQ had also been mired in scandals throughout its second mandate, from major investments into failing projects to massive cost overruns for the digitization of government services. Fréchette acknowledged that her party struggled to shake off that baggage.

Legault defended Fréchette’s efforts on social media, saying she has been “a competent minister and premier.”

“She showed a great deal of courage during this election campaign. She is not responsible for the ‘wear and tear of power’ that affects all governments,” he wrote.

Fréchette was first elected under the Caq’s banner in 2022. She served as immigration minister before taking over the energy and economy portfolio.

She is the first woman to serve as premier since PQ leader Pauline Marois, who won a minority government in 2012. Fréchette said she hopes her short time in office will open the door to more women in political leadership roles.

“Quebec was led by women for a total of 25 months in 159 years,” Fréchette said. “It’s too little.”

Experts are divided on whether the CAQ can survive after being wiped off the political map following a vote that handed the sovereigntist Parti Québécois a minority government.

Thierry Giasson, a political science professor at Université Laval, says many Quebecers still believe in the Caq’s core autonomist position.

“It could survive because there are people who believe in this idea of a third way, who have championed it, and who will likely want to ensure that it survive,” he said.

His colleague André Bodet agrees, saying the PQ was also expected to disappear after the last election.

“The Coalition Avenir Québec is not a fringe party in Quebec politics; on the contrary, it has governed for two terms,” he said. “Today’s electorate is primarily looking for charismatic leaders.”

But Martin Papillon, a political science professor at Université de Montréal, points out that Legault did not have the same deep historical roots. Without a single seat, the party is fragile, he adds.

“It will become very difficult for that party to survive, especially since it is a coalition of people who have or had political ties elsewhere and who May return to their former parties, just as voters have decided to do,” he said.

The CAQ has 30 days to name an interim leader. A spokesperson for the party said meetings will be held in the next few days to determine next steps.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

— With files from Pierre St-Arnaud in Montreal

stories.title: Abrupt end to murder trial after accused pleads guilty to manslaughter
stories.summary: The jury at the second-degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott heard about a week and a half of testimony before the Crown and defence lawyers reached a resolution in the case on Tuesday morning.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The jury at the second-degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott heard about a week and a half of testimony before the Crown and defence lawyers reached a resolution in the case on Tuesday morning.

Crown Attorney Kristina Mildred told Justice Patricia Moore, “The Crown will indicate for the record there has been additional evidence not heard by the court that relates to the issue of self-defence...particularly with reference to threats and possession of a firearm by the deceased.”

Last week during the trial, the jury watched video surveillance footage of the killing with the accused pulling up to the coffee shop in a silver Chevy and shooting Clements-Card. The victim would be rushed to hospital where he would later be pronounced dead.

McDermott who was 18 at the time of the shooting, has spent more than 8 years in custody with much of it being at the Maplehurst Detention Centre in Milton.

As the guilty plea was entered the family and friends of Clements-Card were not present in the body of the courtroom. The jury was then called in and were dismissed from the trial.

The case has been adjourned until Wednesday and that’s when a sentencing hearing will be held for McDermott.

stories.title: Ontario emerges as preferred site to build Saab GlobalEye military surveillance plane, sources say
stories.summary: Plane maker prefers factory near Toronto’s Pearson over Dorval, Que., but possible provincial subsidies could ultimately sway decision, sources said
stories.author: Eric Reguly
stories.content:
Bombardier BBD-B-T is aiming to secure a production site for the Saab GlobalEye military surveillance plane by the new year and favours expanding its existing factory near Toronto’s Pearson airport, sources say.

The Montreal aerospace company prefers Pearson largely because its Global 6500 business jet – the airframe for the radar-equipped GlobalEye – is already built there, the sources said.

Saab, Sweden’s biggest aerospace firm, last year said it could build the GlobalEye and its Gripen fighter jet in Canada for both Canadian and overseas customers. Because Saab’s domestic factories lack the capacity to meet demand for both aircraft, the company offered Bombardier the opportunity to build either plane under licence, a scenario that would create thousands of defence-related aerospace jobs in Canada.

But the size of the subsidies that May be offered by either the Ontario or Quebec governments could ultimately determine whether the military aircraft is assembled at Pearson or in Dorval, Que., near Montreal, where smaller Bombardier business jets are made, the sources said.

They said Bombardier hopes to begin construction of an expanded factory in 2027.

The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the negotiations.

Bombardier’s chief executive Éric Martel told The Globe in September that the “GlobalEye is our priority right now,” adding that the company is “focused on building and finishing GlobalEye here in Canada.”

Bombardier CEO Éric Martel sees opportunity for the company in defence as their business jets are adapted to be military platforms. Speaking at a Globe and Mail event, Mr. Martel says Bombardier’s successful partnership with Saab to make the GlobalEye surveillance plane is a sign of their capabilities.

The Globe and Mail

A Bombardier team was in Sweden last month. More recently, another Bombardier team met with senior Ontario government officials to discuss possible subsidies to expand the Pearson assembly site. The sources said Bombardier put the expansion costs at about $500-million. Bombardier’s communications office did not comment on the cost of the expansion.

Late last year, Saab delivered new proposals to Ottawa that forecast the creation of 12,600 jobs if both the GlobalEye and the Gripen were built in Canada. At the time, David Morden, senior sales director of the GlobalEye, said building the entire aircraft in Canada would create 3,000 jobs. “We are offering a made-in-Canada solution by building and installing the plane’s sensors there,” he said.

Mattias Radstrom, head of media relations at Saab, told The Globe on Tuesday that “we stand by our previous estimate” for the number of jobs created.

Saab selected the Bombardier 6000-series business jet, which later evolved into the 6500-series, for the platform for the GlobalEye a decade ago. The plane, minus its interior fittings, is flown to Saab’s main aerospace factory in Linköping, Sweden, where it is stripped down and rebuilt into an airborne early warning and control jet with an array of sophisticated sensors.

Its radar is capable of detecting aircraft, missiles or drones as far as 650 kilometres away. It can also detect and identify objects on the ground, such as tanks, and those on the sea, including submarine periscopes that break the water surface.

So far, Saab has firm orders for a dozen GlobalEyes, mostly from the United Arab Emirates, Sweden and France, but expects many more. They can take the forms of performance-contingent loans, grants, tax credits, research and development support, or a combination. Often the federal government contributes similar amounts. On big projects, Ontario’s contributions can cover 10 to 20 per cent of the projects’ overall capital costs.

stories.title: Martel returns to Conservative caucus, joins the Tory Senate group
stories.summary: Ottawa — Quebec Sen. Richard Martel is back in the opposition caucus after joining the Conservative Senate group today.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Quebec Sen. Richard Martel is back in the opposition caucus after joining the Conservative Senate group today.

Sen. Leo Housakos, the opposition leader in the Senate, says Martel is a “natural fit” in a statement issued today.

Martel left the House of Commons in July when Prime Minister Mark Carney appointed him to the Senate but had not identified which Senate group he would sit with until now.

Martel says he is happy to be joining his Conservative colleagues in the Senate and looks forward to getting to work on the national security, defence and veterans affairs committee.

Martel’s resignation triggered a byelection in his former riding of Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, which the Liberals won in August, increasing their majority in the House of Commons.

All incoming senators join the Upper Chamber as independents, typically joining one of the Senate groups a few weeks after they begin their term.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Breaking: U.S. resident arrested in connection with Tumbler Ridge shooting
stories.summary: A 30-year-old Washington State resident has been arrested on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.
stories.author: Kim Bolan, Stephanie Ip
stories.content:
Seattle — Chilling details of the moments leading up to the devastating Tumbler Ridge shooting were released for the first time on Tuesday, as U.S. and B.C. law enforcement officials announced that a Bellingham resident has been arrested in connection with the attack.

Killer Jesse Van Rootselaar sent a photo of herself “prepared for the attack” to James Cody Bryant, a 30-year-old transgender woman now charged with conspiracy to commit murder, law enforcement officials alleged. The pair had been communicating for months about the logistics of the attack, including what to use, “how to increase the carnage,” and technical aspects of livestreaming the event, officials said.

On Feb. 10, 2026, Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother and half-brother at home before making her way to Tumbler Ridge Secondary. There, she entered the school and opened fire, killing four students and an educational assistant, and wounding several more, before turning the gun on herself.

In a news conference Tuesday in Seattle, officials described finding evidence of communications between Van Rootselaar and an individual in Bellingham, Wash.

U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd, FBI Special Agent W. Mike Herrington and B.C. RCMP Asst. Commissioner Elija Rain alleged Bryant had been communicating with Van Rootselaar on the Discord online platform during the summer of 2025 and continued to do so until the day of the attack.

Floyd called the school shooting “a horrific tragedy” made more disturbing because “a resident of Western Washington had a role in the attack and took steps — providing counsel, technical advice, and money to the shooter planning such a tragedy.”

Rain said the co-operation and expertise from his U.S. counterparts was “invaluable in advancing the work across jurisdictions and ensuring that all available evidence could be thoroughly examined.”

Bryant made a brief appearance in U.S. district court on Tuesday afternoon dressed in what appeared to be pyjama bottoms and a black jacket. The case was held over to Oct. 13.

Revelations about how ChatGPT helped Tumbler Ridge shooter proves need for new criminal law: B.C. attorney general

B.C. launches lawsuit against OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge mass shooting

Details about the connection between the two are further described in a 41-page criminal complaint that has been reviewed by Postmedia.

The documents allege the pair met sometime before 2023 on a video chat platform called Omegle and had stayed in touch. The now-defunct platform randomly pairs users in video chats, and had come under fire for becoming an online network frequented by those participating in the sexual exploitation of minors.

After securing search warrants, investigators combed through the pair’s “thousands” of Discord messages. The online platform co-operated with police, providing details of two Van Rootselaar accounts and another linked to Bryant.

The two casually “discussed preparation and co-ordination relating to the shooting in Discord direct messages from November 2025 to Feb. 10, 2026,” the complaint alleged. “These conversations included discussions about weapons, theft of ammunition, incendiary device construction, target evaluation, logistics relating to livestreaming the attack, and final day-of co-ordination.”

In the messages, “Bryant agreed to record and broadcast Van Rootselaar’s livestream of the murders.” Officials also allege Bryant provided “tactical advice on how to increase the carnage and what firearms to use.”

On Jan. 4, 2026, Bryant assisted Van Rootselaar “in conducting a test run of the livestream,” the complaint alleged. Bryant then sent Van Rootselaar $14.33 through PayPal on Jan. 25 to buy a lighter to be affixed to an explosive device. She also discussed with the killer “the need to conceal the murder conspiracy” by deleting messages and using a virtual private network, or VPN.

“In various conversations between August (2025) and the February (2026) shooting, Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of doing the attack. But ultimately, Bryant did not contact law enforcement and agreed to handle the livestreaming just minutes before the attack,” according to the complaint.

On the day of the shooting, Van Rootselaar sent a photo of herself “prepared for the attack” and asked Bryant if the livestream was ready, according to the criminal complaint, which was filed in U.S. district court.

“R you ready with my twitch account pulled up?” Van Rootselaar messaged Bryant, to which Bryant responded, “Yeah.”

“I’m going now. Fr. Live. I shot them,” Van Rootselaar said after killing her mother and sibling, the complaint alleged. The livestream lasted 20 seconds, before it went down. The complaint said the brief video “showed Van Rootselaar sitting in a vehicle with a rifle and another long gun in her lap.”

It said when Van Rootselaar, who didn’t know how to drive, struggled to start the family car, Bryant told her to hold the start button in.

“Van Rootselaar successfully started the car. A neighbour observed Van Rootselaar crash the car into a snowbank and then regain control,” the complaint said. “Van Rootselaar proceeded to drive to the Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she committed the murders.”

U.S. agents interviewed Bryant just two days after the attack and confirmed “they had been communicating with Van Rootselaar during the months before the murders and had viewed Van Rootselaar’s attempted livestream of the attack.”

Investigators also learned that about six months before the murders, “Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she had stolen guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and was hiding them in her room in preparation for a mass shooting,” the complaint alleged.

“Van Rootselaar also said she convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf. Van Rootselaar told Bryant about the types of guns and accessories she possessed, including a 3D-printed foregrip, firearm magazines, and a ‘switch’ for the SKS (likely referring to a machine-gun conversion device). According to Bryant, Van Rootselaar ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

Bryant told U.S. agents that “Van Rootselaar was fixated on mass shootings and watched livestreamed recordings of past shootings to learn from them. Van Rootselaar wanted to livestream her planned mass shooting,” the complaint said.

The two discussed possible targets for a mass shooting with Van Rootselaar suggesting a school and Bryant instead saying a grocery store or a church would be better.

“Bryant gave Van Rootselaar tactical advice regarding the carrying out of the attack, including that ‘wide open spaces’ are conducive to more casualties. Van Rootselaar should be armed with a handgun, among other weapons, and Van Rootselaar should make a functional suicide vest instead of a fake vest,” the court document alleged.

Officials said Tuesday there was no specific ideology that bonded the two individuals or motivated the shooting but that the messages exchanged between the pair focused on “an intense desire for the shooting to receive that sort of notoriety.”

Bryant remained in custody on Tuesday. Officials say court proceedings will remain in Washington state, as Bryant’s activities were in that jurisdiction.

The victims of the Tumbler Ridge shooting include Emmett Jacobs, 11, and Jennifer Jacobs, 39, who were killed inside Van Rootselaar’s home, and Ezekiel Schofield, 13, Abel Mwansa, Kylie Smith, Zoey Benoit, Ticaria Lampert, all 12, and Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39, who were killed inside the school.

The shooting turned international attention onto the small community in northeastern B.C., and has spawned two separate lawsuits against OpenAI. It is alleged that Van Rootselaar used the artificial intelligence platform to research firearms and plan logistics about how to stage a school shooting.

One lawsuit was filed this fall by the B.C. government , with the goal of securing stronger regulations on AI after the company revealed that it had spotted red flags about Van Rootselaar’s online activity but did not flag it for police leading up to the shooting.

Earlier in the spring, Tumbler Ridge community members and family members of the victims also filed a lawsuit in California court against OpenAI and its founder Sam Altman for negligence and failing to take action that could have prevented the shooting.

“I’m going now. Fr. Live. I shot them,” Van Rootselaar said after killing her mother and sibling, the complaint alleged. The livestream lasted 20 seconds, before it went down. The complaint said the brief video “showed Van Rootselaar sitting in a vehicle with a rifle and another long gun in her lap.”
It said when Van Rootselaar, who didn’t know how to drive, struggled to start the family car, Bryant told her to hold the start button in.

“Van Rootselaar successfully started the car. A neighbour observed Van Rootselaar crash the car into a snowbank and then regain control,” the complaint said. “Van Rootselaar proceeded to drive to the Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she committed the murders.”

U.S. agents interviewed Bryant just two days after the attack and confirmed “they had been communicating with Van Rootselaar during the months before the murders and had viewed Van Rootselaar’s attempted livestream of the attack.”

Investigators also learned that about six months before the murders, “Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she had stolen guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and was hiding them in her room in preparation for a mass shooting,” the complaint alleged.

“Van Rootselaar also said she convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf. Van Rootselaar told Bryant about the types of guns and accessories she possessed, including a 3D-printed foregrip, firearm magazines, and a ‘switch’ for the SKS (likely referring to a machine-gun conversion device). According to Bryant, Van Rootselaar ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

Bryant told U.S. agents that “Van Rootselaar was fixated on mass shootings and watched livestreamed recordings of past shootings to learn from them. Van Rootselaar wanted to livestream her planned mass shooting,” the complaint said.
The two discussed possible targets for a mass shooting with Van Rootselaar suggesting a school and Bryant instead saying a grocery store or a church would be better.

“Bryant gave Van Rootselaar tactical advice regarding the carrying out of the attack, including that ‘wide open spaces’ are conducive to more casualties. Van Rootselaar should be armed with a handgun, among other weapons, and Van Rootselaar should make a functional suicide vest instead of a fake vest,” the court document alleged.

Officials said Tuesday there was no specific ideology that bonded the two individuals or motivated the shooting but that the messages exchanged between the pair focused on “an intense desire for the shooting to receive that sort of notoriety.”
Bryant remained in custody on Tuesday. Officials say court proceedings will remain in Washington state, as Bryant’s activities were in that jurisdiction.

The victims of the Tumbler Ridge shooting include Emmett Jacobs, 11, and Jennifer Jacobs, 39, who were killed inside Van Rootselaar’s home, and Ezekiel Schofield, 13, Abel Mwansa, Kylie Smith, Zoey Benoit, Ticaria Lampert, all 12, and Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39, who were killed inside the school.

The shooting turned international attention onto the small community in northeastern B.C., and has spawned two separate lawsuits against OpenAI. It is alleged that Van Rootselaar used the artificial intelligence platform to research firearms and plan logistics about how to stage a school shooting.

One lawsuit was filed this fall by the B.C. government , with the goal of securing stronger regulations on AI after the company revealed that it had spotted red flags about Van Rootselaar’s online activity but did not flag it for police leading up to the shooting.

Earlier in the spring, Tumbler Ridge community members and family members of the victims also filed a lawsuit in California court against OpenAI and its founder Sam Altman for negligence and failing to take action that could have prevented the shooting.

stories.title: Alberta separatist leaders see Quebec premier-designate Plamondon as an ally
stories.summary: Edmonton - Leading figures in the push for Alberta separation are celebrating the election of Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - Leading figures in the push for Alberta separation are celebrating the election of Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Jeff Rath said Tuesday that St-Pierre Plamondon’s election victory could change the political dynamic of Canada, especially since the premier-designate has already shown willingness to support Alberta’s separatist movement.

“For the first time in Canadian history we have a government in Quebec that supports Alberta independence,” Rath said in an interview.

“That’s huge.”

St-Pierre Plamondon and the separatist Parti Québécois are set to form a minority government after Monday’s election in Quebec, which saw the governing Coalition Avenir Québec wiped from the assembly.

The premier-designate has pledged to hold what would be Quebec’s third separation referendum, but he’s said it won’t happen until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office.

During a visit to Calgary last year, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would recognize an independent Alberta should the province vote to separate.

Rath said he had met with the Parti Québécois leader in Calgary. He said the pair, who are both lawyers, talked for three hours over dinner and have maintained contact.

“I’ve gotten to know him relatively well over the last year. I think people are going to be very surprised at how well he governs,” Rath said.

Corey Morgan, an online commentator and separatist advertiser in the upcoming Alberta referendum, also said the premier-designate was an ally and that his victory bodes well for Alberta’s movement.

“I believe it’s in the interest of independence movements on both sides of the country to … maintain pressure and instability on the federal system,” Morgan said.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on whether they want to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on quitting Canada.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the vote earlier this year, citing two competing petitions on either side of the separation debate that each received hundreds of thousands of signatures. Smith has said she supports Alberta staying in Canada and that she will vote accordingly.

Smith congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon on Monday in a social media post, saying she’s looking forward to working with his government.

“Our provinces and our country are stronger when we work together, stand united and build a stronger future for all Canadians,” Smith wrote.

Smith didn’t address the issue of separation in her congratulatory note, nor did Prime Minister Mark Carney in his own social media post.

Morgan said he thought the two leaders were ignoring the elephant in the room.

“People are kind of dodging that fact that, whether you like it or not, even if that wasn’t the prime driver in this provincial election, Quebec just elected an overtly separatist party to be their government,” he said.

“That’s significant, and that’s going to make a difference in policy in the next two to four years.”

Rath, a fierce critic of Smith for putting off a binding separation vote, also said he took inspiration from St-Pierre Plamondon’s path to victory.

The Parti Québécois saw much of its electoral support come from outside of Quebec’s two major cities and it managed to form government despite an overall vote share of about 28 per cent.

Rath said he thought something similar could happen in Alberta should Smith’s United Conservative Party fracture over the separation issue.

Smith has been adamant that her party, government and caucus are committed federalists, but in recent weeks the premier has seen calls for a leadership review come from two of her UCP constituency associations.

Rath said despite the premier’s assurances that the UCP isn’t a separatist party, he thinks rank-and-file members who want Alberta to go its own way represent a “supermajority” within the party.

“I think this is going to be really interesting for Alberta politics,” Rath said.

Alberta Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi congratulated St.-Pierre Plamondon in a social media post and criticized Smith’s decision to hold a referendum in Alberta.

“We particularly thank him for being clear about being a separatist and for saying it’s much too dangerous to have a referendum while Trump is in power,” Nenshi wrote.

The NDP has been campaigning in favour of a federalist vote.

“Thirteen days from Danielle Smith’s separatist referendum that no one voted for in the last election, we are reminded that while we may have our disagreements across this country, we are stronger when we face them together,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version misspelled Parti Québécois.

stories.title: Ottawa’s budget watchdog says feds need to spend $164 billion by 2035 to reach Nato target
stories.summary: The Liberal government has committed to spending five per cent of its GDP towards defence spending by 2035.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – A new report published by the Parliamentary Budget Office said the federal government will have to spend $163.6 billion in cash on core defence spending by 2035 to meet its spending pledge under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato).

The report published on Tuesday said while the Department of National Defence has increased its capital expenditures in recent years, Canada’s Nato commitments will require defence spending to increase further and remain at “substantially higher levels.”

The Liberal government has committed to spending five per cent of its GDP towards defence spending by 2035, a new spending target set by Nato allies last year.

The breakdown includes 3.5 per cent allocated for core defence spending and 1.5 per cent for ancillary spending, which includes investments in defence infrastructure. Canada only recently achieved its two per-cent spending commitment, first promised in 2014.

In May, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada will reach four per cent by 2030-31, which would mean core defence spending would rise to 2.5 per cent.

The PBO report estimates that it will require $95.7 billion by 2030 for Carney’s pledge to turn into a reality.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan said the federal government’s plan to hit its five per-cent Nato spending target seems to still be “in formation,” noting that key details are missing.

“I think it’s fair to say that the government’s plans in the next five years or over the next 10 years are still in formation,” Ryan told a House of Commons committee this week.

“I think that it is also fair to say that there remain numerous… kind of elements of that plan to be elaborated and set forth over this five-year period, let alone the 10-year period,” she added.

The federal government has been criticized for not showing its work on its defence spending plans. Budget 2025 and the spring economic update from 2026 lacked any breakdown of its defence spending projections.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told reporters more details will come on his government’s defence spending plans, although he provided no timeline.

Ryan and her colleagues confirmed that they have received a remit from the Department of National Defence, which provides a breakdown of the department’s spending, which has been used for the Pbo’s latest projections.

The PBO also noted that Nato measures spending pledges on a cash basis and the Canadian government uses accrual accounting for its financial statements and fiscal indicators.

Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash moves.

“More recent analysis by the (PBO) indicates that the difference between the cash and the accrual impacts of increased defence spending could be upwards of 30 percent per year during this period of rapid investment,” said Ryan. “In other words, borrowing requirements for these measures could be 30 percent higher than recorded in relevant deficits.”

Liberal MP Tim Watchorn listed off several recent defence-related announcements by his government in recent months, including announced investments in the Canadian Patrol Submarine Project, Arctic over-the-horizon radar, armoured combat support vehicles and the replacement of Canadian Armed Forces’ assault rifles.

Conservative members of the committee pointed out that there is a lack of details on cost breakdowns on most of those announcements and the combined investments of the proposed projects still don’t get Canada to its Nato spending targets.

The PBO said the recent spending by DND is encouraging, noting that between 2017-18 to 2023-24, the cumulative shortfall relative to the original capital spending plans was $18.5 billion. The report said more recently the gap between Dnd’s planned and actual spending has decreased.

“Public Accounts data show that expenditures under Dnd’s capital vote increased from $4.9 billion in 2022-23 to $8.8 billion in 2024-25, while lapses fell from approximately $1.0 billion to $0.2 billion,” the report said.

stories.title: Arrest in Washington state over Tumbler Ridge mass shooting
stories.summary: A 30-year-old man from Washington state has been arrested on a charge of conspiracy to murder in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The FBI says that on Feb. 10, Jesse Van Rootselaar told online friend James Cody Bryant that she had dressed for the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., that would claim the lives of eight victims that day.

An FBI complaint that recounts alleged interactions between the pair — including efforts to livestream the murders — shows a photo of someone from their shoulders down, in fishnet stockings and a black miniskirt, holding a rifle with what looks like a silencer in pink, white and blue, the colours of the transgender pride flag

U.S Investigators say a 30-year-old in Washington state gave advice and money to the Tumbler Ridge mass killer and even offered to livestream the attack on Facebook. (Oct. 6, 2026)

“A few moments later, Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she went live with the stream and had just killed her family members at their residence,” says the complaint released on Tuesday.

Minutes later, Bryant is alleged to have helped Van Rootselaar start the family car — she did not know how to drive — before the 18-year-old killer headed to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she shot dead five students and an educational assistant.

The detailed account of the killings and the months leading up to the attack is contained in the complaint filed against Bryant of Bellingham, Wash.

The FBI, the U.S. Attorney in Washington state and the RCMP announced in Seattle on Tuesday that Bryant, 30, had been charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Mike Harrington, special agent in charge with the FBI in Seattle told a news conference that Bryant enabled the shooter for months as they discussed the plan.

The claims have not been tested in court, and Bryant’s lawyer, public defender Greg Murphy, was not immediately available for comment. Bryant appeared in the U.S. District Courthouse in Seattle on Tuesday, with a detention hearing scheduled for Oct. 13.

“In the complaint, Bryant even admits to being maybe the only one who could stop the shooter,” Harrington said.

The complaint quotes extensive alleged exchanges between the two, including from August 2025 when Van Rootselaar said she wanted to surpass the 1989 École Polytechnique massacre in Montreal, which left 14 people dead, in order to complete “the deadliest school shooting in all of Canadian history.”

“If I got more than 22 it’d be simply the deadliest shooting in Canadian history period,” Van Rootselaar is quoted as saying, referring to the Nova Scotia mass murder where 22 people were killed in 2020 by a man posing as a police officer.

But she is said to have added that killing 14 people would be a “lot easier” than 22.

The conversations depicted by the FBI include Bryant repeatedly assuring Van Rootselaar that they would not “snitch,” adding in one conversation that “people die no matter what.”

The FBI says that moments before Van Rootselaar headed to the school, Bryant accessed a livestream account to record and broadcast the killings on the Twitch platform.

Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant, “I’m going now. (for real). Live. I shot them,” after killing her mother and brother at their home.

“Watching now,” Bryant allegedly responded.

Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd said the accused had the information and the ability to alert police, but instead encouraged the murders.

“Today, Bryant is in custody, charged with conspiracy to murder people in a foreign country. That charge carries a penalty of up to life in prison,” Floyd said.

Harrington said the livestream only lasted about 20 seconds, briefly showing the killer sitting in a vehicle with a rifle.

“Without Bryant’s misplaced loyalty and willingness to operate the livestream, we don’t ultimately know if the shooter would have gone through (with) the crime,” Harrington said.

He said the killer was concerned that not enough people would see the livestream without Bryant broadcasting it and was depending on it because Van Rootselaar didn’t have many followers on social media.

The complaint filed by the FBI said Bryant also gave tactical advice “on how to carry out the murders,” including suggestions on target locations, and that hallways had “a lot of ways people can escape” but “open spaces means numbers.”

The document also said Van Rootselaar threw a crude improvised explosive device in the high school and tried to get into classrooms by firing through locked doors.

Earlier chats between Van Rootselaar and Bryant suggest the shooter considered other targets before settling on Tumbler Ridge Secondary.

In a conversation dated Aug. 8, 2025, Van Rootselaar shared a map of Northern Lights College in Dawson Creek, saying it “seems to give me the best chance at getting a lot of time to shoot before the cops show up.”

The document said Bryant met Van Rootselaar about three years ago, but they fell out of contact while the killer was institutionalized after setting her room of fire.

They spoke daily in the six months before the murders, the complaint said.

Bryant — who the FBI says identifies as a women — allegedly told them that Van Rootselaar was becoming increasingly angry and suicidal.

“Van Rootselaar often spoke about planning to use guns to murder her family members and others because she felt she had been mistreated,” the court filing said.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree says it was "devastating" to see allegations that a Washington state resident had conspired with the Tumbler Ridge shooter before and after the deadly attack. MP Bob Zimmer, whose B.C. riding includes Tumbler Ridge, says the suspect's arrest is an important step toward getting answers. (Oct. 6, 2026)

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Tuesday he was informed of the pending arrest on Monday.

“It is absolutely devastating to see the allegations,” Anandasangaree said in Ottawa.

The minister was joined by B.C. Conservative MP Bob Zimmer, who represents Tumbler Ridge, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon and Conservative public safety critic Frank Caputo.

Zimmer said the allegations are “very troubling,” and while there are still many questions about why the Tumbler Ridge shooting happened, this arrest is an important step forward in getting answers.

“To me, it’s a sick individual … that would even consider this. And the result would be eight dead individuals from my community,” he said, while praising the FBI and the RCMP for the investigation.

The charges against Bryant are American, but Anandasangaree did not rule out the possibility of Canadian charges.

“RCMP is working in collaboration with the FBI, if Canadian laws as part of it were broken and based on the circumstances, there is a likelihood that an individual could also face prosecution in Canada,” he said.

The charging of Bryant comes after allegations that an AI chatbot also helped Van Rootselaar ahead of the killings.

OpenAI said shortly after the murders that it shut down the killer’s first ChatGPT account but that she opened a second account that wasn’t discovered until after the attack.

An article published by U.S. magazine Mother Jones in September said ChatGPT gave Van Rootselaar advice about how to circumvent its own safeguards by describing mass shooting scenarios in prompts as fictional or hypothetical.

The District of Tumbler Ridge said in a statement on Tuesday that it was aware of the developments released by the FBI and RCMP, but it wouldn’t not be providing further comment.

“We recognize that new information related to the events of Feb. 10 May be difficult for members of our community. Supports remain available in Tumbler Ridge for all community members,” it said.

Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd and law enforcement officials from Canada and the U.S. take questions on Tumbler Ridge arrest, Oct. 6, 2026.
