stories.title: Toronto advance voting has begun. What you should know
stories.summary: It's advance voting in Toronto with people able to go cast their vote for the mayoral race, as well as city councillors and school board trustees.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Advance voting has begun in the City of Toronto, even as Chris Alexander says he’s dropping out of the mayoral race.

From Oct. 6 to Oct. 11, Torontonians can head to their designated polling places from 10 a.m. until 7 p.m. daily to cast their vote for mayor, city councillor and school board trustees.

Many residents will have likely received their voter information card in the mail which gives the locations of both advance and election day voting locations.

But people can also check out the city’s MyVote website to confirm, add or update voters’ list information, find out polling locations, and see who their candidates are. People can also call 311 to do the same if they cannot access MyVote.

In order to vote, people must show identification that includes their name and a Toronto address.

If you plan to vote in this year’s municipal election, you must be a Canadian citizen, at least 18 and a resident in the city. Alternatively, if you aren’t a resident of Toronto, you can vote if you or your spouse own or rent property in Toronto.

Whether you own or rent one or more properties, the city stresses you can only vote once and you must vote in the ward where you live.

A person cannot vote if they are prohibited from voting under any law. This includes someone serving a sentence of imprisonment in a penal or correctional institution; a person acting as executor or trustee or in another representative capacity, except as a voting proxy; or are a corporation.

The City of Toronto requires identification to vote, but there is a wide range of ID you can bring in order to cast that ballot though it adds you cannot use your voter information card or passport as ID.

Among the acceptable forms of ID include an Ontario issued photo card such as a driver’s licence or motor vehicle permit, a bank account statement, a mortgage statement or lease agreement, or any other document from the federal, Ontario or municipal government.

Also allowed is a utility bill for hydro, any document from a Band Council in Ontario established under the Indian Act (Canada), or a document showing residence in a long-term care home issued by the home’s administrator.

A full list of acceptable ID, including electronic ID, is on the city’s voting website.

I May need help to vote, what can I do?

For voters with accessibility needs or those who are out of the city on voting day, there are still many ways you can vote including Voter Assist Terminals available at all advance voting locations and two election day locations.

If you require assistance at the voting place, you can bring a friend along or ask an election official for assistance. The city they will need to make a declaration if you want them to accompany you behind the voting screen.

Torontonians can also appoint another voter or proxy to vote on your behalf if you, for any reason, are unable to attend any of the voting days.

A proxy must be eligible to vote as well and is someone you trust and only one person can be a proxy. A voting proxy appointment form must be completed and signed by both the person and the proxy and then certified by the city clerk.

Contact the city if you have questions about accommodations at 416-338-1111 extension 6. You can also email accessibleelections@toronto.CA.

I'm working election day, can I vote?

If you can’t make advance voting and are working election day, Oct. 26, you are still entitled to time to vote. Election day polls are open from 10 a.m. until 8 p.m.

You are allowed three hours to cast your ballot, the City of Toronto says, which means you’re allowed to be absent to give yourself three hours to vote.

The city gives an example of this stating if you work 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., you are entitled to leave one hour early so you would have from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m.

People should also speak with their employer if they need time, as the city says an employer could offer you time to vote. For example, if you work 12 p.m. until 6 p.m., your employer could have you start your shift at 1 p.m. instead of leaving work at 5 p.m.

No. Torontonians had until Sept. 24 to request a vote by mail package. Those who have received their package have until 12 p.m. on Oct. 14 to return their package and they can also track the status of their package online.

When people get behind the voting screen, they’ll be casting their vote for mayor, a city councillor and school board trustees.

The ballots are in place for the election, meaning former federal cabinet minister Chris Alexander will still appear as a mayoral candidate even though he announced Tuesday he was no longer running for the role.

People can still vote for Alexander, but he will not become mayor even if you cast your vote for him. He has also not endorsed another candidate.

stories.title: Carney touts Canadian sovereignty in first comments on Parti Québécois win in Quebec
stories.summary: Carney said he spoke with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and promised to work with him towards increasing sovereignty for Canadians.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Hours after the Parti Québécois was elected to a minority government, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he spoke with premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and promised to work with him towards increasing sovereignty for Canadians.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday morning, Carney said he had just congratulated the incoming Quebec premier and discussed ways to work together in the future.

On Monday evening, Quebecers elected a minority Parti Québécois government to replace the Coalition Avenir Quebec, which was completely eradicated from the electoral map.

St-Pierre Plamondon committed to hold a referendum on Quebec’s sovereignty within his first mandate if elected, but only after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the Oval Office.

In the meantime, Carney said he wanted to extend his philosophy of “cooperative federalism” to the separatist leader and argued for the need for a “strong Quebec within a strong Canada.”

Asked if he was concerned about a Quebec referendum, Carney retorted that he too was working towards sovereignty, but for Canada.

“We take advantage of the real opportunities that exist for our country because of Canadians, because of Canadian values, because of Canadian strengths to expand our trading network and to become more sovereign in Canada,” Carney told reporters Tuesday morning.

“It’s sovereignty, but it’s Canada’s sovereignty. It’s Canada’s independence.”

St-Pierre Plamondon was elected with only 28 per cent of the vote, raising questions about if he has a legitimate mandate to hold a plebiscite on the province’s independent.

When the question was put to Carney, the prime minister simply responded with his party’s election numbers in the 2025 federal election.

stories.title: Amendments would let Manitoba cannabis stores drop window coverings for safety
stories.summary: Cannabis stores across Manitoba May soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.
stories.author: Brittany Hobson
stories.content:
Cannabis stores across Manitoba May soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.

The Manitoba government introduced amendments to the provincial Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Control Act on Monday that would eliminate window coverings on all cannabis storefronts amid safety concerns.

The province said the change would increase visibility from outside the store and help make sure workers are not hidden from public view.

Current legislation requires retailers to ensure that cannabis and cannabis products are not visible to people who are not legally allowed to purchase the products.

“We’re still mandating that the cannabis product will not be visible because we want to protect kids, and so we’re finding that balance,” said Justice Minister Matt Wiebe.

“We don’t want cannabis displayed in window fronts. We don’t want kids riding by and seeing cannabis and being enticed into trying a product that’s not appropriate for them, but at the same time we have to prioritize workers’ safety.”

Labour groups have long expressed concerns about the special problems that cannabis stores pose, because they sell a controlled substance and are required by government rules to cover all windows to the outside.

An attack on a cannabis store employee who was working alone at night in May renewed calls from unions for improved worker safety.

Police arrested a man after he allegedly entered a retail store, waiting for a customer to leave, and then locked himself inside with a woman working alone.

They said he sexually assaulted the 24-year-old, who was able to flee the store and call police.

The province is also proposing changes to the act that would allow mandatory minimum staffing levels during certain hours to ensure that workers are not alone during times when there May be a higher risk of violence.

The United Food and Commercial Workers union welcomed the province’s proposals.

It surveyed its members and non-unionized staff on worker safety concerns and found that staffing levels was one of the biggest issues.

“Loud and clear, not working alone was by far the No. 1 issue that they raised,” said Marie Buchan, secretary-treasurer of Local 832.

Wiebe said the proposed amendments would give the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Authority the ability to mandate how many employees May be on a shift at a given period.

The Opposition Progressive Conservatives said they would have to review the bill before commenting.

Other provinces, including Ontario, have scrapped similar rules around window coverings to address safety concerns expressed by employees.

stories.title: Carney says Canada at ‘crucial time’ in conversation with Quebec premier-designate
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says he spoke with Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon after the Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Monday's provincial election.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
QUÉBEC — Quebec’s premier-designate says a referendum on sovereignty is not among his immediate priorities as he focuses instead on homelessness, government spending and attempting to sever the province’s ties to the monarchy as his first acts in office.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon outlined his plans on Tuesday, one day after Quebecers chose to hand his party a minority government in the provincial legislature.

He has promised to call an independence referendum in his first term in government, but not until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in 2029.

“We’ve got time and we’ve got plenty of urgencies and problems to solve,” he said. “I think the upcoming months will be more about topics I mentioned, things that are urgent.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said his first act in government would be to organize a summit on reducing homelessness. His other priorities include freezing the salaries for legislature members and directors of Crown corporations and creating a secretariat to review government spending and bureaucracy. He also plans to name a trade team to chart a path forward in the ongoing trade war with the United States.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he’s also seeking legal advice on how to ensure the province’s lieutenant-governor doesn’t have to be present at his swearing-in ceremony. During the campaign, he pledged to defund the office and redirect the funds to fighting homelessness.

“There’s something abnormal about a foreign king coming to tell us what to do right at the start of a legislative term, a mandate,” he said. “People might say it’s symbolic, but I would reply that it’s still totally abnormal.”

St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged that he would need to work with other parties to implement his agenda in a minority legislature, and committed to meeting with each of their leaders. He also said he had a positive conversation with Prime Minister Mark Carney, in which the two discussed infrastructure, homelessness and immigration.

He said he was open to working with Carney and the provinces, “on the condition that the interests of Quebec are served and the relationship is based on respect.”

Parti Québécois candidates were elected in 59 ridings in Monday’s election, falling five seats short of the 64 needed for a majority government.

The Coalition Avenir Québec was swept out of power in a resounding defeat, failing to win a single seat after eight years in power.

On Tuesday, Christine Fréchette announced that she was stepping down as leader of her party, but would remain as premier until St-Pierre Plamondon is sworn in.

Earlier, Carney and Quebec’s incoming opposition party leaders pledged to work with the sovereigntist party as it prepares to form a government.

On his way into a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney told reporters he spoke with St-Pierre Plamondon after Monday’s election.

Carney called it a “crucial time” for the country, and said it’s important to focus on the now — not issues that are years into the future.

“This is a crucial time for our country, it’s a crucial time for Quebec,” he said. “This is not a time to wait for something a few years down the road. It’s a time to act. It’s a time for boldness.”

Carney said being bold was what his own government has been doing, including on promoting affordable housing, big projects such as the Churchill Falls energy agreement with Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, and support for workers affected by American tariffs.

Carney said he and the PQ leader discussed some of those issues, including infrastructure funding and support for Quebec workers hurt by the U.S. trade war.

While the party had strong support across much of Quebec, it had its weakest level of support in the province’s two largest cities where the Liberals and Conservatives largely dominated. While the PQ failed to win a single riding in the Quebec City region, it won only two seats on the Island of Montreal.

Quebec’s opposition party leaders also said they were open to working with the new government, but made it clear that their support has limits.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, whose party finished with 40 seats, said the election results show that Quebecers want the parties to work together. He said he was open to collaborating on issues such as health care and support for families and businesses, but that none of his members would support a referendum.

“It’s not worth crossing the room to come see us, because for us, it’s no,” he said.

Milliard said St-Pierre Plamondon would likely seek support for his referendum among the members of left-wing sovereigntist party Québec solidaire, which won nine seats.

Québec solidaire co-spokespersons Ruba Ghazal and Sol Zanetti indicated Tuesday that they would work to grow support for independence, but said it was important that the public be on board.

“If there is a single condition for independence, it is that the population wants it,” Ghazal said.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, who will soon be leading a 19-member caucus, following a historic breakthrough, said his party would fulfil its promise to act as a “watchdog” for taxpayers. However, he said he also expected to speak with St-Pierre Plamondon in the coming days to discuss areas of common interest, including eliminating taxes on used goods and reducing state spending.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Chris Alexander drops out of Toronto mayoral race
stories.summary: Former Conservative cabinet minister’s decision was made too late for his name to be removed from the ballot
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Former federal Conservative cabinet minister Chris Alexander says he is dropping out of Toronto ’s mayoral race, as polls have shown him in a distant third.

Mr. Alexander announced the move Tuesday morning at his campaign headquarters, just as advance voting in the Oct. 26 municipal election got under way across the city. His announcement was made too late for his name to be removed from the ballot.

But it appeared to clear the way for a head-to-head race between leading contenders Olivia Chow, a former NDP MP and the city’s incumbent mayor, and Brad Bradford, an east-end city councillor.

“Our path to success, it became clear to me over this weekend, was not obvious, and perhaps not there at all,” Mr. Alexander said Tuesday.

Mr. Alexander also said he is not endorsing any of the remaining candidates.

Public opinion surveys have consistently shown Mr. Alexander well behind the leaders.

A Nanos Research survey released Tuesday showed Ms. Chow at 52.4 per cent among decided voters, Mr. Bradford at 42.6, and just four per cent for Mr. Alexander, CP24 reported. The poll of 755 Torontonians was conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 4. It was commissioned by cable-news channel CP24 and CTV News Toronto. CP24 said the survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Mr. Alexander was elected a Conservative MP for Ajax-Pickering in 2011 and served as federal immigration minister in Stephen Harper’s government from 2013 to 2015. Prior to politics, he worked in the Canadian Foreign Service, including as ambassador to Afghanistan from 2003 to 2005.

Despite sagging poll numbers, he was considered a possible spoiler candidate, potentially drawing centre-right support from Mr. Bradford, whose message has focused on combatting crime and traffic congestion.

Early in the campaign, Mr. Bradford had taken a combative stance toward Mr. Alexander, saying some views he held while in federal cabinet – such as his advocacy for a “barbaric cultural practices” tip line to report incidents of honour killings, forced marriages and polygamy – made him unfit for office.

As Mr. Bradford emerged from early voting on Tuesday, he was more complimentary, appealing directly to Mr. Alexander’s supporters by drawing parallels between the two campaigns. “If you were ever in the change camp, you were always looking at our campaign,” he said.

Ms. Chow also voted on Tuesday. She thanked Mr. Alexander for bringing new ideas to the campaign, but declined to speculate on how the withdrawal might influence the race, other than saying it’s now a stark contest between two opposing visions of Toronto.

“Do we move forward and build an even more affordable and caring city, and safer city,” she asked. “Or do we go backwards to the bad old days where there’s this cut and slash and burns, and neglect of public spaces, and everything falling apart in terms of the infrastructure?”

stories.title: Shoppers to spend less this holiday season, willing to pay more for Canadian goods: PwC
stories.summary: Toronto — A new report suggests Canadians plan to spend less this holiday season compared with last year, but more than half are willing to pay more for Canadian-made products over imported options.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — A new report suggests Canadians plan to spend less this holiday season compared with last year, but more than half are willing to pay more for Canadian-made products over imported options.

The report by PwC Canada says 54 per cent of those surveyed say they would choose a more expensive Canadian-made product over a similar imported option, up from 49 per cent last year.

The shift comes as the firm’s holiday outlook report says Canadians plan to spend an average of $1,487 this holiday season, down 11 per cent from last year.

PwC added that its survey was conducted in July and early August, before the recent escalation in the trade fight with the United States, so the findings May under-represent current Canadian sentiment.

Adam Boutros, partner and national consumer markets leader at PwC Canada, says more Canadians than ever want their money to stay in Canada.

The report was based on an online survey of 1,016 respondents between July 30 and Aug. 6.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian Dental Association report calls for better dental care coverage and more transparency
stories.summary: Claims are being denied without explanations and too many people are confused about what’s covered
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
The national dental care program has “transformed access to care for millions of patients” but claims are being denied without explanations and too many people are confused about what’s covered, says a new report from the Canadian Dental Association.

The association commissioned the report to assess the dental care program’s progress and make recommendations to the federal government on how it can be improved.

“We have a strong program, it’s got a good foundation, but continuous improvement is essential if the program is ever going to reach its potential,” said Dr. Kirk Preston, president of the Canadian Dental Association.

The program, which launched in 2022, was created as part of the supply-and-confidence agreement between the NDP and Justin Trudeau’s minority Liberal government.

The first phase offered coverage for seniors before the program was expanded to include adults with disabilities and children.

The final expansion, which was announced the day before Prime Minister Mark Carney called the 2025 election, opened coverage to all adults with a household income under $90,000 who do not have private insurance.

It’s been billed as the largest single expansion in public health care in decades, with an estimated nine million people eligible. Around 6.5 million have signed on to the program so far.

Colloquially, politicians have referred to the dental care program as free dental care – something that has created lasting confusion.

“I had a patient just last week that came in and he said, ‘I thought it was free,’” Preston said.

The program provides different levels of coverage depending on income. Those in the highest income bracket must cover 60 per cent of their fees.

Coverage is also based on set fees for services the CDA said are often below the cost of treatment.

That leaves many patients with unexpected bills, the report says.

Ondina Love, CEO of the Canadian Dental Hygienists Association, said confusion over what the plan covers has added to the administrative burdens on clinics.

“We are recommending enhanced public education and clear communications regarding what’s covered,” she said.

Preston said dentists’ biggest concerns are about pre-authorization.

Clinics need to submit treatment plans ahead of time for things like root canals, specialist services, or care above what the dental care plan typically covers. The insurance provider, Sun Life, determines if the care will be covered.

Those claims are denied half the time, the report said.

“It’s frustrating for dentists and patients because there’s no clear explanation in most cases as to why the claims are not approved,” Preston said.

The report said denials can lead to a manageable condition getting worse, forcing patients into more invasive and expensive care.

“It’s not consistent and I don’t understand what their guidelines are for approving or denying treatment in the pre-authorization process,” Preston said.

The CDA report calls for better education for care providers, more transparency and clear clinical criteria for pre-authorizations.

It also calls for fee increases to keep up with rising costs in dental clinics, along with better work force planning to address shortages of dental hygienists and assistants.

Love said that last point is critical.

“We do know that in certain regions, there’s a sufficient supply – maybe even oversupply – and in other regions, there definitely is a shortage,” she said.

The report noted that patients, especially seniors, have reported difficulties with reapplying for coverage each year. The income criteria can mean patients who had care one year might lose it the next.

Overall, patients report a high level of satisfaction with the program. The report includes surveys of both patients and dentists, commissioned by the CDA and carried out by Abacus Data.

More than half of the patients surveyed said they’ve been able to free up savings to spend on groceries and other essentials.

“This is a notable achievement for a program of such scale and ambition,” it said.

Notable, too, is the uptake from dentists themselves.

In early 2024, nearly 70 per cent of dentists told the CDA they were opposed to the program.

Its initial phases required providers to opt in, and uptake was so slow that government eliminated that requirement.

The new report says over 90 per cent of dentists are taking part in the program, and 70 per cent are supportive.

The CDA recommends the federal government commission an independent evaluation of the program’s effectiveness, and use that to decide whether it’s reaching the intended patients.

“This is a notable achievement for a program of such scale and ambition,” it said.

stories.title: Crash between cyclist and London police vehicle closes section of Hamilton Road
stories.summary: Police have closed a section of Hamilton Road following a crash between a marked London police cruiser and a cyclist.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Police have closed a section of Hamilton Road following a crash between a marked London police cruiser and a cyclist.

According to police, the crash happened around 6:30 a.m. and has closed Hamilton Road between Pegler Street and Smith Street.

Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and use an alternate route as the road will remain closed for an undetermined period while the investigation continues.

Police said the cyclist was transported to hospital with unknown injuries.

No details have been released regarding the circumstances surrounding the collision.

Further updates are expected as more information becomes available.

stories.title: ‘Degrading’ off-campus sign near St. Francis Xavier University prompts backlash
stories.summary: A sheet draped over the window of a home in Antigonish with a spray-painted message read: ‘Drop-off zone: Acadia girlfriends’
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Two Nova Scotia universities are condemning a sign that was displayed at an off-campus property in Antigonish on the weekend, saying it perpetuated rape culture.

Tara Taylor, a professor at St. Francis Xavier University, posted a photo on social media Friday that showed a sheet draped over the window of a home in Antigonish with a spray-painted message that read: “Drop-off zone: Acadia girlfriends.”

The sign appeared outside the property during the university’s annual homecoming celebrations. The property is used for student housing.

“When I saw it … it felt like a slap in the face,” Taylor said in an interview Monday. “I just thought it was incredibly tone-deaf.”

Elizabeth Yeo, the university’s vice president of student life, issued a statement Saturday calling the sign “offensive,” adding that the university was investigating the incident.

Taylor said the sign was taken down Saturday morning, but it was displayed again that night.

In a statement released Sunday, university president Andrew Hakin said the school made sure the sign was taken down again, adding that the sign’s message was “degrading and deeply concerning.”

“St. F.X. unequivocally rejects misogyny, sexualized and gender-based violence, and the attitudes and behaviours that contribute to rape culture,” the statement said.

Meanwhile, Acadia University in Wolfville, N.S., issued a news release Sunday that said the sign encouraged sexual violence against its students.

“What happened in Antigonish is a symptom of a society-wide problem,” it said. “It is our collective responsibility as higher education institutions to speak out against violence against women and rape culture specifically.”

Coined in the 1970s, the term rape culture refers to behaviour and beliefs that encourage or normalize sexual violence.

Mariana Paludi, who has researched the views of students at Canadian universities about the issue, said she believes the sign is promoting sexual violence against women.

“It’s portraying … this gender imbalance and degrading women … and objectifying women,” said Paludi, an assistant professor at the Universidad Técnico Federico Santa Maria in Chile

Paludi published research earlier this year that looked at how Canadian post-secondary students interpreted rape culture following two high-profile incidents at Nova Scotia universities – a Saint Mary’s University student chant about sexually assaulting underage girls in 2013 and a 2015 Dalhousie University dentistry student group-chat that contained violent sexual messages about female classmates.

Paludi said the new sign posted over the weekend demonstrates how slow society has progressed, more than a decade after those two scandals.

Taylor said it was shocking to see the sign in light of recent online discourse surrounding a high-profile lawsuit in the United States that alleges seven members of the Chi Pi fraternity at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., sexually assaulted a woman in October, 2024.

The professor said the St. F.X. students who displayed the sign must have been aware of the lawsuit, adding that the timing was “very triggering” for her.

“They can’t possibly be ignorant. It’s on social media everywhere,” she said.

Taylor said she shared the photo to raise awareness about a “party culture” at the university that she says contributes to sexual violence.

“I’ve been at St. F.X. for 22 years and I’ve had students every year come to me and say that they are dealing with the consequence of being sexually assaulted,” she said. “And I’m not unique in that.”

In 2018, students at the university criticized its handling of a reported case of sexual assault and called for a review of its sexual violence policy. And in 2023, a student sued the university, alleging she was sexually assaulted while attending the school in 2022.

Taylor said the university has taken steps to address sexual violence on campus and improve support for victims, but more needs to be done.

“There are people at the university who have worked very hard for a long time to make it safer, so it is deeply frustrating that these incidents still happen.”

According to the university’s website, its sexual violence response policy was approved in 2019 and reviewed in 2025. The policy states that the school is committed to fostering a culture where “behaviours that perpetuate sexual violence are discouraged and rejected.”

In his statement, Hakin said the most recent incident has been referred to the university’s disciplinary process, which will be guided by the school’s sexual violence response policy.

stories.title: Two bids for Welland bungalow drive sale price over asking
stories.summary: Two-bedroom townhouse sells for $610,000
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
69 Andrew Lane, Welland, Ont.

Asking price: $599,900 (August, 2026)

Selling price: $610,000 (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not available

Taxes: $4,824 (2026)

Days on the market: 21

Listing agents: Michael St. Jean and Jonathan Scott, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

This two-bedroom townhouse in Welland, southwest of Niagara Falls, came on the market priced at $599,900 during the last week of August. By the second day of September, two guests started purchase talks. The best offer, cleared of conditions in mid-September, came in at $610,000.

“We ended up having a couple of buyers swirling around at the same time, forcing the price over $600,000,” said agent Michael St. Jean.

“We don’t go in expecting that, but it’s a good product not readily available, and it’s a nice neighbourhood.”

The home’s single-storey design is common in the subdivision, called Merritt Meadows, but not in the surrounding area.

“In general, it’s a pretty sought-after type of product, hard to find in many areas of the Golden Horseshoe,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“The property itself is newer; it showed well and had a lot of upgrades.”

Built several years ago, this townhouse has an attached garage and 1,245 square feet of living space, and an unfinished basement.

The combined living and dining area has a nine-foot ceiling, hardwood flooring, and access to an enclosed deck and interlocking patio on the 28- by 104-foot lot.

A laundry room and two full bathrooms are on the main floor, as well as an open-concept kitchen with quartz countertops, an island and tile flooring.

“[The builder] Rinaldi Homes is known in the area to be the best quality,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“Welland Canal is within walking distance, and it’s very close to the highway, with [highway] 406 literally around the corner.”

Asking price: $599,900 (August, 2026)
Selling price: $610,000 (September, 2026)
Previous selling price: Not available
Days on the market: 21
Listing agents: Michael St. Jean and Jonathan Scott, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

This two-bedroom townhouse in Welland, southwest of Niagara Falls, came on the market priced at $599,900 during the last week of August. By the second day of September, two guests started purchase talks. The best offer, cleared of conditions in mid-September, came in at $610,000.
“We ended up having a couple of buyers swirling around at the same time, forcing the price over $600,000,” said agent Michael St. Jean.
“We don’t go in expecting that, but it’s a good product not readily available, and it’s a nice neighbourhood.”
The home’s single-storey design is common in the subdivision, called Merritt Meadows, but not in the surrounding area.
“In general, it’s a pretty sought-after type of product, hard to find in many areas of the Golden Horseshoe,” Mr. St. Jean said.
“The property itself is newer; it showed well and had a lot of upgrades.”
Built several years ago, this townhouse has an attached garage and 1,245 square feet of living space, and an unfinished basement.
The combined living and dining area has a nine-foot ceiling, hardwood flooring, and access to an enclosed deck and interlocking patio on the 28- by 104-foot lot.
A laundry room and two full bathrooms are on the main floor, as well as an open-concept kitchen with quartz countertops, an island and tile flooring.
“[The builder] Rinaldi Homes is known in the area to be the best quality,” Mr. St. Jean said.
“Welland Canal is within walking distance, and it’s very close to the highway, with [highway] 406 literally around the corner.”

stories.title: Driver involved in Saskatchewan crash is grieving deaths of woman, girls: lawyer
stories.summary: A lawyer for the truck driver involved in a deadly crash in Saskatchewan that killed a woman and two girls says the man is overwhelmed with grief.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted October 6, 2026 8:05 am

A lawyer for the truck driver involved in a deadly crash in Saskatchewan that killed a woman and two girls says the man is overwhelmed with grief.

Brian Pfefferle says his client, Kelly Knopf, plans to fully co-operate with authorities as the case moves through court.

RCMP has said the 40-year-old was driving a truck Friday when he allegedly smashed into an SUV while trying to pass a semi on a rural road near Foam Lake, Sask., northeast of Regina.

Three people in the SUV were killed, including the 40-year-old woman driving the car and two girls, who were eight and five years old.

Mounties say a man who was also in the SUV was taken to hospital in serious condition and the semi driver was not injured.

Knopf, who’s from the United States, as well as two other passengers, were also taken to hospital.

Knopf is facing charges for dangerous driving causing death and bodily harm.

Pfefferle says his client was on a hunting trip in Saskatchewan, and he remains hospitalized with serious injuries.

stories.title: Canadian firms say cybersecurity budgets falling short as attacks grow: survey
stories.summary: A new survey suggests some Canadian companies are losing confidence in their cybersecurity budgets' ability to handle the increasingly frequent and complex threats they face.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

Posted October 6, 2026 8:00 am.

Last Updated October 6, 2026 8:16 am.

A new survey suggests some Canadian companies are losing confidence in their cybersecurity budgets’ ability to handle the increasingly frequent and complex threats they face.

The Canadian Internet Registration Authority surveyed 503 people responsible for making cybersecurity decisions and found 76 per cent represented organizations that have increased their cybersecurity budgets over the past year.

Most organizations reported information technology budgets of at least $50,000, though several said they were even more well-capitalized with funding stretching beyond $100,000.

However, most organizations said only five to 15 per cent of those overall IT budgets were dedicated to cybersecurity.

Seventeen per cent thought that amount wasn’t sufficient to keep pace with the threats, sixteen per cent were unsure and one per cent refused to answer.

Sixty-seven per cent believed their cybersecurity budget was enough, which was down from 74 per cent last year.

“The survey reflects what we hear from organizations every day: cybersecurity challenges are increasing while resources are becoming harder to secure,” said Jon Ferguson, vice-president of cyber and domain name system at Cira.

“Security teams are facing more threats, greater complexity and higher expectations, all amid economic and operational uncertainty.”

Over the last year, many Canadian schools have continued to grapple with a breach of education software they used, while the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto and Winnipeg’s Health Sciences Centre each warned they had been targeted by cyber attackers.

The Cira’s survey aimed to look at how organizations are responding to an evolving threat landscape, where artificial intelligence and vast troves of data bought and sold online are being weaponized.

The online survey conducted between June and July found four in ten organizations that were polled experienced a cyber attack in the past year.

Among those that experienced a ransomware attack, 75 per cent said they paid ransom demands. Organizations that paid a ransom typically forked over at least $25,000.

Cybersecurity experts often discourage companies from paying ransoms because they feel it incentivizes attackers to continue breaching organizations.

They instead encourage companies to beef up their security and better train staff to handle threats.

The Cira survey found 87 per cent of participants had a response plan in place for cybersecurity incidents.

Eighty-two per cent pay for cybersecurity insurance, which is unchanged from last year but up from 59 per cent in 2021.

Two-thirds of organizations surveyed also said they have AI tools integrated into their workflows and operations, but more than eight in 10 cybersecurity decisionmakers are concerned about AI-based threats.

The survey also looked at sovereignty — a hot topic as the trade war rages on and Canada aims to protect its assets and partner with countries other than the U.S.

The Cira found Canadian ownership and data residency have shifted from a preference to a requirement for many respondents.

Ninety-one per cent said it matters that cyber records are stored and processed in Canada and 89 per cent cared that vendors they partner with are Canadian-owned, headquartered or operating here.

Nearly seven in 10 prioritize data sovereignty over price when selecting a cybersecurity vendor, but four in 10 said they have at least reviewed U.S.-based or other foreign cybersecurity firms in the past year.

Cost and limited availability of Canadian vendors were the primary barriers to choosing a domestic cybersecurity vendor.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Eight buyers bid on North York bungalow
stories.summary: The home has formal living and dining rooms and three bedrooms with hardwood flooring
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
16 Jocada Rd., Toronto

Asking price: $849,000 (June, 2026)

Selling price: $1.2-million (June, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not available

Taxes: $5,392 (2025)

Days on the market: Five

Listing agent: Andre Kutyan, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

This 53-year-old bungalow is in original condition on a 42- by 137-foot lot near Keele Street and Highway 401. Agent Andre Kutyan wagered that more people, builders and families alike, would be willing to gauge the property’s potential if it were priced low.

“Things were sitting around on the market in that $1-million plus range,” said Mr. Kutyan.

“I priced it in a way that would make it attractive to a lot of buyers, whether to tear it down, add on, or live in.”

Over five days in June, the bungalow had 27 visitors. By Monday afternoon, the time the seller had set to assess offers, eight bids were registered. The final offer added $351,000 to the asking price.

“Ultimately, most bids I saw were from people looking to live in the house,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“It’s a sizable lot in a relatively central location, and the house is in very good shape.”

The home has formal living and dining rooms and three bedrooms with hardwood flooring.

There is an eat-in kitchen and a four-piece bathroom on both the main and lower level. All have ceramic tile flooring.

The basement also has a dining area with a wet bar and a recreation area with a wood-burning fireplace and an exit to exterior steps leading up to the yard.

There is a built-in, double garage and a private driveway.

“Another great thing about this house was it has a walkout basement, which is not typical for the area,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“A lot of buyers were looking at it as a potential basement apartment because it has a separate entrance, a walkout and a kitchen.”

stories.title: 5 takeaways from Quebec election as Parti Québécois forms minority government
stories.summary: Quebec voters elected a Parti Québécois minority government Monday, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Quebec voters elected a Parti Québécois minority government Monday, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.

Here are five takeaways from the evening.

1. PQ comes back from the brink

After being reduced to three seats in the 2022 election, the Parti Québécois stormed back to form a government, falling short of the 64 seats needed to form a majority in the Quebec legislature. The party was able to capitalize on Quebecers’ desire for change after eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec rule in the province.

2. PQ has promised a referendum

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon won his party’s leadership in 2020 with a promise to hold a referendum if he formed a government. Although his party fell short of a majority government, he May have an opportunity to work with Québec solidaire, a left-wing sovereigntist party that could support his plans to stage a referendum after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029. The Parti Québécois and Québec solidaire combined for more than 40 per cent of the popular vote on Monday evening. Together, the two sovereigntist parties also captured a majority of the seats in the national assembly.

Voters chose the Quebec Liberals as the official Opposition for the third general election in a row. The party more than doubled its seats in the legislature, finishing the evening with 40 elected members. Leader Charles Milliard said his party was the only federalist party committed to remaining in Canada, although he is not the only leader who has pledged to block plans for a referendum.

4. Quebec Conservatives elected for first time in modern Quebec history

Conservatives last elected a member to the Quebec legislature in 1935. The party will now form a strong contingent in the legislature with a caucus of 19. Under Éric Duhaime’s leadership, the party surged from a marginal formation that captured less than two per cent of the vote in 2018 to a main player. The party ran a campaign that was largely targeted on key ridings, after failing to capture a seat in 2022 despite getting close to 13 per cent of the vote. Duhaime has also pledged to stop the PQ from staging a referendum on sovereignty.

5. A fragmented political landscape

Five parties ended the evening with more than 10 per cent of the vote and none had more than 30 per cent of the votes that were counted. The PQ came close to forming a majority government, even though it only received about 28 per cent of the total number of votes counted on Monday. The Liberals had about 24 per cent, while the Conservatives had about 21 per cent. Coalition Avenir Québec had about 13 per cent of the vote, but failed to win any seats, while Québec solidaire, which had about 12 per cent of the vote, won nine seats.

stories.title: Canadian Dental Association report finds dental care program limits coverage
stories.summary: Ottawa — The national dental care program has "transformed access to care for millions of patients" but claims are being denied without explanations and too many people are confused about what's covered, says a new report from the Canadian Dental Association.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The national dental care program has “transformed access to care for millions of patients” but claims are being denied without explanations and too many people are confused about what’s covered, says a new report from the Canadian Dental Association.

The association commissioned the report to assess the dental care program’s progress and make recommendations to the federal government on how it can be improved.

“We have a strong program, it’s got a good foundation, but continuous improvement is essential if the program is ever going to reach its potential,” said Dr. Kirk Preston, president of the Canadian Dental Association.

The program, which launched in 2022, was created as part of the supply-and-confidence agreement between the NDP and Justin Trudeau’s minority Liberal government.

The first phase offered coverage for seniors before the program was expanded to include adults with disabilities and children.

The final expansion, which was announced the day before Prime Minister Mark Carney called the 2025 election, opened coverage to all adults with a household income under $90,000 who do not have private insurance.

It’s been billed as the largest single expansion in public health care in decades, with an estimated nine million people eligible. Around 6.5 million have signed on to the program so far.

Colloquially, politicians have referred to the dental care program as free dental care — something that has created lasting confusion.

“I had a patient just last week that came in and he said, ‘I thought it was free,'” Preston said.

The program provides different levels of coverage depending on income. Those in the highest income bracket must cover 60 per cent of their fees.

Coverage is also based on set fees for services the CDA said are often below the cost of treatment.

That leaves many patients with unexpected bills, the report says.

Ondina Love, CEO of the Canadian Dental Hygienists Association, said confusion over what the plan covers has added to the administrative burdens on clinics.

“We are recommending enhanced public education and clear communications regarding what’s covered,” she said.

Preston said dentists’ biggest concerns are about pre-authorization.

Clinics need to submit treatment plans ahead of time for things like root canals, specialist services, or care above what the dental care plan typically covers. The insurance provider, Sun Life, determines if the care will be covered.

Those claims are denied half the time, the report said.

“It’s frustrating for dentists and patients because there’s no clear explanation in most cases as to why the claims are not approved,” Preston said.

The report said denials can lead to a manageable condition getting worse, forcing patients into more invasive and expensive care.

“It’s not consistent and I don’t understand what their guidelines are for approving or denying treatment in the pre-authorization process,” Preston said.

The CDA report calls for better education for care providers, more transparency and clear clinical criteria for pre-authorizations.

It also calls for fee increases to keep up with rising costs in dental clinics, along with better workforce planning to address shortages of dental hygienists and assistants.

Love said that last point is critical.

“We do know that in certain regions, there’s a sufficient supply — maybe even oversupply — and in other regions, there definitely is a shortage,” she said.

Health Minister Marjorie Michel said Tuesday the government is looking to work with the CDA on its recommendations.

“As we are moving forward and we are (getting) feedback, we are taking action,” she said.

The report noted that patients, especially seniors, have reported difficulties with reapplying for coverage each year. The income criteria can mean patients who had care one year might lose it the next.

Overall, patients report a high level of satisfaction with the program. The report includes surveys of both patients and dentists, commissioned by the CDA and carried out by Abacus Data.

More than half of the patients surveyed said they’ve been able to free up savings to spend on groceries and other essentials.

“This is a notable achievement for a program of such scale and ambition,” it said.

Notable, too, is the uptake from dentists themselves.

In early 2024, nearly 70 per cent of dentists told the CDA they were opposed to the program.

Its initial phases required providers to opt in, and uptake was so slow that government eliminated that requirement.

The new report says over 90 per cent of dentists are taking part in the program, and 70 per cent are supportive.

The CDA recommends the federal government commission an independent evaluation of the program’s effectiveness, and use that to decide whether it’s reaching the intended patients.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Former B.C. Conservative leader Findlay and husband Chapman were threatened, OneBC says
stories.summary: Chapman announced he was joining OneBC to run as a candidate in the Oct. 24 election after Findlay resigned as the Conservative party leader amid a caucus revolt
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
Political party OneBC says former Conservative legislator Brent Chapman and his wife, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, have been subjected to a “torrent of threats and abuse from insiders.”

Chapman announced last month that he was joining OneBC to run as a candidate in the Oct. 24 election after Findlay resigned as the Conservative party leader amid a caucus revolt.

But Chapman’s name wasn’t on the final list of candidates released Sunday by Elections BC, and OneBC says in a statement that the party and Chapman mutually decided that he wouldn’t run in the riding of Surrey South.

The statement says OneBC was excited to have Chapman join the team but the “strains of the last few months have been enormous.”

Following weeks of division and defections, Findlay resigned as Conservative leader just days before NDP Leader David Eby called the snap election.

Findlay’s resignation came less than four months after winning the party leadership, and OneBC’s statement says that “strong conservative values” are not acceptable to the appointed leaders of the Conservative Party of British Columbia.

“Politics is important, but so is family and security,” it says. “That is why we are grateful for [Chapman’s] principled stance, but also in full support of his decision to step back at this time and wish him all the best.”

OneBC emerged as a splinter group from the B.C. Conservatives shortly after the party came close to winning the last provincial election.

OneBC’s interim leader, former Conservative legislator Dallas Brodie, is running to retain her riding, but the party lacked the two members required for official status when the election was called because Chapman hadn’t informed the Speaker or the clerk’s office in time.

stories.title: B.C. sees development of specialized space for life-sciences sector
stories.summary: Developers face complexities building property for biotech companies
stories.author: Alexandra Petros
stories.content:
British Columbia’s growing life-sciences sector is creating a new commercial real estate opportunity, but the specialized requirements of biotech companies mean developers face a different and more complex building challenge than conventional office or industrial developments.

Aspect Biosystems , a Vancouver-based biotechnology company, develops therapies designed to restore or supplement biological functions in the body and to offer functional cures to several diseases. The company recently announced a $280-million expansion, supported by $79-million in federal funding, to complement a separate $200-million co-investment from the federal and British Columbia governments in 2024.

According to Vancouver-based non-profit Life Sciences British Columbia , the province’s life-sciences sector generated approximately $4.6-billion in revenue in 2024, a 27 per cent increase from 2021. That same year, life-sciences companies in B.C. secured approximately $700-million in venture capital.

The interest in the life-sciences sector extends across Canada, with some provincial organizations and governments bullish on investment in the space. For example, Ontario’s Life Sciences Innovation Fund (Lsif) provides early-stage capital to companies in the sector, while the Government of Quebec is providing nearly $271.5-million for its renewed Quebec Life Sciences Strategy between 2025 to 2028.

Alain Rivère, senior vice-president of the High Technology Facilities Group at Cbre in Vancouver, says the life-sciences sector boomed after the pandemic, but investment has normalized over the past two years. “We had massive investment and funding happening in the sector, and that propelled much real estate development, particularly in the Mount Pleasant area,” he says.

Despite interest, the sector faces a unique challenge: access to lab space, according to John Waslen, associate vice-president at Colliers in Vancouver.

“Supply of quality, built-out lab space is extremely limited, and it’s often leased before it ever reaches the open market,” he says. “At the same time, there’s no shortage of demand at the smaller end of the market.”

New graduates from local universities start new companies every year, consistently absorbing smaller blocks of lab space, Mr. Waslen says, adding that the real challenge comes when these companies are ready to scale into larger spaces. For example, a startup May initially only need 2,000 or 3,000 square feet, but May not be in a position to commit to a larger space in the years before it requires it.

Mr. Rivère says the life-sciences sector is cyclical, with tenants outgrowing their space and moving to expand, leaving vacancies for smaller companies. He notes that smaller and medium-sized companies make up most of the current demand.

To secure financing, developers often need to secure pre-leases for as much as 50 per cent of a building, Mr. Waslen says. For a 200,000-square-foot building, that could mean finding tenants that occupy about 100,000 square feet before construction begins. Pre-lease agreements can also require tenants to commit three to four years in advance, indicating the steps required before spaces become readily available.

“Without enough larger tenants in Vancouver’s market, it makes it very difficult for developers to clear that hurdle and get projects moving,” he says.

Depending on the starting point and specific facility requirements, building costs can vary widely.

For a new construction, a vivarium can cost roughly $800 to $1,200 per square foot, a chemistry lab approximately $500 to $800 per square foot, and office and common areas roughly $100 to $300 per square foot, says Brad Cowden, partner and senior client executive at Fusion Projects, an active design-build firm specializing in commercial construction. These are hard construction costs alone before considering demolition, building infrastructure upgrades, professional fees and laboratory equipment.

A proper lab build-out requires much more than a conventional office, explains Mr. Waslen. Fume hoods, specialized Hvac, ventilation, emergency power and higher electrical capacity all require significant capital and time to install. Lab tenants also often have specific requirements for air changes, exhaust, floor loading and ceiling heights that a regular office building isn’t designed to accommodate. This is part of the reason why converting a conventional office building into a life-sciences space can be difficult.

It’s a much bigger engineering feat, which is why many developers seek anchor tenants to kick-start new projects, Mr. Rivère says.

For smaller companies, this creates a catch-22: they need purpose-built space to grow, despite developers needing substantial tenant commitments before they can finance construction.

National life-sciences organization adMare BioInnovations’ recently completed M4 Innovation Centre in Vancouver’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood is helping to bridge this gap, offering purpose-built space for early-stage and growing life-sciences companies.

B.C. has a strong talent pipeline for the life-sciences sector and is home to world-class institutions such as the University of British Columbia, British Columbia Institute of Technology and Simon Fraser University.

Biotech companies in Vancouver’s growing Mount Pleasant neighbourhood include Aspect Biosystems, AbCellera, Zymeworks and Stemcell Technologies, alongside hospitals such as Vancouver General Hospital and Mount Saint Joseph Hospital.

“What we have happening in Vancouver is a very vibrant biotech sector that is clustered in areas around the Greater Vancouver area,” says Wendy Hurlburt, president and CEO of Life Sciences BC. “In addition to advancing their own innovations, these organizations are playing a huge role in attracting and developing talent.”

At a macro level, British Columbia has the capacity to sustain further industry growth, provided land policies support this expansion, she says. Continued infrastructure and policy investments are also needed to foster a competitive environment for companies to remain and grow in Canada, she adds.

For Mr. Rivère, the life-sciences landscape offers promising prospects for further growth.

“We’re past the beginning phase. It’s established and growing – Vancouver is now a global player,” he says.

stories.title: The wrong way to treat the right to know
stories.summary: The Ford government is increasingly allergic to transparency
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Less is more is a fine approach to interior design. But it’s a terrible way for government to approach public disclosure. Unfortunately, it’s the ethos adopted by Ontario Premier Doug Ford .

Evidence is piling up that the three-term government is increasingly allergic to transparency. This is self-serving behaviour from politicians with no shortage of scandals, making it harder for the media and public to hold them to account.

Especially now, with the province facing major threats, Mr. Ford needs to remember that the public is his boss. They have a right to know what he is doing.

In a few ways, though, the premier has made it harder for the people to keep tabs on him.

One example is the no-press press conference. One of these happened last month.

On that day, Mr. Ford livestreamed a housing announcement on YouTube. Although this looked on its face like a press conference it was lacking one crucial element: journalists. In fact, the media didn’t find out about the event until Mr. Ford’s social media account posted that it had happened.

The lack of reporters suited Mr. Ford just fine. He quipped , as the pseudo-event wrapped up, “Thank God we don’t have the media. No questions, no answers. We’re good to go.”

This is insulting both to the men and women at Queen’s Park whose job it is to cover provincial politics and also to the people of Ontario. Putting out a message without having to answer questions about the policy being announced – or whatever else is on the public mind – is ducking responsibility.

Unfortunately, this is not a new impulse for the Ford government. In its first term, there was actually a pseudo-newscaster creating videos to post online. What was called Ontario News Now began during the 2018 election campaign and then continued as the party formed government. According to a Canadian Press analysis , Mr. Ford appeared at least 100 times on the fake news operation in his first year as premier.

This led to some grating moments for the actual reporters whose job it was to cover Mr. Ford. It was not uncommon for him to take a few questions and then his staff would announce he had no more time, only for him to give generously of his calendar to the Ontario News Now pseudo-newscaster, which was also at the scene.

The façade of journalism is not the only trick the Ford government has used to manage its message. Earlier this year Mr. Ford clamped down on freedom of information access.

Such legislation is designed to allow the media or any member of the public to request internal documents. These often contain information that can be embarrassing to government. One way to avoid that is to keep everything above-board. Another way – Mr. Ford’s choice – is to change the law to exempt himself, his cabinet and their political staff.

He also made the rules retroactive, killing any access to information request that was in process at the time of the legislative change.

This was such a sweeping clampdown on information that bureaucrats were initially unsure about just what to do. And then, according to recent reporting by Global News , came the edict: stop all freedom of information work. This directive, which was conveyed only by Microsoft Teams, in spite of some bureaucrats asking for email confirmation, lasted more than a week.

Although parts of the freedom of information system then resumed, the change in legislation has thrown a blanket of secrecy over the inner workings of the Ford government.

At the same time, the Ford government has extended the legislature’s “summer” break until the last week of this month. The legislature will not sit for 21 weeks, after a 14-week winter break.

This leaves the government untroubled by Opposition or reporter questions at Queen’s Park for months on end. The protracted current break is ostensibly to avoid sitting during municipal elections, a risible defence given how Mr. Ford has meddled in city affairs – including cutting Toronto’s council in half in the middle of an election campaign .

Mr. Ford May find it convenient to keep the public in the dark. But he seems to have learned the wrong lesson when he bragged about saving the taxpayer money as a Toronto city councillor. Less May be more when it comes to office expenses. It doesn’t work with political transparency.

stories.title: Local fire departments encouraging battery safety during Fire Prevention Week
stories.summary: Local fire departments are encouraging battery safety this Fire Prevention Week. The theme is ‘Charge into Fire Safety.’
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Local fire departments are encouraging battery safety this Fire Prevention Week. The theme is ‘Charge into Fire Safety.’

Some everyday charging habits you are reminded to follow to reduce the risk of lithium-ion battery fires include:

Use manufacturer-approved batteries and chargers

Never charge on beds, couches, or other combustible surfaces

Avoid charging batteries overnight or while unattended

Stop using batteries that are swollen, leaking, damaged, or unusually hot

Never dispose of lithium-ion batteries in your household garbage

The Canadian government also offers the following warning signs.

You should stop using a battery or device immediately if you notice:

Swelling or bulging

Discolouration or deformation

Hissing, popping, or crackling sounds

If any of these signs are present and it’s safe to do so, move the device away from flammable material and contact the manufacturer.

If a battery fire ignites, evacuate the area, close doors behind you, when possible, call 911, and do not try to fight a large battery fire.

More information on battery fire safety can be found on Canada’s website .

stories.title: Neutrino experiment pioneer Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics
stories.summary: University of Wisconsin-Madison professor is best known for his work establishing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Francis Halzen, a University of Wisconsin-Madison professor who pioneered the detection of ghostly particles from outer space, has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

On Tuesday, members of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences named Dr. Halzen the sole winner of this year’s physics prize.

Dr. Halzen is best known for his work establishing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole. Using a one cubic kilometre volume of the Antarctic ice sheet as its detection medium, the experiment can spot flashes of light that occur when high-energy neutrinos from the distant universe occasionally collide with atoms in the ice.

Completed in 2011, the experiment ushered in a new era of particle astrophysics.

Winning the Nobel “was a great surprise,” said Dr. Halzen when reached by phone during the announcement.

“When I reflect on this moment I have to emphasize how lucky I was because when we started this project, everybody realized this was maybe a good idea but very few thought it would work, including myself.”

Born in Belgium in 1944, Dr. Halzen received his PhD from KU Leuven university in 1969. In 1971, he began his research career in Wisconsin where he continues to lead the IceCube project.

The goal of IceCube is to detect neutrinos, particles that interact so infrequently with other forms of matter that they can easily pass through miles of solid lead as though through thin air.

Starting in the 1960s, experimental physicists began devising experiments to spot neutrinos produced by nuclear reactions in the sun’s core. Such experiments are typically located underground because the surrounding rock is invisible to neutrinos but screens out cosmic rays – electrically charged atomic fragments that are constantly raining down to Earth from collisions in the upper atmosphere.

In 2015, Canadian physicist Arthur McDonald shared the Nobel Prize for leading a solar neutrino experiment built in a mine in Sudbury, Ont., which in the early 2000s helped to establish that neutrinos have mass.

Meanwhile, Dr. Halzen sought to extend the reach of neutrino detectors into the larger universe beyond our solar system.

His goal was to spot high-energy neutrinos that are produced in extreme environments, including massive stellar explosions and jets of material accelerated by the powerful magnetic fields that surround supermassive black holes.

High-energy neutrinos are far more rare than those from the sun. Spotting them requires a much larger detector than can fit inside a mine. Starting in 1987, Dr. Halzen and colleagues began exploring whether the giant sheet of clear glacial ice buried under snow at the South Pole would make an ideal place to build a giant neutrino detector.

Their initial effort was called Amanda, for Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array. Built between 1995 and 2000, it consisted of hundreds of optical detectors. These were lowered into bore holes melted into the ice using hot water, which was then allowed to refreeze, locking the detectors in place. Passing neutrinos interacting with atomic nuclei in the ice generated telltale flashes of light that the detector could spot.

Though cosmic rays drowned out the neutrino signal from above, Dr. Halzen and his colleagues took this into account by only paying attention to particles moving upward from below, effectively using the bulk of Earth as a filter through which they could view neutrinos arriving from the northern sky on the other side of the planet.

Amanda showed the approach could work, paving the way for IceCube, a much larger version of the experiment.

Over the years that it has been operating, IceCube has confirmed the existence of neutrinos arriving from distant galaxies and provided new information about high-energy events in the cosmos. It has also helped to pin down key properties of neutrinos themselves.

As leader of IceCube, Dr. Halzen has also helped to set a course for parallel efforts to spot high-energy neutrinos, including P-ONE, an underwater experiment in development off the coast of Vancouver Island.

Jodi Cooley, a particle astrophysicist and director of Snolab, the successor to Dr. McDonald’s facility in Sudbury, began her research career working on Amanda. In an interview she said she considers Dr. Halzen one of her research mentors and expressed her joy at the news that he had won this year’s physics Nobel.

“He combined extraordinary scientific vision with an infectious enthusiasm for discovery, inspiring generations of scientists to pursue the bold idea that neutrinos could reveal a previously hidden universe,” Dr. Cooley said.

She added that Dr. Halzen also navigated an important transition when Amanda grew into IceCube, becoming a much larger and costly experiment that required hundreds of researchers giving a large share of their careers to help the effort succeed.

“That takes real leadership,” Dr. Cooley said.

With Tuesday’s announcement, the physics prize has been awarded 120 times to 230 individuals since it was established in 1901.

The most recent Canadian winner was Geoffrey Hinton , a University of Toronto professor and pioneer of artificial intelligence who was awarded the physics Nobel in 2024 for is work on neural networks.

stories.title: Parliament's crane operators face unique challenges at lofty heights
stories.summary: Andrée-Anne Pare is one of the handful of Canadian female construction crane operators.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Ottawa — Andrée-Anne Pare is one of the handful of Canadian female construction crane operators on Parliament Hill during the second phase of the estimated $4.5 billion to $5 billion renovation of the buildings.

In this video she tells us of the unique challenges of operating one of the five cranes labouring over Parliament Hill.

The first phase of this massive Parliamentary project, the deconstruction, which included both demolition and excavation, is now complete. The second phase, the rebuilding, is currently in progress. This phase is the creation of the new parliamentary welcome centre and upgrades to the historic Centre Block, including restoring all of the heritage elements while modernizing the old structure and its facilities. The third phase, the “fit-out,” has not yet begun, and involves putting in the final finishes and restored heritage elements.

Main construction will be complete between 2030 and 2031. The Centre Block will reopen about one year later.

The video includes some stunning high aerial footage provided to Postmedia by Public Services and Procurement Canada, who for safety reasons don’t allow media to film on their active construction site.

As of March of this year, up to 800 workers are on site daily (this number will peak at over 1,500). Approximately 95 per cent of the companies that have worked on the project are Canadian owned, with involvement from over 400 companies across eight provinces, including some direct Indigenous participation.

Crane operators bring home some of the biggest paycheques on big construction sites but that’s partly because they work 10 to 11 hour shifts. Becoming a crane operator requires both in-class study and an apprenticeship. Most programs require a high school diploma (Grade 12), a clean driver’s record, and often a specific commercial driver’s license (like a Class 3 or Class 1 with air brake endorsement) especially for mobile cranes.

stories.title: Business leaders want capital gains deferral to keep money in Canadian firms
stories.summary: Toronto - Canadian business leaders are calling on the federal government to reform some of its tax policies in hopes of bolstering investments in domestic firms.
stories.author: Tara Deschamps The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Canadian business leaders are calling on the federal government to reform tax policies in hopes of bolstering investments in domestic firms.

More than 150 investors and executives signed a letter sent to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne on Tuesday, asking him to consider two policies they claim will bolster entrepreneurship in Canada.

The first encourages the country to adopt a program akin to the U.S. qualified small business stock incentive, which allows capital gains from qualified small business stocks to be excluded from federal tax.

The second proposes allowing more entrepreneurs and investors to defer paying some capital gains taxes when proceeds from some domestic business transactions are reinvested in another homegrown venture.

Benjamin Bergen, chief executive of one of the letter’s orchestrators the Canadian Venture Capital and Private Equity Association, said signatories feel deferring but not eliminating the tax would incentivize people who have built successful businesses to put their money to work again rather than take it out of the country, possibly to the U.S.

“This doesn’t impact a tremendous amount of people, but it impacts entrepreneurs and people who are willing to take big risks and it’s in those big risks that you get companies of the future,” he said.

“That is how you get the Googles, the Amazons, the Facebooks, these huge tech firms ... so we want to create an environment where we keep individuals in the country who are willing to take big risks on themselves, ON the country.”

Bergen’s organization put the letter together with the Council of Canadian Innovators.

Signatories include Dayforce chief executive David Ossip, Koho Financial Inc. founder Daniel Eberhard, Borrowell co-founder Andrew Graham, Two Small Fish Ventures co-founder Eva Lau and Float Financial co-founder Rob Khazzam.

Champagne’s office would not directly comment on the letter.

“While the government regularly reviews the tax system, it would be inappropriate at this time to speculate on any potential or prospective changes to the tax system,” said John Fragos, the minister’s press secretary, in an email.

Jack Mintz, the president’s fellow of the School of Public Policy at the University of Calgary, said the ideas the signatories are pressing for have some drawbacks.

He pointed to a June paper from University of Florida researchers who studied the U.S.‘s qualified small business stock incentive.

They found when a tax program like that is available, venture capitalists shift toward investing in riskier ventures, like pre-commercial stage startups and firms carrying pre-existing debt.

Venture capitalists also become more likely to invest across state lines, and provide a company’s first funding, contributing to tax-qualified startup investments experiencing higher failure rates and greater funding gaps.

“You’re basically subsidizing risk,” Mintz said, summarizing some of the paper.

But the policy isn’t all bad. He said the research has also found that the U.S. tax incentives on small business stocks also help companies achieve higher valuations and makes them more likely to reach unicorn status.

Unicorn status is derived when a startup lands a valuation exceeding $1 billion.

“So whether (the signatories’ proposed policies are) a good or a bad thing, I think depends on how you look at these things,” Mintz said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Sunshine sticks around, holiday weekend weather looks promising
stories.summary: Beautiful, sunny conditions across midwestern Ontario this morning, with the high reaching a comfortable 17 degrees.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Beautiful, sunny conditions across midwestern Ontario this morning, with the high reaching a comfortable 17 degrees. “Sunshine holds into Wednesday,” explained CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison, adding temperatures are on the rise.

“We pick up a southerly flow today and that will push temperatures above 20 degrees as we hit Wednesday.” Atchison says sunshine remains for your Thursday as well, with a high of 19 degrees. We will see a mix of cloud move in for the holiday weekend, but the probability for rain is on the lower end.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Tuesday: Mainly sunny. Wind becoming southwest 20 km/h late in the morning. High 17. UV index 4 or moderate. Tuesday night: A few clouds. Wind southwest 20 km/h becoming light in the evening.

Low 11. Wednesday: A mix of sun and cloud with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 23. Thursday: Sunny. High 19. Friday: A mix of sun and cloud with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 18. Saturday: A mix of sun and cloud.
