stories.summary: The film about a father and son trying to survive in a harsh new country is a testament to the power of pushing through obstacles
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
A Breed Apart

Written and directed by Adam Belanger and David Lafontaine

Starring Joshua Close and Isaac Highams

Classification N/A; 131 minutes

Opens at the Carlton Cinema in Toronto Oct. 9

Critic’s Pick

It is the 1850s, somewhere in a remote corner of Northern Ontario, and life is hard. Extremely, brutally, soul-crushingly hard.

But for the lonely English farmer Sydney (Joshua Close) and his nine-year-old son Emmett (Isaac Highams), hard is simply all that they know. Sydney’s wife, and Emmett’s mother, has recently died. The weather in this new country is harsh, and the approaching winter threatens to be even worse. The prized cattle that Sydney is raising shows promise, but one stroke of bad luck, and his meagre sustenance could be wiped away. And neither father nor son know how to relate to one another outside of sullen looks and rigorous discipline.

These are the unforgiving terms and conditions of A Breed Apart , an endearingly tough and robust drama of fathers and sons that doubles as a testament to the power of pushing through this difficult country’s many obstacles to make something of yourself, such as, say, a low-budget Canadian film. There are cold lessons here, but lessons all the same – and if you happen to be a young, aspiring filmmaker in this country, it would be wise to pay attention to just how Sydney and Emmett’s story unfurls.

The film marks the directorial debut of Adam Belanger and David Lafontaine, two long-time collaborators from Toronto’s indie theatre scene who graduated to the film world with their 2021 short, Rivals . (Some might recognize Belanger’s name as a crucial member of Matt Johnson’s Zapruder Films production company; as a production designer, Belanger won a Canadian Screen Award for BlackBerry , and is also working on Johnson’s upcoming Toronto-set comedic thriller tentatively titled Journalism 101 .)

Yet A Breed Apart is, in its ambitions and determination, so far past any of the duo’s previous work on stage or screen that it’s beyond impressive. Even more so when you realize the film was produced under Telefilm’s micro-budget Talent to Watch program, which hands starry-eyed filmmakers a relative pittance and dares them to emerge out the other end unscathed.

That is not unlike the journey that Sydney and Emmett are put on, and there are moments when audiences would be right to think that Belanger and Lafontaine are unfairly testing their endurance at the same time they’re undergoing their own existential dilemmas in putting the dang thing together. Yet there is a deft wryness to the film, even a sentimental compassion, that carries the weight. This is especially felt once the religious Pender family, neighbours to the father and son, enter the picture with eyes toward helping the pair survive, and perhaps find salvation, too. You can practically feel the air getting warmer, the ground getting softer.

Shot in the rural northeastern Ontario community of Powassan, and designed with the kind of meticulous detail that Belanger is known for, the film can feel like a museum piece come to life, but without any dust or creakiness. (There are also some moments involving animals that are, simply put, eye-popping in their sense of verisimilitude.) But Belanger and Lafontaine are also careful to balance the specific time and place that they’ve recreated with characters, and performances, that feel modern in their motives and flaws.

As Sydney, Close is necessarily tough and stubborn, but the actor brings an anxious, empathetic desperation to the father, too, who comes face to face with the masculine facade he is unintentionally passing down to his blank-slate of a boy. And Highams, of whom is asked a whole lot for such a young performer, brings as much to the role as any filmmaker could ask for.

Just as the father and son must embrace discipline and hope in equal measure, so, too, must Close and Highams remain rigidly committed to making it through their own season of trials and tribulations conjured by Belanger and Lafontaine. Well done, lads. Each and every one of you.

stories.title: This rewards program wants to help you purchase a home – no credit card required
stories.summary: Quarters is a rewards program that gives points to consumers based on their spending data
stories.author: Salmaan Farooqui
stories.content:
Rewards programs are generally geared toward travel benefits, retailers or cash back. But in 2024, Romir Joshi founded a reward program that can help you buy a house, and it doesn’t require a credit card to start using it.

Mr. Joshi’s Toronto-based company is called Quarters, and it awards points toward the purchase of a home based on the spending information found in bank accounts and credit statements.

For most consumers, shopping at partnered gas stations, grocery stores, restaurants and retail shops can generally earn between one and five cents back per dollar spent. Users grant access to their accounts through a third-party service.

For users in rural areas without major brands, Quarters automatically switches to a system that provides one cent back per dollar on almost all transactions, regardless of whether the retailer is partnered with Quarters.

Even paying your rent on time can earn you points that could take thousands of dollars off your closing costs.

Quarters is among a wave of new rewards programs that are giving points to consumers based on their spending data across all bank accounts and credit cards, rather than just one payment method. Rbc’s Avion rewards and Blue Rewards (formerly known as Air Miles) have also made it possible to earn without a credit card by processing your spending data. The novel aspect to Quarters is that it banks those rewards toward a down payment or realtor commissions, potentially saving consumers thousands of dollars on what will likely be the biggest purchase of their life.

Members who aren’t planning to purchase a home can also use their points toward a damage deposit for their rental unit.

“Our goal is to make housing rewards the next version of loyalty,” Mr. Joshi said.

“If there’s points you can use to take a flight, there should be points you can use to rent or buy a home.”

Landlords can also pay Quarters to offer their tenants more points for every dollar they spend as a way to attract renters, or to reward tenants for paying rent on time and renewing a lease early.

Mr. Joshi says the system is financially feasible because it produces income from retail brands and property managers that want to drive loyalty, and realtors that want to generate referrals. In the case of realtors, Mr. Joshi said the vast majority make only one or zero transactions a year, and they’re willing to honour the rewards because Quarters hands them clients that are already confirmed as financially sound because of their spending data.

“Every other brokerage is fighting for the same user,” said Mr. Joshi, who said brokers are competing especially hard during the current housing downturn.

“So I thought there was an opportunity to use real estate commissions as a new form of reward currency.”

Nazeer Gaffoor, an early user who started collecting rewards 18 months ago, said he redeemed roughly $8,000 in rewards from the program when he bought a home this year. He said he earned many of his points from purchases on things such as Uber Eats, which he used often as a shift worker.

The savings allowed him to make a bigger down payment, and Mr. Gaffoor said he liked how the Quarters app allowed him to activate bonus rewards offers to max his earnings.

Nilima Pathak, a user for two years living in the Toronto-area, said she has accumulated roughly $1,000 in points on everyday purchases on groceries and other household items, and the program has made the idea of buying a home one day feel a little more realistic.

“It’s been extremely hard with the cost of living to put aside money to save for a house,” Ms. Pathak said.

“These were things I was going to buy anyway, so it feels nice to not think about it and get these rewards to eventually hopefully use on a home.”

Calgary-based rewards expert Patrick Sojka says the program is worth a try because it allows you to stack your rewards on top of existing credit-card rewards, and there’s no upfront cost. For example, a Quarters member could use their Aeroplan credit card to order food on Uber Eats to earn both Aeroplan points and Quarters rewards. And because Uber Eats is a partner with both rewards programs, you would get an enhanced return rate twice.

However, Mr. Sojka said consumers should watch to see if Quarters can continue offering good return rates. He said many new rewards programs start strong and offer great returns, but they often have to pare down their benefits as early investment capital dries out and profitability becomes a concern.

Mr. Sojka added that Canada’s lack of an open banking system (a system that allows financial institutions to securely share data with each other) means that some consumers May be unwilling to trust companies such as Quarters to access their banking data through third-party applications.

Quarters is in its early stages of growth. In September, Mr. Joshi said it had roughly 10,000 members with $100-million in transaction data, with another 10 to 15 users joining daily.

The program started by offering rewards at local businesses within the GTA, but is now expanding nationally and working with larger businesses including DoorDash, McDonalds and Booster Juice.

stories.title: What Avi Lewis thinks Ottawa got wrong with Bill C-39
stories.summary: In today’s The Big Story podcast, Ottawa is furthering its pursuit of building a stronger, more sovereign Canada. Bill C-39, the Build Canada Strong Act is the latest omnibus legislation that aims to reform parts of the Canadian Labour Code, as well as streamline projects deemed of “national interest.” Critics, however, say the bill throws […]
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
In today’s The Big Story podcast, Ottawa is furthering its pursuit of building a stronger, more sovereign Canada. Bill C-39, the Build Canada Strong Act is the latest omnibus legislation that aims to reform parts of the Canadian Labour Code, as well as streamline projects deemed of “national interest.” Critics, however, say the bill throws environmental protection, Indigenous consultation and workers’ rights all into limbo.

Among those critics is Federal NDP Leader, Avi Lewis.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Mr. Lewis to discuss who he thinks gets left behind in the bill, what tweaks are needed to protect workers, and why Prime Minister Carney’s goals seem to be less in the interest of Canadians and more in the interest of foreign investors.

You can subscribe to The Big Story podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

stories.title: Five takeaways from the Quebec election results
stories.summary: The province voted in separatist Parti Québécois for the first time in more than a decade, while Coalition Avenir Québec was wiped off the map
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee, Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Quebec has voted in a separatist Parti Québécois government for the first time in more than a decade, after an election campaign marked by a desire for change and pronounced regional divisions.

The results of Monday’s election will shake up Quebec’s political landscape, with the PQ returning to power after being nearly wiped out four years ago, while the Coalition Avenir Québec is facing extinction after eight years in government.

The PQ has won a minority mandate with just 28 per cent of the vote, the lowest vote share for any government in Quebec’s history. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised his government will hold a referendum on independence within a first mandate, though not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

Here are five things to know about the Quebec election and the next chapter in the province’s political history.

The PQ victory has brought Quebec closer to a sovereignty referendum than it has been in decades, but a minority mandate will make it difficult for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon to follow through on his pledge, even if his government outlasts Mr. Trump’s time in office.

The PQ Leader reaffirmed his commitment to independence during his victory speech Monday night, calling it a “question of survival.” But the party would require support from the opposition to adopt a referendum question in the National Assembly, and the Liberals and Conservatives have both made it clear they will not play ball.

The left-leaning Québec Solidaire, which also supports sovereignty, has not said clearly whether it would support a PQ bid to hold a referendum. Co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal has called for an extensive public consultation before holding a vote on independence, and on Monday said she wants to build a country that “leaves no one behind.”

André Lamoureux, a political scientist at University of Quebec at Montreal, said a referendum will be a “dead end” for a PQ minority. “There are too many obstacles,” he added.

The arrival of a PQ government could herald a thornier relationship between Quebec City and Ottawa, as Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon looks to bolster support for independence. At a time when threats to Canada’s sovereignty are coming from both inside and outside the country, the PQ Leader’s agenda could be an irritant for Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette sought to build ties with the federal government, and appeared alongside Mr. Carney at several announcements in recent months. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon pointed to those announcements as evidence of federal interference in the Quebec election intended to benefit the CAQ.

Late in the campaign, the PQ Leader vowed to break with the monarchy in Quebec if he became premier, promising to pass a law to abolish the office of lieutenant-governor. Critics say such a move would likely be subject to a constitutional challenge.

On Monday, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said he is willing to collaborate with Mr. Carney. “He will find in me someone who is direct, frank, and transparent – but above all, someone who will defend, first and foremost and at all times, the interests of the people of Quebec.”

After winning two majority mandates in 2018 and 2022, the Coalition Avenir Québec was wiped off the map on Monday, losing every one of its 79 seats. It was a dramatic fall from grace, prompting speculation that the party May disappear altogether.

The CAQ rose to power eight years ago as an alternative to the federalist Liberals and the separatist PQ, promising a nationalist government that would not hold a referendum on independence. After the party’s first victory, it seemed the decades-old debate over sovereignty might have been permanently shelved.

Now, however, it seems the CAQ May have been “just a parenthesis in our political history,” said political analyst Raphaël Melançon. “It seems like we’re going back to these old battles.”

The Quebec electorate expressed a clear desire for change on Monday, with more than 90 of the province’s 127 seats switching hands. But voters remained divided throughout the six-week campaign about the kind of change they wanted to see. The PQ’s victory and the Caq’s collapse in the final seat count mask the fact that all five main parties won between 12 per cent and 28 per cent of the vote.

Though a PQ government was declared shortly after polls closed Monday evening, tight races played out in ridings across the province. Early Tuesday morning, candidates were leading or elected by fewer than 1,000 votes in 15 seats.

The final map shows important regional divisions. The Liberals have retained their traditional stronghold in ridings in and around Montreal, while the left-leaning Québec Solidaire held onto a handful of urban seats in Montreal and Quebec City.

The Conservatives, meanwhile, claimed seats in Quebec City and surrounding regions.

The real winner Monday night was arguably Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, who led his party to claim seats in the National Assembly for the first time. With 19 seats, the Conservatives will obtain official party status in the Quebec legislature and could hold the balance of power.

A Conservative party had not won seats in Quebec since 1935, after which the original party was dissolved to form the right-leaning Union Nationale, which would govern the province for the next two decades under the leadership of Maurice Duplessis.

The modern iteration of the party was founded in 2009 and has been led by Mr. Duhaime since 2021. He campaigned on major cuts to taxes, public sector jobs and government spending and has promised to act as a watchdog to guard against government waste.

On Monday, Mr. Duhaime said the Conservatives will embody Quebeckers’ desire for change. “Finally, hope will be present within the walls of the National Assembly.”

stories.title: Demolition plan turns the birthplace of ringette into a political arena
stories.summary: In 1963, North Bay created a new Canadian sport. Now, a debate about that legacy threatens to spill into the Ontario town’s municipal elections
stories.author: Patrick White, Photography by Cory Wright
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections.

The Pete Palangio Arena in North Bay has all the shabby charm of 100 other arenas in 100 other Canadian towns, right down to the olfactory bouquet of rubber mats and foot sweat.

But on this busy Thursday night, there’s a key difference here: tranquility.

As a dozen high-school-age members of the West Ferris 63s hustle up and down the ice, they swish a blue rubber ring from stick to stick. There’s no rifle-crack of pucks, no barking coaches, no bodies crashing against the boards. “It’s nothing like hockey,” says Steve Hamilton, a long-time ringette referee and coach keeping a close eye on the scrimmage. “It’s got a real strategy to it. It’s like a combination of basketball and lacrosse on ice.”

Ringette is North Bay’s gift to the world. Invented in 1963 in this northeastern Ontario city of roughly 60,000 people, its popularity stalled in the 1990s, when the arrival of women’s Olympic hockey began drawing girls away from the sport and created uncertainty around ringette’s future. Now, the sport is slated to lose a piece of its storied past.

On the other side of North Bay from Pete Palangio, the arena considered the place where ringette was born is slated for possible demolition. Some residents have vowed to make the preservation of that building, the now-shuttered West Ferris Centennial Community Centre, an issue in coming municipal elections.

Rinks form the social backbone of countless Canadian towns and cities, yet half of all single-pad arenas need urgent refurbishment, according to Statistics Canada. Those costs often stretch cash-strapped municipalities, leaving few options aside from demolition.

“We can’t keep tearing down our history,” said Bill Antler, who’s leading a local charge to save the rink. “That’s the birthplace of ringette. That’s the history of North Bay. That’s women’s sports history. You can’t do that.”

The origins of ringette can be traced to the Great Depression, when a director at Toronto’s West End YMCA, Sam Jacks, developed rules for floor hockey, then played with broomsticks and a felt ring.

Almost 30 years later, in 1963, recreation directors in Northern Ontario wanted to come up with a no-contact sport for girls that would break up the male domination of ice sports in the region. By then, Mr. Jacks was North Bay’s head of parks and recreation. He suggested a version of his ring-based floor hockey game – but played on ice.

There was just one problem. Hockey ruled North Bay. Team managers and local bureaucrats had no interest in giving up ice time to an experimental girls’ sport. The first games had to be played 200 kilometres away, in Espanola, fuelling perpetual arguments over the game’s true birthplace.

When West Ferris opened in 1967, its manager, Don Pecore, battled hockey leagues and municipal politicians to secure three hours of ice a week for ringette, according to his memoir.

Karen Cook recalls sitting in grade school when someone came to recruit players. “They said all we needed was our mother’s broom handle, skates and a helmet,” she recalled.

She played her first season outdoors before moving into West Ferris. “That rink was the centre of the universe – for us, if not for the entire sport,” she said.

By the 1980s, there were 50,000 players across the country, with sizable involvement in Finland, Sweden and the U.S. Big games featured prominently on CBC and TSN. Ms. Cook led efforts to erect a highway sign declaring North Bay the birthplace of ringette in 2005. A few years later, the sport got its own postage stamp.

But much of the 2000s marked a period of stagnation. Registration plateaued at around 30,000 players as women’s hockey boomed from 8,000 players in 1990 to 120,000 today.

The highway sign is gone now, and city staff say the arena has reached its end. Inspections have found cracks in the rink walls and foundation. The brine piping system needs a $2-million replacement, and the heaters have been defunct for years. A full renovation would likely cost upward of $12.4-million, the price Orillia recently paid to upgrade Brian Orser Arena.

With the recent completion of a $63-million twin-pad facility, North Bay has five rinks without West Ferris, enough to meet demand in an environment where boys’ hockey and ringette participation are both declining, according to reports commissioned by the city.

In May, the infrastructure committee voted to demolish the 59-year-old rink. Council later punted the decision back to committee, effectively delaying any decision on the rink’s fate until after the Oct. 26 municipal election.

Mayor Peter Chirico, who is not running for re-election, cast the lone vote against a delay, saying the millions of dollars required to renovate a surplus rink would be wasteful.

The council vote came after a presentation from Mr. Antler, a self-described rink rat who spent much of his youth in the arena.

He said none of the publicly shared reports show fatal flaws in the structure and that rink participation studies are inaccurate.

“I wouldn’t be surprised to see it become one of the major issues in the election,” he said.

Mr. Antler co-chairs a golf tournament that has raised hundreds of thousands of dollars for the Nipissing Association for Disabled Youth and attracts the likes of retired NHLers Doug Gilmour and Wendel Clark. He has offered to help raise money for rink repairs.

Not everyone is convinced.

“For us, the rink means a lot,” said West Ferris Ringette Association president Erin Johns. “It was our home arena. It was the birthplace of ringette. But change is inevitable. We have to embrace the new.”

Ms. Cook said she’ll understand if the building must come down for engineering reasons, but she won’t like it. She hopes the city will work to recognize ringette and the Jacks family in the new arena.

“We’re all going to cry our eyes out if it’s knocked down,” she said.

stories.title: Toronto home sales fall for second straight month
stories.summary: The decline comes during a worsening trade dispute with the U.S., rising borrowing costs and prolonged war in the Middle East
stories.author: Rachelle Younglai
stories.content:
Toronto home sales fell 5.2 per cent in September, declining for the second straight month as higher mortgage rates and economic uncertainty weighed on prospective buyers.

There were 5,174 sales last month after removing seasonal influences, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board. Before August’s drop in purchases, there had been five months of increasing sales.

“We started to see sales ebb as we moved into fall,” Jason Mercer, the board’s chief information officer, said in an interview.

Mr. Mercer attributed the reversal to the worsening trade dispute with the U.S., the prolonged war in the Middle East and rising borrowing costs.

Although mortgage rates did not immediately increase when Canada walked away from trade talks with the U.S. in August, home loans are starting to become more expensive.

The five-year fixed mortgage rate from national lenders averaged 4.87 per cent in early October, according to data from Wowa.CA , a personal finance website that tracks mortgage rates. That compares to 4.62 per cent in mid-August, prior to the collapse of the trade talks.

The last time monthly sales dropped this much was in February, when the number of transactions declined by 5.2 per cent.

Home values also fell for the second straight month. The home price index, which is the industry’s preferred measure, was $924,600 in September, according to the board. That was a month-over-month decrease of 0.5 per cent, after a 0.2-per-cent fall in August.

Compared to last September, the home price index was down 4.8 per cent. Condos continue to lose the most value, falling 6.7 per cent year over year.

Overall, condos in the city of Toronto did not lose as much value as the areas to the west and north of the city. In the Peel and York regions, the home price index for condos fell more than 8 per cent year over year.

Mr. Mercer said prospective homebuyers want to take advantage of the lower prices. But he said in a press release that they need confidence that “their employment situation will remain solid and inflation will not put pressure on borrowing costs over the long term.”

Last month, the number of homeowners that put their properties up for sale declined. New listings fell 3.8 per cent month over month.

stories.title: Five takeways from Quebec election as Parti Québécois forms minority government
stories.summary: Quebec voters elected a Parti Québécois minority government Monday, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec voters elected a Parti Québécois minority government Monday, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.

The PQ won 59 seats out of 127 seats in the Quebec legislature.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon gave a victory speech in Montreal after his party was projected to form a minority government in Quebec. In the Eastern Townships region, Liberal party leader Charles Milliard promised to be a unifying force and a balance to the new government's promise of a referendum. (Oct. 6, 2026)

Here are five takeaways from the evening.

1. PQ comes back from the brink

After being reduced to three seats in the 2022 election, the Parti Québécois stormed back to form a government, falling five seats short of the 64 needed to form a majority in the Quebec legislature. The party was able to capitalize on Quebecers’ desire for change after eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec rule in the province.

2. PQ has promised a referendum

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon won his party’s leadership in 2020 with a promise to hold a referendum if he formed a government. Although his party fell short of a majority government, he May have an opportunity to work with Québec solidaire, a left-wing sovereigntist party that could support his plans to stage a referendum after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029. The Parti Québécois and Québec solidaire combined for more than 40 per cent of the popular vote on Monday evening. Together, the two sovereigntist parties also captured a majority of the seats in the national assembly.

3. Quebec Liberals form strong Opposition

Voters chose the Quebec Liberals as the official Opposition for the third general election in a row. The party more than doubled its seats in the legislature, finishing the evening with 40 elected members. Leader Charles Milliard said his party was the only federalist party committed to remaining in Canada, although he is not the only leader who has pledged to block plans for a referendum.

4. Quebec Conservatives elected for first time in modern Quebec history

Conservatives last elected a member to the Quebec legislature in 1935. The party will now form a strong contingent in the legislature with a caucus of 19. Under Éric Duhaime’s leadership, the party surged from a marginal formation that captured less than two per cent of the vote in 2018 to a main player. The party ran a campaign that was largely targeted on key ridings, after failing to capture a seat in 2022 despite getting close to 13 per cent of the vote. Duhaime has also pledged to stop the PQ from staging a referendum on sovereignty.

5. A fragmented political landscape

Five parties ended the evening with more than 10 per cent of the vote and none had more than 30 per cent of the votes that were counted. The PQ came close to forming a majority government, even though it only received about 28 per cent of the total number of votes counted on Monday. The Liberals had about 24 per cent, while the Conservatives had about 21 per cent. Coalition Avenir Québec had about 13 per cent of the vote, but failed to win any seats, while Québec solidaire, which had about 12 per cent of the vote, won nine seats.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Victoria - The British Columbia Conservatives plan to repeal the province’s no-fault auto insurance system, in a major policy proposal revealed by a leaked letter from the party’s interim leader to lawyers and insurance executives.

Lorne Doerkson says in the letter that if elected on Oct. 24, the Conservatives would bring in legislation to restore accident victims’ rights to sue, under a new “hybrid system” designed to keep rates affordable while protecting people hurt by reckless drivers.

stories.title: A buy Canadian Thanksgiving dinner is well within reach — and budget, experts say
stories.summary: Experts say an all-Canadian meal on a budget isn't hard, as long as it's grounded in the abundance of harvest season and simple recipes.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

Posted October 6, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated October 6, 2026 5:47 am.

A slow-roasted turkey, buttery stuffing, root vegetables tossed in rosemary and olive oil, creamy mashed potatoes and a cranberry sauce forgotten in the fridge.

It sounds like a table set for Thanksgiving dinner.

A resurgence of patriotism among Canadians have some looking more closely at ingredients and product origins to make sure their festivities are really about celebrating the bounties of the country’s harvest — and whether it’s possible to serve that Canadian-sourced feast within a budget.

Experts say an all-Canadian meal on a budget isn’t hard, as long as it’s grounded in the abundance of harvest season and simple recipes.

“Thanksgiving is really a harvest feast or harvest festival and coincides with peak agricultural production in Canada,” said Paul van der Werf, adjunct professor at Ivey Business School at Western University in London, Ont.

“Canada produces lots of turkey, lots of potatoes. It’s the world’s second-biggest producer of cranberries,” he said.

Ontario alone produced 45 per cent of the country’s turkey in 2025, according to Statistics Canada. Meanwhile, the country hit an all-time high in potato production in 2024, it said in a separate report.

Van der Werf said a classic Thanksgiving meal is Canadian through and through.

“We’ve always had this real abundance of Canadian agricultural products of world-class quality,” he said.

“We’ve been reminded through geopolitical events that, ‘Hey, you know what, maybe we’ll want to think about that a bit more.'”

Renewed trade tensions with the United States have many shoppers once again examining labels for information about their origin and production. But defining what’s Canadian is not always easy with North America’s intertwined food supply chains.

For example, U.S.-based co-op Ocean Spray processes some Canadian cranberries into a jelly sauce.

Knowing what labels mean is important when zeroing in on Canadian-made items, whether that’s based on the origin of ingredients, manufacturing plants or who owns the brand, said Jeff Stewart, executive director of non-profit Food Day Canada, which promotes Canadian food culture.

He said convenience is often why people go for boxed or prepared foods, such as stuffing or a box of store-bought mashed potatoes. But it May be hard to know how much of that food is truly local.

Stewart suggested working backwards with a holiday menu to keep it local and within budget: walk around the grocery store or farmers market to see what’s in season. Then build a menu as you go.

“Whatever is in abundance is what you’re going to find the best prices on,” said Stewart, who is also a chef in Elora, Ont.

Farmers usually harvest a wide array of fresh produce in the fall — pumpkins, squash, potatoes, apples and pears. But if shoppers are looking for blueberries, which finished harvest season last month, they would likely pay more for the imported fruit.

The menu would also look different, based on where you live — mirroring what the region has to offer.

For Stewart, an Ontario celebration would mean a homegrown turkey. “(But) if I was in British Columbia with my brothers, probably there’d be some kind of fish.”

But pantry items can thwart attempts to serve a 100-per-cent-Canadian meal.

A pumpkin or apple pie without a tinge of cinnamon or nutmeg May not feel quite right, for example. But Canada doesn’t grow spices such as cinnamon and black pepper or produce olive oil.

“You can get the pumpkins here, you can get the flour here, you get all the ingredients of your pumpkin pie here except for cinnamon,” van der Werf said.

“Cinnamon probably makes up 0.1 per cent of the pie, so maybe that’s OK.”

Sugar is produced with imported sugar cane, and some brands such as Redpath are owned by American multinationals. But there are some substitutions to make it truly local, such as sugar beets that are grown in southern Alberta and processed at the Rogers factory in Taber, Alta., he said.

Stewart said grounding the menu in simpler recipes can also make the journey easier.

“I remember back to meals with my grandparents and the effort that was put into things a long time ago, when there weren’t options for this kind of convenience,” he said. “Maybe it’s time for people to think about simpler things in simpler times and go back to some of the ways that were maybe forgotten or maybe never learned.”

Serving a truly Canadian meal can take effort, Stewart said.

“If you choose to go 100 per cent Canadian, then you’ll find that you’ll get there, even if it’s a little bit difficult at first,” he said.

“If you make the commitment, then over time, it gets easier and easier.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: 37 fallen stars: Starbucks’ grinds down Canadian locations.
stories.summary: Starbucks has recently closed over 37 locations in Canada, two of which were in London. The two closed Starbuc...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
Starbucks has recently closed over 37 locations in Canada, two of which were in London. The two closed Starbucks restaurants were located downtown at Richmond St, and the other being on the east side of London at Hamilton Rd. Sharmishta Nag, a professor in the Lawrence Kinlan School of Business, says that Starbucks May be facing issues due to what made it famous in the first place, it’s customization.

“T he workers at Starbucks, they get their pay is higher than the average pay (of baristas),” she said. “T he drinks are so customized. So with that customized drink, they are spending more time making a drink. So therefore, they are expected to pay higher wages.”

“I t increases more people waiting in line. So that that reduces the store’s operational efficiency,” Kinlan added. “ I will order from somewhere else, which will be where I get it faster. “

Despite the closure of these Starbucks locations in London, Devika Kumar, the supervisor at the Starbucks location at Fanshawe College, says that she is not concerned about Starbucks potentially closing her location.

“W e are licensee stores, and those are corporate stores,” said Kumar. “I’ve seen most of the corporate stores being shut down, but the licensee stores have been there for a while.”

stories.title: QuickQuotes: Leaders react as Parti Québécois forms minority government
stories.summary: Montreal - The Parti Québécois is projected to form a minority government, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Parti Québécois is projected to form a minority government, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.

The PQ was elected in 59 ridings by late Monday, putting it on track to return to power for the first time in more than a decade.

The Liberals were elected in 40 ridings, the Conservatives were elected in 19 and Québec solidaire were elected in nine.

The Coalition Avenir Québec, which entered the election as the governing party, failed to win a seat and was wiped off the electoral map.

Liberal cabinet ministers react after Quebec elected the Parti Québécois in a provincial election on Oct. 5. Public Works Minister Joël Lightbound says a majority of Quebecers feel, as he does, that Quebec is stronger as part of Canada and the focus will remain building a resilient economy, including in Quebec. (Oct. 6, 2026)

Here are some key quotes from party leaders as the results came in on Monday evening:

“Quebecers have spoken tonight. They decided to elect a Parti Québécois government while also asking it to work with the other parties. I understand that message perfectly, and I will do everything I can to live up to what Quebecers are asking of us.”

— Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon

“(The result) means that the Parti Québécois does not have all the powers to do whatever they want. They’re going to have to discuss, collaborate, and we’ll be collaborating on some issues, but obviously not on the main issue (of a referendum).”

— Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard

“Hope is being reborn in Quebec, because tonight we have just written a page of history. For the first time in 100 years, Quebecers have decided to send a large caucus of Conservative MNAs to the National Assembly.”

— Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime

“What a great campaign. We resisted. It felt like we were starting from pretty far behind. But damn, we fought like only the left knows how to fight.”

— Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal

“Quebecers have spoken. Their choice is clear. I respect it. The result is clearly not the one we were hoping for. And as leader, I take full responsibility. Not our candidates, not our activists, not our volunteers. Me.”

— Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon gave a victory speech in Montreal after his party was projected to form a minority government in Quebec. In the Eastern Townships region, Liberal party leader Charles Milliard promised to be a unifying force and a balance to the new government's promise of a referendum. (Oct. 6, 2026)

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: ‘Luxury’ Muskoka rehab with fake nurses, no on-site doctor is forced into bankruptcy
stories.summary: Muskoka Recovery was the focus of a Star investigation into the "Wild West" of private addiction treatment centres in Ontario.
stories.author: Kevin Donovan
stories.content:
A “luxury” Muskoka addiction clinic staffed with fake nurses and no doctor has been forced into bankruptcy by creditors amid allegations of sexual abuse and a suspicious death.

When it opened, Muskoka Recovery was billed as the perfect place to beat an addiction to drugs and alcohol — a log-and-stone cottage in a serene location on a dead-end road in lake country. It promised trained therapists, 24/7 medical care, counselling, massage and yoga. Clients with serious addictions paid between $30,000 and $150,000 for a six-week stay.

But as the Star found in its late 2024 investigation , the claims were false. None of the staff had the credentials the clinic promised. Clients interviewed by the Star said they noticed numerous problems. Among them, the clinical director liked to party in a hot tub with staff; the only “therapy” they received came from PowerPoint reels and YouTube videos; and clients were left unattended and unmonitored during the all-important “detoxification” phase, when drugs and alcohol are cleared from a person’s system and withdrawal symptoms can be severe.

One person arriving for treatment reported he was first taken to a bar and allowed to have several drinks before being driven to the clinic; clients interviewed by the Star said they would have been better off not going.

Two creditors — the Bank of Montreal, which loaned the clinic $5.5 million, and the wife of a co-manager of the clinic — have successfully petitioned a court to push Muskoka Recovery into bankruptcy. Last August, Justice Jana Steele of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice appointed the firm of Albert Gelman Inc. as receiver, according to court records.

Muskoka Recovery has been shuttered since the summer, though earlier this year an attempt was made by the owners to rebrand it as “The Northern Lights.” The still-functioning website of the rebranded clinic promises those addicted to alcohol and drugs “compassionate support and evidence-based therapies” in a “serene environment.” Where Muskoka Recovery made promises of professional medical and trained therapists, Northern Lights advertisements are more carefully worded, saying people being treated had “access” to that type of care.

“Our unwavering priority has been the well-being of our clients and their loved ones as they navigate mental health challenges including substance

Frank, a former client who was interviewed for the Star series (the Star used clients’ first names to protect their privacy while recovering from addictions), said he was pleased to hear the clinic is closed. Muskoka Recovery was a “house of horrors,” Frank said.

“People with zero credentials in addiction treatment should not be allowed to run a clinic,” said Frank. “I also think there needs to be legislation in place that oversees places like this.”

After the Star series was published, there were calls from legitimate clinics for a regulatory scheme run by the government. But the province said that was not necessary, since all professionals — nurses, doctors, therapists — were overseen by their own regulatory colleges. As the Star series showed, none of the people working at the clinic were licensed professionals.

The Star found that Damien Delaney, the clinical director, had recently been found guilty of professional misconduct by the Ontario College of Social Workers and Social Service Workers for having sex with a client from another addiction rehab clinic where he had worked.

At one point, Delaney was filmed by a resident in the Muskoka Recovery hot tub, with loud music playing, when clients were inside going through the detoxification stage of treatment.

The people at the centre of Muskoka Recovery were Ewa Ricci and Ralph Canonaco, who had previously partnered in real estate projects. In 2021, they purchased the 10-bedroom cottage on 25 acres near Lake Muskoka, paying $2.6 million. “Recover in affordable luxury” read the sign down the road, beckoning people with addictions to choose this clinic to heal and recover. Their “silent partner” was Canonaco’s wife, who has said in court pleadings that she invested to help her husband, who was himself recovering from an addiction.

Business was so good in the first few years that the clinic secured a $5.5-million loan from Bank of Montreal to expand. She had plans to double the number of client beds. The bank loan was secured by the Muskoka clinic property and three small properties in nearby Gravenhurst.

The co-owners of Muskoka recovery, developers Eva Ricci, left, and Ralph Canonaco, centre, with Damien Delaney, the clinical director, seen right in a still from video taken on-site.

The bank, in court filings, said the Star’s stories in 2024 “raised serious concerns,” both for “the well-being of patients and the risk to the bank’s loans.”

The court documents do not describe what due diligence was done by Bank of Montreal before the loan was provided. As the Star found, Ricci and Canonaco had no experience in this type of business.

Seeing the story on the front page of the Star, the bank immediately asked for “a quarterly profit and loss statement.” The bank said that when it did not receive this statement, it demanded immediate repayment. When Muskoka Recovery did not repay the $5.5 million owing, the bank went to court to have a receiver appointed.

Around the same time, Corradina (Cora) Canonaco, the wife of Ralph Canonaco, went to court, saying the clinic owed her money. Cora, in her pleadings, said she was a 50 per cent silent partner in Muskoka Recovery. She said she went into business with Ricci because she wanted to “support” her husband.

Part two of a two-part investigation into the “Wild West” of private addiction treatment centres in Ontario.

Cora said that when her husband told her the Star was about to do an investigative series on the clinic, she became concerned, as she was a part owner with Ricci. Cora said both Ricci and her husband told her everything the Star then published was “false,” according to her bankruptcy pleadings.

Soon after the Star series was published, business dropped off. Cora said Ricci shut her out of any of the decision-making related to the clinic. Cora then tried to get Ricci to sell all the assets. When that failed, Cora went to court to get a receiver appointed, putting Muskoka Recovery into bankruptcy. The bank filed documents supporting Cora.

As receiver, Albert Gelman Inc. has full authority over the business, including the power to sell assets to pay off creditors. As this process only began in late summer, the public files do not yet reveal what actions have been taken. Neither the receiver, Ralph Canonaco, nor Ricci have responded to requests for comment.

A promotional photo of the former Muskoka Recovery addiction clinic.

Meanwhile, at least three separate court actions against Muskoka Recovery are making their way through the courts.

A group of former clients have launched a $40-million lawsuit against Muskoka Recovery, alleging the owners and staff “deliberately and systemically misled, lured, financially exploited, abused and endangered vulnerable people seeking treatment at the facility,” according to a statement of claim filed in Ontario’s Superior Court of Justice. The suit alleges that people trying to get off drugs were given the same drugs they were addicted to and that, in one case, the rehab’s owners told a suicidal patient “only weak people kill themselves.”

When the former clients filed the joint lawsuit, Domenic Saverino, a lawyer for the defendants, told the Star: “My clients will vehemently defend this action and will only present their Defence and position in the court proceedings.”

Meanwhile, the family of the late Dawn Susanne Rose is suing Muskoka Recovery, alleging the clinic was responsible for the death of Rose, who went for treatment, suffered a seizure and died. A “wrongful death” lawsuit against Muskoka Recovery alleges clinic staff were negligent, breached a duty of care, and misrepresented the type of treatment available at the clinic.

In a third suit, a woman described in a court action with the pseudonym “Samantha Doe” has sued Muskoka Recovery, alleging she “suffered serious harm” as a result of the “sexualized and other misconduct” of a senior staff member at the clinic while she was undergoing treatment for substance abuse.

None of these allegations have been tested in court.
paragraphs: A “luxury” Muskoka addiction clinic staffed with fake nurses and no doctor has been forced into bankruptcy by creditors amid allegations of sexual abuse and a suspicious death.

When it opened, Muskoka Recovery was billed as the perfect place to beat an addiction to drugs and alcohol — a log-and-stone cottage in a serene location on a dead-end road in lake country. It promised trained therapists, 24/7 medical care, counselling, massage and yoga. Clients with serious addictions paid between $30,000 and $150,000 for a six-week stay.

But as the Star found in its late 2024 investigation , the claims were false. None of the staff had the credentials the clinic promised. Clients interviewed by the Star said they noticed numerous problems. Among them, the clinical director liked to party in a hot tub with staff; the only “therapy” they received came from PowerPoint reels and YouTube videos; and clients were left unattended and unmonitored during the all-important “detoxification” phase, when drugs and alcohol are cleared from a person’s system and withdrawal symptoms can be severe.

One person arriving for treatment reported he was first taken to a bar and allowed to have several drinks before being driven to the clinic; clients interviewed by the Star said they would have been better off not going.

Two creditors — the Bank of Montreal, which loaned the clinic $5.5 million, and the wife of a co-manager of the clinic — have successfully petitioned a court to push Muskoka Recovery into bankruptcy. Last August, Justice Jana Steele of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice appointed the firm of Albert Gelman Inc. as receiver, according to court records.

Muskoka Recovery has been shuttered since the summer, though earlier this year an attempt was made by the owners to rebrand it as “The Northern Lights.” The still-functioning website of the rebranded clinic promises those addicted to alcohol and drugs “compassionate support and evidence-based therapies” in a “serene environment.” Where Muskoka Recovery made promises of professional medical and trained therapists, Northern Lights advertisements are more carefully worded, saying people being treated had “access” to that type of care.
“Our unwavering priority has been the well-being of our clients and their loved ones as they navigate mental health challenges including substance

Frank, a former client who was interviewed for the Star series (the Star used clients’ first names to protect their privacy while recovering from addictions), said he was pleased to hear the clinic is closed. Muskoka Recovery was a “house of horrors,” Frank said.
“People with zero credentials in addiction treatment should not be allowed to run a clinic,” said Frank. “I also think there needs to be legislation in place that oversees places like this.”

After the Star series was published, there were calls from legitimate clinics for a regulatory scheme run by the government. But the province said that was not necessary, since all professionals — nurses, doctors, therapists — were overseen by their own regulatory colleges. As the Star series showed, none of the people working at the clinic were licensed professionals.

The Star found that Damien Delaney, the clinical director, had recently been found guilty of professional misconduct by the Ontario College of Social Workers and Social Service Workers for having sex with a client from another addiction rehab clinic where he had worked.
At one point, Delaney was filmed by a resident in the Muskoka Recovery hot tub, with loud music playing, when clients were inside going through the detoxification stage of treatment.

The people at the centre of Muskoka Recovery were Ewa Ricci and Ralph Canonaco, who had previously partnered in real estate projects. In 2021, they purchased the 10-bedroom cottage on 25 acres near Lake Muskoka, paying $2.6 million. “Recover in affordable luxury” read the sign down the road, beckoning people with addictions to choose this clinic to heal and recover. Their “silent partner” was Canonaco’s wife, who has said in court pleadings that she invested to help her husband, who was himself recovering from an addiction.

Business was so good in the first few years that the clinic secured a $5.5-million loan from Bank of Montreal to expand. She had plans to double the number of client beds. The bank loan was secured by the Muskoka clinic property and three small properties in nearby Gravenhurst.
The co-owners of Muskoka recovery, developers Eva Ricci, left, and Ralph Canonaco, centre, with Damien Delaney, the clinical director, seen right in a still from video taken on-site.
The bank, in court filings, said the Star’s stories in 2024 “raised serious concerns,” both for “the well-being of patients and the risk to the bank’s loans.”
The court documents do not describe what due diligence was done by Bank of Montreal before the loan was provided. As the Star found, Ricci and Canonaco had no experience in this type of business.

Seeing the story on the front page of the Star, the bank immediately asked for “a quarterly profit and loss statement.” The bank said that when it did not receive this statement, it demanded immediate repayment. When Muskoka Recovery did not repay the $5.5 million owing, the bank went to court to have a receiver appointed.

Around the same time, Corradina (Cora) Canonaco, the wife of Ralph Canonaco, went to court, saying the clinic owed her money. Cora, in her pleadings, said she was a 50 per cent silent partner in Muskoka Recovery. She said she went into business with Ricci because she wanted to “support” her husband.
Part two of a two-part investigation into the “Wild West” of private addiction treatment centres in Ontario.

Cora said that when her husband told her the Star was about to do an investigative series on the clinic, she became concerned, as she was a part owner with Ricci. Cora said both Ricci and her husband told her everything the Star then published was “false,” according to her bankruptcy pleadings.

Soon after the Star series was published, business dropped off. Cora said Ricci shut her out of any of the decision-making related to the clinic. Cora then tried to get Ricci to sell all the assets. When that failed, Cora went to court to get a receiver appointed, putting Muskoka Recovery into bankruptcy. The bank filed documents supporting Cora.

As receiver, Albert Gelman Inc. has full authority over the business, including the power to sell assets to pay off creditors. As this process only began in late summer, the public files do not yet reveal what actions have been taken. Neither the receiver, Ralph Canonaco, nor Ricci have responded to requests for comment.

stories.title: Gillian Steward: Danielle Smith finds out that playing both sides of the fence is a losing strategy
stories.summary: It’s about time Smith got caught in her own trap. Pushing separation while at the same time pretending to be a federalist was never going to work.
stories.author: Gillian Steward
stories.content:
The Alberta referendum on separation is less than two weeks away and it appears most Albertans have decided they want to remain in Canada; not just by a simple majority but overwhelmingly. That’s a relief. Now those voters just have to turn out to cast a ballot.

In a recent poll , 72 per cent of Albertans said they wanted to stay in Canada, while only 23 per cent would choose the option to hold a second vote on a binding referendum on separating the province from the rest of the country. The poll was carried out by the queen of pollsters in Alberta, Janet Brown Opinion Research, for the CBC.

That’s a definite softening of the separatist vote — about a 6 per cent drop in support from April when the last poll was taken.

Brown also discovered that Prime Minister Mark Carney is more popular in Alberta than Premier Danielle Smith . Fifty-two per cent of Albertans said they were very impressed with Carney while only 30 per cent said the same about Smith; 51 per cent were not at all impressed.

Carney’s favourable standing in the province is no doubt due to his promises about the west coast oil pipeline — Pacific Link. In Fort McMurray, Thursday he announced that it had been approved as a project of national interest , another step forward to getting shovels in the ground by the fall of 2027. The timing — just before the referendum — will undoubtedly convince some undecided voters to choose to remain in Canada.

From left, Scott Burrows, CEO of the Pembina Pipeline Corp, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney shake hands after speaking in Fort McMurray on Thursday. Prime Minister Mark Carney declared the Pacific Link pipeline project to be in the national interest.

The poll also suggested that Smith is losing support to the NDP, the official opposition. Three weeks ago Smith’s United Conservative Party lost a byelection to the NDP in a heavily conservative Calgary constituency. The results of the Brown poll found that Smith’s overall support had dropped by 10 per cent, which left her in a tie with NDP leader Naheed Nenshi.

Brown says it appears the party is shedding support on both sides of the independence debate: from separatists who wish Smith had taken their side, and federalists frustrated by the question in the first place.

True to form, Smith is not actually campaigning for a “yes” vote. The provincial government’s $4 million advertising campaign about the separation

“She’s trying to walk the middle of the road, between the moderate, business conservatives and the far-right populist base that’s still angry over COVID restrictions,” said John Santos, data scientist with Janet Brown Opinion Research.

“And she’s getting hit by traffic on both sides of the road.”

Another surprise from the poll : Among those polled who said they would vote for the UCP, 53 per cent said they’d vote for the separation option. Forty per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada. That trumped all demographic groups studied by Brown and her team

It’s about time Smith got caught in her own trap. Pushing separation while at the same time pretending to be a federalist was never going to work. She’s been doing it for so long now voters have had a chance to see through the ruse. They don’t approve and are supporting a unified Canada.

Smith can read polls too and obviously decided the separatists would lose. But she kept throwing them red meat by continuing to blame the federal government at every opportunity for all the “problems” plaguing Alberta.

Concerns over lineups contributed to what Elections Alberta is reporting as a surge in requests for mail-in ballots, also known as special ballots.

She and her advisers concocted the 10 questions, nine of which are contradictory and confusing. And she muddled the last question on separation from Canada by giving voters two options; vote to stay, or vote for a second binding referendum on separation to be held at some future date. Likely next year.

The referendum with its 10 complicated questions is a waste of time and money — last count about $130 million. But here we are, all because Smith wanted to save her premiership and remain in power.

She could have tackled the separatist leanings after she was elected leader of the UCP and automatically became premier. But instead, at the opening of the Legislature she introduced the Alberta Sovereignty Act, which later became the Alberta Sovereignty Act within a United Canada. And that was just the beginning of her tirades against the federal government.

But it didn’t pay off, which she is just beginning to realize.

Brown says it appears the party is shedding support on both sides of the independence debate: from separatists who wish Smith had taken their side, and federalists frustrated by the question in the first place.
True to form, Smith is not actually campaigning for a “yes” vote. The provincial government’s $4 million advertising campaign about the separation

“She’s trying to walk the middle of the road, between the moderate, business conservatives and the far-right populist base that’s still angry over COVID restrictions,” said John Santos, data scientist with Janet Brown Opinion Research.
“And she’s getting hit by traffic on both sides of the road.”

Another surprise from the poll : Among those polled who said they would vote for the UCP, 53 per cent said they’d vote for the separation option. Forty per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada. That trumped all demographic groups studied by Brown and her team

It’s about time Smith got caught in her own trap. Pushing separation while at the same time pretending to be a federalist was never going to work. She’s been doing it for so long now voters have had a chance to see through the ruse. They don’t approve and are supporting a unified Canada.

Smith can read polls too and obviously decided the separatists would lose. But she kept throwing them red meat by continuing to blame the federal government at every opportunity for all the “problems” plaguing Alberta.
Concerns over lineups contributed to what Elections Alberta is reporting as a surge in requests for mail-in ballots, also known as special ballots.

She and her advisers concocted the 10 questions, nine of which are contradictory and confusing. And she muddled the last question on separation from Canada by giving voters two options; vote to stay, or vote for a second binding referendum on separation to be held at some future date. Likely next year.
The referendum with its 10 complicated questions is a waste of time and money — last count about $130 million. But here we are, all because Smith wanted to save her premiership and remain in power.

She could have tackled the separatist leanings after she was elected leader of the UCP and automatically became premier. But instead, at the opening of the Legislature she introduced the Alberta Sovereignty Act, which later became the Alberta Sovereignty Act within a United Canada. And that was just the beginning of her tirades against the federal government.
But it didn’t pay off, which she is just beginning to realize.

ByEdward Keenan Columnist

Good morning. This is the Tuesday, Oct. 6 edition of First Up, the Star’s daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox.

Municipal election day across Ontario isn’t until Oct. 26, but advance voting starts today in Toronto (and Mississauga and some other cities). So if you’ve already decided who you’re voting for, you can go lock it in. If you’re still making up your mind, I’m moderating a debate of Toronto’s mayoral candidates this evening at 7 p.m. that will be livestreamed at thestar.com. And you can compare your ideas to those of the candidates through our Vote Compass tool, which is free to use. More on the elections in a moment.

But first up, here are six things to know on Tuesday morning.

Quebec voters elected a sovereigntist Parti Québécois minority government on Monday. Here are some takeaways from the election.

The public safety minister says no decision has been made, but a new spy agency for Canada is an option on the table.

Everyone who was aboard the missing Ontario air ambulance jet, including the four Canadian crew members, has been identified.

Toronto-area home sales fell 9 per cent in September. Listings were also down.

After the Star found American corporations received $7.8 billion in federal contracts, Pierre Poilievre accused Mark Carney of “sending our money south.”

Mark Carney’s government is demanding answers from Stelco on layoffs and threatening legal action if commitments aren’t upheld.

Correction: Yesterday’s newsletter said a crash on Highway 427 early Sunday killed six people. As noted in the article, the crash sent six people to hospital.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Now let’s get into today’s news.

Mississauga voters are not happy with the insult-heavy tone of recent mayoral debates there. Alyshah Hasham reports that a recent poll by Liaison shows voters overwhelmingly dislike the personal attacks that have come to dominate headlines in the three-way race that’s emerged. Meanwhile in Toronto, columnist Richard Warnica recently wrote that Brad Bradford’s negativity has become a burden for his campaign, while Olivia Chow’s good-vibes-only demeanor might not match the city’s mood. But today, contributing columnist Matt Elliott offers a different complaint: he wishes Chow’s big smile was matched by big policy ambitions.

State of the race: The latest polls show this to be an unusually close race for an incumbent Toronto mayor, as Bradford stays within striking distance of Chow’s lead.

Key moment: Could the next week decide Toronto’s mayoral election? Last time around, advance voting was the key to Chow’s victory.

Ishtar Samano was 21 when cancer took away her appetite, her hair and her education. She fought hard to ensure it wouldn’t take her potential to have children, too.

A Muskoka addiction clinic staffed with fake nurses and no doctor has been forced into bankruptcy amid allegations of sexual abuse and a suspicious death, Kevin Donovan reports.

The trial of the former Air Canada employee accused in the largest gold heist in Canadian history began Monday.

Two 25-year-olds were charged in the murder of a man found dead in a burning car in Scarborough last month. Police are looking for another suspect.

The federal NDP have requested an emergency debate in Parliament about whether Republican party-affiliated operatives mobilizing Alberta separatist votes amounts to foreign interference.

Andrew Phillips’ take: There are a lot of differences between Quebec sovereigntists and Alberta separatists. Including that the PQ never sold out to the United States.

A giant loophole in Trump’s molasses ban means Canada’s sugar industry is breathing easy.

We know that leaders from Canada and the European Union will meet in Quebec at the end of this month to discuss a closer relationship. We know why Carney is pursuing that — as Bob Rae wrote this weekend, “We are at a unique and difficult moment in our national journey, a journey in what I have called a ‘ruptured world.’ We are seeing on a daily basis how difficult, erratic, and, yes, malevolent, the leadership of the United States has become.” That’s a world where Canada needs more, and different, partners.

So we know why, and who, and where and when. What we don’t know yet is exactly what this partnership will look like. It seems to be billed either as “Associate Membership” or, in Carney’s apparent preferred phrasing, an “Alliance for the Future.” But no one really knows what either of those terms means yet.

No doubt you have questions about these upcoming negotiations and the partnership that may result. Our Ottawa bureau chief Tonda MacCharles and Paris-based reporter Allan Woods will join readers for a live Q&A today at 10 a.m.

In advance, readers have already been posting their queries: On whether European models of health care might be imported in the deal, whether we’d be better off focusing on our own regulatory regime first, and whether freer movement of people to Europe would come with portability of pension programs.

What are your questions about Canada and the EU?Ask away in the comments here, and join Tonda and Allan at 10 a.m. for the live chat.

SUSAN DELACOURT:Trump’s America doesn’t view Canada’s sovereignty as inviolable. That’s a new factor in Alberta, and might be in Quebec, too.

ROSIE DIMANNO:Toronto’s most vulnerable are losing their last lifelines — and a church is left holding the bag.

ÉRIC BLAIS:Spain outlaws votes on separation. Meanwhile Quebec and Alberta will determine Canada’s fate.

“I never realized how many people around the world watched the show”: John Reardon returns to “Hudson and Rex” after tonsil cancer forced him to leave.

My family likes pickles. A lot. But hearing a radio hit from a “pickle festival” this weekend, my teenage daughter insisted it must be satire. Just in time, Briony Smith explains Toronto’s sudden love affair with the humble pickle.

Gideon Arthurs recently stepped down as executive director of Soulpepper. Now he’s been announced as the new CEO of Harbourfront Centre.

Yesterday, in response to a book excerpt about the pre-fame band Neil Young and Rick James played in while living in Yorkville, I asked for Toronto music memories and obscure trivia. Here’s an astounding one that appears to be absolutely true according to both celebrities involved:

“I read or heard somewhere that during the time that they all lived in Toronto, Alice Cooper was Keanu Reeves’ and his sister’s after-school babysitter while their mother was at work.” — Susan

Others were interested in the still-going-strong bars where you can drink where the musical legends did:

“I had no idea that The Pilot was famous for jazz (and hosted various legends) and was frequented by the likes of Bob Dylan and Gordon Lightfoot!” — AB

Before you go: The salmon are spawning in the Humber and Don Rivers right now, one of the most gob-smacking annual phenomena inside city limits. As I once wrote, watching them offers an inspiring lesson in resilience we can all use as we, like the salmon, fling ourselves ever upstream.

Thanks for starting your day with us. If you enjoy First Up, please share it with a friend. And let us know what you think of the changes we’ve made, and what you’d like to see. Email firstup@thestar.ca. I’ll see you back here tomorrow morning.

Everyone who was aboard the missing Ontario air ambulance jet, including the four Canadian crew members, has been identified.
Toronto-area home sales fell 9 per cent in September. Listings were also down.
After the Star found American corporations received $7.8 billion in federal contracts, Pierre Poilievre accused Mark Carney of “sending our money south.”
Mark Carney’s government is demanding answers from Stelco on layoffs and threatening legal action if commitments aren’t upheld.

content_blocks.text: Correction: Yesterday’s newsletter said a crash on Highway 427 early Sunday killed six people. As noted in the article, the crash sent six people to hospital.
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem
Now let’s get into today’s news.
TODAY’S TOP STORIES
Mayoral vibe check: less mudslinging, more inspiring?

Mississauga voters are not happy with the insult-heavy tone of recent mayoral debates there. Alyshah Hasham reports that a recent poll by Liaison shows voters overwhelmingly dislike the personal attacks that have come to dominate headlines in the three-way race that’s emerged. Meanwhile in Toronto, columnist Richard Warnica recently wrote that Brad Bradford’s negativity has become a burden for his campaign, while Olivia Chow’s good-vibes-only demeanor might not match the city’s mood. But today, contributing columnist Matt Elliott offers a different complaint: he wishes Chow’s big smile was matched by big policy ambitions.

items: State of the race: The latest polls show this to be an unusually close race for an incumbent Toronto mayor, as Bradford stays within striking distance of Chow’s lead.
Key moment: Could the next week decide Toronto’s mayoral election? Last time around, advance voting was the key to Chow’s victory.

content_blocks.text: The new face of cancer

items: Ishtar Samano was 21 when cancer took away her appetite, her hair and her education. She fought hard to ensure it wouldn’t take her potential to have children, too.

content_blocks.text: Justice

items: A Muskoka addiction clinic staffed with fake nurses and no doctor has been forced into bankruptcy amid allegations of sexual abuse and a suspicious death, Kevin Donovan reports.
The trial of the former Air Canada employee accused in the largest gold heist in Canadian history began Monday.
Two 25-year-olds were charged in the murder of a man found dead in a burning car in Scarborough last month. Police are looking for another suspect.

content_blocks.text: Politics

items: The federal NDP have requested an emergency debate in Parliament about whether Republican party-affiliated operatives mobilizing Alberta separatist votes amounts to foreign interference.
Andrew Phillips’ take: There are a lot of differences between Quebec sovereigntists and Alberta separatists. Including that the PQ never sold out to the United States.

content_blocks.text: Business

items: A giant loophole in Trump’s molasses ban means Canada’s sugar industry is breathing easy.

content_blocks.text: THE CONVERSATION
What do we want to know about Canada and the EU?

We know that leaders from Canada and the European Union will meet in Quebec at the end of this month to discuss a closer relationship. We know why Carney is pursuing that — as Bob Rae wrote this weekend, “We are at a unique and difficult moment in our national journey, a journey in what I have called a ‘ruptured world.’ We are seeing on a daily basis how difficult, erratic, and, yes, malevolent, the leadership of the United States has become.” That’s a world where Canada needs more, and different, partners.

So we know why, and who, and where and when. What we don’t know yet is exactly what this partnership will look like. It seems to be billed either as “Associate Membership” or, in Carney’s apparent preferred phrasing, an “Alliance for the Future.” But no one really knows what either of those terms means yet.

No doubt you have questions about these upcoming negotiations and the partnership that may result. Our Ottawa bureau chief Tonda MacCharles and Paris-based reporter Allan Woods will join readers for a live Q&A today at 10 a.m.

In advance, readers have already been posting their queries: On whether European models of health care might be imported in the deal, whether we’d be better off focusing on our own regulatory regime first, and whether freer movement of people to Europe would come with portability of pension programs.
What are your questions about Canada and the EU?Ask away in the comments here, and join Tonda and Allan at 10 a.m. for the live chat.
OPINION
SUSAN DELACOURT:Trump’s America doesn’t view Canada’s sovereignty as inviolable. That’s a new factor in Alberta, and might be in Quebec, too.
ROSIE DIMANNO:Toronto’s most vulnerable are losing their last lifelines — and a church is left holding the bag.
ÉRIC BLAIS:Spain outlaws votes on separation. Meanwhile Quebec and Alberta will determine Canada’s fate.

items: “I never realized how many people around the world watched the show”: John Reardon returns to “Hudson and Rex” after tonsil cancer forced him to leave.

content_blocks.text: Food

items: My family likes pickles. A lot. But hearing a radio hit from a “pickle festival” this weekend, my teenage daughter insisted it must be satire. Just in time, Briony Smith explains Toronto’s sudden love affair with the humble pickle.

content_blocks.text: Arts

items: Gideon Arthurs recently stepped down as executive director of Soulpepper. Now he’s been announced as the new CEO of Harbourfront Centre.

content_blocks.text: YOUR SAY

Yesterday, in response to a book excerpt about the pre-fame band Neil Young and Rick James played in while living in Yorkville, I asked for Toronto music memories and obscure trivia. Here’s an astounding one that appears to be absolutely true according to both celebrities involved:
“I read or heard somewhere that during the time that they all lived in Toronto, Alice Cooper was Keanu Reeves’ and his sister’s after-school babysitter while their mother was at work.” — Susan
Others were interested in the still-going-strong bars where you can drink where the musical legends did:
“I had no idea that The Pilot was famous for jazz (and hosted various legends) and was frequented by the likes of Bob Dylan and Gordon Lightfoot!” — AB

Before you go: The salmon are spawning in the Humber and Don Rivers right now, one of the most gob-smacking annual phenomena inside city limits. As I once wrote, watching them offers an inspiring lesson in resilience we can all use as we, like the salmon, fling ourselves ever upstream.
