stories.title: Oakville pilot among 4 Canadian crew members on missing air ambulance flight
stories.summary: Ontario-based Latitude Air Ambulance has released more details about the four Canadian crew members.
stories.author: Raju Mudhar
stories.content:
As friends, family and coworkers grieve the loss of the four-person Canadian crew of the Latitude Air Ambulance medevac plane that went down in the Atlantic Ocean over the weekend, Canada’s Transportation Safety Board (TSB) is making arrangements to start the recovery operation and fully investigate what happened.

According to Craig Johnston, the Tsb’s director of air investigations, the hope is to start this part of the recovery process as soon as possible.

“We are trying to find a ship that can take us out and look for the aircraft. We don’t have one and we certainly don’t have one close by, so we’re looking at a bunch of options — U.S. assets, Canadian assets, private for-hire assets, any state or federal assets we can use,” he said in an interview on Tuesday afternoon.

The conditions, large search area and challenging location — off the coast of the U.S., but in international waters south of Nantucket Island — will all be factors.

The Gulfstream G100 jet, operating under the call sign “Heartbeat 104,” crashed early Saturday morning while operating a routine medevac flight from Bermuda to Boston.

The jet was carrying four Canadian crew, along with a patient and an accompanying family member, both Bermudian nationals.

The crew have been identified as pilots Philip Gregory Childerhose and Thomas Henry Farquhar, and medical staff Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir, all based in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area.

The two passengers they were escorting were Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, a senior vice president with a Bermudian insurance firm.

The cause of the crash has not been determined. The pilots were last heard speaking to air traffic controllers shortly after 1 a.m. Saturday, soon after they made a swift descent of around 11,000 feet.

In recordings, a controller can be heard repeatedly asking the pilots if they wished to report an emergency, to no apparent response.

The U.S. Coast Guard called off its search for the plane late Sunday evening after using several planes, helicopters and boats, including additional support from the U.S. National Guard.

TSB describes challenging investigation

“Given the time of year, the sea state and the sea conditions are not great, we need a fairly large vessel to handle the ocean,” Johnston said. “Ideally, we want to get out sooner rather than later. The evidence is perishable and things degrade in salt water, so we always like to find it as soon as we can.”

He said the TSB is in contact with the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, Massachusetts Police and other partners in co-ordinating efforts, but the TSB is leading the investigation. Initially, three investigators will go on the search vessel, and depending on what is found, the team could expand up to 20.

Any evidence that is recovered will be brought to the Tsb’s Ottawa office for examination.

The investigation will be looking for the jet’s black boxes — the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder — as well as any other debris.

All times converted to EDT.

Friday, Oct. 2, 7:15 p.m. — The Gulfstream G100 jet C-Grjp departs Hamilton, Ont., for Bermuda, arriving at 10:45 p.m.

11:42 p.m. — The jet departs Bermuda’s L.F. Wade Airport, with a scheduled two-and-a-half-hour flight time to Boston’s Logan International Airport. The medevac flight is carrying four Canadian employees of Latitude Air Ambulance, including two pilots and two medical staff, as well as a patient and an accompanying passenger.

Saturday, 1:05 a.m. — Data from the website flightaware.com shows the jet descending about 11,000 feet before resuming stable flight.

Around 1:10 a.m. — Pilots contact air traffic control. In recordings, a controller says he is having problems hearing the pilots and repeatedly asks if they are declaring an emergency.

Around 1:30 a.m. — The U.S. FAA loses contact with the plane about 20 minutes from its destination.

6:20 a.m. — The U.S. Coast Guard says it is searching for the jet south of Nantucket Island.

11:45 a.m. — The Coast Guard says the search is ongoing, involving two aircraft, a helicopter, a search-and-rescue lifeboat, and a Coast Guard cutter.

Sunday, around 6:45 p.m.— The U.S. Coast Guard suspends the search for six people who were aboard the missing air ambulance.

9:49 p.m. Latitude Air Ambulance issues a statement regarding Heartbeat 104 Medevac: “It is with profound sadness that we acknowledge the decision by the United States Coast Guard to conclude active search and rescue operations and transition to recovery efforts.”

Johnston said he is also hoping the plane has a functioning underwater beacon that is still operable, which could be very helpful in finding the aircraft. The full investigation and final report could take up to two years, but the TSB aims to give an initial report of findings within 30 days.

Those findings will be important to the many friends, families and coworkers of the crew, who have been posting memories and tributes online.

On Monday evening, Latitude Air Ambulance released more details about its four Canadian crew members.

“This is the part of this tragedy that is hardest to put into words,” said company President Peter Byl.

“To all of us at Latitude, our crew were much more than names. They were colleagues, friends and members of our family. Each brought something special to our company, to the people they worked beside, and to the patients and families entrusted to their care.”

Philip Childerhose, captain

Childerhose was the captain of the flight and was “a person of great integrity, incredibly kind-hearted and extremely passionate about aviation. He was dedicated to his family, friends, and colleagues. He touched the hearts of everyone he talked to and helped anyone who was in need.”

According to his LinkedIn page, Childerhose was with Latitude for almost four years and had been a flight instructor since 2007.

His profile said he lived in Oakville.

Thomas Farquhar, first officer

Farquhar was the first officer on the flight and “was loved by everyone who ever met him. He was a gentle giant who reflected Jesus’ love: a safe place and a helping hand to all,” according to Latitude’s release.

His LinkedIn profile indicated he had been with the company for two years, and that he lived in Brantford.

Sarah Paton, flight nurse

Paton was the flight nurse on board. The company said she was “a bright, joyful presence whose kindness, humour and generosity touched everyone around her. A dedicated nurse, she devoted her life to caring for others and was known by her family as selfless, hardworking, determined and full of life.”

Paton was a “larger than life daughter, mother and friend,” the release continued.

According to the College of Nurses of Ontario, she had been a registered nurse since 2016 and was also registered to work in New York state.

Jolene Weir, respiratory therapist

Weir was listed as the respiratory therapist on board.

“Jolene was a presence unlike any other who loved her family and friends and had a passion for helping others,” Latitude said.

The company said she had years of experience working as a respiratory therapist in a hospital, and that Latitude “truly was her dream job” because it meant caring for others while getting to travel the world.

“Her incredible ability to care for and love others extended not only to her patients, but showed even more in her most favourite roles as a wife, mother, daughter, sister and friend,” said the release.

Her daughter, Mackenzie, posted a tribute on Facebook, saying: “She worked her whole life saving lives and more recently, changing people’s lives for the better helping them get to where they needed to be. This same mentality and care for others wasn’t just her life at work, it was her entire life … I love my mom so much and cannot believe this is real.”

Latitude said it will provide support to the families of its crew and to its employees as they grieve.

“Our colleagues dedicated themselves to helping people at some of the most vulnerable moments of their lives,” Byl said.

“That was the mission they were carrying out aboard Heartbeat 104. We want their families to know that we will remember not simply how we lost them, but how they lived, how they served, and what they meant to the people around them.”

Latitude said that it would co-operate fully with all authorities investigating the flight, including the TSB, the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, as well as any recovery efforts.

stories.title: Delta plane clips Air Canada aircraft at LAX, FAA investigating
stories.summary: A Delta plane clipped an Air Canada aircraft from Toronto at LAX Tuesday morning. No injuries were reported, and the FAA is investigating.
stories.author: Amarachi Amadike
stories.content:
An Air Canada plane collided with a Delta aircraft after arriving at Los Angeles International Airport from Toronto Tuesday morning.

According to the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) spokesperson Donnell Evans, Delta Air Lines Flight 7 was taxiing for departure when its left wingtip “clipped the horizontal stabilizer of Air Canada Flight 785.”

“The Air Canada flight was being towed when it stopped short of its gate,” Evans said, adding that the FAA is still investigating the events that led to the collision.

The jet was carrying four Canadian crew, along with a patient and an accompanying family member, both Bermudian nationals.

Air Canada says its aircraft was “at the gate” at the time of the collision.

In an emailed statement, an Air Canada spokesperson told the Star there have been no reported injuries, but the damaged aircraft “will be taken out of service for inspection and repairs.”

Delta, whose plane was carrying 275 customers and 15 crew members, also reports no injuries.

“Nothing is more important than the safety of our customers and people, and we apologize to our customers for the experience and delay in their travels,” a Delta Airline spokesperson said.

While the FAA says the Air Canada aircraft was being towed at the time of collision, Air Canada says the its aircraft was “at the gate.”

Jayson Lowe watched the aftermath from the window of his United Airlines flight as it crept toward the gate after arriving from Denver.

“I was looking out the window as we were taxiing to our arrival gate and a Delta A350 managed to hit a parked Air Canada plane,” he shared in a Facebook post. “I cannot stress this enough. Parked!”

Just a few feet away from the parking position, Lowe says the plane he was in had to be towed the rest of the way.

“The pilot of our United flight came on the PA and told us that the system that guides aircraft into the gate was not functioning,” Lowe told the Star.

Delta says maintenance crews and airport teams are now examining the aircraft, though the extent of the damage remains unclear.

The airline says it’s ready to cooperate with the National Transportation Safety Board on any investigation, and is “working to accommodate customers and evaluate recovery options.”

stories.title: Althia Raj: Quebec’s election results mean Mark Carney must finally address the province
stories.summary: Monday’s election results in Quebec delivered a Parti Québécois minority government that will prove thorny to handle, but the prime minister escaped the worst-case scenario, a sovereigntist premier with a strong majority government.
stories.author: Althia Raj
stories.content:
Monday’s election results in Quebec delivered a Parti Québécois minority government that will prove thorny to handle, but the prime minister escaped the worst-case scenario: a sovereigntist premier with a strong majority government.

Only 28 per cent of Quebec voters cast a ballot for incoming premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party, which won 59 seats. His pledge to hold a referendum during his first mandate likely cost him votes and sent voters flocking to three other federalist options. The Liberals under untested leader Charles Milliard won 40 seats, and will form the official Opposition. Éric Duhaime’s Conservatives (PCQ) won 19 seats and will now court Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) supporters. The CAQ, which got 12 per cent of popular vote, won no seats.

The balance of power in the National Assembly will also be shared with the left-wing sovereigntist party Québec Solidaire (QS), which emerged from the election with nine seats and more political power. The PQ needs only one dance partner and has natural allies on key issues: the PCQ on immigration, QS on increases to social programs. All three opposition parties must band together if they want to defeat the PQ and return to the polls.

For now, it is in each party’s interest to build on the gains made, grow their teams, and prove their worth.

Plamondon may wish to demonstrate that the Canadian federation doesn’t work, that federal immigration policies contribute to Quebec’s linguistic challenges, and that federal interference obstructs Quebec’s ability to protect and promote its own culture. But as premier, he also must prove that he can be trusted, that he can competently govern — without getting embroiled in petty arguments — so that an eventual vote for sovereignty is not cast as vote for chaos, but for a more promising future.

Monday evening, Plamondon, who at times can be quarrelsome, bitter and unpleasant, struck a mature and conciliatory tone. During his victory speech, he promised to collaborate with the other parties, even pledging to incorporate pieces of their electoral platforms in his government’s first budget.

Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his party will govern for all Quebecers following its election victory and that he intends to work with Ottawa when Quebec’s interests are served. (Oct. 6, 2026)

He promised his would be a government that would courageously take on initiatives regardless of public opinion polls.

On his core promise, Monday he remained firm: a referendum on sovereignty is coming.

“We simply want to exist as a nation, and decide for ourselves, just like the 200 other countries in the world,” he explained. But during a news conference Tuesday, he noted it wouldn’t be for several years. “We’ve got time,” he said.

To Carney, Plamondon said, “He will find in me, someone who is direct, frank, transparent, above all, someone who will defend, first, foremost, and at all times, the interests of Quebecers …

“But I also want to tell him, that every time he defends the interest of Quebec, he will find in me a partner for dialogue and collaboration.”

What happens when their interests do not align? Plamondon did not elaborate.

If we’re frank, Carney has not focused much attention on Quebec.

In the last six months, Carney scheduled 10 trips to Alberta, he was in B.C. — now in the throes of an election — seven times, including on Quebec’s national day. He made eight visits to Quebec, the last one on Aug. 24.

Although polls flagged a PQ surge this spring, the federal government’s focus has been on Alberta’s separatist movement and placating a premier who branded a new pipeline as a proof point of whether the Canadian federation works. Carney gave Premier Danielle Smith much of what she wanted, including rollbacks on Liberal energy and climate policies, but Smith still chose to put a referendum to have a referendum on separation to voters this fall, on Oct. 19. Her timelines forced action. Carney was in Alberta four times this past month.

Liberal cabinet ministers react after Quebec elected the Parti Québécois in a provincial election on Oct. 5. Public Works Minister Joël Lightbound says a majority of Quebecers feel, as he does, that Quebec is stronger as part of Canada and the focus will remain building a resilient economy, including in Quebec. (Oct. 6, 2026)

There are lessons here.

While the PQ leader has pledged not to hold a referendum until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office, Carney can afford to dispense some political capital in the province. Polls suggest he remains the most popular politician in Quebec, and controversial issues are about to bubble up — with the Supreme Court’s ruling on Bill 21 and the use of the Charter’s notwithstanding clause this fall.

On Tuesday, a phone call between both men suggests both realize they have more to gain by working together than against one another — for now.

Plamondon said he told Carney he wanted to be treated with “respect” and expected to be consulted when Quebec’s interests were at stake, notably in talks with the Trump administration.

He also hinted he asked for federal money for big infrastructure projects and help towards the PQ’s goal of halving homelessness in the next four years. Plamondon also said Carney reassured him that he has no immediate plans to increase immigration levels .

“It is a call that went very, very well, and we agreed to meet,” he said.

Support for sovereignty hovers around 30 per cent — in Quebec and in Alberta — but having addressed Smith’s demands, it’s not unreasonable for Plamondon, and Quebecers, to expect Carney address theirs too.

Plamondon said he told Carney he wanted to be treated with “respect” and expected to be consulted when Quebec’s interests were at stake, notably in talks with the Trump administration.

He also hinted he asked for federal money for big infrastructure projects and help towards the PQ’s goal of halving homelessness in the next four years. Plamondon also said Carney reassured him that he has no immediate plans to increase immigration levels .
“It is a call that went very, very well, and we agreed to meet,” he said.

stories.title: What new court records reveal about the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting
stories.summary: Co-conspirator allegedly told the killer that it was a "bad idea to attack a school ... too many young victims."
stories.author: Raisa Patel; Mark Ramzy
stories.content:
Ottawa — A Washington state resident has been charged with allegedly conspiring to help the shooter behind the Tumbler Ridge tragedy , a revelation that has unearthed new details about how the deadly February attack was carried out.

Thirty-year-old James Cody Bryant was arrested and charged Tuesday with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, American officials said, after the “co-conspirator” allegedly aided Canada’s Jesse Van Rootselaar in committing a shooting that left eight people dead in a B.C. community on Feb. 10.

Here’s what U.S. court records detailing chat logs between the pair, and findings from interviews with Bryant, reveal about how one of the country’s worst mass shootings was allegedly plotted and how it unfolded.

The pair, who both identified as transgender, first met approximately three years ago on Omegle, an online chat website designed to connect strangers, which was shut down in 2023 after its founder admitted it was being “misused.”

Officials said Tuesday that Bryant and Van Rootselaar kept in contact intermittently over the following years. Court documents reveal that the pair began communicating daily in the six months preceding the shooting, using the messaging platform Discord to discuss the attack.

“Bryant and Van Rootselaar had numerous conversations relating to Van Rootselaar’s planning and preparation for the murders, including discussing potential attack locations, the way the attack would unfold, and related topics. During some of these conversations, Bryant gave Van Rootselaar tactical advice regarding the carrying out of the attack,” the documents note.

U.S Investigators say a 30-year-old in Washington state gave advice and money to the Tumbler Ridge mass killer and even offered to livestream the attack on Facebook. (Oct. 6, 2026)

FBI special agent W. Mike Herrington said Tuesday that he found the chats “particularly difficult to read, in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used.”

Chat logs show Bryant sent Van Rootselaar money to purchase items to use in the shooting, including a pair of shoes Van Rootselaar wore during the attack — having expressed desire for “cute shoes for when I do my violence” — and a lighter the killer used to detonate an explosive device inside the school.

“As part of the investigation, we had to get subpoenas and warrants to get copies of communications,” said Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, adding that investigators had to sift through “thousands” of messages.

According to the logs, Van Rootselaar mused to Bryant about potentially becoming one of the most notorious mass killers in Canadian history, discussing the death tolls linked to the country’s worst shootings and wondering if it was possible to “steal that title” and whether she would “have fans.”

“Van Rootselaar was insistent that the murders be livestreamed, recorded, and broadcast over the internet for the public to view,” the documents note, with Bryant helping the shooter test livestreaming methods and agreeing to share the video online.

On the day of the attack, Bryant and Van Rootselaar succeeded in briefly broadcasting a video on the livestreaming platform Twitch, right after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and half-brother at their residence, the court records show.

“The livestream lasted approximately 20 seconds before it was disconnected. According to records obtained from Twitch, Van Rootselaar’s livestream was viewed by only one Twitch account,” the documents state.

According to an investigator’s interview with Bryant, the co-conspirator told Van Rootselaar in the months before the attack that it was a “bad idea to attack a school because there would be too many young victims.”

A month before the shooting, documents reveal Bryant sought to convince Van Rootselaar to reconsider the attack after learning she planned to conduct it imminently.

“I truly hope you reconsider today. I wish there were any other path for you, you shouldn’t have to do something like this. I wish I knew what I could say or do to change your mind,” Bryant wrote to Van Rootselaar in a January chat log.

Bryant told the 18-year-old there was “more you can do with your life” and said: “I know you can get better.”

Police say Bryant never reported Van Rootselaar to authorities.

The chat logs and interviews with Bryant show that the pair discussed weapons, parts and ammunition before the shooting.

“Approximately six months prior to the Tumbler Ridge school shooting, Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she had stolen guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and was hiding them in her room in preparation for a mass shooting,” the documents note, describing how Van Rootselaar also convinced someone else to buy her ammunition and how she told Bryant “about the kinds of guns and accessories she possessed.”

The 18-year-old sent Bryant videos of her testing out using a firearm with a 3D-printed silencer. Chat logs reveal Van Rootselaar asked Bryant to buy her a gun kit for a semi-automatic handgun, and two weeks later, requested a 3D printed firearm kit, neither of which Bryant sent.

The RCMP has refused to disclose the specific weapons used, citing ongoing investigations.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: U.S. Coast Guard identifies all six on missing Canadian air ambulance
stories.summary: Boston - The U.S. Coast Guard has named all six people, including four Canadians, aboard an Ontario-based air ambulance that went missing off the coast of Massachusetts on Saturday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The six souls who were on board a Canadian-owned air ambulance that went down off the coast of Massachusetts on the weekend have been identified.

A news release from the U.S. Coast Guard late Monday said the Gulfstream G100 jet carried 66-year-old Marilyn Lavonne Bean and her 41-year-old son Sergio Wayne Lottimore, both of Bermuda.

Lottimore, who worked in insurance, was remembered by his alma mater as a scholastic prefect and by his work as a respected leader.

Meanwhile, the four Canadian crew members, employed by Ontario-based Latitude Air Ambulance, were identified as Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir.

“During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident,” said Rear Adm. Matthew Lake from the U.S. Coast Guard in Monday’s release.

“We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation.”

Coast guard officials have said the plane was en route to Boston with a patient and a family member from Bermuda when it lost contact with air-traffic control early Saturday.

The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net .

The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to about 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

The coast guard later said debris from the plane was recovered 32 kilometres off Nantucket, though officials wouldn’t share specifics. The 66-hour search ended Sunday after scouring roughly 7,000 kilometres of ocean.

Officials said Monday a civilian vessel also found debris associated with the plane. They said it’s not uncommon, and mariners who find such debris should contact the Transportation Safety Board of Canada.

The TSB said it would send crews to Massachusetts to help search for and recover the aircraft.

Latitude Air Ambulance, the medical transport company based in Hamilton, Ont., that owned the jet known as Heartbeat 104, shared more about the crew members late Monday.

The company said captain Philip Childerhose was a man of great integrity who touched the hearts of everyone he talked to, and first officer Thomas Farquhar was a “gentle giant who reflected Jesus’ love.”

Flight nurse Sarah Paton was bright and joyful, and devoted herself to helping others, the company said. Respiratory therapist Jolene Weir loved to travel the world and had an “incredible ability” to care for others.

Peter Byl, company president, said each of the four crew brought something special to the company.

“Our colleagues dedicated themselves to helping people at some of the most vulnerable moments of their lives,” Byl said in a statement. “That was the mission they were carrying out aboard Heartbeat 104.

“We want their families to know that we will remember not simply how we lost them, but how they lived, how they served, and what they meant to the people around them.”

The company, which offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, said it would support the families of the crew members and its employees as they grieve.

It also asked for privacy for their families, and added it would co-operate with Canadian and American flight investigators and not speculate about what happened.

Early tributes to those killed were shared across social media Monday.

“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized and so our first thoughts are with the families of those so tragically lost,” said Bermuda Premier David Burt in a statement.

“Let us open our hearts to the families in the hope that our expressions of love, support and compassion will bring some comfort as they attempt to deal with this terrible loss.”

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said she was heartbroken and expressed condolences to everyone affected by this tragedy.

Investigators have said a black box, a recording device found in airplanes that is used to investigate accidents, has not yet been recovered.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: CPNewsAlert: PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon projected to win riding
stories.summary: The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will win his Montreal-area riding of Camille-Laurin.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had his work cut out for him after the 2022 election.

His party won only three seats in 2022 and watched as the Coalition Avenir Québec won a second majority government, presenting itself as a “third way” between federalism and sovereignty.

Four years later, the leader of the separatist party was able to bring his party back from the brink, and into power.

Although his party fell short of the 64 seats needed to form a majority in Quebec’s national assembly, St-Pierre Plamondon could be well positioned to work with the sovereigntist Québec solidaire party to plan a third referendum on independence in Quebec.

St-Pierre Plamondon won the PQ leadership in 2020 after promising to hold a referendum if the party formed government. Just before this year’s electoral campaign period began, the PQ leader said he would wait until U.S. President Donald Trump is out of the White House to do so.

The PQ hasn’t been in power since former premier Pauline Marois’s minority government dissolved in 2014.

Historically known as a social democrat party whose raison d’être was to separate from Canada, the PQ struggled to connect with voters in elections after the Marois government fell.

However, the party started to gain momentum by winning four more seats in byelections before the Quebec legislature was dissolved in August.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s election victory comes two weeks before Alberta holds its own referendum on the possibility of separation.

“People are going to vote. And nobody thinks there’s any danger in going to vote and being in a democracy,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in a recent interview with Cjad radio.

But while the PQ leader is now an ardent separatist, he once accused the independence movement of having “split Quebec in two.”

He donated over $2,000 to the Liberal Party of Canada between 2004 and 2008. A spokesperson would later say he made the donations during a period when he was a corporate lawyer at Stikeman Elliott, while attending fundraisers tied to his work at the firm.

He also worked on lawsuits stemming from the federal sponsorship scandal that erupted over a program introduced while former prime minister Jean Chrétien was in power. Sometimes describing himself as a “disappointed federalist,” St-Pierre Plamondon later joined the PQ in 2016 under former cabinet minister and party leader Jean-François Lisée.

He made headlines after the 2022 election, when he refused to swear the oath to the King. The government passed a bill making the oath optional soon after, allowing him to sit at the legislature.

During his campaign, he once again attacked the monarchy, calling it a symbol of “domination by force,” and pledging to defund the office of the lieutenant-governor, which represents the King in Quebec.

The PQ leader has described himself as “spontaneous,” admitting to sometimes speaking to media without considering possible backlash. Meanwhile, his rivals deem him to be “hotheaded,” “belligerent” and “quarrelsome.”

The father of three has also said he has found the campaign difficult since it has forced him to be away from his children for days at a time.

Throughout the campaign, the PQ leader leaned on nationalist sentiment and a desire for change to drum up support from those who were disillusioned after eight years of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec.

He also relied on identity politics and linked “uncontrolled immigration” to problems such as the housing crisis, the decline in the French language, the struggling education system and strain on public services.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal compared St-Pierre Plamondon to former premier François Legault, who won two consecutive majority governments by making language, identity and autonomy core governing themes.

But St-Pierre Plamondon’s detractors did little to stop his momentum during the campaign.

The PQ leader also downplayed his plans for a referendum in the last stretch of the campaign, noting that he believes voters will need to decide whom they want to trust to lead Quebec.

“It’s not totally accurate to say that this election is only about whether we would hold a referendum in three years from now,” he told Cjad. “It’s about changing or not changing a government that has catastrophic results in many areas of our society and choosing who could do a good job and who could be reliable in terms of what they do and what they say.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s election victory comes two weeks before Alberta holds its own referendum on the possibility of separation.
“People are going to vote. And nobody thinks there’s any danger in going to vote and being in a democracy,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in a recent interview with Cjad radio.
But while the PQ leader is now an ardent separatist, he once accused the independence movement of having “split Quebec in two.”

He donated over $2,000 to the Liberal Party of Canada between 2004 and 2008. A spokesperson would later say he made the donations during a period when he was a corporate lawyer at Stikeman Elliott, while attending fundraisers tied to his work at the firm.

He also worked on lawsuits stemming from the federal sponsorship scandal that erupted over a program introduced while former prime minister Jean Chrétien was in power. Sometimes describing himself as a “disappointed federalist,” St-Pierre Plamondon later joined the PQ in 2016 under former cabinet minister and party leader Jean-François Lisée.
He made headlines after the 2022 election, when he refused to swear the oath to the King. The government passed a bill making the oath optional soon after, allowing him to sit at the legislature.

During his campaign, he once again attacked the monarchy, calling it a symbol of “domination by force,” and pledging to defund the office of the lieutenant-governor, which represents the King in Quebec.

The PQ leader has described himself as “spontaneous,” admitting to sometimes speaking to media without considering possible backlash. Meanwhile, his rivals deem him to be “hotheaded,” “belligerent” and “quarrelsome.”
The father of three has also said he has found the campaign difficult since it has forced him to be away from his children for days at a time.

Throughout the campaign, the PQ leader leaned on nationalist sentiment and a desire for change to drum up support from those who were disillusioned after eight years of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec.

He also relied on identity politics and linked “uncontrolled immigration” to problems such as the housing crisis, the decline in the French language, the struggling education system and strain on public services.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal compared St-Pierre Plamondon to former premier François Legault, who won two consecutive majority governments by making language, identity and autonomy core governing themes.
But St-Pierre Plamondon’s detractors did little to stop his momentum during the campaign.
The PQ leader also downplayed his plans for a referendum in the last stretch of the campaign, noting that he believes voters will need to decide whom they want to trust to lead Quebec.

“It’s not totally accurate to say that this election is only about whether we would hold a referendum in three years from now,” he told Cjad. “It’s about changing or not changing a government that has catastrophic results in many areas of our society and choosing who could do a good job and who could be reliable in terms of what they do and what they say.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: London man charged after striking ambulance, fleeing scene
stories.summary: A London man is facing charges after an impaired driving incident involving a collision with an ambulance.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
A London man is facing charges after an impaired driving incident involving a collision with an ambulance.

According to police, the incident happened around 9:30 p.m. Sunday by a residence on Duchess Avenue near Dane Street.

Investigators were told by paramedics at the scene that the driver struck a parked ambulance before colliding with a second parked vehicle in a driveway and fleeing the area.

Then, police began receiving reports of a silver sedan being driven dangerously in the area of Western Road and Sarnia Road. They say the vehicle was driving on sidewalks, down a flight of stairs, through red lights, and nearly striking pedestrians.

Later, officers found the suspect vehicle entering the Base Line Road East entrance of Victoria Hospital on Commissioners Road East.

Before the man was arrested, police say two officers were assaulted.

The 46 year old is charged with the following:

Two counts of assault peace officer

Operation while impaired

Flight from peace officer

Dangerous operation

Fail to stop after accident

stories.title: Parti Québécois projected to form government in Quebec
stories.summary: Separatist party promises to hold an independence referendum once Trump leaves office in 2029
stories.author: Maura Forrest, Eric Andrew-Gee, Nicolas Van Praet
stories.content:
Quebec has elected the separatist Parti Québécois to a minority government, setting the stage for years of uncertainty about the party’s promised independence referendum, which will now require support from elsewhere in the province’s fragmented political landscape.

After a five-way race that revealed a divided province and a splintered federalist vote, incoming premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party was leading or elected in 59 of the province’s 127 seats in Monday’s provincial election as of early Tuesday morning, fewer than the 64 needed to secure a majority in the National Assembly.

With 97 per cent of polls reporting, the PQ was on track to receive less than 30 per cent of the popular vote – which would be the lowest share of support for a government in Quebec history.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon was thwarted in his quest for a majority by late surges from the Quebec Liberal Party and the Quebec Conservatives. Both parties oppose a separation vote and have vowed to block one in the National Assembly.

The governing Coalition Avenir Québec, meanwhile, was wiped off the map after running the province for eight years. Leader Christine Fréchette lost her own seat as the party was completely shut out on Monday.

The election results come at a delicate moment for national unity, with a referendum in Alberta two weeks away, and persistent threats to Canada’s sovereignty and economy from U.S. President Donald Trump. Among the provinces, Quebec has been the biggest casualty of Mr. Trump’s protectionist trade agenda, which has targeted its aluminum and forest product industries in particular.

The PQ Leader has promised a vote on the province’s place within Canada once Mr. Trump leaves office in 2029, at which point Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon says Quebec can have a “serene” discussion about its future.

With a minority in the National Assembly, the PQ would need support from other parties or individual MNAs to trigger a referendum, and to stay in power. The PQ’s comeback comes after years in the wilderness. The party was last in government in 2014; in 2022, it had just three seats.

Despite saying little about independence during the election campaign, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon spoke at length about sovereignty during his victory speech in Montreal on Monday.

“The Quebec we want to build for ourselves will be French-speaking. It will be prosperous and modern, but above all, it will be among the most exemplary democracies on the planet,” he said.

“We simply want to exist as a nation and make our own decisions, just like the other 200 countries in the world... We must not let fear prevent us from fulfilling our destiny. And that destiny lies before us. The courageous struggle of francophones in America to preserve their cultural identity will find meaning when that people obtains its own country and the recognition that comes with having their own country and their own democracy.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon suggested the PQ could launch a referendum with the backing of opposition lawmakers who support independence and “would make this commitment possible.”

He also sent a message directly to the rest of Canada. “The independence project we are pursuing is not directed against you, and Quebec will always be a partner in good faith, open to collaboration, just as we have always been,” he said.

The PQ Leader could make relations with the federal government far more contentious. He is vowing to eliminate the role of lieutenant-governor in Quebec and fight any increases in immigration at a time when Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking inter-provincial peace in the face of U.S. economic aggression.

Mr. Carney congratulated Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon on his victory on social media on Monday night, and said he looks forward to working together “to support Québec’s businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec.”

Polls show only about 30 per cent of Quebeckers support independence, a historically low level in the province, where previous referendums led by then-PQ governments in 1980 and 1995 tallied 40 and 49 per cent support respectively.

The new government May struggle to defend the legitimacy of holding an independence vote, while calls to reform the provincial electoral system are likely to grow louder.

Québec solidaire, a left-wing separatist party that focuses more on social justice than independence, was projected to finish fourth, but could now wield the balance of power in the National Assembly after retaining many of its stronghold seats in Montreal.

It remains uncertain whether QS would support the PQ’s referendum ambitions. The two parties diverge sharply on immigration and identity issues, while Ruba Ghazal, the co-leader for QS, has promised a more wide-ranging consultation on the nature of an independent Quebec.

On Monday, Ms. Ghazal said she wants to build an independent Quebec alongside immigrants, Indigenous people and anglophones. “We’re going to be there to build a country that leaves no one behind,” she said. “A country for and by the people, a country for everyone.”

The election marks an unforgiving end to the eight-year reign of the Coalition Avenir Québec, which won consecutive majorities under former premier François Legault. Its brand of nationalism without independence – a vaunted “third way” between federalism and separatism – strongly resonated with voters, but the party was undone by several episodes of financial mismanagement in recent years.

Under Ms. Fréchette, the CAQ was unable to counter an overwhelming appetite for change. An early polling bump spurred by the U.S. trade war gave the outgoing Premier a chance to portray herself as a defender of Quebeckers. But as the shock of the conflict diminished, voters’ attention drifted elsewhere.

At the Caq’s election night event at the Delta Hotel in Trois-Rivières Monday, supporters had almost nothing to cheer about. Some stared at live results on a jumbo screen with stone-faced expressions.

“This result is clearly not what we’d hoped for and as party leader, I assume the entire responsibility for it,” Ms. Fréchette said in her concession speech. “Quebeckers wanted change and I respect their choice. I want to tell you that the convictions that united us will continue. The Coalition will continue to promote a third way – that of a Quebec that affirms its identity, protects its language and culture, maintains our autonomy, and gives itself the means to protect and transform its economy.”

Ms. Fréchette has vowed to stay on as party leader and work with Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon to ease the transition to his government.

The Quebec Liberal Party under new Leader Charles Milliard struggled to distinguish itself from other parties opposing a referendum, despite a strong end to the campaign, and the party was poised to finish in second place. The most resolutely federalist party in Quebec now faces being locked out of power for a decade or more, its longest stretch in opposition since the 1950s.

Still, the party’s projected 40 seats were more than many PLQ faithful hoped for entering Monday night, and the mood at Mr. Milliard’s gathering in Magog was upbeat. The incoming Opposition leader vowed to work with the new PQ government on some issues, but block its referendum hopes.

“A minority government means they don’t have a blank cheque to do what they want,” said Mr. Milliard. “We’ll collaborate on the housing crisis, the homelessness crisis. On the sovereignty crisis, we won’t be collaborating.”

The anti-referendum vote was further splintered by a relatively new force in Quebec politics, the provincial Conservative Party, unrelated to its federal namesake, which is projected to win 19 seats, entering the National Assembly for the first time with a flourish. Under the leadership of former radio host Éric Duhaime, the party captured voters in the traditionally right-leaning Quebec City and Beauce regions who felt government spending has become bloated and wasteful.

The geopolitical context largely took a back seat in this campaign to more prosaic concerns about deteriorating public services and the cost of living. A majority of parties proposed cuts to the size of the public service and immigration. A small-c conservative mood prevailed, with even the historically social-democratic PQ moving to the right.

Despite the upsurge in pro-Canadian sentiment in recent years, Quebeckers also remain anxious about the state of the French language and Quebec culture after years of sharply rising immigration under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and the expansion of an overwhelmingly English-language digital sphere.

The governing Coalition Avenir Québec, meanwhile, was wiped off the map after running the province for eight years. Leader Christine Fréchette lost her own seat as the party was completely shut out on Monday.

The election results come at a delicate moment for national unity, with a referendum in Alberta two weeks away, and persistent threats to Canada’s sovereignty and economy from U.S. President Donald Trump. Among the provinces, Quebec has been the biggest casualty of Mr. Trump’s protectionist trade agenda, which has targeted its aluminum and forest product industries in particular.

The PQ Leader has promised a vote on the province’s place within Canada once Mr. Trump leaves office in 2029, at which point Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon says Quebec can have a “serene” discussion about its future.

With a minority in the National Assembly, the PQ would need support from other parties or individual MNAs to trigger a referendum, and to stay in power. The PQ’s comeback comes after years in the wilderness. The party was last in government in 2014; in 2022, it had just three seats.
Despite saying little about independence during the election campaign, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon spoke at length about sovereignty during his victory speech in Montreal on Monday.
“The Quebec we want to build for ourselves will be French-speaking. It will be prosperous and modern, but above all, it will be among the most exemplary democracies on the planet,” he said.

“We simply want to exist as a nation and make our own decisions, just like the other 200 countries in the world... We must not let fear prevent us from fulfilling our destiny. And that destiny lies before us. The courageous struggle of francophones in America to preserve their cultural identity will find meaning when that people obtains its own country and the recognition that comes with having their own country and their own democracy.”
Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon suggested the PQ could launch a referendum with the backing of opposition lawmakers who support independence and “would make this commitment possible.”

He also sent a message directly to the rest of Canada. “The independence project we are pursuing is not directed against you, and Quebec will always be a partner in good faith, open to collaboration, just as we have always been,” he said.

The PQ Leader could make relations with the federal government far more contentious. He is vowing to eliminate the role of lieutenant-governor in Quebec and fight any increases in immigration at a time when Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking inter-provincial peace in the face of U.S. economic aggression.

Mr. Carney congratulated Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon on his victory on social media on Monday night, and said he looks forward to working together “to support Québec’s businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec.”

Polls show only about 30 per cent of Quebeckers support independence, a historically low level in the province, where previous referendums led by then-PQ governments in 1980 and 1995 tallied 40 and 49 per cent support respectively.
The new government May struggle to defend the legitimacy of holding an independence vote, while calls to reform the provincial electoral system are likely to grow louder.

Québec solidaire, a left-wing separatist party that focuses more on social justice than independence, was projected to finish fourth, but could now wield the balance of power in the National Assembly after retaining many of its stronghold seats in Montreal.

It remains uncertain whether QS would support the PQ’s referendum ambitions. The two parties diverge sharply on immigration and identity issues, while Ruba Ghazal, the co-leader for QS, has promised a more wide-ranging consultation on the nature of an independent Quebec.

On Monday, Ms. Ghazal said she wants to build an independent Quebec alongside immigrants, Indigenous people and anglophones. “We’re going to be there to build a country that leaves no one behind,” she said. “A country for and by the people, a country for everyone.”

The election marks an unforgiving end to the eight-year reign of the Coalition Avenir Québec, which won consecutive majorities under former premier François Legault. Its brand of nationalism without independence – a vaunted “third way” between federalism and separatism – strongly resonated with voters, but the party was undone by several episodes of financial mismanagement in recent years.

Under Ms. Fréchette, the CAQ was unable to counter an overwhelming appetite for change. An early polling bump spurred by the U.S. trade war gave the outgoing Premier a chance to portray herself as a defender of Quebeckers. But as the shock of the conflict diminished, voters’ attention drifted elsewhere.

At the Caq’s election night event at the Delta Hotel in Trois-Rivières Monday, supporters had almost nothing to cheer about. Some stared at live results on a jumbo screen with stone-faced expressions.

“This result is clearly not what we’d hoped for and as party leader, I assume the entire responsibility for it,” Ms. Fréchette said in her concession speech. “Quebeckers wanted change and I respect their choice. I want to tell you that the convictions that united us will continue. The Coalition will continue to promote a third way – that of a Quebec that affirms its identity, protects its language and culture, maintains our autonomy, and gives itself the means to protect and transform its economy.”
Ms. Fréchette has vowed to stay on as party leader and work with Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon to ease the transition to his government.

The Quebec Liberal Party under new Leader Charles Milliard struggled to distinguish itself from other parties opposing a referendum, despite a strong end to the campaign, and the party was poised to finish in second place. The most resolutely federalist party in Quebec now faces being locked out of power for a decade or more, its longest stretch in opposition since the 1950s.

Still, the party’s projected 40 seats were more than many PLQ faithful hoped for entering Monday night, and the mood at Mr. Milliard’s gathering in Magog was upbeat. The incoming Opposition leader vowed to work with the new PQ government on some issues, but block its referendum hopes.

“A minority government means they don’t have a blank cheque to do what they want,” said Mr. Milliard. “We’ll collaborate on the housing crisis, the homelessness crisis. On the sovereignty crisis, we won’t be collaborating.”

The anti-referendum vote was further splintered by a relatively new force in Quebec politics, the provincial Conservative Party, unrelated to its federal namesake, which is projected to win 19 seats, entering the National Assembly for the first time with a flourish. Under the leadership of former radio host Éric Duhaime, the party captured voters in the traditionally right-leaning Quebec City and Beauce regions who felt government spending has become bloated and wasteful.

The geopolitical context largely took a back seat in this campaign to more prosaic concerns about deteriorating public services and the cost of living. A majority of parties proposed cuts to the size of the public service and immigration. A small-c conservative mood prevailed, with even the historically social-democratic PQ moving to the right.

Despite the upsurge in pro-Canadian sentiment in recent years, Quebeckers also remain anxious about the state of the French language and Quebec culture after years of sharply rising immigration under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and the expansion of an overwhelmingly English-language digital sphere.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Québec solidaire's Ruba Ghazal projected to win riding
stories.summary: Montreal - The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal will win her Montreal-area riding of Mercier.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ghazal was a founding member of the left wing sovereigntist party in 2006, alongside Françoise David and Amir Khadir.

She first entered the legislature when she won the riding in 2018.

She was re-elected in 2022.

Ghazal was born in Lebanon to a family of Palestinian refugees in 1977.

She arrived in Quebec at the age of 10 and grew up between Montreal and Laval.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stevenson would realign London’s addiction and homelessness strategy, but Morgan refutes disconnect with province
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson took aim at London’s response to the homelessness and addiction crisis at a campaign announcement on Monday, but incumbent candidate Josh Morgan was quick to fire back.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson took aim at London’s response to the homelessness and addiction crisis at a campaign announcement on Monday, but incumbent candidate Josh Morgan was quick to fire back.

“I want London to lead Ontario in building a recovery-oriented system of care,” she said during her latest campaign platform announcement.

“People choosing recovery, people coming out of ten-day detox, or rehab programs, deserve (before and after) shelters that are abstinent and some access to housing where abstinence is there,” Stevenson said afterwards.

She suggested that an insufficient number of spaces for sober living in local shelters and the supportive housing system jeopardizes efforts by some homeless Londoners to stay off drugs.

If elected, Stevenson pledged:

To seek Council support to align London’s response with Ontario’s recovery-oriented direction by bringing provincial, health, housing and community partners together to address recovery gaps

Pursue a provincial addiction treatment centre that would coordinate with existing services and the London Hart Hub

Review Project Home and overhaul Housing Stability programs by retaining effective services and changing services that fall short

Launch a Homeless Response Review (2020-2025) to track how provincial funding and the privately donated Fund For Change were utilized

“These policies chosen by this mayor and approved by this Council have failed us,” she asserted. “And it’s time for something new.”

Incumbent candidate Josh Morgan shot back, asserting that no municipally-funded programs are required to provide harm reduction services.

He added that the city, and the Ontario Big City Mayors (Obcm) have already been lobbying the provincial government to fund new addiction treatment centres.

“The current system is not complete, it’s got a huge gap in it. It needs more treatment and recovery spaces,” Morgan tells CTV News. “That’s why there’s a standing position of Council saying we support building a treatment and recovery facility right here, funded by the province of Ontario.”

Morgan rejects Stevenson’s suggestion that London’s response to homelessness and addiction are not in alignment with the provincial government.

“We’re not out of alignment with the province. We are a partner with the province working to try to solve a very complex issue,” he explained. “That partnership requires focus, collaboration, and ongoing dialog-- not pointing fingers at each other.”

Stevenson suggested the prevalence of harm reduction at local frontline agencies proves otherwise, “ (Ontario) abandoned the failed harm reduction model and said we are going to the Alberta recovery model. It happened in April of 2024.”

“(The province is) our biggest funding partner when it comes to treatment, health, and housing,” she added. “To align with them makes sense, especially when we are worse off than we were four years ago.”

Also on Monday, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose released her 10-year Homelessness and Housing Strategy in an emailed news release.

“We need to prevent people from becoming homeless, correct the systems that are not working together, and create the housing and supportive spaces our community actually needs,” Krose writes.

Her strategy includes three pillars:

Prevent: Understand and address why people are becoming homeless

Correct: Make City policy work toward the same goal

Create: Build the spaces London actually needs

“The Prevent. Correct. Create. framework would guide a 10-year strategy with annual targets, defined responsibilities, measurable outcomes and transparent public reporting,” the statement by Krose concludes.

stories.title: How the separatist Parti Québécois took back power in Quebec
stories.summary: The separatist party, which was nearly wiped off the electoral map four years ago, came roaring back on Monday night.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL, QC — The rest of Canada will be waking up on Tuesday to a slightly less painful hangover than expected after Quebec elected a minority Parti Québécois government led by leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

The separatist party, which was nearly wiped off the electoral map four years ago, came roaring back just a few seats shy from a majority. However, the party underestimated support for Éric Duhaime’s Conservatives that stopped the PQ from getting to the magic number of 64 seats.

St-Pierre Plamondon promised to collaborate with other parties in a minority situation, including working with Québec Solidaire — which is also vying for the independence of Quebec — to hold another referendum.

He also had a message for the rest of the country that is apprehending the return of his party in power.

“I want to reiterate the following: the independence project we are championing is not directed against you. Quebec will always be a partner acting in good faith and open to collaboration — as we have always been,” he said.

National Post spoke to over a dozen people in the PQ’s orbit — candidates, political staff and people who know the leader well — in an attempt to understand just how the PQ pulled off the feat of winning government with 28 per cent of the vote.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s party had been first in the polls, almost without interruption for nearly three years. And he was facing a new incumbent premier in Christine Fréchette who, many would agree, was performing well in the role.

It was easy for political adversaries to point out that, in that sense, the situation could become similar to Pierre Poilievre’s Conservative Party of Canada who lost against Mark Carney’s Liberals last year despite dominating poll numbers for years.

But with a fixed election date set for Oct. 5 and with five main political parties at play — including three splitting the federalist vote — the situation was entirely different.

Louis Lyonnais, one of St-Pierre Plamondon’s closest aides, said the PQ was well aware that Fréchette’s Coalition Avenir Québec was going to use the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. to scare voters into re-electing her government.

“We knew the CAQ would play that card. That was all they had left,” he said.

That is why on Aug. 18, days before the election, St-Pierre Plamondon made the formal announcement that a PQ government would only hold a referendum on the separation of Quebec after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029.

It wasn’t exactly a new promise, as the PQ was already planning to hold the referendum near the end of a first mandate in government. But making that announcement would lessen the attacks that the PQ would destabilize Quebec in already unstable times.

“We took away their strongest argument,” Lyonnais said of the PQ’s main adversaries.

The days that followed saw the collapse of trade talks between Canada and the U.S. which caused the “rally ‘round the flag” even in Quebec. Trump imposed further tariffs on Canadian exports and Canada shot back with counter-tariffs on U.S. imports.

The sequence of events benefitted Fréchette, who was presenting herself as the person best placed to face Trump. Her party was creeping up in the polls, in second place, and many were wondering if the “Trump effect” could push her just over the edge.

Lucas Medernach, director of communications for the PQ, said the party was expecting the CAQ to slightly go up in the polls, but he wasn’t anticipating the counter-tariffs which helped the incumbent party go up a bit higher than anticipated.

However, the CAQ never saw a “stratospheric” rise in the polls either, he said.

The only party that was able to rise to the PQ’s levels was the Liberal party which, back in the spring, was toe-to-toe with the separatist party. But leader Charles Milliard’s perceived ambiguity on the question of the French language and religious signs in recent months set him back.

The PQ was especially keeping a close eye on the vote of people aged 55 and up, which were heavily leaning towards the CAQ because of the trade war with the U.S. Medernach admitted that trend was a little “worrisome” at the start of the campaign.

What also irked the Péquistes was the fact that Carney and Fréchette were often seen together for major announcements in the days leading up to the campaign, whether it was for the Churchill Falls energy deal or Davie Shipyard’s icebreakers contract.

“Let’s be honest: Mark Carney had chosen his winner,” Medernach said.

Carney’s team has denied that was the case, and that they were simply working with the team in place to land some major deals. If anything, the federal government was more concerned about its own results in the Chicoutimi byelection on Aug. 31.

Fréchette would use every opportunity to tout just how in sync she was with Carney’s team, saying that she had influenced Canada’s counter-tariffs. That was promptly denied by Ottawa, in a move seen by the PQ to create a distance between the two.

In the weeks that followed, the CAQ leader was forced to admit she was not consulted about some of Ottawa’s major initiatives before they were announced.

That was the case about the plan to privatize operations at the Montreal airport and the productivity mega deduction that would deprive Quebec from an estimated 1 billion annually in corporate tax revenue as it would need to harmonize its rules.

Fréchette also struggled to say early on whether she was a federalist or a sovereigntist — she worked for the PQ during the Pauline Marois government — and eventually settled on being an “autonomist” vying for more powers for Quebec within Canada.

Medernach said the electorate took notice of these contradictions and it reinforced the need to have someone who is authentic and straightforward with voters.

Before the debates, St-Pierre Plamondon and his team seemed tense . The CAQ was still too close for comfort in many critical ridings around the Montreal area, and his small team was struggling to keep up with the daily flow of announcements.

“How could we not be stressed? We were the target of all the attacks,” said Medernach.

Furthermore, the PQ had much less financial resources than its competitors, having elected only three members of the National Assembly (MNAs) back in 2022. The caucus eventually grew to seven members after the PQ elected four more in byelections.

Overall, the campaign was too crowded with too many promises from all five parties.

One PQ staffer admitted it was a boring campaign, where parties were proposing different nuances of the same thing because there is no money in government coffers.

Lyonnais said there is simply nothing to spend: “You can’t invent money.”

For instance, the PQ, the Quebec Conservatives and Québec Solidaire said they would abolish the provincial tax on used goods, such as cars, electronics and clothes. The PQ and the Conservatives also vowed to cut taxes on gas at various degrees.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s team decided to put a lot of energy into preparing for the debates, even keeping him from making public events in the days preceding the first one. The leader was even absent from presenting his party’s financial framework.

“Paul is a sprinter,” said one former PQ staffer. He said the leader is at his best when he is able to focus on a few things at a time. Working with him, the staffer said St-Pierre Plamondon would often have three intense days and three with a lighter schedule.

Lyonnais said the strategy was for the leader to arrive at the debates in good shape.

“Our job is to turn him into a marathon runner too,” he said.

By all accounts, St-Pierre Plamondon performed relatively well in the debates. But even his team acknowledges that he got off easily and wasn’t the target of many attacks.

“We had braced ourselves for many, many, many attacks,” Lyonnais said. “But indeed, yes —perhaps we weren’t attacked as much as we thought we would be.”

Fréchette, ON the other hand, was forced to defend eight years of the Caq’s record.

She made the bizarre choice, some PQ officials remarked privately, to distance herself from the founder of the party in the first debate. “I am not François Legault. I am Christine Fréchette, and I bring my own way of doing things,” she said.

“I think Quebecers saw right through the Caq’s strategies, which tried to claim it was a brand-new team with a new vision. It was the same old CAQ,” said Pascal Paradis, former PQ MNA for Jean-Talon in the Quebec City area.

St-Pierre Plamondon has the reputation of looking angry or having a short fuse. So, his team had to keep him “grounded” to make sure he would stay calm and collected.

As the father of three young children, he would spend a half-day each week with his family. And during the debates, he had a picture of his children in front of him — a way for him to remember that not every shot at him is worth getting worked up about.

Former PQ MNA Alex Boissonneault, who lost his seat on Monday night to the Conservatives, said there already was an understanding at the onset of the campaign that Quebecers were ready for change after eight years of a CAQ government and that the PQ could embody that change.

While he felt around the mid-campaign mark that people’s impressions of the different leaders had “crystallized” and that voters were ready to make their choice, it did not quite benefit him in this election.

Medernach said that, after the third debate, seeing that the leader had not made mistakes and that the polls were still good, that the PQ thought this could be it.

“Our stress was replaced by the question: will we win a minority or a majority?”

The fatal blow for the CAQ was without a doubt the allegations of foreign interference , 48 hours away from the opening of advance polls. A report claimed that an obscure U.S. think tank was attempting to help the PQ get elected to divide the country.

Fréchette, after claiming she would ask for a meeting with Carney on the matter, was forced to admit that her own officials had contacted Csis on the matter days prior. She eventually said there was no proof of interference in the Quebec election.

It eventually came out that the CAQ was shopping around the story to reporters.

Lyonnais said it was at that moment that people told themselves, “Wow, this is getting ridiculous.” And that was 48 hours before the advanced polling. The polls in the final week would show that the Caq’s numbers had dropped to fourth place.

“I think that when people base their campaign on fear, it often ends up backfiring,” Lyonnais said. “That’s what happened here, because it was too heavy-handed.”

More than a quarter of Quebecers — 1.6 million — opted to vote early.

In the last week, St-Pierre Plamondon picked up the speed in the campaign.

He was, in his own words, putting “the pedal to the metal” to try to win a majority government. And, yes, he was repeating the expression in English.

With the CAQ out of the picture — or almost — the PQ was especially focused on visiting ridings where there would be tight races with the Quebec Conservatives or the Liberals in the Quebec City area, and Quebec Solidaire in the Montreal area.

The Quebec Liberals and the CAQ, meanwhile, were doing their best to try to convince voters not to vote for the PQ because they are promising to hold a referendum.

But for Medernach, that was never the ballot box question — it was change.

St-Pierre Plamondon was smiling again effortlessly.

In a coffee shop in the Quebec City area, the PQ leader even started joking with reporters that he could see a “phoenix rising from the ashes” in his latte art.

In one pit stop in Laval — a Liberal stronghold — St-Pierre Plamondon became teary as he hugged his father, Jacques Plamondon. The nearly 200 people were chanting his name as the PQ leader was swarmed with selfies in a Trudeauesque manner.

“That’s our future premier, right there!” yelled one person.

Medernach said he expected the party to end up with a minority. To have it come so close to a majority was a win, said the director of communications. And seeing the CAQ wiped off the electoral map is a plus.

But the faces of the PQ supporters on election night told another story. While they were happy to finally be back in government, they lost some of their best MNAs in the Conservative wave that swept the Quebec City area. And the perspective of possibly heading into another election in 18 months as a minority is especially daunting.

Jacques Plamondon has other concerns. The day before the election, he candidly said he is “more nervous than proud” about his son becoming the premier of Quebec because of all the headwinds he will face.

“These are the most difficult moments now, because he is championing a specific cause — the cause of Quebec as a sovereign nation. That is the greatest challenge.”

“So, he faces nothing but enemies.”

stories.title: Fanshawe students having conversations about consent, party culture in light of “Cornell Seven” case
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/GvYMwLs9g90 With the "Cornell Seven" case continuing to make headlines around the world, stud...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
With the “Cornell Seven” case continuing to make headlines around the world, students at Fanshawe are having conversations about parties and consent on and around campus, as well as sharing how they and the people around them can stay safe.

The conversations come in the shadow of the ongoing case from the prestigious Ivy League university located in Ithaca, N.Y., where a woman known only as “Jane Doe” has accused seven male students of sexually assaulting her during a party at a fraternity house in 2024.

Many Fanshawe students living in housing on Kestrel Court have said they are aware of the case, but in their own opinions and experiences, they said the party scene in the student housing bloc is not especially rowdy.

“Nothing really big happens, to be honest,” said accounting student Olivia Reees. “Everybody’s just like getting together and talking to one another.”

At the same time, some students said they had been to parties outside of Kestrel, and described them as being “pretty busy.” As well, multiple students said that the bar scene at Western University and other places in London was concerning.

“I have had friends who have some stories with … people being a little bit inappropriate in terms of words and trying to get them to get into their Ubers,” said second-year nursing student Brooklyn Fisher.

Many students at Fanshawe said that at parties they or their friends had been to, the prioritization of consent by the people there was mixed.

“I guess it depends on who you are, and like if you’re drinking and how that type of person is,” said child and youth care student Charleigh Borell. “If you feel responsible and you’re feeling friendly at other people, then … yes, but if you’re not and they’re just going to look for something, then

A list of support resources provided for Fanshawe students by the Centre for Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (Cedi). The “Cornell Seven” case has inspired many conversations about safety and consent at Fanshawe. Photos by: Curtis Stokman

Concerns such as these were prevalent among the students interviewed. All of them shared similar strategies that they use to keep themselves and the people around them safe at parties. Jaylene MacLean, a business international law student at Conestoga College who was visiting Fanshawe, said she doesn’t drink as much when in public.

“I always like to stick with a friend no matter where I go,” said Borell. “Whether it’s a party or anywhere I like to be.”

Reees and fellow child and youth care student Madison Armstrong said they share the same strategy as Borell, and that all three of them look out for others when at parties.

XFM News also reached out to Fanshawe sexual violence and prevention consultant Xieling Zhang for comment. While she was unable to answer questions, the Centre for Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (Cedi) office that she works in did provide a list of resources available to students who May be in need of support.

Ultimately, while the “Cornell Seven” case May still be ongoing, some students believe the conversations that it has started are important.

“I’m glad that a lot more awareness is being spread about this,” said Fisher.
