stories.title: Air Canada's woeful security at cargo warehouse at time of Toronto's airport gold heist detailed in court
stories.summary: An employee testified that though she was not working that day, someone logged in under her name to remove a high-security code on the shipment
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
When the largest gold heist in Canadian history was pulled off at Air Canada’s cargo warehouse at Toronto airport in 2023, security was so lax that almost any employee could change critical information on any shipment from any computer, court heard.

On the opening day of trial for Parmpal Sidhu, a 56-year-old former Air Canada cargo warehouse employee, an Air Canada manager testified that someone used her log-in credentials to change an important code that allowed the gold to be passed off as a shipment of salmon.

Elizabeth Zaritskaya, now the manager of Hub Operations at Air Canada, testified that even though she was not at the airport on the day of the Toronto Pearson gold heist, her password was used to redirect the shipment that was worth more than $22 million.

“I was not working that day, but yes, my user ID was used to perform one of the functions” that allowed the spectacular heist, she testified in court.

Security inside Air Canada’s warehouse at Toronto’s Pearson airport is key to unravelling the gold heist in April 2023 that led to a shipping crate stuffed with 400 kilograms of nearly pure gold and $2.5 million in currency being stolen shortly after it arrived on an Air Canada flight from Switzerland without anyone noticing for hours.

Whoever logged in under Zaritskaya’s name used it to delete the code “VAL” from the shipment’s listing in the Air Canada cargo management system, court heard. VAL, short for valuable, flags precious cargo for high-security handling.

The VAL code would have alerted staff unloading the crate from a flight from Zurich that it needed to be placed in a secure storage location, which is both locked and guarded, until armed Brink’s guards arrived to collect it. Without the VAL code, staff handled it like regular cargo and placed it in a routine spot in the warehouse.

As a result, Zaritskaya said, the valuable crate was treated as “a basic shipment and it could pass for fish” — and that was step one in the plot that allowed someone supposedly picking up salmon from Scotland to drive away with gold from Switzerland.

India's search for missing loot from Toronto airport gold heist prevents alleged inside man from returning to Canada for trial

Two men charged in the Toronto Pearson Airport gold heist have their charges dropped

“So it was a very critical and crucial change,” Zaritskaya said.

She said she didn’t know who had used her credentials.

Court heard that a second change was made to the gold shipment’s handling on the internal system using the login credentials of a different Air Canada manager. That change told cargo workers not to breakdown or separate the contents of the crate, even though the gold and the currency were going to different destinations, the gold to the TD Bank in Toronto and the currency to a foreign exchange in Vancouver.

A third element crucial to pulling off the heist was a handwritten notation on an Air Canada waybill changing the internal warehouse location code that tells employees where to pick up a specific shipment for a waiting customer.

While changing the VAL code disguised a valuable shipment as regular cargo, changing the warehouse storage space meant that when a truck driver presented the altered paperwork at the counter, the crate of gold was brought out by a forklift and loaded onto his truck.

Court heard that security has improved at the warehouse, but at the time of the gold heist the evidence painted a picture of a security mess where computer credentials, profiles, and logins were frequently shared among employees out of convenience, shared workspaces, shared computers and staff forgetting to log out.

Sometimes Zaritskaya would sit down at a computer and find it already logged in by someone else with crucial internal systems still accessible.

“You would have a direct opportunity to change something or do whatever functions and, unfortunately, we used to do that,” she said under questioning by Crown prosecutor Tyler Powell.

Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, later pressed her further on the point.

“Security, you would agree, was very lax at Air Canada cargo at that time,” Wagman asked Zaritskaya.

“Do I have to answer to this question,” Zaritskaya asked the judge.

“There’s nothing wrong with the question,” said Judge Gordon Cudjoe of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton.

“Not in every area,” Zaritskaya answered, “but it clearly was lacking since we have stolen gold, so I have to answer yes.”

Asked whether one of Sidhu’s co-accused in the gold heist, a fellow former Air Canada employee named Simran Preet Panesar, had access to Sidhu’s computer at the warehouse, Zaritskaya said she did not specifically know, but it is likely.

“It is safe to assume that anybody would have access to (Sidhu’s) computer or to my computer or to any computer,” she said.

Similarly, she was asked by Powell about the official Air Canada stamps used on the doctored waybill that made it look official. Could any employee access them, he asked?

“Yes,” Zaritskaya said. “Usually all of them (the stamps) are at the counter… Probably the customer cannot reach out to grab them but anybody who is behind me or around me, they can just come and grab it. We didn’t monitor them or anything like that before.”

Zaritskaya was asked by prosecutors if she knew Sidhu, who sat beside his lawyers in court wearing a white button-up shirt under a light beige jacket, and periodically whispered to them.

She said they used to be colleagues at the Air Canada warehouse, where he worked for several year before the gold theft.

Sidhu was a lead cargo service agent. People often called him “Paul” at work.

“Anything I needed as a manager, he was there. Never was problematic or dramatic or anything else that unionized employees could be. So, at the time when I was working with him, there was no issues.

“I have to say he is very knowledgeable. He always knew everything.”

That meant he had the knowledge to use any of the Air Canada computers or equipment and knew the codes and processes that impact all the shipments, she said.

Sidhu pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to steal more than $5,000.

The trial continues Tuesday.

stories.title: Business as usual after deadly day-time shooting
stories.summary: Nearly a week after a fatal shooting in broad daylight on Richmond Street, it appeared to be business as usual...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
Nearly a week after a fatal shooting in broad daylight on Richmond Street, it appeared to be business as usual Monday.

London police have charged a 21 year old man in the shooting at the corner of Central Ave., and Richmond St. on Sept. 29. He is expected to appear in court Oct. 7. The suspect and victim are said to have known each other.

“Everything is pretty much business as usual, same every day.” says Samantha Simpson, the day-time bartender at Richmond Tavern.

The sentiment was echoed by many of the businesses XFM spoke to. However, Simpson questioned how long that might continue.

“Downtown is getting worse and worse all the time,” She said. “It is getting more dangerous, that’s for sure.”

Fae Clare, a new-hire at the YOU Made It Café, however, feels differently.

“Hearing about it now, I do feel less safe, and I do think that people would come in less often if they think that the street is dangerous.”

stories.title: First Nation demands more info on Bell AI data centre near Regina: ‘We have to live here’
stories.summary: The Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation penned a letter to Bell Canada requesting documentation and information regarding the AI data centre that is under construction near Regina.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A Saskatchewan First Nation wants more information, including potential environmental impacts, as Bell Canada continues construction of an AI data centre outside of Regina.

The Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation in Fort Qu’appelle, Sask., penned the letter to Bell Canada and Bell Canada Enterprises, or BCE Inc., Oct. 2.

It called on the company to allow the nation to make its own assessment of the AI data centre project being constructed in the RM of Sherwood.

The letter copied provincial and federal officials, including Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The nation’s process would involve Bell applying for, and being granted, a permit, as well as meetings with its Elders oversight committee, its chief said.

“These data centres are going to be impacting the traditional territories,” Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation Chief Rodger Redman told Global News in an interview.

“Our issue is that we haven’t even addressed that yet. Yet these projects are coming through. That’s what I’m saying — that these issues have to be addressed.”

2:01 Bell’s AI Data Centre approved by council amidst chaotic protest

The letter states the Sherwood data centre is being built on unceded, traditional Dakota territory.

As a result, the nation is seeking documents, including ecological and cultural baseline studies, in addition to assessments of the expected effects across all the project phases.

“Industry and government, with other companies, will move on to the next area. We have to live here,” Redman said.

“Nothing is going to be able to grow in this area. The farmers aren’t going to be able to grow crops. Our people aren’t going to be able to sustain, provide sustenance from the animals because they’re going to be contaminated.

“(This is) the whole issue of the byproducts that’s coming from these data centres — what’s going to happen with that?”

Bell Canada previously said the centre will run with an air-cooled heat rejection system to reduce the amount of water used for normal operation.

The cooling fluid will be trucked in and added to the system, where it will remain until it must be replaced, according to Bell’s website .

2:02 Bell AI Data Centre quadrupling expansion raises questions

The Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation is requesting further information on that system. Namely, it wants engineering specs, details on how the system will be maintained and how the water will be disposed of, when necessary, according to its letter.

“When we talk about sustainability and looking for the future, it’s not just to deal with and create large amounts of money. Because when you contaminate the land, the water, the air, every living thing that’s surrounding that area, the economies are going to change. Health care is going to change,” Redman said.

Bell was also asked to provide expected replacement schedules for equipment at the facility. The nation’s letter asked the company for details on how equipment will be determined to be ready for disposal, instead of being repaired or refurbished to extend their lifespans.

“I actually don’t want to leave a cesspool of toxic waste for my grandchildren. I don’t think anybody does. So, we need to do our due diligence in looking at impacts of these projects (of) this size and what it means,” Redman added.

The letter ended by calling on Bell to engage with the Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation or to provide the requested documentation within 30 days.

In an email statement for Global News, Bell Canada said it is “committed to ongoing, meaningful engagement with local communities, including First Nations” as it continues developing AI infrastructure.

“Bell AI Fabric projects are developed in accordance with all applicable regulatory and environmental requirements, and we will continue to provide relevant information about potential impacts through the appropriate processes,” the company’s statement continued.

Global News reached out to the Saskatchewan government for comment, but none was received at the time of publication.

stories.title: Trailblazer Jay Levine made Fashion Television a cultural phenomenon
stories.summary: The show he created ran for 27 years, went into global syndication and spawned a magazine plus a 24-hour specialty channel
stories.author: Diane Peters
stories.content:
Television producer Jay Levine knew little about clothing or designers when he changed both broadcasting and the fashion world with the launch of the first Fashion Television ( FT ) broadcasts in 1985. He was creator and founding producer of the show, which ran for 27 years, went into global syndication and spawned a magazine and a 24-hour specialty channel.

“We were strangers in a strange land,” said Jeanne Beker, the former host of FT , of the early days of the show. “I didn’t know much about fashion and neither did Jay. He wasn’t Mr. Fashionista, but he did understand what would be compelling to watch.”

When it launched, the only other mainstream fashion-related television program on air was Cnn’s staid Style With Elsa Klensch. FT differentiated itself by focusing on lively storytelling; the approach had many imitators.

“One of the keys to success of the show is it never discussed hemlines or colours or trends or anything insipid like that. It was about people – the arbiters of style around the world. FT felt elevated compared to its competition,” said Tyler Levine, Mr. Levine’s half-brother, who worked on FT with him for many years.

Jay Levine, 69, died on Sept. 1 of complications related to lung cancer.

Ms. Beker and others say he set high standards for the show.

“A show about fashion could have been this trivial, superficial show. But he was always encouraging us to dig deeper,” recalled Howard Brull, who worked on FT for its entire run, starting as an editor and later senior producer. He said the team pushed themselves every day to do better, often to impress Mr. Levine. “He brought a certain level of excellence and professionalism.”

Ms. Beker said his innovative ideas for segments meant that she, Mr. Levine and crew members would visit the world’s fashion capitals but also went to Japan in 1986 to cover the fashion scene, visited Russia after the Berlin Wall came down and did a one-hour special on Israeli design. “I’m always coming across pictures of Jay and I in the trenches in Milan or other places,” she said.

The show’s early years coincided with the ascendance of runway fashion and supermodels in pop culture, and FT capitalized on the trend, garnering interest from around the world – it was syndicated in as many as 140 countries.

FT was nominated repeatedly for Gemini Awards (which merged with the Genie Awards and are now called the Canadian Screen Awards) but the show never won; Tyler said Jay did not care. Mr. Levine’s documentary Naked in the House: A Photographic Competition , which he produced under the FT brand, won a Gemini in 2002 for best editing. (The Globe and Mail called it an “amazing, different hour of television.”)

FT used pop music to back its runway footage and featured enticing – and often skin-revealing – visuals; its tagline was “sexy, stylish and spectacular.” It proved sexy enough to trigger viewer complaints, but the Canadian Broadcast Standards Council ruled that the show did not breach the broadcast code.

Those who worked for City-TV at its Queen Street West location in Toronto recall the early FT era as an exciting time when creative and even rebellious ideas were welcome – and Jay fit right in. “He was naturally a very cool guy,” Tyler said.

Mr. Levine had also studied economics and understood the business side, often going to bat for the show when budget cuts threatened it. “He was very charming. He would talk to the corporate people and he got our shows at least an additional five years,” Mr. Brull said. FT was cancelled in 2012.

Mr. Levine was always reading at his desk, but seldom about fashion, Mr. Brull said. “[In] most of our conversations in the over 25 years we worked together, I don’t think we discussed fashion. We were discussing life.”

He taught Tyler to be well-versed in what was going on in the world in order to make smart television. “His part of being a producer of Fashion Television required reading every newspaper and listening to every interview he could. So I kept up that kind of scouring, just always hunting for a good story.”

Ms. Beker said Mr. Levine served as a mentor to many young people. “I’m now hearing so many stories from people about how when they were newbies, he was very much there to support them,” she said.

Jay Lawrence Levine was born on May 9, 1957, in Toronto. His father, Norman Levine, was an entrepreneur and his mother was Beverley (née White, later Rosen). He had an elder brother, David, and a younger one named Harvey. His parents later divorced; Norm Levine remarried and the union produced a son, Tyler, who is 18 years younger than Jay.

Jay studied economics and film at York University, graduating in 1979. His father was close friends with director and producer Perry Rosemond, who died in August , and he helped Jay get his start in television. That included serving in junior roles on the CTV sketch show Bizarre .

Tyler said Jay drove a taxi early in his career and, one day, Moses Znaimer, then head of City-TV, got into his cab; by the end of the ride the media executive offered him a job.

Mr. Levine wrote in The Canadian Jewish News in 2022 that he had pitched a review show about theatre to City-TV, which he described as “the channel where I always wanted to work.” Instead, Mr. Znaimer asked him to produce the 10 p.m. newscast. “And that was the City-TV aesthetic: Getting someone who knew nothing about news to do the news. It was enough to assure me a few years later that I could make a show about fashion,” Mr. Levine wrote.

It was through his extensive reading that Mr. Levine hit on the idea: He found out that Paris designers were filming their collections for American buyers who could not attend the fashion shows in person. “I figured if we could get our hands on that footage, we could make a show about that.”

Mr. Levine’s first concept was tentatively titled Vogue on Video , but that morphed into FT, Tyler recalled. Ms. Beker, who was working on The New Music and wanted a change, advocated to become the host.

Fashion Television started in 1985 as 15-minute segments and launched as a half-hour show a year later. It quickly found viewers and Mr. Levine, Ms. Beker and their camera operators were soon travelling the world, asking fashion icons what it was it like having their names on people’s underwear and who their favourite architect was.

The show, “created a world appetite for television fashion programs …and inspired others to try to imitate its style and content,” an article on the History of Canadian Broadcasting website said. This even led to a copyright infringement lawsuit, a case FT lost.

In 2001, Chum Limited, which owned City-TV, launched Fashion Television Channel, a 24-hour station. It aired a full slate of fashion and art-related content in its early years. It stopped operations in 2021.

Meanwhile, in 2004, the team at FT launched a magazine with Ms. Beker at the helm.

While working at FT and after the show ended, Mr. Levine took on other projects as well, such as the two-season talk show Spectacle: Elvis Costello with… , which launched in 2008, and a series about architecture. Outside of television, he developed digital content for the Andy Warhol Museum, in Pittsburgh, in 2013.

When he became ill, Mr. Levine was working on a project about music managers who were pivotal to the career of their artists and the music scene. “I was excited to see what he was going to come up with. I knew he was capable of doing anything,” Mr. Brull said.

Mr. Levine is remembered as a great friend, a talented television producer and a cool and funny guy who could talk intelligently and wittily about any topic. “He was hilarious and he was brilliant,” Mr. Brull said.

Mr. Levine leaves his brothers and their families.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

Ms. Beker said his innovative ideas for segments meant that she, Mr. Levine and crew members would visit the world’s fashion capitals but also went to Japan in 1986 to cover the fashion scene, visited Russia after the Berlin Wall came down and did a one-hour special on Israeli design. “I’m always coming across pictures of Jay and I in the trenches in Milan or other places,” she said.

The show’s early years coincided with the ascendance of runway fashion and supermodels in pop culture, and FT capitalized on the trend, garnering interest from around the world – it was syndicated in as many as 140 countries.

FT was nominated repeatedly for Gemini Awards (which merged with the Genie Awards and are now called the Canadian Screen Awards) but the show never won; Tyler said Jay did not care. Mr. Levine’s documentary Naked in the House: A Photographic Competition , which he produced under the FT brand, won a Gemini in 2002 for best editing. (The Globe and Mail called it an “amazing, different hour of television.”)

FT used pop music to back its runway footage and featured enticing – and often skin-revealing – visuals; its tagline was “sexy, stylish and spectacular.” It proved sexy enough to trigger viewer complaints, but the Canadian Broadcast Standards Council ruled that the show did not breach the broadcast code.

Those who worked for City-TV at its Queen Street West location in Toronto recall the early FT era as an exciting time when creative and even rebellious ideas were welcome – and Jay fit right in. “He was naturally a very cool guy,” Tyler said.

Mr. Levine had also studied economics and understood the business side, often going to bat for the show when budget cuts threatened it. “He was very charming. He would talk to the corporate people and he got our shows at least an additional five years,” Mr. Brull said. FT was cancelled in 2012.

Mr. Levine was always reading at his desk, but seldom about fashion, Mr. Brull said. “[In] most of our conversations in the over 25 years we worked together, I don’t think we discussed fashion. We were discussing life.”

He taught Tyler to be well-versed in what was going on in the world in order to make smart television. “His part of being a producer of Fashion Television required reading every newspaper and listening to every interview he could. So I kept up that kind of scouring, just always hunting for a good story.”
Ms. Beker said Mr. Levine served as a mentor to many young people. “I’m now hearing so many stories from people about how when they were newbies, he was very much there to support them,” she said.

Jay Lawrence Levine was born on May 9, 1957, in Toronto. His father, Norman Levine, was an entrepreneur and his mother was Beverley (née White, later Rosen). He had an elder brother, David, and a younger one named Harvey. His parents later divorced; Norm Levine remarried and the union produced a son, Tyler, who is 18 years younger than Jay.

Jay studied economics and film at York University, graduating in 1979. His father was close friends with director and producer Perry Rosemond, who died in August , and he helped Jay get his start in television. That included serving in junior roles on the CTV sketch show Bizarre .
Tyler said Jay drove a taxi early in his career and, one day, Moses Znaimer, then head of City-TV, got into his cab; by the end of the ride the media executive offered him a job.

Mr. Levine wrote in The Canadian Jewish News in 2022 that he had pitched a review show about theatre to City-TV, which he described as “the channel where I always wanted to work.” Instead, Mr. Znaimer asked him to produce the 10 p.m. newscast. “And that was the City-TV aesthetic: Getting someone who knew nothing about news to do the news. It was enough to assure me a few years later that I could make a show about fashion,” Mr. Levine wrote.

It was through his extensive reading that Mr. Levine hit on the idea: He found out that Paris designers were filming their collections for American buyers who could not attend the fashion shows in person. “I figured if we could get our hands on that footage, we could make a show about that.”

Mr. Levine’s first concept was tentatively titled Vogue on Video , but that morphed into FT, Tyler recalled. Ms. Beker, who was working on The New Music and wanted a change, advocated to become the host.

Fashion Television started in 1985 as 15-minute segments and launched as a half-hour show a year later. It quickly found viewers and Mr. Levine, Ms. Beker and their camera operators were soon travelling the world, asking fashion icons what it was it like having their names on people’s underwear and who their favourite architect was.

The show, “created a world appetite for television fashion programs …and inspired others to try to imitate its style and content,” an article on the History of Canadian Broadcasting website said. This even led to a copyright infringement lawsuit, a case FT lost.

In 2001, Chum Limited, which owned City-TV, launched Fashion Television Channel, a 24-hour station. It aired a full slate of fashion and art-related content in its early years. It stopped operations in 2021.
Meanwhile, in 2004, the team at FT launched a magazine with Ms. Beker at the helm.

While working at FT and after the show ended, Mr. Levine took on other projects as well, such as the two-season talk show Spectacle: Elvis Costello with… , which launched in 2008, and a series about architecture. Outside of television, he developed digital content for the Andy Warhol Museum, in Pittsburgh, in 2013.

When he became ill, Mr. Levine was working on a project about music managers who were pivotal to the career of their artists and the music scene. “I was excited to see what he was going to come up with. I knew he was capable of doing anything,” Mr. Brull said.

Mr. Levine is remembered as a great friend, a talented television producer and a cool and funny guy who could talk intelligently and wittily about any topic. “He was hilarious and he was brilliant,” Mr. Brull said.
Mr. Levine leaves his brothers and their families.

stories.title: Catholic, Anglican bishops urge Albertans to consider referendum’s impact on vulnerable
stories.summary: The Anglican bishops said they don't normally wade into political issues, but the referendum questions ultimately come down to choosing what kind of society we aspire to have.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
Alberta’s Catholic bishops are imploring parishioners to think about how the province’s upcoming referendum proposals May affect vulnerable people.

The five Catholic Bishops of Alberta, in a joint public letter , ask parishioners to consider the effects of the ballot proposals on children, those in poverty, the sick and the isolated.

“A person’s worth does not depend on citizenship, income, ability or contribution to society,” they state in the letter, dated Oct. 1.

On Oct. 19, Premier Danielle Smith’s government is asking Albertans a series of questions as it seeks a mandate to put limitations and fees on newcomers.

The questions include whether Alberta should seek more control over immigration and put more rules around which newcomers can access services like health care and education.

It also asks if it’s time to put in minimum residency requirements and fees on health and education for some newcomers.

The premier is urging Albertans to vote yes to those proposals, saying immigration is welcome but if not managed places a debilitating burden on public services.

1:57 Alberta referendum questions causing division

The bishops, in the letter, acknowledge those are legitimate concerns but say, “They must be addressed in ways that respect human dignity and avoid making any segment of our population the object of resentment or blame.”

They add, “Decisions concerning health care, education and public resources should promote equitable access and responsible stewardship, with due regard for future generations.”

The province’s three Anglican bishops have also issued a public statement on the referendum that echoes the concerns of the Catholics.

“Jesus is clear that our neighbour is not just those who we think truly belong,” the Anglican bishops wrote in the Sept. 29 letter to their community .

“We have a responsibility to support and protect the lives, dignity and worth of everyone we meet, regardless of their identity or status in our eyes.”

The Anglican bishops say they do not normally wade into political issues, but say the referendum questions ultimately come down to choosing what kind of society we aspire to have.

The Catholic bishops say that while the church remains independent of party politics, the faithful have a responsibility to bring Christian wisdom and sound judgment to moral questions in public life.

Neither letter tells people how to vote, but both make appeals to the common good.

The Catholic Bishops of Alberta letter was signed by Archbishop of Edmonton Rev. Stephen A. Hero, Bishop of Calgary Rev. William McGrattan, Ukrainian Eparchy of Edmonton Bishop Rev. David Motiuk, Archbishop of Grouard-McLennan Rev. Charles Duval and Bishop of St. Paul Rev. Gary Franken.

The Anglican Bishops in Alberta letter was signed by Bishop of Calgary Rev. Greg Kerr-Wilson, Bishop of Athabasca Rev. David Greenwood and Bishop of Edmonton Rev. Stephen London.

2:22 Republican influence in Alberta separatism movement revealed in Globe and Mail investigation

Asked for a response, Sam Blackett, the premier’s press secretary, said in a statement the government is looking forward to getting direction from voters on Oct. 19.

“The questions on immigration simply address the current unsustainable immigration levels in Canada that are putting real pressures on critical public services,” he said.

Blackett added the questions also reflect feedback they heard from Albertans during a series of public town halls last summer.

At one such event in Lloydminster, the prospect of mass deportations drew loud cheers from the crowd.

The immigration questions are part of a package of nine introduced by Smith on Feb. 19.

The day prior to that, Bruce McAllister, executive director in Smith’s office, pointed to religious values when decrying what he called unmanageable population growth in Canada.

“Why import from nations with failed systems when our Judeo-Christian heritage and principles have worked so well here?” McAllister wrote on social media.

The rest of the nine questions address concerns about the Constitution.

The 10th was added later and has become the focus of attention. It asks whether Alberta should stay in Canada or whether it’s time to hold a second, binding vote on leaving Canada.

stories.title: Here is the latest news from the Quebec election
stories.summary: Montreal - Voters in Québec's 127 ridings headed to the polls Monday in an election that could change the party in power.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec voters elected a Parti Québécois minority government Monday, possibly paving the way for another sovereignty referendum.

Here’s the latest on the race (All times Eastern):

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard says the new PQ minority government has responsibility to listen to other parties.

But he says, when it comes to a referendum, there will be no collaboration with the Liberals.

Milliard’s party will form the Official Opposition in the legislature.

Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says Quebec just wants to exist on its own like other countries of the world.

He says it’s a question of survival for a population of French-speaking people who represent such a small fraction of North America.

He says a referendum is about people making their own decision.

The PQ has pledged in the campaign to launch a referendum to separate Quebec from Canada, but not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal says her party’s results prove that the left is still alive and well in the province.

The party is leading in nine seats and could hold the balance of power in a minority legislature.

Ghazal said her sovereigntist party is looking forward to building a country that doesn’t leave anyone behind, with the help of immigrants, Indigenous people and English-speakers.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is congratulating Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Carney says he looks forward to building a stronger Quebec and Canada with the Parti Québécois leader.

He also thanked outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, whose CAQ party was on track to not win any seats.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette has lost her seat in the provincial riding of Trois-Rivières.

Fréchette has been the premier of Quebec and leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec since she won the party’s leadership race in April.

She replaced former premier François Legault who led the party to two consecutive majority governments in 2018 and 2022.

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting a Parti Québécois minority government.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has won his Montreal-area riding of Camille-Laurin.

St-Pierre Plamondon has represented the area in the Quebec legislature since 2022.

The riding was previously known as Bourget and is located in the east-end of Montreal.

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette says Quebec voters have spoken and she respects the results no matter how difficult they are for her party.

Her party, which had won two consecutive majority governments, was in danger of not winning a single seat.

In her concession speech, she thanked party supporters and urged them to hold their heads high in defeat.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Sol Zanetti has won his Quebec City area riding of Jean-Lesage.

He has held the riding since 2022.

It is shaping up to be a disastrous night for the Coalition Avenir Québec, with the party in danger of going from government to being wiped off the electoral map.

Prominent former cabinet members Simon Jolin-Barrette, Bernard Drainville, Sonia Bélanger and France-Élaine Duranceau have already been declared defeated.

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette trails in the riding of Trois-Rivières.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard has won the Orford riding in the province’s Eastern Townships region.

This was Milliard’s first election as leader and his first attempt at winning a seat in the Quebec legislature.

The pharmacist turned politician was acclaimed as leader of the Quebec Liberals in February.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal has won her Montreal-area riding of Mercier.

Ghazal was a founding member of the left wing sovereigntist party in 2006, alongside Françoise David and Amir Khadir.

She first entered the legislature when she won the riding in 2018 and she was re-elected in 2022.

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting the Parti Québécois will form the next government in Quebec.

It is unclear if the government will be a majority or minority.

Conservative Party of Québec Leader Éric Duhaime has won his riding of Bellechasse, south of Quebec City.

Duhaime has been leader of the party since 2021.

It the first time a member of Quebec’s Conservatives has been elected to the legislature since 1935.

The mood is festive at the PQ headquarters in Montreal.

The party jumped out to an early lead in several seats as the initial tallies came in.

Many supporters are decked out in blue and white and candidates are pumping up the crowd with speeches.

The polls have closed in the Quebec election.

Securing a majority government requires winning 64 out of the 127 seats in the legislature.

When the election was called, the CAQ held 79 seats, the Liberals had 18, Québec solidaire 11 and the PQ held seven seats. There were nine Independents and one Conservative.

A boisterous group of protesters gathered outside the PQ’s main watch party in Montreal as voting entered its final hour.

They chanted slogans critical of police, racism, transphobia and what the PQ’s plans to separate would mean for First Nations.

Security was tight with several police officers keeping watch over the crowd.

With only a few hours left to vote, Élections Québec pegged the preliminary voter participation rate at slightly over 45 per cent.

Roughly 66 per cent of eligible voters ended up casting ballots in the last two provincial elections.

Polls close at 8 p.m. ET.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: The Karate Kid: The Musical review: A pleasantly serviceable version of the movie
stories.summary: The juxtaposition of the show’s two mentors, which could be biting social commentary with a more deliberate structure, frustratingly falters
stories.author: Ilana Lucas
stories.content:
Title: The Karate Kid: The Musical

Music and lyrics by: Drew Gasparini

Book by: Robert Mark Kamen

Director: Amon Miyamoto

Actors: Adrian Pang, Gino Ochello, Jodie Jacobs, Abigail Amin

Company: Mirvish Productions

Venue: The Princess of Wales Theatre

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Nov. 1

There aren’t too many musicals where four words get their own applause break, but The Karate Kid: The Musical , based on Robert Mark Kamen’s 1984 movie that spawned a franchise, is one of them.

When Adrian Pang’s terse but kind Mr. Miyagi instructs the 17-year-old Daniel LaRusso (Gino Ochello) in repetitive movements of self-defense cleverly disguised as car maintenance, the phrase “wax on, wax off” briefly stops the show for a nostalgia-fuelled cheer.

I wasn’t among those feeling heady nostalgia upon hearing the famous line, having missed the film in my formative years. When I watched the source material before opening night, though, I quickly understood why the underdog story of intergenerational friendship means so much to so many.

The musicalized adaptation at Mirvish’s Princess of Wales Theatre in Toronto, written by Kamen with music and lyrics by Drew Gasparini and directed by Amon Miyamoto, carries the appropriate theme of rewriting one’s story, treading the boards as its martial arts-savvy characters break them with an open palm. A pleasantly serviceable version of the movie that expands on some of its characters while flattening others, the show moves satisfyingly through its paces (or, perhaps, kata), but could use a more memorable score to justify its revised medium.

Like a powerful punch that veers to the left or a fighter who falls before the final match, the show’s fun choreography and flashes of creativity offer promise that needs further training and balance to fully soar in crane pose.

As in the movie, Daniel’s widowed mother Lucille (Jodie Jacobs, getting good mileage out of a blend of tough love and tender concern) chases a job opportunity from New Jersey to California, transplanting Daniel in his last year of high school. While he quickly makes a friend (Finley Oliver) in their rundown apartment complex and attracts the eye of rich girl Ali Mills (Abigail Amin), this unfortunately comes with the attention of her violent ex, Johnny Lawrence, and his Cobra Kai gang. Daniel’s regular beatdowns come to a temporary end when the complex’s reclusive but caring maintenance man agrees to teach him karate in advance of a winner-take-all tournament showdown.

The Karate Kid advances or gets chopped based on how much we like its scrappy lead’s interplay with his beloved sensei. Ochello is appropriately charming as the fish-out-of-Jersey-Shore-water Daniel, and has plenty of chemistry with Pang, who leans into Miyagi’s comedic quips to contrast his moments of stoicism.

While the plot hews closely to the original, stage Daniel has less agency than his film counterpart, more helpless newb than chill sports instructor or cheeky prankster. The bouncy and banal songs that replace these characteristics largely tell us what we already know about his feelings, making it more difficult for Ochello and Amin to demonstrate their relationship is compelling; luckily, Amin’s self-possessed Ali has a bit of sparkle and a right hook worthy of the ring.

Kamen efficiently expands on the film’s villains, allowing Joe Simmons as Johnny to practise nasty psychological warfare with Daniel in the cobra’s den, and contrasting the war service of the two instructors to develop a richer conflict.

The leader of the Cobra Kai dojo, John Kreese (Matt Mills), sows division, wanting to humiliate and dominate outsiders and foreigners at all costs. While the film merely insinuates that this mentality comes from his Vietnam War service, the musical makes the connection explicit, detailing his anger and hatred in an entertaining act-ender worthy of a Disney villain. Mills fuels the character with his powerful stage presence, stalking around under the blazing red eyes of the dojo’s serpent mascot and similarly exuding genuine menace.

Mr. Miyagi’s service in the Second World War, fighting for a country that held his family in an internment camp, is the wound at his story’s core and informs the character’s underlying desire for connection and kindness toward victims of bullying. To Kreese, martial arts are a way to inflict pain; to Miyagi, they are a defence against it.

Subtlety can be a beautiful thing, but in a musical with otherwise loud emotions, it sometimes reads as absence. The juxtaposition of these two mentors, which could be biting social commentary with a more deliberate structure, frustratingly falters at almost . In the second act, Kreese’s trauma fades into barked orders, and a crucial song about Miyagi’s past has a touching melody but lyrics too generic to truly convey the betrayal of internment; distracted patrons might not even catch the phrase “relocation centre.”

The death of Daniel’s father, too, hints at a rich vein of backstory – one that’s left untouched until a climactic argument. With some thoughtful continuity, it could become a lovely character arc about accepting risk.

Visually, though, the snappy fight choreography by Keone and Mari Madrid (with fight consultant Kev McCurdy) packs a wallop, clearly differentiating between Cobra Kai’s short, choppy movements and Miyagi’s fluid strokes. Derek McLane’s set design uses attractive rolling Japanese shoji screens as backdrops to evoke the feeling of a dojo and bonsai trees representing the incremental process of human growth, while Peter Nigrini’s projections conjure a colourful 1980s arcade or the serenity of a beach.

In the show’s most creative theatrical touch, a spiritual chorus wearing karate gi often follows Mr. Miyagi, twining together to form the communal force that powers his quiet yet explosive strength. It’s moments like these that argue for the sweet story’s potential as an adaptation, even though, as a musical, it waxes and wanes.

stories.title: LHSC program gives high school students firsthand look at careers in health care
stories.summary: A rare opportunity is giving high school students a firsthand look at what it’s like to work in health care at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A rare opportunity is giving high school students a firsthand look at what it’s like to work in health care at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

For Grade 11 student Anviksha Singh, the experience helped shape what she wants to do after high school.

Singh spent a month this summer in LHSC’s pediatric surgical program, observing health care professionals and getting an inside look at several potential career paths.

“My biggest takeaway was it really solidified my interest in health care, because I was able to get that one-to-one exposure and really see how patient interactions actually work,” said Singh.

Singh rotated through several areas, including pediatric plastic surgery, orthopedics, and general surgery.

“It was great to just be able to observe and really see the day-to-day life of those career paths,” she said.

Dr. Andreana Bütter, chair of pediatric surgery at LHSC, says exposing students to health care early is intentional, “The point is for high school students to learn about health care and all the different positions that we have in the hospital and outside, and for them to get interested in it, get excited about it, and then think about hopefully doing that as a career.”

The program gives students an opportunity to see the realities of health care careers before they have to choose a post-secondary path.

For Singh, the experience was also a chance to better understand where she sees herself in the future, “By having that exposure start out early, you’re really able to see and set your path very well.”

Singh hopes more high school students learn about opportunities that allow them to explore health care careers firsthand.

For her, a month inside pediatric health care did more than offer a glimpse of the profession, it helped give her a clearer idea of where she wants her future to go.

stories.title: Canadian Opera Company’s Così fan tutte is invariably glorious
stories.summary: The production, deftly directed by Atom Egoyan, teems with palpable gaiety and infectious charm
stories.author: Nirris Nagendrarajah
stories.content:
Title : Così fan tutte

Written by : Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart

Conductor : Johannes Debus

Director : Atom Egoyan

Company : Canadian Opera Company

Venue : Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts

City : Toronto

Year : Runs until Oct. 18

It’s easy to forget that opera can be a site for serious amusement too.

The Canadian Opera Company’s revival of Mozart’s Così fan tutte , deftly directed by Atom Egoyan and agilely conducted by Johannes Debus, teems with palpable gaiety and infectious charm. Like its dogged male protagonists, it will surely, in spite of its archaic attitudes, seduce you.

Staged in the science lab of a preppy school, where hypotheses linger in the air and students wear cream-coloured uniforms, the opera begins with a conversation between Ferrando (tenor Laurence Kilsby), Guglielmo (bass-baritone Joel Allison) and their grey-haired professor Don Alfonso (bass-baritone Daniel Okulitch). Alfonso makes the claim – based on his experiences but passed off as fact – that all women are unstoppably unfaithful, especially their own supposedly faithful lovers: sisters Fiordiligi (soprano Lauren Fagan) and Dorabella (mezzo-soprano Martina Myskohlid).

To prove him wrong and earn some coin, they are convinced into a wager: They must pretend to leave for the military, then return furnished with moustaches and masks to earnestly ensnare each other’s partners. If only it were so simple, and the girls’ will – initially at least – not so iron-clad.

Debra Hanson’s set and costume design outfits the lab with a dusty chalkboard, beaker-filled shelves, over-sized pins and projections of mounted butterflies. A giant frame in Act 2 acts as a wall between the girls’ room and a garden; later, when Fiordiligi and Ferrando open up their hearts, a projection of Frida Kahlo’s The Two Fridas appears and is zoomed in on to create a dizzying contrast. Elsewhere, in pivotal moments – such as when the trio performs Soave sia il vento or when Alfonso urges the boys to marry the deceived – Michael Walton’s relatively subtle lighting design drastically dims the stage to spotlight the performers, allowing their intermingling to better resonate.

Lorenzo Da Ponte’s libretto, written in the shadows of the Enlightenment, explores the various anxieties that arise when the students’ beliefs are placed under extreme external pressures, including the boys faking drinking arsenic or bringing a blade to their necks, which accelerate the narrative inevitabilities. Wedded to Mozart’s lush, serene score – which the COC’s orchestra passionately performs, particularly the regal percussion, a trilling piano and a sinuous clarinet – the risk with this zany plot is that it can quickly devolve into a trite and unconvincing farce.

But with such a committed, vivacious cast and Egoyan’s thoughtful, original direction, which plays into and past the screwball conditions, the work evolves into a sardonic investigation into the mutability of desire and – as the philosopher Edward Said put it in an essay on Così – the inconstancy of character and identity. “I don’t understand how a heart can change in just a single day,” Fiordiligi sings, bewildered by her moral metamorphosis.

On opening night, Fagan’s full-bodied gravitas and swagger suited Fiordiligi’s steely resolve; Allison’s darkly resonant registers reflected Guglielmo’s gnawing guilt and belated double consciousness; and Kilsby’s noble, angelic tones radiated the purity of Ferrando’s amorous torment. Moreover, Okulitch seemed to derive much pleasure exaggerating Alfonso’s more despicable aspects, and soprano Tracy Dahl, reprising her role as the wise, spritely and shape-shifting Despina – who aids Alfonso in urging the girls’ icy hearts along – was a crowd-pleasing, comic tour-de-force.

But Myskohlid, making her COC mainstage debut, delivered a most remarkably dynamic and effervescent performance. From her endlessly evocative facial expressions – ranging from jaw-dropping excitement to eye-widening terror – to her ravishing, bronzed mezzo, her Dorabella was invested with a knowing irony that made her internal fluctuations more engaging and entertaining. It brought me such joy watching her repeatedly throw herself to the floor in melodramatic despair, twirl around one too many times and candidly deliver stupefied asides directly to the audience.

At the end of this incessantly amusing and invariably glorious three-hour affair, the deceptions – from the insecure boys and unsuspecting girls to the conniving adults – prove to have been part of a calculated act of disillusionment. Alfonso concludes to his humbled students that the capacity for infidelity doesn’t necessarily cancel out faithfulness, but proves that the possibility always has and always will exist. We must live with that discomfort.

“What is love?” Despina had asked the girls toward the end of Act 1.

Unlike the butterflies that appear throughout the production – projected, humongous, magically lit-up – love is the thing that can’t be pinned down.

stories.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney to take 'active role' in new AI advisory council
stories.summary: rime Minister Mark Carney will “play an active role” in setting the agenda for Ottawa’s new AI advisory council.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney will “play an active role” in setting the agenda for Ottawa’s new AI advisory council.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office says the new group, announced Friday, will take an “all of government” approach to advising on AI.

The advisory council includes AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio, as well as a experts in economics, business and AI.

The government already has an advisory council housed at Innovation Canada, which the spokesperson says is more focused on technical advice to the minister.

The Liberal government has also launched a new advisory council on AI and labour, which held its first meeting Monday.

The government also launched a separate advisory council on AI and culture in March.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Forensic evidence surrounding blood stains and bullets heard at murder trial
stories.summary: As the second week of testimony got underway at the second-degree murder trial of 26-year-old Zachary McDermott, the jury heard forensic evidence surrounding shooting.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
As the second week of testimony got underway at the second-degree murder trial of 26-year-old Zachary McDermott, the jury heard forensic evidence surrounding shooting at the Tim Hortons on Dundas Street East on Sept. 12, 2018.

London Police Detective Andrea McGrath-Wheatley testified about collecting photo evidence from the bloody scene in the hours following the gunfire.

“There was some staining believed to be blood on the doorway,” said McGrath-Wheatley. When referring to another photo, she said, “There is staining that is consistent with blood on the floor.”

The jury heard that bullet casings were also found in the coffee shop as well as in a laneway outside in the parking lot.

Christopher Clements-Card, 21, of London died after being shot twice in the back.

McDermott, who was 18 at the time of the incident, has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder.

The trial resumes on Tuesday.

stories.title: Late Fame, starring Willem Dafoe, is the quintessential pick for the Ageless Film Festival
stories.summary: Screenwriter Samy Burch talks about the ‘universal’ story that inspired the 2025 film
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
The mandate for Toronto’s Ageless International Film Festival is to present movies that explore stories and perspectives that connect viewers across generations. Which makes Late Fame a quintessential Ageless title.

The 2025 film stars Willem Dafoe as a former poet in New York whose work from the 1970s is rediscovered by a group of young, well-off, self-styled bohemians. Dafoe’s Ed Saxberger is now a post-office worker − “a man of letters,” as one of his youthful admirers puts it.

Helmed by former New York Film Festival artistic director Kent Jones, the film was written by Samy Burch, who based the screenplay on a 19th-century Austrian novella by Arthur Schnitzler that wasn’t published until 2014.

What’s old is young again.

Screenwriter Burch previously wrote 2023’s May December (which was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay) and this year’s Looney Tunes movie Coyote vs. Acme . She spoke with The Globe on a video call from Los Angeles.

Late Fame, about a poet from decades earlier who is rediscovered, is based on an unpublished novella rediscovered and published more than 100 years later. Could it get any more meta?

It was a coincidence. My brother-in-law recommended the book and I loved it. Arthur Schnitzler‘s writing is so modern and clean, and the feelings are so universal, unfortunately. A lot about ego, insecurity and petty jealously.

How much updating did the original story need?

The main thing was transforming it from 1895 Vienna to present day New York. I was fairly loyal to the novella. The plot, if there is one, is pretty simple. What I was tracking more was how Ed, the poet, feels about himself. Is he overconfident? Is he insecure?

In the novella, there’s a romanticization of an earlier era of Viennese writers. It was written in 1895. Which makes me wonder, are people ever happy about the present?

I don’t know. I lived in New York for a while. There was a sense of ‘You just missed it.’ It was really popping in the 1990s when independent film was going crazy. Or you stand in Washington Square and you feel the last 100 years. Bob Dylan and all of that. There are these ghosts that sit above the city.

I’m curious about the poem Willem Dafoe reads in the film. Where did it come from?

I know I didn’t want to write it. There was a lot of discussion with Kent and Willem about what we wanted the poem to be. Then one afternoon I was sent a poem. I thought it was perfect and asked Kent where he found it. He said, ‘Oh, I just wrote it.’

There’s a line I like: ‘A poem that won’t end till it finds you.’

Yes, that has a nice quality to it. Willem in particular was very invested in the way the poem felt and how it sounded. It was an interesting process.

Last year there was a viral video of him being interviewed on the streets of New York. The interviewer, who didn’t seem to know who he was, asked Willem what he did for a living. It could have been a scene out of the movie.

That clip happened right around the time we were shooting. He’s wearing the same cap, and we were filming in the same area. A lot of things about the character Ed came from Willem’s experience. He and Kent both moved to New York at the same time as Ed did. There’s something personal about the role for Willem. I’m sure there are people he knew at the time who didn’t follow the same path as him.

How did he come to be cast?

Initially the character was much older. But then Kent was on a plane from Los Angeles to New York and sat next to Willem. They knew each other from the New York Film Festival and had a nice conversation. Later Willem called his manager and told him he wanted to work with Kent. Turns out Kent was thinking the same thing.

Did they talk about Late Fame on the plane?

No. And when Willem found out that the project was Late Fame , he said he had a copy of the novella in his bag on the plane. That felt like a real kismet for everyone. I still can’t believe it happened. But it did.

Late Fame screens on Oct. 6, 7 p.m., at Alliance Française, 24 Spadina Rd. Ageless International Film Festival runs to Oct. 13, at Innis Town Hall, Alliance Française, Hot Docs Ted Rogers Cinema and Tiff Lightbox.

The 2025 film stars Willem Dafoe as a former poet in New York whose work from the 1970s is rediscovered by a group of young, well-off, self-styled bohemians. Dafoe’s Ed Saxberger is now a post-office worker − “a man of letters,” as one of his youthful admirers puts it.

Helmed by former New York Film Festival artistic director Kent Jones, the film was written by Samy Burch, who based the screenplay on a 19th-century Austrian novella by Arthur Schnitzler that wasn’t published until 2014.
What’s old is young again.

Screenwriter Burch previously wrote 2023’s May December (which was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay) and this year’s Looney Tunes movie Coyote vs. Acme . She spoke with The Globe on a video call from Los Angeles.
Late Fame, about a poet from decades earlier who is rediscovered, is based on an unpublished novella rediscovered and published more than 100 years later. Could it get any more meta?

It was a coincidence. My brother-in-law recommended the book and I loved it. Arthur Schnitzler‘s writing is so modern and clean, and the feelings are so universal, unfortunately. A lot about ego, insecurity and petty jealously.
How much updating did the original story need?

The main thing was transforming it from 1895 Vienna to present day New York. I was fairly loyal to the novella. The plot, if there is one, is pretty simple. What I was tracking more was how Ed, the poet, feels about himself. Is he overconfident? Is he insecure?
In the novella, there’s a romanticization of an earlier era of Viennese writers. It was written in 1895. Which makes me wonder, are people ever happy about the present?

I don’t know. I lived in New York for a while. There was a sense of ‘You just missed it.’ It was really popping in the 1990s when independent film was going crazy. Or you stand in Washington Square and you feel the last 100 years. Bob Dylan and all of that. There are these ghosts that sit above the city.
I’m curious about the poem Willem Dafoe reads in the film. Where did it come from?

I know I didn’t want to write it. There was a lot of discussion with Kent and Willem about what we wanted the poem to be. Then one afternoon I was sent a poem. I thought it was perfect and asked Kent where he found it. He said, ‘Oh, I just wrote it.’
There’s a line I like: ‘A poem that won’t end till it finds you.’
Yes, that has a nice quality to it. Willem in particular was very invested in the way the poem felt and how it sounded. It was an interesting process.

Last year there was a viral video of him being interviewed on the streets of New York. The interviewer, who didn’t seem to know who he was, asked Willem what he did for a living. It could have been a scene out of the movie.

That clip happened right around the time we were shooting. He’s wearing the same cap, and we were filming in the same area. A lot of things about the character Ed came from Willem’s experience. He and Kent both moved to New York at the same time as Ed did. There’s something personal about the role for Willem. I’m sure there are people he knew at the time who didn’t follow the same path as him.
How did he come to be cast?

Initially the character was much older. But then Kent was on a plane from Los Angeles to New York and sat next to Willem. They knew each other from the New York Film Festival and had a nice conversation. Later Willem called his manager and told him he wanted to work with Kent. Turns out Kent was thinking the same thing.
Did they talk about Late Fame on the plane?

No. And when Willem found out that the project was Late Fame , he said he had a copy of the novella in his bag on the plane. That felt like a real kismet for everyone. I still can’t believe it happened. But it did.

Late Fame screens on Oct. 6, 7 p.m., at Alliance Française, 24 Spadina Rd. Ageless International Film Festival runs to Oct. 13, at Innis Town Hall, Alliance Française, Hot Docs Ted Rogers Cinema and Tiff Lightbox.

stories.title: The steel jobs May never come back. Ottawa should consider nationalizing Stelco
stories.summary: All ideas should be on the table to protect jobs as steel workers are caught in the middle of trade tensions with the U.S.
stories.author: Nicolas Lamp
stories.content:
Nicolas Lamp is an associate professor at the faculty of law at Queen’s University.

Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N has said it would lay off of up to 500 steelworkers at the Stelco plant in Hamilton and Lake Erie Works site in Nanticoke, Ont.

As Canadians digest the devastating news, it’s a natural reaction to hope that what some refer to as the “trade dispute” between the U.S. and Canada will soon come to an end, so that such job losses can be averted.

Even Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves says as much, saying that if a deal is reached, the company would recall all laid off workers.

However, what’s happening between Canada and the U.S. is not a traditional trade dispute, where the two parties disagree about whether one of them is playing by the rules. Instead, what triggered the trade war was an attempt by the U.S. to unilaterally change the rules.

The Trump administration seeks to bring manufacturing jobs back to the U.S. and therefore no longer wants to provide the duty-free access to the U.S. market that Canadian industry depends on. It could not care less that this is a radical departure from decades of U.S. trade policy and inconsistent with its international trade commitments.

There is thus no “dispute” in the narrow sense that could be resolved by knocking heads together or through some sort of international mediation or dispute settlement. Canada and the U.S. want fundamentally irreconcilable things. Canada wants to keep its manufacturing jobs; the U.S. wants those jobs in the U.S., and if that means the deindustrialization of Canada, so be it. The steel workers in Hamilton are thus not collateral damage in the trade war; they are the target.

Fortunately, this is not the case for all the trade barriers the U.S. is currently imposing. The most recent tariffs and import bans are retaliatory in nature, and they will come off when Canada and the U.S. eventually reach a settlement. However, that settlement is unlikely to bring relief to the steelworkers in Hamilton because the steel tariffs are not retaliatory; they are a key element of the U.S.’s new trade order.

What can the Canadian government do? First, it needs to decide what is at stake in Hamilton. If the primary concern is the welfare of the workers and their families, the government should use the funds it has offered to keep the workers employed to instead help them retrain and potentially relocate to other parts of Canada where their skills are in need, as difficult and painful as that will often be.

If, however, the government decides that the steel industry is of strategic importance, that the workers are being “ betrayed ” by their Trump-supporting CEO and would fare better under more sympathetic management, it could nationalize the company and put Canadian management in charge, as the U.K. government as recently done with British Steel.

The caveats are obvious. It’s unclear whether the Canadian steel industry has a future without access to the U.S. market, there is massive steel overcapacity globally and the financial commitment could be enormous.

The government has to carefully weigh different policy objectives – national security and resilience, the jobs and expertise at stake, the affordability of steel for steel-using businesses, and the most efficient use of public funds. But these are times of fundamental transformation, and no idea should be off the table.

stories.title: 2nd potential AI data centre worries Saint John residents: ‘We have questions’
stories.summary: A second potential A.I. data centre in Saint John, N.B., is raising new questions for residents already fighting one proposed near the community of Lorneville.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
A second potential data centre in Saint John, N.B., is raising new questions for residents already fighting one proposed near the community of Lorneville.

Data centres are used in artificial intelligence (AI) and other high-tech industries, and require massive amounts of electricity not just to run, but also cool the computer servers.

Residents say they’re worried about the impact of these large-scale data centres on the environment, people’s health, and the power grid.

“A lot of this is very concerning because the technology that we’re dealing with, AI and data centres, it’s moving faster than government regulations,” said resident Lauren Smith.

“So, we’re very concerned that noise ordinances, industrial uses, 24/7 pollution (…) these things should be addressed and they have not been addressed.

“This is new technology. Our regulations are very poor, very old, and they do not meet the standards of today.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This is new technology. Our regulations are very poor, very old, and they do not meet the standards of today."

Smith is a member of the local advocacy group, Save Lorneville, which has been vocally opposed to a proposed centre at the Spruce Lake Industrial Park that is currently under environmental review.

That proposal, from U.S.-based VoltaGrid and Beacon Data Centers from Alberta, includes a 390-megawatt centre and gas plant.

The group Save Lorneville recently secured documents from the province under a right to information request.

Those documents, which were shared with Global News, reveal a second large-scale data centre has been proposed for Saint John by another U.S. company: Cross River Infrastructure Partners.

Correspondence between the company and Opportunities New Brunswick shows the project is initially requesting 50 megawatts of network-firm power, with potential future expansion opportunities to incorporate grid responsive capacity and further economic development.

Opportunities New Brunswick, a provincial Crown corporation that leads economic development in the province, was unable to comment by deadline.

In a statement, the City of Saint John said it “did receive preliminary inquiries and correspondence from Cross River Infrastructure Partners,” but doesn’t have any updates on the proposal.

Smith and other advocates say limited public dialogue leaves questions over what such projects would pay for power and water, and how those resources would be made available.

“Who is going to pay for the electrical grid build out? Will that be the responsibility of the ratepayers? Will there be subsidies for projects like this?” said Smith.

NB Power tells Global News projects of this size need “contractual flexibility” to protect the grid and rates, and must fit within its long-term supply plan.

Smith also points out there are many unknowns about the impact on human health and greenhouse gas emissions.

Other parts of the country are also grappling with how to regulate AI data centres.

In recent months, Canada announce a new AI strategy that includes plans for large-scale AI data centres .

In neighbouring Nova Scotia, Premier Tim Houston recently softened his stance on the prospect of new data centres, saying if a company can protect the water, ratepayers and create economic opportunity, “we will hear them out.”

In contrast, several municipalities in Ontario have voted on whether to place moratoriums on the centres while they study possible guardrails.

There’s also been opposition in Alberta, where several provincial townhalls were dominated by heated questions and angry remarks over possible environmental risks, water usage and the cost of energy associated with the data centres.

Smith says she believes the New Brunswick government owes it to residents to have open dialogue and properly consult with them about potential projects.

“We are concerned citizens and we have questions,” she said.

“If a data centre goes into Lorneville, this won’t be Lorneville’s problem. This will be New Brunswick’s problem. Whoever is paying for electricity in the province should be concerned about a hyperscale data centre.”

Smith is a member of the local advocacy group, Save Lorneville, which has been vocally opposed to a proposed centre at the Spruce Lake Industrial Park that is currently under environmental review.
That proposal, from U.S.-based VoltaGrid and Beacon Data Centers from Alberta, includes a 390-megawatt centre and gas plant.
The group Save Lorneville recently secured documents from the province under a right to information request.
Those documents, which were shared with Global News, reveal a second large-scale data centre has been proposed for Saint John by another U.S. company: Cross River Infrastructure Partners.

Correspondence between the company and Opportunities New Brunswick shows the project is initially requesting 50 megawatts of network-firm power, with potential future expansion opportunities to incorporate grid responsive capacity and further economic development.
Opportunities New Brunswick, a provincial Crown corporation that leads economic development in the province, was unable to comment by deadline.
In a statement, the City of Saint John said it “did receive preliminary inquiries and correspondence from Cross River Infrastructure Partners,” but doesn’t have any updates on the proposal.
Smith and other advocates say limited public dialogue leaves questions over what such projects would pay for power and water, and how those resources would be made available.
“Who is going to pay for the electrical grid build out? Will that be the responsibility of the ratepayers? Will there be subsidies for projects like this?” said Smith.
NB Power tells Global News projects of this size need “contractual flexibility” to protect the grid and rates, and must fit within its long-term supply plan.
Smith also points out there are many unknowns about the impact on human health and greenhouse gas emissions.
Other parts of the country are also grappling with how to regulate AI data centres.
In recent months, Canada announce a new AI strategy that includes plans for large-scale AI data centres .

In neighbouring Nova Scotia, Premier Tim Houston recently softened his stance on the prospect of new data centres, saying if a company can protect the water, ratepayers and create economic opportunity, “we will hear them out.”
In contrast, several municipalities in Ontario have voted on whether to place moratoriums on the centres while they study possible guardrails.

There’s also been opposition in Alberta, where several provincial townhalls were dominated by heated questions and angry remarks over possible environmental risks, water usage and the cost of energy associated with the data centres.
Smith says she believes the New Brunswick government owes it to residents to have open dialogue and properly consult with them about potential projects.
“We are concerned citizens and we have questions,” she said.

“If a data centre goes into Lorneville, this won’t be Lorneville’s problem. This will be New Brunswick’s problem. Whoever is paying for electricity in the province should be concerned about a hyperscale data centre.”

stories.title: U.S. officials allow liquor deliveries to resume to isolated New Brunswick island
stories.summary: New Brunswick’s provincial liquor agency says it has resumed deliveries to an isolated island where the only land route is through Maine.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s provincial liquor agency says it has resumed deliveries to an isolated island where the only land route is through Maine.

U.S. border officials stopped a truck carrying mail, milk and about 1,000 bottles of alcohol to Campobello Island, N.B., last Tuesday.

A U.S. ban on Canadian liquor imports went into effect the same day as part of the ongoing trade war started by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Campobello’s only land connection to Canada is a bridge to Maine, followed by an 80-kilometre drive through the state to the border crossing at St. Stephen, N.B.

NB Liquor spokesperson Marie-Andrée Bolduc said in an email Monday that the agency was looking for alternative ways to deliver its products to the island, but she said that’s no longer necessary.

When reached Monday, U.S. Customs and Border Protection did not respond when asked if there had been a change at the border.

The truck that was stopped at the border last week eventually made it to the island via a private ferry, but that service is scheduled to end for the season later this month.

stories.title: Suncor sells of N.L. offshore assets, other oilsands giant bulks up Alberta holdings
stories.summary: Suncor is selling offshore assets in Atlantic Canada as it focuses on its oilsands holdings, while Cenovus is buying a smaller peer to grow its own footprint in northern Alberta.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
One of Canada’s biggest energy companies is selling offshore assets in Atlantic Canada as it focuses on its oilsands holdings, while another is buying up a smaller peer to grow its own footprint in northern Alberta.

The announcements from Suncor Energy Inc. and Cenovus Energy Inc. come days after a proposed million-barrel-a-day pipeline to the West Coast was deemed the first national-interest project under federal legislation passed last year.

There have been questions over whether oilsands firms would be willing to invest in enough production growth to fill that massive pipeline by the time it starts up around 2032, as well as several other pipeline expansions set to come online sooner.

Calgary-based Suncor announced Sunday that U.K.-based Ithaca Energy PLC is to purchase its interest in the Terra Nova, White Rose and West White Rose developments off the coast of Newfoundland for $1.2 billion in cash.

Ithaca has also agreed to an additional contingent payment of up to $350 million, based on future oil prices, the news release said.

“This transaction further focuses our efforts on opportunities that generate the greatest long-term shareholder value,” said Rich Kruger, Suncor’s CEO.

“We are aligning our portfolio around our competitive advantages and the strengths of our unparalleled, physically-integrated business, underpinned by large-scale, long-life oilsands resources.”

A Suncor spokesperson said the company will keep its stakes in two other Newfoundland offshore oilfields, called Hibernia and Hebron. The sale to Ithaca is expected to close in early 2027.

The company also announced it’s increasing share repurchases under its normal course issuer bid to $750 million per month from $500 million, starting in October.

“In our view, the transaction further increases Suncor’s flexibility to accelerate in situ development opportunities such as Firebag and Lewis, particularly given the increasingly constructive backdrop for the oilsands in Canada,” Desjardins Securities analyst Robert Mann wrote in a report Monday.

Mann is referring to projects that use steam wells, instead of open-pit mining, to extract bitumen from deep underground. Such operations tend to be smaller, less expensive and quicker to build than a brand new mine.

Cenovus is also a major oilsands player with East Coast assets.

CEO Jon McKenzie told analysts on a conference call Monday that Cenovus has no plans to shake up its holdings in Atlantic Canada, where it operates the White Rose offshore field and its planned extensions. It is also a partner in Terra Nova.

Startup at the West White Rose expansion is “imminent,” he said.

“I’m sure Suncor had their own reasons for doing what they did. We continue to see that as a profitable area of the world in which we exist. We understand what our footprint is there. We understand what our competitive advantage is within that footprint,” McKenzie said.

“I don’t think it’s ever going to be something that is materially bigger than what we’ve got today, but we are excited about bringing on West White Rose and look forward to first production there.”

McKenzie made his remarks after his company announced a $5.7-billion cash-and-stock deal to buy Athabasca Oil Corp .

Athabasca has 40,000 barrels per day of oilsands production currently, but Cenovus sees the opportunity to ratchet that up to 115,000 by 2032.

“That represents one of the most significant organic growth opportunities available in Canadian oilsands today,” McKenzie told analysts.

McKenzie said the federal and Alberta governments have taken “positive steps” toward boosting the sector’s competitiveness.

“These steps will have a meaningful impact on our ability to advance growth projects, like the ones we are contemplating at Leismer and Corner,” he said, referring to two Athabasca assets that will be added to its portfolio.

Last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced businesses will be able to immediately deduct the cost of a broader range of investments against their taxes than they had been previously. McKenzie said that move “is not immaterial” to its ability to speed up growth.

He also cited forthcoming royalty incentives the Alberta government has said it expects to announce in November to spur more oilsands production.

“All of that fits together to draw capital back into the resource in the Athabasca Basin and probably accelerate growth as well,” McKenzie said.

Under the terms of the agreement, Athabasca shareholders will have the option to receive $12 in cash or 0.264 of a Cenovus common share for each share they hold, subject to limits on the total cash and shares available.

“While the transaction does not come cheap … we view the acquisition as strategically compelling given the scarcity value of top-tier long-duration thermal inventory and the increasingly constructive backdrop for oilsands development,” wrote Mann, the Desjardins analyst.

— With files from The Canadian Press reporter Sarah Smellie in St. John’s, N.L.
