stories.title: Cenovus Energy looks to grow as it signs $5.7B deal to buy Athabasca Oil
stories.summary: Athabasca Oil has 40,000 barrels per day of oilsands production currently, but Cenovus Energy sees the opportunity to ratchet that up to 115,000 by 2032.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Cenovus Energy Inc. is adding to its already hefty steam-driven oilsands holdings with a $5.7-billion cash-and-stock deal to buy Athabasca Oil Corp., and its chief executive says recent government policy shifts will help unlock production growth from the properties it’s acquiring.

Athabasca has 40,000 barrels per day of oilsands production currently, but Cenovus sees the opportunity to ratchet that up to 115,000 by 2032.

“That represents one of the most significant organic growth opportunities available in Canadian oilsands today,” CEO Jon McKenzie told a conference call with analysts Monday.

The deal comes days after the federal government deemed a proposed million-barrel-a-day pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia the first national-interest project under legislation passed last year. The designation means the pipeline will be subject to a streamlined regulatory review through the major projects office.

There have been questions over whether Cenovus and its oilsands peers would be willing to invest in enough production growth to fill that massive pipeline by the time it starts up around 2032, as well as several other pipeline expansions set to come online sooner.

McKenzie said the federal and Alberta governments have taken “positive steps” toward boosting the sector’s competitiveness.

“These steps will have a meaningful impact on our ability to advance growth projects, like the ones we are contemplating at Leismer and Corner,” he said, referring to two Athabasca assets that will be added to its portfolio.

Last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced businesses will be able to immediately deduct the cost of a broader range of investments against their taxes than they had been previously.

McKenzie said that move “is not immaterial” to its ability to speed up growth.

He also cited upcoming royalty incentives the Alberta government has said it expects to announce in November to spur more oilsands production.

“All of that fits together to draw capital back into the resource in the Athabasca Basin and probably accelerate growth as well,” McKenzie said.

Under the terms of the agreement, Athabasca shareholders will have the option to receive $12 in cash or 0.264 of a Cenovus common share for each share they hold, subject to limits on the total cash and shares available.

The total cash available is capped at $4.3 billion, while the number of Cenovus shares available under the offer is limited to 44.4 million.

“While the transaction does not come cheap … we view the acquisition as strategically compelling given the scarcity value of top-tier long-duration thermal inventory and the increasingly constructive backdrop for oilsands development,” wrote Desjardins Securities analyst Robert Mann in a note.

Just under a year ago, Cenovus closed another multibillion-dollar acquisition of a smaller oilsands peer. After a bitter bidding war with Strathcona Resources Ltd., Cenovus bought MEG Energy for $8.6 billion.

Cenovus shares were trading down four per cent at $44.41 midday Monday, while Athabasca’s were up almost 14 per cent at $12.04.

Cenovus says it expects to close the deal in December, subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory and shareholder approvals.

stories.title: ‘Poppy rocks’ mark graves of more than 1,200 Bruce County soldiers
stories.summary: Hundreds of ‘poppy rocks’ mark over 1,200 Bruce County gravestones of soldiers who went to war and returned.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Hundreds of ‘poppy rocks’ mark over 1,200 Bruce County gravestones of soldiers who went to war and returned.

“We cannot forget. We can’t forget the sacrifices that not only the people who served, but also their families made,” said Jan Briggs-McGowan of the Bruce County Genealogical Society .

Soldiers like John Dentinger, who saved Clarence Kieffer’s father’s life, ON the battlefield.

“It’s a great thing that he did, or I wouldn’t be here. It’s an honor to come and pay the respects to him today, and to have the poppy rock there to recognize him as a veteran,” said Clarence Kieffer, a local military historian.

John Callahan’s family was proud to lay a poppy rock on his grave near Teeswater.

“This means everything. I wouldn’t miss it,” said his son, Tom Callahan.

Local school children made and laid poppy rocks for local soldiers and their families as part of the No Stone Left Alone initiative .

Briggs-McGowan has spent the past five years researching and laying stones across Bruce County’s 138 cemeteries.

“Laying a poppy rock means the next time somebody goes through this cemetery, they’re going to see those poppy rocks and they’re going to remember. They’re going to say, ‘oh, look, there’s another one, there’s another one, there’s another one over there.’ That’s really important we cannot forget,” said Briggs-McGowan.

Kieffer says matching up the soldiers’ names and their gravestones is no simple task, but an important one.

“Once you get the names listed and find them in the cemetery, that takes considerable time. Cemeteries are not laid out well,” said Kieffer.

But that won’t stop Kieffer and Briggs-McGowan and many other committed volunteers in Bruce County from finding the estimated 6,000 Bruce County soldiers who returned from the battlefield and laying a poppy-painted rock at their gravestone.

“It’s important for our kids to know who came home, who served, who got married, who has children, who opened the butcher store when they came back, or whatever. Those things are important, too,” said Briggs-McGowan.

For the families, the No Stone Left Alone initiative is a sense of closure for those that fought overseas, returned home, and made lives back in Canada.

“It’s necessary,” said Tom Callahan.

stories.title: Schulich Leader inspired by curiosity: ‘My passion for science drives everything I do’
stories.summary: First-year integrated science student Autumn Wright is among 11 Western University recipients of the Schulich Leader Scholarship.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
From an early age, Autumn Wright’s father taught her to be curious and search for answers.

“He really encouraged me to ask ‘why,’” Wright said. “I would work on his car with him, and we would do science experiments on weekends and for my birthday parties. It was a big thing for both of us.”

Sharing an interest forged a bond between Wright and her dad, who served two tours in Afghanistan as a combat engineer with the Canadian Armed Forces. That connection became even more meaningful after he died in a car crash when Wright was nine.

“My dad sparked my love of science. When he passed, I wanted to make him proud by continuing to be curious and working through questions to figure out solutions,” said Wright, a first-year integrated science student from Braeside, Ont.

“My passion for science drives everything I do.”

Wright is one of 11 first-year Western students to receive a Schulich Leader Scholarship. Valued at $120,000 for students pursuing an engineering degree and $100,000 for students pursuing degrees in science, technology or math, the scholarships are among the most competitive undergraduate awards in the country.

Out of 1,300 nominees across Canada, 110 students are selected to receive the award.

Businessman and philanthropist Seymour Schulich established the $200 million scholarship fund in 2012, recognizing “the increasing importance and impact the STEM disciplines have on the prosperity of future generations.”

“As we celebrate the 15th cohort of Schulich Leaders, we are proud to have supported more than 1,000 exceptional Canadian students pursuing STEM degrees at our country’s top universities,” said Judy Schulich, president of the Schulich Foundation. “By supporting their ambition and creating conditions for them to succeed, we can ensure their innovations drive Canada’s future prosperity.”

Earning a $100,000 scholarship has been life-changing for Wright, who, after her father’s death, became more of a caregiver to her younger brother as the family adjusted to their single-parent household.

“I had to become self-sufficient and make strong efforts to be optimistic every day,” she said.

Her perseverance paid off.

Wright received academic excellence awards throughout high school and merit points for leadership and participation in robotics, student council, rugby and track and field. As a top-performing athlete, she overcame significant setbacks, including a severe concussion at age 15 and TMJ (a jaw joint disorder) from a rugby injury.

Autumn Wright (right) with her mother, Sarah. (Submitted)

Wright credits her mother, Sarah, a small restaurant owner, for instilling the work ethic and determination that helped her succeed.

“My mom has always been insistent that I can do whatever I’d like to do and that she will figure out how to get me there,” Wright said. “She works very hard and I didn’t want to put any more pressure on her. I was so relieved to receive this award. Now I can make my own way.”

Wright said an entrepreneurial mindset helped her identify a need in her community and led her to found and run a youth STEM club through her local museum.

“I approached one of the curators and told her I felt very passionate about science and how I explored it as a kid because of my family’s encouragement. I wanted that for other kids too,” she said.

Wright organized hands-on science activities, including making Popsicle-stick balloon cars, to spark curiosity and inspire younger students to explore science and innovation.

“I feel kids don’t have the same curiosity for science because they only have access to it in a classroom setting, where they’re being assessed. I wanted to create an environment where they could play with it and see the joy in it first, thinking if I can even inspire one kid through that program to care about the climate, our world and innovation, I’ve done my job.”

The following Western Schulich Leaders received $100,000 each and are pursuing degrees in the Faculty of Science:

Will Clark Brooklynn Gonyea Lina Hout Autumn Wright Lenny Yu

Will Clark, Science. (Lindsay, Ont.)

The following Western Schulich Leaders received $120,000 each and are pursuing degrees in the Faculty of Engineering:

Esha Gill Matthias Lodewyk Jimmy McLaren Angelo Placido Ron Tismenetski Ava Yeung

Esha Gill, Engineering. (Kincardine, Ontario)

Valued at $120,000 for students pursuing an engineering degree and $100,000 for students pursuing degrees in science, technology or math, the scholarships are among the most competitive undergraduate awards in the country.
Out of 1,300 nominees across Canada, 110 students are selected to receive the award.

Businessman and philanthropist Seymour Schulich established the $200 million scholarship fund in 2012, recognizing “the increasing importance and impact the STEM disciplines have on the prosperity of future generations.”

“As we celebrate the 15th cohort of Schulich Leaders, we are proud to have supported more than 1,000 exceptional Canadian students pursuing STEM degrees at our country’s top universities,” said Judy Schulich, president of the Schulich Foundation. “By supporting their ambition and creating conditions for them to succeed, we can ensure their innovations drive Canada’s future prosperity.”
Leading others through a love of science

Earning a $100,000 scholarship has been life-changing for Wright, who, after her father’s death, became more of a caregiver to her younger brother as the family adjusted to their single-parent household.
“I had to become self-sufficient and make strong efforts to be optimistic every day,” she said.
Her perseverance paid off.

Wright received academic excellence awards throughout high school and merit points for leadership and participation in robotics, student council, rugby and track and field. As a top-performing athlete, she overcame significant setbacks, including a severe concussion at age 15 and TMJ (a jaw joint disorder) from a rugby injury.
Autumn Wright (right) with her mother, Sarah. (Submitted)
Wright credits her mother, Sarah, a small restaurant owner, for instilling the work ethic and determination that helped her succeed.

“My mom has always been insistent that I can do whatever I’d like to do and that she will figure out how to get me there,” Wright said. “She works very hard and I didn’t want to put any more pressure on her. I was so relieved to receive this award. Now I can make my own way.”
Wright said an entrepreneurial mindset helped her identify a need in her community and led her to found and run a youth STEM club through her local museum.
“I approached one of the curators and told her I felt very passionate about science and how I explored it as a kid because of my family’s encouragement. I wanted that for other kids too,” she said.
Wright organized hands-on science activities, including making Popsicle-stick balloon cars, to spark curiosity and inspire younger students to explore science and innovation.

“I feel kids don’t have the same curiosity for science because they only have access to it in a classroom setting, where they’re being assessed. I wanted to create an environment where they could play with it and see the joy in it first, thinking if I can even inspire one kid through that program to care about the climate, our world and innovation, I’ve done my job.”

stories.title: American officials have ‘concerns’ about Trump’s Canada attacks, MPs hear
stories.summary: Senior Global Affairs officials stressed the deep and enduring ties between Canada and the U.S., noting that disagreements have been worked out before.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
American officials have privately confided “concerns” with U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggressive stance towards Canada, MPs on the House of Commons’ foreign affairs committee were told Monday.

Niall Cronin, the director general of Global Affairs Canada’s North America bureau, told MPs that Canada has a network of diplomats that spend a considerable amount of time arguing Canada’s side of the conflict with American politicians and business leaders.

“What we’ve heard from our network in the United States is broad support for the Canada-U.S. relationship and affection for Canada and understanding of the benefits that a relationship with Canada brings to the United States,” Cronin said.

“We’ve also heard people raise their concerns with some of the steps the (Trump) administration has taken, in private. Few are willing to be more public about it, and that’s their decision.”

“But our network across the United States spends a lot of its time raising awareness about the benefits of the trading relationship, the security partnership and other aspects of the relationship, and has a very receptive audience from a number of sections across the United States,” Cronin added.

During the first Trump administration’s trade war, former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government presided over a full-court press of premiers, mayors, business leaders and diplomats targeting sub-national politicians and decision makers across the U.S. in the first “Team Canada” push.

The objective was to convince Americans of the value in the Canada-U.S. relationship, in hopes that message would trickle up to — or become pressure against — Trump and his inner circle.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s approach to dealing with Trump’s second administration has been different, or at least less public-relations focused than his predecessor. Trade talks between the two countries collapsed in late August, with Carney saying Trump had demanded terms including control over who Canada could trade with.

Carney and senior Canadian officials have said their side is willing to head back to the negotiating table, but the Trump administration — currently attempting to prosecute a shooting war in Iran and under the shadow of next month’s midterm elections — have not appeared in a rush.

“I don’t know. Canada behaves very badly with the United States, and I don’t know, we’ve caught them in the act,” Trump told reporters on Monday when asked if he would resume trade talks with Canada before the midterms on Nov. 4.

But Cronin noted the Canada-U.S. relationship has endured through disputes in the past, and stressed that, away from the headlines, cooperation between the two countries is still strong.

“I was actually in British Columbia last month, meeting with B.C. officials, they have regular interactions with their counterparts in Alaska and Washington State dealing with all sorts of issues … and those relationships are deep and enduring, and the conversations very, very positive,” Cronin said.

“I think that goes across the board.”

stories.title: Steven Galloway accuser will not testify in defamation trial
stories.summary: Woman who levelled sexual-assault allegations against author won’t offer any evidence ‘for reasons pertaining to her own welfare,’ court hears
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Bestselling author Steven Galloway’s career was abruptly destroyed, his finances ruined and his mental health damaged so badly he would often convulse in the fetal position after he was accused of sexual assault and was dismissed as head of Ubc’s creative writing program, B.C. Supreme Court heard Monday during the first day of a defamation trial against four people.

The start of the high-profile trial more than a decade in the making focused on the profound impact the November, 2015, allegations – and wider online debate of the incident – had on the mental health of two people at the centre of it: Mr. Galloway and a former UBC student A.B., who is also one of the defendants. The other three defendants are people who repeated her claims online.

“It’s hard to imagine the nightmare one lives through of being accused of being a rapist,” Mr. Galloway’s lawyer Daniel Burnett said on the first day of the judge-only trial scheduled to run 20 days.

His opening statement explained how his client’s “star” literary career ended immediately at the age of 40 when allegations of sexual assault were made in 2015 by A.B. Her identity is being protected by a pre-trial publication ban that Justice Neena Sharma will either extend or end on Tuesday. A.B. will not testify at the trial.

Mr. Burnett told the court in Vancouver his client is seeking aggravated and special damages and will be calling a publishing expert to testify to the earnings Mr. Galloway could have expected if the author of the 2008 international bestseller The Cellist of Sarajevo continued his writing career.

After Mr. Burnett’s statement, he called his first witness to testify: Mr. Galloway’s wife Katie Wagner. She said that in the immediate aftermath of the accusation Mr. Galloway was briefly hospitalized due to concerns about his mental health while on a work trip in Ohio. In the months that followed, she told the court, he would frequently throw up in the mornings, rarely eat and have severe panic attacks related to the public’s perception he was a rapist.

“He’d turn over into the fetal position, he’s shaking, full body shaking,” she testified.

At one point, Ms. Wagner testified, the couple were staying at her parents’ house on Vancouver Island when she woke up to find her husband gone and rushed to the boathouse to find Mr. Galloway standing next to a knotted rope he had tied and looped over a beam.

A.B.’s lawyer, Arden Beddoes, told the justice that his client will not be offering the defences of truth or fair comment to refute Mr. Galloway’s allegations.

Instead, he told the court, A.B. will contest the evidence provided by lawyers for Mr. Galloway, who is scheduled to testify this week.

Mr. Beddoes said his client has been in a prolonged mental health crisis herself and that when she was told at the beginning of June she would need to appear soon for a discovery hearing, she attempted to kill herself the following day. Her medical records also noted a previous suicide attempt earlier this year, he said.

He urged Justice Sharma to extend the ban on identifying A.B. through the trial, reading out an example of the hate mail she received to her e-mail inbox stating and explaining how the lawsuit has created extreme stress.

Between 2011 and 2013, the pair had an affair Mr. Galloway has described as consensual and A.B. has characterized as abusive.

UBC fired Mr. Galloway in 2016, even after a retired judge hired by the university to investigate A.B.’s complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established he committed sexual assault or assault. He was not charged by police.

In 2018, Mr. Galloway’s original defamation suit was filed against two dozen defendants, but only A.B. and three others remain: Mandi Gray, Dana Kagis and Glynnis Kirchmeier.

The case has wound its way through various courts over the years as judges have had to weigh whether those accused of sexual assault have a right to sue their accusers for defamation. In 2024, the B.C. Court of Appeal upheld a lower-court decision that said someone accused of being a rapist must be allowed to defend their reputations in court.

When the accusations against Mr. Galloway first surfaced, sexual misconduct by powerful men was rising in the public consciousness. Once-admired celebrities were facing allegations that would eventually lead to the #MeToo movement.

Margaret Atwood, the popular Canadian author who has written publicly about what she says was a lack of due process afforded to Mr. Galloway, told The Globe recently she hopes the trial finally reveals the truth of what happened a decade ago.

Ahead of this trial, one former defendant, Chelsea Rooney, who was a student of Mr. Galloway’s when he taught at UBC, released a public apology for what she characterized as her “harmful” conduct in spreading accusations against Mr. Galloway.

“Everyone deserves fairness, including Mr. Galloway, who was the subject of very serious allegations,” Ms. Rooney said in a statement, posted online alongside the apologies of eight others. She said she regrets playing a role in collecting and soliciting complaints about Mr. Galloway, and building a case against him.

Ms. Wagner, a screenwriter and teacher, testified that she met Mr. Galloway while studying in Ubc’s creative writing program in the summer of 2013, began dating him a year later then moved her two kids in with his two children in the summer of 2015 before getting married early the following year.

She ended Monday’s court session testifying how she has tried to maintain a normal family life whilst Mr. Galloway often retreated to their bedroom as he grappled with intense sadness and anxiety.

She said it has been very hard on his two daughters, who share his surname and would often read online “their dad’s a rapist.”

With a report from Chris Hannay

stories.title: In the age of AI, why Canadian travel agencies just saw revenues rise
stories.summary: The operating revenue of the travel arrangement and reservation services industry rose 8.8 per cent to $18.3 billion in 2025, Statistics Canada said in a report on Monday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
While artificial intelligence and the internet are making it easier to find and compare travel options and book them with the click of a button, many Canadians are still turning to the old-fashioned way of planning a vacation – going to a travel agent.

The operating revenue of the travel arrangement and reservation services industry rose 8.8 per cent to $18.3 billion in 2025, Statistics Canada said in a report on Monday. This follows an even bigger increase of 9.3 per cent in 2024.

The 2025 increased happened despite Canadian travel to and from the U.S. falling 25.4 per cent compared to 2024.

This comes at a time when AI chatbots can compare flights and hotels for users and point them to websites. Meta’s newly launched agentic AI Muse is even able to book flights across hundreds of airlines.

The information overflow that comes with AI and internet searches does not necessarily translate to greater clarity, said Suzanne Acton-Gervais, president of the Association of Canadian Travel Agencies and Travel Advisors.

“A search engine can offer a thousand answers. A great travel agency and travel advisor knows which questions to ask first. That is the value of human judgment,” she said.

When planning a vacation, many Canadians value a human connection, she added.

“Ultimately, our business is not simply travel. Our business is people. It is human connection, human judgment and human care,” Acton-Gervais said.

Booking airline seats is still a big focus, accounting for 35 per cent of travel agencies’ operating revenue. However, packaged tours are not far behind, accounting for a quarter (25.2 per cent) of the revenue.

“It reflects a broader desire for travel that is curated, seamless and designed around the individual,” Acton-Gervais said.

While customers of travel agencies tend to skew older, younger customers are a “growing opportunity,” she added.

“What’s particularly interesting is that these are highly digitally fluent consumers. They May discover a destination through social media, use AI to research it and compare options online, and still turn to a professional agency and advisor for expertise, personalization and support,” Acton-Gervais said.

“They are not choosing between technology and human advice, they are using both.”

However, the Canadian travel industry is facing significant headwinds from declining U.S. travel.

Since U.S. President Donald Trump launched a trade war against Canada in 2025, Canadians have been avoiding travel south of the border.

This presents a problem for travel agencies in Canada, since 60 per cent of their operating revenue came from U.S. travel, Statistics Canada said.

The industry’s growth could be further constrained in 2026, the report warned, but added that non-U.S. travel could present an opportunity.

From January to June 2026, Canadian-resident return trips from the United States fell 4.6 per cent compared to the same period one year earlier, while return trips from other countries rose 4.8 per cent, Statistics Canada said.

stories.title: Mother and son aboard Ontario-based air ambulance lost off Massachusetts coast identified
stories.summary: Bermuda nationals Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41, were aboard when plane went down, police say
stories.author: Philip Marcelo
stories.content:
The six souls who were on board a Canadian-owned air ambulance that went down off the coast of Massachusetts on the weekend have been identified.

A news release from the U.S. Coast Guard late Monday said the Gulfstream G100 jet carried 66-year-old Marilyn Lavonne Bean and her 41-year-old son Sergio Wayne Lottimore, both of Bermuda.

Lottimore, who worked in insurance, was remembered by his alma mater as a scholastic prefect and by his work as a respected leader.

Meanwhile, the four Canadian crew members, employed by Ontario-based Latitude Air Ambulance, were identified as Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir.

“During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident,” said Rear Adm. Matthew Lake from the U.S. Coast Guard in Monday’s release.

“We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation.”

Coast guard officials have said the plane was en route to Boston with a patient and a family member from Bermuda when it lost contact with air-traffic control early Saturday.

The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net.

The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to about 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

The coast guard later said debris from the plane was recovered 32 kilometres off Nantucket, though officials wouldn’t share specifics. The 66-hour search ended Sunday after scouring roughly 7,000 kilometres of ocean.

Officials said Monday a civilian vessel also found debris associated with the plane. They said it’s not uncommon, and that if mariners find such debris they should contact the Transportation Safety Board of Canada.

The TSB said it would send crews to Massachusetts to help search for and recover the aircraft.

Latitude Air Ambulance, the medical transport company based in Hamilton, Ont., that owned the jet known as Heartbeat 104, shared more about the crew members late Monday.

The company said captain Philip Childerhose was a man of great integrity who touched the hearts of everyone he talked to, and first officer Thomas Farquhar was a “gentle giant who reflected Jesus’ love.”

Flight nurse Sarah Paton was bright and joyful, and devoted herself to helping others, the company said. Respiratory therapist Jolene Weir loved to travel the world and had an “incredible ability” to care for others.

Peter Byl, company president, said each of the four crew brought something special to the company.

“Our colleagues dedicated themselves to helping people at some of the most vulnerable moments of their lives,” Byl said in a statement. “That was the mission they were carrying out aboard Heartbeat 104.

“We want their families to know that we will remember not simply how we lost them, but how they lived, how they served, and what they meant to the people around them.”

The company, which offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, said it would support the families of the crew members and its employees as they grieve.

It also asked for privacy for their families, and added it would co-operate with Canadian and American flight investigators and not speculate about what happened.

Early tributes to those killed were shared across social media Monday.

“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized and so our first thoughts are with the families of those so tragically lost,” said Bermuda Premier David Burt in a statement.

“Let us open our hearts to the families in the hope that our expressions of love, support and compassion will bring some comfort as they attempt to deal with this terrible loss.”

Investigators have said a black box, a recording device found in airplanes that is used to investigate accidents, has not yet been recovered.

stories.title: A developer agreed to sell 23 condos at a discount. The lender said no
stories.summary: B.C. lawsuit lays bare that developers don’t have final say on pricing
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
As completed unsold homes continue to pile up in Metro Vancouver, politicians are seeing opportunity.

Earlier this year, B.C. Premier David Eby unveiled a plan to buy up completed unsold condos with financial support from the federal government, convert them into rental homes and make them available to British Columbians via a rent-to-own program.

The proposal received widespread criticism , the NDP-led government opted to call a snap election, and Mr. Eby recently proposed a new tax on completed unsold condos. The tax would start at 2 per cent for units that have been vacant for one year before increasing by 1 per cent every year thereafter.

At a news conference in Burnaby on Sept. 25, Mr. Eby cited reports of thousands of completed unsold condos in Metro Vancouver and blamed developers for not lowering prices to meet buyers.

“Some of them have been sitting for more than two years. More than 10 developers own over half of those condos. They’ve been built and they won’t sell them at the price that people are willing to pay.”

It’s a line of thinking that has been repeated by many pundits, but it misses the fact that developers often don’t have final say on pricing.

“In most construction loans, there will be a minimum sale price clause,” said Aman S. Bindra, a partner at KSW Lawyers. “There will be a loan agreement or commitment letter saying ‘here’s what we value the units at, here’s what we think you’re gonna be able to sell them for, and you can’t sell them for 90 or 95 per cent of that number without our consent.’”

Say a developer and lender enter into a $100-million loan agreement for a project with 100 units. If the developers agreed to sell 90 units for a discounted price totalling $80-million, that would mean they would have to sell the remaining 10 units for $20-million to pay off the loan.

That is easier said than done, particularly in today’s market, and if the developer is unable to achieve the latter, it’s the lender that May take the loss. This is the situation lenders try to avoid, says Mr. Bindra.

A prime example of this has been at the centre of a lawsuit in the Supreme Court of British Columbia involving 1397676 B.C. Ltd. and prominent developer Westbank.

According to a civil claim filed by the numbered company in February, it entered into an agreement with Westbank in October, 2025, to buy 23 completed but unsold condos at Sanctuary – a 158-unit luxury condo project along Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver – for $30-million and had plans to assign 17 of the 23 units – flip them – for a profit of $3.6-million.

The plaintiff said that the agreed-upon prices “were below or significantly below” the price the units were previously marketed for, meaning Westbank agreed to a bulk discount.

The transactions were scheduled to be completed on Nov. 28, 2025, but ultimately did not complete because Westbank was unable to discharge a mortgage held by QuadReal Property Group – the real estate subsidiary of the British Columbia Investment Management Corporation. Westbank notified the buyer on Nov. 27 and returned the deposit with accrued interest.

The numbered company initiated the lawsuit alleging that Westbank made certain misrepresentations that resulted in damages, including “incurring the costs of the investments with little to no return.” Westbank and QuadReal argued that the presale contracts stated that in the event the transactions failed to close, remedies would be limited to the return of the deposits with accrued interest.

In its own filing, QuadReal said that it refused to discharge the mortgage and consent to the bulk sale because “the proposed sale contemplated a purchase price below the ‘minimum discharge amount’ as required by the credit agreement, and was otherwise significantly below fair market value.”

According to QuadReal, the average sale price was $700 per square foot, which was below fair market value by an average of $400 per sq. ft. and would’ve resulted in “a loss of revenue in the millions of dollars.”

Reached by The Globe and Mail, Mr. Sager said he assembled the assignees and negotiated the deal with Westbank on behalf of a friend and that he would not have received the $3.6-million in profit. He added that he was removed as a corporate director some time after the lawsuit was filed and has not been involved in the proceeding.

Documents filed more recently in the proceeding allude to the numbered company as now having two directors with an Austrian mailing address. Although the civil suit was active as of earlier this month, Mr. Sager told The Globe that the parties have settled the dispute.

Explaining his involvement, he said he became aware of the unsold units at Sanctuary last year, was impressed by the building, and wanted to see it filled with locals instead of offshore investors or speculators.

“Before proceeding, I specifically asked the District’s municipal lawyers whether my involvement in putting this group of buyers together presented a conflict of interest,” said Mr. Sager. “I was advised that it did not. And to be absolutely clear: I was not receiving a side payment, I had no undisclosed financial arrangement, and I was not making a profit from this transaction. Mr. Sager also commented on the issue of unsold condos and the dynamic between developers and lenders that has been laid bare by the incident.

“We have completed buildings with significant numbers of empty units, while prices sometimes remain disconnected from what buyers are actually prepared to pay. Financing arrangements can make it difficult for developers to adjust prices to current market conditions, and that can prevent the normal market process of prices responding to actual demand. The community pays a price for that.”
paragraphs: As completed unsold homes continue to pile up in Metro Vancouver, politicians are seeing opportunity.

Earlier this year, B.C. Premier David Eby unveiled a plan to buy up completed unsold condos with financial support from the federal government, convert them into rental homes and make them available to British Columbians via a rent-to-own program.

The proposal received widespread criticism , the NDP-led government opted to call a snap election, and Mr. Eby recently proposed a new tax on completed unsold condos. The tax would start at 2 per cent for units that have been vacant for one year before increasing by 1 per cent every year thereafter.
At a news conference in Burnaby on Sept. 25, Mr. Eby cited reports of thousands of completed unsold condos in Metro Vancouver and blamed developers for not lowering prices to meet buyers.

“Some of them have been sitting for more than two years. More than 10 developers own over half of those condos. They’ve been built and they won’t sell them at the price that people are willing to pay.”
It’s a line of thinking that has been repeated by many pundits, but it misses the fact that developers often don’t have final say on pricing.

“In most construction loans, there will be a minimum sale price clause,” said Aman S. Bindra, a partner at KSW Lawyers. “There will be a loan agreement or commitment letter saying ‘here’s what we value the units at, here’s what we think you’re gonna be able to sell them for, and you can’t sell them for 90 or 95 per cent of that number without our consent.’”

Say a developer and lender enter into a $100-million loan agreement for a project with 100 units. If the developers agreed to sell 90 units for a discounted price totalling $80-million, that would mean they would have to sell the remaining 10 units for $20-million to pay off the loan.

That is easier said than done, particularly in today’s market, and if the developer is unable to achieve the latter, it’s the lender that May take the loss. This is the situation lenders try to avoid, says Mr. Bindra.
A prime example of this has been at the centre of a lawsuit in the Supreme Court of British Columbia involving 1397676 B.C. Ltd. and prominent developer Westbank.

According to a civil claim filed by the numbered company in February, it entered into an agreement with Westbank in October, 2025, to buy 23 completed but unsold condos at Sanctuary – a 158-unit luxury condo project along Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver – for $30-million and had plans to assign 17 of the 23 units – flip them – for a profit of $3.6-million.
The plaintiff said that the agreed-upon prices “were below or significantly below” the price the units were previously marketed for, meaning Westbank agreed to a bulk discount.

The transactions were scheduled to be completed on Nov. 28, 2025, but ultimately did not complete because Westbank was unable to discharge a mortgage held by QuadReal Property Group – the real estate subsidiary of the British Columbia Investment Management Corporation. Westbank notified the buyer on Nov. 27 and returned the deposit with accrued interest.

In its own filing, QuadReal said that it refused to discharge the mortgage and consent to the bulk sale because “the proposed sale contemplated a purchase price below the ‘minimum discharge amount’ as required by the credit agreement, and was otherwise significantly below fair market value.”

According to QuadReal, the average sale price was $700 per square foot, which was below fair market value by an average of $400 per sq. ft. and would’ve resulted in “a loss of revenue in the millions of dollars.”

Explaining his involvement, he said he became aware of the unsold units at Sanctuary last year, was impressed by the building, and wanted to see it filled with locals instead of offshore investors or speculators.

stories.title: Two Canadian Armed Forces members arrested in organized crime, kidnapping probe: DND
stories.summary: Toronto - The Department of National Defence says two members of the Canadian Armed Forces were arrested by Toronto police on charges related to organized crime, kidnapping and firearms theft.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The Department of National Defence says two members of the Canadian Armed Forces were arrested by Toronto police on charges related to organized crime, kidnapping and firearms theft.

The department says Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau, both members of the 7 Toronto Regiment, have been removed from duties and their access to military facilities and bases has been restricted after their arrests on Aug. 11.

stories.title: Dr. Abbas Jessani named one of Canada’s Top 40 Under 40
stories.summary: Western University's Dr. Abbas Jessani was named one of Canada’s Top 40 Under 40 for advancing oral health equity, community service education
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
When Dr. Abbas Jessani came to Canada in 2011 to pursue graduate studies, being named one of Canada’s Top 40 Under 40was far beyond anything he could have imagined.

Fifteen years later, his work to improve access to oral health care for underserved communities in Canada and internationally has earned him a place among the 2026 recipients of the national award, which recognizes 40 Canadians under the age of 40 for their leadership, impact in the community and achievements.

“I feel immense gratitude to everyone who has shaped my work and my journey,” said Jessani, a professor in dentistry and epidemiology and biostatistics at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry. “I also feel very lucky and blessed to be part of a team, an institution and a family that have been so supportive and have contributed to this prestigious honour.”

Born and raised in Pakistan, Jessani completed an undergraduate dental degree at the University of Karachi. When he decided to pursue graduate studies in Canada, his family made significant financial sacrifices to support his journey.

“Growing up, I saw the financial challenges my family faced and how hard my parents worked to support my education. When I moved to Canada for graduate studies, I had enough resources to cover my first semester’s tuition,” he said. “Those experiences shaped my journey and strengthened my commitment to advancing equity and access to care.”

Jessani went on to complete his MSc and PhD studies at the University of British Columbia, focusing on public health dentistry. He began his academic career at University of Saskatchewan, College of Dentistry, before joiningSchulich Medicine & Dentistry in 2020.

Throughout his career, Jessani has focused on making oral health care accessible to everyone.

“Equitable oral healthcare means that everyone is treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial status, race, skin colour, or sexual orientation,” he said.

At Schulich Dentistry, Jessani leads the Community Service Learning (CSL) in Oral Health program, which works with communities in Southwestern Ontario and East Africa to improve access to oral health for socially marginalized populations.

The program brings together community partners, experiential student learning and research to develop and deliver care that reflects local and global health needs, particularly in communities that have historically faced barriers to oral health services.

Jessani is also the co-director of the master of health sciences in global health systems program at Schulich Medicine & Dentistry.

### “My work focuses on reaching out to the most vulnerable and socially marginalized people in our communities who cannot advocate for their oral health. These are the people who have lost trust in our health-care system. I want to show them that we care about them and that we want to empower them.” – Dr. Abbas Jessani, Schulich Dentistry professor

For Jessani, some of the most meaningful examples of that work have come through the students he teaches.

He recalls a dental student who had arrived in Canada as a refugee from Iraq and wanted to give back to the settlement centre – London Cross Cultural Learning Centre– that had supported her family.

“We were able to develop a CSL partnership with the Cross Cultural Learning Centre because of the student’s intention and passion to serve,” he said. “I watched her go back to the centre where she had first arrived as a refugee 20 years ago, this time as a dental student serving the community – that’s what the CSL program is all about – empowering our learners and communities.”

It’s an example of the broader impact Jessani hopes to create by championing community-engaged dental education.

For him, the Top 40 Under 40 recognition is also a chance to reflect on the path that brought him to Canada and the people who supported him along the way.

Over the years, he says his success has rested on four main pillars: “Work hard, be kind, dream big and always take care of your mom.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all.

“Equitable oral healthcare means that everyone is treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial status, race, skin colour, or sexual orientation,” he said.
Bringing community service learning to dentistry students

At Schulich Dentistry, Jessani leads the Community Service Learning (CSL) in Oral Health program, which works with communities in Southwestern Ontario and East Africa to improve access to oral health for socially marginalized populations.

The program brings together community partners, experiential student learning and research to develop and deliver care that reflects local and global health needs, particularly in communities that have historically faced barriers to oral health services.
Jessani is also the co-director of the master of health sciences in global health systems program at Schulich Medicine & Dentistry.

### “My work focuses on reaching out to the most vulnerable and socially marginalized people in our communities who cannot advocate for their oral health. These are the people who have lost trust in our health-care system. I want to show them that we care about them and that we want to empower them.” – Dr. Abbas Jessani, Schulich Dentistry professor
For Jessani, some of the most meaningful examples of that work have come through the students he teaches.
He recalls a dental student who had arrived in Canada as a refugee from Iraq and wanted to give back to the settlement centre – London Cross Cultural Learning Centre– that had supported her family.

“We were able to develop a CSL partnership with the Cross Cultural Learning Centre because of the student’s intention and passion to serve,” he said. “I watched her go back to the centre where she had first arrived as a refugee 20 years ago, this time as a dental student serving the community – that’s what the CSL program is all about – empowering our learners and communities.”
It’s an example of the broader impact Jessani hopes to create by championing community-engaged dental education.
For him, the Top 40 Under 40 recognition is also a chance to reflect on the path that brought him to Canada and the people who supported him along the way.
Over the years, he says his success has rested on four main pillars: “Work hard, be kind, dream big and always take care of your mom.”

stories.title: Report of Republicans working with Alberta separatists is ‘concerning,’ says Tory MP
stories.summary: 'Absolutely nobody has a right to promise away Alberta's birthright, which is our natural resources,' said Dane Lloyd, the Tory MP tasked by with convincing Albertans to stay.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
The Conservative MP tasked with leading his party’s efforts to convince Albertans to stay in Canada says he is concerned by reports of separatists going to Washington and offering up fresh water and oil in exchange for American support.

Dane Lloyd, who represents the Parkland riding directly west of Edmonton, said no one has the right to promise away Albertan resources and he will not condone any of the province’s revenues going to a foreign government.

Speaking outside a House of Commons committee on Monday, Lloyd said he wouldn’t speculate on whether the reported activity amounted to foreign interference, or on how the matter should be investigated by Canadian officials.

“Absolutely nobody has a right to promise away Alberta’s birthright, which is our natural resources,” he said.

The Globe and Mail also reported over the weekend that Republican political operatives were in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist cause.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree deferred questions about the reporting to CSIS.

“What I will say, in general terms, is as electoral events take place, democratic events take place, we expect them to be governed under democratic principles where foreign interference or actors influencing local electoral events does not occur,” he said.

Albertans will vote on Oct. 19 on whether to hold a binding referendum on legal separation from Canada.

Premier Danielle Smith has said she will vote against separation but has been accused of not doing enough to quell separatist sentiment in the province.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas, a staunch critic of Alberta’s separatist movement, said The Globe and Mail’s reporting shows how independence leaders are putting the province’s future at risk.

“They say (separation) is about taking back control, then go begging to Washington for support,” Farkas said in a video posted to social media on Monday.

“You don’t protect Alberta’s sovereignty by seeking help from a foreign government. And you sure as hell don’t defend Alberta by discussing what parts of us you’ll carve up for the Americans.

“That’s not taking back Alberta. That’s selling Alberta out.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That's not taking back Alberta. That's selling Alberta out."

— More to come…

— With files from The Canadian Press reporters Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa and Jack Farrell in Edmonton

stories.title: Canada closely following reports of plague in Russia, health minister says
stories.summary: Ottawa — Health Minister Marjorie Michel says Canada is very closely following reports that a woman who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia has died.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada is very closely following reports that a woman who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia has died, Health Minister Marjorie Michel said on Monday.

Russian authorities say the woman contracted pneumonia from an unknown source. They also say there’s no evidence it was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.

Media outlets in Siberia have suggested the woman died of pneumonic plague, a less common but still severe form of plague that infects the lungs.

The World Health Organization says this particular form of plague is always fatal if left untreated, but antibiotics are effective against the bacteria that causes plague if it is treated early.

Pneumonic plague can be spread between humans via respiratory particles or through contact with infectious bodily fluids or contaminated materials. It can be fatal within 24 hours of disease onset if it’s not treated.

Russian state TV reports said the woman died last week at a hospital just outside Irkutsk.

Local authorities have placed the hospital in Shelekhov in quarantine and are monitoring people who were in contact with the woman.

Michel said there is no risk to Canada and the federal government is working with the World Health Organization and other countries to stay on top of the situation.

When asked if she had concerns with Russian officials being transparent and forthright about the situation, Michel said the United States is in close contact with officials in Russia “and we are in close contact with the United States.”

“So I feel that in this specific case, we will work together for the benefit of the world,” she said.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday the United States is watching the situation closely.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Public safety minister admits security 'gaps' after Nato intern arrest
stories.summary: Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree conceded there are "gaps" in the government's security clearance process.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree conceded there are “gaps” in the government’s security clearance process, after the arrest of a Canadian woman of Chinese origin charged with spying at Nato headquarters.

“I think there’s over 200,000 screenings that are undertaken every year,” said Anandasangaree, who was grilled by MPs of all stripes at the Commons public safety committee on Monday.

“By and large, it is an unimpeachable record. Of course, there are gaps here, and I recognize that there are gaps, and that’s what I think we need to improve on.”

But the meeting provided few answers to key questions such as what are those gaps, what did the government know or not know about Biwei Zhang’s checkered professional past and how was the former federal public servant allowed to keep her clearance despite previous concerns about her integrity.

That raised the ire of Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs, who described the Zhang saga as a stain on Canada’s international reputation.

“I don’t feel like we have any further … answers, I should say, ON something that is a very serious matter,” said Conservative MP Frank Caputo towards the end of the public meeting with the minister and top Csis, RCMP and Treasury Board Secretariat officials.

Bloc MP Claude De Bellefeuille went a step further, telling the minister and bureaucrats that she was seeing “sizeable incompetence and a lack of rigour” in this case.

“I cannot believe that this person who had fake names… applied twice to Cbsa and (has) Facebook accounts under two names succeeded in getting her security clearance,” said Bloc MP Claude DeBellefeuille.

“Sure, because of the investigation you can’t tell us anything, but it’s a demonstration of the weakness of your processes… and if I was the public safety minister, I would not be happy to see that the group that is meant to protect us are very lax,” she added.

House public safety committee votes to investigate vetting of accused Nato spy

Canadian Nato intern arrested on espionage charges by Belgian police

On July 24, Belgian authorities laid espionage charges against the Canadian who was working as an intern at Nato’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (Shape) headquarters in Mons, Belgium.

The suspect was later identified by media as 33-year-old Biwei Zhang, who also went by Claire Zhang. Belgian and Canadian officials have neither confirmed nor denied her identity.

According to Belgian authorities, Zhang is suspected of “spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization.” She was denied bail in August and remains imprisoned in Belgium.

During the hearing, Anandasangaree revealed that he had learned of the impending charges against Zhang one week before they were made public in July.

He promised there would be “serious learnings” from the Zhang case at the conclusion of the Canadian and Belgian investigations.

Granting any level of security clearance to an employee rests with the deputy minister at the top of a federal organization but is informed by information from the RCMP and Csis, Anandasangaree told the committee.

The arrest sparked international headlines and intense scrutiny on the Canadian public service and intelligence apparatus, which is charged with approving the security clearance of public servants who intern at Nato.

Following her arrest, various media outlets revealed that she had worked for the Canadian public service for a decade, often in jobs that required security clearance.

A 2024 Federal Court decision revealed that Zhang had committed fraud while applying for a job at the Canadian Border Services Agency by submitting two applications using different names in order to increase her chances of getting the job.

During the committee meetings, Liberal, Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs all agreed that it was crucial for the government to prevent any such failings in the future.

Csis, Public Safety and Treasury Board Secretariat (TBS) officials all said they were reviewing their own processes all the while investigating what happened in the Zhang case.

Public safety assistant deputy minister Richard Bilodeau noted that his department had recently implemented a mandatory “Internet inquiry” as part of the screening process of clearances ranked “secret” and above.

Tbs’s Adam Hatfield also said there needs to be much better information sharing between departments regarding personnel files.

“There’s room for improvement there. A lot of that turns into an IT and data problem. Where we would see improvement is speed, transferability, consistency. It wouldn’t necessarily affect the rigour of the system, but it would certainly let us use our resources far more effectively and hopefully cut down some of those times,” he said.

stories.title: 2 Canadian soldiers arrested by Toronto police on organized crime charges
stories.summary: Two Canadian Armed Forces members stationed in Toronto are facing several charges connected to organized crime, kidnapping and theft.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Two Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) members stationed in Toronto are facing several charges connected to organized crime, kidnapping and theft.

A spokesperson for the Department of National Defence said Bombardiers Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau were arrested by Toronto police on Aug. 11.

Fernando and Moreau, members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, are facing charges related to organized crime, kidnapping and the theft of firearms and weapons.

Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in March 2018 and Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in January 2020, the spokesperson said.

Fernando has not been deployed on a CAF operation, whereas Moreau served on Operation Laser in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Following their arrests, both individuals were removed from military duties and their access to CAF equipment, facilities, and bases was restricted,” the spokesperson said.

“They remain members of the CAF pending the outcome of an administrative review. An administrative review is a formal process used to assess matters that May affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.”

The spokesperson added the army is assisting Toronto police as it investigates.

stories.title: Health Canada warns of possible false positives in pregnancy test recall
stories.summary: Rapid response tests are used for the early detection of pregnancy by determining the presence of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) in urine.
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
Health Canada is issuing a safety notice and recall for HCG one-step pregnancy tests from Innovacon Inc . over concerns that they May show a false positive result.

“The product May detect low levels of HCG below the stated assay sensitivity, which May result in false-positive test results in samples from non-pregnant individuals,” the agency wrote in the notice.

“The package insert is being updated to note that low HCG levels can occur at or after the onset of perimenopause. Customers should consider this when interpreting results,” the warning added.

2:10 Sunnybrook medical team adapts procedure to help pregnant people manage fibroids

Rapid response tests are used for the early detection of pregnancy by determining the presence of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) in urine. It is a hormone produced in the placenta, and its levels begin rising after a fertilized egg implants in the uterus.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

During early pregnancy, the amount of HCG in blood and urine doubles every two to three days, the Mayo Clinic says . That means waiting a day or two after a missed period to take the test makes it more likely that it will detect HCG and show a positive result.

Most tests produce a result within a few minutes.

Many home pregnancy tests claim to be 99 per cent accurate, but several factors can impact the results or lead to a false positive.

A false positive might happen if a miscarriage occurs soon after the fertilized egg attaches to the uterine lining, the Mayo Clinic notes. It also says a false positive is possible if a person takes a pregnancy test soon after taking fertility medicine that contains HCG.

HCG is present in the body only during pregnancy, the clinic added, though problems with the ovaries and menopause May also lead to a false positive test result, it warns.

Irregular menstrual cycles can also impact pregnancy test results, as they can make it hard to decipher when a period should start.

Home pregnancy tests can also vary in sensitivity. More sensitive tests need less HCG in urine to show a positive result.

On the contrary, false negatives are more likely if a person takes a test too soon. The most accurate results usually occur the first day after a missed period.

Pregnancy tests have been recalled in Canada before, for issues ranging from unreliable results to faulty packaging.

stories.title: Suspect wanted in connection with Point Edward break-and-enter
stories.summary: Lambton OPP are searching for a suspect wanted in connection with a Point Edward break-and-enter.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Lambton OPP are searching for a suspect wanted in connection with a Point Edward break-and-enter.

On Sept. 24, police received a report of a break-and-enter at a Marina Road property. They said just before 2 a.m., an unknown person went to the property and got onto a docked boat.

The suspect allegedly stole a surveillance camera before they left.

Police describe the suspect as a white man, around 30 years old with a slim build, shaggy hair, a moustache and short beard. They were seen wearing a hoodie under a plaid shirt.

Anyone who can identify the suspect is asked to contact Lambton County OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be sent to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Florida could slash property taxes – but not for Canadian snowbirds
stories.summary: For snowbirds, it is important to understand what is actually on the ballot and how these changes will affect their properties, the Canadian Snowbirds Association said.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Voters across the United States will go to polls in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, but Florida voters will also cast their ballots on a question that affects Canadian snowbirds – whether to significantly cut property taxes.

The question is a part of a proposal from Florida Governor Ron DeSantis to amend the state’s constitution, called Amendment 3.

Currently, Florida tax law gives residents or “homesteaders” something called a homestead tax exemption. This cuts up to US$51,411 of taxable value from the assessed value of your home.

If the vote passes with a 60 per cent supermajority on Nov. 3, this homestead exemption would be raised to US$150,000 in 2027 and US$250,000 in 2028. Starting in 2029, the value of a Florida resident’s home shielded from tax exemptions will rise automatically every year, with the limit being indexed to inflation.

DeSantis has indicated that he intends to raise taxes on “residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial” properties to make up for the shortfall, he told Fox Business earlier this year.

“That’s a lot of money that they have,” DeSantis said.

In a March press conference, DeSantis said he wants “Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists subsidizing the state.”

“I don’t want to give Canadians a tax cut,” he said.

The eventual goal is the full elimination of property taxes, since the amendment would require the legislature to prepare “a schedule for full elimination.”

The move could cause a tax shortfall of US$12 billion for municipalities, nonprofit tax research group Florida TaxWatch estimates.

Advocates are warning of service cuts across cities and towns in Florida for everything from fire departments, police and the ability to fight against mosquito-borne diseases.

“If this amendment passes, every Florida community will face critical shortfalls,” an advocacy coalition called Vote No on 3 says on its website.

6:00 What to know about new U.S. border rules

What do snowbirds need to know right now?

For Canadian snowbirds, it is important to understand what is actually on the ballot and how these changes will affect their properties, said Evan Rachkovsky, spokesperson for the Canadian Snowbirds Association.

“The constitutional amendment voters will consider (on Nov. 3) is a much more measured approach than what was originally proposed,” Rachkovsky said.

Typically, property taxes for non-homesteaders, including Canadians, go up around one to two per cent annually, but the increases are capped at 10 per cent.

The amendment lowers the cap to five per cent.

“This provides property owners with greater predictability and limits how quickly their assessments can increase,” Rachkovsky added.

Canadians are the single largest group of foreign buyers in the Florida real estate market, accounting for 37.8 per cent of all international demand in the first three months of 2026, according to Florida Realtors data.

In some communities, as many as seven out of 10 foreign buyers were Canadian.

However, data suggests Canadian snowbirds are turning away from the U.S.

According to a 2025 Travel Health Insurance Association of Canada (Thia) most Canadians said they would skip U.S. travel in the winter, with only 26 per cent saying they will head south – a 37 per cent drop from 2024.

The pullback is sharpest among baby boomers, traditionally the snowbird generation, with only 10 per cent planning U.S. trips, the report said, noting that this is a 66 per cent decline compared with 2024.

The Sunshine State is also getting the cold shoulder from Canadian tourists.

In the final three months of 2025, Florida saw a 13.1 per cent drop in visits from Canadians compared to the same period in 2024, according to data from Visit Florida.

stories.title: Frost advisory issued as temperatures set to dip near freezing
stories.summary: A frost advisory has been issued for parts of southwestern Ontario as temperatures are expected to drop near the freezing mark overnight, according to CTV meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A frost advisory has been issued for parts of southwestern Ontario as temperatures are expected to drop near the freezing mark overnight, according to CTV meteorologist Julie Atchison.

After a cool start to the week, Atchison said a northwest wind kept temperatures feeling brisk Monday afternoon, with readings ranging from 11 C to 16 C across the region.

Skies are expected to clear overnight as high pressure moves into the area, allowing temperatures to fall to between 0 C and 2 C by early Tuesday morning.

“The coldest temperatures are likely to occur just before sunrise, with a couple of hours of frosty conditions expected in some areas,” Atchison said.

The frost advisory covers Essex County, Chatham-Kent, Lambton County and the Sarnia area. While temperatures in Windsor are expected to remain just above the freezing mark, Atchison said patchy frost could still develop in outlying rural locations.

Residents with sensitive outdoor plants are being encouraged to take precautions overnight, including covering vegetation vulnerable to frost damage.

The chilly start is not expected to last long.

Atchison said temperatures will rebound Tuesday under mainly sunny skies, reaching a high of 18 C. Even warmer weather is expected Wednesday, with a mix of sun and cloud and a high near 23 C.

Sunshine is also forecast to continue into Thursday, when temperatures are expected to reach 19 C.

“We are in for a nice stretch of sunshine over the next few days,” Atchison said. “It’s shaping up to be a beautiful week across southern Ontario.”

stories.title: Mother and son from Bermuda named as passengers on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
stories.summary: The two people aboard an air ambulance that crashed in the waters off Massachusetts over the weekend while flying from Bermuda to Boston were identified Monday as a mother from Bermuda and her son.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The United States Coast Guard has released the names of all six passengers and crew who were aboard an air ambulance that crashed in the waters off Massachusetts over the weekend while flying from Bermuda to Boston.

The Canadians aboard were identified late Monday evening as: Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir.

Earlier in the day, Bermuda police said Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41, both Bermudian nationals, were aboard a Gulfstream G100 along with four crew members when it went missing off Nantucket around 1 a.m. Saturday. Bermuda is about 750 to 780 miles (roughly 1,200 to 1,250 kilometers) southeast of Boston.

Searchers later found a “debris field” off the coast of the island, but with no sign of the six people on board after a 66-hour search that spanned more than 4,400 miles (7,081 kilometers), the U.S. Coast Guard suspended rescue efforts Sunday.

“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized,” Bermuda Premier David Burt said in a statement . “Let us open our hearts to the families in the hope that our expressions of love, support and compassion will bring some comfort as they attempt to deal with this terrible loss.”

Warwick Academy, the school Lottimore attended in Bermuda, remembered him as a school prefect and an “ outstanding person .” Hamilton Re, the Bermuda insurance firm where he served as a senior vice president, said it had lost a “ respected leader, colleague and friend.”

Latitude Air Ambulance, the Ontario-based company that owned the plane, said Sunday that its staff faces the “heartbreaking reality” that all aboard the plane are now presumed dead, even if they have not been officially declared dead.

“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family,” the company said in a statement. “They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred. We are grieving their loss deeply.”

Peter Byl, president of Latitude Air Ambulance, said Monday the company’s immediate focus was on supporting the victims’ families and cooperating fully with authorities.

“We will not speculate about the circumstances or cause of the accident while that work is underway,” he wrote in an email.

The Canadian-registered jet had departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport on a nighttime flight to Massachusetts. Air traffic audio indicates that the plane May have been “coming in blind” as a storm loomed. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.

Canada’s Transportation Safety Board said it will send investigators in the coming days to assist in the search for and recovery of the aircraft. The agency said it is leading the investigation into the crash with assistance from its U.S. counterpart, the National Transportation Safety Board.

Philip Marcelo, The Associated Press

stories.title: 2 Canadian armed forces members face organized crime, kidnapping charges: Department of National Defence
stories.summary: The Department of National Defence (DND) confirms with CityNews that two Canadian Armed Forces members have been arrested by Toronto police on charges related to organized crime, kidnapping, and the theft of firearms and weapons. The suspects, Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau, are current members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, based at Moss Park Armoury […]
stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
The Department of National Defence (DND) confirms with CityNews that two Canadian Armed Forces members have been arrested by Toronto police on charges related to organized crime, kidnapping, and the theft of firearms and weapons.

The suspects, Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau, are current members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, based at Moss Park Armoury in Toronto, the DND said.

The DND says Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a Reservist in January 2020 and has not deployed on a Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) operation.

Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a Reservist in March 2018 and deployed on Operation LASER in 2020.

“Following their arrests, both individuals were removed from military duties and their access to CAF equipment, facilities, and bases was restricted,” the DND statement adds.

“They remain members of the CAF pending the outcome of an administrative review. An administrative review is a formal process used to assess matters that may affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.”

CityNews has reached out to Toronto police for comment and is awaiting a response.

More to come

stories.title: Two First Nations members dead in northern Labrador boating accident
stories.summary: Two members of a First Nation in northern Labrador are dead after an accident on the water yesterday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nain — Two members of a First Nation in northern Labrador are dead after an accident on the water yesterday.

The Mushuau Innu First Nation said in a social media statement Sunday that two of its members had lost their lives in an accident near Nain, N.L.

RCMP say a distress signal came from a vessel Sunday afternoon.

Police supported local ground search and rescue volunteers and the Canadian Coast Guard, which led the response.

The Mounties said two people were found dead and the chief medical examiner’s office is involved.

The First Nation’s statement thanked first responders and said the tragedy will have a profound impact on the community.

“We also echo the (First Nation’s) call to avoid speculation and discussion online, out of respect for all those impacted,” the RCMP said in a statement.

No further details were released.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Chief justice says democratic institutions must be protected
stories.summary: Canada's democratic institutions need protection in the face of unrelenting pressures, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said Monday.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Canada’s democratic institutions need protection in the face of unrelenting pressures, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said Monday as the Supreme Court of Canada opened a new judicial year.

Wagner said the world feels increasingly uncertain due to deepening polarization, the non-stop pace of events and the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence.

When seas grow rough an anchor keeps a vessel from drifting, and democratic institutions play the same role in society, Wagner said.

“The strength of an anchor is not measured in calm waters,” he added. “It is measured in a storm. The same is true for the rule of law.”

Wagner, flanked by the other members of the Supreme Court, spoke at a ceremony in the court’s temporary new building.

The top court is settling in at the West Memorial Building, not far from Parliament Hill, while the court’s permanent home across the street undergoes extensive renovations.

Refurbishing the stately Supreme Court building is expected to take at least 10 years.

A formal welcome for the court’s newest member, Glenn Joyal, is set to take place next month.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser told the courtroom full of dignitaries Monday that provinces, communities and groups of people are asking questions about their roles within the Canadian federation.

“If we expect to preserve national unity, we must constantly improve the public’s belief that the systems that we enjoy serve their interests over time,” he said. “The law has an important role to play in this regard.”

Fraser said that at a time “when it’s difficult to discern between truth and fiction, particularly with the rise and deployment of artificial intelligence, the truth-seeking function of this court and courts across Canada could never be more important.”

Refurbishing the stately Supreme Court building is expected to take at least 10 years.
A formal welcome for the court’s newest member, Glenn Joyal, is set to take place next month.
Justice Minister Sean Fraser told the courtroom full of dignitaries Monday that provinces, communities and groups of people are asking questions about their roles within the Canadian federation.

“If we expect to preserve national unity, we must constantly improve the public’s belief that the systems that we enjoy serve their interests over time,” he said. “The law has an important role to play in this regard.”

Fraser said that at a time “when it’s difficult to discern between truth and fiction, particularly with the rise and deployment of artificial intelligence, the truth-seeking function of this court and courts across Canada could never be more important.”
