stories.title: Quebec voters heading to the polls for provincial general election
stories.summary: Montreal - Voters in Quebec's 127 ridings are heading to the polls today to choose a new provincial government.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Parti Québécois has won a minority government, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.

The party captured 59 seats after the votes were counted late Monday, falling short of the 64 needed to form a majority in Quebec’s legislature.

The Coalition Avenir Québec, which has governed the province for the past eight years, was wiped off the map. Even leader Christine Fréchette, who took over after former premier François Legault’s resignation earlier this year, failed to win a seat in her hometown of Trois-Rivières.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon gave a victory speech in Montreal after his party was projected to form a minority government in Quebec. In the Eastern Townships region, Liberal party leader Charles Milliard promised to be a unifying force and a balance to the new government's promise of a referendum. (Oct. 6, 2026)

Charles Milliard’s Liberals were elected in 40 ridings and form the official Opposition for the third straight election, while the Quebec Conservatives led by Éric Duhaime make a historic entry into the legislature and gain official party status with 19 elected members.

A crowd of PQ supporters exploded with cheers at a watch party in Montreal as they learned their party was declared elected, with supporters dressed in blue and white chanting “Quebec, a country,” in French.

“There is a new chapter in our nation that is starting over the next few years,” PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon told a boisterous crowd Monday.

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to launch a referendum to separate Quebec from Canada, but not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

The premier-designate said a future independent Quebec would be rich, modern and democratic.

“A referendum is an opportunity to decide for ourselves,” he told the crowd, some of whom sported merchandise from the “Yes” campaign in the 1995 referendum. “It’s an act of democracy. It’s not up to anyone but us, as a people, to decide our national future.”

However, his path is complicated by the fact that both the Liberal and Conservative leaders have said their parties would fight to stop a sovereignty vote. Québec solidaire, another sovereigntist party, could hold the balance of power and support the PQ’s plans for a referendum. Québec solidaire elected nine members to the legislature.

The PQ has also promised to more than halve temporary immigration in Quebec and table legislation to abolish the monarchy, diverting funds used to pay the lieutenant-governor to tackle homelessness.

In his speech Monday, St-Pierre Plamondon pledged to include elements from the other parties’ platforms in his future budget. He also promised to work with the province’s English speakers and Prime Minister Mark Carney — when it serves Quebecers.

“I want to tell him that every time he’ll defend the interests of Quebec, he’ll find in me a partner in dialogue and collaboration,” he said.

Carney congratulated the PQ leader for his victory, pledging to work with the new government in Quebec City.

“Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada,” Carney said in a statement on social media. “I look forward to working with you to support Québec’s businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec.”

Carney also thanked Fréchette for her service, noting they had accomplished a lot together.

The Parti Québécois won only three seats in 2022, the lowest total ever since the party was founded in 1968. That number increased to seven by the start of the campaign, after four straight byelection wins.

The sovereigntist party capitalized on Quebecers’ desire for change after eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec rule. The outgoing governing party struggled to connect with voters due to a series of scandals, unpopular decisions and high-profile departures from its caucus in recent years, culminating in Legault’s resignation in January.

The Liberals also more than doubled their seat count, finishing with about 24 per cent of the popular vote, close behind the PQ, which finished the evening with about 28 per cent of the votes that were counted.

Milliard, the 47-year-old former pharmacist-turned-politician, warned St-Pierre Plamondon that the PQ would need to secure support beyond its own ranks to govern, and said he was open to collaborating on matters that improve Quebecers’ lives.

“But to prepare your referendum, you’ll find a determined opposition,” he said.

Duhaime and the rest of his Conservative team are the first candidates to be elected under the Conservative banner in modern history, although the party has had a recent presence in the legislature in former CAQ member Maïté Blanchette Vézina, who joined the party.

Under Duhaime’s leadership, the party surged from a marginal formation that captured less than two per cent of the vote in 2018 to a main player. The party ran a campaign that was largely targeted on key ridings, after failing to capture a seat in 2022 despite getting close to 13 per cent of the vote.

Duhaime has promised to use his leverage to act as a “guard dog” that would protect taxpayer interests and attempt to block a referendum vote.

“The voice of Quebecers who no longer recognize themselves in the old parties and who want to modernize the old bureaucratic model will finally be heard,” Duhaime said.

It was a quiet night at a Coalition Avenir Québec watch party in Trois-Rivières, where more than half the tables remained empty. The party entered the campaign with 79 seats, and ended the night with none.

Fréchette, who replaced Legault as leader and premier in April, took the blame for her party’s crushing defeat.

“Quebecers wanted change, and I respect their choice,” Fréchette said.

She spent much of her campaign warning of the dangers of a referendum at a time when the U.S. trade war is destabilizing the economy, and argued that her party was best placed to guide the province through the storm.

Despite an early boost in the polls, she largely failed to make the case that she could offer Quebecers a change in leadership without a change in government.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal was declared elected in her Montreal riding, as the left-wing sovereigntist party appeared poised to hold onto most of its seats.

She told supporters that her party’s results prove that “the left is still alive and well in the province,” and promised to fight the “four shades of right” that the other parties offer.

The same cheers of “Quebec, a country” — heard at the PQ watch party — also echoed through Québec solidaire’s gathering in Montreal, as Ghazal said the sovereigntist party was looking forward to building a country inclusive of everyone, including immigrants, Indigenous people and English speakers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: MPs return for break with debate set on key legislation and new bill on the table
stories.summary: Parliamentarians are back in Ottawa where debate is set to continue on the government's 243-page economic and labour bill, with plans to introduce legislation focused on national defence and security procurement.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Parliamentarians returned to Ottawa on Monday and Opposition members of Parliament had their sights trained firmly on the government’s 243-page economic and labour bill.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also squared off in question period Monday over whether the government has done enough to prioritize Canadian materials in its sweeping infrastructure agenda.

Key to that agenda is the Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, which was introduced on the first day of the fall sitting on Sept. 21.

The government’s landmark economic legislation proposes measures to create a one-year timeline for federal project decisions, create zones of “national interest” where certain projects are pre-approved, and change when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute — a move aimed at reducing the number of work stoppages.

Conservative MPs speaking to the legislation as debate resumed Monday were broadly supportive of getting projects built more quickly but questioned whether Bill C-39 would help Canada do that.

Conservative MP David McKenzie, who represents the riding of Calgary Signal Hill, said Liberal promises to approve projects with one assessment within one year are not the same as the government getting out of the way and letting private proponents build.

Bill C-39’s proposed “regions of national interest” — zones where pre-emptive consultations can pave the way for project pre-approvals and exemptions from certain laws — are akin to letting the government prioritize certain developments above others, he argued.

“It is an uncertainty, it’s a political process, and it is not going to be helpful in moving things forward,” McKenzie said.

Conservatives have largely criticized Bill C-39 since its introduction but have yet to say whether they would support the legislation or seek to amend it.

The bill’s passage is not in doubt, as the Liberals hold a majority of seats in the House of Commons now.

Bloc Québécois MP Christine Normandin criticized the bill’s proposed centralization of powers.

Speaking in French, Normandin compared the “national interest” exemptions to U.S. President Donald Trump bypassing the checks and balances of the United States Congress. She said Canada should not imitate Trump as it responds to the economic crisis he caused.

Liberal MPs argued in response that Bill C-39 is about giving businesses and private investors the certainty they need to get projects moving.

The legislation is expected to go before a committee for study, however instead of sending it to a regular standing committee, the House of Commons will create a special committee to study the wide-ranging bill.

Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has warned the government against “abusing” its majority powers to pass the bill, adding it could affect First Nations rights if it limits mandatory consultation.

The bill has also faced pushback from labour groups, including the Canadian Labour Congress, which says the proposed powers threaten the right to strike.

People in the business sector, meanwhile, have said the bill doesn’t go far enough to stave off labour disruptions.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the bill will put “guardrails” around ministerial powers to intervene in a strike or lockout and force people back to work.

Poilievre has said his party will call on the government to set a goal for Canada to produce one million barrels of diesel per day in response to high fuel prices.

He said in a video released Sunday that target could be reached through emergency permits and tax relief for refining, storage and transportation.

The Conservative motion also calls on the government to extend the fuel excise tax exemption until at least July 1, 2027.

Poilievre added the government should create a strategic energy reserve so there are stockpiles in the event of shortages driving up prices.

“We are the only G7 country that has no such reserve, even though we have the most oil right beneath our feet. So we could be joining them to release the 100 million barrels of oil they’re putting on the market right now,” Poilievre said.

The International Energy Agency stipulates that member nations must maintain a 90-day supply of their net fuel imports that can be used in the event of shortages. Canada is exempt from this rule because it exports more fuel than the country consumes.

Last week closed with near record-high diesel prices, while the Canadian average was about $2.60 per litre.

The Conservatives have two opposition days this week. The first is Tuesday, when they could introduce a motion that would be voted on Wednesday. They’ll be able to bring forward another motion Thursday that would go to a vote on Oct. 19.

The current fuel excise tax pause, which was extended last month until Jan. 31, 2027, will see the tax gradually rise until it’s fully in place on April 1, 2027.

Procurement Minister Joel Lightbound put a piece of legislation on the notice paper Friday entitled “an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security.”

Lightbound’s portfolio includes the Defence Investment Agency, created a year ago to overhaul defence procurement.

The government has been ramping up its defence spending with the goal of meeting the Nato target of investing five per cent of annual GDP in defence.

Parliamentarians will be in Ottawa until Friday, when they return to their ridings for another constituency week to coincide with Thanksgiving.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

— With files from Alessia Passafiume.

Craig Lord and David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Author Steven Galloway 'destroyed' by sex assault allegations, lawyer says
stories.summary: Vancouver - The lawyer for author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says his life and career were “destroyed” by sexual assault allegations, while his defamation lawsuit has been delayed for years as he tried to clear his name.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The lawyer for author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says the man’s life and career were “destroyed” by sexual assault allegations, while his defamation lawsuit has been delayed for years as he tried to clear his name.

Daniel Burnett told a B.C. Supreme Court judge on Monday that Galloway’s case is mostly about how to calculate damages against the defendants, who spread unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against Galloway.

Burnett said Galloway was once “a star in the literary world” with a bright future that was “cut very short” when the allegations were made publicly by a former student, and were then spread by others in the academic and literary world.

He said at the opening of the defamation trial that Galloway’s reputation was “tarnished to a degree that is incomparable.”

The sexual assault accusations were made against Galloway in late 2015, and since then, his accusers have fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming their accusations were protected speech.

The high court refused to hear the case, after a lower court said that if the defendants’ arguments held, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.

In the months after the information came out, dozens of high-profile representatives in Canada’s literary community, including Margaret Atwood and Yann Martel, signed a letter that raised concerns about the university’s process to investigate the complaints against Galloway, calling them secretive and unfair.

Galloway was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at the University of British Columbia when rumours swirled and spread, and while he was never charged, he was fired from the university.

A report that was later produced for the university by former judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the accusations against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

The defamation trial was originally scheduled for 60 days, but Justice Neena Sharma said it will likely take 20 days.

Nine of the people who accused Galloway or repeated accusations against him online have apologized, all of which have been posted on the website gallowayapologies.com .

Chelsea Rooney, one of the original defendants, issued a lengthy apology to Galloway over the weekend, saying she was genuinely sorry for the part she played in causing harm to him.

Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know if the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them, and she has come to better understand his position and commitment to clear his reputation.

“I should not have listened only to one side, or allowed that one-sided understanding to shape my communications, my tweets or my participation in the process,” her statement said, much of which was published in the National Post newspaper on Saturday.

Rooney is no longer a defendant in the case.

The court heard that four defendants remain, including his accuser only known as A.B., who isn’t going to attend court to testify.

Glynnis Kirchmeier, who is representing herself as a defendant, told the judge that the court will hear evidence about “how UBC utterly failed to have any reporting mechanisms available” for the proper reporting of sexual assault and that A.B. did “as best she could in a context where it was impossible to do so in the right way.”

Author Mandi Gray and Dana Kagis are also defendants.

After Burnett completed his opening on Monday, Galloway’s wife, Katie Wagner, told the court that Galloway was taken to a mental health facility in Ohio when the allegations came to light in 2015.

She testified that Galloway would become physically ill; he would cry, shake and vomit; and was distraught after the “outlandish” allegations went public in news articles and spread over social media.

Wagner became emotional during her testimony, telling the court that Galloway had panic attacks and sleep troubles that were “horrible.”

When they returned home to Vancouver, she said reporters started calling and showing up to their home with cameras, and the family retreated to Vancouver Island “for a long time” to avoid the publicity.

After the Boyd report came out and found the allegations against Galloway unsubstantiated, she said the faculty association at the university indicated that he should get his job back, but he didn’t.

She said Galloway would withdraw and she became a sort of caretaker for him, driving him to therapy and medical appointments and portioning out medications, taking a toll on her life for the last 10 years.

“I would feel torn. I want to go out and take care of my kids, or do normal things, or go to things, and he would be in there, you know, obsessing over the situation that was so horrible and couldn’t just be dropped. He couldn’t just shed it all, like go downstairs and, you know, live life.”

She said Galloway reacted with “hopelessness” and defeat as the allegations would be repeated, and she tried shielding him from social media.

Wagner told the court that she brought Galloway to a writer’s festival event, insisting that he go, and he “sat in the corner” and later told her how “absolutely awful it felt to go there and see his former life that way.”

The defamation trial continues in Vancouver on Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: University of Toronto launching $100-million scholarship fund to attract PhD students
stories.summary: New program aims to help school compete for bright minds at a time when elite U.S. universities are under attack by the Trump administration
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The University of Toronto is launching a $100-million scholarship fund for PhD students that will double the pay of recipients and help the school compete for bright minds at a time when elite U.S. universities are under attack by the Trump administration.

The new U of T program, unveiled Monday, will see the university recruit 12 or 13 new PhD candidates a year to conduct cross-disciplinary research on a predetermined theme, such as sovereignty and the Arctic, or health and artificial intelligence.

Winners will be paid $80,000 a year for four years, twice the current minimum base funding for PhD candidates at U of T. Half of the $100-million endowment comes from an anonymous donation, the rest from the university.

“We’ve got an unprecedented opportunity right now to bring back Canada’s best and keep Canada’s best here,” U of T president Melanie Woodin said in an interview. “The Prime Minister has spoken about the prioritization of talent as it relates to Canada’s economic resiliency and sovereignty, and as Canada’s flagship university, we’re fully aligned because we’re in the talent business.”

The new U of T awards are called the Presidents’ Impact Scholarships. If the name sounds familiar, it could be because Mark Carney’s Liberal government last year promised $1.7-billion over 12 years for an academic recruiting blitz with a similar moniker – The Canada Global Impact+ Research Talent Initiative.

That federal campaign is part of a wider push by Canada’s top-flight universities and hospitals to capitalize on uncertainty at postsecondary institutions south of the border. Donald Trump’s government has cut funding for scientific and scholarly research, sued top universities and expressed a general disdain for science.

The infusion of public funding and attention for science and scholarship in Canada is also something of a departure from the past.

In 2023, an advisory panel’s report on the federal research support system found the funding dispersed by Canada’s three main granting councils – the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada; and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada – had “not kept pace with evolving needs” or with Canada’s international competitors.

One of the shortfalls the report singled out was pay to graduate students, which they often receive via their professors’ grants.

The panel, led by Frédéric Bouchard, dean of the faculty of arts and sciences at the University of Montreal, concluded that financial support for graduate students in Canada was “at a breaking point.” The value of Ottawa’s awards for university research trainees had been stagnant for two decades, the panel’s report noted.

The new U of T scholarship program is an acknowledgment that paltry pay for graduate students can be a barrier to doctoral research, especially for those who have racked up debt as undergraduates or who are considering leaving the private sector to pursue a PhD, Dr. Woodin said.

She added that the Presidents’ Impact Scholarships will be, to U of T’s knowledge, the most lucrative PhD funding package in Canada. “Globally, it puts us pretty close to the top – so above Princeton, Harvard, Cambridge and Oxford,” Dr. Woodin said.

All that said, pay packages are just one of many factors that promising PhD candidates weigh when choosing a university.

U of T is hoping candidates for the new scholarship will be enticed by the interdisciplinary nature of the awards, which require doctoral students to work with two faculty supervisors from different disciplines.

For stem cell scientist Derrick Rossi, a Canadian co-founder of the pharmaceutical company Moderna Inc., money didn’t matter as much as living somewhere interesting and finding a PhD program that was the best fit for him.

He studied at U of T before moving to Paris and ultimately getting his PhD at the University of Helsinki.

More important, Dr. Rossi said in an interview, is the message that U of T is sending with a large scholarship for doctoral students.

“The U.S. government right now is very anti-science,” he said. “The signal that [U of T] is sending to the globe is that Canada is not anti-science and we’re serious about science.”

stories.title: PM Mark Carney pledged to ‘Buy Canadian.’ Since then, $7.8 billion in contracts went to American corporations
stories.summary: A Star analysis reveals U.S. firms dominated federal contracts despite PM Mark Carney’s ‘Buy Canadian’ promise.
stories.author: Frédérik Plante
stories.content:
Since assuming office a year and a half ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney has repeatedly promised that his government would “build Canadian and buy Canadian .”

But American-controlled multinational corporations have dominated the most lucrative federal contracts under Carney’s leadership, a Toronto Star analysis of government data shows. The share of government contract dollars going to U.S. companies also increased.

Since Carney was sworn in as Prime Minister in March 2025 and up to the end of July 2026 — the latest available data — Ottawa awarded $25 billion in contracts to buy everything from cloud services to military vehicles and office furniture.

The vast majority of it, $22.4 billion, went to Canadian companies, according to federal contract data. United States businesses come at a distant second place, with nearly $1.2 billion.

But that’s not the full picture; procurement data does not distinguish between a homegrown shop and the locally-incorporated subsidiary of an American corporation. This is how well-known U.S. brands such as defence contractor Lockheed Martin , which has received about $86 million in contracts under Carney, or tech giant Amazon, which has received about $49 million, sometimes show up in procurement data as Canadian companies.

The Star cross-referenced procurement data with another federal data set, the Inter-corporate Ownership (ICO) review’s index , which includes information on more than 50,000 companies and their “country of control” — where the people controlling the firm live. That metric is used to measure “the extent and impact of foreign control within the Canadian economy,” according to the ICO review, which reports on its findings to Parliament.

The Star also reviewed reports filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, company websites and other public records to confirm American ties among some of Ottawa’s largest contractors. Where there was no ICO match for smaller contractors, the Star used procurement data to establish an organization’s country.

The results show that while Carney has promised to uphold Canadian sovereignty and make the country’s economy less dependent on the U.S., his government has been reliant on its businesses. They also illustrate the limits of Ottawa’s Buy Canadian Policy, which went into effect in December to give “priority to Canadian businesses and Canadian-made content for large federal purchases.”

In its first 16 months in power, the Carney government gave an estimated $7.8 billion in federal contracts to American-controlled corporations. Contracts with Canadian companies over the same period amounted to $14.9 billion.

Public Services and Procurement Canada did not answer the Star’s questions on the proportion of contract dollars going to U.S.-controlled companies. Spokesperson Jean-François Létourneau said that the government “continues to take action to increase domestic participation, strengthen Canadian supply chains, and support Canadian workers, businesses, and communities.” He said that since December, 34 contracts worth $1.5 billion have been awarded under the Buy Canadian Policy.

The Prime Minister’s office declined to comment.

The share of federal contract dollars heading south went from one-fifth in the 16 months before Carney took office to nearly a third under his watch.

Canada’s secretary of state for defence procurement defended a decision on Wednesday to narrow the contest for at least 1,600 new light utility

Don Davies, the Vancouver Kingsway MP and New Democratic Party finance critic, said that this level of contracting with U.S.-controlled firms is “completely unacceptable” and “wrong in the current situation.”

“But it’s consistent with the Carney approach to (U.S. President Donald Trump) from the beginning of his election, which is to talk tough and act weakly,” Davies said. “If we can’t find Canadian companies” for procurement contracts, “then I think we should be looking for non-U. S. sources,” he added.

Shuvaloy Majumdar, the Calgary Heritage MP and Conservative Shadow Minister for Canada-U. S. Relations, said that the federal government should favour Canadian companies in procurement and be more transparent about contractors’ origins.

“If Mark Carney wants the world to choose Canada, maybe his own Liberal government should start by choosing Canadian,” Majumdar said, in reference to the Prime Minister’s push to attract investment.

“Canadians should be able to clearly see whether their tax dollars are supporting Canadian businesses and workers who are being hit hardest by unjustified U.S. tariffs, or if they are being funneled out to American companies,” he said.

The four highest-grossing federal contractors under Carney are all American-controlled. Tech giants IBM and Microsoft charged Ottawa more than $1 billion each for software license fees and IT services, among other things. Defence contractor L3Harris earned more than $1.2 billion, the majority of it for aircraft parts and engineering services, while General Dynamics got $846 million, mostly for ammunition and engineering consultants.

Canadian company Bombardier closes the top five with $710 million in contracts, mainly for aircraft parts.

The Department of National Defence, which is responsible for some of the largest contracts with U.S.-controlled companies, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Neither did Minister of National Defence David McGuinty, nor Joël Lightbound, the minister responsible for procurement.

But American-controlled multinational corporations have dominated the most lucrative federal contracts under Carney’s leadership, a Toronto Star analysis of government data shows. The share of government contract dollars going to U.S. companies also increased.

Since Carney was sworn in as Prime Minister in March 2025 and up to the end of July 2026 — the latest available data — Ottawa awarded $25 billion in contracts to buy everything from cloud services to military vehicles and office furniture.
The vast majority of it, $22.4 billion, went to Canadian companies, according to federal contract data. United States businesses come at a distant second place, with nearly $1.2 billion.

But that’s not the full picture; procurement data does not distinguish between a homegrown shop and the locally-incorporated subsidiary of an American corporation. This is how well-known U.S. brands such as defence contractor Lockheed Martin , which has received about $86 million in contracts under Carney, or tech giant Amazon, which has received about $49 million, sometimes show up in procurement data as Canadian companies.

The Star cross-referenced procurement data with another federal data set, the Inter-corporate Ownership (ICO) review’s index , which includes information on more than 50,000 companies and their “country of control” — where the people controlling the firm live. That metric is used to measure “the extent and impact of foreign control within the Canadian economy,” according to the ICO review, which reports on its findings to Parliament.

The Star also reviewed reports filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, company websites and other public records to confirm American ties among some of Ottawa’s largest contractors. Where there was no ICO match for smaller contractors, the Star used procurement data to establish an organization’s country.

The results show that while Carney has promised to uphold Canadian sovereignty and make the country’s economy less dependent on the U.S., his government has been reliant on its businesses. They also illustrate the limits of Ottawa’s Buy Canadian Policy, which went into effect in December to give “priority to Canadian businesses and Canadian-made content for large federal purchases.”

In its first 16 months in power, the Carney government gave an estimated $7.8 billion in federal contracts to American-controlled corporations. Contracts with Canadian companies over the same period amounted to $14.9 billion.

Public Services and Procurement Canada did not answer the Star’s questions on the proportion of contract dollars going to U.S.-controlled companies. The Prime Minister’s office declined to comment.

stories.title: Éric Blais: Spain outlaws votes on separation, meanwhile Quebec and Alberta will determine Canada’s fate
stories.summary: The only borders that truly matter, in the end, are not the ones drawn on a map, but the ones a country agrees to put to a vote. Spain forbids
stories.author: Éric Blais
stories.content:
On a break during a long day walking on the Camino de Santiago in Spain, I checked my phone — not for tomorrow’s weather forecast, but for news from Quebec’s election to be held today. I am a pilgrim who followed the polls and promises while admiring and learning about churches along the way from the 11th century.

There is something a bit absurd about reading all of this from here. Yet, I began this journey in the Basque Country, a place where, like Quebec and Alberta, an independence movement wants to pull out of the country.

In 2008, when the lehendakari Juan José Ibarretxe wanted to hold a simple popular consultation — not even a referendum on independence, but a consultation on the idea of opening negotiations — the Spanish Constitutional Court did not weigh the pros and cons. It ruled the question itself illegal, stating that an autonomous community does not have the right to call on its citizens regarding sovereignty.

The constitution states that everyone can be autonomous but no one can be sovereign. Catalonia asked anyway in October 2017. Its organizers went to prison.

Quebecers, ON the other hand, have voted twice on a question about sovereignty. And they might do so a third time if the PQ forms the government following Monday’s provincial election .

Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon repeated his commitment to hold a referendum during a first mandate. That he prudently postpones it — not while Donald Trump occupies the White House, which brings us to 2029 at the earliest — does not change the essential point: the question remains open and no one in Ottawa is thinking of declaring it illegal.

While Mark Carney has been clear about where he stands on Alberta independence, his position on nine other referendum questions is far less so.

And two weeks after Quebec, Alberta will vote in turn. Premier Danielle Smith , pushed by the secessionist wing of her own party, added a question to the ballot asking if the province should begin the process leading to a binding referendum on leaving Canada.

Two provinces, two votes, two nationalisms. One for the nation and the language. The other for grievance and oil.

Seen from Spain, it is genuinely unthinkable.

The temptation is great to conclude that Canada possesses a fine democratic spirit. What an admirable country, submitting its own dissolution to a vote rather than forbidding it.

Except I am suspicious of this version. Because Canadian openness was not born out of grace. It was born out of fear.

In October 1995, coming within roughly 50,000 votes, Canada narrowly dodged its own end. That night, it understood that it could not lock a door that half a province wanted to walk through.

The 1998 Reference re Secession of Quebec, and then the Clarity Act, were the answer: not a prohibition, but a procedure. A clear question, a clear majority, and the obligation to negotiate. Ottawa did not open the door out of generosity. It did so out of necessity.

It is a lesson that Spain has never wanted to learn. Madrid forbids asking. Canada, for its part, eventually understood that letting people vote, ON its own terms, is a firmer stance than a ban.

Alberta serves as a reminder that this openness is far from smooth. There, the question collides with treaties, opposition from First Nations and the constitutional duty to consult. A province’s sovereignty thus runs up against other sovereignties older than itself.

Days ago, I crossed the border between the Basque Country and Navarre without realizing it, and in the same step, that of France and Spain. Neither was marked.

At a window in Puente la Reina, someone hung an ikurriña, the Basque flag. On the flag were these words: ” Euskal Herriak erabaki .” Let the Basque Country decide. In the heart of Navarre, ON land that Madrid does not recognize as Basque, residents demand the right to ask the question.

The only borders that truly matter, in the end, are not the ones drawn on a map, but the ones a country agrees to put to a vote. Spain forbids asking the question. Canada prefers to answer it.

content_blocks.text: And two weeks after Quebec, Alberta will vote in turn. Premier Danielle Smith , pushed by the secessionist wing of her own party, added a question to the ballot asking if the province should begin the process leading to a binding referendum on leaving Canada.

content_blocks.text: Seen from Spain, it is genuinely unthinkable.

content_blocks.text: The temptation is great to conclude that Canada possesses a fine democratic spirit. What an admirable country, submitting its own dissolution to a vote rather than forbidding it.

content_blocks.text: Except I am suspicious of this version. Because Canadian openness was not born out of grace. It was born out of fear.

content_blocks.text: In October 1995, coming within roughly 50,000 votes, Canada narrowly dodged its own end. That night, it understood that it could not lock a door that half a province wanted to walk through.

content_blocks.text: The 1998 Reference re Secession of Quebec, and then the Clarity Act, were the answer: not a prohibition, but a procedure. A clear question, a clear majority, and the obligation to negotiate. Ottawa did not open the door out of generosity. It did so out of necessity.

content_blocks.html: Letting people vote

content_blocks.text: It is a lesson that Spain has never wanted to learn. Madrid forbids asking. Canada, for its part, eventually understood that letting people vote, ON its own terms, is a firmer stance than a ban.

content_blocks.text: Alberta serves as a reminder that this openness is far from smooth. There, the question collides with treaties, opposition from First Nations and the constitutional duty to consult. A province’s sovereignty thus runs up against other sovereignties older than itself.

In the heart of Navarre, ON land that Madrid does not recognize as Basque, residents demand the right to ask the question.

stories.title: How blood donors like Glen save up to three lives at a time
stories.summary: October 5, 2026
stories.content:
Above: Glen Dietz, Laboratory Quality Consultant at LHSC, sits proudly completing his 300th donation with Canadian Blood Services. He holds a sign that says, “This is my 300th donation and I’m coming back for more.”

October 5, 2026

Glen Dietz didn’t think skipping English class at 17 would turn into something so important. Yet, 55 years later with 300 blood donations up his sleeve, donating blood when he was supposed to be reading Shakespeare shaped a massive part of his life.

“ I first donated blood when H.B. Beal hosted a blood donation clinic. My biggest motivation was skipping English class to donate with my friends.”

Although he didn’t think about it much afterwards, a few months later a friend asked him to donate again.

“The second time I donated, my grandfather was in the hospital and required blood transfusions. That changed donating blood from no big deal into something personal. I knew my blood wasn’t going directly to my grandfather, but I saw the need.”

That year, Dietz excelled in high-school science, earning a unique placement at an LHSC lab, which motivated him to go to medical technology school and continue donating.

Before he knew it, Dietz had achieved a 50-year-long career in medical technology, and in January 2026, rolled up his sleeve for his 300 th donation with Canadian Blood Services.

Once donors like Dietz make their contributions, their blood goes on an incredible journey. Donations travel to Brampton, where each unit is separated into red blood cells, plasma, and platelets. That separation allows patients to receive exactly what they need, making it possible for one donation to help save up to three people.

Then, LHSC’s Transfusion Medicine Laboratory, which operates 24/7, orders blood components from Brampton to maintain the stock needed for patients.

When the blood products arrive back at LHSC, skilled Transfusion Medicine technologists collaborate with physicians and nurses to match patients with the blood products they need. The team completes crucial antibody testing, interprets lab results and perform compatibility tests, all before nurses administer transfusions to a variety of patients. This meticulous and detailed work makes it possible for the right blood product to get to the right patient at the right time.

Blood products support a vast range of patient needs, not just those involved in physical traumas or surgery or transplants. Dietz learned through his work that “blood is used daily for chronic transfusions, like dialysis patients or patients that have cancer. In some cases, patients needed blood transfusions for the rest of their lives.” The Transfusion Medicine Laboratory also reserve up to four coolers of blood products for the Ornge air ambulance team so they can meet the needs of patients in the field.

There is no existing substitute for real blood products, making donation critical to maintaining national supply. Thankfully, Dietz isn’t alone in his commitment to blood donation. Many members of Team LHSC give:

“I have been donating blood since high school. Working in healthcare I knew it was always important. When my grandfather was in intensive care he needed blood. Our family promised to "repay" those eight units. I celebrated by 40th donation in June and my mom just reached 51” - Amanda Johnston, Medical Imaging

“When I was in university a lot of people around me were diagnosed with cancer. I couldn’t help financially but wanted to make an impact. I started donating whole blood and my hair. I eventually switched into platelet donations. where some are direct matches with patients.” – Serge Parent, Paediatric Critical Care

“Life happens; we never know when we’ll be a giver or a recipient. I’ve been both! Donating blood is one of the few times being ‘full of it’ is a good thing! It's a chance to do something meaningful and spend a few relaxing minutes in a comfy chair. One donation can make a big difference. And the free snacks afterward don't hurt either!” – Tracy Harrison, Patient Experience

“Initially, I donated because it felt right and fit my schedule. Now, 20 years in, I make time because two close family members required blood transfusions during their cancer journeys. Donating takes very little time, the staff are always welcoming, and the process is efficient. It's one of the simplest ways I can give back and help someone in need.” – Elaine Hunter-Gutierrez, Infection Prevention and Control

Until October 31, donate blood as part of Team LHSC and help us win the Canadian Blood Services Hospital challenge for the third year in a row.

Check your eligibility with this quiz on the Canadian Blood Services website

Log in/Create an account and Join existing Team LHSC donors (Team code LOND012624)

Schedule an appointment at a convenient location across London and Middlesex County, including the Canadian Blood Services donation centre at 820 Wharncliffe Road South in London.

Team LHSC is a proud member of the Canadian Blood Services Partners for Life program .

stories.title: Fatal motor vehicle collision
stories.summary: London, ON (October 5, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Frontline Division and Road Safety Section are investigating a fatal motor vehicle collision that took place yesterday in the northwest end of the city.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 5, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Frontline Division and Road Safety Section are investigating a fatal motor vehicle collision that took place yesterday in the northwest end of the city.

On Sunday, October 4, 2026, at approximately 6:20 p.m., emergency crews responded to a collision involving a motorcycle and a motor vehicle in the area of Fanshawe Park Road West and Aldersbrook Gate. Upon arrival, the motorcyclist was located deceased. Roads in the area were closed while emergency crews remained on scene.

All roads have since reopened.

The driver of the motor vehicle remained on scene.

The investigation has been reassigned to members of the London Police Service Road Safety Section and is ongoing.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area on Sunday, October 4, 2026, between 6:10 p.m. – 6:30 p.m., and May have witnessed the collision, or who has dashcam, residential, or business surveillance footage, to please contact the London Police Service.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Missing Vulnerable Person – Brandon Kipp
stories.summary: London, ON (November 5, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 32-year-old Brandon Kipp, of London.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 5, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 32-year-old Brandon Kipp, of London.

He is described as male, White, approximately 5’9”, medium build, short brown hair and brown eyes. He was last seen wearing grey shorts, a blue shirt, a black hat with the letter “S” on the front, yellow socks, black shoes with white soles and a blue backpack.

He was reported missing on Sunday, October 4, 2026, and was last seen at approximately 5:15 p.m. in the area of Horton Street and Ridout Street.

Police and family are concerned for his welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Collision results in charges
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (October 5, 2026) – A London man is facing charges after a motor vehicle collision over the weekend.

On Saturday, October 3, 2026, at approximately 1:10 p.m., a man was driving eastbound on Euclid Avenue near Wharncliffe Road South when the vehicle he was operating struck two parked vehicles and rolled on to its roof. The involved driver exited the vehicle and attempted to flee the scene. Witnesses contacted police, and a citizen restrained the man until officers arrived and arrested him.

There were no reported injuries.

As a result of the investigation, Christopher Ulm, 46, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

· Impaired operation of a conveyance; and

· Fail to comply with demand made by Peace Officer

The accused was released from custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on November 12, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Bermudan passengers on missing Ontario air ambulance are identified
stories.summary: The Canadian pilots and medical staff on the plane have not yet been identified.
stories.author: Raju Mudhar
stories.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard has identified the Canadian crew who died on board the Ontario-based air ambulance flight that went missing off the coast of Nantucket this past weekend.

The four Canadians were pilots Philip Gregory Childerhose and Thomas Henry Farquhar and medical staff Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir. Earlier in the day, Bermudian authorities released the names of the two passengers they were escorting, which the Coast Guard confirmed. They were Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada is now leading the investigation into what happened with the aircraft.

On the pilots’ LinkedIn pages, Childerhose is listed as having been with Latitude for almost four years, but having had a career involving flight instruction since 2007. His residence is listed as Oakville. Farquhar, the first officer on the flight, is listed as having been with the company for two years and his residence is stated as Brantford. Latitude had said that four crew members lived in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton area.

The Gulfstream G100 jet C-Grjp had the call sign “Heartbeat 104,” and went missing early Saturday morning off the coast of Nantucket in the Atlantic Ocean.

A Latitude spokesperson told the Star on Sunday evening that company staff, many of whom rushed to the office and worked overnight Saturday, are in contact with family members of the crew and are planning to release more details.

“Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search and rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient’s family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died,” Latitude said in a press release late Sunday night.

“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family. They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred. We are grieving their loss deeply and will continue to support their families and our employees through the difficult days ahead,” said the release.

On Monday, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada put out a statement saying it is leading the investigation.

Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41.

“Pursuant to international agreements, the investigation shall be conducted by the State of registry, which is Canada. The TSB will be assisted by the (U.S.) National Transportation Safety Board as accredited representatives, and in the coming days will deploy investigators to assist in the search and recovery of the aircraft,” said the release .

Warwick Academy, the school Lottimore attended in Bermuda, remembered him as a school prefect and an “ outstanding person .”

Hamilton Re, the Bermuda insurance firm where he served as a senior vice-president, said it had lost a “ respected leader, colleague and friend.”

“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized, and so our first thoughts are with the families of those so tragically lost.”

A search remains ongoing off the Massachusetts coast for an air ambulance carrying six people that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. A “debris field” was found later Saturday off the coast of Nantucket, the Coast Guard said. (Oct. 4, 2026)

Air traffic controllers lost contact with the flight around 1:30 a.m. Saturday eastern daylight time (EDT), about 20 minutes outside its destination of Boston’s Logan International Airport.

Very little is known about what happened in the final moments of the flight.

The plane went missing early Saturday carrying four staff and crew from the GTA and Hamilton areas, along with a patient and family escort.

The jet made its departure from Bermuda around 11:42 p.m. Friday EDT Records from the website flightaware.com show the plane climbing normally to 24,000 feet and remaining at that altitude until shortly after 1 a.m. The jet then made a descent of about 11,000 feet before resuming stable flight until its disappearance.

Around 1:10 a.m., air traffic control recordings show the pilots made contact with a U.S.-based controller. The controller can be heard saying he is having problems hearing the pilots.

At one point, the controller describes the plane as “coming in blind,” after which he repeatedly asks if they wanted to declare an emergency.

While the U.S. Coast Guard has called off the search and rescue mission, it is unclear whether recovery efforts are underway.

At a press conference on Sunday morning, Coast Guard officials said that the plane’s black box recorder had not been recovered.

Authorities have said they plan to use sonar to comb the seabed where a field of debris spanning roughly 30 metres was discovered Saturday, about 160 kilometres short of the flight’s planned destination.

stories.title: Report linking Alberta separatists to Americans sparks call for emergency debate
stories.summary: The NDP wants a debate in Parliament about whether work by Republican party-affiliated operatives with Alberta separatists is foreign interference.
stories.author: Tonda MacCharles; Mark Ramzy; Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa —The Speaker of the House of Commons has rejected a New Democrat Party request for an emergency debate in Parliament about whether work by Republican party-affiliated operatives to help mobilize Alberta separatist votes amounts to foreign interference, as Canada’s public safety minister deferred such questions Monday to the national spy service.

Responding to new concerns raised by a Globe and Mail story that detailed the connections between Alberta separatists and Republican party strategists who developed a voter mobilization app, and that detailed the Albertans’ pitch to U.S. State Department officials about future exports of Alberta resources like water and oil to the U.S., Gary Anandasangaree declined to say whether it is foreign influence or worse, foreign interference.

He twice referred reporters to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis).

“What I will say in general terms is, as electoral events take place, democratic events take place, we expect them to be governed in … democratic principles, where foreign interference or actors influencing local electoral events does not occur,” he said.

New Democrat MP Heather McPherson made the case for an emergency debate in Parliament, saying that the revelations, coming two weeks before Alberta’s vote on Oct. 19, are “a serious threat to our democracy and our sovereignty.”

Quebec’s sovereigntists never tried to advance their cause by selling out to the United States.

“These are not simply Albertans having a political disagreement with Ottawa. These are extremists seeking foreign assistance to break up Canada. There is a word for people who put foreign interests ahead of their own country: traitors,” she said. “Under Canadian law, they would be investigated, and if convicted, they should face the full force of the law.”

However, Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia refused her request, saying “at this time” it didn’t meet the bar for a debate, which is usually granted when Parliament confronts a matter requiring urgent consideration.

McPherson told the Star she does not believe the federal government is “taking this as seriously as they need to.”

The Prime Minister’s Office declined to offer specific answers Saturday when the Star asked about Prime Minister Mark Carney’s knowledge of and response to the concerns raised in the Globe story.

“There is regular and ongoing engagement between national security agencies and the relevant authorities in Alberta to ensure the security of the referendum,” said spokesperson Audrey Champoux. “This is the case any time Canadians go to the polls federally or provincially, as part of a continued commitment to protecting our democratic processes.”

But Conservative MP Dane Lloyd, whose group Conservatives for Canada is campaigning for the federalist or “remain” side of the referendum question, said it is cause for concern.

“Nobody, absolutely nobody, has a right to promise away Alberta’s birthright, which is our natural resources,” Lloyd said.

“Those belong to the people of Alberta, and I will never condone even one cent of Alberta’s royalties going towards any foreign government.”

Lloyd stopped short of saying the reported activity amounts to foreign interference. “I think we have to get more information on this, but it’s obviously very concerning,” he said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has not publicly addressed the concerns, but her spokesman distanced Smith from any connection to the activity that’s raising alarms.

“The premier is not affiliated with these individuals and has no knowledge of these alleged meetings. She also opposes separation or becoming a U.S. state,” Sam Blackett said in a written statement. “In fact, many of these individuals in question have been relentlessly attacking the premier for her support for remaining in Canada.”

Last week, the U.S. embassy said it had not identified which U.S. State Department officials had met with representatives of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project, whose organizers acknowledged in January that they had travelled to Washington. The Globe reported two of the Alberta participants disputed what was discussed in Washington.

For weeks, the Star has sought clarity from the federal government about concerns around potential foreign influence or interference in the Alberta referendum, and whether it had directed the Security and Intelligence Threats to Elections (Site) task force — comprised of officials from Csis, the Communications Security Establishment (CSE), Global Affairs Canada and the RCMP — to report on those threats.

The Privy Council Office, answering for Site, and Csis have consistently offered non-responsive replies. PCO spokesman Pierre Coguen said the agencies involved take “any attempts” at foreign interference with “the utmost seriousness” and “will take action to protect Canadians … This work includes regular and ongoing engagement with relevant authorities in Alberta.”

Similarly, Csis offered little other than to say it remains “vigilant” and declined to answer questions in any more depth.

“In order to protect sources, tradecraft and methods, we do not, however, confirm nor disclose investigative details, including whether an investigation is ongoing. Csis will continue to release information at appropriate times about specific threats when it is able to do so and when it’s in the interests of Canada’s national security,” said spokesman Eric Balsam.

Foreign interference is a higher level of suspicious activity than foreign influence. The first is generally understood to be covert, while the latter is seen as overt activity that falls below the interference threshold.

In the wake of nationwide concern about the extent of foreign interference in Canada by countries like Russia, China, India, Iran and other players identified by a public inquiry, Ottawa established an Office of the Foreign Influence Commissioner of Canada to register people or organizations who might be subject to foreign actors trying to flex their muscles in Canada.

That office said two weeks ago that it was “aware” of concerns about foreign influence in Alberta, and had reached out to individuals and organizations there to remind them of their public reporting obligations.

But it has turned down repeated requests since then for more information or an interview with commissioner Anton Boegman, who said in August that his main job is to ensure transparency for Canadians.

“We cannot disclose the identities or number of individuals and organizations contacted, nor can we comment on potential registrants or compliance matters,” said a media communications response, signed only by a “Charlaine S.”

In another email Monday, Boegman’s office said submissions about foreign influence will only be publicly disclosed on the registry after the office has evaluated whether it is required by the law. The office defended such secrecy, saying it is “committed to transparency and accountability, while complying with the Privacy Act and other legal requirements governing the collection, use and disclosure of information.

“The office does not comment on potential registrants or ongoing investigations, as doing so could compromise the integrity of those processes and affect procedural fairness.”

It said it will provide transparency “through the public registry, public reporting, and the publication of enforcement outcomes.

“Under the act, the commissioner must make public confirmed violations, including the nature of the violation, the name of the person who committed it, and any administrative monetary penalty imposed. While the office cannot comment on potential or ongoing compliance matters, Canadians will be informed of violations where disclosure is required by law.”

At the same time, the commissioner’s office defended its own secrecy even around the name of its media spokesperson, saying it “does not publicly disclose employee information to protect the safety and security of our staff.”

Anandasangaree shrugged off questions about why the office isn’t proactively providing transparency about the Alberta separatist connections with foreigners.

“The process of registration and ongoing reporting is just in the early stages, so we’re hoping in the coming months and years that (it) would become more of a robust registry for information to be gathered and for disclosures,” he said.

stories.title: Bermudian mother and son on missing Ontario air ambulance are identified
stories.summary: The Canadian pilots and medical staff on the plane have not yet been identified.
stories.author: Raju Mudhar
stories.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard has identified the Canadian crew who died on board the Ontario-based air ambulance flight that went missing off the coast of Nantucket this past weekend.

The four Canadians were pilots Philip Gregory Childerhose and Thomas Henry Farquhar and medical staff Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir. Earlier in the day, Bermudian authorities released the names of the two passengers they were escorting, which the Coast Guard confirmed. They were Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada is now leading the investigation into what happened with the aircraft.

On the pilots’ LinkedIn pages, Childerhose is listed as having been with Latitude for almost four years, but having had a career involving flight instruction since 2007. His residence is listed as Oakville. Farquhar, the first officer on the flight, is listed as having been with the company for two years and his residence is stated as Brantford. Latitude had said that four crew members lived in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton area.

The Gulfstream G100 jet C-Grjp had the call sign “Heartbeat 104,” and went missing early Saturday morning off the coast of Nantucket in the Atlantic Ocean.

A Latitude spokesperson told the Star on Sunday evening that company staff, many of whom rushed to the office and worked overnight Saturday, are in contact with family members of the crew and are planning to release more details.

“Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search and rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient’s family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died,” Latitude said in a press release late Sunday night.

“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family. They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred. We are grieving their loss deeply and will continue to support their families and our employees through the difficult days ahead,” said the release.

On Monday, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada put out a statement saying it is leading the investigation.

Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41.

“Pursuant to international agreements, the investigation shall be conducted by the State of registry, which is Canada. The TSB will be assisted by the (U.S.) National Transportation Safety Board as accredited representatives, and in the coming days will deploy investigators to assist in the search and recovery of the aircraft,” said the release .

Warwick Academy, the school Lottimore attended in Bermuda, remembered him as a school prefect and an “ outstanding person .”

Hamilton Re, the Bermuda insurance firm where he served as a senior vice-president, said it had lost a “ respected leader, colleague and friend.”

“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized, and so our first thoughts are with the families of those so tragically lost.”

A search remains ongoing off the Massachusetts coast for an air ambulance carrying six people that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. A “debris field” was found later Saturday off the coast of Nantucket, the Coast Guard said. (Oct. 4, 2026)

Air traffic controllers lost contact with the flight around 1:30 a.m. Saturday eastern daylight time (EDT), about 20 minutes outside its destination of Boston’s Logan International Airport.

Very little is known about what happened in the final moments of the flight.

The plane went missing early Saturday carrying four staff and crew from the GTA and Hamilton areas, along with a patient and family escort.

The jet made its departure from Bermuda around 11:42 p.m. Friday EDT Records from the website flightaware.com show the plane climbing normally to 24,000 feet and remaining at that altitude until shortly after 1 a.m. The jet then made a descent of about 11,000 feet before resuming stable flight until its disappearance.

Around 1:10 a.m., air traffic control recordings show the pilots made contact with a U.S.-based controller. The controller can be heard saying he is having problems hearing the pilots.

At one point, the controller describes the plane as “coming in blind,” after which he repeatedly asks if they wanted to declare an emergency.

While the U.S. Coast Guard has called off the search and rescue mission, it is unclear whether recovery efforts are underway.

At a press conference on Sunday morning, Coast Guard officials said that the plane’s black box recorder had not been recovered.

Authorities have said they plan to use sonar to comb the seabed where a field of debris spanning roughly 30 metres was discovered Saturday, about 160 kilometres short of the flight’s planned destination.

stories.title: Impaired driver
stories.summary: London, ON (October 5, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple criminal charges after an impaired driving incident that began with a collision involving an ambulance and ended with his arrest at a local hospital following reports of dangerous driving across the city.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 5, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple criminal charges after an impaired driving incident that began with a collision involving an ambulance and ended with his arrest at a local hospital following reports of dangerous driving across the city.

On Sunday, October 4, 2026, at approximately 9:30 p.m., members of the London Police Service responded to a report of an ambulance being struck by a vehicle by a residence on Duchess Avenue near Dane Street. Paramedics at the scene contacted police.

Investigators learned that the driver struck a parked ambulance before colliding with a second parked vehicle in a driveway and fleeing the area.

Shortly after the initial call, police received multiple reports of a silver sedan being driven dangerously in the area of Western Road and Sarnia Road. The vehicle was reported to be driving on sidewalks, down a flight of stairs, through red lights, and nearly striking pedestrians while operating with significant damage to one of its tires.

Officers searched for the suspect vehicle and located it as it entered the Base Line Road East entrance of a local hospital on Commissioners Road East. Police utilized their police cruisers to prevent the vehicle from continuing to move and attempted to arrest the driver.

During the arrest, a Conducted Energy Weapon (CEW) was deployed but was ineffective. The suspect male resisted officers and assaulted two members of the London Police Service before being taken into custody at approximately 9:50 p.m.

There were no reported injuries.

As a result of the investigation, Neil Anthony Salters, 46, of London, has been charged with:

Two counts of assault peace officer;

Resist arrest;

Operation while impaired;

Flight from peace officer;

Dangerous operation; and

Fail to stop after accident.

The accused remains in custody and appeared in London court today in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Air ambulance passengers identified; crew remembered as 'valued members' of Hamilton company
stories.summary: The Hamilton-based company is “grieving their loss deeply” after the presumed death of the crew, plus the patient and family escort.
stories.author: Fallon Hewitt; Laura Sebben
stories.content:
Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance is remembering the four crew members lost when a medevac flight disappeared off the coast of Massachusetts early Saturday as “valued members” of its team, acknowledging they are presumed dead.

The two pilots and two medical staff, along with a patient and a family escort, were travelling from Bermuda to Boston when their Gulfstream G100 jet vanished over the Atlantic Ocean near Nantucket, Mass., spurring a massive search over the weekend.

“This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104,” Latitude Air Ambulance president Peter Byl said in a statement late Sunday. “We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism and commitment they brought to their work every day.”

On Monday, the Bermuda Police Service identified the passengers as Bermudian nationals Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore.

The identities of the crew members have not been publicly released. No further details have been issued on the mother and son.

The U.S. Coast Guard announced late Sunday it had suspended its search of an extensive debris field off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., where pieces of the missing plane had been spotted a night earlier.

The U.S. Coast Guard searches for the missing Latitude Air Ambulance plane that went missing off the coast of Nantucket in this Oct. 3 photo. The search has since been called off.

Authorities said a black box associated with the flight — designed to preserve evidence after a crash — had yet to be recovered.

Canada’s Transportation Safety Board (TSB) will lead the investigation into the accident, it announced Monday.

In a statement, the TSB said the aircraft “was approaching the Boston area when the crew reported electrical difficulties.”

“The aircraft subsequently descended rapidly and contact with air traffic control was lost south of Nantucket.”

The investigation is being led by the TSB because international agreements state they must be conducted by the aircraft’s state of registry. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (Ntsb) will assist.

Investigators will be deployed in the coming days to assist in the search and recovery of the aircraft, the TSB said.

Late Sunday, Latitude said in a statement that with the end of the search, the company must “face the heartbreaking reality” that all those on the flight have likely died.

“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family,” said the statement from the company, which is based out of Hamilton’s airport. “They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred.”

The company offered extended condolences to the families, loved ones, friends and colleagues of the crew.

The company noted it is “grieving their loss deeply” and pledged to support their families and its staff in the “difficult days” ahead.

The Spectator reached out to Latitude Monday, but the company declined to comment beyond its statement. More details are expected to be released from the company in the coming days.

Latitude also shared condolences to the family and friends of the patient and family escort on the flight.

Warwick Academy, a long-standing private school in Bermuda, mourned the loss of Lottimore (Class of 2002) and his mother in a LinkedIn post shared Monday.

The school described Lottimore as a “school prefect” and an “outstanding person” in the post, noting that he will be remembered with “great fondness by those who knew him.”

The company said it will continue to “co-operate fully” with the Ntsb, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada and other authorities as recovery efforts and the investigation continue.

“Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred,” said the company.

Latitude thanked all those who took part in the search, noting their “professionalism, determination and compassion will never be forgotten.”

All four crew were from Ontario and lived “within one to two hours” of Latitude’s headquarters at Hamilton’s John C. Munro International Airport, operations manager Clarence Togeretz told The Spectator on Saturday. The passengers were from Bermuda.

The plane lost contact and disappeared from radar around 1:30 a.m. Saturday, about 20 minutes outside its destination, Boston Logan International Airport. The Coast Guard was notified and responded at 2 a.m.

Over the ensuing hours, the Coast Guard covered a stretch of 7,355 square kilometres, deploying a heavy mix of specialized air and sea assets, including two fixed-wing search planes, a recovery helicopter, an unsinkable motor lifeboat and a 154-foot fast response cutter.

By Saturday night, the Coast Guard had identified a debris field about 30 kilometres off the coast of Nantucket, where flight trackers had for hours shown search planes flying in loops.

The depth of the water in that area is approximately 80 to 90 feet.

Industry partners and health-care colleagues posted dozens of condolence messages on LinkedIn over the weekend and Monday.

Mayor Andrea Horwath wrote on social media that she was “heartbroken” by the loss of those on the flight, sharing that her “heart goes out” to the families of those who were aboard as well as the entire Latitude team.

“Latitude is part of our Hamilton community, operating out of Hamilton International Airport,” said Horwath, extending condolences on behalf of the city to all affected by the tragedy.

stories.title: London Knights blown out in first loss of season
stories.summary: The Flint Firebirds have put an end to the London Knights (4-1) perfect start to the Ontario Hockey League season.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Flint Firebirds have put an end to the London Knights (4-1) perfect start to the Ontario Hockey League season.

The Firebirds came into Canada Life Place Sunday and pounded London 7-2.

Outshooting the Knights 35-24, the visitors chased starting goaltender Aleksei Medvedev from the net after five goals in early in the third period.Jimmy Lombardi had a goal and four assists for the Firebirds to earn first star honours.

London’s Thomas Zocco had his fourth goal of the year, while rookie defenceman Juho Piiparinen scored his first career goal.

stories.title: Missing for 22 years: Frank Davis found in Kootenay River
stories.summary: For 22 years, the disappearance of Frank Davis remained an unanswered mystery for his family. Frank was 40 when he went missing from Creston, B.C.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
For 22 years, the disappearance of Frank Davis remained an unanswered mystery for his family.

Davis was 40 when he went missing from Creston , B.C., leaving behind loved ones who would spend years wondering what happened to him.

Now, a team of divers called Adventures with Purpose uncovered a discovery beneath the waters of the Kootenay River near Creston: Frank’s car, flipped upside down at the bottom of the river, with his remains inside.

The divers start by identifying a person’s last known location and using available information to map out potential areas where their vehicle May have entered the water. The team then uses sonar to scan beneath the surface, methodically ruling out locations until they find a lead.

For Davis, the search stretched into its eighth hour before the team located his car on the opposite side of the river.

“The 11th search was where his car was on the other side of the river. We can work very fast,” said Bryon Leisek, a diver with Adventures With Purpose.

Adventures with Purpose is an American dive team known for its YouTube channel, where it documents searches for missing people and vehicles believed to be underwater.

The team works with families and law enforcement to help bring answers to long-unsolved cases and doesn’t charge the families or police departments for its recovery searches.

For families who have spent years wondering what happened to a loved one, the team’s work can help provide answers and a sense of closure.

For Davis’ brother, Reid Davis, the discovery brought back a ton of emotions. After 22 years without answers, Reid says he had almost stopped believing he would ever know what happened.

“It was numbing at first; after so long, you kind of think that you’re not going to have this moment ever, and then just a flood of memories again, all these things that you kind of put away over the years,” Reid said.

Now, Reid hopes the family can move forward by sharing stories about Frank, especially with his youngest son, who was just two years old when his father disappeared.

Frank’s niece, Lenelle Davis, remembers being young when he disappeared. But she has not forgotten the uncertainty that followed, especially for her grandmother, Frank’s mother, who died without knowing what happened to her son.

“How could you ever have any peace not knowing what has happened to your child?” Lenelle said. “I always felt heartbroken for her.”

While the discovery has finally answered where Davis was found, it has not explained exactly how he ended up in the river.

Kade Pigg, a producer with Adventures With Purpose, said the team believes the car went into the water near the abandoned ferry crossing.

“We just determined the where, not the why,” Pigg said.

Police say Davis’ death is not considered suspicious and foul play is not suspected.

For his family, the discovery means they no longer have to wonder where Frank was. As Lenelle put it, there is relief in knowing “he’s home and he’s resting and we’re just not wondering.”
