stories.title: B.C. man sentenced for 'hateful' messages written on Victoria historic synagogue
stories.summary: Victoria - A British Columbia man who defaced a historic synagogue in Victoria with "unquestionably hateful" statements has been sentenced to eight months in jail.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - A British Columbia man who defaced a historic synagogue in Victoria with “unquestionably hateful” statements has been sentenced to eight months in jail.

B.C. provincial court Judge Micah Rankin’s ruling released this week says Arthur Roberts pleaded guilty to mischief and uttering threats, after he admitted to defacing the Congregation Emanu-El synagogue in downtown Victoria in the summer of 2025.

stories.title: Another oilsands boom? Smith, Carney say this time Canada will be ready
stories.summary: The last boom from the mid-2000s to 2010s came with the side-effects of cost inflation, labour scarcity and housing shortages — the industry has changed significantly since then.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
It’s been a relatively quiet decade in the Alberta oilsands , but the federal and provincial governments believe a new West Coast pipeline coupled with policy shifts might help turn up the volume.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Fort McMurray, Alta., this week to announce the first proposal to be deemed in the national interest under legislation passed last year: the million-barrel-per-day Pacific Link pipeline from Alberta to a tanker export terminal in southern B.C.

The designation means the proposal will be subject to a streamlined review process, shepherded by the Calgary-based major projects office.

2:20 Pipeline receives national interest designation

The pipeline’s economic fate hinges on oilsands companies being willing to spend on expanding their output.

At a news conference, Carney was asked whether he expected a return to boom times in the northeastern Alberta oilsands hub city.

“I wouldn’t use the term ‘boom,'” he replied.

“I would use ‘sustained growth.'”

The last oil boom from the mid-2000s to mid-2010s came with the side-effects of cost inflation, labour scarcity and housing shortages. Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith say that if oilsands companies start building again — as they hope — it will be different this time around.

Oilsands companies have for years shied away from the multibillion-dollar megaprojects of more than a decade ago.

The last mine to be built from scratch was Fort Hills, operated by Suncor Energy Inc.

From when it got the final go-ahead decision in 2013 to its startup in 2018, its cost ballooned to more than $17 billion from $13.5 billion.

Lately, instead of so-called “green field” projects, companies have opted to instead tweak their existing operations to squeeze out more bitumen or add to their existing footprints.

Executives have cited a dearth of pipeline capacity, a convoluted regulatory regime and onerous environmental regulations for the chill on large-scale growth projects.

But also around the time investment fell off a decade ago, global crude prices cratered amid a supply glut and didn’t have much of a chance to recover before the COVID-19 pandemic virtually obliterated demand.

2:02 Peak oil demand could be reached by 2030: report

Fast forward to 2026, and the Mideast war has laid bare the vulnerability of global energy supply chains and left countries clamouring for stable providers.

A host of Trudeau-era energy policies loathed by oilpatch players have been undone and Pacific Link has taken a big step forward to becoming a reality, potentially enabling more oilsands crude to reach lucrative Asian markets.

“We learned lessons from the past in building infrastructure,” Carney told reporters on Thursday. He said local mayors are thinking ahead for what their communities need and early participation from First Nations leaders means “a much broader spread of the economic benefits.”

He also cited “another phase of technical innovation” in the industry that didn’t exist previously.

At the news conference, Smith noted the autonomous oilsands haul trucks in the backdrop.

Previously, human drivers for those gargantuan vehicles would have received six-figure salaries and might have been flown in and out of the site from elsewhere in Canada, living in work camps, for a week or two at a time.

“(Companies) have managed to find a way to increase production without having the kind of dramatic pressure that we saw in the past of a large number of people moving here, not able to find homes,” Smith said.

The premier said she’s also talked to local municipal leaders about the bridge and road infrastructure that might be needed if production ramps up.

She mentioned upgrades to Highway 881, a road to the east of the main Highway 63 route north, that winds through several steam-driven oilsands sites south of Fort McMurray.

“There’s lots of ways that we can partner with the federal government to make sure those key infrastructure projects get built, so we build on a pace that allows us to keep up,” she said.

Andrew Botterill, who leads Deloitte Canada’s oil, gas and chemicals practice, said the Alberta oilpatch has matured since the last boom.

“What we have is a more efficient, far more aligned group of producers up there than maybe what it was 10, 15 years ago,” he said.

“They’ve come together as an alliance and really recognize that ‘We’ve got to share labour, we’ve got to be less competitive, we’ve got to find ways that we can do things together and not just drive up costs.'”

2:10 Ottawa fast tracks ‘Pacific Link’ pipeline, designates as project of national interest

Oilsands properties are also concentrated in fewer hands than had been the case a decade or more ago.

Erstwhile producers including Husky and MEG Energy have been bought out and international players like Shell and Total have exited or sharply reduced their holdings.

Lance Mortlock, managing partner at EY Canada, flagged a bigger-picture concern over the availability of workers with multiple major projects in the works — not just the Pacific Link pipeline and new oilsands projects, but potentially mines, transmission lines and hydro dams.

“We’re going to need tens of thousands of workers across the country to build this stuff: engineers, professionals, welders, pipe fitters. I’m not sure where all these people are going to come from if we do half the projects that we have the desire to construct,” he said.

“So I’m hoping that there’s going to be more conversation about the workforce and more conversation about how do we sequence these things so we optimize the system from a labour force perspective?”

stories.title: Western climbs Pitchbook Rankings for top entrepreneurship universities
stories.summary: Western University rose in the Pitchbook Rankings 2026, up to 36th globally for undergraduate alumni entrepreneurs raising venture capital.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Western University improved in the 2026 Pitchbook Rankings , climbing several spots on the undergraduate, MBA and undergraduate female founder charts based on the number of alumni entrepreneurs who have raised capital in the last decade.

In the Top 100 Universities for Entrepreneurs for 2026, Western University was ranked:

PitchBook, a financial data company, compiles the ranking based on an analysis of more than 222,000 founders raising capital between Jan. 1, 2015, and Aug. 1, 2026.

One of eight Canadian universities on the list, Western placed above prestigious global institutions such as Oxford, Cambridge and Johns Hopkins University. It rose several spots compared to Pitchbook’s 2025 rankings.

Notable alumni founders listed by Pitchbook included 1Password founder David Teare, BSc‘00; Wealthsimple CEO Michael Katchen, HBA‘09; Lazada Philippines co-founder James Chang, HBA ’08; Flexiti founder Peter Kalen, HBA‘95, MBA‘01; and Substack co-founder Hamish McKenzie, MA‘06.

“We are very excited to see so many of our alumni featured in these rankings,” said Eric Morse, executive director of the Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship Powered by Ivey.

“It’s a testament to the incredible work Western graduates are doing around the world in a variety of industries.”

While Pitchbook provides an important snapshot of entrepreneurs raising capital for their ventures, Morse said it’s not the full picture of Western graduates pursuing entrepreneurship.

Less than one percent of all start-ups raise venture capital, and most successful companies grow purely through revenue or angel capital. These include small businesses that become the beating heart of communities throughout Canada, to multi-million dollar companies that hire hundreds, even thousands, of people across the country.

What Pitchbook does capture is an important segment of the entrepreneurship community.

“The companies that are raising venture capital are wrestling with big ideas and pushing the boundaries of innovation,” Morse said.

Despite the gains by Western, the University of Waterloo, McGill University, and the University of Toronto, Canadian entrepreneurship has struggled over the last two decades, with estimates showing 100,000 fewer entrepreneurs active today in comparison to 20 years ago. One of the major factors associated with this decline has been the lack of capital available to Canadian founders, forcing many to seek opportunities in the United States.

Two of Western’s current initiatives that support alumni start-ups and scale-ups are Western Angels’ Demo Day and the Western Propel Fund. Demo Day is a bi-annual investor event that brings together entrepreneurs and investors from the Western alumni community to forge mutually beneficial partnerships and create a new generation of great Canadian companies.

The Western Propel Fund , in partnership with the Ivey Business School and the Morrissette Institute, enables the university to fuel the growth of high-potential Western-founded companies across a broad range of industries. The fund will enable up to six investments of $150,000 annually, along with comprehensive support and mentoring for portfolio companies through Morrissette.

“We want to change Canada’s entrepreneurship story and help the country rediscover its roots,” said Morse.

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: B.C. extortion investigation leads to arrests of five foreign nationals, RCMP say
stories.summary: From Jan. 1 to Sept. 28, the department has had 142 reported extortions
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Five foreign nationals are in police custody and face a string of charges arising out of an RCMP extortion investigation involving members of British Columbia’s South Asian community.

Supt. Harm Dosange, with the Langley RCMP, said Friday that the investigation into arsons, shootings and extortions started in June 2025 when owners of an auto dealership reached out to police.

The criminals’ demands were followed up by shootings and arsons in Langley and neighbouring Surrey, B.C., he said.

Dosange said it was a long and difficult case for investigators as they worked across Canada and internationally.

“ They faced numerous daunting challenges and some unprecedented things we have not seen before,” he said, although he wouldn’t elaborate as the case is before the courts.

The five accused are in their 20s and face a variety of charges, including extortion, damaging property by fire explosion and throwing an explosive substance, along with numerous drug and firearms allegations.

“We obtained evidence identifying additional suspects, evidence that supports other extortion-related offences throughout Western Canada,” Dosange said during a news conference.

One of the accused was arrested getting off a plane in Toronto from India, police said.

Investigators “determined that it was in the public interest to have him appear before the courts in Canada,” police said in a news release.

The RCMP said investigators worked with immigration and border services officials as well as international police to facilitate a “controlled operation” to allow the suspect to enter Canada in order to arrest him.

The arrests are among a series of cases being investigated by police after a provincewide extortion task force was launched last year, while police in Surrey and Abbotsford also diverted officers to the cases.

The City of Surrey set up a $250,000 reward for convictions, while the Surrey Police Service started keeping statistics for the year.

From Jan. 1 to Sept. 28, the department has had 142 reported extortions, 21 related shots-fired cases, three arsons and 76 victims, although 39 of them are repeated victims.

The extortionists are aiming their threats at business owners and those in the South Asian community.

Chief Supt. Duncan Pound with B.C.’s extortion task force said the trial for those accused will hear if the India-based Lawrence Bishnoi gang is involved.

“I will say there are lots of these investigations where we’ve seen that the perpetrators will allege that they’re connected to high-profile gangs to try and increase the level of intimidation,” he said.

It’s also a way to make money, he noted.

The Lawrence Bishnoi gang has been labelled a terrorist entity in Canada. Bishnoi has been accused of running his operation while in prison in India.

Both Dosange and Pound say the victims’ courage to come to police made the difference in their investigation.

“Truly, without really timely reporting and the courage to come forward and provide as many details as they can, it’s very difficult for the police anywhere to get to a point like we are at today, where we can announce arrests and charges being laid.”

stories.title: Memorial ride planned for motorcyclist killed in city's northwest end
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 8:19 PM | Last Updated: 21 hours ago
stories.author: Andrew Lupton
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 8:19 PM | Last Updated: October 2
A London motorcycle club will hold a group ride Saturday in honour of one of their members killed in a collision in late September.
Steven Steinsland, 36, died Sept. 21 when his motorcycle and another vehicle collided at the intersection of
Sarnia Road and Castlegrove Boulevard in northwest London.
Steinsland was a member of

London Free Riders group. On Saturday about a hundred riders are expected to gather at noon at the Tim Hortons on Admiral Drive at Veterans Memorial Parkway. From there they will ride together to a memorial set up in
Steinsland's honour at Sarnia and Castlegrove.
His mother Kim Davies told CBC News Steinsland's death has been a huge blow to the wide group of people who knew him.
"He was larger than life, helped everybody, loved his friends and his family," she said. "It's overwhelming how many people knew him and loved him."
His father Mark Steinsland said Steven had an extended group of friends, including many who worked with him at Labatt brewery.
"It's an amazing group of people, they liked to have fun and help people," he said.

Davies said Steven "would be blown away" by the idea of a group ride. Riders are asked to gather in the Tim Hortons parking lot starting at noon with kickstands up at 1 p.m. The ride will be pushed to Sunday in the event of rain.
According to a memorial notice posted online , a celebration of life for Steve will be held at a later date.

His mother Kim Davies told CBC News Steinsland's death has been a huge blow to the wide group of people who knew him.

"He was larger than life, helped everybody, loved his friends and his family," she said. "It's overwhelming how many people knew him and loved him."

His father Mark Steinsland said Steven had an extended group of friends, including many who worked with him at Labatt brewery.

"It's an amazing group of people, they liked to have fun and help people," he said.

Davies said Steven "would be blown away" by the idea of a group ride. Riders are asked to gather in the Tim Hortons parking lot starting at noon with kickstands up at 1 p.m. The ride will be pushed to Sunday in the event of rain.

According to a memorial notice posted online , a celebration of life for Steve will be held at a later date.

stories.title: 2 injured in Cnrl gas plant fire east of Calgary; 1 in critical condition
stories.summary: Stars air ambulance said a man in his 70s was transported from the gas plant, about 88 kilometres east of Calgary, to hospital in critical condition.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted October 2, 2026 4:04 pm

Two people were injured in a gas plant fire in southern Alberta on Friday.

A spokesperson for STARS air ambulance said a man in his 70s was transported from the plant, about 88 kilometres east of Calgary, to hospital. He was listed in critical condition.

Wheatland County Fire Services responded to the fire at the Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. facility at 5:30 a.m.

The blaze was later declared under control.

Fire crews said the surrounding area was evacuated as a precaution.

There were no details about the condition of the second person injured.

— More to come…

stories.title: Retailers face tougher search for space as construction drops to 10-year low: JLL
stories.summary: Toronto - Store owners might be having a harder time finding rental property as the amount of retail space under construction in major Canadian markets dropped to its lowest level in a decade.
stories.author: Tara Deschamps The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Store owners might be having a harder time finding rental properties as the amount of retail space under construction in major Canadian markets dropped to its lowest level in a decade.

Retail construction starts amounted to 1.5 million square feet in the first half of this year, commercial real estate firm JLL said in a new report.

That was down from 2.7 million square feet a year prior and 5.3 million square feet in the first half of 2016.

The previous low during the decade came in 2023, when retail construction starts totalled 1.9 million square feet.

Jll’s senior vice-president of retail Paul Ferreira attributed the drop in starts to rising building costs, the increasing redevelopment of existing retail space, particularly in malls, and the cancellation of some residential projects that would have had stores on the ground floor.

Ferreira said these factors have left some businesses with fewer rental options.

“Retailers that want to grow are finding it more challenging today to find space than they would have five or 10 years ago,” he said Friday. “It means that they have to adapt their formats to the kind of space that is becoming available.”

Adding to the challenge are low vacancy rates across most categories of retail space.

Leasing has also declined, the company said.

That’s because “first and foremost, there isn’t space to move into or some of the larger blocks of space that are available have more homework to be done,” Ferreira said.

“Supply is tough to deliver ... so I think landlords who do have the supply are being much more careful in how they are merchandising the space they have and making their long-term decisions.”

Many of them have their eye on supermarkets, he said. On the heels of the COVID-19 pandemic, grocers are seen as more stable tenants because they didn’t have to temporarily close like other businesses when the economy shut down.

They also drive weekly visits from customers and because they sell essential items, are resilient in the face of inflation and other economic swings.

Plus, other tenants like pharmacies, banks and businesses providing personal services always like to be near a grocer, helping landlords with vacancies, Ferreira said.

Jll’s research found that 96 per cent of new properties built since 2022 in what it calls the “daily needs” category are being anchored by grocery tenants, up from 74 per cent between 2016 and 2021.

Grocers had the third highest number of new opening announcements in the first half of this year.

Supermarkets trailed dining establishments, which made up 33 per cent of the opening announcements, and apparel and accessories retailers, which sat at 26 per cent, in Jll’s analysis.

Ferreira suspects restaurants are dominating openings because there’s still an appetite to dine out after the COVID-19 pandemic and because people are being lured in by new concepts and brands that have moved into major Canadian markets.

“We’ve seen a lot of growth in quick-service restaurants and fast casual restaurants ... but I don’t know how sustainable continued growth in those sectors are,” he said.

“As the consumer gets challenged for how much they can eat out of home, I think we’ll start to see the market respond to that.”

stories.title: Fredericton chief says police are making progress since collapse of two murder trials
stories.summary: The chief of police in Fredericton says the force has made significant changes after an investigation into an error that forced the Crown to abandon two murder trials last year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The chief of police in Fredericton says the force has made significant changes after an investigation into an error that forced the Crown to abandon two murder trials last year.

Gary Forward told a municipal public safety committee meeting Thursday that the police force had hired staff, introduced new training and implemented better oversight measures.

The moves were in line with 19 recommendations made by Ontario lawyer Ian D. Scott, as part of his review of the cases.

Scott released his report late last year, saying an “insurmountable evidentiary issue” brought both cases to an end, though he included few details, citing the Canada Evidence Act.

1:59 Fredericton police ‘error’ forced homicide cases to be stayed, report can’t disclose why

Forward said the police force has implemented 10 of Scott’s recommendations, and it is on track to complete all 19 by June of next year.

The collapse of the trials before they began in the Court of King’s Bench meant no one was convicted for the murders of 41-year-old Corey Christopher Markey, originally from Woodstock, N.B., and 27-year-old Brandon Patrick Donelan of Fredericton.

On Dec. 21, 2021, Markey was shot on Paul Street in Sitansisk First Nation, ON the north side of the Saint John River in Fredericton. He died in hospital eight days later.

Donelan was reported missing in January 2022, and his body was found in a wooded area off a snowmobile trail northeast of Fredericton on March 31, 2022.

The Fredericton Police Force led the investigation into Markey’s death, and the RCMP investigated Donelan’s killing.

Scott’s report made it clear the mistake made by the municipal police force prompted the Crown to scuttle both cases.

Forward said the municipal police force has begun discussions with other New Brunswick police forces to explore whether a provincial investigative unit for homicides could work, as per Scott’s recommendations.

He said he would provide another update to the city early next year.

stories.title: The next Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit goes out on Monday
stories.summary: Another Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit payment for the fiscal year, and the last of 2026, will arrive in bank accounts and mail boxes of qualifying Canadians as of Monday.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The second Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (Cgeb) payment for the fiscal year, and the last of 2026, will arrive in bank accounts and mailboxes of qualifying Canadians as of Monday.

The benefit replaced the former GST credit in July of this year, and featured a bigger payment from the federal government designed to help millions of low and modest-income households keep up with the heightened cost of living , including to buy food and other essentials.

Payments are issued by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) every quarter, or every three months in a year, and are tax-free.

The final payment for this year is scheduled for Oct. 5.

Here’s how to know if you qualify and how much you could receive.

In order to qualify for the Cgeb, there are two foundational requirements that must first be met.

First, one must be a resident of Canada for tax purposes both in the month before the CRA makes a payment and at the start of the month when a payment is made.

For the payment expected on Monday, this means a recipient must have met the first qualification both in September and as of Wednesday, Oct. 1.

Get expert insights, Q&A on markets, housing, inflation, and personal finance information delivered to you every Saturday.

Second, recipients must also be at least 19 years of age, unless they have (or had) a spouse or common-law partner, or are (or were) a parent and live (or lived) with your child.

Once these two qualifications are met, the CRA will determine eligibility of payments and how much they will be based mostly on their declared incomes.

Starting next year, for these individuals and households with lower incomes and simple tax situations. When these changes were announced last year, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said it will “ensure they receive government benefits they qualify for, such as the GST/HST credit [now the Cgeb], the Canada child benefit, the Canada Disability Benefit.”

If an individual or household’s declared income is below the maximum income threshold, they typically will qualify for Cgeb payments.

The 2025 maximum annual income level thresholds for a single person without children and single-parent families are as follows.

With no children – $60,012

With one child – $68,912

With two children – $73,592

With three children – $78,272

With four children or more – $82,952

For married or common-law individuals to receive Cgeb payments, the combined maximum income thresholds for the 2025 tax year are as follows.

With no children – $64,232

With one child – $68,912

With two children – $73,592

With three children – $78,272

With four children or more – $82,952

The CRA says parents who are in a shared custody situation May be eligible for half of the Cgeb payment for that child.

The agency also says it will only send out notices to individuals and families if they are entitled to receive the Cgeb, either electronically through their online accounts, or by mail if they are not registered for CRA services online.

2:12 Feds extend gas tax break into 2027

The amount one can receive for Cgeb payments varies greatly depending on incomes and whether someone is single, married or in a common-law relationship, and if they have children.

The payment amounts are also updated every July, meaning the current payment cycle runs from July 2026 and June 2027, making the Oct. 5 payment the second of this cycle.

Some examples of payment amounts for qualifying recipients of the Cgeb are as follows.

If a single individual with no children has a declared 2025 income of $11,564, they May receive up to $445 in the period between July 2026 and June 2027. Over the course of four quarterly payments, that works out to $111.25 each — including on Monday.

If a single individual with no children has a declared 2025 income of $55,000, the payment amount totals $250.60 over four payments. That works out to $62.65 per Cgeb payment.

If a single individual has two children and a declared income in 2025 of $45,000 or less, they could receive $1,358 over four payments. That means four payments of $339.50, including on Monday.

paragraphs: The second Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (Cgeb) payment for the fiscal year, and the last of 2026, will arrive in bank accounts and mailboxes of qualifying Canadians as of Monday.

The benefit replaced the former GST credit in July of this year, and featured a bigger payment from the federal government designed to help millions of low and modest-income households keep up with the heightened cost of living , including to buy food and other essentials.
Payments are issued by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) every quarter, or every three months in a year, and are tax-free.
The final payment for this year is scheduled for Oct. 5.
Here’s how to know if you qualify and how much you could receive.
In order to qualify for the Cgeb, there are two foundational requirements that must first be met.
First, one must be a resident of Canada for tax purposes both in the month before the CRA makes a payment and at the start of the month when a payment is made.
For the payment expected on Monday, this means a recipient must have met the first qualification both in September and as of Wednesday, Oct. 1.

Second, recipients must also be at least 19 years of age, unless they have (or had) a spouse or common-law partner, or are (or were) a parent and live (or lived) with your child.
Once these two qualifications are met, the CRA will determine eligibility of payments and how much they will be based mostly on their declared incomes.

Starting next year, for these individuals and households with lower incomes and simple tax situations. When these changes were announced last year, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said it will “ensure they receive government benefits they qualify for, such as the GST/HST credit [now the Cgeb], the Canada child benefit, the Canada Disability Benefit.”
If an individual or household’s declared income is below the maximum income threshold, they typically will qualify for Cgeb payments.

With two children – $73,592
With three children – $78,272

With no children – $64,232

stories.title: Senators have doubled overseas trips with costs to taxpayers jumping 88%, according to CTF
stories.summary: Why is "an unelected senator should be travelling anywhere outside of the country on (the) taxpayers’ dime,” says Ctf's Franco Terrazzano.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Canadian senators are costing taxpayers extensive amounts for overseas trips even though Members of Parliament are regularly representing Canada on the same trips, according to the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.

A national overview of province-by-province senator overseas travel , released by the CTF this week, states that international trips undertaken between Jan. 16, 2023 and March 17, 2026 by 65 senators cost Canadian taxpayers $1,850,420. Overall, says the CTF, senators have nearly doubled their international travel spending in the last two years, with the costs climbing 88 per cent from $391,095 in 2023 to $736,165 in 2025, according to its analysis of parliamentary financial disclosures.

The CTF takes the position that senators are unelected and as such should not be travelling anywhere outside of the country on the taxpayers’ tab. “Nobody votes for senators so these people represent exactly nobody,” said Kris Sims, spokesperson for the Canadian Taxpayers Federation in an email to National Post.

Ontario Senator Salma Ataullahjan ‘s international travel topped the CTF list, totalling $131,706 between January 2023 and March 2026 for 14 overseas trips. The CTF says Ataullahjan travelled to Mozambique, Botswana, Switzerland twice, Uzbekistan, the United States, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Angola, Costa Rica, Ghana, the Dominican Republic, Chile, Bahrain, Senegal and Cabo Verde.

Otherwise, looking at the Ctf’s top Senate travellers on a per province basis across the rest of the country, Nova Scotia Senator Michael MacDonald took 17 trips abroad costing $85,000. B.C. Senator Margo Greenwood went on 11 trips abroad costing more than $80,000, then P.E.I. Senator Percy Downe ($67,000), New Brunswick Senator René Cormier ($64,000), Manitoba Senator Gigi Osler ($61,000), former Saskatchewan Senator Brent Cotter ($19,000) and on the lower end, Alberta Senator Scott Tannas ($10,795). (Terrazzo told National Post in an email that the organization is holding off on a report about Quebec senators until after that province’s election on Monday.)

Ataullahjan’s office responded to National Post with an emailed statement on Thursday, noting that the Ctf’s “characterization of these expenses as having been incurred or billed by the Senator (is) not accurate. These are costs incurred by Parliament and administered by parliamentary personnel in the execution of parliamentary association responsibilities.”

Senate speaker spent close to $1M on 'courtesy calls' and other foreign travel, Taxpayers Federation finds

Alcohol, mini-golf helped double Canadian Senate's hospitality bill since 2019, says taxpayers group

The statement said that the parliamentarians, which includes both MPs and senators, “selected to participate in these activities do not control or authorize these expenses.”

Further, the statement noted that “Senate expense rules do not permit Senators to undertake international travel in their capacity as Senators. Senators travel internationally when selected to do so in their capacity as members of a parliamentary association or, ON rare occasions, a committee.”

Sims said the “senators are absolutely spending taxpayers’ money on international trips, regardless of what label is being put on their travelling entourage. If senators are upset by being held accountable for this expenditure of taxpayers’ money, they can refuse to go on any international trips.”

The CTF analysis points out that taxpayers paid $173,041 for seven trips by senators to be “observers” to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (Pace), where Canada is not a member . Therefore, senators travelled to meetings as observers, where they could only speak with permission. Sometimes, says the CTF, the senators simply submitted written speeches instead of participating in the proceedings. Further, Pace sessions are live-streamed and viewable from anywhere in the world. Meanwhile, Canadian MPs were also at these sessions representing Canada.

Some senators incurred costs for international trips to attend meetings that were also held by videoconference, according to the CTF. For example, it says Manitoba Senator Gigi Osler went to New York in 2023 and 2024 to attend parliamentary meetings. During the 2023 trip, Osler discussed the benefits of hybrid parliamentary sittings. The same parliamentary group regularly holds meetings and workshops by videoconference . Osler went in person both times, costing taxpayers $4,677.

Nova Scotia Senator Michael MacDonald cost taxpayers $2,869 to attend the Canadian Embassy’s Trump inauguration event, even though Parliament sent three MPs. The delegation watched the proceedings from the Canadian embassy on a live-stream, says the CTF.

Former Saskatchewan senator Brent Cotter cost taxpayers $7,694 for a six-day European trip, though Parliament also sent three elected MPs. Cotter and the delegation arrived in Tallinn, Estonia, ON a Sunday when no officials “ were available ” to meet with them, notes the CTF. So they visit ed “important landmarks in the city.”

Senators René Cormier, Percy Downe and Michael MacDonald went on a $76,236 trip to Argentina and Uruguay, along with elected MP. Parliament did not release a report on the trip, says the CTF. However, it says Argentinian records identify MP Richard Cannings as speaking on behalf of the Canadian delegation during a meeting with Argentine lawmakers. No remarks were attributed to any of the senators, according to CTF.

Ataullahjan cost taxpayers $12,887 for a trip to Cabo Verde and Senegal. Four other senators, René Cormier, Amina Gerba, Manuelle Oudar and Rebecca Patterson, went on the same trip. The whole delegation cost $95,795 . Canada only exports about $2.4 million worth of goods annually to Cabo Verde, says the CTF.

Claudine Courtois, director of Parliamentary Affairs for Senator Wells, says that parliamentary diplomacy is an increasingly important dimension of Canada’s international relations. Regarding Wells’ European travel, Courtois points out that he is the elected vice president of the Canada-Europe Interparliamentary Association, and “regularly represents Canada in a number of international fora, including the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe … and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, and he regularly speaks on issues important to Canada.”

With regard to speaking and submitting speeches to Pace she adds that “delegates register to speak and there is a finite time allotted for the rapporteurs, respondents and delegates on each of the given topics. If the time for the full debate expires before all speakers have an opportunity to speak, their speeches are registered and are submitted for the record. Speeches will not be registered unless the delegate is in the chamber, so it’s inadmissible if the delegate doesn’t attend.”

Courtois also says that Wells “recognizes the responsibility that comes with the expenditure of public funds and takes that responsibility seriously.”

Tony Spears, a Senate spokesperson, said the travel cited by the CTF relates to parliamentary associations, which include both senators and MPs and has remained stable over the past five fiscal years.

“Strong international relationships have rarely mattered more,” he said in a prepared statement.

stories.title: Man charged in London Hydro data breach: LPS
stories.summary: The London Police Service has charged a man in connection with a London Hydro data breach.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The London Police Service has charged a man in connection with a London Hydro data breach. On June 19, police received a report from London Hydro about a suspected compromise of its customer information. Investigators said between June 5 and June 17, a suspect accessed customer accounts unauthorized, gaining customer information.

The LPS executed a search warrant a home on Aug. 13, part of investigation efforts. Several devices were seized and examined. Police said they found evidence that linked the suspect to the data breach. A 40-year-old man of London has been charged with fraudulently obtaining any computer service and mischief over $5,000.

Given the complexity of cases like this, charges are not commonly laid. Today’s announcement speaks to the expertise, skill and dedication of our police partners.”

stories.title: Alberta Mountie found not guilty of using database to help Rwanda
stories.summary: RCMP Const. Eli Ndatuje was charged under the Criminal Code and the Security of Information Act for alleged illegal use of the police database but has been found not guilty.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
An Alberta Mountie accused of using a police database to help the country of Rwanda was found not guilty Friday of several charges.

Const. Eli Ndatuje was arrested following an extensive investigation dubbed “Operation Salt Mine,” involving wiretaps and up to 30 officers and civilian staffers.

Ndatuje admitted to using the database to check up on a missing person but said he didn’t pass the information on.

He called it a dumb move but said he wasn’t a spy or a traitor.

Court of King’s Bench Justice Jason Wilkins agreed.

“The effort put into that investigation was not lacking, but the resulting evidence is,” he said.

However, the judge said it’s clear why the RCMP would do a thorough investigation.

“In recent years, Canada has seen a significant increase in the frequencies, sophistication and illegality of foreign interference,” Wilkins said.

“The government of Canada is compelled to respond.”

Ndatuje faced three charges — under the Criminal Code and the Security of Information Act — for the alleged illegal use of the database to assist the High Commission of Rwanda in Ottawa.

At trial, court heard the 39-year-old Ndatuje and his family fled war-torn Uganda and moved to Ottawa when he was a teen.

He was arrested in February 2024 by the RCMP’s federal policing team. It identified Rwanda as the alleged “foreign actor” in the case.

Ndatuje’s lawyer, Robb Beeman, told the trial that his client had been in touch twice with the Rwandan High Commission, and both times were for innocent purposes.

The first time, Beeman said, was in April 2022. He said it was for Ndatuje to clear up confusion over his wife’s travel documents.

On the second occasion, the lawyer said, Ndatuje was contacted by a friend at the Rwandan High Commission who was worried about the disappearance of a housekeeper working at the Ottawa residence of the Rwandan ambassador.

Ndatuje, on his own initiative, checked the police database to see if anyone had reported the housekeeper missing, court heard. There was no record of the housekeeper being missing, and the employee was later found unharmed.

“(Ndatuje) did the search because he cared about a missing person,” Beeman told the trial.

“One would hope that every police officer in this country would share that attitude.”

— More to come…

stories.title: Indigenous newcomer brings her ancestors teachings to Huron County community
stories.summary: Cory Bilyea May be relatively new to North Huron, but she’s making her mark, leading a full week of events, marking Truth and Reconciliation.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Cory Bilyea May be relatively new to North Huron, but she’s making her mark, leading a full week of events, marking Truth and Reconciliation.

“I’m actually really overwhelmed. I am so humbled to see so many youths come out to honor Indigenous people, to honor residential school survivors, and those that didn’t make it home,” said the Wingham area resident.

Bilyea, who just moved to the Wingham area a few years ago to work for the local newspaper, is amongst a small handful of North Huron residents, with Indigenous heritage.

As such, in previous years, the community marked Truth and Reconciliation Day with a small ceremony, but Bilyea has brought Indigenous authors and speakers to town for a week full of events to share her Indigenous culture with the greater community.

“When I started writing my columns about Truth and Reconciliation, I found that the community at large here in North Huron was really receptive, and really curious to know the truth, and were not afraid to ask the hard questions,” she said.

Bilyea says she is proud of her ancestry and hopes other First Nations people in small towns across Canada, step forward to share their heritage, with their neighbours.

“It’s exciting to know that minds are changing. People are starting to accept the truth, learn the truth, and want to reconcile, and want to stand together. We don’t want people to feel guilty. We want people to recognize the truth and honour us as First Nations. We’ve been here since time immemorial,” she said.

Bilyea says she already has ideas for next year’s Truth and Reconciliation week, and even throughout the year, to share her indigenous culture, with her community.

We want people to recognize the truth and honour us as First Nations. We’ve been here since time immemorial,” she said.
Bilyea says she already has ideas for next year’s Truth and Reconciliation week, and even throughout the year, to share her indigenous culture, with her community.

stories.title: Cooler air arrives in London area after warm spell
stories.summary: After a recent period of above-seasonal warmth and overnight rain, cooler air is coming to London, Ont.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner, Gary Archibald
stories.content:
After a recent period of above-seasonal warmth and overnight rain, cooler air is coming to London, Ont.

CTV meteorologist Gary Archibald says to expect a significant temperature swing over the next few days.

The Environment Canada forecast predicts a mix of sun and cloud with a daytime high of approximately 18C on Friday. Overnight, temperatures will drop to around 9-11C. The recent band of rain is sliding south and east, making way for clearer conditions and cooler northerly air.

Friday night, a ridge of high pressure will bring clear skies, offering a beautiful starry night. Winds will be calm or light from the north.

Saturday will start cool, with temperatures around 5C at 8 a.m., accompanied by light winds from the north-northeast. The day is forecast to be mostly sunny, with a projected daytime high of 18C.

Looking ahead to the weekend and early next week for the London area, expect fluctuating temperatures and a mix of fair weather and showers. Lows will be in the single digits, potentially dipping near freezing by Tuesday and Wednesday across much of Southern Ontario.

stories.title: Assault charges laid in Malahide Township
stories.summary: Elgin OPP have laid assault charges against a Niagara Falls resident after an incident in Malahide Township.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Elgin OPP have laid assault charges against a Niagara Falls resident after an incident in Malahide Township.

On Aug. 31, OPP launched an investigation after altercations were reported at an address on Hacienda Road between Aug. 27 and Aug. 28.

Police arrested a 21-year-old Niagara Falls man on Sept. 18. He was charged with three counts of assault causing bodily harm.

No further information was released and police said nothing more will be released as it is before the courts.

stories.title: 2 men charged in August northeast London shooting, police say
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 6:20 PM | Last Updated: October 2
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 6:20 PM | Last Updated: October 2
No injuries reported in Aug. 9 incident near Kipps Lane and Arbour Glen Crescent
Two London men are facing charges in connection with a previously unreported shooting nearly two months ago in the city's Kipps Lane neighbourhood, London police said Friday.

No one was hurt in the Aug. 9, 2026 incident, which happened around 12:30 a.m. near Kipps Lane and Arbour Glen Crescent, but police said a vehicle leaving the area was hit by gunfire and cartridge casings were found at the scene. It's unclear whether the vehicle was targeted.

Two suspects were determined to have discharged firearms and were seen fleeing on foot before officers arrived. Police arrested both late last month after what they said was an "extensive investigation."

The accused, a 19-year-old man and a 20-year-old man, both from London, have been jointly charged with discharging a firearm in a reckless manner and possessing a restricted or prohibited firearm while knowingly not holding a licence, police said.
The 20-year-old also faces one count of possessing a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking, police said.
Few other details about the incident itself have been released.
Police said their investigation is ongoing and have appealed for witnesses or residents who May have dash or surveillance camera video to come forward.
It brings the number of shootings in the city this year to at least 12, following Tuesday's shooting at a Richmond Row apartment building that left
Robert Rico Rivard, 48, dead. Mohamed Abdel Aziz Soumahoro, 21, of Laval, Que., faces a second-degree murder count and other charges.

stories.title: Manitoba park trail where boys drowned reopens with safety upgrades
stories.summary: A trail in a Manitoba park has reopened with safety upgrades after two boys who were swept into fast-moving rapids and drowned.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted October 2, 2026 2:19 pm

A trail in a Manitoba park has reopened with safety upgrades after two boys who were swept into fast-moving rapids and drowned.

The Sturgeon Falls trail in Whiteshell Provincial Park closed in July, when Aaron Au Ramirez, 13, and his 10-year-old brother, Maximo Au Ramirez, disappeared into Nutimik Lake.

Their bodies were later recovered by searchers.

The Manitoba government says it has installed fencing in viewing areas to keep the public from hazardous terrain.

It has also updated signage to warn visitors about drowning risks and strong currents, and it has created a new portage path for canoeists and kayakers.

Mike Moyes, the environment and climate change minister, says the upgrades were based off of feedback from families, community members and local business owners.

Allison Baker-Thiessen, owner of the Nutimik Lodge, says the changes will help protect Manitobans and provide peace of mind for visitors.

stories.title: Keeping the Cree language alive in Saskatchewan
stories.summary: With language being stripped away from students during residential schools, people are now left finding new ways to keep the Cree and Dene language alive.
stories.author: Payton Zillich
stories.content:
The Cree language is more than just a means to communicate. It represents culture, spirituality, and identity, something stripped away from hundreds of Indigenous peoples during their time at residential schools. Nevertheless, work is still being done to ensure the next generation knows how to speak their language.

One way is through the hard work and efforts of elders and Indigenous leaders, passing language, stories and the significance of using your native tongue. Events like the Keep Our Language Alive (Kola) conference allows for everyone to workshop these ideals under the same roof.

“The people are lost, those people have lost their way, (and) they’ve lost their cultural identity,” shares Milton Tootoosis, the founder of the Kola convention.

This year, the convention was completely sold out.

“It’s absolutely dynamic, very inspiring because I spend most of my time engulfed in the mainstream dominant culture which is the English language here in Saskatchewan of course,” says Tootoosis.

A big theme highlighted by the speakers this year was focusing on delivering the language to the youth. With talks on how to further incorporate Cree in institutions, school and technology.

“Teach our children the value of learning Cree or the value of learning Dene. The most important thing is that (we) keep language alive,” adds Buckley Belanger, Secretary of State for Rural Development and Kola Speaker.

With modern day technology at our fingertips, learning a new language is easier than ever. This, inspiring one Cree teacher to create an app to teach his students how to say phrases in Cree.

“They are saying, ‘can we go to the gym?’ and they have asked in Cree. And I said, ‘well if you ask me in Cree, I’ll say yes’,” explains Vernon Lewis, creator of the How do you say this in Cree app .

The app, inspired by Lewis’ granddaughter is simple to use. Just type in a word or phrase and it will show how to say it in Cree. Lewis added the use of phrases, so users actually learn how to use the language, not just random words.

“I wanted to make sure that it wasn’t a dictionary. You can go online anywhere and look up the word dog,” explains Lewis. “But now that you know the word, the word for dog, how do you use that word in a phrase? ‘Do you see that dog?’ is the phrase that would be more common or ‘don’t go close to that dog’.”

The work to restore the Cree and Dene language to the not end here. There is a push to encourage more politicians and government officials to learn the language. With elders sharing no matter who you are or where you come from, you are more than welcome to ask them more about the Cree language.

“We learn a lot from the language about our identity, our purpose and our spirituality. I think if other people want to join our spirituality and our efforts to promote good humanity, (then) they are more than welcome,” adds Sturgeon Lake elder Willie Ermine.

Watch the video above to see footage from the Kola convention.

stories.title: 'Disturbing': Belleville, Ont., synagogue receives antisemitic flyers after shooting
stories.summary: Antisemitic flyers were distributed this week to a Belleville, Ont., synagogue targeted in a shooting last month as well as the surrounding neighbourhoods, the synagogue’s president said Friday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Antisemitic flyers were distributed this week to a Belleville, Ont., synagogue targeted in a shooting last month as well as the surrounding neighbourhoods, the synagogue’s president said Friday.

Norman Weddum said he woke up Thursday morning to find four different flyers blaming Jewish people “for everything under the sun” had been distributed overnight to the Sons of Jacob synagogue and throughout the city’s east end.

“The number of flyers that were distributed and posted, it couldn’t have been done by one person,” he said.

Police said they’re aware of the flyers and are “actively investigating.”

Weddum said the incident is particularly “disturbing” in the wake of the Sept. 20 attack police have described as a thwarted mass killing of Jewish worshippers at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

Police have said the shooter, 29-year-old Sean Ward, had multiple guns, large amounts of ammunition, gasoline and the motive to carry out an extended attack when he opened fire on an officer stationed outside the synagogue.

Const. Jeff Smith suffered multiple gunshot wounds but “stayed engaged” with the shooter and soon after, a second officer arrived and joined the shootout, they said.

No one inside the synagogue was hurt but Smith is expected to undergo multiple surgeries. Ward was fatally injured and died in hospital the next day.

The Canadian Armed Forces have since said that Ward was a former soldier who served for about five years before he was released from the military at the rank of corporal in 2022.

The shooting was widely condemned by politicians and prompted synagogues and Jewish institutions elsewhere to review their security measures.

Weddum said Sons of Jacob has held some services since the attack and will hold another Friday evening.

“We’re trying to get people back into the building, and I think it’s helping,” he said in a phone interview Friday.

Norman Weddum said he woke up Thursday morning to find four different flyers blaming Jewish people “for everything under the sun” had been distributed overnight to the Sons of Jacob synagogue and throughout the city’s east end.
“The number of flyers that were distributed and posted, it couldn’t have been done by one person,” he said.
Police said they’re aware of the flyers and are “actively investigating.”

stories.title: Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime admits to using AI to write book
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec Conservative Party Leader Éric Duhaime admitted to using artificial intelligence to write his latest book.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec Conservative Party Leader Éric Duhaime admitted to using artificial intelligence to write his latest book.

Duhaime told reporters Friday morning that he used AI as “a tool among others” to write the book, titled Destination Autonomie, which was published in April.

Duhaime, who previously worked as a columnist and radio host, said he used AI to structure his thoughts and that the ideas in the book are all his.

“AI is important to us. It’s part of reality. That said, it has to be done under human supervision. And that’s exactly what happened,” Duhaime said.

Using the AI-detection software Pangram, Quebecor media outlets reported on Thursday that 62 per cent of the book was machine-generated.

The introduction, written by Conservative candidate Maïté Blanchette-Vézina, was reported to have been completely AI-generated. Blanchette-Vézina had previously crossed the floor to join Duhaime’s party after being shuffled out of former premier François Legault’s Coalition Avenir Québec cabinet.

Duhaime’s rivals on the campaign trail made light of the revelation about his book. Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Liberal Leader Charles Milliard both joked about whether Duhaime used AI to generate his party’s platform.

Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette also took a political jab at Duhaime, saying she now understands how he found time to write a book as a politician. Meanwhile, Québec solidaire posted a joke about Duhaime on social media featuring co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal looking through a telescope, saying she was searching for sections of his book that were written by humans.

Duhaime has supported the use of AI throughout his campaign, saying it could be useful to cut bureaucracy.

He also admitted on Friday to using AI in his campaign materials, including to generate charts, a table of contents and the layout of the party’s financial framework.

“Social progress has been achieved thanks to technology, not in spite of it. So, for us, it was a step forward for society, not a step backward,” he said, questioned on the ethics of his use of AI.

In his book, Duhaime reflects on how Quebec can gain more autonomy within the Canadian Confederation.

Duhaime has published four other books. He came out as gay in his 2017 book, titled La fin de l’homosexualité et le dernier gay (“The end of homosexuality and the last gay man” in French).

He has also written books critical of labour unions, baby boomers and the monopoly of Quebec’s government-owned liquor corporation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Extortions, fire bombings, shootings lead to arrest of 5 foreign nationals, RCMP say
stories.summary: Langley - Five foreign nationals are in police custody and face a string of charges arising out of an RCMP investigation into extortion of members of British Columbia's South Asian community.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Langley - Five foreign nationals are in police custody and face a string of charges arising out of an RCMP extortion investigation involving members of British Columbia’s South Asian community.

Supt. Harm Dosange, with the Langley RCMP, said Friday that the investigation into arsons, shootings and extortions started in June 2025 when owners of an auto dealership reached out to police.

The criminals’ demands were followed up by shootings and arsons in Langley and neighbouring Surrey, B.C., he said.

Dosange said it was a long and difficult case for investigators as they worked across Canada and internationally.

“They faced numerous daunting challenges and some unprecedented things we have not seen before,” he said, although he wouldn’t elaborate as the case is before the courts.

The five accused are in their 20s and face a variety of charges, including extortion, damaging property by fire explosion and throwing an explosive substance, along with numerous drug and firearms allegations.

“We obtained evidence identifying additional suspects, evidence that supports other extortion-related offences throughout Western Canada,” Dosange said during a news conference.

One of the accused was arrested getting off a plane in Toronto from India, police said.

Investigators “determined that it was in the public interest to have him appear before the courts in Canada,” police said in a news release.

The RCMP said investigators worked with immigration and border services officials as well as international police to facilitate a “controlled operation” to allow the suspect to enter Canada in order to arrest him.

The arrests are among a series of cases being investigated by police after a provincewide extortion task force was launched last year, while police in Surrey and Abbotsford also diverted officers to the cases.

The City of Surrey set up a $250,000 reward for convictions, while the Surrey Police Service started keeping statistics for the year.

From Jan. 1 to Sept. 28, the department has had 142 reported extortions, 21 related shots-fired cases, three arsons and 76 victims, although 39 of them are repeated victims.

The extortionists are aiming their threats at business owners and those in the South Asian community.

Chief Supt. Duncan Pound with B.C.‘s extortion task force said the trial for those accused will hear if the India-based Lawrence Bishnoi gang is involved.

“I will say there are lots of these investigations where we’ve seen that the perpetrators will allege that they’re connected to high-profile gangs to try and increase the level of intimidation,” he said.

It’s also a way to make money, he noted.

The Lawrence Bishnoi gang has been labelled a terrorist entity in Canada. Bishnoi has been accused of running his operation while in prison in India.

Both Dosange and Pound say the victims’ courage to come to police made the difference in their investigation.

“Truly, without really timely reporting and the courage to come forward and provide as many details as they can, it’s very difficult for the police anywhere to get to a point like we are at today, where we can announce arrests and charges being laid.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Expert insight: How Canada and the U.S. entered a cycle of hostility and how they can break it
stories.summary: Researchers explain how Canada-U.S. relations entered a cycle of hostility and what could help Canadians and Americans break it.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
For decades, the relationship between Canadians and Americans was defined by proximity, economic interdependence and a shared sense of partnership.

Millions of jobs in both countries depended on bilateral trade, and the two countries have supported each other as key allies and defence partners. Despite occasional disagreements, the relationship was treated as a stable feature of North American life.

Since Donald Trump returned to office as president of the United States in January 2025, that assumption has changed. Trade disputes and escalating political tensions have transformed how many Canadians view their southern neighbour.

Today, 48 per cent of Canadians have an unfavourable view of Americans, with many saying that Canada should approach the U.S. with caution (29 per cent), as a potential threat (36 per cent) or as an enemy (six per cent).

How did a relationship built on decades of partnership reach this point, and where does it go from here?

The 10-reason cycle of hate, developed by our team of researchers at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research BMB (Boundaries, Membership and Belonging) Program, helps explain why hostility toward Americans flared so quickly in Canada, and why it has the potential to become long lasting.

The cycle of hate shows how social, political and historical conditions can reinforce hostility between groups over time. (Canadian Institute for Advanced Research BMB Program), CC BY-NC

Hate is not simply a spontaneous emotion that emerges within individuals. It develops through a combination of social, political and historical conditions. These conditions can be created, fuelled and mobilized by people and institutions.

The cycle has four interconnected components: the current context, a call to arms, justification and history. Once the cycle of hate is initiated, the four components continually reinforce each other, making hostility more difficult to reverse.

The current state of Canada-U.S. relations contains many of the conditions that can fuel hostility: perceived threats to identity and shared norms, competition and loss, a lack of control and uncertainty.

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state and circulated maps showing Canada covered by the American flag. He has also referred to the Canadian prime minister as “governor.”

These actions challenge Canada’s status as a sovereign nation and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s position as leader of an independent country. Many Canadians have interpreted these statements as threats to Canadian identity and as violations of diplomatic norms between neighbouring allies.

At the same time, American tariffs have intensified feelings of economic competition and vulnerability. Surveys show Canadians are feeling frustration and anger, as well as anxiety, fear and uncertainty. These feelings can reliably accelerate hatred toward Americans.

When a threatening context emerges, the next stage in the cycle is often a “call to arms.” This occurs when leaders and groups mobilize people around the need to defend themselves against a perceived threat.

In Canada, political leaders have responded to these tensions with the U.S. using language that emphasizes resistance to competition and threat.

Carney has stated that Canada is in a trade war with the United States that was not our choice. “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.”

The hockey phrase “Elbows Up” was introduced by comedian Mike Myers and taken up by Carney as an expression of the need to defend Canada against the American enemy. It was a political strategy that reinforced themes of resilience and resistance.

There have been other examples of resistance, including boycotts of American products and cancellations of travel to the U.S.

Once a call to arms is in place, the next stage in the cycle involves justifying the hostility. Hostility becomes easier to sustain when it is framed as necessary.

Current justifications for anti-American sentiment increasingly rely on moral arguments. Hatred is seen as justified because Canada is defending its sovereignty, values and dignity. The “Buy Canadian” and “Don’t Travel to the U.S.” movements have taken on a patriotic dimension, with resistance framed by some as a civic responsibility.

Canadians have not broadly engaged in dehumanizing Americans. However, the same cannot be said for Americans. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, for example, recently compared Canada to a little yippy dachshund trying to fight with a German Shepherd.

Such comparisons can reinforce perceptions of disrespect and deepen antagonism between groups.

The fourth stage of the cycle is history: the process by which present conflicts become part of a group’s shared identity and collective memory.

Current tensions could become part of a Canadian historical narrative in which the country sees itself as having resisted American pressure.

As former MP and activist Charlie Angus has written:

“We are making history right now. And our grandchildren will hear the stories of how we handled ourselves. They will learn how we stood our ground and defended our lands. They will know what it means to be elbows up in the face of injustice.”

When conflicts become part of collective memory, they can continue shaping attitudes long after the original events have passed.

Some commentators suggest that Canada and the U.S. are now “dug in,” and that worsening public attitudes could prevent a return to the bargaining table.

If the cycle of hate continues, the Canadian public May prefer this outcome. However, being trapped in the cycle and seeing Americans as permanent adversaries is not inevitable.

An important strategy that can help break the cycle of hate is focusing on a shared identity that includes both Canadians and Americans as North American partners who depend on each other for well-being.

This was the dominant way in which many Canadians and Americans viewed their relationship before tariffs and diplomatic tensions changed the conversation.

That shared identity and respect May yet be recovered in the years ahead. But political leaders and the media will need to communicate this inclusive identity and justify the value of Canadian-American co-operation when relations return to a context in which Canada is no longer under attack.Image 2: The Conversation

stories.title: Two London men charged in north-end shooting: LPS
stories.summary: London police have charged two men in connection with a north-end shooting in the city.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
London police have charged two men in connection with a north-end shooting in the city.

On Aug. 9 around 12:30 a.m., police were called with multiple reports of gunfire near Kipps Lane and Arbour Glen Crescent.

Officers said two suspects ran from the area before police arrived on scene.

Through an investigation, they learned two people fired guns. Nobody was hurt, but a vehicle was hit by gunfire. Police recovered multiple cartridge casings.

London police say an extensive investigation led to the arrest of two suspects in late September.

A 19-year-old man and a 20-year-old man were both charged with:

Discharging a firearm in a reckless manner

Possess a restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a license

The 20-year-old was also charged with one count of possession of a schedule one substance for the purpose of trafficking.

“Gunfire in our neighbourhoods is unacceptable. Every time a firearm is discharged in our community, there is the potential for devastating consequences for innocent people,” said Det. Sgt. Micah Bourdeau of the LPS Major Crime Section.

“Those who choose to use firearms in our city should expect our investigators to pursue every available avenue to identify those responsible and bring them before the courts. These arrests are the result of a determined and thorough investigation by our Major Crime investigators.”

The investigation is still ongoing. Anyone who was in the area between 12 a.m. and 12:45 a.m. on Aug. 9, or who has dash cam or security footage of the incident, is asked to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Crime Stoppers can also be contacted online .

stories.title: Palmerston manufacturing company granted $3.9 million to expand
stories.summary: Hammond Manufacturing Company Ltd. in Palmerston has been granted more than $3.9 million for expansion through the Southwestern Ontario Development Fund (Swodf).
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Hammond Manufacturing Company Ltd. in Palmerston has been granted more than $3.9 million for expansion through the Southwestern Ontario Development Fund (Swodf).

Matthew Rae, MPP for Perth-Wellington, announced the grant Friday. It will allow the 97,000 sq. ft. facility to grow to 182,000 sq. ft.

“Our government will be there to support our small businesses across Ontario during this economic trade war, including right here in Perth-Wellington,” said Rae.

“This nearly $4 million investment will support Hammond Manufacturing’s continued growth in Palmerston, helping protect 128 good-paying local jobs and strengthen our local economy.”

The expansion will cost a total of $26,475,000. Hammond Manufacturing says it will increase automation, create a new spot-welding cell, and increase painting capacity. It will also allow the company to buy two punch laser machines, a powder coat paint line, brakes, storage racks, and other equipment.

“The support provided by the government of Ontario has allowed Hammond Manufacturing to accelerate investments that strengthen our manufacturing capabilities and enhance our ability to serve customers across North America,” said Rob Hammond, CEO of Hammond Manufacturing Company Limited.

“These investments are helping us expand our capacity, improve productivity, remain competitive within our industry, and position the company for sustainable long-term growth”

Hammond Manufacturing specializes in the design and manufacturing of electrical and electronic enclosures, server racks and cabinets, outlet strips, small enclosures, and low-voltage electronic transformers.

stories.title: PM Carney to visit Turkiye this month in first for Canadian leader: Reuters
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to visit Turkiye this month to meet President Tayyip Erdogan in what would be the first dedicated bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian leader, four sources with knowledge of the visit said.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to visit Turkiye this month to meet President Tayyip Erdogan in what would be the first dedicated bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian leader, four sources with knowledge of the visit said.

One of the sources said Carney and Erdogan could discuss the free-trade talks they launched on the sidelines of a Nato summit in Ankara in July, as well as potential energy and defense cooperation. Canadian and Turkish trade ministers agreed this week to accelerate the talks ahead of the leaders’ meeting, two sources said.

The visit would mark Carney’s latest break with Canadian diplomatic convention as he seeks to reduce the country’s reliance on the United States, by far its biggest trading partner, after a collapse in trade talks in August.

Carney has vowed to double Canada’s non-U.S. trade over the next decade and has rushed to establish ties with a host of countries, including China and India, with which it had past strains.

He has focused less on human rights than his predecessors to forge ahead, backed by polls showing strong support among Canadians for his efforts to reinforce the economy in the face of U.S. tariffs.

Erdogan, Turkiye’s leader of 23 years — whom rights groups have criticized for a crackdown on the political opposition since 2024 — seeks new markets and collaboration for the regional military power’s burgeoning defense industry. Erdogan says an independent judiciary is probing the opposition and rejects claims it is politically motivated.

Turkiye, an emerging market economy whose biggest trading partner is the European Union, also seeks partnerships and investment in energy, infrastructure and mining.

The sources did not share the dates or agenda of the visit planned later this month.

Carney’s office and Erdogan’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Less focus on rights

Western powers have grown relatively silent on Turkiye’s rights record as it has become a leading defense-industrial power and a bulwark against Russian aggression.

Since last month, a wave of arrests and restrictions has targeted Turkiye’s Lgbtq+ community in a probe the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and some European officials.

No Canadian prime minister is known to have made a standalone bilateral visit to Turkey in recent decades, though they have met Erdogan and other Turkish leaders on the sidelines of multilateral gatherings, including Nato and G20 summits hosted by Turkiye.

Modest bilateral trade

At the Nato leaders’ summit in July, Carney and Erdogan formally launched negotiations for a ‌free-trade agreement.

That month, Turkiye agreed to join Canada’s Defense Security and ‌Resilience Bank as one of 10 founding member nations of Carney’s multilateral “middle powers” bank.

The two countries’ trade ministers met in June and planned to expand cooperation on renewable and nuclear energy, a Canadian government statement said, listing aerospace, defense and security as areas of potential new partnerships.

Turkiye has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis Atrl.TO as well as South Korea’s Korea Electric Power Corporation and China’s State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its second and third nuclear power plants, and Russia’s Rosatom is building its first.

An executive at AtkinsRealis, which holds the exclusive licence for Canadian-designed Candu reactors, told Reuters this year that it anticipates Turkiye will complete an early review of its Candu reactors ​following an information exchange, which May lead to concrete talks for a plant bid.

In a step that helped thaw bilateral ties in 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkiye, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkiye exports to dozens of nations.

Yet bilateral trade is small.

Turkiye accounted for less than 0.3 per cent of Canada’s total merchandise trade in 2025, or C$4.34 billion, compared with C$1 trillion with the U.S., Statistics Canada data shows.

Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkiye, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry.

($1 = 1.4227 Canadian dollars)

(Reporting by Jonathan Spicer, Promit Mukherjee and David Ljunggren; Additional reporting by Huseyin Hayatsever in Ankara; Editing by Rod Nickel)

Since last month, a wave of arrests and restrictions has targeted Turkiye’s Lgbtq+ community in a probe the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and some European officials.

No Canadian prime minister is known to have made a standalone bilateral visit to Turkey in recent decades, though they have met Erdogan and other Turkish leaders on the sidelines of multilateral gatherings, including Nato and G20 summits hosted by Turkiye.
Modest bilateral trade
At the Nato leaders’ summit in July, Carney and Erdogan formally launched negotiations for a ‌free-trade agreement.
That month, Turkiye agreed to join Canada’s Defense Security and ‌Resilience Bank as one of 10 founding member nations of Carney’s multilateral “middle powers” bank.

The two countries’ trade ministers met in June and planned to expand cooperation on renewable and nuclear energy, a Canadian government statement said, listing aerospace, defense and security as areas of potential new partnerships.

Turkiye has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis Atrl.TO as well as South Korea’s Korea Electric Power Corporation and China’s State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its second and third nuclear power plants, and Russia’s Rosatom is building its first.

An executive at AtkinsRealis, which holds the exclusive licence for Canadian-designed Candu reactors, told Reuters this year that it anticipates Turkiye will complete an early review of its Candu reactors ​following an information exchange, which May lead to concrete talks for a plant bid.
In a step that helped thaw bilateral ties in 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkiye, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkiye exports to dozens of nations.
Yet bilateral trade is small.
Turkiye accounted for less than 0.3 per cent of Canada’s total merchandise trade in 2025, or C$4.34 billion, compared with C$1 trillion with the U.S., Statistics Canada data shows.
Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkiye, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry.
