stories.title: What 'threat' worries Canadians most and other key findings of State of the Nation poll
stories.summary: More Canadians think the federal government should stand up to the United States than to the People's Republic of China.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
An ambitious new poll by British-based Ashcroft Polls surveyed 10,098 Canadian adults on a wide range of topics , from their thoughts on who is the country’s No. 1 enemy to their top kitchen-table issue. Here are the key findings.

After a trade war with the Americans (47 per cent), the most serious threat to Canadians as a whole was the risk of a new economic and financial crisis (38 per cent) followed by immigration (32 per cent). Climate change was fourth overall, followed by loss of jobs to robotics, AI and machine learning.

Allies or adversaries?

The U.K, Australia and France were more likely to be seen as allies of Canada, while Russia, Iran and the U.S. were the most likely to be seen as an adversary or threat.

In 2022, 73 per cent of Canadians saw the U.S. as an ally. Today, only 25 per cent do.

The U.S. vs China: Who should Canada stand up to?

When asked if they had to choose, 72 per cent of Canadians as a whole said they’d prefer a government that stands up to the United States versus 28 per cent who said the government should seek accommodations with the U.S.

By comparison, 59 per cent of Canadians would prefer to seek cooperation with China rather than stand up to Beijing (41 per cent).

Trump will still be a threat even after he’s no longer in the White House

Most Canadians feel the same tensions with the U.S. will exist even after Donald Trump is no longer president by the time of the next federal election in 2029: 40 per cent said managing the Canada-U.S. relationship will be as important as it is now, with a further 42 per cent saying it will be even more important.

The party and their leader’s approval ratings

Canadians are more likely to have a net positive view of Mark Carney than of the Liberal party: 60 per cent had a positive view of Carney, compared to 55 per cent who had a positive view of the Liberals.

Poll of 10,000 Canadians finds half consider U.S. to be an adversary and 45% feel worse off today than a year ago

Mark Carney’s support surge coming largely from former Conservatives, poll finds

The reverse was true for Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who scored a lower positive score (43 per cent) than his party (49 per cent).

Who would you never vote for?

A slightly higher proportion of voters said they would never vote for the Conservatives (27 per cent) than said the same for the Liberals (24 per cent) or NDP (22 per cent).

What are the most important issues facing Canada today?

The cost of living was chosen by 60 per cent of respondents as the most important issue facing Canada today, followed by health care, the economy and jobs, housing, and trade and tariffs with the U.S.

Source: Ashcroft Polls interviewed 10,098 Canadian adults online between July 31 and Aug. 17 A poll sample of this size has a margin of error or plus or minus one percentage point.

stories.title: Sarnia Police Association ratifies new collective agreement
stories.summary: The Sarnia Police Association (SPA) has ratified a new collective agreement.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The Sarnia Police Association (SPA) has ratified a new collective agreement.

A vote took place on Thursday, deciding on a proposed 2025-2027 collective agreement.

“After a long process, we are pleased to have reached a fair agreement with the PSB [Police Service Board] for the SPA membership,” said Gavin Armstrong, president of the SPA.

The SPA is a professional police labour relations organization, which offers members of the Sarnia Police Service support via bargaining and labour contracts, but also while promoting a healthy and safe work environment, it said.

“We are very pleased to see the ratification of the collective agreement and the successful conclusion of this bargaining process,” said Kelly Ash, board chair for the Sarnia PSB.

“Through respectful dialogue, good-faith negotiations, and a commitment to finding common ground, the parties were able to achieve a fair contract that recognizes the interests of our members, the Service, and the community. The board thanks everyone involved for their dedication and professionalism throughout these negotiations.”

stories.title: After arson attack, Liberal MP warns violent rhetoric puts all MPs at risk
stories.summary: Ottawa — Liberal MP Salma Zahid says she's concerned about escalating violent rhetoric directed at MPs — including the leader of another party.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Liberal MP Salma Zahid says she’s concerned about escalating violent rhetoric directed at MPs — including the leader of another party.

“We need to lower the temperature,” Zahid told The Canadian Press. “The reality we are living in is (that) sadly, it is not uncommon for online rhetoric to cross over into real-world violence.”

In August, a man was filmed setting vehicles on fire outside Zahid’s home in the Toronto suburb of Scarborough. Police have said they believe it was an arson attack.

Zahid said she now has 24-7 security at her home and she believes the incident could be linked to rising rhetoric against her fellow MPs.

“For me and my family, it has been very traumatic, because I really need to know who is behind this and what is their motive,” she said.

Toronto Police have arrested one person in connection with the case. Zahid said the person arrested is a driver hired by the individual spotted in security camera footage pouring gasoline and lighting five cars on fire.

She said police told her the driver would not identify the person who hired him and the primary culprit remains at large.

“That might have been the purpose, to frighten us,” she said. “And it has changed in many ways the way we do the work.”

House of Commons officials have helped arrange full-time security outside Zahid’s house and are vetting all invitations she receives. Her constituency office has shifted to appointments-only, barring walk-in visits until new cameras are installed and a security assessment is complete.

“I have always said that I want to be an accessible MP. This is not how I want to function. But this is how I have been put in a situation,” said Zahid, an MP since 2015.

She spoke out this week about backlash against NDP Leader Avi Lewis over his public statements on Israel. Zahid said she believes some of the language used by Lewis’s critics could put him at risk.

Zahid said she can stand up for MPs from other parties when they face violent rhetoric and others should voice their support.

Her comments come after three recent arrests for death threats against Prime Minister Mark Carney, incidents Zahid said are symptoms of a broader problem.

“I worry that this language, if it is used like that, risks fuelling antisemitism, Islamophobia, and anti-Palestinian racism. I see incidents of all sorts increasing, and I think it is unacceptable,” she said.

“Incitement and hateful rhetoric is wrong and dangerous.”

Zahid is of Pakistani origin, was born in the U.K. and wears a hijab. She said hateful rhetoric makes it harder to convince minorities to run for office, and to preserve the vigorous debate democracy requires.

“As politicians, I think we need to bring people together, so that everyone is part of the Canadian team here and everyone can live freely,” she said.

Former Liberal MP Pam Damoff announced she would not seek re-election last year due to constant threats, misogyny and harassment.

Damoff said at the time that all MPs know they must have a thick skin but she feared that someone was going to be killed, with harassment intensifying since the COVID-19 pandemic.

In June 2022, Commons officials started giving MPs panic buttons in response to threats and harassment of parliamentarians.

Known as “mobile duress alarms,” the devices are meant to immediately alert Parliamentary Protective Services or local police when MPs face a threat anywhere in Canada.

Commons security also offered to install alarms and cameras in MPs’ offices and to provide training on de-escalating potentially violent situations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Avoid packing ‘Canadian-origin products’ when travelling to U.S., snowbird group advises
stories.summary: The Canadian Snowbird Association has advised travellers to the U.S. to avoid packing some dairy products and Canadian alcoholic beverages for their trips.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
The Canadian Snowbird Association (CSA) has advised travellers to the U.S. to avoid packing Canadian alcoholic beverages and some dairy products for their trips.

The advisory was published Monday , a day before U.S. President Donald Trump’s ban on Canadian alcohol and some dairy imports came into effect.

The CSA advised snowbirds to keep the ban in mind when travelling south of the border and to “check their vehicles, RVs and luggage.”

The ban, announced on Sept. 8, barred Canadian exports of more than 30 different alcohol products including beer, wine and spirits such as whiskies, vodka and gin. It also barred different whey products, some types of molasses, non-alcoholic beer and some motorcycles.

Trump announced the ban in response to Canada’s retaliation measures on nearly $28 billion of U.S. imports, announced the same day.

It isn’t clear if the new import restrictions apply to Canadians bringing their own personal supply of Canadian alcohol or dairy.

However, the organization warned: “Do not bring Canadian-origin products that are subject to the new import bans. All food, agricultural products and alcohol must be declared to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).”

On Tuesday, a truck carrying “over 1,000 bottles of spirits” was denied entry into the U.S. by border officials at the St. Stephen-Calais crossing between New Brunswick and Maine, despite the driver holding a U.S. customs permit.

Border officials said the cargo violated the import restrictions that went into effect earlier this week.

Canada and the United States have been embroiled in a weeks-long tariff war after talks of a trade deal broke down in late August. On Aug. 21, Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion of Canadian goods.

Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said on Tuesday that trade talks aren’t currently underway, but officials from both countries are still in contact.

With files from CTV News Atlantic’s Melanie Price and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney plans to visit Turkiye this month, sources tell Reuters
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to visit Turkey this month to meet President Tayyip Erdogan in what would be the first dedicated bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian leader, four sources with knowledge of the visit said.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to visit Turkiye this month to meet President Tayyip Erdogan in what would be the first dedicated bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian leader, four sources with knowledge of the visit said.

One of the sources said Carney and Erdogan could discuss the free-trade talks they launched on the sidelines of a Nato summit in Ankara in July, as well as potential energy and defense cooperation. Canadian and Turkish trade ministers agreed this week to accelerate the talks ahead of the leaders’ meeting, two sources said.

The visit would mark Carney’s latest break with Canadian diplomatic convention as he seeks to reduce the country’s reliance on the United States, by far its biggest trading partner, after a collapse in trade talks in August.

Carney has vowed to double Canada’s non-U.S. trade over the next decade and has rushed to establish ties with a host of countries, including China and India, with which it had past strains.

He has focused less on human rights than his predecessors to forge ahead, backed by polls showing strong support among Canadians for his efforts to reinforce the economy in the face of U.S. tariffs.

Erdogan, Turkiye’s leader of 23 years — whom rights groups have criticized for a crackdown on the political opposition since 2024 — seeks new markets and collaboration for the regional military power’s burgeoning defense industry. Erdogan says an independent judiciary is probing the opposition and rejects claims it is politically motivated.

Turkiye, an emerging market economy whose biggest trading partner is the European Union, also seeks partnerships and investment in energy, infrastructure and mining.

The sources did not share the dates or agenda of the visit planned later this month.

Carney’s office and Erdogan’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Less focus on rights

Western powers have grown relatively silent on Turkiye’s rights record as it has become a leading defense-industrial power and a bulwark against Russian aggression.

Since last month, a wave of arrests and restrictions has targeted Turkiye’s Lgbtq+ community in a probe the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and some European officials.

No Canadian prime minister is known to have made a standalone bilateral visit to Turkey in recent decades, though they have met Erdogan and other Turkish leaders on the sidelines of multilateral gatherings, including Nato and G20 summits hosted by Turkiye.

Modest bilateral trade

At the Nato leaders’ summit in July, Carney and Erdogan formally launched negotiations for a ‌free-trade agreement.

That month, Turkiye agreed to join Canada’s Defense Security and ‌Resilience Bank as one of 10 founding member nations of Carney’s multilateral “middle powers” bank.

The two countries’ trade ministers met in June and planned to expand cooperation on renewable and nuclear energy, a Canadian government statement said, listing aerospace, defense and security as areas of potential new partnerships.

Turkiye has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis Atrl.TO as well as South Korea’s Korea Electric Power Corporation and China’s State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its second and third nuclear power plants, and Russia’s Rosatom is building its first.

An executive at AtkinsRealis, which holds the exclusive licence for Canadian-designed Candu reactors, told Reuters this year that it anticipates Turkiye will complete an early review of its Candu reactors ​following an information exchange, which May lead to concrete talks for a plant bid.

In a step that helped thaw bilateral ties in 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkiye, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkiye exports to dozens of nations.

Yet bilateral trade is small.

Turkiye accounted for less than 0.3 per cent of Canada’s total merchandise trade in 2025, or C$4.34 billion, compared with C$1 trillion with the U.S., Statistics Canada data shows.

Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkiye, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry.

($1 = 1.4227 Canadian dollars)

(Reporting by Jonathan Spicer, Promit Mukherjee and David Ljunggren; Additional reporting by Huseyin Hayatsever in Ankara; Editing by Rod Nickel)

stories.title: How international junior hockey players find support overseas
stories.summary: Junior hockey is the next step for player development and is a big change for players, especially overseas. Th...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Junior hockey is the next step for player development and is a big change for players, especially overseas. The Greater Ontario Hockey League (Gohl) is on it’s 20th year of an organized league and it’s second year as a development league for the Ontario Hockey League OHL. The Gohl has become more international than it has ever with 7 different overseas countries represented .

Nikolai Felin-Henrikson from Oslo, Norway is a goaltender for the Strathroy Rockets in the Gohl and moved to Canada on August 10th, 2026. One difference Felin-Henrikson found difficult to start was the philosophy difference from Canada to Norway.

Nikolai Felin-Henrikson in goal (Credit: Colleen Wiendels)

“In Norway we have the mind set practice makes you better, so we’re on the ice two times a day. While in Canada you’re on two times a week, which made me focus on practice more and felt I needed to be perfect.” said Felin-Henrikson.

He stats the hockey skill cap in Norway is around the junior level creating a big skill gap between teams.

“The game is faster, more skilled players, and a smaller rink in Canada. In Norway you would have 3-5 teams dominate the league, while over here the skill gap is much closer where their isn’t a clear team that will win.” he said.

Vladimir Romankov is from Minsk, Belarus he is teammates and roommates with Felin-Henrikson. Romankov found much support when coming over to Canada from his billet family.

Vladimir Romankov going for the puck along the boards (Credit: Colleen Wiendels)

“They told me to make myself at home and that they will take good care of me.” Romankov said. Billet families are meant to provide a ‘home away from home’ for international players coming over to play in higher leagues.

When coming over from Belarus, Romankov did struggle to getting used to the Canadian play style, but caught on very quickly.

One thing both Romankov and Felin-Henrikson like about Canada is how nice and welcoming Canadians are, as well as the food.

Both shared there favourite national food, with Romankov’s being Borscht a type of stew, and Felin-Henrikson’s being Salmon as the fish in Norway tastes amazing according to him.

stories.title: 'Disgusting' antisemitic flyers distributed in Belleville weeks after synagogue shooting
stories.summary: The president of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue called it "disgusting" as police ask community to share any video evidence.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Not even two weeks after a hate-motivated attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., antisemitic flyers were distributed in the city’s east end, according to police.

Norman Weddum, the president of the synagogue that was targeted, called it “disgusting.”

“It was so soon after the shooting,” he said. “What’s going on here?”

The Jewish community in the area is still recovering from the Sept. 20 shooting at Sons of Jacob Synagogue, which left Const. Jeff Smith seriously injured. He was stationed outside the building on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, when 29-year-old Sean Ward opened fire.

Weddum was inside with around 25 congregants for the evening prayer service. Doug Lobel was also attending that service when dozens of shots rang out.

“Just over a week ago, I was there that night of the shooting, and like many in our community, I had only begun the process of trying to heal and regain a sense of safety,” he told National Post.

“Seeing these flyers posted around the east side of Belleville near the synagogue yesterday has brought that night and all those emotions rushing back. Yesterday was a very difficult day.”

Weddum said he’s not sure how many people were involved with handing out the flyers, or if it was only one person, but there were “a lot” distributed.

Copies of the flyers shared with National Post showed messaging that promoted conspiracy theories blaming the Jewish community for the COVID-19 pandemic, abortion, gun control and mass immigration.

The synagogue shooter reportedly “spouted” a theory that blamed Jews for COVID and was discharged from the Canadian Armed Forces due to his refusal to receive the COVID vaccine. After the attack, police shared a video where Ward could be heard shouting “You are going to die for the Jews” before shooting at Smith.

Police said the shooting deliberately targeted the Jewish community and Ward had the “means, the motive and the mechanisms” to carry out a bigger attack.

J.D. Tuccille: After the Belleville attack, Jews face tough decisions about security

Belleville shooting a wake-up call for Canadians, survivor says in new statement

Ward later died in hospital. Smith is in critical but stable condition.

The Belleville Police Service said it was aware of “flyers being distributed in the east end of Belleville containing antisemitic messaging” on Oct. 1. It is asking anyone with information or video evidence to share it. Police have been in contact with community leaders and are “taking proactive steps to support the safety and well-being of residents.”

Increased patrols are continuing in Belleville at places of worship as well as other community gathering spaces.

Jewish advocacy groups, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs and the UJA Federation of Greater Toronto released a statement on X saying that the flyers are “more than hateful rhetoric.”

“Libels and conspiracies about Jews and Israelis are fuelling hate and violence against Canadians,” it said. “Canada’s security services have sounded the alarm of the current situation in which acts of antisemitism become so prevalent and frequent that they create an environment that influence extremists toward more violent pathways.”

Although McCurdy was not injured, the description of the fundraiser online says “the emotional toll of this experience is significant, and mental recovery is just as vital as physical healing.”

stories.title: Boy, 16, charged with threatening Pickering school, manufacturing firearm parts
stories.summary: Pickering - Police say a 16-year-old boy is facing charges after allegedly threatening to carry out a shooting at a Pickering, Ont., high school and making firearm parts with a 3D printer.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Pickering - Police say a 16-year-old boy is facing charges after allegedly threatening to carry out a shooting at a Pickering, Ont., high school and making firearm parts with a 3D printer.

Durham regional police say they received reports from multiple sources, including international policing partners, about comments the suspect allegedly made online about printing a firearm for a shooting.

stories.title: N.S. privacy commissioner questions transparency around cabinet records
stories.summary: Nova Scotia’s information and privacy commissioner says new rules regarding public access to provincial cabinet records will result in less transparency.
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Nova Scotia’s information and privacy commissioner says new rules regarding public access to provincial cabinet records will result in less transparency.

In a letter to the ministers of justice and Service Nova Scotia, David Nurse said legislative changes coming into effect on April 1, 2027, will completely shield all cabinet records from requests made under the province’s freedom of information law.

Nurse’s letter, released Friday as part of an annual report, said current rules already limit disclosure of records that would reveal the substance of cabinet discussions, but background information is generally disclosed if a cabinet decision has already been released to the public.

If a request for cabinet records is denied, the public still can request the background information five years later and it must be handed over. Under the new rules, that time limit will be extended to 15 years.

“To me, (the changes) just feel like an unnecessary step backwards,” Nurse said in an interview Friday. “We don’t need more secrecy around government decision making …. We want to see more openness, more trust that the public can handle the truth.”

Nurse noted that Progressive Conservative Premier Tim Houston used freedom of information requests when he was in opposition. At the time, Houston was keen to learn why then Liberal premier Stephen McNeil was refusing to disclose details about the government’s contract with the operator of the ferry service that links Yarmouth, N.S., with Maine.

“That obviously proved to be a very beneficial tool and a way to hold the previous government accountable,” said Nurse. “So why deny future journalists and future opposition parties and members of the public the ability to hold the government accountable?”

Houston’s government introduced changes to freedom of information laws as part of a controversial omnibus bill in February 2025.

Among other things, one change would have allowed the government to fire the auditor general without cause. Another change would have given cabinet ministers the power to block the release of auditor general reports. But those proposed changes were both withdrawn before the bill passed.

Nurse said some of the changes, however, were positive, such as the plan to make the privacy commissioner an officer of the legislative next April. The commissioner was also granted the power in 2025 to tell departments to disregard information requests deemed frivolous and vexatious.

Nurse said the government has responded to his letter by saying it is not considering further changes to the legislation. Still, he said he’s hopeful improvements will be made.

Justice Minister Scott Armstrong and Service Nova Scotia Minister Jill Balser issued a joint statement Friday saying the new act brings Nova Scotia in line with other jurisdictions and provides strong oversight and access rights.

“We respect the role of the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner, who was given the opportunity to comment ahead of this legislation’s introduction, and will continue working with them as the new act is implemented,” said the statement.

“We are focused on practical implementation and will continue working through regulations, tools and guidance to support consistent application of the act.”

NDP Opposition Leader Claudia Chender said in a statement Friday that Nurse was right to raise his concerns, and that the changes take away transparency, moving the province in the wrong direction.

“Nova Scotians deserve a government that doesn’t hide their spending or decision making from the people who elected them,” Chender said. “People want to know what’s going on, not just what the government wants them to hear.”

One of Nurse’s duties is to review information requests if the applicant does not agree with a department’s decision. His report says 80 per cent of those disputes were resolved informally in 2025-26.

Meanwhile, the office’s backlog on those files, previously four-years long, has been cut to three years.

stories.title: Nexus application rules are changing for Canada and the U.S.
stories.summary: Changes are coming for Canadians who need to renew their Nexus memberships, according to Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa), with shorter timelines to schedule interviews.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Changes are coming for Canadians who need to renew their Nexus memberships, according to the Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa), with shorter timelines to schedule required interviews.

The changes were detailed in a release Thursday.

Starting April 1, 2027, applicants will have up to two years to schedule a Nexus enrolment interview upon receiving a conditional approval.

Under the current requirements, applicants have up to five years to schedule interviews, which was a temporary measure put in place since the disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the Cbsa says.

Since the pandemic years, the agency says its enrolment interview capacity has improved, which prompted the change to the original two-year time limit.

For applicants that were conditionally approved for a Nexus membership before April 1, 2027, the five-year time limit will still be honoured provided an interview is scheduled within that timeframe, or by April 1, 2029 — whichever comes first.

Nexus, the Cbsa says, is an exclusive membership program designed to speed up processing and wait times for approved “low-risk” travellers to cross the border into Canada or the United States.

This is mainly done by pre-screening passengers, allowing access to priority lanes to reduce wait times and other benefits.

The program is run jointly by the Cbsa and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (Uscbp), and memberships are valid for five years.

4:32 Will Nexus price hike impact demand?

To qualify for Nexus, the Cbsa says one must be considered admissible to Canada and the U.S. under immigration laws, provide complete and accurate information on the application, and not have violated any customs, immigration or agriculture laws.

An application May also be denied if an applicant has been convicted of a criminal offence in any country, unless a pardon for that offence has been granted.

Members over 18 years of age also have to pay a non-refundable processing fee of US$120, while those under 18 years are free.

Once an application is filed, it then goes through both the Cbsa and Uscbp for approval. Each agency then assesses an applicants risk to determine if they meet all Nexus requirements, and May then be granted a conditional approval.

The Cbsa says applicants May have to undergo a criminal background check, be questioned by either agency about any arrests, charges or convictions, and be asked to provide fingerprints to determine eligibility.

If an applicant passes the risk assessment phase, they May be granted a conditional approval. It’s at this point where an applicant will have up to two-years to schedule an interview to finalize a Nexus membership.

Those interviews must be done with both agencies before a Nexus card can be issued. The Cbsa portion can be conducted at a Nexus enrolment centre, while the U.S. CBP portion May be completed at a CBP enrolment center or through Enrolment on Arrival at various border crossings and airports.

The Cbsa is also warning anyone currently waiting for an interview to book an appointment as soon as possible, because applications are considered expired once the applicable timelines are exceeded.

stories.title: Canada the 10th smartest country in the world, well ahead of U.S., study finds
stories.summary: Canada's "smartness score" puts it ahead of 18th-place United States, but trails other commonwealth countries and first-place Singapore.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A report on “global intelligence” has placed Canada 10th in a list of 80 countries that were analyzed, eight places ahead of its neighbour the United States, but trailing the U.K., Australia and first-place Singapore.

To create its ranking, researchers combined several pieces of information. One was data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa), an international study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (Oecd) that tests the skills and knowledge of 15-year-old students in various countries.

They also looked at the per capita publication of high-quality scientific publications last year, and the average IQ scores from the International IQ Test , a website that has been active since 2018 and gathered more than 1.2 million scores last year alone.

Canada’s Pisa scores were relatively high, and it placed 6th in the number of scientific publications and 18th when adjusted for population. Its IQ averaged 102.09, putting it in 11th place in that category among a cluster of countries with scores between 102 and 103.

Combined, these figures gave Canada a “smartness score” of 59.36 and a ranking of 10th place. Singapore topped the list with a score of 87.13, while New Zealand (59.9) and Britain (60.6) narrowly edged out Canada.

The United States was 18th with a score of 53.88 and trailed Canada in all the categories. Although it remains the world leader in scientific papers published, it drops to 23rd place in that category when adjusted for population.

“The teenagers performed particularly well in science, scoring 510 points, while mathematics and reading scores stood at 485 and 490, respectively,” the study noted. “Canada also scored 525 points in the new computational problem-solving assessment, which measures students’ ability to use digital tools to solve problems.”

It added: “Canada is undoubtedly a scientific powerhouse, with its institutions producing 5,647 high-quality scientific publications in 2025, (but) while this remains a strong result, it falls well below the elite levels produced by Switzerland (507.12), Singapore (411.12) and Denmark (374.86).” Canada’s per-capita publication rate was 139.54.

China was excluded from the ranking, the study noted, in part because the Oecd only tests a subset of Chinese provinces and municipalities, “which cannot be reliably compared to whole-country results elsewhere in this dataset.”

Diliana Hristova, a data analyst behind the study, lauded that move as a smart way to turn the uncertainty surrounding U.S. universities and research funding under the Trump administration into an opportunity. But there is an obvious question hanging over the move: Why is a country with such a strong higher education system having to go abroad for talent in the first place?

She added: “Canada already produces the sixth-highest volume of scientific research among the 80 countries we analyzed, yet it has spent years losing talented researchers in fields such as AI and quantum computing to better-funded labs overseas.

stories.title: Pwhl establishes Eastern and Western conferences, expands to eight-team playoffs
stories.summary: The Professional Women’s Hockey League is establishing Eastern and Western conferences this season and increasing the number of playoff teams from four to eight. The 12-team league – which will have four expansion clubs on the ice this season – will begin play Dec. 5 when Seattle faces Vancouver, while expansion teams Hamilton and San […]
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
The Professional Women’s Hockey League is establishing Eastern and Western conferences this season and increasing the number of playoff teams from four to eight.

The 12-team league – which will have four expansion clubs on the ice this season – will begin play Dec. 5 when Seattle faces Vancouver, while expansion teams Hamilton and San Jose square off against Montreal and Minnesota, respectively. The season ends April 18.

The Pwhl says Eastern Conference teams will include the Boston Fleet, Pwhl Hamilton, the Montreal Victoire, the New York Sirens, the Ottawa Charge and the Toronto Sceptres.

Western Conference clubs include Pwhl Detroit, Pwhl Las Vegas, the Minnesota Frost, Pwhl San Jose, the Seattle Torrent and the Vancouver Goldeneyes.

The league says each team will play 30 regular-season games, including 18 within its conference and 12 interconference games.

All teams will observe a one-week break around the debut of Pwhl All-Star on March 7, 2027, to be played at Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena.

The top four teams in each conference will qualify for the playoffs. Best-of-three first-round series will be followed by best-of-five conference finals and then a best-of-five league final for the Walter Cup. The league will continue and expand a playoff tradition, awarding the first-place team in each conference the opportunity to select its first-round opponent, choosing between the third or fourth-place team within their respective conference.

stories.title: ‘Buy Canadian’ movement just as strong 19 months since trade war began: poll
stories.summary: In February 2025, Trump first announced tariffs against Canada. Abacus conducted a poll of Canadians asking if they intend to boycott American products.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canadians are just as enthusiastic about avoiding American products and buying Canadian as they were nineteen months ago when U.S. President Donald Trump launched his trade war against Canada , new polling shows.

The share of Canadians who intend to avoid American products is “unchanged,” a report from Abacus Data said on Thursday.

In February 2025, Trump first announced tariffs against Canada. Abacus conducted a poll of Canadians asking them if they intend to boycott American products, with 78 per cent saying they would.

Nineteen months later, the figure is virtually unchanged at 77 per cent.

Many are putting their intentions into action. In February, more than half (53 per cent) said they had bought more Canadian goods, while on Thursday that figure was 61 per cent.

2:10 Buy Canadian app sees spike in popularity

The largest swing came among Canadians who said they would not make any travel plans to the U.S., with the number rising from 32 per cent in February 2025 to 52 per cent in 2026.

Canadians are also making smaller behaviour changes, such as avoiding American gas stations (rising from 33 per cent to 39 per cent), avoiding American retailers such as Walmart (20 per cent to 26 per cent), reducing purchases on Amazon (21 per cent to 26 per cent) and cancelling American streaming services (14 per cent to 20 per cent).

The demographic where the Buy Canadian movement was softening was older Canadians, with 54 per cent saying they planned to avoid American products in February 2025 and 48 per cent in September 2026.

Over the same period, Canadians under 30 went from 31 per cent to 32 per cent during the same period.

But challenges remain, with 61 per cent of Canadians saying buying Canadian-made goods would cost more money, up from 60 per cent in February 2025.

In February 2025, the week the first U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect, Abacus Data surveyed 3,000 Canadian adults (February 5 to 11, 2025) about how the tariffs would change what they buy. In September 2026 Abacus asked the same questions again of 1,479 Canadian adults from September 4 to 9, 2026.

stories.title: Gas tax: Why Canadians are paying more at the pump in some provinces
stories.summary: Canadian Taxpayers Federation is calling on Nova Scotia to join Alberta and others who have announced a tax holiday for gas levies.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
As gas prices remain stubbornly high across Canada, gas taxes at both the federal and provincial level vary from high to non-existent, as groups like the Canadian Taxpayers Federation (CTF) call for relief.

A Nova Scotia flashpoint

The CTF is calling on Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston to suspend the province’s gas tax amid continued high prices at the pumps. This comes as several other provinces as well as the federal government have enacted full or partial rollbacks on gasoline taxes.

The CTF notes that the Nova Scotia gas tax amounts to 15.5 cents per litre on gasoline, the highest in Atlantic Canada. “Houston has never cut it,” Devin Drover, Ctf’s Atlantic Director and General Counsel, told National Post by email.

He added: “The government has never given a real reason. When affordability comes up, the Houston government points to its one-point HST cut, but it has never touched the 15.5-cent-per-litre provincial gas tax.”

National Post has reached out to the premier’s office for comment.

Suspending the provincial gas tax would save Nova Scotians almost $10 on a 64-litre minivan fill-up, according to the CTF.

Drover said the fuel tax brings in about $297 million a year, per the province’s own budget estimates “A four-month suspension like P.E.I.’s would run roughly a third of that, about $100 million.”

Alberta takes a three-month break

Last month, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced that her government would eliminate its fuel tax for three months to help fight costs. The cut took effect yesterday, Oct. 1, and amounts to a 13-cent-a-litre savings on gasoline and diesel fuel.

Most Canadians oppose Ottawa's planned September gas tax hike

New fuel surcharges on groceries and more making 'almost everything in the economy' more expensive

In June she opted to keep the tax but instead invited Albertans to apply for a $100 energy rebate cheque, available for households making less than $225,000. But Smith admitted the program was not well received, noting: “We have to be willing to take criticism and adjust and change course.”

Albertans still have until Oct. 31 to apply for the rebate, after the province extended the deadline.

Ontario, Newfoundland make change permanent

Newfoundland and Labrador had cut its provincial gas tax by 8.05 cents per litre in June 2022, and this year passed legislation to make that decrease permanent, a move applauded by the Retail Council of Canada . It keeps the province’s gasoline taxes at 7.5 cents per litre of gas and 9.5 cents for diesel.

Ontario made a similar move in the same timeframe, cutting taxes on a gas by 5.7 cents and on diesel by 5.3. The rate is now nine cents per litre for both.

In August, Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote to Prime Minister Mark Carney asking him to extend the federal gas excise tax holiday until at least the end of the year, which eventually happened. Ford added: “The federal government could also match Ontario’s ambition to lower costs by making the suspension permanent.”

P.E.I.’s temporary rollback

Prince Edward Island, meanwhile, has announced a four-month hiatus on gasoline taxes. The cut took effect Sept. 26 and lasts until Jan. 31, 2027. The change saves Islanders 8.47 cents per litre on gasoline and 14.15 cents per litre on diesel until then.

P.E.I.’s move follows a decision by the federal government to extend its own moratorium on gas taxes. Ottawa had already announced in April that the federal tax of 10 cents a litre on gasoline and four cents on diesel would be removed until Sept. 7.

Five days before the end of that period came another announcement that the suspension would continue until Jan. 31, 2027. At that point, the tax will come back at a 50 per cent rate through March 31.

A politically agnostic choice

Nova Scotia has a Conservative government, but Drover said cutting gas taxes is not a party-dependant decision. The Liberal government in Ottawa suspended its tax in April, while Progressive Conservative premiers did it in P.E.I. and Ontario. In Newfoundland and Labrador, a Liberal government cut the tax in 2022 and a Conservative government later made the cut permanent.

“And Manitoba’s NDP ran a full-year fuel tax holiday in 2024, then brought the tax back 10 per cent lower,” he noted.

Even with the federal gas tax suspended, taxes make up 26 per cent of the price at the pumps in Nova Scotia, according to Ctf’s recent Gas Tax Honesty Report . Nova Scotia drivers also pay a tax-on-tax of about three cents per litre, because sales taxes are charged on top of all the per-litre taxes.

That report also noted that Montreal has the highest gas taxes in the country at 61 cents per litre, or 35 per cent of the price of gasoline. Drivers in Montreal pay a transit tax when fuelling up in the city, in addition to provincial and federal levies. The rest of Quebec had gas taxes amounting to 33 per cent of the total price.

Similarly, drivers in Vancouver and Victoria also pay transit taxes at the pumps, and had total taxes of 28 and 25 per cent, respectively. Manitobans pay just 17 per cent tax on their gas, with Saskatchewan at 18 per cent.

“Ottawa, P.E.I., Alberta and Newfoundland and Labrador have all delivered meaningful relief at the pumps,” said Drover. “Houston controls Nova Scotia’s gas tax and he needs to suspend it now.”

stories.title: September auto sales in Canada up 3.4%, DesRosiers says
stories.summary: But warns sales could be weaker in the fourth quarter, compared with stronger activity seen in 2025
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Auto sales in September in Canada were up from a year ago, marking the fourth consecutive month of gains, according to DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc.

The firm estimates 168,000 vehicles were sold in the month, up 3.4 per cent from September 2025.

Andrew King, managing partner at DesRosiers, says the market has shown stability in recent months despite conflict in the Middle East and a tariff dispute with the United States.

But DesRosiers says sales could be weaker in the fourth quarter, compared with stronger sales seen in 2025.

On a year-to-date basis, auto sales are still 0.7 per cent lower than 2025 levels.

Despite the winning streak, auto sales have slowed this year as gas prices remain elevated and Canadian households pull back on spending amid geopolitical uncertainties.

stories.title: Ontario police officer charged after woman pepper sprayed following arrest
stories.summary: A 33-year-old woman was arrested shortly before 2 a.m. on April 29. According to police, Const. Brandon Mihalides used pepper spray following the arrest.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A London, Ont. police officer has been charged with assault after allegedly using pepper spray on a woman following her arrest earlier this year.

A 33-year-old woman was arrested shortly before 2 a.m. on April 29, London police said in a news release.

According to police, Const. Brandon Mihalides used pepper spray following the arrest.

In Ontario, the use of pepper spray is subject to mandatory use-of-force reporting requirements and a subsequent review process, police said.

During that process, concerns were raised about the use of force, and the matter was referred to the Major Crime Section to investigate possible criminal conduct.

As a result of the investigation, the 29-year-old officer is facing one count of assault with a weapon.

The officer has been reassigned to non-operational administrative duties, police said.

stories.title: Poll of 10,000 Canadians finds half consider U.S. to be an adversary and 45% feel worse off today than a year ago
stories.summary: The U.S. trade war poses the most serious threat to Canada for Canadians as a whole, according to a new poll of more than 10,000 Canadians.
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Canadians are feeling relatively “jaunty” in the face of a trade war with a country they now view as an adversary and no friend, even while saying they feel worse off than they did a year ago, according to a new poll of more than 10,000 Canadian adults .

Most believe Prime Minister Mark Carney and his Liberal government are best suited to handle trade negotiations and American designs on Canada, and most voters overall feel the Liberals are making headway and “doing some good things” — or they’re at least giving them the benefit of the doubt that they will.

But while Carney is polling stronger than his party, which isn’t the case for Pierre Poilievre, the high cost of living and other bread-and-butter issues were ranked as more personally pressing than the trade war.

According to the poll, Carney leads on attributes like “understands the lives of people like me,” though only 32 per cent thought this was true of him, according to U.K.-based pollster, Lord Ashcroft Polls.

“If living standards continue to stagnate, it’s easy to see how an air of calm authority could, over time, turn into aloof technocracy,” Lord Michael Ashcroft, a British businessman, philanthropist and former deputy chair of the British Conservative party, wrote in a commentary for National Post .

While the poll found 47 per cent of Canadians think the country is heading in the wrong direction compared to 40 per cent who believe Canada is on the proper path, the numbers are notably less pessimistic than in other Western nations, Ashcroft wrote.

“Overall, Canadians say the country is on the wrong track by a margin of just seven points — positively jaunty numbers compared to their equivalents in Europe and the U.S.”

Recent U.S. polls put the “wrong direction” camp ahead by 20 to 30 points, with a similar picture in Britain.

Majority of Canadians now see U.S. as an enemy, and Trump is the reason: poll

What 'threat' worries Canadians most and other key findings of State of the Nation poll

U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and bombastic rhetoric “didn’t just help to swing the 2025 election; they continue to shape Canadian politics” Ashcroft wrote. “Many see Carney almost as a wartime leader, his economic credentials making him the man for the times.”

In all, 10,098 adults in Canada were surveyed online between July 31 and Aug. 17. A poll sample of this size has a margin of error or plus or minus one percentage point.

In addition, 16 focus groups involving 128 participants — equal numbers of men and women drawn from a range of backgrounds — were held in four locations in B.C, Alberta, Quebec and Ontario.

While the poll found support for the way Carney is handling Trump, people were more likely to worry the country is off track, a finding that surprised Carleton University’s Richard Nimijean, given more recent polls have reported more upbeat results, with the “right direction” overtaking the wrong. It could come down to timing, said Nimijean, an associate professor of Canadian studies.

The Ashcroft poll was conducted at a time “when people were feeling pretty tired of and stressed by” the trade conflict, Nimijean said.

Days after the Ashcroft polling stopped, Carney pulled his negotiating team out of the trade talks, telling reporters: “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.”

The prime minister’s rallying call might have marked an important mood shift that could explain why more recent polls found higher optimism, and why the jaunty sentiment has continued, Nimijean said.

Still, when asked whether they feel better or worse off than they did a year ago, 45 per cent of Ashcroft poll respondents said they felt worse off, rather than better (17 per cent); 37 per cent said they felt about the same.

Those aged 45-54, the most hard-pressed group, felt worse, rather than better off, by a 37-point margin: only 15 per cent said they felt better off, versus 52 per cent who said they feel worse off.

Despite the “we won’t be bullied sentiment,” issues around affordability, housing and cost of living still deeply matter, Nimijean said. “Getting affordable housing hasn’t gone away. Accessible health care as an issue hasn’t gone away,” and people in vulnerable sectors are legitimately worried about their jobs, he said. This week, steelmaker Stelco Holdings announced plans to lay off up to 500 workers at its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities.

When looking at political party affiliation, one third of Liberal voters (32 per cent) said they feel worse off than they did a year ago. More than half (57 per cent) of Conservative voters shared that sentiment.

On the economic outlook, while people were more likely to say they expect the economy will do poorly over the next year for Canada as a whole, they were more optimistic about how things will fare for themselves personally.

It’s a phenomenon seen globally, according to the pollster. People feel they have no control over issues like tariffs, the Iran war and international uncertainty. “But closer to home, when people think about their own lives and careers and prospects, things feel somewhat less gloomy and more within their power to determine,” the Ashcroft team said in an email.

Men tend to be more bullish about the economy, and women more guarded, according to the poll.

Canadians across all age groups and parties named the cost of living as the top concern facing Canada today. Housing was the second most important issue for voters up to age 44. Health care took second spot for the 45 and older.

Conservatives were more likely to name immigration and border control, followed by the economy and jobs.

Trade and tariffs came in fifth spot for Canadians as a whole.

When asked which party, regardless of how they intend to vote, does the best job handling issues they consider most important, “the economy was the most tightly contested issue among those who named it as a priority,” according to the poll. The Conservatives had a slight lead (43 per cent) over the Liberals (42 per cent).

On energy and natural resources, 71 per cent of those polled said they’d rather have a government that lets Canada use its own natural resources to reduce energy costs over a government that preserves its natural resources “even at a time of higher energy prices.”

Even a majority of NDP voters (57 per cent) preferred using natural resources to keep energy bills down.

In focus groups, a new oil pipeline to the West Coast drew mixed reviews. “Some saw it as a welcome and overdue investment that would promote energy independence and economic resilience, while others — particularly those who had switched from the NDP (in the last federal election) — worried about the environmental impact and the effect on First Nations,” according to the poll.

“I know sometimes it doesn’t seem like the woke options, but I feel like a lot of people don’t think about the alternative being to buy from countries like Saudi Arabia where they have terrible human rights,” remarked one Liberal participant from the B.C. focus group.

“I also think there are ways to get oil here where Indigenous people are partners and there is responsible stewardship of the land. And with gas being like $1.80, it’s really important to have our own supply.”

Overall, 51 per cent of respondents said they see the U.S. as an “adversary or threat,” and just 25 per cent viewed their southern neighbour as a friend or ally.

Four years ago, in 2022, the opposite was true: 73 per cent of Canadians saw the U.S. as an ally; 23 per cent saw the Americans as a threat.

“Those who voted Conservative in 2025 were the only group more likely to call the U.S. an ally than an adversary” by a four-point margin, according to the poll.

Focus groups supported the push to make the country more economically self-sufficient “though many felt this was long overdue and regretted that it had taken the Trump presidency to force action on this front,” according to the poll.

A closer relationship with China, however, was slightly more worrisome.

For Canadians as a whole, including for Liberal, Bloc and NDP voters, a trade war with the U.S. was the most serious threat to Canada. For Conservatives, it was immigration, followed second by trade tensions.

More than eight in 10 people polled (82 per cent) said managing relations with the U.S., even after Trump is no longer in office, would be at least as important as it is now in deciding their vote in Canada’s next federal election, “partly because they see Trump as a symptom as much as a cause of the movements in American politics over the last decade or more,” the Ashcroft team said in an email. Among the Republican Party, whoever succeeds Trump could have a similar agenda.

Overall, Canadians have a generally positive view of Carney and the Liberal government: 42 per cent, including one in five Conservative voters, said the Liberals are “making progress and doing some good things.”

Only just over a quarter, including just over half (52 per cent) of Conservative voters, said the Carney Liberals “won’t achieve anything good” and want them out as soon as possible.

On the leadership question, 34 per cent of Canadians as a whole said they would be more likely to consider voting Conservative in the next election if someone other than Pierre Poilievre led the party.

Among those who said there was some chance they’d vote Conservative in the next election, but probably won’t, 34 per cent said what most put them off was that “I don’t like Pierre Poilievre.”

Roughly another third said the party feels too close to engaging in U.S.-style politics; 23 per cent said they worry about what the Conservatives would do in government.

“The Conservatives have struggled to find a narrative or a story to tell Canadians that speaks to the moment, that speaks to how Canadians are feeling,” Nimijean said. “The challenge for Mr. Poilievre is, how do you reach out more to the centre or to the moderates while also speaking to the base you have? It’s not easy.”

The poll echoes what an annual public survey — the Confederation of Tomorrow survey of 5,600 adults — has found when Canadians are asked if they are satisfied, or not, with the way things are going. “It’s basically 50-50,” said Charles Breton, executive director of the Centre of Excellence on the Canadian Federation in Montreal.

What isn’t clearly captured by the new poll “is that Canadians still feel a relationship with the U.S. is an important relationship — not the way things are going now. We do not want that relationship,” Breton said.

“But it is an important relationship, nonetheless.”

stories.title: Hudson Williams’s sweater by Canadian Indigenous designer triggers sales frenzy
stories.summary: The actor put the spotlight on designer Justin Jacob Louis
stories.author: Erica Commisso
stories.content:
Justin Jacob Louis almost forgot it was happening.

The Indigenous designer, who is based in B.C.’s Fraser Valley, had taken the day off to spend the National Day of Truth and Reconciliation with his family. And then a picture of Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams wearing one of his designs hit the internet. The orders started coming in almost immediately.

“Probably within one to two hours of the sweater hitting the feeds, it was gone,” Louis says of the sweater, the Journey Knit Cardigan from his label Section 35. It brought attention to his other work, too, and people – as they often do with the clothes Williams and his costar Connor Storrie wear – are eager to get their hands on it when it becomes available again. “There’s been a bit of a waterfall of other sales, too, and a major request for restocking of the cardigan.”

On a heavy day of reflection for Louis, Williams’s decision to support an Indigenous designer was a bright spot. “It’s pretty cool. I think what stands out, though, was the genuine intention and support that he showed. He didn’t ask for it for free. He purchased it, which is so important for an independent designer,” Louis says (the sweater retails for $350). “And he could have worn any designer, but he chose to represent an Indigenous designer on that day. He even messaged me directly to thank me for getting him that piece. So he was very genuine and intentional, and that meant a lot to me.”

Williams is from British Columbia originally, and he hand-selected the piece from Louis’s collection to wear to an event happening that day, the announcement of Heated Rivalry ’s charity, the Irina Foundation (a nod to the one main characters Shane, played by Williams, and Ilya discuss in the show). It supports established non-profits that offer organized sports and arts programs and champion inclusivity and mental health with a focus on Lgbtq and underserved communities.

A member of his team drove to Louis’s Fraser Valley studio on Sunday to pick the sweater up since shipping wasn’t an option because of time constraints and, by Wednesday, Williams was on stage in New York wearing the cardigan paired with a necklace from Bvlgari’s Save the Children collection, which sends parts of its proceeds to programs that provide opportunities to the world’s most vulnerable youth.

Louis has been a designer for more than 10 years. His work has appeared at New York Fashion Week and the 2025 Met Gala and has earned him a nomination for Menswear of the Year at the Canadian Arts & Fashion Awards.

The Journey Knit Cardigan’s inspiration is deeply personal. “It’s based on a dream I had. At the time, I was feeling far from home and disconnected from my community. And I had a dream about being back home on my reserve in Alberta,” Louis says. Home, for him, is the Samson Cree Nation in Maskwacîs, Alta.

“In the dream, I was walking across the field at my dad’s, looking across the prairies during a winter night.” The blue hues represent the moonlight shining across the prairies during winter, he explains. “At that time, I was asking where my people and my ancestors were, and I was told to look into the sky,” he says. “So the stars represent my ancestors in the sky watching down over us.”

The tipi, stars and moon are woven throughout the collection the sweater belongs to, called Collection One, and pay homage to Louis’s Indigenous identity. And that’s exactly what clothing represents to Louis. “For me, it’s about storytelling. Sharing who I am, where I come from, how I see the world,” Louis says. “It’s a form of true expression and something that allows us to truly be and represent who we are. Our people have been dressing each other for a long time, and I’m just an extension of that.”

stories.title: Construction of Bell Canada’s AI data centre in Saskatchewan scaling up
stories.summary: Saskatchewan’s Crown investments minister stood Thursday in front of a skeleton of steel beams to tout progress on an artificial intelligence mega facility.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes
stories.content:
Saskatchewan’s Crown investments minister stood Thursday in front of a skeleton of steel beams to tout progress on an artificial intelligence mega facility, while the Opposition again called on the province to consult first, then build.

“We have just an amazing thing going on here behind us,” Jeremy Harrison told reporters at the site, southeast of Regina.

“Literally millions of pounds of steel.”

Harrison and Bell Canada held a news conference at the company’s 65-hectare site. Behind them, construction crews moved heavy equipment.

Framing is done for three of four data halls. Paneling for one wall is also nearing completion.

Surrounding the structures are dozens of trailers, stacks of steel pipes and piles of dirt. Security cameras keep an electronic eye on comings and goings.

Harrison said there are 500 workers on the site at any given time.

The $1.7-billion, 300-megawatt centre is to be one of the country’s largest data facilities.

John Watson, group president with Bell, told reporters the first two halls are set to start operating in the first half of next year. Its anchor tenants are CoreWeave and Cerebras.

Bell also has its sights set on expansion. It plans to quadruple the size to 1.2 gigawatts, which would cost $50 billion and require a dedicated natural gas plant.

Watson said there are no timelines on when the expansion would happen.

“It needs to be probably twice as large as this one,” he said. “It will be in proximity to here.”

Bell and the province are promising the expansion would produce bigger economic benefits.

Harrison said it could support 500 permanent jobs at the site, plus up to 3,000 off site and community jobs.

Bell would also move its AI fabric headquarters to Regina, he said, which would add 100 management jobs to the city.

Regina Mayor Chad Bachynski said the project would make the province a hub for innovation and growth.

“These are the kinds of jobs that will help us retain talented young people (and) attract new workers and families,” he said.

Bell has said it plans on partnering with the University of Regina for research, including the possibility of capturing the facility’s heat for greenhouses.

The centre has met with public pushback.

There have been protests this past year, with critics saying they worry about how the megaproject will affect the environment and electricity grid. They’ve also taken issue with what they say is a lack of public consultation, as the project was quickly approved.

Asked if the province should hold town hall meetings about the centre, Harrison said people already support it.

“Elected representatives are here speaking on behalf of their constituents, which I think reflects the broad support that exists out there,” he said.

The Opposition NDP has called on the Saskatchewan Party government to impose a moratorium on large-scale centres, arguing robust consultation isn’t happening.

Sally Housser, the Ndp’s energy critic, told reporters at a separate news conference that the province should be holding town hall meetings.

“I think that is the most basic thing, particularly around the areas that are most affected,” she said. “People have genuine concerns about how this is going to affect their power bills, how this is going to affect the area they live in.”

Watson has said the data centre won’t use groundwater but rather a closed-loop system, where a fluid continuously runs through it for cooling. Bell also said the facility won’t cause power rates to increase.

stories.title: Michael J. Fox to be promoted within Order of Canada at Rideau Hall
stories.summary: Rideau Hall says the honour stems from Fox’s ‘powerful global advocacy and unflinching honesty about Parkinson’s’
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Celebrated actor and Parkinson’s disease activist Michael J. Fox said he felt both “pride” and “humility” while receiving a promotion within the Order of Canada on Friday.

Spectators stood and applauded Fox at Rideau Hall as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially named him to the companion level of the Order of Canada.

Rideau Hall says Fox was elevated to the companion level to honour his “powerful global advocacy and unflinching honesty about Parkinson’s.”

“It’s so many things. But mostly it’s just growing up in Canada, loving this country, loving what it stands for and how it’s progressed and corrected course when it needed to, and stayed the course when it needed to,” Fox told The Canadian Press following the ceremony.

“I picked all that up growing up. I love Canadian music, I love that Canadian content thing. At the end, you have a 65-year-old guy who’s uniquely Canadian because of all those things.”

Parkinson’s is a progressive nervous system disorder that causes tremors, stiffness and slowness, and is linked to depression and memory problems.

Fox, who went public with his Parkinson’s diagnosis in 1998, has raised $2.5 billion for research into the disease and has shared candid experiences about the challenges faced by those living with its symptoms.

“Canada was one of the early proving grounds for (deep brain stimulation),” Fox said, pointing to advances in Parkinson’s research in Canada.

He was among 51 people inducted into, or promoted within, the Order of Canada on Friday.

Arbour said each inductee has demonstrated excellence and thanked them for their work.

“You could have used your talents solely to further your own success. Instead, you have chosen to use your skills, influence and energy to help others,” said in French.

“Because talent, as exceptional as it May be, is not sufficient on its own. It also takes the will to get involved and to take action to improve one’s community and contribute to the common good.”

Arbour said Fox is a “shining example of this.”

“Your example reminds us of something that’s very fundamental: sustainable progress requires that we move forward with courage, imagination and determination,” she said.

“After all, back to the future has always been a much better idea than forward to the past.”

The comment was in reference to Fox’s iconic roles in the Back to the Future trilogy of movies.

“She’s very funny. Very sweet, very welcoming,” Fox said of Arbour, joking that her “average height” made him feel tall.

Yusuf Altintas, a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of British Columbia, was inducted as an officer of the Order of Canada along with Nada Jabado, a professor at McGill University who is being honoured for her work in pediatric neuro-oncology.

Former Bank of Canada governor Stephen Poloz was inducted an officer for helping to facilitate Canada’s international trade and promote its economic well-being.

Sculptor Ruth Elsie Abernethy was inducted as a member. Rideau Hall said she has created iconic life-size bronze pieces showcased around the world, and that her work explores themes of gender, heritage and nation-building.

Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporter Susanne Craig was inducted as a member for her work with The New York Times, The Globe and Mail and The Wall Street Journal.

Rideau Hall described her as one of the most outstanding journalists of her generation, citing her coverage of contemporary issues in the United States.

Colin Roswell Clarke was inducted a member for his work as founder and artistic director of the Toronto Youth Wind Orchestra program. Marcelle Dubois was inducted a member for her work on revitalizing Quebec playwriting.

Patrick Joseph Lahey, co-founder of Triton Submarines, was inducted a member for being one of the world’s leading experts on submersibles and a leading voice for safe practices in the deep diving industry, Rideau Hall said.

stories.title: London police officer faces assault-with-a-weapon charge
stories.summary: According to the London Police Service, a 33-year-old woman was arrested by officers at about 2 a.m. on April 29. During the arrest, oleoresin capsicum (OC) spray was deployed.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A London police officer is facing charges in connection with an on-duty incident earlier this year.

According to the London Police Service, a 33-year-old woman was arrested by officers at about 2 a.m. on April 29. During the arrest, oleoresin capsicum (OC) spray was deployed.

Police said the use of OC spray in Ontario is subject to mandatory use-of-force reporting and review requirements. Concerns were identified during that review regarding the circumstances surrounding the use of the spray, prompting a criminal investigation by members of the Major Crime Section.

As a result of the investigation, Const. Brandon Mihalides, 29, of London, has been charged with one count of assault with a weapon. He has been reassigned to non-operational administrative duties.

“As this matter is now before the courts, no further information will be provided at this time,” London police said in a statement.

Mihalides is scheduled to appear in court on Dec. 30.

stories.title: Tsawwassen First Nation remembers elders killed in B.C. crash
stories.summary: Two women were killed and two others were seriously injured by a pickup truck whose driver was in apparent medical distress
stories.author: Marissa Birnie
stories.content:
Family members of two Tsawwassen First Nation elders killed in a collision outside a shopping centre in Delta, B.C., ON Wednesday say the women were “cultural pillars” of their community.

Statements shared by the nation on social media on Thursday say that wilapiya, also known as Barb Joe, and Virginia Splockton died in the collision at the Tsawwassen Mills mall.

The women were killed and two others were seriously injured by a pickup truck whose driver was in apparent medical distress and drove into an area where nation members were to unveil four traditional carvings known as house posts.

Joe’s family said in the statement that she was a knowledge keeper and matriarch who revived the nation’s language.

The Splockton family described Virginia Splockton as a generous great-grandmother who “touched countless lives” and loved crafting, drumming and singing.

“We recognize the profound impact this tragedy has had on our community as a whole,” the nation wrote in its statement. “We also extend our sincere gratitude to the first responders, emergency personnel, and all those who assisted at the scene.”

Delta police said the driver involved has been released from hospital as investigators assessed whether their medical emergency played a role in the crash.

Police said in a news release on Thursday that there is no information to suggest the collision was intentional.

The nation was hosting a community walk in recognition of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation near the time of the crash and had invited people to meet at the mall’s entrance for the posts’ unveiling after the walk.

Police said the collision was not related to the walk and there is no evidence to suggest any connection between the collision and the house post event.

They said the driver received medical attention and was interviewed by investigators before being released from hospital.

The two injured people remain in hospital in critical condition, and while the investigation remains ongoing, no charges have been laid, police said Thursday.

Dylan Kruger, a city councillor who is running for mayor in the Oct. 17 local elections, said he was taking part in the community walk that was about halfway through when the crowd saw emergency vehicles drive by and two helicopters land in the mall’s parking lot.

“Obviously everybody at that point was getting very nervous. They knew something had gone very seriously wrong,” Kruger said in an interview Thursday.

He said he thought some in the crowd were “flashing back” to the deadly ramming attack at the Lapu Lapu Day festival in Vancouver last year.

But Kruger said organizers kept the crowd calm amid the initial confusion and panic, and people returned safely to their vehicles.

He said it was traumatic for some people in the crowd, which included many families with young children, as they had to walk past the scene that was eventually obscured with screens.

He said the tight-knit First Nation is grieving but has full support from the community of Delta.

“We’re giving them space to do that, but everyone will be there when they’re ready,” he said.

First Nations, politicians and community leaders were among those who expressed condolences over the deaths and injuries.

The Indian Residential School Survivors Society said in a post on social media that the loss of the two “beloved” elders was devastating, while the Huu-ay-aht First Nations on Vancouver Island said it felt the tragedy deeply as one of the elders who died was a grandparent of one of its citizens.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith began her news conference on Thursday about the proposed Pacific Pipeline between her province and B.C., saying her heart was with the grieving families and community.

The pipeline would carry crude oil to the Roberts Bank Terminal in Delta on the waterfront of the Tsawwassen First Nation.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and leaders on the B.C. election campaign, David Eby, Emily Lowan and Lorne Doerkson, also expressed their condolences to the families and the First Nation after the crash.

Video from the scene of the crash on Wednesday shows a pickup truck with the logo for the company Alpine Building Maintenance printed on its side.

The company released a statement on Thursday and confirmed one of its vehicles was involved in the collision.

“We are co-operating with the appropriate authorities to support their investigation. Our thoughts are with everyone affected,” it said.

stories.title: The property tax time-bomb, house-sitters save big and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Oct. 2
stories.summary: Plus, this week’s lowest fixed and variable mortgage rates in Canada
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: Why your property tax bills are a ticking time bomb, and an unconventional way to save for a downpayment. Plus, the case against making mortgage interest payments tax-deductible, and one property worth a look.

If you own a home in Ontario, be prepared to take cover. Ever since the province froze the price estimate that municipalities use to calculate property taxes in 2020, your bills have been a ticking time bomb. And as Jeff Gray reports, lifting the freeze could have explosive political and financial consequences – but so could leaving it in place.

As you probably well know from your property tax bills, the freeze at 2016-assessed values hasn’t stopped municipalities from raising property tax rates. But if Premier Doug Ford ends the six-year halt, people whose home values rose more than the average in their communities are in for some major sticker-shock when their next bills come in. On the other hand, if your home sank in value, you’ve probably been paying more than you otherwise would have, perhaps by thousands of dollars a year.

So is it time to rip the Band-Aid off? Not everyone agrees, and the Ontario government says it’s consulting on the issue. But if you’re curious about whether you’ve been overpaying or might see your property tax bill skyrocket if the freeze lifts, read Jeff’s story on which homeowners have been most affected .

Could you live for 18 months with no permanent address? One couple decided to give up renting and house-sit full-time in order to save for a downpayment. And while no path to homeownership is easy, not paying rent certainly helps.

Nicholas, 35, an electrician, had discovered the unconventional savings approach in Yellowknife, where he house sat and took care of pets for three months. Then about a year before he and his 36-year-old fiancée, a speech therapist, planned to move to Whitehorse, they gave up renting full time and decided to house-sit full-time for as long as they could. “I was like, ‘This is pretty sick,’” he told Zahra Khozema. “I get this whole house by myself and I get to enjoy some pets.”

To be sure, there were drawbacks: the chaos of living out of boxes and your car, figuring out where to send mail and moving sometimes every few weeks. But how much did they save, and what did it mean they could afford in Whitehorse? Read the story to see where they landed.
