content_blocks.text: By happenstance, on March 10, the MPs on the health committee who had voiced concern the previous summer voted to summon Grifols to testify during a series of hearings on pharmaceutical sovereignty. Conservative MP Matt Strauss noted Grifols had turned down an earlier invitation to appear, but he pressed his colleagues to take the unusual step of requesting the company’s presence so it could explain why some of its products from Montreal were being sold overseas. The testimony was set for two weeks later.

content_blocks.text: Then the following day, news of the deaths broke. CBC and Globe and Mail reporters had been chasing tips that two Winnipeg donors had died and on March 11, the news outlets began reporting on the deaths. The accounts of what happened to Ms. Alabede relied on her friends, who had gone to the hospital to identify her body after she passed. Health Canada and Grifols confirmed the deaths, but provided few other details.

content_blocks.text: On March 25, Grifols filed its final investigation report on Ms. Alabede’s death with Health Canada. The report was substantially similar to the one the company had filed in November, but now contained a copy of a report from Manitoba’s chief medical examiner. The short report included the results of the autopsy in October and declared her cause of death as “sudden cardiac death” linked to “dilated cardiomegaly,” a medical term for an enlarged heart. Ms. Alabede’s family believes she was unaware she had an underlying heart condition.

content_blocks.text: The next day, March 27, an unspecified Health Canada staff member wrote an internal medical summary of Ms. Alabede’s case. The staff member based their summary entirely on Grifols’s report and the attached document from the medical examiner. The summary said Ms. Alabede’s death was “temporally coincident” with the plasma donation but not caused by it. The autopsy noted Ms. Alabede’s cardiac problems began while she was donating, but did not say the activity did or did not contribute to her death.

content_blocks.text: The medical summary also said all standard operating procedures were followed – language that echoed the Grifols report, but was at odds with the investigation from Health Canada inspectors, which found procedures were not followed properly. Health Canada has never explained the discrepancy and has since qualified its comments about the medical summary by saying it is not the department’s role to determine a cause of death.

content_blocks.text: The following Monday, March 30, Health Canada imposed terms and conditions on Grifols’s licence, which covered 16 of the company’s 17 locations. (The Winnipeg site on Innovation Drive was on a separate licence.) The regulator said the move was necessary because of deficiencies uncovered during its virtual inspection of the company’s head office. Those deficiencies included donors not being screened properly and staffing not being appropriate, such as physicians or physician substitutes not always being present.

content_blocks.text: And then on April 3, Good Friday, Health Canada communications staff sent out an e-mail to reporters: The regulator had determined there was “no linkage” between the deaths of the two donors in Winnipeg and the plasma donation process. content_blocks.text: Throughout the spring, CBS remained relatively quiet about the controversy. Dr. Sher suggested at an open CBS board meeting on June 18 that the problems weren’t critical if Health Canada allowed Grifols sites to remain open.

content_blocks.text: That state of affairs wouldn’t last much longer. The following week, on June 23, Health Canada inspectors made a surprise visit to the Taylor Avenue location in Winnipeg. They yet again found problems with donor screening and standard procedures not being followed, among other concerns, and said the company was not abiding by the conditions that had been imposed. Health Canada warned of further consequences that could include suspending operations.

stories.title: Dynamic race underway to see who will be Ottawa’s next mayor
stories.summary: Four top candidates are vying to prove who can best manage the city’s top issues, including homelessness, transit and municipal taxation
stories.author: Ian Bailey, Marie Woolf
stories.content:
Federal politics and Parliament dominate the typical Canadian perspective on Ottawa , the nation’s capital. The phrase “Ottawa says” has long been synonymous with decisions by the federal government.

But, with municipal elections across Ontario on Oct. 26, Ottawa voters are getting set to make decisions of their own, including choosing who will be the next mayor of their city, the second-most populous in Ontario and home to more than one million people.

There’s a debate underway about who can best manage the issues that are top-of-mind for local voters, including crime, homelessness, public disorder, transit and municipal taxation.

Although there are 14 names on the mayoral ballot, polling shows that incumbent Mark Sutcliffe is facing a concerted challenge from at least three of the candidates: veteran city councillor Jeff Leiper; businessman Alex Lawson; and Neil Saravanamuttoo, a former senior economist with the federal Finance Department.

Pollster David Valentin, the principal at Liaison Strategies, says the mayoral race in Ottawa is one of the most interesting ones in Ontario right now.

“It seems more competitive,” he said in an interview. “I think, all things being equal, that [Sutcliffe] will probably get re-elected. The field is so split, it seems unlikely to me that that would not be the case.”

With a big field of candidates, Mr. Valentin said that Mr. Sutcliffe could win another term with 35 per cent or so of the vote.

“But the chemistry is there that something interesting could happen. There could be an upset.”

Whoever wins on Oct. 26 gets to govern a municipal area created by the provincial government in 2001 to combine the former Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton and 11 other municipalities into a single city.

Canada has many large cities, but only one national capital.

“It’s a city unlike any other in Canada,” said Mr. Sutcliffe, a former broadcaster who was new to politics when he was first elected in 2022. He succeeded Jim Watson who had a 14½-year run over two stints between 1997 and 2022.

The city faces Quebec on the other side of the Ottawa River. Key players that any mayor has to deal with include the federal government and the National Capital Commission, a federal Crown corporation that manages 11 per cent of all the land in the capital region, ON both the Ontario and Quebec sides of the river. Ottawa is also home to scores of embassies and diplomatic residences.

“It’s a unique city with unique challenges, but it’s also a big city with many of the same challenges as other big cities in Canada,” said Mr. Sutcliffe.

Mr. Valentin has tracked traffic, transit and city spending affecting property taxes as issues in the mayoral race. And there’s crime. “Perceived, increased homelessness, whether it’s real or not. Graffiti. All of these things are feeding into a feedback loop now where people are increasingly telling us they feel unsafe in different parts of the city,” he said.

Key rivals for the mayor’s job are pushing the narrative that Mr. Sutcliffe has been idle, which he rejects by citing movement on a number of files.

“I think we have gotten a lot done in the last four years.”

He notes his administration has negotiated an agreement with the province that would see Ontario Premier Doug Ford ’s government take on responsibility for the O-Train LRT; has ordered scores of new buses; enjoyed solid relations with the federal and provincial governments; hired more police officers; and committed to end youth homelessness by 2030.

Six Ottawa Liberal MPs, including Defence Minister David McGuinty and former treasury board president Mona Fortier, have issued a statement in support of him.

Five prominent conservatives, including former federal cabinet ministers John Baird and Lisa Raitt, did the same.

In an interview, Mr. Sutcliffe acknowledged visible downtown homelessness, a concern for many. “I understand why residents feel that way because it does feel, at times, like the problem is growing faster than the solutions we are able to provide,” he said.

“That’s the reality, not just in Ottawa, but elsewhere,” he said. “It does feel, at times, like whenever we help one person, there’s another person who is in need of help and that’s why we need to step up our efforts.”

A 2024 city-led count found 2,952 people experiencing homelessness in the nation’s capital, up slightly from 2,612 in the previous count in 2021.

Mr. Leiper, a city councillor for 12 years, has pledged to boost crisis response in Ottawa to help tackle homelessness, and says he would build more supportive housing on city-owned land for people who are relying on shelters, as well as more affordable not-for-profit housing.

As part of a wider investment program in city services, he would restore bus routes cut under Mr. Sutcliffe’s tenure.

Mr. Leiper said he is “open to some affordable and predictable tax increases” to raise the $12-million required to pay for the buses, as well as to cover other costs. But he says the claim by Mr. Sutcliffe that he is planning 7-,8- or 9-per-cent tax increases is not true.

“My commitment is not to do that. My tax increase will be affordable, and my tax increase will be predictable,” he said, so there are not “big spikes.”

In an interview, Mr. Leiper says there is a currently a $10.8-billion funding gap to maintain the city’s infrastructure, including roads, sewers and community recreation centres. On top of tax rises, he would introduce an infrastructure levy, estimated at about $40 per Ottawa household a year, to maintain repairs, raising $25-million annually.

Mr. Leiper says bringing in money for infrastructure improvements will provide greater leverage with the federal and provincial governments when it comes to asking for funding.

Although their political styles May be different, Mr. Leiper believes he could work with Premier Ford.

He would seek to build a “productive and good” relationship with Mr. Ford but be “more vocally firm with Queen’s Park” than Mr. Sutcliffe has been about the needs of Ottawa residents, he said.

Ottawa’s intransigent homelessness and addiction problem is a focus of the mayoral campaign of Mr. Lawson, a 38-year-old carpenter who runs a company building wooden frames for houses in the capital.

His campaign headquarters is in the heart of Chinatown, near a now-shuttered safe injection site, with dozens of addicts milling about the streets nearby.

Not only do such clusters of addicts keep customers from downtown businesses, Mr. Lawson says, but drugs are fuelling crime and kids on their way to school are finding needles on the street. The failure to adequately address the problem is also a blight on the lives of addicts, who deserve help, he says.

Mr. Lawson has consulted addicts themselves and spent time with outreach teams, shelters and the police to try to find answers. If elected, he says he would build a rehab facility that would provide wrap-around supports, including training to get people back into the workplace and help to find housing.

He said, in an interview, that his upbringing in a lower-income Ottawa neighbourhood and his business experience give him a multidimensional perspective on the city’s needs, including on public transport. One of his first acts, if elected, would be to reintroduce express bus routes.

His most eye-catching policy has been his pledge to remove every on-street parking meter in the city, saying they are deterring residents from shopping on metered streets.

Mr. Lawson says he never saw himself getting into politics. He voted for Mr. Sutcliffe last time but was looking for an alternative after seeing no tangible improvements on crime, traffic, transit and affordability and “seeing nobody.”

“It started as a joke a couple of times. People saying, “Well, why don’t you do it? Eventually it was just like, you know what - why don’t I do it?”

Mr. Saravanamuttoo said he was driven to run for mayor after trying to influence municipal policy as a community organizer. But he found working from the outside just did not lead to the changes he wanted to see.

His flagship “buck a ride” policy for public transit will, he says, attract more people to use the system and cost the city $83-million a year.

To address Ottawa’s lack of affordable housing and prohibitively high rents, the economist wants the city to invest heavily in public housing not just for low-income residents but for middle-income residents as well. Rather than creating more suburban sprawl, with its attendant infrastructure costs, he believes more housing could be built on surplus municipal and federal land near the centre of the city.

And to address the capital’s homeless problem, Mr. Saravanamuttoo wants to build a “village” of micro homes made of shipping containers as a transitional fix until permanent housing can be found for unhoused people. He has yet to seize on a location for this but says such projects have been established successfully in New Brunswick and nearby in Gatineau.

“Location is going to be key,” he said in an interview. “It is something that needs to be quite frankly discussed and negotiated with residents of Ottawa.”

stories.title: Slow down. It’s a school zone not the Twilight Zone
stories.summary: On September 9, a truck driver was clocked going 81 kilometres an hour in a 30 km/h school zone in Prince George, B.C.
stories.author: Andrew Clark
stories.content:
At around noon on September 9, a truck driver operating a tractor-trailer was clocked going 81 kilometres an hour in a 30 km/h school zone in Prince George, B.C. The Prince George Citizen reports that the truck driver, who hails from Edmonton, was caught by the BC Highway Patrol as they conducted school zone safety enforcement. They called in Commercial Vehicle Safety and Enforcement, which found that the tractor-trailer had ineffective brakes. The incident occurred outside Pineview Elementary School.

What can you say? How can someone be that bad, that incompetent, that willfully inept at the one single thing (“truck driver”) that they are supposed to do for a living? To me, it’s on the same level as a news story that reads “At around noon on September 9, an Edmonton soup-eater was caught trying to eat a bowl of clear beef broth with a fork in a restaurant called ‘Just Soup for Kids’ in Prince George, B.C.”

Reckless soup eating leaves you hungry. Reckless driving in a school zone can leave people hurt or dead.

But hey, that’s what you get when you add motorized vehicles to school zones. Dangerous driving is never good but it’s extra egregious when it happens in a school zone. And guess what? Parents and children are terrified. A recent study conducted for the Governors Highway Safety Association (Ghsa), a U.S. nonprofit that advocates for safer roads, has found that almost half of parents “whose children ride a school bus say their child has experienced a close call involving dangerous driving near a school bus or school zone.”

A 2026 CAA study found 84 per cent of parents reported seeing at least one dangerous driving behaviour near their child’s school. Only 37 per cent of parents consider their child’s school zone very safere.

According to Ghsa, of the U.S. parents surveyed:

36 per cent say their own child has experienced a close call

43 per cent know another child who has experienced a close call

91 per cent support the use of automated stop-arm enforcement (cameras that catch drivers who illegally pass school buses)

88 per cent support the use of school-zone speed enforcement cameras

95 per cent say speeding in school zones is a serious threat

53 per cent believe dangerous driving continues because drivers assume they won’t get caught.

Respondents also recounted personal experiences with reckless driving. For instance, “A couple of years ago, my neighbor’s child was stepping off the bus and starting to cross the two-lane residential street. The bus had its red lights flashing and the stop sign arm fully extended. A distracted driver in an SUV completely ignored the bus signals and sped right past the driver’s side of the bus. Luckily, the bus driver honked the horn loudly, which made the child freeze in place just in time as the car flew by.”

Or the more succinct, “My child was getting on the bus and someone tried passing on the side my child was walking on and almost struck my child.”

There was a time when most kids walked to school or took the bus. I took the school bus to kindergarten but that was back when dinosaurs roamed the earth and bell-bottoms were king. School zones have sadly become Nascar rallies. I’ve written frequently about the bedlam that occurs weekday mornings as stressed parents attempt to drop their kids off before heading to power the corporate capitalist machine. Parents are often the worst offenders when it comes to school zone driving.

The driving is so bad that you often wonder if any of the moms and dads dropping their kids off graduated from elementary school. As a parent, how can you not know that you must stop and not pass a school bus when its upper red lights are flashing and its stop arm is extended?

And yet I’ve witnessed this firsthand. Each time I’ve been overwhelmed by a melancholy wonder, as I watch a never-ending cycle in which dumb begets more dumb which begets more dumb. Let’s clear up any confusion over school zone rules. In many places in Canada, the school zone speed limit during weekdays is 30 km/h (except Nova Scotia which has a two-tiered school zone rule). Speeding fines are generally doubled in school zones.

Adam Snider, Ghsa’s director of communications, says that the 91 per cent support for automated stop-arm camera enforcement was the survey’s most surprising result.

“That’s about as close as you’ll get to a consensus on anything nowadays,” he said in an email. “Automated stop-arm camera enforcement can be hugely beneficial, with data showing that more than 90 per cent of drivers who receive a citation do not reoffend. While these programs are incredibly effective, they must be part of a comprehensive approach that utilizes all proven strategies to address the dangerous driving behaviors that put children and everyone else at risk.”

And speaking of putting everyone at risk, here’s a skill-testing question:

According to the Prince George Citizen, along with a seven-day impound for excessive speeding, what other tickets did the truck driver from Edmonton receive?

A ticket for excessive speeding, with a fine of $368

A ticket for failing to produce an out-of-province registration

A ticket for failing to produce insurance

A ticket for failing to properly mount an Electronic Driver’s Log, for a fine of $598.

All of the above.

If you chose “all of the above” give yourself a gold star. The paper estimates the total costs of “tow, impound, tickets, inspections and repairs” will be more than $3,000. Which, to be fair, is a lot less costly than all the bad things that could happen when you drive 81 km/h in a 30 km/h school zone.

stories.title: Michael J. Fox to be promoted within Order of Canada at Rideau Hall today
stories.summary: Ottawa - The actor and Parkinson’s disease advocate Michael J. Fox is set to be honoured at Rideau Hall this morning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Celebrated actor and Parkinson’s disease activist Michael J. Fox said he felt both “pride” and “humility” while receiving a promotion within the Order of Canada on Friday.

Spectators stood and applauded Fox at Rideau Hall as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially named him to the companion level of the Order of Canada.

Rideau Hall says Fox was elevated to the companion level to honour his “powerful global advocacy and unflinching honesty about Parkinson’s.”

Spectators stood and applauded Michael J. Fox at Rideau Hall Friday morning as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially inducted the celebrated actor and Parkinson’s disease activist to the companion level of the Order of Canada. Rideau Hall says Fox was elevated to the companion level to honour his “powerful global advocacy and unflinching honesty about Parkinson’s.” (Oct. 2, 2026)

“It’s so many things. But mostly it’s just growing up in Canada, loving this country, loving what it stands for and how it’s progressed and corrected course when it needed to, and stayed the course when it needed to,” Fox told The Canadian Press following the ceremony.

“I picked all that up growing up. I love Canadian music, I love that Canadian content thing. At the end, you have a 65-year-old guy who’s uniquely Canadian because of all those things.”

Parkinson’s is a progressive nervous system disorder that causes tremors, stiffness and slowness, and is linked to depression and memory problems.

Fox, who went public with his Parkinson’s diagnosis in 1998, has raised $2.5 billion for research into the disease and has shared candid experiences about the challenges faced by those living with its symptoms.

“Canada was one of the early proving grounds for (deep brain stimulation),” Fox said, pointing to advances in Parkinson’s research in Canada.

He was among 51 people inducted into, or promoted within, the Order of Canada on Friday.

Arbour said each inductee has demonstrated excellence and thanked them for their work.

“You could have used your talents solely to further your own success. Instead, you have chosen to use your skills, influence and energy to help others,” she said in French.

“Because talent, as exceptional as it May be, is not sufficient on its own. It also takes the will to get involved and to take action to improve one’s community and contribute to the common good.”

Arbour said Fox is a “shining example of this.”

“Your example reminds us of something that’s very fundamental: sustainable progress requires that we move forward with courage, imagination and determination,” she said.

“After all, back to the future has always been a much better idea than forward to the past.”

The comment was in reference to Fox’s iconic roles in the Back to the Future trilogy of movies.

“She’s very funny. Very sweet, very welcoming,” Fox said of Arbour, joking that her “average height” made him feel tall.

Yusuf Altintas, a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of British Columbia, was inducted as an officer of the Order of Canada along with Nada Jabado, a professor at McGill University who is being honoured for her work in pediatric neuro-oncology.

Former Bank of Canada governor Stephen Poloz was inducted an officer for helping to facilitate Canada’s international trade and promote its economic well-being.

Sculptor Ruth Elsie Abernethy was inducted as a member. Rideau Hall said she has created iconic life-size bronze pieces showcased around the world, and that her work explores themes of gender, heritage and nation-building.

Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporter Susanne Craig was inducted as a member for her work with The New York Times, The Globe and Mail and The Wall Street Journal.

Rideau Hall described her as one of the most outstanding journalists of her generation, citing her coverage of contemporary issues in the United States.

Colin Roswell Clarke was inducted a member for his work as founder and artistic director of the Toronto Youth Wind Orchestra program. Marcelle Dubois was inducted a member for her work on revitalizing Quebec playwriting.

Patrick Joseph Lahey, co-founder of Triton Submarines, was inducted a member for being one of the world’s leading experts on submersibles and a leading voice for safe practices in the deep diving industry, Rideau Hall said.

With files from Alessia Passafiume.

stories.title: Court records show Ontario's 'serious concerns' about three career colleges
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario government officials who inspected three career colleges found evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn't name their school or program, they alleged in reports filed in court.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario government officials who inspected three career colleges found evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program, they alleged in reports filed in court.

Inspection reports for three Academy of Learning locations are among hundreds of pages of documents that make up the record in a court challenge as the schools seek to overturn a government decision that cut off their ability to offer financial aid.

“Inspection findings indicate that AOL Bay is unable to demonstrate that Osap-funded students are actively participating in the programs they are enrolled in,” the government’s Osap compliance unit wrote in a September 2025 inspection report for a downtown Toronto location.

Experts say data suggests some issues around compliance and enforcement, but institutions say they don’t have any control over students after they

“This raises serious concerns about the reliability of the institution’s admissions practices, student identity verification, and the accuracy of academic progression and attendance records.”

The schools deny most of the allegations and also say they have taken the government’s concerns seriously, including already implementing numerous corrective actions.

The three Academy of Learning locations are among 10 that Career Colleges Ontario flagged for the government in January 2025 as having “concerning” levels of growth in applications for the Ontario Student Assistance Program — jumping 500 and 600 per cent in two years — while other schools’ activity was largely flat, the college association said in a letter.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request found that about 14,800 students at those three Academy of Learning franchise locations received more than $219 million in Osap grants in 2024-25.

Meanwhile, students at all publicly funded colleges across Ontario qualified for about $385 million in Osap grants that year, freedom-of-information data shows.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn informed five career colleges, including the three Academy of Learning locations, ON May 1 that they would not be Osap eligible as of Aug. 1. The three schools, which share a parent company, have applied for judicial review of that decision, alleging Quinn did not have the power to predetermine their eligibility for this year and that his decision is unreasonable.

Court records show Quinn’s decision followed inspections last year and earlier this year that inspectors say the schools failed, with the ministry listing similar concerns in both reports. One report covers two sites, as a North York location is a branch campus of Academy of Learning Brampton East.

One student’s account showed all of their quizzes and final exam in their business writing essentials course were completed on the same day, with the final exam taking six minutes, the Brampton inspection report said.

Another Brampton student’s account shows their final exam for a business course was completed on the first day they accessed the course, inspectors wrote. Yet another student viewed all of their business writing essentials modules and completed all quizzes on the same day in less than 15 minutes, inspectors wrote.

The credentials of a student at the North York campus were used to log into their school account from at least 211 IP addresses, inspectors wrote.

At the Bay Street location, 39 out of 42 student files examined by inspectors had IP addresses that were used to access accounts belonging to other students, who were all referred by the same recruiter, the report said.

“This pattern suggests shared login credentials, unauthorized access, and/or co-ordinated activity among users,” the report said.

“While shared networks or communal access points, such as residences or campus locations, could explain IP address overlap, the frequency and concentration of these shared IP addresses within specific community partners is notable.”

The nature of the inspectors’ findings prompted them to drill down further and contact six students, three of whom were available for a phone call.

Interviews revealed “inconsistencies,” including students unable to name their institution, program or courses, students unable to communicate in English and students claiming to attend classes in person despite being enrolled in asynchronous online programs, the inspectors wrote.

The federal government also expressed concerns about the Bay and Brampton locations in September 2025, according to letters sent to the institutions that are also part of the court record.

The government alleged unusually high growth in the amount of financial aid claimants from the schools, that there was evidence that multiple applications were completed by the same person or group, significant increases in loan default rates and that a large amount of people could not be confirmed as qualifying students.

In a February 2026 letter to the province, also in the court record, Career Colleges Ontario said the federal government’s concerns and subsequent investigations led to reduced Osap application volumes at those schools, but “application activity shifted to other institutions rather than declining.”

“This pattern aligns with complaints received from CCO members indicating that certain schools were using third-party agents who offered to redirect students to other institutions if those institutions would misrepresent or falsely report attendance in order to facilitate continued Osap disbursement,” executive director Kate Bartz wrote.

None of the findings and allegations from either level of government have been proven in court. The Academy of Learning denies most of the allegations from both levels of government and the ways in which some of their evidence is being interpreted.

Students May not have responded to the federal government’s verification attempts because they believed them to be scam calls, and other students having difficulty answering questions in interviews “can be reasonably attributed to situational and linguistic factors,” the school wrote in response to the government.

The Academy of Learning also offered up, in its response, figures showing their loan default rates to not be high, and it suggested the high growth in applications was due to offering programs relevant to workforce needs.

The schools also wrote to the province to rebut any nefarious assumptions about students’ log-ins from multiple IP address, saying Bell, Rogers and Cogeco customers are assigned dynamic IP addresses.

“The presence of the same IP address among different users does not, by itself, establish misconduct, misrepresentation, or unauthorized activity,” they wrote.

As well, the schools had submitted corrective action plans in response to their failed inspections, showing dozens of actions taken to remedy problems identified by the province.

The Academy of Learning said in a statement that many of the government concerns relate to a historical period that has since been the subject of “extensive regulatory review, corrective action plans, internal reviews, and independent compliance monitoring.”

“Since these concerns were raised, we have put in place significant additional controls across admissions, identity verification, financial aid, and academic participation and progress,” the school wrote in a statement.

“These include two-factor authentication and investigation of unusual login activity. We have co-operated extensively with both reviews and will continue to strengthen our controls wherever issues are identified.”

The instances of unusually rapid completion of courses warrants review, the Academy acknowledged, and said it has implemented additional monitoring of files before exam codes are issued.

“It’s also important to note that time spent in our online learning platform is not, ON its own, a complete measure of a student’s learning,” the Academy said in its statement.

“Students learn in different ways, some programs include third-party learning materials, and many students download textbooks and course materials to study off-line before completing their assessments. A short period of online activity or a quick assessment does not by itself mean the required learning did not take place.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

stories.content:
Montreal - Anne Latendresse retired from her job as a university professor and researcher in June. But instead of taking time to relax, the 65-year-old jumped right into a new challenge: running as a candidate for left-wing party Québec solidaire in the Oct. 5 election.

Latendresse says the timing was right. Her 26-year-old son is not only grown, but serving as her campaign manager. She also felt like her 25-year career in the Université du Québec à Montréal’s geography department, as well as involvement with social movements and non-profit organizations, had given her the skills and confidence needed to make the leap.

“I’m coming in with a sense of maturity and greater depth of knowledge,” she said in a recent interview at her campaign headquarters in the Maurice-Richard riding north of downtown Montreal. “I think it’s a good time for me to champion issues, push initiatives forward, and develop expertise.”

While Latendresse has good reasons to enter politics in her 60s, her choice is less common for women of her age.

Data from Élections Québec shows that 42.6 per cent of the candidates running in the provincial election are women. However, men outnumber women nearly two to one among candidates 60 and older, with 104 men to 58 women.

Valérie Caron, the executive director of a non-profit group that promotes parity between women and men in politics, says there could be several reasons for the underrepresentation of older women.

She said legislatures have only started nearing parity in recent years, which means older women have had fewer examples to follow. “It’s possible that women of 60 and older didn’t project themselves in that kind of role, since the role models were really limited,” she said in a phone interview.

She also notes that women generally have to be recruited in order to run, which raises questions about whether parties are approaching candidates in that age group.

Coalition Avenir Québec candidate Sonia Bélanger says ageism is an unfortunate reality in politics. “It’s very easy to do, I’ve seen it,” the outgoing health minister said in a phone interview. “I noticed certain things — not directed at me, not at my level, but toward colleagues.”

Bélanger decided to run for office in 2022 after a career spent mainly as a manager and administrator in the public health system. Like Latendresse, the now-65 year-old believes it was the right moment to run, with her two children grown and her career at its peak.

“I feel like I’m in better shape than when I was 40,” Bélanger said.

She also believes women still face more scrutiny than men, whether as managers or politicians.

“If a woman speaks loudly during a debate, people say she’s shouting,” Bélanger said. “If she tries to assert herself, they say she’s interrupting others. But that never happens with men.”

Caron’s group works with women to help develop the skills and confidence they need to run for office. But she also advocates for broader change, including the adoption of a law that would require parties to select a certain percentage of female candidates. She also pushes parties to name women in ridings that are considered winnable.

In recent years, politicians of all stripes have faced a surge of online hate and threats. While that can turn some people away from running, Caron says the main reason female politicians leave office is because they feel like their skills aren’t being used to the fullest.

Bélanger agrees that this is an important motivation. Since being elected in 2022, she’s served in a number of cabinet posts that use her expertise, including in the health, social services and seniors and caregivers portfolios.

Bélanger credits former premier François Legault’s choice to elevate women to top jobs — including current Premier Christine Fréchette — as part of the reason why 54 per cent of the Coalition Avenir Québec’s candidates are women.

Québec solidaire, which has an even higher percentage of female candidates at 59 per cent, also has a woman, Ruba Ghazal, as co-spokesperson and choice for premier.

Caron, Latendresse and Bélanger all believe that it’s important to have women of all ages in politics, and believe that older women have important expertise, experience and energy to share.

Latendresse says she’s happily spending 12 hours per day on her campaign, filling her days with debates, meet-and-greets, and canvassing by phone and door-to-door.

Bélanger says her time in government has made her believe more strongly than ever in the value of female leadership skills, including a tendency to seek dialogue and collaboration rather than conflict.

While she’s happy to see so many young women entering politics, she believes older women also need to take their place.

“Politics is the right place to keep moving initiatives forward and to serve the public well,” she said. “I believe that women aged 60 and over certainly have a place in government.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Was this Susan Stevenson campaign announcement allowed under city policy?
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 8:00 AM | Last Updated: October 2
stories.author: Andrew Lupton
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 8:00 AM | Last Updated: October 2
London’s election policy prohibits candidates from using city facilities for campaign activities

Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson held a campaign announcement outside London city hall on Wednesday, prompting questions about whether the event complied with the city’s policy governing the use of municipal property during an election.
Stevenson, the Ward 4 councillor who is running for mayor, set up a podium in Reginald Cooper Square, steps from the north wall of city hall.
A sign at the base of the podium listed campaign promises that include greater oversight of city operations and a smaller local government.
The City of London has a policy governing the use of city resources during election campaigns.

It says candidates cannot rent or use city-owned facilities for meetings that directly or indirectly benefit an election campaign or for election-related purposes. It also says campaign-related signs or materials cannot be displayed or distributed at city-owned or leased facilities.
The city's election information also says city property, including parks, cannot be used to host campaign events.
Asked by CBC News at Wednesday's announcement whether she was violating the policy, Stevenson said she did not believe she was.
"I don't think this is a big concern to the voters," she said. "This is not inside city hall."
Asked again whether she was breaking the rules, Stevenson said, "I don't believe so."

The city clerk's office told CBC News it does not comment on specific enforcement actions, saying those matters fall within the purview of enforcement agencies, prosecutors and the courts and are determined on a case-by-case basis.
The city policy is intended to prevent municipal resources from being used to directly or indirectly benefit an election campaign and to ensure candidates do not receive an unfair advantage.
Mayor Josh Morgan, who is running for re-election, said in a statement that the rules apply to all candidates.

"The rules for campaigning on city property are clear," he said. "And they apply to every candidate, me included. But accountability isn't something you only ask of others. It starts with yourself. That matters more when someone is asking to be mayor. If you want to run city hall, following its rules is the easy part."
Mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose said the space outside city hall is be off-limits for campaign announcements.
"It's clearly laid out in the policy," said Krose. "One rule should apply to everyone."
"When you're a councillor and a candidate for mayor, the line between city business and campaign business needs to be unmistakeable."
Another mayoral candidate, Tariq Kahan, said he would not hold a campaign event at city hall.
"The rules are clear," he said.
Stevenson is not the only mayoral candidate to have used city hall as a backdrop.

Mayoral candidate Mustafa Zeboon was shooting a social campaign video at city hall on Wednesday. Zeboon has made social media videos directed at younger voters a focus of his campaign. The topic of Wednesday's video was encouraging people to vote in advance polls, but also closed with a call for people to vote for him.

Zeboon said he wasn't aware there was a policy barring the use of city-owned facilities for election campaigns. He pointed out that one of his first campaign videos was shot at city hall and he didn't hear a word of complaint.
"Nobody told me it was an issue," he said. "It seemed like it was a law that no one really cared about."
It's unlikely that people would see someone using city property in a campaign video or announcement, and not understand the message is coming from a candidate, Zeboon said.
"No one is seeing these videos and thinking 'Oh that's the mayor,'" he said. "It's very clear from the video what my intensions are."
Stevenson has also used city hall as a backdrop for campaign videos posted to social media.
At Wednesday's announcement, Stevenson outlined several proposals she says would make city finances and council decisions more transparent, including:
Earlier access to agenda items and financial information coming to council and committee meetings.
Quarterly review of city finances including a "line-by-line" reporting of spending.
An independent auditor general and a fraud waste hotline.
A review of how senior administration spends money including "responsibilities, vacancies and executive costs" with an eye to restructuring to trim costs while "protecting front-line delivery."
Advance voting for the municipal election began on Thursday. Voting Day is on Oct. 26.

| CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 8:00 AM | Last Updated: October 2

London’s election policy prohibits candidates from using city facilities for campaign activities

Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson held a campaign announcement outside London city hall on Wednesday, prompting questions about whether the event complied with the city’s policy governing the use of municipal property during an election.

Stevenson, the Ward 4 councillor who is running for mayor, set up a podium in Reginald Cooper Square, steps from the north wall of city hall.

A sign at the base of the podium listed campaign promises that include greater oversight of city operations and a smaller local government.

The City of London has a policy governing the use of city resources during election campaigns.

It says candidates cannot rent or use city-owned facilities for meetings that directly or indirectly benefit an election campaign or for election-related purposes. It also says campaign-related signs or materials cannot be displayed or distributed at city-owned or leased facilities.

The city's election information also says city property, including parks, cannot be used to host campaign events.

Asked by CBC News at Wednesday's announcement whether she was violating the policy, Stevenson said she did not believe she was.

"I don't think this is a big concern to the voters," she said. "This is not inside city hall."

Asked again whether she was breaking the rules, Stevenson said, "I don't believe so."

The city clerk's office told CBC News it does not comment on specific enforcement actions, saying those matters fall within the purview of enforcement agencies, prosecutors and the courts and are determined on a case-by-case basis.

The city policy is intended to prevent municipal resources from being used to directly or indirectly benefit an election campaign and to ensure candidates do not receive an unfair advantage.

Mayor Josh Morgan, who is running for re-election, said in a statement that the rules apply to all candidates.

"The rules for campaigning on city property are clear," he said. "And they apply to every candidate, me included. But accountability isn't something you only ask of others. It starts with yourself. That matters more when someone is asking to be mayor. If you want to run city hall, following its rules is the easy part."

Mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose said the space outside city hall is be off-limits for campaign announcements.

"It's clearly laid out in the policy," said Krose. "One rule should apply to everyone."

"When you're a councillor and a candidate for mayor, the line between city business and campaign business needs to be unmistakeable."

Another mayoral candidate, Tariq Kahan, said he would not hold a campaign event at city hall.

"The rules are clear," he said.

Stevenson is not the only mayoral candidate to have used city hall as a backdrop.

Mayoral candidate Mustafa Zeboon was shooting a social campaign video at city hall on Wednesday. Zeboon has made social media videos directed at younger voters a focus of his campaign. The topic of Wednesday's video was encouraging people to vote in advance polls, but also closed with a call for people to vote for him.

Zeboon said he wasn't aware there was a policy barring the use of city-owned facilities for election campaigns. He pointed out that one of his first campaign videos was shot at city hall and he didn't hear a word of complaint.

"Nobody told me it was an issue," he said. "It seemed like it was a law that no one really cared about."

It's unlikely that people would see someone using city property in a campaign video or announcement, and not understand the message is coming from a candidate, Zeboon said.

"No one is seeing these videos and thinking 'Oh that's the mayor,'" he said. "It's very clear from the video what my intensions are."

Stevenson has also used city hall as a backdrop for campaign videos posted to social media.

At Wednesday's announcement, Stevenson outlined several proposals she says would make city finances and council decisions more transparent, including:

Earlier access to agenda items and financial information coming to council and committee meetings.

Quarterly review of city finances including a "line-by-line" reporting of spending.

An independent auditor general and a fraud waste hotline.

A review of how senior administration spends money including "responsibilities, vacancies and executive costs" with an eye to restructuring to trim costs while "protecting front-line delivery."

Advance voting for the municipal election began on Thursday. Voting Day is on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Quebec party leaders work to shore up support as campaign enters final stretch
stories.summary: Quebec's main party leaders are shifting their campaigns into top gear, with the election just days away.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was the primary target on Friday as his political rivals urged Quebec voters not to elect a sovereigntist government with less than three days to go in the provincial election campaign.

Leaders of the Coalition Avenir Québec and the Conservative Party both started their days by delivering warnings about a referendum that the PQ has promised to hold after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

For his part, Charles Milliard pitched his Quebec Liberals as the only federalist option, suggesting Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime and Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette were closet separatists.

“We don’t want Quebec to leave Canada,” said Milliard during a news conference on Montreal’s South Shore. “Fréchette is unable to take a stance on the national question. As for Mr. Duhaime, he voted yes in 1995.”

The Liberal leader visited five ridings, all outside of Montreal.

Duhaime used some buses in a garage as props to make his point at a news conference in Quebec City. One bus had a sign featuring the logo and slogan of the “Yes” side from the 1995 Quebec referendum, while the other had a sign with the logo of the “No” side’s campaign.

He and candidate Maïté Blanchette-Vézina closed the garage door, promising that the buses for a potential referendum campaign would never leave if the Conservatives win enough seats to hold the balance of power at the legislature.

“We’re going to make sure that the ‘Yes’ bus and the ‘No’ bus remain nothing more than a fantasy of Charles Millard and Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, and that they certainly don’t become a nightmare for Quebecers over the next four years,” he said, attacking both the PQ and Liberal leaders.

Vézina previously crossed the floor in the provincial legislature, leaving the governing Coalition Avenir Québec to join the Conservatives, which have yet to have an elected official at the national assembly.

Fréchette campaigned in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, west of Montreal, with her finance minister, Eric Girard. She warned that a PQ government would cause “colossal damage” to Quebec’s economy and trigger instability that would be felt “the very day after the election.”

She said companies that have been considering investing in Quebec “will think twice.”

“They’re asking themselves, ‘Well, in two and a half years, where will we be?’ … There are decisions that will outright exclude Quebec,” she said.

She urged Quebecers to remember the effects of the 1995 referendum on the financial sector, when banks implemented risk premiums, “which can have a domino effect on corporate financing, mortgages, the government’s borrowing costs, and infrastructure costs.”

“We’ll pay the price,” Fréchette warned.

Fréchette also told journalists that she would remain the head of the party regardless of election results. Polls show the Coalition Avenir Québec could be wiped off the political map, and Fréchette May lose her seat.

First Nations leaders have also come out against the PQ’s sovereignty plan, saying it would need their approval.

“We are not asking you to make room for us in your political agenda. We are asking you to recognize our status as a government and our right to self-determination,” wrote Lucien Wabanonik, Chief of the Anishnabe Nation of Lac Simon, in an open letter to St-Pierre Plamondon published Friday.

“Once that relationship is established, we can lay the foundation for a shared future.”

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to consult Indigenous communities in Quebec before holding a referendum, but specified they would not get a veto.

Campaigning in Quebec City, the PQ leader accused his opponents of intensifying their “fearmongering campaigns” because they have “lost credibility.”

“It becomes a caricature,” he said. “I think this actually helps the Parti Québécois a little, because it’s reached such a level that it’s obvious … that it’s a bit of a last-ditch effort. So, I’ll let my opponents say whatever they want.”

However, he walked back his comments on the role of First Nations in achieving sovereignty, saying he wants consensus. He also promised to be the premier “of absolutely everyone” in Quebec if elected.

Leftist party Québec solidaire is also sovereigntist and expecting to win seats on Monday. Co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal was in Trois-Rivières and focused her campaign on unionized workers and families.

She promised to ban lockouts during strikes, saying it’s an “outdated practice” that goes against workers’ rights. She also promised to increase family allowances and to create more spots in subsidized daycares.

The five party leaders are expected to make their final pitches to the public over the weekend before the election day on Oct. 5.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

stories.title: LPS officer facing charge in relation to on-duty incident
stories.summary: London, ON (October 2, 2026) – A London Police Service (LPS) officer has been charged following an investigation by the LPS Major Crime Section into an incident that occurred during an arrest earlier this year.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (October 2, 2026) – A London Police Service (LPS) officer has been charged following an investigation by the LPS Major Crime Section into an incident that occurred during an arrest earlier this year.

On April 29, 2026, shortly before 2 a.m., a 33-year-old woman was placed under arrest by LPS officers.

Following her arrest, Oleoresin Capsicum (OC) spray was deployed. The use of OC spray in Ontario is subject to mandatory use-of-force reporting requirements and a subsequent review process.

During that review, concerns were identified regarding the circumstances surrounding the use of force. As a result, the matter was referred to members of the LPS Major Crime Section to investigate possible criminal conduct arising from the use of the OC spray.

Following the investigation, Constable Brandon Mihalides, 29, of London, has been charged with one count of assault with a weapon and has been reassigned to non-operational administrative duties.

Policing depends on public trust and confidence. Maintaining that trust requires police services to have effective systems of oversight and accountability, and to ensure that when concerns regarding police conduct are identified, they are addressed appropriately, transparently and thoroughly.

Accountability is a fundamental principle of policing and public service. Our community rightly expects police officers to exercise their authorities professionally and lawfully. It also expects its police service to identify concerns when they arise, examine the evidence objectively and take appropriate action where warranted.

As this matter is now before the courts, no further information will be provided at this time.

The accused is scheduled to attend court on December 30, 2026, in relation to the charge.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Two charged in north-end shooting
stories.summary: London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section have charged two London men following an extensive investigation into a shooting in the city’s north end this summer.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section have charged two London men following an extensive investigation into a shooting in the city’s north end this summer.

On August 9, 2026, at approximately 12:30 a.m., police responded to multiple reports of gunfire in the area of Kipps Lane and Arbour Glen Crescent. Two suspects were reported fleeing the area on foot before police arrived.

Investigators determined that two individuals had discharged firearms. While no one was injured, a vehicle leaving the area was struck by gunfire and multiple cartridge casings were recovered at the scene.

Following an extensive investigation, members of the LPS Major Crime Section identified two suspects. Both were arrested in late September.

Dante Guerrero, 19, and Kaleb Forden, 20, both of London, have been jointly charged with:

Discharge a firearm in a reckless manner; and

Possess restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a licence.

Forden has additionally been charged with one count of possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking.

“Gunfire in our neighbourhoods is unacceptable. Every time a firearm is discharged in our community, there is the potential for devastating consequences for innocent people,” said Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau of the LPS Major Crime Section. “Those who choose to use firearms in our city should expect our investigators to pursue every available avenue to identify those responsible and bring them before the courts. These arrests are the result of a determined and thorough investigation by our Major Crime investigators.”

The investigation remains ongoing. Investigators continue to ask anyone who was in the area between 12 a.m. and 12:45 a.m. on August 9, 2026, and who May have dash-cam, residential or business surveillance footage, to contact the London Police Service.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Man facing charges following investigation into data breach
stories.summary: London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Cyber Crime Unit have charged a London man following an investigation into the unauthorized access of London Hydro customer information.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Cyber Crime Unit have charged a London man following an investigation into the unauthorized access of London Hydro customer information.

On June 19, 2026, police received a report from London Hydro regarding a suspected compromise of its customer information.

Investigators learned that between June 5 and June 17, 2026, an individual accessed customer accounts and obtained customer information without authorization.

As part of the investigation, police executed a search warrant at a London residence on August 13, 2026. Several electronic devices were seized and subsequently examined.

Through a forensic examination of the seized electronic devices, investigators located evidence that linked the suspect male to the unauthorized access of London Hydro customer information.

As a result of the investigation, Rony Hotimsky, 40, of London, has been charged with:

Fraudulently obtain any computer service; and

Mischief over $5000.

The accused was arrested this morning and is expected to re-appear in London court on December 29, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information related to this investigation is asked to contact the London Police Service Cyber Crime Unit at 519-661-5670 or CyberCrime@londonpolice.CA . Anonymous information can also be provided through Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477) or online through London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Stephen Harper warns Albertans against supporting separatists
stories.summary: "I love my country, and I love my province," the former prime minister wrote. "I do not wish to pit one against the other. I believe that is how most
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — Stephen Harper is warning Albertans against setting the province on a path toward secession by using their votes in an upcoming referendum in an attempt to send Ottawa a message.

In an essay published Friday in the Calgary Herald , Harper also expressed optimism over how he sees the Liberals under Prime Minister Mark Carney turning a page from the “anti-Alberta” policies of Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

“As a former prime minister of Canada, staying silent on the upcoming referendum on Alberta secession is not an option. But I wish it were,” he wrote.

“I love my country, and I love my province. I do not wish to pit one against the other. I believe that is how most Albertans feel.”

It is one of the fullest arguments the former Conservative leader has made in support of the federation and against the push for separation ahead of the referendum on Oct. 19.

Alberta Conservative MPs are defending their efforts in the province’s sovereignty referendum, arguing they’re doing all they can to keep the

But it came as some separatist leaders seek to sway Albertans by painting a vote for “Option 2” on the ballot as not a vote to actually separate, but as a way to express how they feel about their province’s treatment by Ottawa.

A towering figure within the Conservative movement, Harper served as prime minister from 2006 to 2015 as a member of Parliament from Calgary. He was first elected as a member of the populist Reform Party, which was birthed out of backlash to Ottawa’s actions in Western Canada, before he helped create the modern Conservative party and became its leader.

His call for national unity follows those of former members of his government, including Jason Kenney, a Conservative cabinet minister who later led Alberta as premier. Former Conservative MP Monte Solberg has joined Kenney in backing a third-party advertising group urging Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

This week, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre appeared at a fundraiser in Edmonton to drum up support for another third-party group, led by one of his Alberta MPs, which is focused on getting Conservative voters in the deep blue province out to vote to secure a victory to stay .

While Albertans, Harper wrote, “are naturally inclined to love Canada and have made disproportionate contributions to every facet of national life,” they have been left to wonder “why Canada periodically seems to not love them.”

Carney has said he has looked to the former prime minister for advice since coming to power. Last month, Harper was one of the headline speakers at a summit for foreign investors Carney held in Toronto, where he declared the gathering was such a good idea that “I wish I had thought of it.”

In that speech, Harper also threw his support behind Carney’s decision to suspend trade talks with the United States, and praised his plans for regulatory overhauls to get more major projects off the ground.

He offered a similar message to Albertans after placing the blame for the bubbling up of separatist sentiments at the feet of Trudeau and his environmental policies.

“Fortunately, I believe things are already changing. While I remain a committed Conservative, the reality is that the Liberal party has not always been as an anti-Alberta as the two Trudeaus,” Harper wrote, referring also to Trudeau’s father, former prime minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau.

“At other times, it has openly enabled the growth of our energy sector. Like (Alberta) Premier Danielle Smith, I see strong evidence that this Liberal government is returning to those roots.”

When it comes to the upcoming referendum vote, Harper said he stands against separation, adding that beyond the risk that path carries “there is nothing resembling the credible leadership necessary to establish a new country.”

“However, the truth is that the referendum is not really about separation,” he wrote.

“It is a ‘referendum to have a referendum.’ Most voting for it will do so just to ‘send a message,’ in other words, to keep the threat alive in the hope of retaining the benevolent attention that the province has recently been receiving from Ottawa. I believe that approach is mistaken.”

Pointing to past battles over Quebec independence, Harper warned of the consequences of similar debates playing out in Alberta for years to come, saying he believes those “downsides” are not “fully understood” in the province.

“Did Quebec gain some favours as a consequence of the separation threat? Yes, at first,” Harper wrote.

“But that dissipated badly over time as Quebec’s image was increasingly damaged in the rest of Canada. It vanished altogether when the separatists were actually in power, leading to major constitutional amendments without Quebec’s consent.”

stories.title: Software problem caused widespread 911 outage last month, Bell says
stories.summary: The outage in the early hours of Sept. 17 lasted for 87 minutes, according to the telecom giant’s report.
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
A software problem sparked the outage that shut down 911 emergency lines for nearly an hour and half last month, Bell says.

The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (Crtc) required the telecom giant to submit a post-outage report within two weeks of the incident, and Bell submitted it Thursday .

Here’s what Bell disclosed in an abridged version of the report:

On Sept. 17, “a software failure in Bell’s Next-Generation Core Services (Ngcs) platform — the call-routing platform of Bell’s NG9-1-1 network — caused the platform to stop accepting new 9-1-1 calls or new call transfers to public safety answering points (PSAPs) through the NG9-1-1 network,” Bell said Thursday.

In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the company attributed the outage to a “network problem,” saying at the time that it was still investigating the root cause.

The outage lasted from 3:13 a.m. to 4:40 a.m., a period of 87 minutes, Bell said.

The incident affected 911 calls transiting through the NG9-1-1 network to 79 PSAPs and 63 originating network providers in Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, according to Bell.

On Sept. 17, the Nova Scotia government said intermittent 911 outages could affect some cellphone and VoIP (voice over internet protocol) users.

At the time of the outage, Bell spokesperson Elise von Scheel said it was not caused by a cyberattack.

The company reiterated that in its report Thursday, adding that the outage wasn’t caused “by any change activity, planned or unplanned.”

“The root cause was identified on the day of the outage and has been fixed,” Bell wrote.

“Bell has since developed and deployed new independent monitoring mechanisms as a further failsafe,” the company said in the report. “Bell takes its responsibility as a 9-1-1 Service Provider with the utmost seriousness and is committed to the reliability, resilience, and continuous improvement of emergency calling services.”

The company also pledged to implement more automated alarm systems to allow for earlier call-outs to experts, among the “next steps” it listed in the report.

Bell added that it plans to hold a post-incident debrief session for PSAPs and for third-party call operators to share what it learned from the incident, and that it already had a call with other NG9-1-1 providers to do so.

The Star reached out Friday night to all five police departments in the GTA — Toronto as well as Durham, Halton, Peel and York regions — and asked whether they have changed any protocols in the wake of the outage.

“As part of our standard practice, we continually review significant incidents to identify any lessons learned and opportunities to strengthen our response,” Toronto police spokesperson Nadine Ramadan said in an email Saturday night.

Toronto police have been in contact with Bell about the outage, Ramadan added, while noting that the outage originated with the 911 service provider and “was not related to Toronto Police Service technology.” She referred any questions about changes to Bell’s systems or processes to the telecom giant.

Peel police spokesperson Tyler Bell-Morena said in an email Friday night that his department couldn’t comment until Monday at the earliest, while the other three police forces have not replied.

stories.title: PQ leader’s vow to break with monarchy raises prospect of constitutional showdown
stories.summary: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says a PQ government would introduce legislation to abolish the office of lieutenant-governor
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
The leader of the Parti Québécois says he will break with the monarchy in Quebec if he becomes premier, invoking the spectre of a constitutional battle that critics say could help him drum up support for an unpopular referendum on independence.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said this week that it’s “unacceptable” for a representative of the British Crown to have a role in Quebec’s Parliament. If the PQ wins the provincial election on Oct. 5, he said his government will pass a law eliminating the role of lieutenant-governor.

Quebec has for decades taken steps to reduce the visibility of the monarchy in its legislature, including when the Coalition Avenir Québec government scrapped a mandatory oath of allegiance to the Crown four years ago – a change that was also driven by the PQ Leader.

But experts say a move to unilaterally abolish the function of lieutenant- governor is transparently unconstitutional and would inevitably wind up in court.

“It’s almost being done intentionally just to cause a constitutional crisis that then bolsters the impetus for a referendum,” said Lawrence David, who teaches constitutional law at the University of Ottawa.

The PQ is widely expected to win Monday’s election and could claim a majority of the seats in the province’s National Assembly. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold the province’s third sovereignty referendum by 2030, even though support for independence in Quebec is currently below 30 per cent.

On Tuesday, the PQ Leader said that it’s “not normal” for a representative of King Charles III to “tell us what to do.” Lieutenant-governors swear in premiers and cabinet ministers, open legislative sessions and grant royal assent to bills passed by provincial legislatures.

“There is nothing preventing the National Assembly from acting as a sovereign legislature and passing a law that abolishes the lieutenant-governor’s duties and stops allocating funds to this charade, which wastes money that could be put to better use,” he told reporters.

He said he would redirect the provincial government’s contribution to the lieutenant-governor’s office – about $1.3-million in the 2026-27 fiscal year – to fighting homelessness. The lieutenant-governor’s salary and pension are paid by the federal government, while the province covers a portion of office expenses.

But Mr. David said any such constitutional amendment would require the unanimous consent of the federal Parliament and every provincial legislature, and cannot be carried out unilaterally.

“Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon knows that there is no way to argue that it’s not manifestly unconstitutional,” he said. If a court struck down the Quebec law, he added, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon could argue that the only way to rid Quebec of the monarchy is through separation.

Speaking to reporters Thursday, the PQ Leader denied that he’s spoiling for a fight with Ottawa ahead of a referendum, which he has said would not take place until U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

“I am preparing Quebeckers for three years of true democracy, with my sole loyalty being to the interests of Quebeckers,” he said.

Patrick Taillon, a professor of constitutional law at Laval University, said Quebec has a long history of taking steps to make the monarchy “invisible” in the province without abolishing it outright.

In Ottawa, the governor-general typically delivers the Speech from the Throne to open sessions of Parliament. After Mark Carney became Prime Minister last year, the King delivered the speech himself during a visit to Canada.

But in Quebec, the lieutenant-governor since 1973 has given only a short inaugural address. The opening speech is then delivered by the Premier.

Prof. Taillon pointed out that Quebec has also replaced the word “Crown” with “state” in provincial laws, and earlier this year announced that it would remove the British crown from the province’s official coat of arms.

On Tuesday, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said he would ask the province’s lieutenant-governor, Manon Jeannotte, not to attend the opening speech at the National Assembly if the PQ forms government. His caucus has previously boycotted the lieutenant-governor’s address.

Such cosmetic changes have a low chance of provoking constitutional challenges, Prof. Taillon said. But scrapping the role entirely would have a “high risk of being challenged.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has for years called for the monarchy to be excised from Quebec. In 2021, the new PQ Leader published a sardonic video in which he listed several reasons to “love the monarchy,” including that it “reminds us of our colonial heritage.” He then called on the legislature to abolish the office of lieutenant-governor.

After he was elected to the National Assembly in 2022, he and his caucus members were denied entry to the legislature after they refused to swear allegiance to the King.

The move propelled the CAQ government to pass a law stating that only an oath of allegiance to the Quebec people would henceforth be required. Mr. David is now challenging that law in court.
