stories.title: B.C.'s large parties on track to field candidates in all ridings as deadline looms
stories.summary: Victoria - The major parties running in British Columbia's election appear to be on track to fill each of the 93 ridings, but smaller parties are struggling ahead of the Oct. 3 nomination deadline.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Promises to lower the cost of gasoline from B.C. New Democrat Leader David Eby and praise for a planned pipeline from Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson fuelled British Columbia’s snap election campaign on Thursday.

Eby’s platform for relief at the gas pumps comes in two parts: a temporary reduction of the provincial motor fuel tax by 10 cents per litre on both gasoline and diesel, and a permanent “price guard” to regulate the price at the pumps.

The leader said the measures would save the average two-car family up to $100 per month, but would also cost the provincial treasury about $250 million, with additional details forthcoming.

The fuel promise was criticized by Lorne Doerkson, the interim B.C. Conservative leader, who reminded reporters that Eby made a financial promise before the 2024 election that he didn’t keep.

“Just two years ago, there were promises made for a thousand-dollars of relief to families and to homes and to people in this province, and he failed to deliver that, and I think he needs to answer that,” Doerkson said.

Eby had promised a direct rebate of $1,000 to the average household as one of his campaign’s signature planks in the 2024 election.

In February 2025, then-finance minister Brenda Bailey said that government could not pay the so-called “grocery rebate” because of the provincial deficit.

Asked whether voters could trust his promises, Eby pointed to the elimination of the carbon tax, which he said was “probably the largest” tax cut in provincial history at $2 billion.

He acknowledged that “circumstances” changed after the 2024 election but said they’ll “make sure the tax cut actually reaches the pockets” of B.C. residents.

The Ndp’s proposed measures against price gouging mirror rules that already exist in Atlantic Canada, where they have worked, he added.

“We’re going to ensure stability for gas prices, predictability and transparency,” Eby said. “These are pieces that have been missing, and as a result, British Columbians are paying too much for gas.”

Eby said Thursday that if the NDP was re-elected in the Oct. 24 election his government would ask the B.C. Utilities Commission to set the maximum price that fuel stations can charge.

It would be updated weekly as the benchmark price for crude oil fluctuates, he said.

“Yes, government needs to step up and say, ‘we’ll reduce the tax on gas in this time to support families,’” he said. “But also, government needs it to use its force. We need to use our authority. We need to use our rules to make sure that British Columbians are not gouged.”

Big oil and gas companies have been exploiting conflicts overseas to make record profits, leaving ordinary drivers and truckers paying the price every time they fill up, Eby said.

He made the announcement at a gas station in Surrey, a riding-rich area that the NDP needs to win if it’s to form government.

Doerkson spoke at a campaign event in Vancouver, where he praised the federal government’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project of national interest.

He said his party supports a second pipeline from northern Alberta to B.C.‘s southern coast, because the world desperately needs Canadian energy.

“We welcome it because British Columbia’s economy desperately needs a boost. And the events of the last few years have shown just how important this is to be self-sufficient,” Doerkson said.

Eby said during a later media availability that the province has an important role to play in the pipeline process to protect the interests of B.C. residents, “but we also recognize that our projects, our priorities, need the same level of attention from the federal government,” he said.

That is why, Eby said, his province fought so hard for the Canada-British Columbia Co-operative Prosperity Agreement announced in July.

The accord calls for federal investments worth about $20 billion into infrastructure and resource projects across B.C.

The B.C. Green Party announced a high-profile candidate on Thursday as it released its platform on the toxic drug crisis.

Former B.C. chief coroner Lisa Lapointe will run under the Green banner in Saanich South, the same riding where former Global TV reporter Richard Zussman will run for the NDP.

Lapointe was B.C.‘s chief coroner for 13 years and made recommendations to save lives, some of which were rejected by the NDP government.

“I recognize that the toxic drug crisis will only be solved when politicians are willing to show leadership; when regulated alternatives are available, when voluntary treatment is available when people need it, and when people who use drugs have the same access to resources, medical care, housing, dignity and respect as anyone else,” Lapointe said in a statement issued Thursday.

She said in testimony to a B.C. Supreme Court last December at a constitutional challenge by founders of a compassion club that the NDP government ignored multiple recommendations from experts to create a safer drug supply that did not require a prescription.

The judge in that case tossed out criminal convictions for the founders this week and gave the government six months to rework the law because the act that prohibited them from selling safer drugs “criminalizes life-saving conduct” by the pair.

Lapointe’s name has not yet appeared among the 11 candidates officially running for the Greens.

CentreBC has five official candidates, while OneBC has two official candidates.

All three parties say their candidate count is higher than that, but all are under 20 each and the cut off to register candidates looms on Oct. 3.

Elections BC lists 55 official candidates for the B.C. New Democrats, while there are 45 people confirmed for the Conservatives as of Oct. 1.

Both parties say on their websites that those numbers are much higher and both appear on track to field candidates in all 93 ridings.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec parties make final pitches with election days away
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec’s political parties are making their final pitches to voters with just days to go before the provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The leader of the Parti Québécois asked voters on Thursday to give him a majority government, as his party continues to lead in the polls with just days to go before the provincial election.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon delivered the message in separate morning radio show interviews in both English and French.

He says he needs a majority government to get things done and to implement his program.

In an interview with English-language radio station Cjad, St-Pierre Plamondon said his party was considering the scenarios of either a minority or majority PQ government as serious possibilities.

He repeated that sentiment later in the day in an address to supporters, who he urged to not take anything for granted.

“It will be tight, there will be tight battles in every region until the end,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon also told Radio-Canada Thursday that his government would be “handcuffed” in a minority scenario, and called for a strong and stable government to reverse the damage from eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec leadership.

Later, St-Pierre Plamondon urged each Parti Québécois voter to try to convince one undecided person to vote for his party, and launched an appeal to voters who haven’t yet made up their minds.

“We believe that the change we want to see will come through the quality of the team, but also through the stability and strength of a government that will truly have the means to realize its promises.”

The major party leaders spent much of the day on the defensive, working to shore up support in ridings that are expected to be tight.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard spent time in the Eastern Townships regions, where he’s battling to secure himself a legislature seat.

Québec solidaire’s Ruba Ghazal was in Montreal to pitch a plan to ban evictions during the winter, as polls suggest her party could be in trouble in some of the ridings it won in 2022.

Ghazal noted that the race isn’t over, and urged people to vote “with their hearts,” instead of strategically.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, meanwhile, suggested that St-Pierre Plamondon and U.S. President Donald Trump both want to “weaken Canada,” even as she faced a new round of questions about her response to allegations of foreign interference earlier in the election.

Fréchette had made an early statement saying she was “very concerned” by a report of possible interference coming from the U.S., before later saying there was no reason to be concerned about the integrity of the election.

Fréchette admitted that she should have waited to have more information before sounding the alarm.

Quebecers go to the polls on Oct. 5.

stories.title: Advocates say Quebec rules keep unhoused voters from polls as election nears
stories.summary: Montreal - Marcel Dionne Jr. says he won’t let homelessness stop him from voting.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Marcel Dionne Jr. says he won’t let homelessness stop him from voting.

The 66-year-old has been living in transitional housing for the last four months, and plans to list the address of that facility as his residence when he casts his ballot in the Oct. 5 Quebec election.

“I don’t want to be forgotten, I want to be heard,” he said.

Dionne Jr. has followed the campaign closely. He said he has been worried about escalating costs for rent and hasn’t heard any promises that would address his concerns. Still, he said participating in the democratic process is important.

But while the challenges faced by Dionne Jr., and other unhoused people have dominated the campaign’s final weeks, it will likely be difficult for many of them to cast their ballots.

Quebec’s rules for voters without a fixed address are more restrictive than federal rules, and advocates say the gap is disenfranchising a population that has grown to over 12,000 people, increasing by nearly 20 per cent in four years.

Scarlett Martinez of the community group Tapaj Québec wants the provincial government to change election voting rules to eliminate the barriers that make it harder for unhoused people to vote.

She estimates that less than one per cent of those experiencing homelessness cast a ballot.

“For people who live in situations where there May be fewer options, it can be more restrictive,” she said. “At the federal level, it’s much simpler.”

Elections Canada has long allowed polling stations to be set up inside community organizations, like shelters and soup kitchens.

Élections Québec asked the national assembly to approve a pilot project to make voting more accessible to those experiencing homelessness. But PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon objected to the proposal in the legislature last spring, citing concerns about “electoral fraud.”

“If third parties approach certain groups and say, ‘Go vote,’ … we’re opening the door to possibilities that, in my opinion, need to be considered more seriously,” the PQ leader told journalists last March, when his party voted against the proposal.

That objection contrasts with the PQ’s platform in the current campaign. The party has said homelessness was its “top priority,” with St-Pierre Plamondon pledging to make himself the homelessness superminister if elected.

In Quebec, unhoused voters can confirm their identity with a statement signed by a community organization where they receive services. However, Élections Québec acknowledged in an email that this measure “May not be suitable for everyone experiencing homelessness,” since many would not have access to community support.

At the Old Brewery Mission, a shelter in downtown Montreal, about a dozen people gathered in the cafeteria to watch the final debate of the campaign Sept. 23. Some were scanning the local newspaper waiting for the debate to start. Others scoffed or nodded along as the five leaders presented their visions for the province.

A handful said they planned to cast a ballot.

There are posters around the shelter with information related to the election, and staff are trained to accompany residents to the nearest polling station.

Supervisor Marie-France Chauvin says staff make sure residents feel that they can be heard and affect change. While some are very politically engaged, others are disillusioned, she says.

“Some feel so neglected by politicians that they’ve lost faith in politics,” said Chauvin.

Montreal’s public consultation office recommended in a 2025 report that the province change its rules in line with those of Elections Canada. It noted that community organizations want to assist people in the voting process from start to finish.

“Excluded individuals … are cut off from the means that allow them to participate in decisions that affect their neighbourhood, their city, their region, and their country, leading them to see themselves as having no rights and no voice,” the report says.

Robert Brunet, who works for a local rights defence group, says people experiencing homelessness can also experience social profiling at the polling station, which discourages them from voting. Having experienced homelessness in the 2000s, he adds that it’s crucial for society’s most vulnerable to participate in the democratic process.

“Generally speaking, public funds and the party in power are directed toward communities that exercise their right to vote,” said Brunet. “And it’s going to take a lot of money to solve homelessness.”

Michel A. Messier, who has a room at the Old Brewery Mission, said he didn’t know he could vote using the shelter’s address. The man, who is turning 74, added he hasn’t cast a ballot in over 30 years.

“It doesn’t change anything,” he said. “But if someone brings me (to the polls), I’ll vote.”

Montreal’s public consultation office recommended in a 2025 report that the province change its rules in line with those of Elections Canada. It noted that community organizations want to assist people in the voting process from start to finish.

“Excluded individuals … are cut off from the means that allow them to participate in decisions that affect their neighbourhood, their city, their region, and their country, leading them to see themselves as having no rights and no voice,” the report says.

Robert Brunet, who works for a local rights defence group, says people experiencing homelessness can also experience social profiling at the polling station, which discourages them from voting. Having experienced homelessness in the 2000s, he adds that it’s crucial for society’s most vulnerable to participate in the democratic process.

stories.title: Carney's electoral Trump card is falling flat in B.C., Quebec elections
stories.summary: With the opposition in disarray, Eby never mentioned the new interim Conservative leader, but referenced Donald Trump at least 20 times.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — When British Columbia Premier David Eby took the risky step last week of calling an election with almost exactly half of his mandate left, he didn’t seem too clear why he was doing so.

But there was no doubt who he wanted to run against.

With the opposition conservatives in disarray, Eby never mentioned the new interim B.C. Conservative leader in his Sept. 22 campaign-opening speech. But he referenced U.S. President Donald Trump at least 20 times, saying it was an “existential moment” and that the New Democratic government would erect a “firebreak” against the American threat.

Less than a month earlier, Québec Premier Christine Fréchette opened her campaign by making it clear that she wanted Trump on the ballot too. Fréchette called the unpopular U.S. leader “her main opponent.”

In both cases, the two premiers seemed to be following the path created by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who won big in the 2025 federal election because he presented himself as the best defender of Canadian interests against Trump’s threats to the country’s economy and sovereignty.

And in both provincial cases, the plan, at least so far, has failed.

“(Voters are) not looking for a rhetorical opposition to Trump,” said Stewart Prest, a political scientist at the University of British Columbia.

That view is backed up by the polls. Both Eby and Fréchette’s numbers have plunged and are now at risk of being tossed out of office.

So what happened to playing the Trump card? Has that move lost its potency for incumbents in Canadian politics?

Or is there something unique to Carney — or his job as prime minister — that makes it work?

Analysts say voters seem to have made a distinction in this case that international trade and dealing with Washington are not the provinces’ jobs, so they’re not buying the effort to play the Trump card.

In Eby’s case, they say it was a gross miscalculation to call the election early and to emphasize the province’s need to stand up to Trump, instead of waiting to hold the vote and then focusing on more traditional provincial matters such as health care, education and B.C.’s economic development. The province’s large deficit under Eby is expected to be an election issue at either time, analysts say.

Trump attacks still good news for federal Liberals as lead increases among decided voters: poll

Trump derails the Quebec campaign, but the PQ leader would rather not talk about that

Prest said Eby’s effort to link the election call to Trump might have worked if the Conservatives hadn’t switched leaders just a couple of days earlier.

The previous leader, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, resigned Sept. 20 following a caucus revolt and other internal strife. The former federal MP was seen as more sympathetic to Trump’s Maga movement and therefore, more vulnerable to the NDP charge that she wouldn’t defend B.C.’s interests against him.

The party’s new interim leader is Lorne Doerkson, a more moderate figure who is also more critical of Trump. He will lead the party into the Oct. 24 election.

Sanjay Jeram, a political scientist at Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, said voters aren’t usually very good at distinguishing between the responsibilities of the different levels of government, but seemed to have sussed out almost immediately this time that the New Democrats’ election call and efforts to play the Trump card were “disingenuous.”

“It’s a little far-fetched,” said Jeram.

And recent polls reflect that view. When the election was called, Eby’s New Democrats had a solid lead of between four and 10 percentage points over the Conservatives. Since then, depending on the poll, the NDP had fallen as many as six to eight percentage points, with those votes seeming to go straight to the Conservatives. Some recent polls in recent days have the Tory lead down to just a couple of points.

The Ndp’s fall should be seen as a “ballot backlash,” said Shachi Kurl, president of the Angus Reid Institute. “There’s a lot of unhappiness with this government.”

Unlike B.C. where there’s some flexibility on election dates, Quebec has fixed elections, leaving Fréchette and her Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) party no choice but to face voters. With the Oct. 5 election less than a week away, Caq’s polling numbers have fallen five to seven points since the election call.

André Lecours, a political science professor at the University of Ottawa, said Fréchette also had little choice but to play the Trump card because she’s the leader of an unpopular CAQ government that had been in power for almost eight years.

“There was no other card to play,” said Lecours. “She had to play it.”

Analysts are divided over whether the potency of the Trump card has faded in Canadian politics or just won’t work as well at the provincial level.

Lecours said Canadian voters are getting used to the Trump threats and rhetoric and their impact is fading.

Recent polls have Carney’s Liberals with the support of almost half of Canadian voters and the Conservatives almost 20 percentage points behind. If the Trump factor has faded, Carney May be attracting support more for his plan and policies, analysts say, not just his defence of Canada.

If the Trump card has faded as a weapon for incumbents in Canada, some Conservatives acknowledge their challenge May have grown. Carney maintains a big lead without the full boost that he earned last year from his defence against Trump, many voters May now be buying into his policies and plan for the country.

“I think we have to start looking more at Carney for Carney’s success,” says Jeram.

stories.title: Albertans could save cash at the pumps as gas tax holiday begins
stories.summary: Edmonton - Albertans filling their tanks May soon be saving cash as the province's gas tax holiday starts today.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Albertans filling their tanks May soon be saving cash as the province’s gas tax holiday starts today.

Premier Danielle Smith’s government is pausing its tax of 13 cents per litre on gasoline and diesel until the end of the year to ease the pressure of high everyday costs.

It comes as the oil-rich province’s treasury reaps the benefit of steep global energy prices.

Eligible adults also have until the end of October to apply online for $100 fuel tax rebates that started rolling out in July.

Smith had said the province went with payments out of concern that tax cuts don’t always get passed on to consumers.

Smith later acknowledged Albertans weren’t happy with the rebate program.

The online application portal was criticized by some as invasive and onerous, although the government tweaked the process to try to make it smoother.

On the heals of a projected $2-billion budget surplus, Smith ditched the rebate, and reverted to cutting the fuel tax until the end of the year.

Alberta’s fuel tax suspension will cost government coffers far more than the rebate. The province estimates it will forego $350 million in revenue in the coming three months.

Nearly 3.4 million adult Albertans are eligible for the rebate, but Finance Minister Jason Nixon said Wednesday only about 1.5 million people have applied.

Nixon previously said he’s not entirely confident the tax cut will be passed on to consumers.

But he has said the low number of rebate applications made it clear the government couldn’t dole out the cash efficiently.

The federal government has also stepped up to try to help Canadians dealing with the high cost of living.

It has extended its fuel excise tax relief until the end of January, which is expected to save drivers up to 10 cents a litre on gas, or four cents per litre on diesel.

Albertans are already paying less, ON average, than drivers across the country.

On Wednesday, the Canadian Automobile Association pegged the average price of gas in Canada at $1.77 per litre. The gas price tracking website GasBuddy, as of Wednesday afternoon, estimated Alberta’s average to be $1.67 per litre.

Fuel prices have soared since the U.S. war on Iran began in late February, choking the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane at the mouth of the Persian Gulf.

The impact has turned Alberta’s finances around.

Its budget is heavily dependent on oil exports, and before the conflict in the Middle East, was predicting a $9.4-billion deficit this fiscal year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Sexual assault trial begins for 'Trailer Park Boys' actor Mike Smith
stories.summary: Dartmouth - A three-day sexual assault trial is scheduled to begin today for Nova Scotia-based actor Mike Smith, best known for playing Bubbles on the TV comedy "Trailer Park Boys."
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Dartmouth - The sexual assault case against the Nova Scotia-based actor known for playing Bubbles on the TV comedy “Trailer Park Boys” was dismissed Thursday after Crown lawyers said they would not be presenting any evidence.

The case was dismissed by provincial court Judge Jill Hartlen as Mike Smith’s three-day trial was about to begin.

Outside the courtroom, Crown prosecutor Bryson McDonald said an assessment of the case led to the determination that the “prosecution standard” had not been met. He declined to elaborate.

“We’re not going to go into specific facts or discuss prosecutorial discretion,” he said.

McDonald also declined to say whether the complainant was willing to testify during the trial. He said the Crown had originally anticipated that three witnesses would testify: the complainant, a civilian witness, and police officer.

“It is an ongoing assessment of whether the prosecution standard is met,” the lawyer said. “We evaluate at every step, and based on ... the ongoing information and evidence that was provided to us (and) that keeps coming in throughout the process, that’s how we arrived at this determination.”

McDonald said the Crown determined this week it would not be presenting any evidence.

Smith had pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault stemming from an alleged incident in 2017. The actor was charged on Oct. 2, 2025.

Court documents did not provide details about the allegations. The complainant’s identity is protected from publication by a standard, court-ordered ban.

Smith’s lawyer, Stan MacDonald, told reporters that his client was pleased with the dismissal.

“Mr. Smith is pleased that this matter is now behind him, and he’s ready to move forward,” MacDonald said.

Nova Scotia-based Trailer Park Boys Inc., where Smith is listed as a director, issued a statement saying he will resume his responsibilities with the company. Other company directors include John Paul Tremblay, who plays Julian on the show, and Robert Wells, who plays Ricky.

Smith has had legal troubles before. In April 2016, he faced a battery charge in Los Angeles for an incident at a Hollywood hotel involving a woman. The misdemeanour domestic battery charge was dropped a month later.

At the time, the Los Angeles City attorney’s office said it decided not to pursue the charge due to a lack of sufficient evidence.

Smith denied any wrongdoing in a written statement issued shortly after his arrest on April 1, 2016, saying the woman involved was a friend with whom he had a “loud and heated dispute.”

“At no time did I assault her,” Smith’s statement said. “I am not guilty of the misdemeanour charged against me.”

Not long after news of Smith’s arrest surfaced in 2016, his co-star at the time, Lucy DeCoutere, announced she was leaving the television show.

DeCoutere took to social media at the time to say: “If I find out that somebody is abusive, I cut them out of my life.” She later said she remained friends with the cast and crew of the show, despite saying her departure was linked to Smith’s arrest.

Trailer Park Boys Inc. announced in August that the company had completed filming for the show’s 13th season, which will coincide with the 25th anniversary of its debut.

The show is a mockumentary-style comedy set in the fictional Sunnyvale Trailer Park, where Bubbles and his friends Julian and Ricky routinely get involved in get-rich-quick schemes that go awry.

The original show, created by Mike Clattenburg, ran for seven seasons before spawning four feature-length films, two spinoff series and a Christmas special. Meanwhile, Trailer Park Boys Inc. announced in July it was launching its own streaming service to host its content.

Many recognizable Canadian actors and directors have appeared on the show. John Dunsworth and Patrick Roach were part of the main cast, playing trailer park supervisor Jim Lahey and assistant Randy. Jonathan Torrens has appeared throughout the show’s run as fan-favourite J-Roc.

As well, a number of internationally known actors have been featured in several episodes, including Elliot Page, who played Treena Lahey in the early seasons. Tom Arnold and Brian Austin Green each appeared, and rapper Snoop Dogg guest-starred in five episodes.

Smith has won a Canadian Comedy Award and two Gemini Awards for his work on the show. He was also the guitarist for rock band Sandbox in the mid-1990s, when they were nominated for Best New Group at the Juno Awards in 1996.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: News Alert: Sexual assault trial for ‘Trailer Park Boys’ actor Mike Smith dismissed
stories.summary: A three-day sexual assault trial is scheduled to begin today for Nova Scotia-based actor Mike Smith, best known for playing Bubbles on the TV comedy "Trailer Park Boys."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Dartmouth — The sexual assault case against the Nova Scotia-based actor known for playing Bubbles on the TV comedy “Trailer Park Boys” was dismissed Thursday after Crown lawyers said they would not be presenting any evidence.

The case was dismissed by provincial court Judge Jill Hartlen as Mike Smith’s three-day trial was about to begin.

Outside the courtroom, Crown prosecutor Bryson McDonald said an assessment of the case led to the determination that the “prosecution standard” had not been met. He declined to elaborate.

“We’re not going to go into specific facts or discuss prosecutorial discretion,” he said.

McDonald also declined to say whether the complainant was willing to testify during the trial. He said the Crown had originally anticipated that three witnesses would testify: the complainant, a civilian witness, and police officer.

“It is an ongoing assessment of whether the prosecution standard is met,” the lawyer said. “We evaluate at every step, and based on … the ongoing information and evidence that was provided to us (and) that keeps coming in throughout the process, that’s how we arrived at this determination.”

McDonald said the Crown determined this week it would not be presenting any evidence.

Smith had pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault stemming from an alleged incident in 2017. The actor was charged on Oct. 2, 2025.

Court documents did not provide details about the allegations. The complainant’s identity is protected from publication by a standard, court-ordered ban.

Smith’s lawyer, Stan MacDonald, told reporters that his client was pleased with the dismissal.

“Mr. Smith is pleased that this matter is now behind him, and he’s ready to move forward,” MacDonald said.

Nova Scotia-based Trailer Park Boys Inc., where Smith is listed as a director, issued a statement saying he will resume his responsibilities with the company. Other company directors include John Paul Tremblay, who plays Julian on the show, and Robert Wells, who plays Ricky.

Smith has had legal troubles before. In April 2016, he faced a battery charge in Los Angeles for an incident at a Hollywood hotel involving a woman. The misdemeanour domestic battery charge was dropped a month later.

At the time, the Los Angeles City attorney’s office said it decided not to pursue the charge due to a lack of sufficient evidence.

Smith denied any wrongdoing in a written statement issued shortly after his arrest on April 1, 2016, saying the woman involved was a friend with whom he had a “loud and heated dispute.”

“At no time did I assault her,” Smith’s statement said. “I am not guilty of the misdemeanour charged against me.”

Not long after news of Smith’s arrest surfaced in 2016, his co-star at the time, Lucy DeCoutere, announced she was leaving the television show.

DeCoutere took to social media at the time to say: “If I find out that somebody is abusive, I cut them out of my life.” She later said she remained friends with the cast and crew of the show, despite saying her departure was linked to Smith’s arrest.

Trailer Park Boys Inc. announced in August that the company had completed filming for the show’s 13th season, which will coincide with the 25th anniversary of its debut.

The show is a mockumentary-style comedy set in the fictional Sunnyvale Trailer Park, where Bubbles and his friends Julian and Ricky routinely get involved in get-rich-quick schemes that go awry.

The original show, created by Mike Clattenburg, ran for seven seasons before spawning four feature-length films, two spinoff series and a Christmas special. Meanwhile, Trailer Park Boys Inc. announced in July it was launching its own streaming service to host its content.

Many recognizable Canadian actors and directors have appeared on the show. John Dunsworth and Patrick Roach were part of the main cast, playing trailer park supervisor Jim Lahey and assistant Randy. Jonathan Torrens has appeared throughout the show’s run as fan-favourite J-Roc.

As well, a number of internationally known actors have been featured in several episodes, including Elliot Page, who played Treena Lahey in the early seasons. Tom Arnold and Brian Austin Green each appeared, and rapper Snoop Dogg guest-starred in five episodes.

Smith has won a Canadian Comedy Award and two Gemini Awards for his work on the show. He was also the guitarist for rock band Sandbox in the mid-1990s, when they were nominated for Best New Group at the Juno Awards in 1996.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

Lyndsay Armstrong, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Mark Carney must be more than anti-Trump for a real shot at the Nobel Peace Prize
stories.summary: The question around Carney’s Nobel nod is whether he has accomplished enough beyond the country’s borders—and ahead of the Jan. 31, 2026, nomination deadline—to merit the award.
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
The world loves him and Washington loathes him, but that alone will not secure Prime Minister Mark Carney the Nobel Peace Prize next week.

This is not to rain on the annual parade of prediction-market speculators who get fired up every October for the awarding of one of the world’s most prestigious honours.

It is, like every year, a crowded field of candidates, according to the Nobel committee, with 208 individuals and 79 organizations in the running — all of them anonymous.

But if Carney’s name has floated to the top (and again, we don’t even know if he’s in the running), the panel of judges tasked with announcing the 2026 winner on Oct. 9 would do well to skim the Liberal party leader off, place him to the side and dig a little deeper.

Carney has won his current position in politics as a national leader willing to stand up to U.S. President Donald Trump and his tariff threats. For the moment, he is already something of a Canadian laureate, as evidenced by his high standing in public opinion polls and his party’s majority in the House of Commons.

The question around Carney’s Nobel nod is whether he has accomplished enough beyond the country’s borders — and ahead of the Jan. 31 nomination deadline — to merit the award.

That deadline date is important.

Carney, the former central banker and United Nations special envoy for climate action and finance, has long been a man of the world. But his real global coming out as the world leader most willing to stand up to Trump occurred 11 days earlier, when he delivered his speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos.

Experts analyze Prime Minister Mark Carney’s World Economic Forum speech and what it could mean

With it, he began inspiring his fellow heads of state and government to believe that they too have choices beyond submitting to the will of the White House.

But 11 days is a short runway for the lofty launch pad that the Nobel Peace Prize represents.

In this, Carney’s supposed candidacy most closely resembles the “Yes We Can!” spirit surrounding the 2009 peace prize winner, U.S. president Barack Obama .

Obama’s Nobel win just nine months into his presidency celebrated, in the judges’ words , “his extraordinary efforts to strengthen international diplomacy and co-operation between peoples.”

Left unsaid was that Obama was a symbol, a cathartic contrast to George W. Bush, whose eight years as president were defined by the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

In a 2015 book, the former Nobel Peace Prize secretary Geir Lundestad wrote that the committee’s intention was to “strengthen Obama,” but he lamented that “it didn’t have this effect.”

A few months after his prize was announced, Obama sent an additional 30,000 U.S. troops to fight the war in Afghanistan.

The so-called “troop surge” flew in the face of Alfred Nobel’s last wishes for the honour that would bear his name: that it be given to a person who has worked for “fraternity between nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies and for the holding and promotion of peace congresses.”

Invoking that spirit, the Nobel has rightly been awarded to the likes of Jimmy Carter, who spent just one term in the White House but emerged as a standard bearer for world peace — as the Nobel committee said , “the best ex-president the country ever had.”

It has gone to Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk , to Desmond Tutu and Albert Lutuli for opposing or dismantling apartheid in South Africa. Mikhail Gorbachev won for the “radical changes” he brought to the Soviet Union, which would crumble just a year later. Yasser Arafat, Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin were celebrated for the Oslo Accords, which allowed people to imagine, however briefly, the prospect of peace in the Middle East.

Canada’s Lester B. Pearson received his Nobel in 1957 for putting together a multinational United Nations Emergency Force — the precursor to UN peacekeepers or Blue Helmets — to resolve a dispute over control of the Suez Canal.

The point being that the Nobel Peace Prize stands on firmer ground when it celebrates an individual or organization that has delivered on their great promise in the name of a global good.

Carney is certainly international in his experience and his outlook. But his concrete actions and accomplishments in the year and a half since he took office have primarily been domestic efforts to Trump-proof the Canadian economy. In doing so, he has scrubbed the country’s emissions targets, eased environmental regulations and standards, weakened labour protections and reduced Canada’s foreign aid budget.

And this summer, the Canadian Armed Forces also effectively ended its participation in UN peacekeeping operations — ironic in the current context because the so-called Blue Helmet force was the recipient of the 1988 Nobel Peace Prize .

Carney has been chiefly concerned with the speedy construction of Canadian infrastructure and energy projects and the opening of critical mineral mines, less so in building bridges between warring factions and opening eyes to the world’s suffering.

On the global stage, Carney has made important propositions about the need for middle-power countries to work together to defend common values and the rule of law against aggressive superpowers.

He has proposed the creation of a “technology stability board” to oversee the growth and implementation of artificial intelligence and to set international safety standards.

He has doubled down on the two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict, but in partnership with a host of other nations. Ditto with Partners for Multilateralism , a weeks-old initiative that is aimed at supporting peace, sustainable development and international law.

These are all worthy contributions to the pressing issues of the day. But they are opening moves — not yet hard-fought outcomes.

Up against peace in Europe, in Northern Ireland, in East Timor, in the Middle East; up against the existential threat of nuclear annihilation; up against lifetimes spent fighting for human rights and against despots, Carney’s accomplishments to date don’t measure up to those that Nobel’s noble prize has recognized.

stories.title: Marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation at Fort Edmonton Park
stories.summary: Edmonton's oldest historic site served as a place to remember the history of Canada's Indigenous people on the sixth annual National Day of Truth and Reconciliation.
stories.author: Joel Gotlib, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Edmonton’s oldest historic site served as a place to remember the history of Canada’s Indigenous people on the sixth annual National Day of Truth and Reconciliation .

The day is a sombre remembrance of 150,000 Indigenous children who suffered malnutrition and abuse over decades in Canada’s residential school system.

“Days like today are not necessarily happy days for us — they’re actually quite sad and heavy,” said Jasmine Hannig, an Indigenous social worker who took in the commemorative event at Fort Edmonton Park.

Many at the gathering wore bright orange shirts, the symbol for the children who attended residential schools. Some ate bannock and sipped on warm beverages on the chilly autumn morning.

The Federal statutory holiday was established after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission called on the Canadian government to recognize the impact residential schools had on survivors, their families and their communities.

In 2015, the commission concluded the schools were central to a state-backed policy of cultural genocide.

“Truth and reconciliation, definitely for Indigenous people, is not just one day. It’s a life that we live,” said Chief Desmond Bull from the Louis Bull First Nation in Maskwacis. “More importantly, the acknowledgement of our ancestors that went through residential school.”

Experts and First Nations advocates have cited the violence and abuse inflicted upon several generations of Indigenous children at the schools as the reason why Indigenous communities experience disproportionately higher rates of violence, psychological distress and substance use and abuse.

The trauma was compounded by events like the Sixties Scoop — a government policy that forcibly removed Indigenous children from their birth parents and sent to foster homes and other families for adoption.

Hannig wants people to know the day commemorates more than just Canada’s dark history with residential school.

“Not only residential schooling had an impact, but so did the Sixties Scoop, day schools, boarding schools, the 90s scoop and many other colonial aspects,” she said of the intergenerational trauma Indigenous peoples have suffered.

“I think it’s really important we talk about the impact of all that harm collectively, and the echoes that has had within our community.”

2:00 How residential school trauma is passed down from generation to generation

The day is full of mixed feelings for Hannig.

“In one way, it’s really emotional because it’s so beautiful that we’re having this conversation — finally. But another way, I feel like there’s a lot of conversations that we’re not having collectively.”

On Wednesday, about 2,000 people were expected to walk through the Indigenous People’s Experience at Fort Edmonton Park, which is opened year-round.

“The immersive experience in here is really about the fact that you’re learning about us in a broader sense,” Evert Poor, an event manager at Fort Edmonton Park, said of the exhibit.

“A lot of people have a lot of myths and stereotypes about Indigenous people.

“This space basically teaches you the true history of our people.”

1:58 Indigenous Peoples Experience at the heart of Fort Edmonton Park reopening

Chief Bull said listening to those whose lives were impacted is also encouraged.

“There’s much more you can learn from sitting down with a person of Indigenous background and hearing their story of where they are now, and how they came about where they are,” Bull said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre, Mayor Andrew Knack, leaders from First Nations near Edmonton and other officials took part in a commemorative ceremony at the interactive historical site.

Carney, who was born in the Northwest Territories and raised in Edmonton, recalled in his speech the numerous visits to Fort Edmonton in his youth.

Carney said the ceremony urged everyone to hear the stories of those affected by the residential school system and “reflect on a dark chapter in Canada’s past and to commit to move forward together.”

“This is not a distant chapter in Canada’s past, but a truth that endures,” said Carney, who wore an orange tie and a pin of a beaded orange T-shirt on his lapel.

“Reconciliation is a journey, not a destination. It’s an attitude, not an achievement. Our job is to move together as far and as fast down the path as we can.”

2:01 Mark Carney reiterates Indigenous partnerships for major projects in Ndtr speech

Alberta’s Minister of Indigenous Relations released a statement about the day.

“Reconciliation is about more than a single day,” the statement from Rajan Sawhney said. “Reconciliation takes time, care and sustained effort. It is shaped by relationships built on listening, respect and a willingness to learn, and by supporting Indigenous-led knowledge, perspectives and priorities.”

Anyone experiencing pain or distress as a result of their residential school experience can access this 24-hour, toll-free and confidential National Indian Residential School Crisis Line at 1-866-925-4419.

With files from Daniela Germano, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Fanshawe raises awareness on Truth and Reconcilliation day.
stories.summary: Fanshawe's students are honouring Indigenous students on Truth and Reconciliation day through many ways. Inclu...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
Fanshawe College honoured Indigenous students on Truth and Reconciliation Day with events and conversations across main campus. An art gallery displaying Indigenous students’ creations, a market to support Indigenous businesses and a speaking event called Approachable Conversations with an Indigenous Man, were among Wednesday’s events.

In Approachable Conversations, Oneida knowledge-sharer Ray John Jr. and the Canadian Mental Health Association’s Pam Tobin discussed the importance of women in Indigenous communities.

“I salute the women in my life,” said John Jr. “Thank you for giving us that life and for giving us a chance.”

Kristen Longdo, the Indigenous Strategic Learning Guide for the Institute of Indigenous Learning at Fanshawe, told XFM News that art plays a major role in how many Indigenous people express themselves.

“ It’s important to highlight the wonderful parts of Indigenous cultures ,” said Longdo. “We wanted to utilize September 30 to highlight Indigenous artisans from our surrounding communities and give them a platform to display their work.”

Longdo also discussed how Truth and Reconciliation day has changed over the years, being officially recognized in as a statutory holiday by Canada in 2021, but according to Longdo, was celebrated across Indigenous communities since 2015.

“Truth and Reconciliation day has continued to change and evolve over time the more truth has come out.” said Longdo. “Each year we see more people showing up and more people engaging in reconciliation efforts.”

Many students wore orange shirts designed by Fanshawe student Robin Cornelius.

“ I am Indigenous and recently I just got a job working for the Indigenous Centre,” said one Fanshawe student. “I’m supporting my culture and all my friends, my family, stuff like that. “

“ I think we need to have more non-indigenous people showing up to these types of events,” said another.

Longdo said she’d like to see more non-Indigenous at the events.

“ Non-Indigenous people need to continue to educate themselves on our truths. Listen, learn, show up and support your local indigenous communities,” said Longdo. “A great way of doing this is giving Indigenous people a platform to speak about their truths, to buy from local Indigenous artists, to use your social media platforms to give Indigenous people, stories, and businesses a voice.”

stories.title: Canadian astronaut set to take off for six-month stay on space station
stories.summary: Joshua Kutryk is part of a four-person crew scheduled to blast off from the Kennedy Space Center on Thursday
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Canada’s next space traveller is fast approaching his scheduled departure – but the weather May have other ideas.

On Wednesday afternoon, officials at Nasa’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida said there was a 55 per cent chance of favourable conditions for the launch of a four-person crew heading to the International Space Station for half a year.

The group includes Joshua Kutryk, a native of Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., and an air force pilot who was selected to be an astronaut by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.

Colonel Kutyrk is scheduled to fly with Jessica Watkins, crew commander, and Luke Delaney both of the United States, as well as Sergey Teteryatnikov of Russia. The team is set to lift off aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket Thursday at 11:10 a.m. ET and dock with the space station about eight hours later.

“I’m excited to do the science, I’m excited to look at the Earth, but I’m also excited to do it as a Canadian,” Col. Kutryk said during a press conference after he and his crewmates arrived on Sunday in advance of their launch.

He also stressed the value of the partnership that has enabled Canadians to work together with Nasa colleagues.

Col. Kutryk’s planned six-month stint on the ISS is another example of how active that partnership has been this year.

In April, Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen and his U.S. crewmates captured the world’s attention with Artemis II, the first mission to take humans around the moon and back in more than half a century.

Now, it’s Col. Kutryk’s turn to begin his nearer but far longer residency in Earth’s orbit.

During that time he will conduct a wide range of science experiments and help keep the station running in whatever way is needed.

And while it’s tempting to call the mission a marathon – especially when compared with Col. Hansen’s 9½ day lunar sprint – there is a more apt comparison.

“It’s a Tour de France,” said Robert Thirsk, a retired astronaut and physician who became the first Canadian to spend multiple months in space in 2009. “You get up and you go hard every day.”

Dr. Thirsk said he picked up the metaphor from Gennady Padalka, a seasoned Russian cosmonaut who was the station’s commander when he first arrived there for a 188-day stay.

“Gennady was a master at what I had to learn,” Dr. Thirsk said. “Every mission is going to have contingencies and inevitable malfunctions. So you need to have the physiological, but also the psychological reserves to deal with that.”

He said that while astronauts on short duration missions tend to train for specific tasks they need to complete on a tight timeline, those who expect to spend many months in orbit instead focus on skills that May be required to deal with the unexpected and maintain their physical and mental capacity over the long haul.

Dr. Thirsk said that Col. Kutryk was well suited for the challenge.

“During the fifth month of his expedition, he is going to need as much energy and enthusiasm to perform his tasks and his experiments as he will during this first week,” Dr. Thirsk said.

Col. Kutryk is set to become the fourth Canadian to undertake a long duration mission in space. Besides Dr. Thirsk, only Chris Hadfield and David Saint-Jacques have had comparably long flights aboard the ISS.

One way that Col. Kutryk’s mission differs is in how he will reach the station. Unlike his predecessors who were all launched from Kazakhstan in Soyuz spacecraft, Col. Kutryk will be transported in a SpaceX Dragon capsule as part of Nasa’s commercial crew program.

Because it is the 13 th regular flight under the program that relies on industrial partners to take astronauts to and from the station, the mission is referred to as Crew-13.

The flight was originally scheduled for mid-September, but was held up when engineers detected an oxidizer leak and decided to investigate. This led to the replacement of a valve – a delicate operation while the rocket was in its vertically stacked configuration.

During a call with reporters last week, Col. Kutryk said the problem was a minor one, but the decision to delay “makes us all feel that much more confident” in the safety of the vehicle.

Another way that Col. Kutryk’s trip is likely to be unique among Canadian astronauts is the fact that he and his wife Heather are expecting their third child to be born later this year while he is still in space.

Mathieu Caron, director of astronauts, life sciences and space medicine with the Canadian Space Agency said that Col. Kutryk would have access to enhanced communications with his family during his time on orbit.

“We have a team that’s dedicated to making sure that we support Josh and that the Kutryk family will receive whatever support is needed during the mission,” he said.

stories.title: Survey of candidates in municipal elections show differences between London politicians and voters
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/8bFKBD9DAgc Researchers at Western University recently published the results of a recent surv...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
Researchers at Western University recently published the results of a recent survey of candidates running in municipal elections across Ontario, and with it came a variety of potential differences between candidates and voters that one candidate said he has seen for himself.

According to its media release, the survey was conducted by the Local Democracy Project at Western, and surveyed close to 900 candidates running in municipal elections across Ontario. The stated purpose of the survey was to learn what drives candidates in terms that included their campaigns, demographics and what they think about local politics.

“It’s actually a national project,” said political science professor and the survey’s co-lead Zachary Taylor. “The goal is to look for trends across the entire country.”

The media release stated that the project has just sent out surveys to B.C., which is undergoing snap elections.

Because of the broad scope of the survey, finding data points about specific regions can be difficult. Taylor said that while the survey’s results May not be able to determine how London can deal problems like its lack of youth voter engagement , he believes it is linked to how candidates wage their campaigns, which the survey does examine.

However, Ward 12 candidate and Western student Ribal Zebian believes that the differences between candidates and the voting public can reflect on who tries to run in elections.

“When it’s … very hard to get by, you won’t really find the average voter going in,” he said. “You’ll find someone who doesn’t really represent them.”

Taylor said the survey data he collected showed that plenty of people are already showing up to run for elections, and that the barriers for running are very low.

“In the vast majority of races you have 2, 3, 4 candidates running, so I suppose that means things are working,” he said.

London City Hall. The survey conducted by Western researchers seems to point to financial and age differences between municipal politicians and the voting public. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

The survey also speaks to how money can be a barrier in municipal politics. The survey results showed that the average Ontario candidate has a yearly income over $100,000, that the average cost of a campaign is $2,600 and that campaigns are mostly self-funded.

“As places get bigger, the game changes,” said Taylor. “It is true that the people who run for office are generally better off financially … than the public they would seek to represent.”

Zebian said he has seen financial obstacles reflected in campaigns around Ward 5, where Western is located.

“They’re spending significantly beyond [$2,600],” he said. “When you look and you see some of the candidates … they have a lot more resources and a lot more to take advantage of.”

Money is only one characteristic of what the survey found was a part of the average candidate. It also found that the average age of candidates was 56, they are mostly men, they have a university degree and they own a home.

“There’s lots of examples of people in their late teens and 20s running for office and they often get picked up in the media because they’re such a novelty,” said Taylor.

Zebian, who is 19 years old, sees this for himself as well.

“If you look at the current mayor, you look at some of the councilors … [they are] in the age of 40s, 50s, have a degree whether it’s a bachelor’s or a master’s, they have an established career, all those types of things,” he said.

At the same time, Zebian believes he’s seeing a change in some of the survey’s averages. He says as well that candidates with less money May try to engage more directly with voters by knocking on doors and exchanging ideas, and that even if they don’t win their first election they can build a strong voter base for the future.

“You’ll see candidates who don’t have too too much, but they’ll still get themselves in,” he said. “And as we’re going through the years we’re seeing more people just getting themselves together, getting a little bit more brave … and eventually that leads you a very long way.”

stories.title: ‘We come here for healing’: Saskatoon holds fifth annual truth and reconciliation powwow
stories.summary: Hundreds of orange shirts dotted the SaskTel centre on Wednesday to mark a day filled with reflection to honour residential school survivors.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Irene Nippi sees National Truth and Reconciliation Day as a way to show pride in a culture she was once told to abandon.

The elder from Kinistin Saulteaux First Nation was six years old when she was first sent to a residential school, an experience that compels her to take part in reconciliation ceremonies.

“I went to a residential school for a long time, and there are a lot of things that happened like sexual abuse, physical abuse, emotional abuse and spiritual abuse,” said Nippi.

Beginning in the 19th century, over 150,000 Indigenous children were separated from their families and communities and sent to church-run, government-funded residential schools where abuse, malnutrition and inadequate health care were rampant.

For Nippi, the schools stripped away more than family.

“It was taken away from us to be proud of who we are,” Nippi said, adding that the loss also extended to her culture, traditions, belief system and ceremonies.

On Wednesday, Nippi was among hundreds of others who donned an orange shirt and lined the inner bowl of the SaskTel Centre in Saskatoon for the Saskatoon Tribal Council’s fifth annual Truth and Reconciliation Powwow — a day marked by dancing, singing and reflection.

“All of them who went to the school are slowly getting their lives back but are still not ready to talk about what they experienced at the residential school,” she said, adding that she hopes events like Wednesday’s powwow can help start conversations.

Travis Toto, a drummer from Whitefish River First Nation, said he and his fellow members of the Eagle Boys Singers come for healing.

“It warms our hearts,” Toto said. “Just being around the drum and being around each other, it’s a good day.”

The federal government officially established Sept. 30 as the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021 following recommendations in a report commissioned by the federal Truth and Reconciliation Commission six years earlier.

For some, attending the powwow in Saskatoon has already become a tradition.

“The grand entry always makes me weep. Even just talking about it makes me teary,” said Koreen Geres, an attendee at the powwow.

“I believe we need to get to know each other, that’s the best way for reconciliation,” Geres added.

Walking through the crowded concourse minutes before the grand entry, attendees of all ages could be seen meandering about. For some, the powwow marks a learning opportunity for future generations.

“My kids are extremely young, so the fact that they can come out to this particular event is quite special,” said Jordan Baptiste, adding he wants to show his kids to be proud of who they are.

In 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission put forward 94 Calls to Action.

Since then, only 14 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 calls to action have been completed in the last 11 years, according to the independent monitor Indigenous Watchdog.

Another 41 recommendations are considered in progress, while 24 are stalled and 15 have not been started.

Saskatoon Tribal Chief Mark Arcand said reconciliation remains an ongoing process, and that progress is not coming fast enough.

“There’s still a lot of outstanding calls to action, and it’s been a few years, and that’s where we talk about accountability,” Arcand said. “It’s good to have them, but if we’re not enacting them, we have major problems.”

Arcand said the real measure of reconciliation is what happens beyond the one day set aside to mark it.

“Let’s start making a change together as a city, as a province, as a country, to be the leaders of working together because it’s tough when people don’t recognize the negative things that happen to First Nations people, and we have to have some hard, uncomfortable discussions,” he said.

— with files from Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney vows ‘true partnership’ with Indigenous people on major infrastructure projects
stories.summary: PM spoke at National Truth and Reconciliation Day event in Fort Edmonton Park on eve of expected West Coast oil pipeline announcement
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to create a true partnership with Indigenous people, including on operating and owning major infrastructure projects, as he marked the sixth annual National Truth and Reconciliation Day.

Mr. Carney’s comments at a commemorative event in Fort Edmonton Park Wednesday were made on the eve of an expected announcement to designate a West Coast oil pipeline as a project of national interest.

The pipeline is a key part of Mr. Carney’s suite of policy changes that aim to reset federal relations with Alberta and diversify Canadian exports away from the United States. But some First Nations have accused his government of a lack of meaningful consultation.

The Prime Minister, wearing an orange tie on what is known as “Orange Shirt Day,” addressed his government’s desire to build major projects across the country, but to do so sustainably.

“Sustainably means embedding Indigenous knowledge and leadership in our conservation efforts, and it means building in true partnership with Indigenous peoples,” Mr. Carney said.

He added that involves “meaningful opportunities to develop, operate and own major infrastructure, to share truly in the prosperity that’s created.”

“My point is, we are making some progress, but we know the work of reconciliation is far, far from finished,” Mr. Carney said.

“The wounds are still too deep, the gaps are still too wide. Reconciliation is a journey, not a destination. It’s an attitude, not an achievement. Our job is to move together as far and as fast down the path as we can.”

The Assembly of First Nations declined to comment on Mr. Carney’s remarks but said it would respond on Thursday.

In May, Mr. Carney’s government said it would designate the proposed pipeline a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act by Oct. 1. That process is being led by the federal Major Projects Office, headquartered in Calgary.

One of the groups opposing the fast timeline for the process is the Coldwater Indian Band, in British Columbia. The group also opposed the Trans Mountain Expansion Project owing to concerns about risks to the community’s aquifer.

On behalf of the band, Vice-Chief Michael Smithers said in an e-mail earlier this week that there has been a lack of meaningful consultation between the community and the Major Projects Office about the new pipeline.

In his speech Wednesday, Mr. Carney called residential schools a “dark chapter” and said it’s the government’s responsibility to respond to the findings uncovered by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which documented the stories of residential-school survivors and the historical inequities faced by Indigenous people.

Beginning in the 1800s, more than 150,000 Indigenous children in Canada were sent to church-run residential schools, where abuse and malnutrition were rampant.

In 2015, the TRC concluded the schools were central to a state-backed policy of attempted cultural genocide.

Mr. Carney said that while the “gaps are still large,” the government is responding, including by improving opportunities in education to ensure children on reserve have access to high-quality learning that respects and embraces their culture.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said it's important to reflect on a 'dark chapter' in Canada's history and honour the children who survived residential schools and those who never made it home. He made the comment Wednesday on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation at an event in Fort Edmonton Park.

The Canadian Press

He said the government is building homes for families on reserve and throughout the country, improving access to drinking water, as well as placing an emphasis on mental wellness, primary care and culturally relevant care for First Nations.

NDP MP Leah Gazan, her party’s critic for Indigenous affairs, said in an interview that Mr. Carney’s comments on a day dedicated to residential-school survivors, who were removed from their families in the name of “nation-building,” show “how out of touch this government [is], and how uncommitted this government is to true reconciliation.”

She pointed to the release Wednesday of a report from the Permanent Peoples’ Tribunal, a human-rights organization, that called on the government to rescind the Building Canada Act, which allows it to accelerate projects designated in the national interest. The report said the law “uses ‘projects of national interest’ to justify the persistent land dispossession of Indigenous Peoples.”

Ms. Gazan also noted that the government in its June legislation removed language stating that those living on First Nations have a “human right” to clean drinking water, instead focusing on furthering progress toward that goal.

“As an Indigenous person – but not even as an Indigenous person, as a human being – I feel deeply hurt by the ongoing human-rights violations of the Carney Liberal government,” said Ms. Gazan, a member of Wood Mountain Lakota Nation in Saskatchewan.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s office did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday. But in a statement posted to X, he said residential schools “were a massive intrusion of government coercion imposed on Indigenous families.”

“On the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, we honour these children, their families and their communities, and recommit to reconciliation built on self-determination, opportunity, and true partnership,” he wrote.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Fact File: Masked agitators at First Nation in B.C. not a false flag action
stories.summary: Claims have spread online this week that a white nationalist group's demonstration at a First Nation in British Columbia, which has been denounced by authorities as "disgusting" and "cowardly," was in fact a false flag operation. The claims say the action was the work of government agents with purported goals ranging from stifling free speech to influencing…
stories.author: Timon Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Claims have spread online this week that a white nationalist group’s demonstration at a First Nation in British Columbia, which has been denounced by authorities as “disgusting” and “cowardly,” was in fact a false flag operation.

The claims say the action was the work of government agents with purported goals ranging from stifling free speech to influencing the upcoming provincial election. But a number of elements, including statements by prominent members of the organization, point to the action being carried out by white nationalists.

On Sunday, a group of masked individuals dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops, B.C., with a message mocking reports of unmarked graves at the nearby site of the former residential school on Tkemlups te Secwepemc First Nation.

As photos of the men and their banner spread online and politicians weighed in, some users on X expressed skepticism.

“They have masks on because it’s fake. They’re government plants. They want to pretend there is some kind of ‘threat’ from ‘hate groups’ in Canada so they can justify further crackdowns on free speech and expression,” one user said in her post Sunday evening, which has received close to 48,000 views.

Other users linked the banner drop to the B.C. election campaign, suggesting it was aimed at damaging either the provincial Conservatives or the OneBC party.

“Now on Sunday a group of 20-30 masked ‘white supremacists’ showed up right at the center of a political minefield for Conservatives.... It’s all just a little too convenient,” one user said in a Sept. 28 post that had drawn close to 84,000 views as of Sept. 30.

Images and a video posted of the demonstration clearly show many members are wearing clothing with logos associated with Second Sons Canada. The Canadian Anti-Hate Network describes Second Sons Canada as a far-right, members-only organization for men inspired by militant white nationalist groups in other countries, often engaging in short-lived demonstrations and training sessions across Canada.

The Second Sons website says the group was established in 2024 and functions as a “fraternal organization dedicated to health and fitness, camaraderie, activism and friendly support for those who share our values.”

In past posts from Second Sons social media accounts, members can be seen wearing the same crests and T-shirt design featuring the Vimy Ridge monument that some members wore in the photo of Sunday’s demonstration.

Evan Balgord, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network, said the group’s merchandise is restricted to members who are vetted before they can join. For that reason, he said it would be highly unlikely for dozens of people to impersonate them.

“Nobody can get their hands on this Second Sons merchandise,” he said.

Furthermore, a few prominent members of the group publicly acknowledged the gathering on their social media accounts.

In a recorded livestream on YouTube on Sept. 27, one of the members referred to the banner questioning reports of human burials at the residential school site. “When we go out and do something like this, my God, does the media come running for comments, pictures, whatever they can from us,” he said.

Second Sons founder Jeremy MacKenzie responded on X to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s denunciation of the action as hateful by writing, “Thank you for confirming that an honest question is considered ‘hate’ by Ottawa.”

Following reports of the group’s presence circulating online, the Tkemlups te Secwepemc First Nation said it was working with the RCMP and exploring additional security measures.

“White supremacy will not instil fear in generations of survivors and intergenerational survivors who have already carried fear for far too long,” the chief’s office said in a statement.

The RCMP’s Kamloops detachment said its officers promptly engaged with the group after receiving reports about their presence. The police said the group later left the area and continued to move through different parts of the city.

The statement described the banner and masks as a “cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division.”

In a video message posted on provincial NDP Leader David Eby’s X account on Sept. 27, he described the gathering as “disgusting behaviour” aimed at provoking fear and intimidation.

In a Sept. 28 post on X, Carney called the gathering “a cowardly act” that has no place in Canada.

“This week, we will mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It is a stark reminder of our shared responsibility to confront the devastating legacy of the residential school system and the consequences still felt today,” he said in the post. “Courageous survivors shared the truth so that all Canadians could take up the work of reconciliation.”

More than 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to attend residential schools, the last of which closed in 1996.

Thousands of children died in the institutions, and researchers at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation have identified 63 children who died at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School. In May 2021, the Tkemlups te Secwepemc First Nation announced ground-penetrating radar had uncovered what were believed to be 215 unmarked graves at the site of the former Kamloops residential school.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

The claims say the action was the work of government agents with purported goals ranging from stifling free speech to influencing the upcoming provincial election. But a number of elements, including statements by prominent members of the organization, point to the action being carried out by white nationalists.

On Sunday, a group of masked individuals dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops, B.C., with a message mocking reports of unmarked graves at the nearby site of the former residential school on Tkemlups te Secwepemc First Nation.
As photos of the men and their banner spread online and politicians weighed in, some users on X expressed skepticism.

“They have masks on because it’s fake. They’re government plants. They want to pretend there is some kind of ‘threat’ from ‘hate groups’ in Canada so they can justify further crackdowns on free speech and expression,” one user said in her post Sunday evening, which has received close to 48,000 views.
Other users linked the banner drop to the B.C. election campaign, suggesting it was aimed at damaging either the provincial Conservatives or the OneBC party.

“Now on Sunday a group of 20-30 masked ‘white supremacists’ showed up right at the center of a political minefield for Conservatives.... It’s all just a little too convenient,” one user said in a Sept. 28 post that had drawn close to 84,000 views as of Sept. 30.

Images and a video posted of the demonstration clearly show many members are wearing clothing with logos associated with Second Sons Canada. The Canadian Anti-Hate Network describes Second Sons Canada as a far-right, members-only organization for men inspired by militant white nationalist groups in other countries, often engaging in short-lived demonstrations and training sessions across Canada.

The Second Sons website says the group was established in 2024 and functions as a “fraternal organization dedicated to health and fitness, camaraderie, activism and friendly support for those who share our values.”

In past posts from Second Sons social media accounts, members can be seen wearing the same crests and T-shirt design featuring the Vimy Ridge monument that some members wore in the photo of Sunday’s demonstration.

Evan Balgord, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network, said the group’s merchandise is restricted to members who are vetted before they can join. For that reason, he said it would be highly unlikely for dozens of people to impersonate them.
“Nobody can get their hands on this Second Sons merchandise,” he said.
Furthermore, a few prominent members of the group publicly acknowledged the gathering on their social media accounts.

In a recorded livestream on YouTube on Sept. 27, one of the members referred to the banner questioning reports of human burials at the residential school site. “When we go out and do something like this, my God, does the media come running for comments, pictures, whatever they can from us,” he said.

Second Sons founder Jeremy MacKenzie responded on X to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s denunciation of the action as hateful by writing, “Thank you for confirming that an honest question is considered ‘hate’ by Ottawa.”
Following reports of the group’s presence circulating online, the Tkemlups te Secwepemc First Nation said it was working with the RCMP and exploring additional security measures.
“White supremacy will not instil fear in generations of survivors and intergenerational survivors who have already carried fear for far too long,” the chief’s office said in a statement.

The RCMP’s Kamloops detachment said its officers promptly engaged with the group after receiving reports about their presence. The police said the group later left the area and continued to move through different parts of the city.
The statement described the banner and masks as a “cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division.”
In a video message posted on provincial NDP Leader David Eby’s X account on Sept. 27, he described the gathering as “disgusting behaviour” aimed at provoking fear and intimidation.
In a Sept. 28 post on X, Carney called the gathering “a cowardly act” that has no place in Canada.

“This week, we will mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It is a stark reminder of our shared responsibility to confront the devastating legacy of the residential school system and the consequences still felt today,” he said in the post. “Courageous survivors shared the truth so that all Canadians could take up the work of reconciliation.”
More than 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to attend residential schools, the last of which closed in 1996.

Thousands of children died in the institutions, and researchers at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation have identified 63 children who died at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School. In May 2021, the Tkemlups te Secwepemc First Nation announced ground-penetrating radar had uncovered what were believed to be 215 unmarked graves at the site of the former Kamloops residential school.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.
