stories.title: 1940s design helps Kingsway home sell $205,000 over asking
stories.summary: Classic brick and stone façade drew many buyers within first two days on the market
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
65 Dunedin Dr., Toronto

Asking price: $2,095,000 (August, 2026)

Selling price: $2.3-million (August, 2026)

Taxes: $10,021 (2026)

Days on the market: Two

Listing agent : Motria Dzulynsky, Re/Max Professionals Inc.

This four-bedroom house, near Dundas Street and Royal York Road, was posted for less than $2.1-million during the last week of August, usually a busy time in the home-selling market. Four buyers among those able to visit the home in its first two days on the market made offers, one of which, at $205,000 over the asking price, the seller accepted.

“We were priced well,” said agent Motria Dzulynsky. “I thought we’d get one really good offer or more than that, and we ended up with four.”

The classic 1940s brick and stone façade drew many buyers. A three-storey addition at the rear was completed in the 1980s.

“The layout was good, and it was in good shape,” Ms. Dzulynsky said. “You could just live there until you wanted to update.”

“It had an ensuite bath and four bedrooms, which is sought-after in the area.”

The two-storey house has a formal dining area and an eat-in kitchen with beamed ceilings and access to a deck. Fireplaces are in three entertaining areas, including one in the basement.

There are three bathrooms and a laundry room on the main floor.

A private driveway and garage are on the 40- by 104-foot lot.

“It’s a very sought-after street because it’s close to schools, like Lambton-Kingsway,” Ms. Dzulynsky said.

“It’s also quiet with no through traffic.”

stories.title: Toronto home sellers see a patch of blue sky in the market
stories.summary: Lighter supply helps to steady the market, with active listings shrinking in August year over year
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
Level-headed sellers and judicious buyers have brought some calm to the troubled Toronto condo segment as lighter supply helps to steady the market.

“It doesn’t feel like we’re free-falling any more. It feels like a lot of the damage has been done,” says Christopher Bibby, broker with Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty.

Active listings for condo apartments in the 416 region of Toronto shrank by 15.3 per cent in August from the same month last year, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board.

In the same period, sales edged down 0.2 per cent while the average price dipped 2.1 per cent.

Mr. Bibby believes slower sales in August were partly a result of potential buyers wanting to wait for fresh listings in September.

Meanwhile, some potential sellers are deciding to hold off for stronger prices or turning to the rental market instead.

So far, Mr. Bibby has not seen a surge of supply this fall in condos or single-family homes.

“I’m not seeing that big push we usually see post-Labour Day.”

As for buyers, Mr. Bibby says some anticipated that mortgage rates will rise. Some of those with pre-approvals for a three-year fixed-rate mortgage, for example, want to lock in a purchase now.

In September, Mr. Bibby says, some negotiations included a quick closing because pre-approved financing was set to expire after three months.

“People want to put these rates to work.”

Mr. Bibby recently sold a unit in the Wrigley Lofts in Leslieville after negotiations fell apart with the buyer earlier in the summer.

He listed the two-bedroom unit at 245 Carlaw Ave. in February with an asking price of $979,000.

In July, he cut the asking price to $925,000, where it remained when the listing expired in August.

“We were close to a deal – then they travelled, and we vanished,” says Mr. Bibby.

Not long after the listing expired, the buyer had their agent call Mr. Bibby to ask if the unit was still available.

The two sides hammered out a deal for $875,000 in September.

Mr. Bibby says buyers often seem indecisive as they hover around properties. But when listings are terminated or sold to another buyer, they regret missing out.

He received two lowball offers for the unit months earlier.

“It’s sometimes this waiting game – then when it disappears, it’s ‘what happened?’ If you want a loft in a converted bubble gum factory, how many are there?”

Paul Maranger and Christian Vermast of Sotheby’s International Realty Canada, recently drew three offers for a two-bedroom condo with 1,740 square feet of living space near Yonge Street and St. Clair Avenue.

Unit 1106 at 10 Delisle Ave. sold for $1.8-million, or $205,000 above the asking price of $1.595-million.

Larger units in walkable neighbourhoods are in high demand, says Mr. Vermast.

Mr. Maranger notes that the downtown area of Toronto is awash in micro condo units, but those are not the units that buyers are looking for in the current market.

“North of Bloor there is a dire shortage of larger suites.”

He estimates that only 11.9 per cent of the condos listed in the city of Toronto in the last week of September have an asking price above $1-million and only 2.6 per cent have an asking price above the $2-million mark.

Those numbers indicate that the large units in desirable neighbourhoods that many empty nesters are seeking are relatively scarce.

Some potential sellers are putting off listing until early 2027 because they are betting on a resolution to the trade conflict with the United States. Others are waiting to see what happens with the federal government’s ban on some categories of foreign buyers, which is set to end on Jan. 1.

Mr. Vermast notes that, as supply contracts, the list-to-sale price ratio is also tightening.

Sellers are probably more sensible in their pricing as well, he notes.

As buyers see more sales, their confidence is bolstered, he adds.

The two say that buyers seem more rational and less fearful this September than last.

“I think it’s a cautiously opportunistic fall market,” says Mr. Vermast.

Mr. Bibby was working to tie up loose ends on four conditional offers as September wound down.

Setting an asking price has become more straightforward, he says, because seller expectations are reasonable. He tends to set asking prices with a small buffer because nearly every buyer is seeking a discount.

“That’s a given,” he says. “We’re going out negotiable.”

In the west end, Mr. Bibby sold a penthouse at 22 Southport St. near South Kingsway for $1.057-million after listing the two-bedroom unit with an asking price of $1.099-million.

Mr. Bibby says the unit with 1,709 square feet of interior space and a 525-square-foot terrace sold after about three weeks on the market.

Units with a terrace are rare in the building, he says, and the large outdoor space in this case provides views of High Park and the city skyline.

The last time a unit with a terrace traded hands on the open market was 2003, he says.

Mr. Bibby, who has six new listings landing on the market in the last week of September, says sellers today are clear-eyed about the downturn in prices.

“Nobody’s really testing the market any more. They’re committed to the sale.”

At National Bank of Canada, economists Daren King and Evelyne Gosselin warn that a major headwind for the country’s housing market is looming in the form of rising interest rates.

Since the start of the conflict in Iran, U.S. and Canadian bond yields have surged, they note, and mortgage rates follow the trend set in the bond market.

Recently, however, mortgage rates have not kept pace with the rise in bond yields, which means a rise in fixed mortgage rates is highly likely in the coming weeks.

Rising financing costs are likely to weigh on affordability and further undermine the already fragile recovery in the housing market, caution Mr. King and Ms. Gosselin.

They say that outcome can still be avoided if there is a significant improvement in the geopolitical landscape, which would help to ease inflationary pressures, or a resolution to the trade turmoil between Canada and the United States, which would support the job market.

Mr. Bibby says the unit with 1,709 square feet of interior space and a 525-square-foot terrace sold after about three weeks on the market.
Units with a terrace are rare in the building, he says, and the large outdoor space in this case provides views of High Park and the city skyline.
The last time a unit with a terrace traded hands on the open market was 2003, he says.
Mr. Bibby, who has six new listings landing on the market in the last week of September, says sellers today are clear-eyed about the downturn in prices.
“Nobody’s really testing the market any more. They’re committed to the sale.”
At National Bank of Canada, economists Daren King and Evelyne Gosselin warn that a major headwind for the country’s housing market is looming in the form of rising interest rates.
Since the start of the conflict in Iran, U.S. and Canadian bond yields have surged, they note, and mortgage rates follow the trend set in the bond market.
Recently, however, mortgage rates have not kept pace with the rise in bond yields, which means a rise in fixed mortgage rates is highly likely in the coming weeks.
Rising financing costs are likely to weigh on affordability and further undermine the already fragile recovery in the housing market, caution Mr. King and Ms. Gosselin.

They say that outcome can still be avoided if there is a significant improvement in the geopolitical landscape, which would help to ease inflationary pressures, or a resolution to the trade turmoil between Canada and the United States, which would support the job market.

stories.title: Seller of three-bedroom Toronto condo holds out for the right buyer
stories.summary: Unit with both north and south views sells for $1.07-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
560 Front St. W., No. 1131, Toronto

Asking price: $1,125,000 (April, 2026)

Previous asking price: $1,125,000 (February, 2026)

Selling price: $1.07-million (June, 2026)

Previous selling price: $530,141 (January, 2012)

Taxes: $4,652 (2025)

Days on the market: 72

Property days on market: 129

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

Down the street from the popular Stackt Market and historic Fort York, the 15-year-old Rêve building has a steady turnover of one- and two-bedroom units, but the last three-bedroom model, like this one, sold several years ago. Agent Christopher Bibby was optimistic the long absence of similar units would generate attention for his client’s offering, and marked it for sale in February.

“At the time, there were other units for sale, but all smaller stuff, and nothing of this size,” said Mr. Bibby.

“It’s really rare to see a three-bedroom unit these days, especially one with windows in all the bedrooms.”

There were no offers for the 1,060-square-foot unit the first time around, and it was relisted with the same asking price in April. It wasn’t until June that a bid came in, though substantially below asking. Negotiations brought the sale price to $1.07-million.

“Showings were consistent, we were just waiting for someone to commit,” Mr. Bibby said.

“It’s a rare unit, centrally located, and the clients had fully renovated the property.”

This unit has north-facing windows in two bedrooms and south-facing windows in the primary bedroom. The adjacent living room has sliding doors to a balcony.

Hardwood flooring was recently installed, and the kitchen and two full bathrooms have been remodelled.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $1,033 cover concierge and use of building amenities, such as a gym, party room and rooftop deck.

“It has both north and south views,” Mr. Bibby said.

“The neighbourhood has really changed in the last few years with the addition of a grocery store directly behind.

“The Well is also down the road. It’s a new development with a collection of new restaurants, shops and boutiques.”

stories.title: Asset manager grows from ashes of rental scheme’s collapse
stories.summary: Company stepped in to rescue Thunder Bay senior-living facility in danger of having heat, electricity cut off
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
A private equity company that was born from the ashes of one of Ontario’s largest private-mortgage insolvencies has stepped in to rescue a senior-living facility in Thunder Bay that was in danger of having the heating and electricity cut off.

The declining conditions at Vickers Manor, formerly known as McKellar Place and McKellar Hospital, have been the subject of many local news stories and growing attention by city officials and politicians in the Northern Ontario city in recent months.

The 109-unit, six-storey building has seen an exodus of residents after dozens of fire code and health code violations were reported in the spring and summer, the latter resulted in the Thunder Bay District Health Unit seeking a court order for compliance from former owner Ongrasothy Masillamany and SMS Property Trust Inc.

The health complaints ranged from bed bugs and excessive heat to overflowing garbage. The fire code violations required repairs to multiple doors and emergency lights, installation of carbon monoxide detectors, in addition to keeping extinguishers and sprinklers inspected and in good working order.

“The priority right now is health and safety and fire code violations; money is in the bank and is being deployed to ensure the security and safety of residents,” said Sophia Pino, director of operations and people for Big North Capital, which backed the acquisition of the property from SMS.

Currently, the building is only about 15 per cent occupied, and some of the remaining tenants are among the most vulnerable residents who were placed there by social service agencies Brain Injury Services in Northern Ontario (Bisno) and Community Services for Independence Northwest.

The record of Sms’s ownership of the Thunder Bay site has been chaotic according to those close to the situation.

Michelle Hamilton’s son, John, a quadriplegic patient who receives support from Bisno, is one of the residents still in the building after being placed there in 2014. While the home wasn’t perfect before, Ms. Hamilton said things took a turn for the worse once SMS purchased the property.

“It was bad; they got rid of a lot of good staff, fired a manager,” she said. “We used to have a nurse practitioner on the main floor. It just went downhill.”

In July, SMS shut down the building’s commercial kitchen, which provided the meals that are included in the tenant’s rental agreements. In response, volunteers ran a GoFundMe online campaign that raised more than $15,000 to keep (at that time) 29 residents fed.

Earlier this year, the building was listed for sale for $18-million (later lowered to $1), but Big North took over the property after SMS defaulted on loan payments to lenders.

SMS itself originally purchased the property in a power of sale process, and just five months after the 2022 purchase it lost control of the building when a previous lender – Barrett Kudlow Capital Management Inc. – filed an application in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to appoint a receiver, saying it had lost faith in the company’s ability to manage the property.

“It appears that SMS has failed to pay many of its expenses since taking over the business, and has taken money from the business and deposited into other related businesses,” the 2022 court records state. However, by May, 2024, a refinancing settlement allowed Barrett Kudlow to exit, and the Court lifted the receivership order, returning control to SMS.

The building is one of the last remaining parts of a campus for the former McKeller Hospital, which was largely demolished after the 100-year-old hospital was decommissioned in 2004. In 2025, SMS rebranded the building Vickers Manor, erasing the property’s historic links.

However, some old troubles showed up even with the new name, with allegations of unpaid bills, maintenance complaints and code violations soon following.

While the project to revive the battered senior-living centre is a new challenge for Big North, Ms. Pino noted that stepping in to clean up messes is how the company was formed. “To an extent, it’s one building; we had to deal with 100 separate properties … that was challenging,” she said.

Ms. Pino said some Big North staff are temporarily moving to Thunder Bay to spearhead the remediation efforts, with phase two designed to address non-critical maintenance and aesthetic needs – painting and cleaning – that had gone unmet under the old owners.

The unit owners of Big North, a private equity company, are largely pulled from a pool of private mortgage lenders who were caught in the 2024 collapse of former child actor Robbie Clark’s rental home business. That turned out to be one of the largest insolvencies in Canadian history involving almost exclusively private lenders, who had contributed more than $135-million worth of private mortgages and promissory notes to Mr. Clarke’s companies to help it purchase more than 400 homes spread across four Northern Ontario cities.

After a year-long legal fight over the insolvency of Mr. Clark’s businesses, Big North was formed to help engineer a credit-bidding process for many of those lenders to band together and take control of 185 properties worth about $44-million. Some of the properties didn’t have roofs; many were untenanted, but over the past two years Big North’s team has poured money into repairs and operations, paring down some of the portfolio and achieving almost full occupancy in the rental homes. It has since expanded into investing in agriculture and finance.

In the future, the company plans to investigate reopening another wing of the Vickers Manor building that’s currently locked off, which has potentially 50 more apartments.

“There’s so much space and potential to make this a thriving community,” said Ms. Pino, who said the company hopes to make the building welcome again for residents who felt they had to flee in recent months. “We’re really thankful for a number of volunteers; everyone has rallied together.”

Ms. Hamilton is hopeful things will improve, but she’s been burned before and is cautious.

“I’m optimistic, but I’m guarded; I have no trust,” she said. “What needs to happen is people need to have follow-through.”
paragraphs: A private equity company that was born from the ashes of one of Ontario’s largest private-mortgage insolvencies has stepped in to rescue a senior-living facility in Thunder Bay that was in danger of having the heating and electricity cut off.

The declining conditions at Vickers Manor, formerly known as McKellar Place and McKellar Hospital, have been the subject of many local news stories and growing attention by city officials and politicians in the Northern Ontario city in recent months.

The 109-unit, six-storey building has seen an exodus of residents after dozens of fire code and health code violations were reported in the spring and summer, the latter resulted in the Thunder Bay District Health Unit seeking a court order for compliance from former owner Ongrasothy Masillamany and SMS Property Trust Inc.

The health complaints ranged from bed bugs and excessive heat to overflowing garbage. The fire code violations required repairs to multiple doors and emergency lights, installation of carbon monoxide detectors, in addition to keeping extinguishers and sprinklers inspected and in good working order.

“The priority right now is health and safety and fire code violations; money is in the bank and is being deployed to ensure the security and safety of residents,” said Sophia Pino, director of operations and people for Big North Capital, which backed the acquisition of the property from SMS.

Currently, the building is only about 15 per cent occupied, and some of the remaining tenants are among the most vulnerable residents who were placed there by social service agencies Brain Injury Services in Northern Ontario (Bisno) and Community Services for Independence Northwest.
The record of Sms’s ownership of the Thunder Bay site has been chaotic according to those close to the situation.

Michelle Hamilton’s son, John, a quadriplegic patient who receives support from Bisno, is one of the residents still in the building after being placed there in 2014. While the home wasn’t perfect before, Ms. Hamilton said things took a turn for the worse once SMS purchased the property.
“It was bad; they got rid of a lot of good staff, fired a manager,” she said. “We used to have a nurse practitioner on the main floor. It just went downhill.”

In July, SMS shut down the building’s commercial kitchen, which provided the meals that are included in the tenant’s rental agreements. In response, volunteers ran a GoFundMe online campaign that raised more than $15,000 to keep (at that time) 29 residents fed.
Earlier this year, the building was listed for sale for $18-million (later lowered to $1), but Big North took over the property after SMS defaulted on loan payments to lenders.

SMS itself originally purchased the property in a power of sale process, and just five months after the 2022 purchase it lost control of the building when a previous lender – Barrett Kudlow Capital Management Inc. – filed an application in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to appoint a receiver, saying it had lost faith in the company’s ability to manage the property.

“It appears that SMS has failed to pay many of its expenses since taking over the business, and has taken money from the business and deposited into other related businesses,” the 2022 court records state. However, by May, 2024, a refinancing settlement allowed Barrett Kudlow to exit, and the Court lifted the receivership order, returning control to SMS.

The building is one of the last remaining parts of a campus for the former McKeller Hospital, which was largely demolished after the 100-year-old hospital was decommissioned in 2004. In 2025, SMS rebranded the building Vickers Manor, erasing the property’s historic links.
However, some old troubles showed up even with the new name, with allegations of unpaid bills, maintenance complaints and code violations soon following.

While the project to revive the battered senior-living centre is a new challenge for Big North, Ms. Pino noted that stepping in to clean up messes is how the company was formed. “To an extent, it’s one building; we had to deal with 100 separate properties … that was challenging,” she said.

Ms. Pino said some Big North staff are temporarily moving to Thunder Bay to spearhead the remediation efforts, with phase two designed to address non-critical maintenance and aesthetic needs – painting and cleaning – that had gone unmet under the old owners.

The unit owners of Big North, a private equity company, are largely pulled from a pool of private mortgage lenders who were caught in the 2024 collapse of former child actor Robbie Clark’s rental home business. That turned out to be one of the largest insolvencies in Canadian history involving almost exclusively private lenders, who had contributed more than $135-million worth of private mortgages and promissory notes to Mr. Clarke’s companies to help it purchase more than 400 homes spread across four Northern Ontario cities.

After a year-long legal fight over the insolvency of Mr. Clark’s businesses, Big North was formed to help engineer a credit-bidding process for many of those lenders to band together and take control of 185 properties worth about $44-million. Some of the properties didn’t have roofs; many were untenanted, but over the past two years Big North’s team has poured money into repairs and operations, paring down some of the portfolio and achieving almost full occupancy in the rental homes. It has since expanded into investing in agriculture and finance.
In the future, the company plans to investigate reopening another wing of the Vickers Manor building that’s currently locked off, which has potentially 50 more apartments.

“There’s so much space and potential to make this a thriving community,” said Ms. Pino, who said the company hopes to make the building welcome again for residents who felt they had to flee in recent months. “We’re really thankful for a number of volunteers; everyone has rallied together.”
Ms. Hamilton is hopeful things will improve, but she’s been burned before and is cautious.
“I’m optimistic, but I’m guarded; I have no trust,” she said. “What needs to happen is people need to have follow-through.”

stories.title: New housing at a former 1940s bombing and gunnery school in Picton, Ont.
stories.summary: With six developers teaming up for the gargantuan project, the various housing clusters won’t lay a finger on the heritage portion
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
I remember having a high-school debate with friends: had we been born 40 or 50 years earlier, what role would we have wanted during the Second World War? While almost no one chose the Canadian Army, the debate over being in the Royal Canadian Navy or the Royal Canadian Air Force was fierce: on a ship, friends argued, you had a chance to jump into the water to save yourself, while being trapped in a metal box hurtling through the air didn’t leave much hope if one’s engines failed.

But, as I stand in the Exhibition Hall of Base 31 in Picton, Ont., and gaze up at the majestic Lancaster bomber (KB882), I can’t help but picture myself in an Rcaf uniform. According to the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum website, the Lancaster was the RAF/Rcaf’s “only heavy bomber capable of carrying the 12,000[-pound] ‘Tallboy’ and 22,000[-pound] ‘Grand Slam’ bombs” and it “won a place for itself in history” at the Ruhr dams in 1943 and the sinking of the German battleship Tirpitz in 1944.

“It’s here until 2034, for now,” says Alexandra De Gasperis, vice-president of Deco Communities Inc. The aircraft is on loan from National Air Force Museum of Canada. “They want to build a permanent home for it in Trenton.”

And speaking of permanent homes, 7,500 of them will eventually surround this almost-intact, 28-hectare 1940 military base on the escarpment above Picton.

“Now that sounds staggering,” continues Ms. De Gasperis, “but it’s important to note that that was a number embedded in the secondary plan and it was a number put forward by the county [Prince Edward County]; this is part of their planned growth area prior to us even purchasing the site.”

At more than 300 hectares, there is plenty of room. And the various housing clusters – which will contain stacked townhouses at $299,900 as well as mews houses, bungalows and two-storey houses at higher prices – won’t lay a finger on the heritage portion, despite (or perhaps because of) the fact that six developers have teamed up for the gargantuan project.

It’s already been a huge undertaking since PEC Community Partners Inc. (the six developers) purchased the site in 2021. I first saw the site two years ago, after PEC had already held an Idea Fair, run focus groups and surveys, and begun regular concerts in the Drill Hall. Yet, the site still felt raw and lacked cohesion.

In September of 2026, I arrived to find a bold, concrete-and-Corten-steel roadside sign, laughing pickleballers on new courts (a partnership with Toronto’s Fairgrounds Public Racket Club), way-finding aplenty, and established amenities such as The Commissary and a much-needed daycare.

“Do you want to sit in the front?” offers Tammy Sweeney, general manager of Base 31. I accept, and our little group – which also includes Kathryn Randle, vice-president of planning and development at Rockport Group – fills the back rows of the golf cart. As we drive, bumpily, to Exhibition Hall, Ms. De Gasperis says that after stormwater management is addressed, the roads will be smoothed out.

After ogling the Lancaster bomber, I peruse Exhibition Hall’s other exhibits, such as a reproduction of the Avro Arrow scale models that were stored and tested here in the 1950s, a series of love letters between an Rcaf member and his girlfriend, and, under glass, uniforms and other artifacts.

“Some of them are actually radioactive,” says Ms. De Gasperis, “so we can’t display them.”

When it opened in 1941, No. 31 Bombing and Gunnery School was part of a network of training bases built in Canada under the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan, and included not only six massive hangars, but officer’s and men’s quarters, two hospitals, a dental clinic, maintenance and paint shops, Quonset huts, a hostess house/fire chief’s cottage, parachute storage building, a theatre/dance hall, and, obviously, a series of runways. Airmen-in-training came from all over the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Base 31 was decommissioned in 1969.

And, says Ms. De Gasperis, many of the men came back: “The men who trained here often took up roots here after the war. … Many of them came back and married here because there was a matchmaker that organized dances.”

En route to the Drill Hall/Gymnasium, we pass one of the very few buildings, an “H-hut,” that will have to come down (due to restoration efforts under Jacqui Burley, manager of the site under previous owners, there are only a few). The Drill Hall, however, has been completely restored with new shingles in the same green as the vintage versions, new flooring in parts (original portions show the basketball markings), along with new plumbing and washrooms; it’s a beautiful room that has hosted acts such as The Sheepdogs, Blue Rodeo and Judy Collins.

Our next stop, Hangar 6, is mostly empty, but fun to experience for scale. But it’s our fourth stop that gets my neck hair standing at attention: the monolithic, buttressed concrete wall that gunners, from the air, would use for target-practice. Since there are only a few pockmarks, I remark that it must have been patched over after every dozen strafings.

Next, we tour “Building 3,” an entirely refurbished H-hut building that contains the Hub Child & Family Centre (daycare), Wildlings Play Café and the Arts Collective. In here, what strikes me, again, is scale: the Hub alone is 3,750 square feet, the café is 2,400 sq. ft. Outside, we admire (and play in) the Sensory Garden by Wild Child Regeneration.

And speaking of gardens, PEC Community Partners is promising 110 hectares of green space, 10,000 metres of walking trails and a great deal of public art; right now, nearby Oeno Gallery has collaborated to create an Art Walk.

It’s heady stuff indeed, made all the richer by the commitment to preservation.

“This is a national treasure,” finishes Ms. De Gasperis. “We haven’t had a single ounce of government funding for anything that we’ve done here.”

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that the Lancaster KB882 bomber is on loan to Base 31 from the Rcaf. It is on loan to the National Air Force Museum of Canada. This article has also been updated to correct the starting price for stacked townhomes in the development; they will be sold for $299,900, not $299,000 as previously stated.

stories.title: How Carney’s infrastructure push is testing reconciliation
stories.summary: In today's The Big Story podcast, as Prime Minister Mark Carney longs for a stronger Canada, his lust for fast-tracking projects signals a threat to meaningful conversation and consultation from Indigenous groups.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted September 30, 2026 7:38 am.

In today’s The Big Story podcast, as Prime Minister Mark Carney longs for a stronger Canada, his lust for fast-tracking projects signals a threat to meaningful conversation and consultation from Indigenous groups.

Earlier this month at his Investment Summit in Toronto, hundreds of protestors across the country gathered in opposition to his pitch for a trillion dollars in exchange for what they feel like is their say in projects. Same goes for the Ontario government’s plans for infrastructure surrounding the Ring of Fire, specifically Bill 5.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Chadwick Cowie, political science professor at the University of Toronto to discuss the Carney government’s relationship with First Nations, Inuit and Métis groups, and why pushing their voices to the fringes is more dangerous than not.

stories.title: Ontario hospitals owed private banks $70 million last year — and one wasn't sure it could even keep operating
stories.summary: One hospital, Strathroy Middlesex General, wasn't sure it could even keep operating.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
Ontario hospitals, forced to borrow privately in order to keep the lights on, owed banks more than $70 million on operating borrowings by the end of fiscal year 2025-26, according to hospital financial statements.

With 80 of the 129 Ontario hospital networks posting operating deficits last year, at least $1.45 million in public health-care dollars went to bank interest payments from just eight hospital networks, the Investigative Journalism Bureau found.

Niagara Health, for instance, paid about $549,000 in operating interest, said the organization’s spokesperson, Erica Bajer. The Huron Perth Healthcare Alliance in southwestern Ontario paid $346,000 in interest on its operating borrowings, according to spokesperson Gerry Rucchin. CEO Andrew Williams said the institution continues “to focus on minimizing debt servicing costs wherever possible” while focusing on patient care.

Strathroy Middlesex Hospital, west of London, Ont., expressed concern in its financial statement about its ability to even continue operating.

And 12 Ontario hospital networks, including Scarborough Health Network, North York General Hospital and The Ottawa Hospital collectively increased their borrowing capacity from the previous year by close to $460 million, according to financial statements.

“The only way for them (hospitals) to survive is to borrow money … That’s totally unsustainable,” said Michel Grignon, a health economist at McMaster University in Hamilton. “It doesn’t make any sense that taxpayers would simply line the pockets of banks, that’s absolutely not the way it was supposed to work.”

The need to increase borrowing capacity last year is a “sign hospitals have been cut to the bone,” he said.

Thousands of Canadians implanted with metal hip devices despite warnings of pain and complications

How successful is egg freezing? Fertility clinics don't have to say

Neither the Ontario Ministry of Health, Ontario Health nor Health Minister Sylvia Jones responded to questions about hospital bank borrowing or provincial funding.

It doesn't make any sense that taxpayers would simply line the pockets of banks, that's absolutely not the way it was supposed to work Michel Grignon, health economist

The true value of interest paid on operating borrowings remains shrouded in secrecy, with some hospitals not disclosing this information in their financial statements. Some declined to provide it to the IJB when asked.

A hospital network spokesperson from Waterloo Regional Health Network said she’d been advised not to disclose the hospital’s borrowing details, adding “there is nothing that’s going to serve our purposes.”

Jennifer Lawrance, CEO of Red Lake Margaret Cornehour Memorial Hospital in northwestern Ontario, said she believes it is “ethically wrong that taxpayers should be paying interest” for hospital borrowing.

“I’m not suggesting that the hospitals who are borrowing are wrong in doing so,” she added. “They’re doing that to keep their doors open, because funding isn’t keeping up with the operational costs.”

One of the biggest percentage deficits recorded this year was from Anson General Hospital in northeastern Ontario, in Iroquois Falls, near Timmins, which finished the year in the red for the fourth consecutive time.

Asked if the hospital expects to find efficiencies that would return it to a balanced position, Paul Chatelain, CEO of the MIC Group, which includes Anson General Hospital, told the IJB, “We don’t have any fat to trim.”

“Our reserves are not keeping up, they’re almost depleted.”

Ontario law requires hospitals to plan for a balanced budget each year but the province can give special dispensation to end the year in the red. Financial records show the province can also provide one-time shortfall funding, including at least $325 million given to 30 hospital networks last fiscal year, according to the IJBs analysis of hospital financial statements.

The latest IJB findings come six months after the Ontario government pledged an additional $1.1 billion in funding for hospitals as part of its 2026 budget, up four per cent from the previous year. The Ontario Hospital Association says costs are increasing by six per cent a year, due to an aging population and inflation.

David McNeil, CEO of Health Sciences North, in the greater Sudbury region, told the IJB that his hospital had identified $18 million in savings over the past three years, mostly by reducing the use of private agencies to staff nurses.

Still, Health Sciences North, which had total revenues of close to $800 million last year, explicitly states in its financial statements the need to rely on “temporary financing through its existing credit facilities” in the short-term.

“We would prefer not to have to rely on lines of credit to sustain the operations of the hospital. That’s the fundamental piece and that’s what we’ve been struggling with as an industry,” McNeil told the IJB. “Efficiency itself is not going to be sufficient enough to close the gap between what hospitals need and what they’re spending today.”

McNeil said his hospital keeps the provincial health ministry “well informed” of its bank borrowing.

Variations in financial reporting across the province’s hospital sector make annual comparisons of indebtedness difficult to monitor.

A January IJB investigation found Ontario hospitals paid at least $4 million in interest on borrowing in the fiscal year 2024-2025. Nearly $2 million of that was paid by Hamilton Health Sciences.

This year, the hospital would not disclose any interest paid on its borrowing for 2025-2026.

Hamilton Health Sciences financial statements show it owed $40 million on its two operating lines of credits by fiscal year-end and intended to “rely on temporary financing through its existing credit facilities” in the short term.

Waterloo Regional Health Network (Wrhn) owed close to $9 million on its operating line of credit in March 2026 and paid close to $1 million in interest on this line and its two operating loans. The hospital reported defaulting on its bank loans in its most recent financial statement.

The network’s spokesperson, Cassandra Easton, told the IJB the loans did not relate to operating borrowing, but declined to disclose how much interest the network paid on its borrowings to sustain daily operations, saying she’d “been advised not to provide anything further.” Easton declined to say who provided that directive.

In March, the hospital’s annual financial statement showed it was “in violation of the covenants” relating to several loans. The hospital network reached an agreement with the bank, which is not named in the financial statement, not to demand a repayment until April 2027.

“Access to credit is a common treasury management tool used by large healthcare organizations to support liquidity and maintain financial stability,” Easton said in an email, adding the hospital “maintains ongoing discussions” with the province about financial pressures.

Among the hospitals that increased their borrowing capacity from last year was the Ottawa Hospital (TOH), which increased its operating lines of credit to $120 million in 2026, up from $24 million in 2025.

“Having sufficient line of credit as a liquidity buffer is a standard industry best practice of managing financial risks actively and does not warrant any funding issues,” TOH spokesperson Michaela Schreiter said in an email.

“TOH recognizes the importance of minimizing the interest burden on taxpayers. Hence, the hospital manages its working capital prudently and draws on the line of credit only when needed,” she added. As of March 2026, it had not drawn on this line of credit.

Scarborough Health Network arranged for a new $120-million operating line of credit, and North York General Hospital took out a new $60-million loan to finance day-to-day operations, the financial records show.

In a response to questions, Scarborough Health Network spokesperson Leigh Duncan said it is “one of Ontario’s most efficient hospital systems,” and “continues to experience significant growth and demand pressures.”

“Any borrowing capacity available to the organization is a financial management tool that helps ensure continuity of operations and patient care while we work within existing funding structures,” Duncan said.

North York General Hospital did not respond to requests for comment.

Strathroy Middlesex General, which worried about its ability to operate, cited an accumulated deficit of over $24 million and an increased use of credit lines.

“As a result, there is material uncertainty that May cast significant doubt on the hospital’s ability to continue as a going concern,” read the hospital’s financial statements.

Julie McBrien, CEO of Middlesex Hospital Alliance, which Strathroy Middlesex General belongs to, declined to comment on the specifics of the hospital’s financials, but said the hospital system “continues to navigate significant system pressures while remaining focused on delivering safe, high-quality care.”

Len Brooks, professor emeritus of business ethics and accounting at the University of Toronto, told the IJB that hospitals borrowing from banks “is not unreasonable” given that the province itself operates in a deficit.

“There’s lots of good work that can be done if hospitals have funds in the short run, even if sourced from banks,” said Brooks. “It might be a very good thing for them from the perspective of patients.”

The problem, says Brooks, is when hospitals routinely cite chronic, structural deficits as reasons for borrowing, which means they are routinely spending more than they are taking in.

“That signals to the government that there’s something to watch for and to look into.”

Health-care workers say ongoing deficits are being felt across hospital floors.

Dr. Raghu Venugopal, an emergency physician who works across three Toronto hospitals, told reporters that despite the uptick in provincial funding, things are “worse than ever before.”

“Hospital budgets are literally the issue of life and death,” he says. “One of the markers that can’t lie is the number of hallway stretchers, and that’s just metastasized like cancer.”

Citing a lack of acute care beds, he said patients have died, “because we didn’t get to them and we didn’t do the medical work because there was nowhere to offload them.”

The Ontario Nurses’ Association has claimed that hospitals have cut more than 1,500 nursing positions since December 2025, attributing the cuts to underfunding. The province has not provided an official number.

“Letting go of those nurses means, of course, the quality of care is going to decrease,” said health economist Grignon. “This is going to translate into more adverse events. It is going to translate into patients not being taken care of in a timely manner.”

The Investigative Journalism Bureau (IJB) at the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana School of Public Health is a collaborative investigative newsroom supported by Postmedia that partners with academics, researchers and journalists while training the next generation of investigative reporters.

Strathroy Middlesex General, which worried about its ability to operate, cited an accumulated deficit of over $24 million and an increased use of credit lines.
“As a result, there is material uncertainty that May cast significant doubt on the hospital’s ability to continue as a going concern,” read the hospital’s financial statements.

Julie McBrien, CEO of Middlesex Hospital Alliance, which Strathroy Middlesex General belongs to, declined to comment on the specifics of the hospital’s financials, but said the hospital system “continues to navigate significant system pressures while remaining focused on delivering safe, high-quality care.”

Len Brooks, professor emeritus of business ethics and accounting at the University of Toronto, told the IJB that hospitals borrowing from banks “is not unreasonable” given that the province itself operates in a deficit.

“There’s lots of good work that can be done if hospitals have funds in the short run, even if sourced from banks,” said Brooks. “It might be a very good thing for them from the perspective of patients.”
The problem, says Brooks, is when hospitals routinely cite chronic, structural deficits as reasons for borrowing, which means they are routinely spending more than they are taking in.
“That signals to the government that there’s something to watch for and to look into.”
Health-care workers say ongoing deficits are being felt across hospital floors.
Dr. Raghu Venugopal, an emergency physician who works across three Toronto hospitals, told reporters that despite the uptick in provincial funding, things are “worse than ever before.”
“Hospital budgets are literally the issue of life and death,” he says. “One of the markers that can’t lie is the number of hallway stretchers, and that’s just metastasized like cancer.”
Citing a lack of acute care beds, he said patients have died, “because we didn’t get to them and we didn’t do the medical work because there was nowhere to offload them.”

The Ontario Nurses’ Association has claimed that hospitals have cut more than 1,500 nursing positions since December 2025, attributing the cuts to underfunding. The province has not provided an official number.

“Letting go of those nurses means, of course, the quality of care is going to decrease,” said health economist Grignon. “This is going to translate into more adverse events. It is going to translate into patients not being taken care of in a timely manner.”

stories.title: Early guilty plea helps earn two year sentence for B.C. man who buried ex's mother in 'surreptitious grave' after killing her
stories.summary: The Crown and defence submitted a joint sentencing submission for Carson MacKay, who pleaded guilty to manslaughter in Jodine Millar's death.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
A man who killed his ex-girlfriend’s bipolar mother and hid her body in the woods to be ravaged by wild animals before her remains could be found will spend two years in prison, a B.C. judge ruled earlier this month.

The Winnipeg native, who was apprehended in Calgary, pleaded guilty to manslaughter charges this January and was sentenced by Justice David M. Layton in a New Westminster courtroom on Sept. 15, after accepting a joint submission from Crown and defence counsel.

Layton said the sentence “reflects a properly functioning justice system, as opposed to one that has broken down, and accounts for the hard decisions Crown and defence counsel must legitimately make in difficult cases.”

According to an agreed statement of facts in his recently published decision , MacKay and Millar’s daughter, Sara, had been in a relationship since 2017. In July 2021, it was agreed that Millar would come to live with them in Kelowna and the trio moved to a home in Coquitlam the following year, where the couple resided on the main floor and she in the basement, with shared common spaces.

“Millar had experienced mental health difficulties, including bipolar disorder, and Sara wanted to look after her,” the judge wrote, noting that the older woman “sometimes failed to take her medication as prescribed.”

By August, the couple had split up and while Sara moved out, Millar stayed in the basement. The decision does not explain why.

Former B.C. teacher, 86, to remain imprisoned on child sex offences pending appeal, court rules

'Hard to imagine a more invasive offence': B.C. man gets 28 months for alleyway rape

On Nov. 26, Millar “was in a manic state, and was acting in a paranoid and erratic manner,” resulting in her overfeeding her dog and the animal vomiting on the stairs outside her bedroom door.

As MacKay was cleaning up the mess, a “paranoid and angry” Millar emerged from her room yelling at him while holding the steak knife she used to cut her pills. The two “got into a physical altercation,” during which MacKay pushed her hard, causing her to fall on her bedroom floor.

He went back upstairs and left Millar “space to calm down.” When he returned some 10 minutes later, he found her in a pool of blood from a wound caused by the knife that had become “lodged in her body” when she fell.

Fearing someone would think he’d intentionally murdered Millar, MacKay wrapped her “body in blankets and bound it with tape, rope and a dog collar” and drove it in her car to “an empty lot on Burke Mountain where he buried it in a clandestine grave in a forested area.” He reported her missing to police the following day.

According to Coquitlam RCMP, her vehicle was involved in a single-vehicle collision along Highway 1 at No. 3 Road in Abbotsford shortly after 9 p.m. on Nov. 28. The vehicle was empty when police arrived.

When discovered under undisclosed circumstances in May 2023, her decomposed remains showed damage “consistent with large animal scavenging.”

In her victim impact statement, read aloud in court, Sara didn’t address Millar’s mental struggles but called her a hard-working and supportive mother who “put herself through trade school to become a journeyman electrician.”

“Not knowing what had happened to her for so many months was traumatic, as was the later knowledge about how her remains had been disrespected and discarded,” the judge summarized.

Layton said he had to consider many aggravating and mitigating factors in determining whether to accept the joint sentencing submission.

“Particularly aggravating,” he said, was MacKay “taking actions that desecrated” Millar’s body by hiding it and not reporting it to authorities. Also working against him was that she was killed in her own home, “which should have been a place of safety,” and the impact on the family by burying Millar “in a surreptitious grave” and depriving her family the chance to mourn and bury her appropriately.

Layton also said MacKay’s youth and his size advantage over Millar — six-foot-three and 160 pounds to her five-foot-five and 125 pounds — was another aggravating factor. In pushing her down, the judge said MacKay was “not protecting himself, but rather was acting out of frustration.”

On the mitigating side were the brevity of the altercation, the single push, the “significant element of chance” in Millar’s death, that it was out of character for MacKay and the strong community support for him.

MacKay also pleaded guilty before even pre-trial applications were heard, thereby sparing Millar’s family from “additional grief and anxiety.”

Layton noted his early plea meant MacKay surrendered several strong arguments that could have helped him fight the charge had it gone to trial. Chief among them was a Jordan application under section 11 (b) of the Canadian Charter — when the defence seeks a stay of proceedings for failing to resolve the matter in a “reasonable time,” as established by the Supreme Court of Canada’s 2016 R. v. Jordan case. In the case of a provincial trial, the period is 18 months.

“The parties acknowledge that the presumptive Jordan ceiling would have been surpassed by six months by the time the trial concluded, that no delay had been waived by the defence, and that despite attempts to schedule earlier trial dates it was not possible to do so,” Layton wrote, noting even the Crown stressed the importance of him forgoing the application.

The plea also meant MacKay gave up “‘very viable’ arguments for excluding Crown evidence, arising from alleged breaches” under sections 7, 8 and 9 of the Charter, which spell out the core legal rights protecting people from unlawful or unfair state interference.

The judge also said MacKay could have made a legitimate argument about identification after the Crown highlighted “numerous areas of weakness in its circumstantial case” during preliminary inquiry, “any of which May have ultimately affected the trial verdict.”

As highlighted by the judge, under the Criminal Code of Canada, a conviction of manslaughter without the use of a firearm normally carries a sentencing “range of four to fifteen years.”

But bearing all the factors in mind, Layton said he had “no difficulty in concluding that this is one of those cases where the circumstances justify a sentence below the range of four to fifteen years’ imprisonment.”

MacKay was sentenced to two years and 99 days, but received credit for 99 days spent in pre-sentence custody. He is also prohibited from owning a firearm for 10 years after release, was ordered to submit a DNA sample, and have no direct contact with the Millar family while in prison.

As MacKay was cleaning up the mess, a “paranoid and angry” Millar emerged from her room yelling at him while holding the steak knife she used to cut her pills. The two “got into a physical altercation,” during which MacKay pushed her hard, causing her to fall on her bedroom floor.

He went back upstairs and left Millar “space to calm down.” When he returned some 10 minutes later, he found her in a pool of blood from a wound caused by the knife that had become “lodged in her body” when she fell.

Fearing someone would think he’d intentionally murdered Millar, MacKay wrapped her “body in blankets and bound it with tape, rope and a dog collar” and drove it in her car to “an empty lot on Burke Mountain where he buried it in a clandestine grave in a forested area.” He reported her missing to police the following day.

According to Coquitlam RCMP, her vehicle was involved in a single-vehicle collision along Highway 1 at No. 3 Road in Abbotsford shortly after 9 p.m. on Nov. 28. The vehicle was empty when police arrived.
When discovered under undisclosed circumstances in May 2023, her decomposed remains showed damage “consistent with large animal scavenging.”

In her victim impact statement, read aloud in court, Sara didn’t address Millar’s mental struggles but called her a hard-working and supportive mother who “put herself through trade school to become a journeyman electrician.”
“Not knowing what had happened to her for so many months was traumatic, as was the later knowledge about how her remains had been disrespected and discarded,” the judge summarized.
Layton said he had to consider many aggravating and mitigating factors in determining whether to accept the joint sentencing submission.

“Particularly aggravating,” he said, was MacKay “taking actions that desecrated” Millar’s body by hiding it and not reporting it to authorities. Also working against him was that she was killed in her own home, “which should have been a place of safety,” and the impact on the family by burying Millar “in a surreptitious grave” and depriving her family the chance to mourn and bury her appropriately.

Layton also said MacKay’s youth and his size advantage over Millar — six-foot-three and 160 pounds to her five-foot-five and 125 pounds — was another aggravating factor. In pushing her down, the judge said MacKay was “not protecting himself, but rather was acting out of frustration.”

On the mitigating side were the brevity of the altercation, the single push, the “significant element of chance” in Millar’s death, that it was out of character for MacKay and the strong community support for him.
MacKay also pleaded guilty before even pre-trial applications were heard, thereby sparing Millar’s family from “additional grief and anxiety.”

Layton noted his early plea meant MacKay surrendered several strong arguments that could have helped him fight the charge had it gone to trial. Chief among them was a Jordan application under section 11 (b) of the Canadian Charter — when the defence seeks a stay of proceedings for failing to resolve the matter in a “reasonable time,” as established by the Supreme Court of Canada’s 2016 R. v. Jordan case. In the case of a provincial trial, the period is 18 months.

“The parties acknowledge that the presumptive Jordan ceiling would have been surpassed by six months by the time the trial concluded, that no delay had been waived by the defence, and that despite attempts to schedule earlier trial dates it was not possible to do so,” Layton wrote, noting even the Crown stressed the importance of him forgoing the application.

The plea also meant MacKay gave up “‘very viable’ arguments for excluding Crown evidence, arising from alleged breaches” under sections 7, 8 and 9 of the Charter, which spell out the core legal rights protecting people from unlawful or unfair state interference.

The judge also said MacKay could have made a legitimate argument about identification after the Crown highlighted “numerous areas of weakness in its circumstantial case” during preliminary inquiry, “any of which May have ultimately affected the trial verdict.”
As highlighted by the judge, under the Criminal Code of Canada, a conviction of manslaughter without the use of a firearm normally carries a sentencing “range of four to fifteen years.”

But bearing all the factors in mind, Layton said he had “no difficulty in concluding that this is one of those cases where the circumstances justify a sentence below the range of four to fifteen years’ imprisonment.”

MacKay was sentenced to two years and 99 days, but received credit for 99 days spent in pre-sentence custody. He is also prohibited from owning a firearm for 10 years after release, was ordered to submit a DNA sample, and have no direct contact with the Millar family while in prison.

stories.title: Refugee claimants strike out after Federal Court says their legal claim is AI fakery
stories.summary: The family's claim was rejected because their appeal was apparently generated by AI tools and riddled with fake cases and false legal arguments.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
A claim for refugee protection in Canada by a family of three has been rejected because their appeal was apparently generated by artificial intelligence tools and riddled with fake cases and false legal arguments.

The Federal Court issued a sharp rebuke of a court filing that challenges an Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) decision that refused asylum to the trio, with Justice Roger Lafrenière saying the appeal is riddled with nonsense and calling it “an abusive document.”

A lawyer representing the failed refugee claimants had requested the court accept the late filing of its documentation in their appeal. The IRB had previously found the asylum claim “manifestly unfounded.”

Lafrenière said the mistake over the filing date might have been excused until he saw the arguments relied on “fictitious citations” and “wholly inaccurate references to legal precedents.”

Lafrenière said the lawyer’s arguments cited case law from five prior Federal Court cases. The “cases,” however, cannot be found at the citations provided, nor do the citations to real cases make the argument the filing claims.

“The Applicants’ Memorandum of Argument is replete with inaccurate and, dare one say, misleading arguments,” Lafrenière wrote in a decision released Monday. In some of the cases, the precedent cited says the opposite of what the filing claims.

For example, the document cites two cases in support of an argument over judicial discretion. “However, nothing of the sort is stated in either of the two cases,” wrote Lafrenière. The document also gives one citation as being found in paragraphs 28–33 of a judgment that has only 10 paragraphs, and it is on an irrelevant subject.

“Citing fake cases in court filings is an abuse of process and is tantamount to making a false statement to the Court,” Lafrenière wrote in his judgment. “In addition, making misleading arguments to the Court violates professional ethics and counsel’s fundamental legal duty of candor.”

Judge slams Ontario lawyer for filing made-up legal quotes; lawyer says it's 'human error' not AI

Toronto prof called 'Godfather of AI' quits Google to warn world about the dangerous technology

Government lawyers flagged concerns over the written material of the three applicants. The parties were given an opportunity to answer the allegations but failed to respond, court said.

“I can only conclude that AI was used in the drafting of the Applicants’ Memorandum of Argument without careful human judgment being applied to the output,” said Lafrenière.

“AI tools promise efficiency; however, their indiscriminate use in drafting legal arguments constitutes a pernicious threat to the integrity of the judicial process. Fabricated case citations distort and corrupt the case law. Superficial fluency also creates an illusion of competence and genuine legal reasoning that masks underlying inaccuracies. In addition, inaccurate legal arguments shaped by AI also results in the waste of scarce resources, both judicial and those of the opposing party.

“Whether accidental or deliberate, reliance on false citations and advancing misleading arguments on matters of substance cannot be condoned by this Court. For these reasons, I decline to exercise my discretion in favour of the Applicants.”

Washim Ahmed, a lawyer with OWS Law in Toronto, is listed as the lawyer of record in the case. He said he is investigating what happened.

“I was shocked to see it,” Ahmed told National Post. He said filings are sometimes made by others at the firm in his name.

“Based on my preliminary review and discussion with the associate lawyer who worked on the file it appears that an earlier draft was inadvertently included when the applicant’s record was compiled. A revised version had been prepared but was not included in the compiled record. This was an inadvertent error,” he said.

Ahmed said his office also did not receive the government’s reply that originally flagged the citations, and was unaware of the court’s concern.

He is preparing a motion asking the court to reconsider the decision on the refugee appeal, to allow him to provide a new version of the document and explain how the error occurred, he said.

Lafrenière’s ruling suggests that even if he had allowed the motion to accept the late filing, it would not have made much difference to the claimants’ prospects of being granted asylum in Canada.

“The determinative issue before the (Irb’s Refugee Protection Division known as the RPD) was credibility. The panel also found that the Applicants’ claim was clearly fraudulent given the repeated reliance by the principal claimant… on fraudulent documents to mislead the RPD on central components of his claim,” Lafrenière wrote on the substance of the applicants’ complaint.

“The result reached (by the RPD) was transparent, intelligible and among the alternatives available to the panel on the evidence and arguments before it.”
