stories.title: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette’s fresh start withers in the end
stories.summary: François Legault’s successor tried to set herself apart, and it seemed to be paying off. But she and the Coalition Avenir Québec are now fighting for survival in Monday’s election
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Christine Fréchette has done her best to outrun her own party.

Since taking over the Coalition Avenir Québec and becoming Premier in April, she has tried less to rehabilitate a tarnished brand than to erase it.

Her strategy was on display at the launch of the Quebec election campaign in late August, when observers quickly noticed that her bus and election signs did not feature her party’s name. “ Avançons ,” her campaign slogan read. Let’s move forward.

Ms. Fréchette, 56, began the first debate of the campaign by declaring that she is not her predecessor, François Legault.

As she faces a restive electorate looking for change, she has attempted to shed the baggage of her party’s eight years in government. In this election, she is selling herself.

For a moment, voters were buying in. Early in the campaign, which began days after trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart, Ms. Fréchette invited comparisons to Prime Minister Mark Carney. Like him, she embodied the sort of unflappable technocrat that seemed a welcome contrast to the erratic and hostile behaviour of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Though the Coalition Avenir Québec had spent months circling the drain, Ms. Fréchette, who declined an interview request from The Globe and Mail, orchestrated an unlikely comeback.

It seemed possible she could achieve what Mr. Carney had done in last year’s federal election and turn near-certain defeat into an improbable victory. If she was a touch bland, well, perhaps that was exactly what Quebeckers were looking for.

But then it went away. Days ahead of the vote on Oct. 5, Ms. Fréchette’s campaign has lost its momentum. The winds of change are blowing in the direction of a Parti Québécois government, regardless of Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s unpopular promise to hold a third referendum on independence.

Despite Ms. Fréchette’s best efforts, the legacy of the CAQ has caught up to her. Now, she is fighting for the survival of the party she would prefer not to name.

Christine Fréchette is not the kind of politician who delivers thunderous oratory or inspires breathless excitement, but in a way, that’s what her supporters like about her.

She has had the unenviable task of reshaping a party built in the image of Mr. Legault, who co-founded the CAQ in 2011 and led it to form government in 2018.

Mr. Legault, who announced his resignation in January after more than seven years as premier, had a folksy, plainspoken style and a hair-trigger reaction to negative press. Though he walked on water during the COVID-19 pandemic, a series of controversies and questionable financial decisions had made him one of the least popular politicians in the country by the time he made his exit.

At a September campaign event on Montreal’s South Shore, supporters told The Globe and Mail they’d joined the party specifically because of Ms. Fréchette.

Marie-France Bilodeau, 69, said she previously voted for the CAQ but grew disenchanted with Mr. Legault’s performance. She became a party member to support Ms. Fréchette’s bid for the leadership earlier this year. “She’s really smart. I think she takes the time to think things through before making decisions,” Ms. Bilodeau said. “She’s calm.”

As the room emptied out after the event, she approached the CAQ Leader. “The only thing that brought me back was you,” she told her.

Ms. Fréchette doesn’t stand out as the type of person who would want to be premier, though she showed an interest in public policy and civic life from a young age.

The cut and thrust of partisan politics appealed less to her, said Vicky Trépanier, a long-time friend. “She wants to have in-depth debates.”

Ms. Trépanier, who is not involved in politics, met the future Premier when they were both part of the student movement of the 1990s. Ms. Fréchette earned a Master’s degree in international relations from Laval University in 1994, and went on to work for a provincewide student union.

In those early years, she rubbed shoulders with a group of future politicos, including Martin Koskinen, who would become Mr. Legault’s long-time chief of staff. “She wasn’t someone who wanted to be the centre of attention,” Mr. Koskinen recalled in an interview.

Several years after completing her studies, Ms. Fréchette began organizing annual simulations of a North American parliament attended by university students from Canada, the United States and Mexico.

It was an impressive achievement, said Ms. Trépanier, who helped out with the paperwork and grew close to Ms. Fréchette during that time. “She created an institution that didn’t exist.”

Starting in 2007, Ms. Fréchette worked at a centre for international studies at the University of Montreal, where she met Jean-François Lisée, a future leader of the separatist Parti Québécois. When Mr. Lisée was elected to the National Assembly in 2012 and named minister of international relations, he hired her to work in his office.

Ms. Fréchette had voted “yes” in 1995, but she was never a “militant sovereigntist,” said Ms. Trépanier, her friend.

Her career with the PQ would be short-lived, however. She left the minister’s office in 2014, unable to accept the government’s proposed charter of values, which would have banned religious symbols for many public servants.

Ms. Fréchette would go on to spend nearly five years as the head of the chamber of commerce of eastern Montreal. But there were signs she was looking for a new political home. Ms. Trépanier recalled that after Ms. Fréchette left the PQ, the two of them attended a meeting of a group of so-called “orphelins politiques” (political orphans) organized by none other than Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who would seek the PQ leadership for the first time in 2016.

As the CAQ gained prominence, Mr. Legault, who had moved in the same circles as Ms. Fréchette in her younger years, tried to recruit her to the party multiple times, according to her partner, businessman Guy Nadeau. She declined his invitation to run for the CAQ in 2018, having started her position at the chamber of commerce not long before.

But when he came calling again four years later, she was ready to take the plunge. Among other things, she was impressed by how Mr. Legault had handled the pandemic, Mr. Nadeau said. “It took shape slowly in her mind,” he said. “She’s not an opportunist.”

Ms. Fréchette won a seat in the National Assembly as the CAQ formed its second majority government. She was named immigration minister, before being moved to the high-stakes energy and economy portfolio in 2024.

In the fall of 2025, after the CAQ’s support had collapsed, colleagues told Ms. Fréchette she should consider running to replace Mr. Legault if he resigned, her partner said. She felt it might be a “unique opportunity” that wouldn’t come along again, he added.

Mr. Koskinen, Mr. Legault’s chief of staff, hadn’t expected the reserved Ms. Fréchette would want the job.

But he now believes her restraint was part of her appeal to party members. “Quebeckers weren’t going to choose a François Legault 2.0.”

After being sworn in as the province’s second-ever female premier in April, Ms. Fréchette hit the ground running.

Political observers suggested the best she could hope for was to save her party from devastation. But ahead of an election set for October that would hinge partly on the question of sovereignty, she took steps to prove she could work within Canada.

While Mr. Legault had an often adversarial relationship with Ottawa, Ms. Fréchette arranged a meeting with Mr. Carney two days after her swearing-in. The two leaders have since made several joint announcements, and the CAQ enjoyed a modest bump in the polls.

Ms. Fréchette kicked off her campaign in late August as a new round of U.S. tariffs loomed, naming Mr. Trump as her prime adversary. Her party’s fortunes rose again, with one survey putting the CAQ neck-and-neck with the PQ.

But the Trump effect didn’t last, said political analyst Antonine Yaccarini. “People have gotten somewhat used to the tariff crisis.”

Ms. Fréchette has proven less adept at campaigning than at being Premier, Ms. Yaccarini said, and her debate performances were underwhelming. She is also an easy mark for her opponents, given the eight years of unpopular CAQ decisions that are all too easy to dredge up.

The CAQ Leader has also prevaricated repeatedly when asked for her personal position on sovereignty, despite her promise not to hold a referendum.

Back in April, before anyone was comparing Ms. Fréchette to Mr. Carney, some were drawing parallels to a different Canadian prime minister. Kim Campbell, who took over from Brian Mulroney in June, 1993, led the Progressive Conservatives to a devastating defeat in an election that November, from which the party never really recovered.

Ms. Fréchette may share the same fate. Quebec’s governing party is once again looking to save the furniture, with projections suggesting it could lose every one of its 79 seats. A majority may be in reach for the PQ.

In the months since becoming Premier, Ms. Fréchette has made it very clear who she is not. She is not François Legault. She is certainly not Donald Trump. And she is not Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

But it is less clear who she is, and that could be her downfall. “The problem is she herself, despite her impressive demeanour, is a bit of an empty shell,” journalist and author Francine Pelletier said in an interview. “What’s the new dream?”
paragraphs: Christine Fréchette has done her best to outrun her own party.
Since taking over the Coalition Avenir Québec and becoming Premier in April, she has tried less to rehabilitate a tarnished brand than to erase it.

Her strategy was on display at the launch of the Quebec election campaign in late August, when observers quickly noticed that her bus and election signs did not feature her party’s name. “ Avançons ,” her campaign slogan read. Let’s move forward.
Ms. Fréchette, 56, began the first debate of the campaign by declaring that she is not her predecessor, François Legault.
As she faces a restive electorate looking for change, she has attempted to shed the baggage of her party’s eight years in government. In this election, she is selling herself.

For a moment, voters were buying in. Early in the campaign, which began days after trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart, Ms. Fréchette invited comparisons to Prime Minister Mark Carney. Like him, she embodied the sort of unflappable technocrat that seemed a welcome contrast to the erratic and hostile behaviour of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Though the Coalition Avenir Québec had spent months circling the drain, Ms. Fréchette, who declined an interview request from The Globe and Mail, orchestrated an unlikely comeback.

It seemed possible she could achieve what Mr. Carney had done in last year’s federal election and turn near-certain defeat into an improbable victory. If she was a touch bland, well, perhaps that was exactly what Quebeckers were looking for.

But then it went away. Days ahead of the vote on Oct. 5, Ms. Fréchette’s campaign has lost its momentum. The winds of change are blowing in the direction of a Parti Québécois government, regardless of Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s unpopular promise to hold a third referendum on independence.
Despite Ms. Fréchette’s best efforts, the legacy of the CAQ has caught up to her. Now, she is fighting for the survival of the party she would prefer not to name.
Christine Fréchette is not the kind of politician who delivers thunderous oratory or inspires breathless excitement, but in a way, that’s what her supporters like about her.
She has had the unenviable task of reshaping a party built in the image of Mr. Legault, who co-founded the CAQ in 2011 and led it to form government in 2018.

Mr. Legault, who announced his resignation in January after more than seven years as premier, had a folksy, plainspoken style and a hair-trigger reaction to negative press. Though he walked on water during the COVID-19 pandemic, a series of controversies and questionable financial decisions had made him one of the least popular politicians in the country by the time he made his exit.
At a September campaign event on Montreal’s South Shore, supporters told The Globe and Mail they’d joined the party specifically because of Ms. Fréchette.

Marie-France Bilodeau, 69, said she previously voted for the CAQ but grew disenchanted with Mr. Legault’s performance. She became a party member to support Ms. Fréchette’s bid for the leadership earlier this year. “She’s really smart. I think she takes the time to think things through before making decisions,” Ms. Bilodeau said. “She’s calm.”
As the room emptied out after the event, she approached the CAQ Leader. “The only thing that brought me back was you,” she told her.
Ms. Fréchette doesn’t stand out as the type of person who would want to be premier, though she showed an interest in public policy and civic life from a young age.
The cut and thrust of partisan politics appealed less to her, said Vicky Trépanier, a long-time friend. “She wants to have in-depth debates.”

Ms. Trépanier, who is not involved in politics, met the future Premier when they were both part of the student movement of the 1990s. Ms. Fréchette earned a Master’s degree in international relations from Laval University in 1994, and went on to work for a provincewide student union.

In those early years, she rubbed shoulders with a group of future politicos, including Martin Koskinen, who would become Mr. Legault’s long-time chief of staff. “She wasn’t someone who wanted to be the centre of attention,” Mr. Koskinen recalled in an interview.
Several years after completing her studies, Ms. Fréchette began organizing annual simulations of a North American parliament attended by university students from Canada, the United States and Mexico.
It was an impressive achievement, said Ms. Trépanier, who helped out with the paperwork and grew close to Ms. Fréchette during that time. “She created an institution that didn’t exist.”

Starting in 2007, Ms. Fréchette worked at a centre for international studies at the University of Montreal, where she met Jean-François Lisée, a future leader of the separatist Parti Québécois. When Mr. Lisée was elected to the National Assembly in 2012 and named minister of international relations, he hired her to work in his office.
Ms. Fréchette had voted “yes” in 1995, but she was never a “militant sovereigntist,” said Ms. Trépanier, her friend.

Her career with the PQ would be short-lived, however. She left the minister’s office in 2014, unable to accept the government’s proposed charter of values, which would have banned religious symbols for many public servants.

Ms. Fréchette would go on to spend nearly five years as the head of the chamber of commerce of eastern Montreal. But there were signs she was looking for a new political home. Ms. Trépanier recalled that after Ms. Fréchette left the PQ, the two of them attended a meeting of a group of so-called “orphelins politiques” (political orphans) organized by none other than Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who would seek the PQ leadership for the first time in 2016.

As the CAQ gained prominence, Mr. Legault, who had moved in the same circles as Ms. Fréchette in her younger years, tried to recruit her to the party multiple times, according to her partner, businessman Guy Nadeau. She declined his invitation to run for the CAQ in 2018, having started her position at the chamber of commerce not long before.

But when he came calling again four years later, she was ready to take the plunge. Among other things, she was impressed by how Mr. Legault had handled the pandemic, Mr. Nadeau said. “It took shape slowly in her mind,” he said. “She’s not an opportunist.”

Ms. Fréchette won a seat in the National Assembly as the CAQ formed its second majority government. She was named immigration minister, before being moved to the high-stakes energy and economy portfolio in 2024.

In the fall of 2025, after the CAQ’s support had collapsed, colleagues told Ms. Fréchette she should consider running to replace Mr. Legault if he resigned, her partner said. She felt it might be a “unique opportunity” that wouldn’t come along again, he added.
Mr. Koskinen, Mr. Legault’s chief of staff, hadn’t expected the reserved Ms. Fréchette would want the job.
But he now believes her restraint was part of her appeal to party members. “Quebeckers weren’t going to choose a François Legault 2.0.”
After being sworn in as the province’s second-ever female premier in April, Ms. Fréchette hit the ground running.

Political observers suggested the best she could hope for was to save her party from devastation. But ahead of an election set for October that would hinge partly on the question of sovereignty, she took steps to prove she could work within Canada.

While Mr. Legault had an often adversarial relationship with Ottawa, Ms. Fréchette arranged a meeting with Mr. Carney two days after her swearing-in. The two leaders have since made several joint announcements, and the CAQ enjoyed a modest bump in the polls.

Ms. Fréchette kicked off her campaign in late August as a new round of U.S. tariffs loomed, naming Mr. Trump as her prime adversary. Her party’s fortunes rose again, with one survey putting the CAQ neck-and-neck with the PQ.
But the Trump effect didn’t last, said political analyst Antonine Yaccarini. “People have gotten somewhat used to the tariff crisis.”

Ms. Fréchette has proven less adept at campaigning than at being Premier, Ms. Yaccarini said, and her debate performances were underwhelming. She is also an easy mark for her opponents, given the eight years of unpopular CAQ decisions that are all too easy to dredge up.
The CAQ Leader has also prevaricated repeatedly when asked for her personal position on sovereignty, despite her promise not to hold a referendum.

Back in April, before anyone was comparing Ms. Fréchette to Mr. Carney, some were drawing parallels to a different Canadian prime minister. Kim Campbell, who took over from Brian Mulroney in June, 1993, led the Progressive Conservatives to a devastating defeat in an election that November, from which the party never really recovered.

Ms. Fréchette may share the same fate. Quebec’s governing party is once again looking to save the furniture, with projections suggesting it could lose every one of its 79 seats. A majority may be in reach for the PQ.
In the months since becoming Premier, Ms. Fréchette has made it very clear who she is not. She is not François Legault. She is certainly not Donald Trump. And she is not Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

But it is less clear who she is, and that could be her downfall. “The problem is she herself, despite her impressive demeanour, is a bit of an empty shell,” journalist and author Francine Pelletier said in an interview. “What’s the new dream?”

stories.title: Hanover shooting leaves man injured, suspect arrested
stories.summary: At least three schools and the town’s hospital were placed in a “hold and secure” Tuesday after gunshots were heard in Hanover.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
One person has been taken into custody following a shooting investigation in Grey County.

According to police, one person was injured in the shooting shortly before noon at a residence in the 300 block of 14th Avenue in Hanover, Ont.

Police said a 37-year-old man was taken to Hanover and District Hospital by Grey County paramedics with gunshot wounds that were not considered life-threatening.

Investigators said a 50-year-old suspect was arrested a short time after the incident, however they have not released details on any charges. Officers also recovered a firearm near the scene.

Hanover police are asking for the public’s help identifying and locating a black van that was seen leaving the area immediately after the shooting.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Hanover Police Service investigators or Crime Stoppers.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Joly presses Stelco’s U.S. owner to present job-saving plan in 5 days
stories.summary: The federal government is turning up the heat on the U.S. owner of Stelco Holdings Inc. over impending layoffs at the Hamilton-based steel plant.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The federal government is turning up the heat on the U.S. owner of Stelco Holdings Inc. over impending layoffs at the Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday laying out her “extreme disappointment” over the company’s plan to lay off up to 500 workers in response to U.S. tariffs and other market pressures.

Canada gave U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs the go-ahead to purchase Stelco back in 2024 under the Investment Canada Act, which regulates foreign takeovers.

Canada’s approval of the deal was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions, Joly said.

Those conditions don’t expire just because “business strategy or market conditions have changed,” she wrote in the letter.

“This is particularly relevant here, where Cleveland-Cliffs has cited trade disruptions as affecting its operations at Hamilton Works, notwithstanding its chief executive officer’s public support for Section 232 tariff measures,” Joly said.

Lourenco Goncalves, the chief executive of Cleveland-Cliffs, has publicly supported U.S. steel tariffs, saying they are a “necessary step” to curb dumped steel imports.

In the letter, Joly said she wants to see Cleveland-Cliffs’ plan to comply with all undertakings of the original acquisition. She asked for a response within five business days or the government could consider legal action.

If the steelmaker does not comply, Ottawa could go to superior court where a judge could order the company to meet its obligations, impose penalties or even order a sale of the business, Joly said.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers local 1005, which represents workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant, said he is pleased the federal government acted “very swiftly.”

“They were very slow to react last time,” he said, referring to an earlier dispute involving the steel mill under a different owner. “We actually had to lobby to get them to react.”

U.S. Steel began laying off hundreds of workers at the former Stelco operations in November 2008 and announced temporary shutdowns affecting another roughly 1,500 jobs the following March.

Then-industry minister Tony Clement did not issue a formal demand under the act until May 5, 2009 — roughly nine weeks after the larger shutdown was announced.

In that case, Ottawa rejected the company’s explanation for falling short of its labour and production commitments and took U.S. Steel to court.

The case was ultimately settled in 2011 after the company agreed to a new set of undertakings.

However, the steel mill entered creditor protection in 2014 and was acquired by Bedrock Industries in 2017, returning to the Stelco name, before Cleveland-Cliffs acquired the company in 2024.

“Cleveland-Cliffs knew exactly what they were agreeing to when they bought the place,” Wells said, referring to the five-year commitments the company made when it purchased the operations.

“We’re hoping that they will recant the layoff,” he said. “But I’m not holding my breath.”

“They’ll drag this through court and try to provide their rationale for how this was out of their control. But they’re all in favour of the tariffs so it’s contradictory.”

The existence of Joly’s letter was first reported by the Toronto Star.

stories.title: Ontario’s medical regulator proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply
stories.summary: The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is looking to clamp down and is set to hold a board of directors meeting next week to decide on the proposed changes.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario’s medical regulator is proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply drugs, The Canadian Press has learned.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is looking to clamp down on the practice and is set to hold a board of directors meeting next week to decide on the proposed changes.

Safer supply refers to prescribing medications as an alternative to opioids obtained on the streets to those who are at high risk of overdose.

The most common form of safer supply is hydromorphone, a powerful opioid often prescribed for pain but significantly less potent than fentanyl and its derivatives that dominate the illicit drug supply chain. Fentanyl is often found laced with other drugs such as benzodiazepines, a depressant, and xylazine, often used to tranquilize animals.

One change the regulator has proposed in a document tucked away on its website is that “physicians must only prescribe safer supply medications in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy.” The therapy uses medications such as methadone to treat opioid addiction.

The college is also proposing an eight-week time limit for physicians to prescribe safer supply, and mandating that it be consumed in front of health-care professionals.

The regulator previously made changes to its drug prescription policy in May that mandated physicians to perform an in-person assessment before prescribing narcotics for safer supply, as well as making it mandatory for doctors to offer opioid agonist therapy before prescribing safer supply drugs and perform followups every three months.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

The rationale behind the new proposed changes centres largely on diversion of patients’ prescription pills to the black market.

“The proposed amendments build on targeted changes introduced in May and respond to ongoing concerns about the diversion of safer supply medication and the resulting risks to patients and communities,” Mickey Cirak, spokesperson for the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, wrote in an email.

“In response, the college has proposed amendments intended to strengthen oversight of safer supply prescribing and enhance safeguards related to physician prescribing practices, consistent with its role as Ontario’s medical regulator.”

The college said it has consulted with a broad range of people and organizations, including physicians, municipalities and health-care partners, as well as the office of Ontario’s chief medical officer of health, Dr. Kieran Moore.

Moore’s office did not respond to a request for comment or an interview. Moore has never granted The Canadian Press an interview about the province’s opioids crisis, despite more than a dozen requests since he took the role in 2021.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons said the initiative to change safer-supply prescription rules is its own and did not come from the provincial government.

Cirak said the college also received feedback from doctors with expertise in addiction medicine.

The proposal has the support of Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“Our government does not and will never support the distribution of illegal drugs, including the illicit use of hydromorphone masked as ‘safer supply,'” said Satnam Grewal, a spokesperson for Jones.

“We welcome any action from Ontario’s 27 regulatory colleges who set standards and obligations for health-care professionals, including the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, to crack down on the predatory prescribing of addictive drugs.”

Ontario has moved to an abstinence-based model under Premier Doug Ford in its approach to the ongoing opioid crisis. The province closed provincially funded supervised consumption sites and passed a law banning them within 200 metres of schools and daycares.

The province has since opened 29 homelessness and addiction recovery treatment hubs, which the government calls HART hubs. It has spent more than $500 million on that plan, which offers primary and mental health care, addiction services and peer supports.

Word of the proposed changes has reached some people who depend on safer supply, said Lorraine Lam, an organizer with the Shelter and Housing Justice Network and a longtime harm reduction worker.

“The changes are really dangerous and very destabilizing,” Lam said.

“People are really, really scared and people are really, really anxious and very angry.”

She said some people using safer supply got jobs or returned to school and she’s worried what will happen to them when they’re cut off.

“The reality is people who are on safe supply are going to be de-prescribed really, really quickly, which will increase the chances of people turning to the street unregulated supply, which will then therefore increase the risk of overdoses and deaths,” Lam said.

The college’s board of directors is set to meet on Oct. 13, when it is expected to vote on the proposed changes.

stories.title: Separation is unpopular in Quebec. Why did the province elect sovereigntists?
stories.summary: Quebecers chose a new government on Monday, handing the Parti Québécois (PQ) minority power in the province’s legislature, raising questions about why a sovereigntist party was elected when polling shows little interest in separating from Canada.
stories.author: Jordan Fleguel
stories.content:
Quebecers chose a new government on Monday, handing the Parti Québécois (PQ) minority power in the province’s legislature, raising questions about why a sovereigntist party was elected when polling shows little interest in separating from Canada.

“I think for now, Quebecers wanted a divided government,” David Heurtel, political analyst and former Quebec cabinet minister, told CTV News Channel on Tuesday.

“They wanted to give the PQ a minority government, and I think right now, what Quebecers want most is to deal with the priorities, the same priorities you see across Canada.”

Quebec’s premier-designate, PQ Leader Paul-St Pierre Plamondon has said that his party will work towards holding a third Quebec sovereignty referendum, but that he will wait until U.S. President Donald Trump has left office .

Minority saves province from ‘fraught territory’

That timeline keeps a referendum off the table for the next two years, by which point Plamondon May no longer be in charge, Heurtel said, noting that minority governments typically only last between 18 and 24 months.

“It’s, for most Quebecers, a big sigh of relief that (the PQ) didn’t get a majority, because then we would have been in some very fraught territory,” Tom Mulcair, CTV News’ political commentator and former federal NDP leader told CTV News Channel Tuesday.

“The fact that they were held to a minority came as a surprise to the PQ but not to those of us who kept our eyes on one number, which was 70 per cent. That’s the percentage of Quebecers that didn’t want another referendum,” he said.

Heurtel made the same observation, noting that even as the PQ surged in the polls during the campaign, “support for sovereignty has not wavered.”

5 takeways from Quebec election as Parti Québécois forms minority government

“Seventy per cent of Quebecers, including 63 per cent of Francophones, do not want a referendum and do not want independence,” said Heurtel.

Mulcair argued that while the PQ’s overarching separatist message was attractive to some voters in Quebec, Plamondon’s campaign mainly revolved around a promise to govern differently than the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which formed majority governments in 2018 and 2022.

Even Plamondon said in the final stretch of the campaign that the election was going to be about who Quebecers trusted most to lead them through the turbulent economic and political times ahead.

“It’s not totally accurate to say that this election is only about whether we would hold a referendum in three years from now,” Plamondon told Cjad, The Canadian Press reported .

“It’s about changing or not changing a government that has catastrophic results in many areas of our society and choosing who could do a good job and who could be reliable in terms of what they do and what they say.”

Collapse of the CAQ

Despite the PQ’s victory, the party received just 28 per cent of the total number of votes cast on Monday, and it has very little representation in the province’s largest urban centres of Montreal and Quebec City.

The collapse of the (CAQ), which failed to win any seats in the legislature, helped other parties gain ground as well. The provincial Liberals maintained opposition status after receiving 24 per cent of the popular vote, while the provincial Conservatives got roughly 21 per cent.

While both parties have said they would not support a referendum, Quebec’s other sovereigntist party, Québec solidaire, won enough seats in the legislature to form a majority with the PQ.

“They’ve got nine seats, so they could support the PQ if it decides to go ahead with the referendum bill, but there’s a lot of differences; they don’t get along very well on the political level,” said Heurtel.

Another important aspect of the political landscape in Quebec to keep in mind, Heurtel argued, is the current popularity of the prime minister.

“So, it’s not like you have that dichotomy with a Justin Trudeau, a Stephen Harper, or even a Jean Chrétien. The dynamic is completely different, and Quebecers don’t have an appetite… for a referendum.”

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario's medical regulator proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's medical regulator is proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply drugs, The Canadian Press has learned.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Ontario’s medical regulator is proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply drugs, The Canadian Press has learned.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is looking to clamp down on the practice and is set to hold a board of directors meeting next week to decide on the proposed changes.

Safer supply refers to prescribing medications as an alternative to opioids obtained on the streets to those who are at high risk of overdose.

The most common form of safer supply is hydromorphone, a powerful opioid often prescribed for pain but significantly less potent than fentanyl and its derivatives that dominate the illicit drug supply chain. Fentanyl is often found laced with other drugs such as benzodiazepines, a depressant, and xylazine, often used to tranquilize animals.

One change the regulator has proposed in a document tucked away on its website is that “physicians must only prescribe safer supply medications in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy.” The therapy uses medications such as methadone to treat opioid addiction.

The college is also proposing an eight-week time limit for physicians to prescribe safer supply, and mandating that it be consumed in front of health-care professionals.

The regulator previously made changes to its drug prescription policy in May that mandated physicians to perform an in-person assessment before prescribing narcotics for safer supply, as well as making it mandatory for doctors to offer opioid agonist therapy before prescribing safer supply drugs and perform followups every three months.

The rationale behind the new proposed changes centres largely on diversion of patients’ prescription pills to the black market.

“The proposed amendments build on targeted changes introduced in May and respond to ongoing concerns about the diversion of safer supply medication and the resulting risks to patients and communities,” Mickey Cirak, spokesperson for the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, wrote in an email.

“In response, the college has proposed amendments intended to strengthen oversight of safer supply prescribing and enhance safeguards related to physician prescribing practices, consistent with its role as Ontario’s medical regulator.”

The college said it has consulted with a broad range of people and organizations, including physicians, municipalities and health-care partners, as well as the office of Ontario’s chief medical officer of health, Dr. Kieran Moore.

Moore’s office did not respond to a request for comment or an interview. Moore has never granted The Canadian Press an interview about the province’s opioids crisis, despite more than a dozen requests since he took the role in 2021.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons said the initiative to change safer-supply prescription rules is its own and did not come from the provincial government.

Cirak said the college also received feedback from doctors with expertise in addiction medicine.

The proposal has the support of Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“Our government does not and will never support the distribution of illegal drugs, including the illicit use of hydromorphone masked as ‘safer supply,’” said Satnam Grewal, a spokesperson for Jones.

“We welcome any action from Ontario’s 27 regulatory colleges who set standards and obligations for health-care professionals, including the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, to crack down on the predatory prescribing of addictive drugs.”

Ontario has moved to an abstinence-based model under Premier Doug Ford in its approach to the ongoing opioid crisis. The province closed provincially funded supervised consumption sites and passed a law banning them within 200 metres of schools and daycares.

The province has since opened 29 homelessness and addiction recovery treatment hubs, which the government calls HART hubs. It has spent more than $500 million on that plan, which offers primary and mental health care, addiction services and peer supports.

Word of the proposed changes has reached some people who depend on safer supply, said Lorraine Lam, an organizer with the Shelter and Housing Justice Network and a longtime harm reduction worker.

“The changes are really dangerous and very destabilizing,” Lam said.

“People are really, really scared and people are really, really anxious and very angry.”

She said some people using safer supply got jobs or returned to school and she’s worried what will happen to them when they’re cut off.

“The reality is people who are on safe supply are going to be de-prescribed really, really quickly, which will increase the chances of people turning to the street unregulated supply, which will then therefore increase the risk of overdoses and deaths,” Lam said.

The college’s board of directors is set to meet on Oct. 13, when it is expected to vote on the proposed changes.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Greater Toronto home sales in September down from year ago, average price also lower
stories.summary: Toronto - Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area in September were down nine per cent compared with a year ago as the average price also edged lower.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area were down in September from a year ago, while average prices continued to decline as soft conditions persist in some parts of the housing market.

The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board said in its monthly report Tuesday that homebuyers were in a holding pattern in September, as uncertainty surrounding the economy, inflation and borrowing costs weighed on sales.

Sales totalled 5,040 in September, down nine per cent year-over-year, it said.

The result came as the average selling price for the month was $1,006,409, down from $1,060,036 a year earlier. The composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.7 per cent year-over-year in September.

Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area in September were down nine per cent compared with a year ago as the average price also edged lower. (Oct. 6, 2026)

Renewed tensions with the United States and a surge in gas prices amid war in the Middle East have kept potential buyers on the sidelines in recent months.

Meanwhile, rising bond yields have pushed fixed mortgage rates higher over the past month, and buyers are expecting the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates, said John Pasalis, president of Move Smartly Realty Inc.

“Higher rates — and the idea of higher rates — is obviously straining on affordability, but also leading buyers to think that the market’s going to be a little bit softer in the future,” he said in an interview on Tuesday.

The slowdown is likely going to continue through the rest of the year, he said.

Slowing home sales come as municipalities across Ontario, including the GTA, hold an election on Oct. 26.

“Housing is one of the biggest issues on voters’ minds, and the upcoming municipal election will help shape housing policy across the GTA and Simcoe County for the next four years,” said Daniel Steinfeld, TRREB president, in a statement.

“The decisions our next mayors and councillors make on affordability, housing supply and the costs associated with buying a home can also influence buyer demand and confidence in the market.”

New listings in September totalled 16,500, down 14.4 per cent year-over-year.

Within the City of Toronto, TRREB said there were 1,937 sales last month, down 5.4 per cent from September 2025. Across the rest of the GTA, home sales decreased nine per cent to 5,040.

Townhouses saw the biggest drop in activity among all housing types, with 12.8 per cent fewer sales year-over-year. There were also 7.8 per cent fewer condos sold last month compared with a year ago.

The semi-detached markets grew 8.2 per cent year-over-year, while detached home sales were up 8.7 per cent.

Toronto real estate broker Cailey Heaps said while some segments of the market suffered, ultra-luxury buyers as well as first-time homebuyers were active.

“First-time homebuyers have accepted that the market that we’re in now is the new normal. It’s no longer about waiting to time a market,” she said.

“You’re going to make a buying decision when it feels right for you, whether that’s because you’re getting married or starting a family or relocating to a new city or because you can afford it.”

The move-up market, or homeowners who can upgrade to a bigger property, largely remained on the sidelines last month, Heaps said.

“They don’t want to take the risk when the economy is not as strong as it was, or they have some job insecurity. So, not many people are moving in that segment,” she said.

A muted market could pick up in the new year but Pasalis said a rebound hinges on economic certainty and market confidence.

That means no new tariff threats, easing tensions with the U.S. and a slight decline in bond yields.

“We don’t even need to see a dramatic change, but if (bond yields) dip a little bit in the new year where mortgage rates are closer to the four per cent range rather than the mid-to-high four per cent range, I think again that can shift buyers off of the sidelines,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Crash between cyclist and London police vehicle closes section of Hamilton Road
stories.summary: Police have closed a section of Hamilton Road following a crash between a marked London police cruiser and a cyclist.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Police have closed a section of Hamilton Road following a crash between a marked London police cruiser and a cyclist.

According to police, the crash happened around 6:30 a.m. and has closed Hamilton Road between Pegler Street and Smith Street.

Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and use an alternate route as the road will remain closed for an undetermined period while the investigation continues.

Police said the cyclist was transported to hospital with unknown injuries.

No details have been released regarding the circumstances surrounding the collision.

Further updates are expected as more information becomes available.

stories.title: Amendments would let Manitoba cannabis stores drop window coverings for safety
stories.summary: Winnipeg - Cannabis stores across Manitoba May soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WINNIPEG - Cannabis stores across Manitoba may soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.

The Manitoba government introduced amendments to the provincial Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Control Act on Monday that would eliminate window coverings on all cannabis storefronts amid safety concerns.

The province said the change would increase visibility from outside the store and help make sure workers are not hidden from public view.

Current legislation requires retailers to ensure that cannabis and cannabis products are not visible to people who are not legally allowed to purchase the products.

“We’re still mandating that the cannabis product will not be visible because we want to protect kids, and so we’re finding that balance,” said Justice Minister Matt Wiebe.

“We don’t want cannabis displayed in window fronts. We don’t want kids riding by and seeing cannabis and being enticed into trying a product that’s not appropriate for them, but at the same time we have to prioritize workers’ safety.”

Labour groups have long expressed concerns about the special problems that cannabis stores pose, because they sell a controlled substance and are required by government rules to cover all windows to the outside.

An attack on a cannabis store employee who was working alone at night in May renewed calls from unions for improved worker safety.

Police arrested a man after he allegedly entered a retail store, waiting for a customer to leave, and then locked himself inside with a woman working alone.

They said he sexually assaulted the 24-year-old, who was able to flee the store and call police.

The province is also proposing changes to the act that would allow mandatory minimum staffing levels during certain hours to ensure that workers are not alone during times when there may be a higher risk of violence.

The United Food and Commercial Workers union welcomed the province’s proposals.

It surveyed its members and non-unionized staff on worker safety concerns and found that staffing levels was one of the biggest issues.

“Loud and clear, not working alone was by far the No. 1 issue that they raised,” said Marie Buchan, secretary-treasurer of Local 832.

Wiebe said the proposed amendments would give the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Authority the ability to mandate how many employees may be on a shift at a given period.

The Opposition Progressive Conservatives said they would have to review the bill before commenting.

Other provinces, including Ontario, have scrapped similar rules around window coverings to address safety concerns expressed by employees.

stories.title: Liberals ask Ontario auditor to probe spending, oversight of Osap at career colleges
stories.summary: Toronto - The Ontario Liberals are asking the auditor general to investigate provincial student financial aid spending at private career colleges.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - The Ontario Liberals are asking the auditor general to investigate provincial student financial aid spending at private career colleges, after reporting by The Canadian Press showed a rapid increase concentrated within a small number of schools.

Liberal colleges and universities critic Tyler Watt requested a value-for-money audit, looking at the spending increases and whether the government was properly overseeing the Ontario Student Assistance Program.

“This has all the makings of Doug Ford’s next billion-dollar scandal,” Watt said Monday at a press conference.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that in 2024-25, career college students received nearly $1 billion in OSAP grants. Just seven career colleges accounted for $385 million of that funding.

Between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 academic years, the province spent $465 million more on Ontario Student Assistance Program grants, and 95 per cent of that went to private career college students, the data showed.

Auditor general Shelley Spence’s office said all 2026 audits are underway, but it would take Watt’s request into account for future audit planning.

The request comes after a series of stories by The Canadian Press showed that OSAP applications at a few career colleges far outpaced the rest of those institutions and publicly funded colleges and universities, and that Career Colleges Ontario has warned the provincial government for years about that.

The association representing career colleges raised concerns with the ministry about “indicators consistent with suspicious activity” in OSAP applications in January 2023, according to a letter filed in court in a case involving three schools.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn earlier this year said the cost of OSAP was becoming “unsustainable” and dramatically reduced the amount of grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges can receive, while also making career college students only eligible for loans.

Watt said the evidence seems to suggest the issue of rapidly growing OSAP costs was limited to a small number of private career colleges, and raises the question of why the government response involves students at all publicly funded institutions taking on more debt to fund their education – or in some cases delaying their schooling.

“Instead of cracking down on the dozen or so private career colleges at the centre of OSAP spending increases, the government took a hatchet to a problem that required a scalpel, and it ruined OSAP for everyone,” he said.

“That’s either a government that is grossly incompetent, or one that has something it desperately wants to hide.”

Zain Baig, president of the Toronto Metropolitan Students’ Union, said the government has penalized students across the province.

“Slashing OSAP for everybody may be the easy thing to do, and it’s simple and straightforward for the higher-ups like Doug Ford and Minister Quinn,” he said.

“But maybe the right thing to do would have been to dedicate more resources to do an independent investigation, look into these things thoroughly, and address the issue on a case-by-case basis, as opposed to just a one-size-fits-all type of solution.”

Quinn earlier this year made five career colleges ineligible even for OSAP loans, and three of the schools – which share a parent company – have asked the courts for a judicial review of that decision, alleging it was procedurally unfair.

Ministry inspection reports filed in court as part of that case show inspectors alleged they found evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework, and students who completed all of a course’s quizzes and exams in a single day.

The three Academy of Learning locations deny most of the ministry’s allegations, saying they have taken concerns seriously. None of the findings and allegations from either level of government have been proven in court.

A statement from the schools said it has implemented dozens of corrective actions, including stricter admission and identity verification controls.

“These include two-factor authentication and investigation of unusual login activity,” the Academy of Learning wrote. “We have co-operated extensively with both reviews and will continue to strengthen our controls wherever issues are identified.”

The instances of unusually rapid completion of courses warrants review, the Academy acknowledged, and said it has implemented additional monitoring of files before exam codes are issued.

stories.summary: Toronto - A hearing before the Ontario Human Rights Tribunal has begun for a blind accessibility advocate who is arguing Elections Ontario failed to ensure he can consistently and reliably mark, verify and cast his ballot independently and in private.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A hearing before the Ontario Human Rights Tribunal has begun for a blind accessibility advocate who is arguing Elections Ontario failed to ensure he can consistently and reliably mark, verify and cast his ballot independently and in private.

By The Canadian Press

David Lepofsky filed a human rights complaint more than seven years ago after an incident during the 2018 Ontario election.

Lepofsky says he had tried to vote using Elections Ontario’s assistive voting terminal for voters with disabilities, but a poll worker inadvertently saw who he voted for.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Lepofsky argues Elections Ontario did not take sufficient action to ensure accessible voting, including before, during and after the incident.

He had said he also experienced barriers to accessible voting in Ontario elections since that June 2018 incident and that constitutes a continuing human rights violation.

Lepofsky argues that Elections Ontario violated his rights under the Ontario Human Rights Code to equal treatment with respect to services and facilities without discrimination because of his total blindness.

The hearing is set to take place over several days this week, with Lepofsky and Elections Ontario expected to provide final submissions later this month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Trial begins for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport
stories.summary: A trial is set to begin today in Brampton for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
BRAMPTON — Prosecutors allege an Air Canada employee provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Toronto Pearson airport cargo bay in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Parmpal Sidhu was one of the “inside men” with the knowledge and access to help carry out the 2023 heist, Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic told a Brampton, Ont., court Monday as Sidhu’s trial began.

The trial is expected to hear evidence that the fraudulent air waybill was printed on site the day before the operation using Sidhu’s profile, and the Crown alleges he was the one who printed it, Vlacic said in her opening statement.

The driver who picked up the gold had an air waybill for a fish shipment, but the document was altered with a handwritten number for the gold shipment, she said.

The Crown alleges the driver is Durante King-Mclean, an Ontario man who U.S. authorities say fled south shortly after the heist. He was arrested in Pennsylvania in September 2023 and has since pleaded guilty in a separate case to conspiring to traffic firearms, U.S. officials said.

“Whoever provided this air waybill to Mr. Durante King-Mclean … knew exactly what he needed to have and what needed to be changed,” Vlacic said.

Sidhu pleaded not guilty Monday to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.

Prosecutors allege Sidhu was working hand in hand with Simran Panesar, another Air Canada employee at the time, to facilitate the theft for the others accused.

Panesar resigned in the months that followed the heist and was interviewed by investigators that July, court heard. The next day, he and his family left Canada and never returned, according to an agreed statement of fact read in court. A Canada-wide warrant has been issued for his arrest.

The altered waybill was only one of the steps needed to pull off the theft without getting noticed immediately, Vlacic said. In the background, the shipment’s designation as high value was removed and notes about its breakdown were changed, she said.

Yelizaveta Zaritskaya, who was Air Canada’s cargo operations manager at the time of the heist, told court her profile was used to remove the high-value designation from the gold shipment on a day when she was not working. Under questioning from the defence later, she clarified it was a crucial change that meant the shipment would be treated as regular cargo that could “pass for fish.”

Back then, she said, there were shared computers in the managers’ offices and it wasn’t uncommon for people to conduct minor functions while the computer was still logged into someone else’s profile.

“It was a bad practice,” she said.

Anyone who had access to the offices would have access to managers’ computers, including Sidhu’s, she said, adding that a lot of Air Canada’s security protocols have changed since then.

Asked by the defence whether security was lax in those days, Zaritskaya paused, then said: “It clearly was lacking since we had stolen gold.”

Zaritskaya highlighted some “concerning” points on the waybill used to pick up the gold. For one thing, she said, the number linking it to the shipment was handwritten on two separate spots when it should be typed out. “Air Canada employees should not write on the air waybill,” she said.

It also specified in which area the shipment should be stored, namely the cold storage, which is not often marked on the waybill, she said. As well, there was a tear in the document that means it wasn’t maintained to standard, she said.

However, an inexperienced attendant may not notice these issues, she said.

Earlier Monday, Peel regional police Const. Clayton Asano, testified about his role in investigating how the air waybill made its way through the cargo facility.

Court watched surveillance video from the cargo facility that showed a white truck back into the loading bay and the driver, dressed in reflective gear and a face covering, go inside and interact with Air Canada staff.

The driver handed over documents including the waybill and eventually an employee with a forklift came with the shipment and helped load it onto the truck. The truck then drove away, with the entire process playing out within an hour, court heard.

Prosecutors said the identity of the driver is not in dispute in this trial.

During cross-examination, Sidhu’s lawyers asked Asano whether handwriting analysis was conducted on the waybill. Asano said no, but clarified under re-examination by the Crown that such an analysis had been considered and ruled out because there wasn’t enough writing on the waybill or enough of a sample to compare it to.

The trial comes after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

Chaudhary, who is considered one of the architects of the heist, is expected to testify for the prosecution in Sidhu’s trial.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial next month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

Parmpal Sidhu was one of the “inside men” with the knowledge and access to help carry out the 2023 heist, Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic told a Brampton, Ont., court Monday as Sidhu’s trial began.

The trial is expected to hear evidence that the fraudulent air waybill was printed on site the day before the operation using Sidhu’s profile, and the Crown alleges he was the one who printed it, Vlacic said in her opening statement.
The driver who picked up the gold had an air waybill for a fish shipment, but the document was altered with a handwritten number for the gold shipment, she said.

The Crown alleges the driver is Durante King-Mclean, an Ontario man who U.S. authorities say fled south shortly after the heist. He was arrested in Pennsylvania in September 2023 and has since pleaded guilty in a separate case to conspiring to traffic firearms, U.S. officials said.
“Whoever provided this air waybill to Mr. Durante King-Mclean … knew exactly what he needed to have and what needed to be changed,” Vlacic said.
Sidhu pleaded not guilty Monday to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.
Prosecutors allege Sidhu was working hand in hand with Simran Panesar, another Air Canada employee at the time, to facilitate the theft for the others accused.

Panesar resigned in the months that followed the heist and was interviewed by investigators that July, court heard. The next day, he and his family left Canada and never returned, according to an agreed statement of fact read in court. A Canada-wide warrant has been issued for his arrest.

The altered waybill was only one of the steps needed to pull off the theft without getting noticed immediately, Vlacic said. In the background, the shipment’s designation as high value was removed and notes about its breakdown were changed, she said.

Yelizaveta Zaritskaya, who was Air Canada’s cargo operations manager at the time of the heist, told court her profile was used to remove the high-value designation from the gold shipment on a day when she was not working. Under questioning from the defence later, she clarified it was a crucial change that meant the shipment would be treated as regular cargo that could “pass for fish.”
Back then, she said, there were shared computers in the managers’ offices and it wasn’t uncommon for people to conduct minor functions while the computer was still logged into someone else’s profile.
“It was a bad practice,” she said.
Anyone who had access to the offices would have access to managers’ computers, including Sidhu’s, she said, adding that a lot of Air Canada’s security protocols have changed since then.
Asked by the defence whether security was lax in those days, Zaritskaya paused, then said: “It clearly was lacking since we had stolen gold.”

Zaritskaya highlighted some “concerning” points on the waybill used to pick up the gold. For one thing, she said, the number linking it to the shipment was handwritten on two separate spots when it should be typed out. “Air Canada employees should not write on the air waybill,” she said.

It also specified in which area the shipment should be stored, namely the cold storage, which is not often marked on the waybill, she said. As well, there was a tear in the document that means it wasn’t maintained to standard, she said.
However, an inexperienced attendant may not notice these issues, she said.
Earlier Monday, Peel regional police Const. Clayton Asano, testified about his role in investigating how the air waybill made its way through the cargo facility.

Court watched surveillance video from the cargo facility that showed a white truck back into the loading bay and the driver, dressed in reflective gear and a face covering, go inside and interact with Air Canada staff.

The driver handed over documents including the waybill and eventually an employee with a forklift came with the shipment and helped load it onto the truck. The truck then drove away, with the entire process playing out within an hour, court heard.
Prosecutors said the identity of the driver is not in dispute in this trial.

During cross-examination, Sidhu’s lawyers asked Asano whether handwriting analysis was conducted on the waybill. Asano said no, but clarified under re-examination by the Crown that such an analysis had been considered and ruled out because there wasn’t enough writing on the waybill or enough of a sample to compare it to.
The trial comes after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.
Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.
Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.
Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.
Chaudhary, who is considered one of the architects of the heist, is expected to testify for the prosecution in Sidhu’s trial.
Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.
The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.
Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.
Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial next month.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.
Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Clocks stay in daylight saving, but analysis backs permanent standard time
stories.summary: An analysis by economic, mental health and sleep experts has concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time, not daylight saving. Here's why.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver — Ralph Mistlberger’s light is adjustable, allowing him to have the full spectrum of options depending on what his internal clock needs.

“You want cool in the morning. You want warm in the evening or warm in the afternoon,” he said.

“And so, it goes from being more bluish in the morning to more reddish in the evenings. Both of those are important because artificial light affects your clock.”

Mistlberger knows real sunlight is better than a lamp, but after more than 40 years as a neuroscientist studying sleep and the body’s circadian rhythms, he’s preparing for what’s to come Nov. 1.

That’s when clocks would normally have turned back an hour for most of Western Canada. But they’re staying where they are, putting residents on permanent daylight time.

Mistlberger said it’s a mistake and he and other researchers from British Columbia have released an analysis warning of the potential risks to health, the economy and students’ well-being with the darker mornings on the way.

The analysis by economic, mental health and sleep experts was published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal and examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time — not daylight saving — in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

Mistlberger, a psychology professor at Simon Fraser University, said people May think they want more sun in the evening, but the impact of starting your winter day in the dark is far-reaching.

“You’re actually waking up at an earlier circadian phase. Your clock May still be telling your brain and your body that this is the sleep period. It’s not time to wake up yet,” he said.

“The same is going to happen in the evening. It’s going to be telling you this is still the wake period, it’s not time to go to bed yet.”

He said not being able to get consistent sleep can lead to what scientists call “social jet lag,” when someone’s life and social calendar doesn’t line up with their biological clock.

Small amounts of sleep deprivation can be reversed with a good, long snooze, he said, but if the issue becomes chronic it can lead to health concerns.

That can include more cases of metabolic disorders, like obesity and diabetes, as well as cardiovascular disease. He said epidemiological studies of large populations have found increases in cancer and some mood disorders.

B.C., Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Manitoba all announced this year that they would adopt permanent year-round daylight time.

The B.C. government pitched that the move would “improve people’s overall health, reduce disruptions for families, simplify scheduling and provide an extra hour of evening light during the winter months.”

It said more than 223,000 people participated in a 2019 online survey and 93 per cent preferred a change to year-round daylight time.

Both Mistlberger and Patrick Baylis, a co-author of the analysis, said the government survey didn’t give the public the option to choose permanent standard time.

“The survey gave two options, which were comparing a switching regime, which is what we have previously had, to permanent daylight time. But those are the only two options. Baylis said.

Baylis, an associate professor at the Vancouver School of Economics at the University of British Columbia, said one of the biggest concerns is what it will mean for students going to school in the dark.

A study of students around the time zone boundary in Florida showed an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores among adolescents. The analysis said it was “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions and largest at puberty when circadian rhythms are most sensitive.”

“At minimum we should be thinking about monitoring for some of these negative effects on schooling outcomes, particularly among adolescents,” Baylis said in an interview.

While there is limited economic research, Baylis said some studies suggest exposure to sunlight can affect productivity.

A study that looked at variation in sunset timing within U.S. time zones found that an hour of later sunset reduces earnings over the long run by about five per cent.

Some countries that tried to make the switch to permanent daylight saving have not fared well.

Russia made the move in 2011 but reversed it three years later.

“Public dissatisfaction grew rapidly, particularly in northern regions, where winter morning darkness was even more prolonged, with critics citing disrupted biological rhythms, morning travel risks and effects on daily functioning,” the study said.

Most of Chile’s decision to change in 2015 was also reversed “after complaints about reduced school attendance, scheduling disruption and agricultural effects,” it said.

In 1974, all of the United States adopted permanent daylight saving as an energy-conservation measure.

“The policy was abandoned within the year after widespread opposition to dark winter mornings, concerns about children travelling to school before sunrise, workplace safety concerns and limited evidence of meaningful energy savings,” the analysis said.

The study recommends that choosing to stay with permanent daylight time should include steps to reduce the potential health effects and to evaluate the change.

Baylis said that could mean more flexible or later school start times or helping schools supplement the lack of real light in the morning.

Mistlberger said educating people on the potential impact is important, using bright lights in morning with adjustable bulbs to dim them by the evening.

“You want to get as much light exposure as you can as early as possible in the day when you go outside. So, even though the sunrise is going to be later than usual, it’s going to help you to get outside as soon as there is some sunrise.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Ashley Joannou, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Trial set to begin for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto's Pearson airport
stories.summary: A trial is set to begin today in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Brampton — A trial is set to begin today in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Parmpal Sidhu is charged with theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist that took place at Toronto’s Pearson airport.

The trial comes soon after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial later this fall.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Supreme Court to open judicial year with ceremony in temporary new building
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada is set to mark the opening of the judicial year with a ceremony in its temporary new building today.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canada’s democratic institutions need protection in the face of unrelenting pressures, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said Monday as the Supreme Court of Canada opened a new judicial year.

Wagner said the world feels increasingly uncertain due to deepening polarization, the non-stop pace of events and the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence.

When seas grow rough an anchor keeps a vessel from drifting, and democratic institutions play the same role in society, Wagner said.

“The strength of an anchor is not measured in calm waters,” he added. “It is measured in a storm. The same is true for the rule of law.”

Wagner, flanked by the other members of the Supreme Court, spoke at a ceremony in the court’s temporary new building.

The top court is settling in at the West Memorial Building, not far from Parliament Hill, while the court’s permanent home across the street undergoes extensive renovations.

Refurbishing the stately Supreme Court building is expected to take at least 10 years.

A formal welcome for the court’s newest member, Glenn Joyal, is set to take place next month.

Kristen Boon, president of the Council of Canadian Law Deans, said during the ceremony Monday that, like many judges, those who lead law schools have been watching with concern the threats to the rule of law around the world.

“We believe that future generations of lawyers will understand their duties as citizens to be central to their professional identity,” Boon said.

“Our classrooms and our campuses should model what reasoned debate and evidence-based decision making looks like. Law faculties protect academic freedom and give professors the space to teach, to research and to debate difficult ideas openly.”

Justice Minister Sean Fraser told the courtroom full of dignitaries that provinces, communities and groups of people are asking questions about their roles within the Canadian federation.

“If we expect to preserve national unity, we must constantly improve the public’s belief that the systems that we enjoy serve their interests over time,” Fraser said. “The law has an important role to play in this regard.”

He said that at a time “when it’s difficult to discern between truth and fiction, particularly with the rise and deployment of artificial intelligence, the truth-seeking function of this court and courts across Canada could never be more important.”

Fraser said that, as a Nova Scotian, he appreciated Wagner’s seafaring analogy about the strength of an anchor being tested in choppy waters.

But the justice minister reflected on one even more familiar to the court.

“It’s been nearly a century since Canadian law was first referred to as a living tree. If we’re to accept that doctrine as part of the laws of this nation, we must similarly accept the obligation placed upon us as caretakers of that tree,” he said.

“And as the branches grow, sometimes in unruly ways to address the changing nature of modern reality, I know and take great comfort in the fact that the court will be here to ensure that its roots remain strong for a generation to come.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.
